"Are all of us Victor?"
That's the first question that was asked when I introduced two more friends to this game. What's better than one Victor Vran? Four Victor Vrans! Anyway. I'm loving this game. Bought it a couple of nights ago on sale, grabbed a two pack and played with a friend who is also loving it. The combat is fun, fluid and punishing! When you get to a certain level you unlock these brilliant little things called Hexes that you can activate and deactivate at will; they make the game harder by upping Armor Regeneration or making monsters hit harder while you're awarded more XP and a higher chance at loot. We instantly turned on 4 out of 5 Hexes and went to town.
The ability to move the camera around opens up the map and lets you discover secrets and hidden areas where there might spawn some cool monsters. It really does feel fresh if you're coming from something like Diablo III (where we've spent XXX hours..). The jump mechanic is pretty cool too, especially when you make it on your first jump instead of jumping needlessly into a wall. But most of all, seriously, most of all - even though it can be hard and all that stuff, it's still a super casual game in my mind. Can't wait for the weekend so I can just play this until sunday.

This is a review from someone that played DS2 after having played the first and third in the trilogy.
I had a great time with this game. I don't think it's as satisfying as the other two, but I also think it doesn't deserve a lot of the hate that it gets. I will definitely say that certain parts feel more difficult than they deserve and I can understand someone having an emotional response as a result.
The main differences in gameplay from the other two games are the health regenerating items and the fact that enemies stop respawning after they've been killed twelve or so times. I think these things make the game tolerable considering that the difficulty is considerably higher. All three games have unfair sections, especially the first one, but this second game has some particularly frustrating parts. You can say Git Gud or whatever, but I beat the last two games with very little help and my experience with this one was different.
One thing that pops into this game that isn't common in the other games is an impaling move that certain bosses and regular enemies have. The hit boxes for these are the size of the boss and it makes for some really frustrating gameplay. I could accept it if the hitboxes were that wide and the move did little damage, but it would often be the case that I would be visibly out of the move's range and still lose three quarters of my health. The ogres spattered about the game have a similar hold move that have impossible hitboxes. I also have an issue with NPCs invading when hollow. It creates an annoying challenge when I just wanted to grab an item and use a Homeward Bone or just rest at a bonfire. Thankfully, the extra healing items can mitigate this.
There are other things people complain about, like certain bosses just throwing enemies at you, like the Rat Authority, but I think the mechanics of dealing with groups is pretty good when the hitboxes are fair. There is also the fact that illusory doors have to be touched with the action button instead of hit or rolled through; something that makes likely well wishers to accidentally block doors with their messages. There is no way to open an illusory door when a message is right on it, no way to dismiss it or to just open it regardless. Thankfully they fixed this in the next game.
The last complaint I want to address is about the level design. I like a lot of the levels, but the sense of interconnectivity isn't there. Shortcuts are not quite as important and there is a lot of extra running around that I think could have been made efficient. I spent over sixty hours in this game and I think a lot of that was retreading old areas that didn't have shortcuts.
The optional DLC areas the Frigid Outskirts and Iron Passage were pretty frustrating to defeat without help and were definitely deserving of an extra bonfire. The Cave of the Dead is much shorter than those two, but the bosses were something I could not defeat without people to help aggro one or two of the three enemies. I understand wanting to have an area where co-op could be necessary, but there should be a way to do it alone.
Some positives:
The combat is still good for the most part. Exploration was pretty fun and stressful, as it should be. The first third of the game was really nice, with the interconnectivity staying pretty apparent. Though it disappears a bit later, it was cool to spend a long time in what felt like a small world, only to see more of it appear. This is probably my favorite part about the Souls series; spending twenty hours thinking you've explored the majority of the game then opening a door or pathway into a whole other realm filled with new dungeons.
I do like how there are multiple ways to get through certain areas just in case you hit a difficulty wall. For instance there are multiple ways to get to The Lost Bastille and The Gutter. You can open the door to Winter Shrine either by beating the four big bosses of the early game or earning one million souls. These sorts of things are clever and kept me curious. I also like that certain areas needed to be revisited without a lot of annoyance. For instance, revisiting the Forest of Fallen Giants reminded me that I had certain keys and left a few doors unopened. While the challenge was no longer there, since my character had leveled up quite a bit, it was nice to find new parts of locations I thought I had already explored.
I like how carrying a torch around the Undead Crypt can reveal the shadows of hidden hollows, and how lighting the statue/crypt can give you new enemies to fight in what is admittedly a small area. I like how going into all the memories gives you souls which weaken Vendrick enough that beating him is not a challenge, if you somehow have the urge to defeat an old decrepit hollow who suffered for his people, you heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
The story is solid. This game gets a lot of flack for being less oblique about the plot, but I accept it. It fits very well into the middle of the trilogy. I was able to pick up a lot of the plot details without having to spend a lot of time reading item descriptions.
There is plenty of environmental storytelling, for example: the Dragon Shrine is filled with enemies who only attack you if you avoid their champions. The average sized soldiers thump their chests in a sign of respect and will let you pass as long as you defeat the largest one in the area. In Dragon Aerie, you can leave many of the dragons alone, but if you're sloppily running through and smashing the eggs, you'll get murdered as you try to cross a bridge. The game has many responsive moments like this, and it really builds immersion.
DS2 also fixes some thing that I had problems with in DS1. I didn't fall off of a slanted surface that should have held me like I did so often in DS1. Overall the geometry is less of a problem and movement is pretty smooth. There aren't any required and uncomfortable platforming parts, which is great. Fast travel is a very welcome feature from the beginning of the game. Vendors also have an expanding product list as you give them souls and this makes farming for upgrade items much easier and less frustrating. Finding and quickly upgrading weapons is a godsend when a person is trying to find the right moveset and damage per srike combination that is so important to play comfortably.
In closing, while this game has a lot of flaws it still carries the addictive qualities the Souls games are well known for. Worth playing, especially if you're craving more Souls experience. This may be my least favorite, but that still puts it miles above other games. Have fun!

Banished is a good concept, and I got some enjoyment out of it, but it's a one-trick-poney, and the trick doesn't go that far. It's a city builder with very little in the way of progression. Only a couple buildings can be upgraded (from wood to stone). The AI is occasionally frustrating. The game is rock hard at the beginning, but if you can survive long enough to get your population under control.... that's it. You expand at a snail's pace, till you're out of room. There's no tech tree, no missions, no customization (beyond where you decide to place the limited number of building types in the game), no unit variety, and no depth. Walk the tightrope between gathering food and building houses.... and you've beaten the game. There's nothing to reach toward beyond survival, and survival is only difficult at the beginning.
It's a city-builder, where the city-building isn't the fun part. I reccomend you wait, and see if there's a content patch or something. There just isn't enough here, to justify a game that's twice the price of Terraria.

All the game's about is left clicking if the word on the screen matches the font color and right clicking if it doesn't. It does a fair job at it and even more when the game throws a few minor "distractions" your way the further you progress its 5 main levels. I find that the "distractions" will no longer become a part of the game if you're too fast since being so activates "Sherlock Mode", which allows you to pretty much skip half or even the entirety of the current level depending on how fast you mash the LMB. The more clicks you pump into "Sherlock Mode", the more you skip ahead to the end of the current level.
Throughout the game, you earn CP which you use to buy levels for the level select and some skills. There are only 3 skills in the game and they really only help with getting the achievements for the game if your reflexes aren't up to par. Their usefulness in beating the game is very short-lived due to length of the main levels in total being only less than an hour long.
It's kind of a shame that it's so small & short but it's at least free and its simplistic gameplay is pretty enjoyable for testing your brain a bit.

Let me first say, if you played and enjoyed DD1, that does not mean that you will enjoy this in early access. I reccomend it for HARDCORE fans of the game, people who are willing to play with issues and help fix the game while enjoying the process. Do NOT buy early access if you are wanting to come home from a hard day of work and kill some orcs. Early access is for people who are paying money to support the game, not to play the game. Having said that, as long as the devs live up to what they have said DD2 will be at the time of release, it will be a must have especially emphazised by the free to play but not pay to win aspect.
Current gameplay is fun... at times. The matchmaking system can be frustrating, as you can be paired with players who are new to Dungeon Defenders entirely and have no clue what they are doing, while you on the other hand are a seasoned veteran with hundreds of hours of experience in DD1. This is due to the fact that in order to win more difficult maps, everyone has to know what they are doing because not one map is designed to be defended by a single player.
Here is why:
Multiple, multiple lanes, enemies seem a bit too tough right now, ranged enemies are almost always outside the range of your defenses, so unless a defender is actively defending a lane, it will go down due to ranged attackers in a matter of (short) minutes.
This makes single player gameplay nearly impossible and with matchmaking appearing to be entirely luck as to being partnered with experienced or nonexperienced players, gameplay has a ways to go.
Content is also lacking, but this is not a surprise as weapons, abilities, towers, maps, and much more are sure to be added within the next year.
The good: Graphics, core mechanics and most map design look and feel very good at max settings. Everything that has been put in the game is quality, nothing feels rushed and heroes are for the most part good.
Thoughts: Melee heroes seem weak compared to ranged heroes as they lose health rather quickly, and do the same DPS as ranged heroes. Towers could use some buffing, or enemies some nerfing *cough* ranged *cough*. Matchmaking and single player modes need work.
After all the negativity, why a thumbs up? DD2 (for early access) is good. I gave it a thumbs up because those who want to help DD2 become a great game will be able to do that without walking away from the game because it sucks orc. Most everything that has been implemented is quality (I'm looking right at matchmaking and singleplayer when I say most)
and I'm sure that is the way new aspects of the game are going to be implemented as well.
To restate: If you are wanting to buy the game to help the development process then you will not be dissapointed, however if you are wanting to buy the game to play it like DD1 STAY AWAY for another year. So far this game has lots of promise, I can't wait to see what it will be like this time next year!

I really wish I could give this a thumbs up, but I can't.  I'm more neutral it than anything.
The biggest issue is there really isn't a sense of progression like Dungeon Defenders 1 had.  I understand that there were balancing issues, but half the fun was dumping all your stats in range or attack speed and watching your towers perform ridiculously.  Dungeon Defenders 2 has more unique towers, but you can't really "play around" with them as everything is tied to equipment. Heroes VI has its problems: required internet connection to play, shoddy save syncing, and a long string of support patches that fix certain bugs while causing others.
However, one thing alone will make Heroes VI a worthwhile purchase for many: Heroes VI is a love letter written by the develoeprs to the fans of the golden days of the Heroes franchise (1, 2, and 3).
A plethora of small details in this game recall the older titles that Heroes fans fell in love with. Just to list a few: they've brought back some of the best of the old musical scores, done away with the worst (although sadly not all) of the shoddy gameplay elements of 4 and 5, and they've even included a Heroes 6 version of one of the most iconic Heroes maps ever created: Broken Alliance.
Long story short, if you've never played a Heroes of Might and Magic game in your life, then the flaws with this game may make it more frustrating to you than it's worth. But if you're a die hard Heroes fan yearning for the glory days, and you're willing to put up with a few bugs, this game is a real gem.
İf you like Strategy Games, you won't be disappointed.

In VVVVVV you have to navigate different screens by alternating the gravity and thus avoiding many pesky spikes and other obstacles. It starts easy but each area expands the simple mechanic with a new twist and some screens can get quite difficult.

It didn't hook me when I first tried it years ago. But since then I started playing fangames (
like games) and when I got back to VVVVVV I could really appreciate it.
The challenging difficult, the fast action where dying is just part of the process and the satisfying and rewarding feeling when you finally beat a screen after multiple fails.
VVVVVV had a big influence on the fangame scene, be it mechanics like gravity flipping and screen wrappings or levels like the infamous gravitron, the equally dreaded tower or the exhausting veni vedi vici and it was a great experience to finally play through these.
VVVVVV is now a well-known classic and the review scores speak for themselves (rightfully so).
If you haven't played it yet and like fangames or hard platformer in general you should really give it a try.

Easily one of the best RPG's I've ever played. I'm a big fan of Morrowind, The Witcher (1), Gothic 3, etc. This game is on par with all of them. The first hour or two of the game, it seems like any other RPG. However, the game just gets better and better (plot wise and gameplay) as the game progresses. The sequel in the developer's pack was also very good, and it looks like there could very likely be a third installment. I'm a pretty harsh critic of rpg's because I have played most of them, and they all follow similiar formulas.
The way you can craft your character is unique, and the armor/item enchantment are really cool and essential for late game survival. The game is very hard, and if it ever isn't challenging enough for you, you can set it to "nightmare mode." The graphics are good but not top of the line, but who really cares about that. Go play crysis if all you want is graphics.
In conclusion Larian Studios has found an avid new fan - for creating an RPG MADE FOR PC GAMERS (so tired of console ports), and you can tell they spent a GREAT deal of time on every aspect of this game.
Ratings:
Gameplay: 9/10 (What other game can you turn into a dragon and attack flying fortresses? The transition is flawless).
Music: 10/10 (Really great original music - made the game that much better).
Plot: 7/10 (It's hard to have a completely original plot, but I don't know of any other dragon knight games...the plot was good enough to keep me interested and the boss fights are awesome).
Graphics: 7/10 (Very good in some areas, okay in other departments).
Game length: 10/10 (Very long game - and the side quests are usually worth it and actually interesting).
Overall: 9/10
GOOD JOB, LARIAN STUDIOS!! THANK YOU TAKING THE TIME TO MAKE A GREAT RPG FOR PC GAMERS!

Can not recommend this game to any new players at all. There are so many issues, bugs and crash problems with this game that Ubisoft has acknowledged and refuses to fix. For more than a year these issues have persisted, you can even youtube these problems with keywords as " The Crew terrain bug ".
Ubisoft has not shown any support in fixing these problems for the duration of the year despite the community having upwards of 40+ pages on both the Steam forum and the Ubisoft The Crew forum. There support consists of " Please give us more information about the crash so we can help fix it " while doing nothing.
The Crew has some of the worst finicky hardware related issues I have seen in a game in my time, you can deck yourself out with the greatest hardware and still have problems, or you can have average to low and have little problems and then vice versa again.
The Crew is a beautiful looking game for it's release date, platforms and multiplayer capacity, I have enjoyed many hours driving around the " virtual usa " map which is not 100% accurate, probably not even 60%, but it has it's moments driving passed landmarks, or through new york city for example. On ultra settings the game will definitely impress for visuals and excitement. Plently of entertainment driving around completing missions or cruising with friends, performing co-op missions, on that note though, you must be aware that anyone in the world can and will affect your gameplay experience.
You are not really 'locked' behind a security blanket in The Crew, your missions can be interupted by other players which will effect your personal experience, due to a lack of any form of moderation or adminship in the game, trolling others is not at all against the rules. Blocking entrances, ends of races, race markers, anything goes.
The Crew's over all performance for game play is a fun and enjoyable experience, if you can enjoy it that is. With constant crashes and terrain issues, or game freezes it becomes a frustrating mess at times. If you're willing to give the game patience and grit your teeth through all it's cancer, you might be able to sit down and have a pretty good time, and godspeed to you.
However, I must conclude with, the price of the game vs it's overall problems, is not worth the buy. Ubisoft shows no support or help / compensation for players so the price will never cover the frustration of it's downfalls. With a 2nd expansion in the works and issues still unresolved and full pricing for the expansion with no compensation for the previous owners who are not able to even load the game due to " The Crew has stopped responding " at startup, I can not give this game a passing score. It is a flop, a fail, a miserable purchase and a game that gets shelfed quickly soon after your bad experiences become more infuriating then attempting to load the game time and time again.
TLDR:  Ubisoft doesn't support it, it's priced heavily for a broken game.

The AI sometimes breaks, and gets stuck trying to get to a checkpoint, or doesn't realize that it's missed a checkpoint and appears at the finish line doing doughnuts while waiting for you.  The game's story is the most cliche and stereotypical street racing story line that's featured in almost every movie and game on the subject.
And it is glorious.
There's a lot to do in the game.  Even more with the expansion pack.  (At the time of writing, Wild Run has been released, but not Calling All Units, which I am eagerly awaiting.)  Several races, including an up to almost four hours (in reality can be finished in around three) endurance race.  A few different game modes, including an annoying "drive over the boxes" mission type, or a few where you need to try to knock out another car.  Lots of pain jobs and "stickers" to apply to cars, as well as some visual customization (though some are quite lacking).  Unlocking everything can take quite some time, and some of the in-game achievements won't trigger properly.  There's PVP, and you can group up with three other friends to do the races and events together.  With the expansion pack you can set up your own races, and accept random stunts.
This is not a serious racing game.  It's pretty arcadey with an open world.  But it is fun.  It's great to laugh at the game when it just goes wrong.  The races can be a lot of fun.  Even just driving around can be enjoyable.  Grab the game and a group of friends and just cruise around the USA.  See who can make the best, or worst, cars.  (No under-lights available, sadly.)  Compete with each other on skill points.  Just don't expect a Forza style realistic simulator.  Accept that this game is DUMB and embrace it, and you can have one of the more entertaining driving experiences out there.
(Note: I played the game on Uplay for months before getting a complete version on Steam.)

Title says it all: it's an ARPG, a genre you can't talk about without mentionning Diablo at some point of the time.
The reason is pretty obvious, Diablo was really the pinnacle of the genre. Especially Diablo II, but that's my opinion.
Thing is, Diablo II was so damn good it became hard to *really* enjoy the genre for more than a few hours, whereas most fans of the genre probably spent hundreds, if not thousands hours into Diablo.
Yet many tried, and many failed. Titan Quest was good and full of good ideas, but due to the lack of promotion and refined online, it didn't work. Torchlight was boring after a playthrough. Plus, it was way too easy to cheat. Van Helsing had its moments, but then again it was so easy to cheat and so short people didn't stick to it. I could mention more and more, but you probably get the idea.
What really differentiates this one from the others, you may ask?
That's the point of this game really. One of the reasons Diablo II succeeded was that the online pretty much prevented cheating (though there were some shady methods, but certainly not as easy and risk free as duplicating your save). Another is that getting loot was damn easy. Sure, the drop rates were terribly low but running a boss again and again was so easy that it pretty much became the point of playing Diablo. Back then, farming was called MF running.
Here, in Victor Vran, I'm not exactly sure about the real profitability of running boss instances over and over, but the game definitely makes up for it.
Here's how.
1) Loot. No good ARPG game without a good loot system. Man, is this one satisfying.
What makes up for the MF runs are not only the MF runs themselves, but also a fantastic addition under the form of bounties and treasure hunts. Basically, you and people can share keys under the chat that you can activate to either receive a bounty or a treasure hunt map. To complete them, you have to visit some maps and either kill some bosses or fetch treasure hints. Upon completing the tasks, you'll get some good loot.
And that's the thing really. This is just the dose of addicting farming an ARPG needs to succeed. Something that keeps you playing and puts you under pressure because the bounties are time limited. As a result, you might feel like doing them with buddies. Oh yeah, there's some online.
2) Online. First of all, whether you prefer playing solo or online with some people, you can still get access to the chat. Meaning you'll get all those damn keys even if you feel like being alone. I haven't tried the game in COOP mode just yet, but I don't see this being anything else than awesome. However, I'm not sure how the loot gets splitted, so you might wanna stick to your friends.
3) Equipement. This is kind of bothering. While there's a neat addition in the form of cards that you can equip to add a various set of features to your build, such as life leech, more melee / ranged damage or cast damage whenever you get it, I'm a bit saddened by the fact there's only one slot for armor. Yep. No gloves, no helmet, just your armor. That said, you can still personnalize your character with the sets of outfits and dye them according to your preference.
Also, the skills are weapon based. How does this translate to gameplay?
4) Gameplay. One of the strong features of Diablo II was that you could be pretty much anything. Your build was the one you decided to use, as even sorceress could be damn powerful in melee. This isn't the case in Victor Vran.
The skills being weapon based, your build is kind of on rails based on which set of weapons you prefer. Set, because it's so damn easy to switch to your other weapon that you are pretty much going to use both sets of skills.
With that being said, Victor Vran is no common hunter as he can uses to "demon powers" which are two bonus spells. Bonus spells that you can actually choose! So in the end, there are some build possibilities. Berserk Aura, one of the demon powers, gives you better damage which is pretty much handy in every scenario. If you're more of a melee guy, Diamond adds you another layer of life in the form of armor. If you wanna stick to the spells, I'm sure Meteors will handle that boss just fine.
The demon powers use your second bar, called the Overdrive. This thing is pretty much based on your outfit which gives it a critical importance. Whether you prefer to gain overdrive over time or after each kill is up to you.
6) Misc.
The game story is quite nice. Hard to tell much about it without spoiling anything, but basically, demons are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and so are the rulers of the people.
The soundtrack is nice though forgettable, but it works fine with the game.
The effects of the spells are pretty cool though they stay simple so it's easy to tell what's going on screen. Marvel Heroes made the error of doing way too fancy effects resulting in a general cluster♥♥♥♥, rest assured that's not the case here.
What else... oh yeah! GET THIS GAME. I'm going to be honest, that's the first time I felt this addicted to an ARPG ever since Diablo II and Marvel Heroes.

Refunct is a refreshingly fluid... experience.
Upon launching Refunct you'll be dropped into a world relatively devoid of color. Your task, well I guess that's up to you ultimately. You can restore color the the pads by stepping on them. There are beacons attached to buttons that when depressed reveal more of the world. There are collectibles that can prove, I don't want to say difficult but may take some thinking on how to traverse to reach them.
The game feels extremely fluid. It reminds me Mirrors Edge without the mechanics of momentum or the visceral awareness of where your characters limbs are. You can wall jump, climb (near on edge) and swim.
The OST is also superb and lends itself well to the ethereal location you'll find yourself in. Its sort of mindless. In a good way. It feels good mechanically, its very aesthetically pleasing. It indeed encourages your mind to wander about. What I found refreshing while “ponderous exploration evoking existentialism” is certainly becoming a trope in indie titles. This one isn't pretentious about it. It lets you go there if you want and get lost in the atmosphere or you can just run around and collect the things, making sure to hit all the platforms.
It's screw or get screwed!

Welcome to the lovingly crafted realtime strategy game/misery simulator that is Banished. Unlike many other RTS titles, Banished is a game that puts far more emphasis on the process of building rather than on using building as a means to an end. There is no combat in this game. No objectives. The goal of this game is to survive, and with a little luck, even to thrive as you create an entire city from just about nothing. This is done by using a number of finely tuned in-game systems and processes which stress careful planning, resource balancing, and long-term strategizing over mindless resource gathering and the spamming of useful buildings.
I certainly do not think this game is for everyone; the gameplay appeals far more to hardcore strategists looking for the subtle sense of achievement that comes from achieving long term goals, such as properly balancing resource deficits and developing effective city layout. Additionally, Banished is not afraid to harshly punish mistakes, or even to create unexpected challenges, even to the point where there will be times when save-scumming cannot save your little town from certain destruction, be it from a natural disaster, an infectious outbreak, or even rampant starvation. The attractive graphics and solid soundtrack (though a bit foreboding, even stranglely intimidating at times) make this a game that is easy to play for hours at a time as one continuously seeks to improve from a humble beginning of just a few citizens and resources into a massive and sprawling  colonial township.
If you're a fan of resource managment game and long-term strategizing, or even urban planning, you're gonna like this game. And even if you're not, the the short and effective tutorial as well as its simple menu and interface system surely will not scare you away before you've had the chance to tackle your first winter.
Certainly worth a buy for any hardcore strategy fans or even those with an interests in applying the recent craze in survival mechanics to a more thoughtful and slower paced strategy application.

I've been waiting a long time for this to come out, and yet here it is December 2014 and this is still only "pre-alpha"??? As other have said, no controller support yet, and no split-screen local multiplayer either!! So those 2 things right there limit my enjoyability for this game since my brother and I have been playing the original DD together for a few years.
Also, I'm not a fan of the forced online "instances", a la MMORPGs. I hate those kind of games. I generally play games alone or locally with a friend, or very rarely with a friend online. I seriously do not have any interest in playing with random people online. I did not know this was the case before I bought it.
And, did something change, because I distinctly remember the Dungeon Defenders website saying that DD2 would be a free-to-play game, with in-game purchase of items, levels, etc. Yet they're asking $24.99 (20% off until 12/12) for this unfinished game! I went ahead and bought it yesterday anyway, though, since I loved DD1, but the current state of the game leaves a lot to ask for.
Yes, I get that they're calling this "pre-alpha" and "early access". But since this game has been in development for a long time now, I would have imagined they be further along, and at least have the same features as the first game (controller support, splitscreen multiplayer, pop up menus for your powers/summons, ability to upgrade your items in your inventory with mana, etc.)
The good: The game looks great; the graphics and animations are well polished. Some neat new game play aspects. Simplified mechanics, each hero now only gets 4 types of powers and 4 kinds of summonable defenses.
The bad: Core features are missing! HELLO? What happened to controller support and split screen multiplayer??? Also, the music gets repetitive very fast. Some of the new aspects and mechanics are confusingly presented. For instance, you can't get your inventory or character stats without visiting the defenders forge. Level ups seem to be automatic, except for points you can distribute, but you must go to the forge.
As others have said, you don't get as much green mana for summoning as DD1. Basically there's now blue mana for powers and green mana for summons. In my 2 hours of play so far, the levels end up littered with blue mana crystals that I can't pick up because I'm already full, yet my green mana is either empty or nearly half full. I guess this is a balance problem, hopefully they'll address it.
RECOMMENDATION: Not worth even the sale price of $19.99. They need to bring back the core features I loved about DD1. Maybe once they've released a few more patches it'll be up to my expectations.

I'm not a big fan of modern indie platformers. Several of them feel like someone's just taken a decades-old game, updated the graphics, and added some modern one-liners. VVVVVV goes in the opposite direction. It looks and sounds like a game from the 80s, with just one new gameplay mechanic: reversing gravity. Yet, by building the whole game around that concept, the devs have managed to put together a game which feels very focused, and is truly unique.
The soundtrack and graphics are a perfect fit for this game - they add to the atmosphere, without distracting you from the puzzles themselves. The game is difficult, but I didn't find it as frustrating as some other precision-jumping games. The hardest puzzles in the main game are optional. Also, with frequent checkpoints, a fail will only set you back a few seconds - you won't have to keep repeating an easy section because of one difficulty spike.
The main plot is relatively short, but the game includes a wide variety of challenges (e.g. speedruns, endurance, no-death runs), and lets you play user-made maps. If you like the style of gameplay here, VVVVVV will provide you with great value for money. Highly recommended.

Keep in mind most of the other (negative) reviews are from early access.
Anyway, I'd give this game a buy with a caveat. If you, like me, are always searching for starship sims (less Tie Fighter more Star Trek Bridge Commander), you might enjoy this game. If you aren't, however, you probably will not like this, as it is a fairly simple, shallow experience. That experience, however, does scratch that utterly maddening starship sim itch.
This game allows you to play like you're Captain Picard or Admiral Adama, which is something a lot of us really want, but not something that's often made. Most of the games in this genre are decades old, rarely talked about or even remembered, and sometimes not even capable of being played on modern machines -- even with DosBox. This game fills that very large gap. If you are looking to sit on the bridge and take command over starship systems and crew, this is for you.
So what is the game like? It basically amounts to a series of simple mobile-like minigames superimposed over a smallish 3d open world and resource management simulator. You can pick and name your captain, crew, ship loadout (everything from weapons systems to what kind of food replicators you ship is equipped with), and starting resources. The controls are not able to be changed, but they are fine as-is and not anything that you'd worry about changing anyway. For that matter the interface is streamlined and easy to use. The mini-games are actually enjoyable, if simplistic, so the game ends up being pretty fun for the price.
The only things I dislike about the game are its lack of depth (the minigames really do feel like minigames and the away missions are just randomly generated die rolls with possible stat bonuses applied as far as I can tell) and its visual style (some may like it, but I find it a hideous mess that's aesthetically similar to the worst of bargain-bin scifi crap--lots of glowing neon, random hexes getting in the way of everything, plastic-looking textures, hideous ship design, etc). These may be deal breakers for some, but I'm willing to put up with it because A) It's cheap and B) it exists in a genre that's very rarely explored.
tl;dr It's a simpler FTL in first person, except you feel more attached to your crew and ship

Dungeon Defenders II is the struggle for a party of usually four adventurers to defend some type of objective, be it a merchant that unbeknownst to him travelled into an area fraught with danger in the recent invasion, now needing the help of the player to defend his merchandise. Or protecting the city's sewersystem, or any other menial low-level task they have you do to level up and progress. It's a sequel, and therefore permits us to compare and contrast the game to its predecessor and figure out if the game isn't samey enough to warrant an actual purchase.
Right away we are met with new contraptions that are fairly interesting, some traps for the huntress has been embellished and made more flashy along with the wizards. But I am missing the old flow of glowing magic missiles. It seems they made things more subtle in terms of world-building, in the process they lost some of the vibrant colorfulness that I enjoyed from the first one. It's also hard to shake the feeling of sameness, that would almost alienate a player of the previous game. Perhaps you find it fun to just have more content, but in reality it means that if you were a hardcore player in this scene you just lost all your characters and would have to be forced to do it all again, those 800 hours for naught. So far I haven't seen what actually sets apart the sequel from the first one.
One things that sets it a part in some regards are the spells, they are flashier and a lot more exciting – like the visceral reaction you get with the wizards hurricane spell which lifts your foes into the air and makes the vulnerable to attacks and thereafter dazes them. It's all in the game-world and doesn't suspend the enemy in an animation beyond your hand, like some other games would have a hurricane ability do. Enemies are instead simply lifted up in the air for you to do as you please with, still within the physical world of the game and not transcended into intangible animations. Your attacks have more impact now, perhaps not substantially enough for praise (but it is still in pre-alpha), but they do have a greater feel to them compared to the previous version, nevertheless, the speed of the game is lost in the process. Your new running animation is woefully sluggish and makes it a drag running to and fro to repair, upgrade and defend: the free flow of movement that made the first ones move-set so wonderful is no longer present.
Level-wise there are actually some new mechanics that provide use with new contingencies in how to plan out and design your defense. There are often “subcores” that when broken, open up new pathways for the enemies to stream in from. This inhibits you from centralizing your defense or making it easy for yourself – especially in singleplayer – in just stacking all your defense in one pathway. Instead you have to separate your defense-points, that serve only to illuminate the slow nature of the game that I keep going on about.
The look of the game has to me improved greatly, in the basic way it looks, not necessarily color-wise or in the sense of uniqueness but still beyond that cell-shaded style we can see everywhere these days. Textures have improved and the maps are more dense with scenic imagery – but in a less fantastical setting, so far. The animations, although slower and the culprit in dulling the game, look a lot better than in the previous game. But is this higher quality animation while more elaborate, better than a lesser quality animation, but that doesn't interfere with high speed exciting gameplay? That's up to you, I suppose. I, for one, prefer the fast gameplay.
To really get by – to really breeze by the levels – you need the co-op. If you want it to be difficult, you can do it on your own. As far as I know, it's not like in the first one where you could use different characters interchangeably to build all the defenses you need to clear the level. Unless you can do this, I do kind of enjoy that co-op becomes a reward in itself, but less that it's so forced and difficult to do without. There are points where you have to snipe specific enemies that some contraptions can't get at, and there are characters designed to do just that and without them your defenses are nullified.
I clocked in at about 800 hours in the first Dungeon Defenders, it's not something I'm proud of but it shows that there was a depth of content which made the game substantial enough to play for that amount of time. There was a set meta of different characters providing different services that after a while were set in their ways, which stagnated the game. Dungeon Defenders II might change a few of its features and have a brand new look, but that stagnation is at the heart of the experience, even though it's after hours and hours of quite enjoyable gameplay, it results in a slow realization of how pointless this ultimately has been. It is still the cartoony game it set out to be. It can be quite beautiful in some locations and Dungeon Defender is now more lively and vibrant in its world-building, even if it at points is comparably lackluster in gameplay. It's a cheap game considering how much content there is, and how much content is yet to come and I would recommend it, especially if you have some friends to play it with.

I'll use this review to compare it to the previous entries since if you're looking at the third game in the series, then you probably already know what you're getting into.
Story: Whereas Rebirth 1 and Rebirth 2 had almost no continuity, Rebirth 3 actually directly follows Rebirth 2 in terms of story, so it may be a good idea to play that (though honestly you won't miss out on much of the story if you haven't played the second game).
Gameplay: Like Rebirth 2, you can have four characters in the front lines during battle. New changes include the removal of the EXE drive (SP is used instead and is generated similarly; SP potions are pretty much gone). EX Finishers are now selected one per category, which makes it easier to tell what they do and makes combat planning a lot easier. Beyond that it's more of the same.
The port is decent too, being stable everywhere aside from a couple areas. No FPS cap, though higher framerates tend to screw with the jump function sometimes (not a big deal).

Angvik, the 2D action platformer from Alastair John Jack, is a bit like Dark Souls and a bit like Angry Birds. Although this combination sounds ridiculous, allow me to recount my first run: after spending two minutes spewing fluffy sheep from my pink staff, my character came into contact with some kind of monkey-dog and exploded into a (rather dainty) pile of bones.  This strange mashing of hardcore gaming and casual visuals allows Angvik to stake out an identity in a relatively crowded market.
While the cute art style deserves attention, Angvik shines brightest through its punishing gameplay.  Don't expect to button-mash your way through combat—instead, prepare for several deaths as you slowly learn enemy patterns.  Admittedly, many games require this type of memorization.  Angvik, however, also requires the player to be very adaptable.  Because nearly all of the game's weapons break after three or four successful attacks, players must constantly shift their offensive and defensive strategies.  Close combat, for instance, isn't necessary with a boomerang—but you'll have to change things up after you switch out the boomerang for a sword that shoots fireballs.  And when you fail, a frequent occurrence, don't expect to load up a save game: you'll be starting from the beginning on each playthrough.
Adding to the difficulty is a subtle timer measured by the player's age.  As you progress throughout each of the five stages, your character grows older (demonstrated by his whitening hair) until he collapses dead.  With only one 'hurry up' warning, this mechanic occasionally caught me off-guard.  That said, it fits well and adds another level of difficulty to the game...even if I don't understand how I can be an old man at the end of the first stage and a teenager at the start of the next.
While the first two mechanics boil down to a durability counter and a timer, the last two are more interesting.  Oils, found by killing enemies and opening chests, are used to transform items.  Green oil turns a paladin's cross into a wooden boomerang, and black oil shifts a stick into a powerful great-sword.  These oils inject a small amount of strategy and experimentation into what is otherwise a very straightforward platformer. Lastly, the player picks up eggs that can be converted into weaponized birds.  I think that's pretty self-explanatory.
As much as I've praised Angvik, I found the game lacking in several areas.  The UI is frustrating—as far as I can tell, you cannot find statistics on equipped armor.  (Yet, for some reason, information is available on unused armor.)  Secondly, the game has a fair amount of bugs.  My computer, according to the developer's website, is perfectly capable of running Angvik; yet the game lags after I play for a few minutes, and it occasionally crashes.  On a more neutral note, the music is decidedly mediocre: it fits, but it doesn't add much to the game.
My biggest issue with Angvik is the way the developer forced it to become a classic arcade experience.  Despite possessing some roguelike elements in random enemy and weapon generation, this game lacks randomly generated levels.  The result is a contradictory experience: sure, the player needs to adapt on the fly, but at the same time the easiest path to success involves memorizing the layout of the world.  The preset map has other disadvantages as well: secrets lose their secrecy because, once discovered, they remain in the same spot on each subsequent playthrough.  Ultimately, Angvik boils down to one big pattern—and while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, it does feel outdated.
I had a lot of fun the first few times I booted up Angvik, and I may play it a few more times after I publish this review.  That said, this game offers little replayability in the face of true roguelikes.  There's a lot to like about Angvik, and I enjoyed it in the short run.  In the long run, however, I'd rather play something else.
FINAL SCORE: 7.2/10

Welcome to the lovingly crafted realtime strategy game/misery simulator that is Banished. Unlike many other RTS titles, Banished is a game that puts far more emphasis on the process of building rather than on using building as a means to an end. There is no combat in this game. No objectives. The goal of this game is to survive, and with a little luck, even to thrive as you create an entire city from just about nothing. This is done by using a number of finely tuned in-game systems and processes which stress careful planning, resource balancing, and long-term strategizing over mindless resource gathering and the spamming of useful buildings.
I certainly do not think this game is for everyone; the gameplay appeals far more to hardcore strategists looking for the subtle sense of achievement that comes from achieving long term goals, such as properly balancing resource deficits and developing effective city layout. Additionally, Banished is not afraid to harshly punish mistakes, or even to create unexpected challenges, even to the point where there will be times when save-scumming cannot save your little town from certain destruction, be it from a natural disaster, an infectious outbreak, or even rampant starvation. The attractive graphics and solid soundtrack (though a bit foreboding, even stranglely intimidating at times) make this a game that is easy to play for hours at a time as one continuously seeks to improve from a humble beginning of just a few citizens and resources into a massive and sprawling  colonial township.
If you're a fan of resource managment game and long-term strategizing, or even urban planning, you're gonna like this game. And even if you're not, the the short and effective tutorial as well as its simple menu and interface system surely will not scare you away before you've had the chance to tackle your first winter.
Certainly worth a buy for any hardcore strategy fans or even those with an interests in applying the recent craze in survival mechanics to a more thoughtful and slower paced strategy application.

This may be one of the most well realized games I've ever played.
The concept is the simplest concept. Left click if the colour matches the word, right click if it doesn't.
This turns out to be sort of like how Osu! and Super Hexagon are for your hands, but for your brain.
First off there are two ways to play, and this might be the most ingenious part of it all.
First, you can play slowly and steadily. Take a moment to think here and there and you'll eventually run down all of the puzzles in an area.
Or you can play fast and loose, which requires you to basically anticipate the next colour on the screen and react in a fraction of a second.
The fact that the game allows both ways to play makes it better balanced than most AAA games.
Also all of the achievements are not only wacky, but fun as well.
Playing the game in a different language, or in monochrome mode, actually introduce you to new ways to have fun with the game when you feel like you've run out. Not to mention attempting to figure out the legendary achievements.
This is offically my new go to game when I'm just looking to burn a couple of minutes. And I don't see another game toppling it ever.

I absolutely recommend this game. While it's not necessarily a game I'll be playing for years, it's a very fun and very engaging strategy/city builder that's well worth the money.
My favorite part of this game, other than the gameplay itself, is the difficulty controls. It's not a simple "easy, medium, difficult." You choose the terrain of the land, the harshness of the winters, whether or not to have disasters on, and the difficulty of your start. This allows the game to be very straightforward or very challenging depending on what the player wants, without taking away from the gameplay. You still need some level of strategy to succeed no matter what, but it's way more forgiving when winter is mild and there are no disasters coming your way. You'll probably still fail a few times before getting it right, but that's all part of the fun!
Additionally, I love the level of detail you can go into if you want to. Once you build a City Hall (which requires a certain level of having your city established), you can see graphs of demographics and production, which I love. I'm all about details like that.
Overall, it's a fun balance of strategy and sandbox! Well worth the money.

One thing before I start: If I could give this game a "maybe" instead of a straight yes or no, I would. I don't dislike this game. I enjoyed my time with it, I just felt like there wan't enough there.
As a Star Trek fan, this game immediatly caught my eye because of the whole "being the captain on the bridge" thing. Comparisons to FTL sold it and, in fact, I'm going to compare it to FTL a few times in this review.
The foundation of the game is solid. You attempt to get from A to B, starting with limited resources and scouring planets to replenish your supplies while evading an alien in race in pursuit of you. You pick a crew at the beginning of the game and level them up as they perform various tasks, such as away missions or dealing with civilian unrest.
The problem I began to encounter very early on is that the potential of this game isn't fully realized. Let me explain: You're given this fairly large space in which to traverse, yet it feels very empty. You'll encounter the Skorn (the alien race chasing you) fairly often, but the only interactions you ever have with other races out in space, as far as I could tell, is limited to trading resources. Contrast this to FTL, where encounters in space can come with any number of outcomes that could end up fundamentally altering how you handle that run. At the very least, something interesting happens. In Into the Stars, you can encounter some aliens when you reach planets and they reward you with stuff, but I quickly found the rewards pretty boring. For example, one event awarded me with a better life support system. This was USEFUL, but it didn't make anything more interesting. Again, compair this to FTL, where getting ship modules and new weapons can greatly alter the way the game plays. Next, the combat. For me, combat quickly became trivial (I'll note here that I was playing on normal difficulty). It was very Trek like, which I appreciated, but I found it to be very easy. Even when I fought two ships at once, after the first encounter even that was lacking in difficulty. I say this not because I need the game to be as brutal as FTL can be, but because I soon found myself completely ignoring the threat level of sectors. The Skorn just weren't a threat, and that's a shame. Lastly (and this may be sort of a nitpick), I thought the game was to short. At the beginning, it seems like you're really in it for the long hall. As you move along, your time is measure in days. But in actual playtime, it actually goes by really fast. I got to the end in maybe an hour and a half.
I want to like this game. I want to LOVE this game. It has so much potential, but there just isn't enough there. I'd love to see some kind of expansion that adds more content. Until then, I don't see myself playing this again.

Dungeon Defenders II is the struggle for a party of usually four adventurers to defend some type of objective, be it a merchant that unbeknownst to him travelled into an area fraught with danger in the recent invasion, now needing the help of the player to defend his merchandise. Or protecting the city's sewersystem, or any other menial low-level task they have you do to level up and progress. It's a sequel, and therefore permits us to compare and contrast the game to its predecessor and figure out if the game isn't samey enough to warrant an actual purchase.
Right away we are met with new contraptions that are fairly interesting, some traps for the huntress has been embellished and made more flashy along with the wizards. But I am missing the old flow of glowing magic missiles. It seems they made things more subtle in terms of world-building, in the process they lost some of the vibrant colorfulness that I enjoyed from the first one. It's also hard to shake the feeling of sameness, that would almost alienate a player of the previous game. Perhaps you find it fun to just have more content, but in reality it means that if you were a hardcore player in this scene you just lost all your characters and would have to be forced to do it all again, those 800 hours for naught. So far I haven't seen what actually sets apart the sequel from the first one.
One things that sets it a part in some regards are the spells, they are flashier and a lot more exciting – like the visceral reaction you get with the wizards hurricane spell which lifts your foes into the air and makes the vulnerable to attacks and thereafter dazes them. It's all in the game-world and doesn't suspend the enemy in an animation beyond your hand, like some other games would have a hurricane ability do. Enemies are instead simply lifted up in the air for you to do as you please with, still within the physical world of the game and not transcended into intangible animations. Your attacks have more impact now, perhaps not substantially enough for praise (but it is still in pre-alpha), but they do have a greater feel to them compared to the previous version, nevertheless, the speed of the game is lost in the process. Your new running animation is woefully sluggish and makes it a drag running to and fro to repair, upgrade and defend: the free flow of movement that made the first ones move-set so wonderful is no longer present.
Level-wise there are actually some new mechanics that provide use with new contingencies in how to plan out and design your defense. There are often “subcores” that when broken, open up new pathways for the enemies to stream in from. This inhibits you from centralizing your defense or making it easy for yourself – especially in singleplayer – in just stacking all your defense in one pathway. Instead you have to separate your defense-points, that serve only to illuminate the slow nature of the game that I keep going on about.
The look of the game has to me improved greatly, in the basic way it looks, not necessarily color-wise or in the sense of uniqueness but still beyond that cell-shaded style we can see everywhere these days. Textures have improved and the maps are more dense with scenic imagery – but in a less fantastical setting, so far. The animations, although slower and the culprit in dulling the game, look a lot better than in the previous game. But is this higher quality animation while more elaborate, better than a lesser quality animation, but that doesn't interfere with high speed exciting gameplay? That's up to you, I suppose. I, for one, prefer the fast gameplay.
To really get by – to really breeze by the levels – you need the co-op. If you want it to be difficult, you can do it on your own. As far as I know, it's not like in the first one where you could use different characters interchangeably to build all the defenses you need to clear the level. Unless you can do this, I do kind of enjoy that co-op becomes a reward in itself, but less that it's so forced and difficult to do without. There are points where you have to snipe specific enemies that some contraptions can't get at, and there are characters designed to do just that and without them your defenses are nullified.
I clocked in at about 800 hours in the first Dungeon Defenders, it's not something I'm proud of but it shows that there was a depth of content which made the game substantial enough to play for that amount of time. There was a set meta of different characters providing different services that after a while were set in their ways, which stagnated the game. Dungeon Defenders II might change a few of its features and have a brand new look, but that stagnation is at the heart of the experience, even though it's after hours and hours of quite enjoyable gameplay, it results in a slow realization of how pointless this ultimately has been. It is still the cartoony game it set out to be. It can be quite beautiful in some locations and Dungeon Defender is now more lively and vibrant in its world-building, even if it at points is comparably lackluster in gameplay. It's a cheap game considering how much content there is, and how much content is yet to come and I would recommend it, especially if you have some friends to play it with.

So. Into The Stars, basically, Battlestar Galactica, you are humanities last hope. A colony ship which moves at best at the speed of a flying space turtle on tranquilisers, moving across a fairly hostile chunk of galaxy in the hope of making it to a habitable planet (Titus Nova). The ship's warp core is more or less dead, you're running on limited resources, everything is going to break slowly, and you're fighting progressively worse situations as you go. It's a bit like a lot of games that involve such mechanics (think FTL and its' ilk).
Now, disclaimer, I kickstarted this game, and I wanted to get involved
because I saw the potential in this to be the big BSG experience that everyone was aiming for. It had the team behind it, it had (and has) the graphics behind it, it has the -music- damn it. What it needed was people who could be dedicated playtesters who could shape the game into something great. People with a lot of experience in the gaming arena who know what works and what doesn't. People who understand the limitations of dev time and therefore could have got the ideas in early so they wouldn't have been going down the wrong track on things like combat and so on.
Problem, the dev team was probably the least communicative that I've ever seen during the KS phase post campaign. It was definitely the least involved KS post release I've been. So I decided to stay well back and wait for the early access release, in the vague hope that hey, these guys looked professional, they'd get this right. I was partially correct.
Into The Stars should be seen as an exercise in why if you have a bad idea, you should discard it as quick as you can, rather than double down on it in an attempt to patch it up and make it playable. The big bugbear in this case was combat. Combat here uses a colour frequency system to determine if a shot gets past your (or your opponents shields) or not.
This is not good gameplay, because it offers no reward to the player, if they do stuff right, they're basically getting the damage from the weapon that they're supposed to get in the first place (presuming it even hits), and if they do stuff right defensively, then their shields function as advertised (yes, it's possible to hit "deflect" and it do -nothing- if your frequency is the wrong colour).
Right from the get go I voiced my criticsm about this system, because I could see this being a major issue with the game, it didn't reward the player, and simply punished the player for lapsing in concentration. It was busywork, and busywork without benefit. Instead of seeing this and discarding the colour frequency idea as one that promoted poor design choices, the team instead decided to try to create workarounds such as the "evade" button (which ironically allows you to dodge fire regardless of frequency) and ways of forcing the opponent to flip their frequency to allow you to line up deflections and attacks easier. In effect, sticking to their original idea in the hope they could make it workable. It's STILL bad, when you've multiple foes to fight and you've got this mess of colours going on, it's chaotic, and it's
, it's annoying.
The civillian city, created to give the events that pop up some meaning and context, was another idea that didn't promote good gameplay, largely because it lacked thematic background and narrative to tie it in to the game proper. It was bolted on as a means to add work and to try and force you to care about the civillians, except in this case it didn't make a great deal of sense, why were you building these extra modules, why did they need arbitrary numbers of minerals, why did the city appear to be entirely divorced from the ship itself?
Had the city mimicked the layout of the ARK, and perhaps had you been building additional modules INTO the available cargo space (or indeed, demolishing habitable space to make room for cargo at the cost of civillian homes), THAT would have made more sense narratively, and could have opened up a lot of interesting decisions. As it stands, it feels like a stub that lacks a real sense of place.
Then there's the mess that is the stat layout and where said stats are used, Engineering being too heavily relied upon with Toughness being a dump stat that seems to have little bearing on much of anything. Again, a matter that was raised before the launch of the game, but not addressed at launch (I fired up the game and to my dismay, you still need engineering for the bulk of your operations, half of your combat duties are reliant on Engineering), my proposal was to slim down the stats from six to five and to more evenly distribute the "workload" of the stats to ensure that each role had a more valid use in the game.
Augh.
And it pains me to say, that I think the devs know there's a good game in here too, but in this case they went down some decisions early on and decided to stick to them too rigidly, rather than fail fast and recover faster. The launch version is polished, but the design issues STILL plague the game.
Had they listened to the posts I made far earlier (as far back as 0.2 even), and changed course, this might be a very different game, and this might be a very different review. For the better or worse? Who knows. I can't claim to have all the answers, but I know that -these- choices didn't end up making sense, when you added them all together. Perhaps with more iteration and patching, this game will be worthy of recommendation, but for now, I can only very cautiously recommend it to people who have a major BSG itch to scratch.

Into the Stars is a cool early access game! If you are a fan of surival simulation games I think you will like this quite a lot. If you are a fan of Star Trek and Battlestar Galactica I think you will love it. For an early access game it is very polished and from the 5 hours I have played I have never experienced a ctd.
presentation-
The graphics in this game are very well done utilizing the unreal 4 engine ( your ship will travel through space in real time with animated meteor fields, and ennemy encounters, etc It looks impressive. You can switch views on the fly from the exterior to the interior of the ship( this is where you will access the various menus and make your decisions.The ui and illustrations are also executed very well.
gameplay-
there is a lot of thought that went into this system. The premise is that humanity is facing extinction and must move thier last colony ship through the dangers of unexplored space to locate a new homeworld. The journey cannot be completed successfully without carefully managing your resources. There are a lot of things you have to consider, and the game does a great job of forcing you to make difficult choices. There are three difficulty settings, and I found myself struggling with normal mode because I was a noob and put all my resources into outfitting my ship with powerful weapons to fight the skorn( the skorn are an alien race trying to wipe you out as you forge a path to the new homeworld.) Because of this all my colonists died of starvation lol. So I started over on easy until I better understood how to balance my ships attributes. Certain parts you choose may be more powerful, but they will also consume more of a specific resource so you really have to be smart about how you initially set up your spacecraft when you start a new campaign. Along the way you will have to restock your resources,( i think there are 8 total attributes?) through mining minigames, and what you focus on mining in these mini games also directly relates to your overall ship composition. I think there is a great deal of customizabilty here and I'm interested in seeing what the devs have in store, regarding possible upgraded parts in the full release?
if you are a fan of these survival simulation strategy games you should definitely check this out. My only gripe is that in order to save your game you have to choose- save AND quit- there is no other option lol! You have to quit out of the game to save...
But this has been mentioned in a lot of other peoples reviews, I'm pretty sure this will be fixed in the final build. so yeah, I'm giving it a positive review. Looking forward to seeing what new content is added in the update.

EA REVIEW: "Into The Stars" is an excellent EA title, particulalrly given so many EA missteps, giving the early access buyer a full-fledged experience of what will be in the final release. If you loved "Star Trek: Bridge Commander", a game I played again only recently, then you have an idea of what to expect. Unlike "ST:BC" though, you are in control of your ship with direct input (think "Independence War 2") and have a civilian population aboard, in a 'city' that you must feed, oxygenate and build support structures for.
You fly an Ark, searching for a new home with your civilian populace - ala "Battlestar Galactica".
At the heart is a "FTL"-like idea that you have to move from sector to sector (basically planet to planet) with an enemy in hot pursuit - the Skorn! Unlike "FTL" though it is both first and third person, in that you are either in 3rd Person with your ship at the centre, or in the Captain's chair navigating from planet to planet in order to send shuttles down on mission, manual drilling or automated resource probe gathering.
There are Shuttle Missions, Shuttle Drilling (for resources), and Probes. The shuttle missions consist of objectives, with choices on how to conduct them with items and modules as rewards if successful. The drilling assignments are a mini-game of sorts where you must direct your drill to collect as many resources as you can before running out of fuel or hitting a block. The automated probe resource gathering assignments consists of assigning a pilot and sending the probe down which if successful results in resources collected.
Careful though, as each planet holds different resources and expending Nitrogen or Hydrogen to collect Biomass to feed the populace might have you running out of fuel and at the mercy of the Skorn. It is up to the player to choose how much of any gathered resource to bring aboard the ship, and this can take some juggling by the player/captain.
You will also interact with pirates and trading vessels, but so far the trades aren't particularly inspiring.
In the third person, you see your ship in all its glory and surrounding planetary bodies, nebulae, suns and asteroids all beautifully rendered using the Unreal 4 engine. It's also an efficient way of spotting Skorn ships, and planets safely in reach away from the enemy (which on your map each sector displays yellow threats and red - attack imminent).Speaking of which….
Battles are handled well, as you micromanage and build the skills of your crew in training, populace alerts and through missions, and assign them to battle stations. You must modulate your shield and weapon frequencies to differ from your attackers, which is fairly simply down, and you have shields and a dodge ability (very useful). Target enemy modules by taking down shield, and then weapons as quickly as you can then attack the hull. You do take damage and casualties though, and this is where the items, such as repair items can be used to fix up the damage taken. Injured crew can be assigned to one of two sick bays to heal and if lost, additional crew members are offered as rewards for shuttle missions.
With much to come and a lot of polishing, according to the Devs this makes the anticipation for launch day high. Don't know if there will be modding tools or a workshop, but the game really would benefit if you could transform your ship into the "Enterprise", the Battlestar "Galactica" or even a Star Destroyer (let alone the Firefly or Normandy).
Have to wait and see...

Wow, this game was hard. I just finished grabbing all the achievements, logging in about 17 hours, I think? And a good chunk of those were spent on the 5 star difficulty level.
The art is simple and controls are easy to understand (I used a controller), so it's easy to get started, but you'll be dying at about every corner as you progress. That's normal. There's a 'great guy' option when choosing your character that starts at one star difficulty and randomizes your character (and the map to some extent in later difficulties). When you beat it two star unlocks, and so on. Birds can be hatched from eggs dropped by all sorts of enemies (Like monkeys!) and the type of bird depends on what hat you're wearing, and weapons and armor can be changed with 'oils.' The classes were simple, a few being more interesting than others. The king is the most OP with full armor and a sword, the bottler has oils and no weapons, and the peasant doesn't get any armor drops throughout the whole game. There are a few more, too.
I didn't really experience any bugs, but sometimes as shepard my sheep would somehow appear in the ground instead of the air and couldn't move.... which was interesting.
Overall, good platformer with relentless enemies and solid gameplay. I enjoyed it while playing but now that I've beaten it I'm not sure I would want to go through 5 star difficulty again.

I am writing this review as someone who played this game first from it's series so I cannot speak for fans of the first.
If you can get in the mentality that you will probably die a lot and a few of those times you will also probably lose a decent chunk of souls ( both level-up and shop currency ) then you can have a great time with this game.
It isn't quite as hard as many may boast since patience and attention to details can save you a lot of headache but it still way ahead of other action rpgs in which you might never die.
The combat is very different than other RPGs as well in that your ability to attack or dodge ( stamina ) is really limited but regenerates very fast when you aren't doing anything. And getting hit even by grunts hurts a lot. Thus a tactical approach is required many times and a simple misstep and aggroing several enemies can easily get you killed.
Still even though I like the game very much it isn't perfect and I have a few complaints, most of them can be put down to taste but still.
Pvping can be somewhat avoided but it can be really costly to do so and a lot of the times might not be worth using the consumable to do so. Thus you can get ganked by players that generally seem better prepared and unless another consumable is used they will be ignored by enemies putting you at a major disadvantage.
Also because of the fact that you lose all souls on you when dying and dying again makes the previous drop of yours vanish, invading players can go from a simple annoyance to rage-quitting frustration when you lose a significant amount of souls.
While most enemies and bosses have varying degrees of difficulty between them there are a few bosses in particular that seem intentionally designate as difficulty spikes and you will spend way more time on those than anything else in the game if you want to solo them.
And finally the game really doesn't go into specifics. Like how weight actually interacts with dodge rolls, how damage is calculated, the fact that infused weapons even when they have the same grade of scaling don't scale as well as natural elemental weapons and so on. Trips to the wiki and googling will almost be required for anyone trying to finish it.
A great game... especially for masochists.

This is one of those games I would like to have had a neutral feedback option for.
I love the concept and the overall presentation as well, designing once you get a hand of it is quite powerful etc and I think this game will end up being quite good.
The physics is modeled quite well with weight, torsion, spring, bounce, collisions etc all being a factor.
You can build just about anything you want with actuators of all shapes and sizes and angles, motors, propellers, wheels etc so your imagination is really the limit here.
The workshop has tens of thousands of examples, some very well done, planes, trains, helicopters, cranes, trucks, dragsters, rock crawlers, atv's, jeeps, trailers and more!
My current gripes are how easily everything falls apart, this topic we are bringing up again and again, I hope it gets fixed soon but in a dynamic manner with say a slider that lets players choose how well "stuck together" the blocks are.
Another thing is multiplayer, currently it "works" but needs a decent amount of additional work and options to become stable and really usable long-term.
There is no dedicated server option (just P2P atm), no password or whitelist feature, no way to promote another player to admin to manage the gaming session and unfortunately crashes especially while changing maps.
Auto-cleanup of debris and abandoned vehicles is also essential for keeping up performance and clearing up the "junk".
Performance is overall quite good with plenty of options to tweak for your system.
It uses the Unreal Game Engine.
Overall I like where this is going, it just needs some attention to specific important details and polishing of multiplayer to take it from its current ok/good status to great.
Keep up the work Dev. you have done a decent job so far and I would love to see this title grow.

I absolutely recommend this game. While it's not necessarily a game I'll be playing for years, it's a very fun and very engaging strategy/city builder that's well worth the money.
My favorite part of this game, other than the gameplay itself, is the difficulty controls. It's not a simple "easy, medium, difficult." You choose the terrain of the land, the harshness of the winters, whether or not to have disasters on, and the difficulty of your start. This allows the game to be very straightforward or very challenging depending on what the player wants, without taking away from the gameplay. You still need some level of strategy to succeed no matter what, but it's way more forgiving when winter is mild and there are no disasters coming your way. You'll probably still fail a few times before getting it right, but that's all part of the fun!
Additionally, I love the level of detail you can go into if you want to. Once you build a City Hall (which requires a certain level of having your city established), you can see graphs of demographics and production, which I love. I'm all about details like that.
Overall, it's a fun balance of strategy and sandbox! Well worth the money.

This game is amazing. A completely new take on city building. A bottom up simulation sets the foundation for this game while a harsh unforgiving environment supplies the challenge. Barns store your resources, markets collect resources from around the city for citizens, and people gather food and supplies from the markets into their homes. People need to eat, idle, and stock their homes with perishables in addition to working. Resource management is crucial and a schedule for building is essential to surviving the first few seasons. Every resource you fail to produce for any reason can kill a substatial portion of your population. Inefficient resource gathering placement can cause you to squander land for resource sinks that could otherwise be used for utility. My only complaint is that the game seems to get easier the larger your city becomes. Once you're over a hundred people you have the man power to ensure a constant supply of every resource. Losing 20-30 people will likely resolve your resource problem and you'll only have to make minor adjustments to your job assignments. The fun is definitely in the early game.
