Sugar (FTL: Faster Than Light). Spice (Out There). And everything nice. These were the ingredients chosen to create the perfect space survival simulation. But Fugitive Games accidentally added an extra ingredient to the concoction... Chemical X (bugs, performance and other issues).
+ The game delivers an excellent captain's hotseat experience. I want to scream "Captain on deck!".
+ A real sense of urgency to reach Titus Nova especially early game where the crew is inexperienced and modules tend to be one sided, highly costly and not very resource friendly. The game brutally teaches you the importance of foresight and progression.
+ Stunning visuals. The ARK-13, distant stars, asteroid field and even solar flares look gorgeous. Nailed it all!
+ Great sound effects and brilliant score by Jack Wall.
+ Planetary exploration, probe deployment and the mining mini game are well done and challenges the player's morals. Planetary exploration could do with more scenarios and variety in rewards - i.e. increase to population, implementable alien city constructs, researchable blueprints.
+ On board city, crew, resource and engineering management tools are nice additions. Could do with greater city management freedom and features.
+ The ability to switch between the Captain's chair and exterior camera helps with navigation and appreciation of the universe.
- There is a performance issue and possibly a memory leak issue too. The game is a CPU hog and demands plenty of juice.
- Slight delay between mouse clicks and game response.
- No hotkeys. Almost entirely dependent on mouse clicks. Controls cannot be reassigned or tweaked in any way.
- The ship alert system needs fixing. Quite often I found it would loop (as if bugged; continuously repeating) the presence + approach of Skorn or trade vessels, depletion of resources or increase in threat level.
- Trade ships, enemy patrols and warped Skorn ships quite often incur bugs and freeze in place or fail/block interaction.
- Lack of variation in alien encounters, Skorn ship types and enemies. I discovered only one other alien race (Menhit) and had a short exchange of fire. Mercenary ships, pirates, hostile alien species also in seek of refuge or other threats in the Gamma and Delta sectors would add to the variety of threats present.
- I enjoyed the overwhelming combat mechanics and 3v1 scenarios, but it becomes a case of constant repetition after the first few playthroughs. Variation in enemy types and Skorn vessels may help spring new combat methods.
- Limited trade features. Previous ship modules are lost rather than scavenged or traded for resources. Also needs a galactic trade or space station of some sort (possibly in the Sigma Sector) where trade rates are a little less unfair and one sided. Can also boast a store to purchase (with resources or other means of currency) specific modules or hire crew members. This might even dare players to plunge into the depths of the Sigma Sector other than to reach Titus Nova in the shortest time possible.

A sequel to the wildly popular and unique Dungeon Defenders game that takes a different direction from its predecessor.
(Note, I originally did not recomment this game, but after hours of playing, I have decided to recommend it.  I'll explain why below.)
Pros
- Personal loot drops make for a more relaxed game where you don't have to constantly keep your eyes out for drops you need (There's no more race to grab the good loot before other players and that is a great design call)
- The classes have some really cool attacks and abilities making each feel unique
- Changes to mana and loot selling have made things much easier, both for sorting through loot and for upgrading it
- Seperation of mana for building and for personal powers was a great call
- Easy group finding system gets you right into the action
- Reputation system makes random players more inclined to be polite
- Synergy system means you can make powerful tower combinations if you have a cooperative team of players.
Cons
- Can't play offline
- Long lags between games.  Due to the fact that a game has no clear leader, everyone has to ready up for the game to progress between levels and after the games.  This doesn't sound too bad, but when people go afk or someone new isn't paying attention, it can end up being 2+ minutes to continue on
- Solo, each classes tower set is lacking (I'll explain more about this below)
- A lack of mana will prevent you from doing much during a combat round (at least at low level)
- The win points and fun-factor strategies to this game aren't as obvious as they were in the original
- Builder specs feel very nerfed thanks to the lack of mana (EDIT: Again, this is only when you don't try to work with the other player's towers)
- Maps are a bit bland, there aren't as many strategic points where you can put towers to have them cover multiple lanes
- Tower synergies are esential to effective play
- Certain specs are almost completely useless right now
- Gating low-level players means that you can't power level your buddies.  It also means that, if your buddies get too far ahead, you can't play with them unless you make a new character.
- Certain monsters outrange your towers.  I'm not sure if this changes at high level, but at low level it's extremely frustrating.  It means that you'll be babysitting your towers instead of being able to place them in different spots and trust them to do their job.
- Due to the fact that you have to babysit your tower clumps, you cannot solo most of the levels (At least as an apprentice)
So I went back and started playing as the monk with a friend who was playing the huntress, and I quickly figured out a pretty devistating combo that made the game much more playable.  I also figured out that one of my mages towers, while not super impressive when combined with his original towers, was extremely effective when combined with one of the monk's auras.
So it seems the devs are really pushing for cooperative gameplay in this one, the game almost feels more like WoW than it does Dungeon Defenders.  To be successful, each player must assume a certain role in their tower construction.  A group of apprentice towers isn't very effective, however an ice tower combined with an electric aura (monk) combined with a water geyser (hunter) is devastating.  The concept is fun when it works out, the big problem is that new players or stubborn players will often build whatever they want, effectively lowering your chances of success.  I feel like this sort of design choice needs to be combined with a matchmaking system that tries to put one of each class in a game together.  (Maybe this is already the design, I don't know, but I was often in games with several members of my own class.)
The good news is, I did start having a lot of fun once I figured out how the devs expected me to play.  However, I had to do a lot of digging to find that answer.  The game needs to guide its new players better so they know what's needed for victory and don't just build whatever, therebye frustrating the other people who are trying to work as a team.
Also, the game needs more towers and more tower synergies.  As of this review, there is one devastating tower/aura/trap combination and everything else is very meh.  Certain towers are very meh and pretty much un-needed.  This needs to be changed so that there are multiple metas (tower building combinations) showing up in the games instead of just 1 or 2.
In closing, the game is fun but very different from the first Dungeon Defenders.  You'll have the most fun when playing with friends, and you may want to watch some videos on how to effectively use your towers depending on your class.
* Update
So the game changes quite a bit at high level.  Once you get your gear established and start the process of farming, you pretty much only need one skilled builder (generally an apprentice or squire) to do the tower setup for the level.  To be honest, it is kind of grindy and not always fun.  And while finding new items to improve your stats can be fun, the actual gameplay isn't.  This may change once more maps are available and harder difficulties are provided.  I'm going to keep my recommendation for now as the game isn't bad and still has potential, but I'm really looking for some new kinds of juicy cooperative gameplay.

Divinity: Developers Cut is a fantastic, under the radar RPG that most people have never heard of. Now, I can't say that you'll pick it up and be immediatley engrossed, it most deafinatley takes some time to get into, but if you're a hardcore RPG gamer, it is absolutely worth your time. When I say hardcore RPG gamer, I mean you've gotta know how to figure things out on your own. Occasionally there is a quest marker, but usually it's just a quest description, the rest you gotta figure out on your own. Some people could be turned off from the crazy difficulty in the beginning, but the only reason it's so hard is because the game demands that you go out and explore, do side quests, and level up, gear up, instead of jumping right into the story. When I started out I went straight for the main story and got anihallated almost instantly by some skeletons. So I went out, explored, killed goblins, did some quests, and about 2 hours in I started the main questline.
The combat is probably the low point of the game, but even then it's not bad, just kind of clunky. You have a pretty standard skill tree but the nice thing is you can branch out and choose whatever skills you want. Wanna be a two handed sword wielding brute that also likes to use healing spells? Go for it. But other than that, it's all pretty basic RPG stuff with some mildly messy hack and slash type combat.
The world is nice and open offering tons of exploration and secrets to be found, just don't expect there to be a huge variety of enemies, because there isn't. As far as I've played, there is really only one real town too. But I dunno if there is another later on.
Now, lets talk about the awesome stuff. If you can give it a chance, about 9-10 hours in the game goes from pretty average but fun, to really really cool. If you can manage to get to the point where you get to own the Battle Tower, things start to look waaaaay up. You have 4 different wings in the Battle Tower that can help you out. You have the Necromancy Chamber which allows you to create your own creature out of dismembered limbs of fallen foes. You have the Alchemy Chamber which allows you to brew potions with probably the most easy to use potion creater ever in a game. Then there is the Enchanting Chamber which allows you to enchant/disenchant armor and weapons. And then there is the Training Chamber which allows you to use gold to buy additional levels for your skills so you can level them past 5. Then aside from the chambers, there is also your team of runners. Runners will go out and find whatever crafting materials you may need. You can also equip them with gear so they don't die while out in the field.
Also awesome is the fact that at the same time you get your battle tower, you also gain the ability to turn into a dragon at will and wreak havoc. If that's not a game seller, I don't know what is.
All in all Divinity 2 is a pretty awesome game. There are some low points like little enemy variety and mildly clunky combat, and the beginning is pretty boring for like the first 2 hours. But if you stick with it (Especially if you make it to the Battle Tower) you will find that it's a pretty rewarding game with lots to keep you busy.
Verdict

I will recommend this game but read carefully!
As always, i read most helpful not recommended reviews and i will try to sum them up here.
My opinion: Huge map is tolerating all the cons of this game. I am just happy about crusing around.
Cons:
Server issues happens sometime and game does not start at all
The wild run expansion changes the game a little bit even you do not have it, but when you see an event and try to enter, message says you have to install wild run. This is ridicuolus.
The concept is wonderful. having a crew to compete against others is what makes racing fun. But there is not much reason to look for players on the map because most online players are busy with PVP events. And the story is not urging you to play as a group. Good concept, bad execution.
PVP events (online races) are open to everyone and if you have not completed most of the game you will most probably be beaten to smoke. Cuz you will not have platinum parts from skills on the map and therefore other players with platinum parts will be flying away from you. This could be understandable, if there were a proper match making algorithm.
Physics are not realistic, mostly like an arcade game.
There are weird glitches like flying to the moon all of a sudden.
And i do not see any other flaws in the game. Here are the pros:
The map is huge and the visuals are aweome. (Some optimizations could be better)
The soundtrack in missions are awesome but they do not play in freeroam. You have to listen to radio in freeroam. Radio contains classical music, ambient music, rap, rock, electornic... A wide range.
Story is easy because most of the time, you are given a car to ride. so you do not have to have an expensive car in your pocket all the time. And when you need one, there are like a hundred of different skill actions which gives you new parts.
Physics are weird for a racing game but just right for an open world game. This is not a simulation. Remember Need for Speed Most Wanted from 2006. The physics reminds me of that game, and it was too an amazing game.
5 different camera angels are all yours to select. Some games has only 2.
Cars are divided into multiple types. So you can go off road with a dirt car or completely out into the wild with a raid car. You can have a hypercar (performance car) to travel in light speed. I actually do not understand the Street cars :D Circuit cars are ideal for point to point agile drivng. How much more diversity do you want?
There is a faction system, which is kind of a mafia wars over the whole map, but it does not much mean to belong to one faction. This is a good idea but no one cares about it.
There are faction races to increase your factions reputation. These races can be less than 10 mins or longer than an hour. There are two particular races, one is like 3.5 hours long dirt race and the other is a 2 hours long performance race. BTW, this was my childhood dream. An hours long race which does not involve looping the same track.
So if you do not mind some server issues, sloppy physics, out of the concept gameplay and some glitches, this game is a great openworld racing game.

Divinity II: If you like RPGs, here's an RPG.
This game will click with some, but it didn't with me. I can't give it a bad review because, quite honestly, I enjoyed it; I just wish I could have enjoyed it more.
The first thing to hit you when you start the game is the talent 'tree.' Or more like a talent wall; there are no pre-requisites asides leveling up, which means you have a lot of freedom in how you want to build your character. At least, you do in the sense that you can pick any talent; cross-picking melee, archery, and magic may not be the best move, but some mixing and matching can be interesting. Great if you like experimentation.
Or, well, until you find some of the broken combos. Find the perfect setup and the game is too easy (to the point where you can one-shot the end-boss). Try to spec to something 'more fun', you'll need a weapon (or two) of the setup you're going for, plus armor that matches, and you aren't guaranteed to like the new spec more. So pretty much like any RPG, right?
The talent tree is a good example of what the rest of the game is; a nerd's wet dream of dragons and magic that would be awesome, but perhaps not executed in the best manner possible. Dialogue choices! Your own fortress! Talents that favor utility over straight combat! Mind-reading NPCs for hidden info! You can turn into an f'in dragon! This game has a crapton of cool mechanics, and it encourages you to use them... except for the part where the cool mechanics fall a bit short in execution.
Yes, you can turn into a dragon, but there are invisible walls everywhere. Yes, there are dialogue choices, but they don't really affect the world. Mind-reading is cool, but without risk; you can tell the importance of the info by the price of the mind-read to determine if you want to delve. The fortress you can eventually own is really just a hub with some utilities (though tastefully made).
And of course, the story is a bit generic. Prophesized hero destined for greatness, as usual. That's not to say the lore surrounding everything is necessarily bad, and there are a lot of details hinting at a well-thought out and coherent universe (and the game occasionally gives you bonuses for reading up on them), but it can feel generic if you're a regular of the RPG genre. Still, I quite like knights and dragons duking it out, so this kind of generic is fine from my point of view, but I just wish it could have done something more.
The world is semi-open; a good number of areas, but a linear progression, sort of like leveling up a character in WoW - you've got a large world, but you can only go X number of places at your current level, and revisiting older places offers no rewards.
Side-quests can be amusing, and the good news is that a lot of them are NOT simply 'go kill X'; there are usually puzzles, traps, and even riddles involved before you can touch target X. Heck, you can even permanently fail some - that kind of pressure is sort of thrilling! That being said, you have to dig for the fun ones - very few would you go back and complete 'just because it is fun.'
If you're really itching for an RPG to play, Divinity 2 isn't bad. You've got to think about gear, specialization, exploration, leveling, and everything else that goes with RPGs. It has everything that goes into an RPG from dialogue choices to various characters to bosses, making it a great game if you "just want an RPG." It just doesn't shine in any one department.
As I said earlier, I can't possibly un-recommend this game since it does everything right and I enjoyed myself. I just wish it could have been more.

Everything is just so cute... On this land where everything and everyone is out to get you. And they will. Time and time again.
Charming, albeit a little bit bland, colorful 2D graphics. Its visual cues are functional, every object and enemy is able to convey what it's able to do, and how you should react.
The levels are quite well crafted, too, specially regarding secrets and different paths. They're not all that obvious, making you feel somewhat clever for finding new things on your first few runs.
(C'mon, even the bloodthirsty butcher looks cute)
The art style is cute, a contradiction in regard to the game brutal difficulty. Yet, it works, and gives that feel that Villager "I will murder you and devour your soul" face gives over at Smash Bros.
It works. The music complements the game well, although I judged it a bit forgettable at first, it grew on me, and I've come to think it matches the tone of the game seamlessly.
The sound effects also work fine, adding to the readability of the graphics.
It's good. It's also quite bland and nothing out of the extraordinary, mind you, but it adds to the charm of the game.
Its main source of inspiration seems to be Ghouls'n Goblins.
The core mechanics of old school platformers is present. You also have a button for each of the characters arms, letting you use one weapon on each hand (I recommend keeping a melee and a ranged one equipped, if available). You can equip three pieces of armor. You can store a few items on your inventory. You can also pickup eggs, which you lose when you're hit and can use to spawn birds that protect you and kill enemies.
Every piece of equipment has a limited number of uses, so you will be managing your resources, trying not to waste anything or else you will be pretty much defenseless. Items can be found on certain (fixed) locations, and can also drop randomly from enemies.
Potions can be used to restore durability and give special traits to items. Weapons will have their kill potential increased, with bonus such as extended reach or piercing trough enemies. Armor will activate additional effects when you're hit, like spawning fireballs. Helmets will also change the birds you can summon by using eggs into another species, for varying effects.
The weapons are: Swords, lances (that really drives the point home on Ghouls'n Goblins as inspiration), magic staves and boomerangs, each with its variations and uses. Pretty much all of them are fun to use.
The items you're able to acquire at the very start of the run depends on "who your father was", you can select it from a few choices or go with "Great Guy" for his profession, which will randomize it. Each time you beat the game with "great guy" for a father, you will collect a white star besides this option, making the game even harder for each star present. If there's a goal on this game besides just having a successful run, it's unlocking "5 stars Great Guy" mode, and then beating it. There are 3 all around classes (Paladin, King and Lancer), 2 pretty different, which translates in unique runs, albeit requiring more strategy and awareness (Shepherd and Alchemist), and Peasant, which transforms the game in one hit kill mode, removing armor spawns and adding difficulty to whoever is masochist enough to try and beat this game with the extra challenge. The classes "Great guy" gives you depending on your difficulty, with the last 3 ones only appearing after clearing this mode a few times.
The levels are linear and the items spawned are fixed. The enemies are randomized, although lightly. Each level, you will see the same enemies every run, although varying in number and spawning locations.
It's straightforward, yet complex enough to be interesting. It gets repetitive, and you might get tired of it before you unlock those 5 stars, but controlling your character is fun.
Its challenging nature gives you that cozy feeling when you succeed.
Controller highly recommended, but not required.
As a somewhat recent update, this game received achievements.
I didn't actually play that much after that, but by looking at the descriptions, I can see pretty much all of them are doable, except for the one that requires you to beat the game with a Peasant as your father...
Just by playing the game you will unlock most of them, but it seems quite hard to 100% it.
It's quite cheap, and gets discounts every once in a while. Also, as of today, it's been featured on five different bundles, which is great.
It's worth full price if you're a fan of the genre and believes you're going to get a few hours of fun out of this title every once in a while.
If you have any interest in the genre, you should at least get it while it's on sale.

That gets old after a while, but you can put the game down and pick it up to play again whenever you're bored. It's also funny to see other people struggling with it.

59/100 (ok)
TLDR
I enjoyed it, after it lowered my expectations.
OVERVIEW
The game can be summarized a mediocre/budget JRPG (with heavily re-used assets and monotonous gameplay) 48% of the time, and the remaining 48% being listening to character interactions 50% of which (so 24% of total) is actually voice acted by the actors, with the remaining 4%  being miscellaneous (like making your character jump while your camera is trying to look up her skirt). It was an overall peaceful and somewhat dull experience, but I did like the relatively calm story which was unprecedented/unusual, & some of the choreography of the animations as well as some of the gimmicks (though I thought the animations were bad), I felt the combat system was deeper than all other other JRPG I played (eternal sonata, quest 64) which is something I enjoyed.
After playing through the entire game, and getting all of the steam achievements (didn't do new game+) I finally feel qualified to make this review.
PLAYSTYLE/PERSPECTIVE
From the perspective of an western gamer, who can only speak/read english.
I played as a semi-completionist, searching through most of the dungeons as they became available, cataloging the monsters and loot drops, but not fretting too much over missed content (locked behind RNG) too much.
I played as a binge player, who would commit entire days to this game.
I actively avoided the free beneficial DLC content (I dislike most/all? DLC on principle) perhaps so I can experience the game as "it was intended" for the average (non steam) buyer.
I came in expecting something of the quality of dota 2, tribes 2, fallout 3, deadcore, perimeter, stalker, delta force 2, halo, the total war series, serious sam, eternal sonata, ETC. Generally things that are AA or AAA quality (sometimes A).
BEGINNING
It was an awful first impression, after even downloading the game I met technical difficulty, where I did not have the required download installed for the game, I came in expecting to be submerged into a pleasant fantasy land of anime girls in a gamey world immediately and conveniently, too bad I had to have my experience halted by this rather rude intrusion of "reality" (the technical problematic lens). Once I got the game to work (by downloading a somewhat vaguely described redistributable on my internet browser), and being relieved, I was met with what I thought was a shockingly bad introduction, where upon my character gets beaten down, but what was bad about it was that the animation quality was surprisingly bad (like a good quality MMD fan animation) and that my character made only 1 pain-scream when being struck, giving the impression of a bad Wii game (might sound small, but it was huge to me). Usually games like this want to leave a good impression, but this one left an awful one, heck, even the game "chex quest" somehow left a better first impression than this game (and that game literally came out of my cereal box). I was planning to get this game refunded during this disappointing phase, but knowing I had 2 hours to "demo" the game before steam refunds were disabled, I continued until I got a better look at the game. In a way, it is quite shocking that a game like this would leave such a bad impression so quickly, as if they aren't aware that there is a refund policy in place.
BEGINNING 2
In a bit of a haze, I proceeded in the game, expecting further disappointments, which showed rather quickly when I found my first segment of storytelling that lacked voice acting, me coming from games like fallout 3, skyrim, and eternal sonata expected that all or most of the lines displayed in the chat box would be uttered by some voice actor, but rather, only about 50% of the main story is voiced, and only about 20% of sidequests (if any) were voiced, I was again further negatively surprised, but this defect was somewhat beneficial/mitigated; as the lack of the voice acting let me fill in the voice acting with my imagination (such as replacing some voices with voices from other games, usually inappropriately), and in a way this somewhat added to my experience. Though, I doubt others would rise to this "challenge", and is still a fault to be considered, I really would have preferred a 60-70% voice acting on the story dialog, but sadly, it was not the case.
There were 2 notable flaws in the game that left somewhat lasting impression which is the dominatrix's lost 3 second static pose when she "transforms into existence" with bad english lip-syncing, and a camera that clips through her segmented sword, and the playstation character's sometimes cringe-worthy "tryhard" deep voice, though I was fond of some of the defects (tryhard voice).
MIDDLE/LATE
The middle of the game was perhaps the best enjoyed part of it, after I had my expectations passively beaten down my the overall quality, and this was a time of discovery. I really started to get into the more difficult content, and I started to notice some of the complexities of the combat system, like how one might want to align turns to initiate a guard break, and use ultimates, and typically having enough complexity to cause me to delay and think what action to do sometimes, and with enough complexity to prevent it from getting too formulaic too quickly, (though formulas are naturally developed) in fact, this would be the most tactically deep JRPG I have played, and I enjoyed it, though the system tends to degrade later on and problems started to crop up (formulas were developed), since I was playing as a semi-completionist, I would do dungeons, but most of the dungeons would only have 1 formulaic way of "clearing them"; 1. beat each enemy until it dropped all of it's items, 2, fight the boss 1-3 times, which typically require 1 of 3 strategies with some permutations (1. power attack spam/use ultimates, for the weakest bosses, 2. Buff your characters, break guard/weaken enemies, then kill with ultimate, 3. buff, weaken guard, buff, align turns (making it so that most of your characters will be able to attack before the bosses turn), use ultimates, then finish off.), 3. Run through the dungeon again, ignoring the enemies, and headbutting the camouflaged boxes so that you can better "catalog" the items that come out of them (because it tends to be random). Then rinse/repeat for every other dungeon you unlock, skipping step 1 for upgraded dungeons that recycle enemies. In a way, step 3 was relaxing, (after I got the upgrade that trivializes finding the boxes but hellish before) so it wasn't that bad. But the boss fight distinctly lacked variety in methodologies to beat, there were some helpful differences such as the 7 elite boss type, and the boss with disabling helpers, but much too rare to be really helpful (about 4% are different), which is surprising, I'd think that more exotic bosses would be easy to implement. There is also a minor concern of stats, there is no explanation of them, while some stats can largely be figured out (like strength being attack power) some can be mistaken for others, one could think that vitality is related to HP amount instead of it functioning as "armor" or "men" (mental?) having some affect on SP(mana) regeneration instead of it being "magic armor", this is largely irrelevant since you cannot really "build" characters to have extreme stat imbalances and/or character specialties, and how the game is generally very easy, (even going so far as to send some story bosses in waves, instead all at once even though it is explicit that the bosses are in a group) thus not really requiring understanding of the stats, but another rather small deficiency.
Due to the character limit, you will need to search the last 3 pages of the comments to find the remainder of the review.

I am writing this review as someone who played this game first from it's series so I cannot speak for fans of the first.
If you can get in the mentality that you will probably die a lot and a few of those times you will also probably lose a decent chunk of souls ( both level-up and shop currency ) then you can have a great time with this game.
It isn't quite as hard as many may boast since patience and attention to details can save you a lot of headache but it still way ahead of other action rpgs in which you might never die.
The combat is very different than other RPGs as well in that your ability to attack or dodge ( stamina ) is really limited but regenerates very fast when you aren't doing anything. And getting hit even by grunts hurts a lot. Thus a tactical approach is required many times and a simple misstep and aggroing several enemies can easily get you killed.
Still even though I like the game very much it isn't perfect and I have a few complaints, most of them can be put down to taste but still.
Pvping can be somewhat avoided but it can be really costly to do so and a lot of the times might not be worth using the consumable to do so. Thus you can get ganked by players that generally seem better prepared and unless another consumable is used they will be ignored by enemies putting you at a major disadvantage.
Also because of the fact that you lose all souls on you when dying and dying again makes the previous drop of yours vanish, invading players can go from a simple annoyance to rage-quitting frustration when you lose a significant amount of souls.
While most enemies and bosses have varying degrees of difficulty between them there are a few bosses in particular that seem intentionally designate as difficulty spikes and you will spend way more time on those than anything else in the game if you want to solo them.
And finally the game really doesn't go into specifics. Like how weight actually interacts with dodge rolls, how damage is calculated, the fact that infused weapons even when they have the same grade of scaling don't scale as well as natural elemental weapons and so on. Trips to the wiki and googling will almost be required for anyone trying to finish it.

Played the GOG version a lot before I also bought the Steam version so I have around 14 more hours than it says I do. Basically, this game is FUN. It might not be perfect, but it does a great job at entertaining.
+ The game is fun as hell, the levels mostly varied, and things remain largely fresh for a lot of the time.
+ It's an Action RPG, best played with a Controller (from my perspective) but KB+M is just as good. There aren't too many good ARPGs around these days.
+ The weapons are interesting and all different, especially some of the late-game weapons.
+ VV is responsive and easy to play with, you aren't likely to die because you tripped over your own feet
+ Did I mention this game is fun? Imagine Diablo's hack-n-slash, except each button press is a single attack instead of having to click and hold to automatically attack until the enemy is dead. Think Isometric God of War.
+ Geralt of Rivia is in it. Kinda.
- The game, however, can be boring in parts. You go through enemy after enemy after enemy and they never seem to stop. The most annoying thing? Some of them require a critical hit to die properly; if they're just hit normally, they break apart and come back together again as good as new, so they need to be killed again (although a normal hit will do it that time). There's no way to guarantee the final blow will be critical, although you can improve your chances of a critical several ways.
- It's less RPG than I'd like. Yes, a deck of cards can be used to increase percentages: Damage, Crit Hit chance, Defense, etc. and outfits act slightly differently (your "mana" for Demon Powers is built up either by Critical hits, taking damage, or over time by itself depending on which outfit you choose). Pick the wrong outfit, and there's no changing your mind 10 minutes later - you're stuck with it for a long time. The problem is there really is no traditional skill progression so to speak, it's all just increased arbitrarily by pickups.
- I don't find Demon Powers all that useful, at least not until they're upgraded significantly. I also wish weapons were balanced differently: You can hit multiple enemies with a sword or hammer, but a shotgun? Nope, not unless it's using one of its "Special abilities".
All in all, great game, I highly recommend you give it a go, it's fun to pass some time with and I can guarantee you'll be coming back to it for a long time to come.

I also expect that the finished version of the game will have a tutorial and a working help button(has a help button now-f1-but its not functional). Outlast is a pretty decent horror game hampered by some issues that stop it from being brown trousers excellence.  The lack of combat and regular chases can be tense, the sheer darkness of the environment and brilliant sound engineering create a great atmosphere, and the reliance on batteries is pretty well done (I never ran out of them and made an effort to find as many as possible, but during the points where it was almost all darkness I ran worryingly low as the game seems to be be stingy with them when you need them most).  Some of the regular characters like The Twins are actually quite interesting too, which can make chases feel a little bit more interesting when you know the people chasing you are butt naked and want your tongue and liver.
However the AI is somewhat frustrating and can be rather predictable, both of which take away from the tension.  If you hide in a locker you can ALWAYS bet the enemy, assuming they didn't see you, will check the locker next to you then give up (only once did they check the right one on my playthrough and I'm pretty sure they saw me go in).  It's also annoying they seem to only patrol the route you need to go, rather than the entire area or where they last saw you, even if they didn't see you move there, which quite often makes it incredilbly difficult to sneak by through certain corridors where the option of stealth would be more fun to try an enact.  It therefore ends up easier to just run round the area slamming doors in their face to delay them while you look for the exit, which isn't very scary or well designed.  The game also has an interesting setup and mysterious surrounding, and then as you uncover more and more information the plot becomes generic and really rather lazy.  It ends up being one of the most cliched explanations in video games or films or whatever whenever spooky♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down.  Furthermore, other than collectable documents which aren't entirely interesting, there isn't much replay value either, but that tends to be expected of more linear horror titles.  It's not an incredibly long game, I finished it in 4 hours, but I feel it's an ok length as the gameplay isn't varied enough to remain interesting for much longer than that.
Fortunately the gameplay overall is interesting enough, and it does so much of the horror aspect of the game correctly it's well worth picking up if horror games rub you up the right way.

A lot of this review sounds  negative, so I'll start straight away with TL;DR... It's fun, and it's going to get more fun. Buy it.
If you've got this far, however, I'll break down the bits I didn't like so much.
Yeah... it's a poor-man's FTL with better graphics. It has combat which looks prettier, but ultimately isn't quite so engaging.
In FTL, you are basically at each decision-point in moments. In ITS you have to point your ship in the right direction and wait a while.   Frantic it is not. Atmospheric, it is.
Occasionally en-route you'll be told something is happening which needs attention, and you assign a crewmember to fix it. Essentially, this takes them out of the command pool, and you might find you wish you hadn't assigned your pilot to sanitary clean-up duty when all hell breaks loose.
Combat is basically FTL without the fun weaponry and targeting.
Your enemy charges a red, yellow or blue weapon... you make sure your shields match to limit damage.
When firing your own weapons, make sure they're a different colour to the enemy shields.
Rinse and repeat.
When you get to where you're supposed to be, the game basically whimpers to a halt and tells you how much you earned. No 'boss-fight' or challenge to face. It felt a bit flat, to be honest.
Don't get me wrong, I think FTL went too far in the other direction... but ITS had nothing.
The main way of getting resources is to mine planets. This feels a bit place-holder. You essentially move a little icon left and right to collect resources of different types. I would really love it if this was improved. Even if it's just a graphical overhaul. That way I don't sit there wondering if I've just paid NZ$17 for something out of the 1980s.
Ship customisation is basically limited to what resources your modules use. You can swap out your magnesium-guzzling engines for hydrogen engines, for example. They might go a little faster. Or not.
I like it though. On the understanding that it's Early Access and that I haven't put a great many hours into it, it's comfortably diverting.  There are a few things I'd like to see improved though:
1. Procedural universe.  At the moment, it isn't.
2. More things to do. Or at-least, more than just dragging crew into "Fix It" slots.
3. A better 'end-game'.
4. More ship customisation.
5. Mining. Fix mining. Please.
6. More captains-chair engagement.  There's so much potential there for crew interaction.
I have high hopes for this one, and - honestly - think it's probably worth taking the punt and putting some money into it. If it gets as good as FTL... and I think the potential is well and truly there... then it's going to be a winner.
It's playable and fun now - with the caveats above - but the potential here is for an amazing piece of kit, and I really am looking forward to it.

TLDR; Excellent visuals, great combination of a Star Trek Sim and FTL: Faster Than Light, Solid Core gameplay IDEAS but balance/execution is lacking. For $20, I’d wait. Find it on sale or wait until the content increases.
At the very beginning I was slightly put off by the character portraits, they seemed like stickers plopped on to the uniforms and backgrounds. The second I got into the game and took a look around I quickly changed my tune. All of the stellar objects (planets, asteroids ect…) look stunning. Solar flares in-circling the stars, the surface of the planets well detailed and each one had its own character to it. The Command Chair view also has a ton of high points, if you ignore the character models and animations. The animations for the different command functions and even the simplified city all look superb. I can forgive the repeated characters (The command deck girls all look pretty much the same) I just hope they look to improve those in the future because against the rest of the game, it seems a tad out of place.
You’re the last hope of humanity running from the Scorn, your typical nomadic, devour everything in their path alien species. Pretty simple and not much explanation behind it.
The core of the gameplay is fairly solid. Combat is fun and the exploration side has its strong points, but the UI and its responsiveness hurts me. Sometimes it seems that what I click on doesn’t register or does slowly. Assigning crew can be a bit of a learning curve for the first few times, and all the small numbers so close to one another can send your head into a spin. One feature I’d love is while assigned to a position, the relative skill number would appear alongside the name of the skill.
The Combat itself is fun and can be intense for the first play through or two until you start to get the hang of it, and even then it has its moments of excitement as you barely bring up shields in time or duck out of the way of a laser. Audio ques are well done, mostly on point and once you learn them, have a huge part in correctly defending yourself. The issue lies in variation, it turns into the same fight over and over again. A simple strategy emerges and the skill cap is frankly quite low. You may fight against 4-5 different ships but they all are fought the same way, by the end of the third play through I was taking almost no damage verses single combatants and maybe one shot when faced against two of them, even when I finally got a 3 ship encounter, I took maybe 3 hits. My request? Toss in some variation in strategy, in enemy modules or even change up the playing field, maybe an asteroid field could provide evading ships even better defenses? Not sure about how but I know a larger variation is needed or else it becomes stale quickly.
I love the resource management, even if it seems VERY overwhelming at first, a full tutorial would go a long way. Finding the correction combination of modules that suits your resource needs is a fun way to change up how you play and can decide if you really are going to stop at the planet or just book it to the next sector. The only complaint I have is the numbers on the civilization side aren’t always very clear, the biggest one being the growth stat. I have a growth of .9%! Okay, is that .9% of my population every day? Week? Month?? None seem to be quite right. Or is it not supposed to be a %, and it’s just + .9 population every day? This last one seems to be the case, but it took until my third play through to come to that conclusion.
To round things off, I love how the game makes you work for your victories, or at least seem like it. I played three runs on normal (each run seems to last 3-4 hours with the slower, more resource efficient engine) and I felt like I earned the two victories I got. I just want a climax, both times I pretty much coasted into the finish line with nothing stopping me (Abit, the second time I was bleeding population with 0 food left :D).
Overall, a great game for someone like me who is absolutely obsessed with space exploration and sim games, the average person might want to wait a bit longer, or pick it up for a few play throughs and come back later when the game receives more content. If you enjoyed FTL: Faster Than Light and have always dreamed of being the next Kirk or Picard, this is a must pick up.

I thought the doc did a good job of presenting a decent range with regards to those involved in the more shadier side of cyber activity in Romania, from (what some might consider a lowly) ebay scammer, to a man on the hunt for truth.
Personally, I wasn't getting the 'Norton ad' vibes which others have eluded to, but on reflection I can see how it may have come across like that, even though I don't recall coming across any actual product placement save for the brand itself.
As it was less than 20 minutes in length, one can't expect too much in the way of in-depth detail, and also I guess it's worth pointing out that given the nature of the doc, there probably wouldn't be too many people willing to come forward with anything to back up their claims anyway, it would be stupid. Even so, I kind of liked the dark tone (literally and figuratively), although it was perhaps a little overdone.

If you are a fan of Heroes III or Heroes V, DO NOT BUY.
Pros: Very nice graphics, good spread of decent units. A few nice concepts, but not well executed. Story isn't bad, though let down by horrid voice acting. Seriously, King's Bounty had better voice acting. Destiny stuff is a neat idea, though all of the extra heroes were free for me, maybe from DLC? The music is mostly ripped off from HOMM5 and reochestrated, so it's alright. I do like the idea that your hero can go on any allied turn instead of having to wait for a specific place in the initiative. Also, when you recruit from a town, It automatically recruits from surrounding structures and other forts etc. No wait time, the troops are just there (by magic I assume). Saves time on re-arming, even if it makes no damn sense.
Cons: HOLY CRAP IS THE VOICE ACTING BAD. Necromancy is nerfed to uselessness, The other racial abilities are frankly meh, All heroes have all of the same abilities to pick from, and spells are just abilities. You get to pick one per level essentially, and a lot of the core spells aren't there (No summoning to speak of, no raise dead, almost no direct damage spells.) Nice 3D rendered towns like HOMM5 you can circle around in? Nope! Static images with overlays. Also, the interface overlay crawls, even if the rest of the game runs great (AMD quad core, Geforce 560)
The real shame is the sheer homoginization of the play styles accross races. Since all heroes have the same ability access and trees, you just pick the tactic you like and then hang some set dressing on it by picking a race. Literally no other flavor involved.
The units are a nice mix, but they all are roughly the same at each tier. Also the AI is balls. Aims for highest tier, or ranged and ignores everything else. Sieges are about as challenging as water baloon fights.
Also adds in the idea of territory control, which is kind of nice and kind of dumb. To control a mine or sawmill etc, you have to control the fort or town it is in the territory of. You don't get any resources from it unless your hero is parked on it otherwise it continues pumping to the local town as normal. This would be neat if you could at least stop production from it by attacking it and sacking it, thus denying resources, but no, the moment you leave it it just reverts back. So again, cool idea, with a flaw in execution.
Overall, if I had played a demo of this game, I would not have bought it. I payed $10 on the autumn sale and uninstalled it within 24 hours, and wish I had my $10 back.

Third person action RPGs are my favorite genre, and I can't believe I missed out on this for so long. The world, its lore and characters, are just so interesting while the combat strung it all together so nicely. As a ranger I would go around launching exploding arrows at groups of enemies while my undead summon pulled aggro. But there was also a lot of moving around and dodging enemy projectiles as well. Lengthy stuns and instantaneous flinch attacks can make fights pretty frustrating, though. And then there is the dragon combat. You fly around hitting towers and other flyers with your fire breath and fireball attacks for the most part. You can't attack or even see ground units which means when you switch back to human form you can drop into the middle of a group of enemies and not even realise it till you're dead. Theres not much else I can say about it other than it makes for a nice change of pace. Overall, there are a lot of side quests and a lot of different places to explore. There weren't many variations on the dungeons, but they never got stale. If you're a fan of the genre I don't see how you could be dissapointed with this game.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I have 3 Jets one Euro jet that will do 1800 mph and 12,000 ft above sea level, my stealth fighter (an F-22 with a working missle bay that holds up to 10 missles or even a spare fuel tank) ... my stealth fighter is actually too smooth and I have had trouble getting air to go into the vents at higher altitudes where the air is thiner thus the F-22 goes only 1300 mph and flies up to 65,000 feet before losing too much thrust to maintain stable flight. I also have an American style super fighter that is just a little bit slower than the Euro fighter both would make an amzing match for each other in real life and it's awesome that the game allows you to put your planes under AI control and the AI will actully fight back, although right now there is now difficulty setting for AI so if you give them a decent plane with the right missles they will kill you and you them since missles are very very accurate in this game.
Pros;
Build your own planes, Jets, VTOLS, even cars, helicopters and boats!
Real life physics are very reward as you learn to overcumb the real life obsticles of flying
Map is very large with 3 Biomes on 4 main islands
Easy basic tools for starting out and advanced tools for as you progress
The Challenge mode is pretty cool
Cons;
Some physics seem stiff and springy while others seem weak and washy, yaw being the worst.
The map is mostly water with most of the land being bare, no rocks no trees and few buildings.
No online multi player mode only single player against the AI.
there is very lil reward in completing challenges and you don't even need to build your own plane you can use premade ones to complete the challenges with no added bonus for if you did it with your own original build.
Overall a very fun game for those who like airplanes and have always wanted to build their own. If you just would like to fly tho and you are looking for a mission based game this is not it. I have spent 80% of my game time building and tweeking my planes 19% of the time testing the planes and 1% of the time actually playing missions or completing challenges. I would like to see that 1% grow as I don't always want to build I would like to fly more missions but for now it is what it is.

I bought this game expecting a rogue-like, but the only roguelike element it has is permadeath. Levels are not random, and there are not many powerups. This is a challenging classic platformer (as was common in the NES days).
That said, if you like classic platformers this one is not bad.
All equipment has a limited number of uses. All weapons and armor collapse and break after it is used 1-4 times. Oils are found occasionally, and can be used to fully repair an armor or weapon while at the same time converting it into another type of armor or weapon.
Levels are linear and the game is fairly short. There are a number of character classes which differ only in their starting equipment, and there is some replayability to be had in beating the game with different classes.
You won't get many hours of entertainment with this, but it's brief and enjoyable fun and the price is right.

You will come to fear the word "buddy". It will send you running for shelter under a bed, or sprinting down a hall. It will give you nightmares of a madman in a leather apron and nothing else, chasing you with bone shears. And you'll record it all, along with your screams, on a video camera.
Some very clever minds clearly went into Outlast. The Production values are incredible. Serious thought went into the level design, and as a result Mount Massive Asylum feels like a real place with an organic layout. This dedication spills into the characters and the presentation as well. The story has few real cutscenes (only three to speak of), and feels very immersive as a result. The story plays out around Miles the protagonist, and as a result missing a horror moment is almost worse. It becomes something glimpsed out of the corner of the eye, a nightmare that hides in your mind.
That's ultimately the game's greatest strength. Only late in the game are the monsters really exposed to your eyes for any length. Their design is...well, it's fine. But it will never measure up to what we imagine it to be. Fortunately, the game gives you plenty of time to mess with your own head. There's no way to fight back, the only options are to run for your life or hide.
Technically, everything serves these two choices. You can peek around corners, you can find batteries to help you find your way in the dark.  It's a well crafted experience.
Which is why the story is such a crying shame. Nazi mysticism, pseudo techno babble, and an asylum for a setting all hold the game back. Parts of it hold up, especially anything to do with "dr." Trager, but overall the story is disappointing and ends abruptly. Additionally, one glimpse of the monsters does a lot to diminish their scares. Yet, it feels like Red Barrel is just finding their feet. I can't wait to see what they make next. Give it a run through, it'll be worth the shrieks.

Outright this game is very enjoyable.  That said, after 10-20 hours of playing and generally figuring things out you'll start to feel an itch.
This game does the fundamentals very well, but after getting to know it the "itch" becomes things it could do better or expand on.  You start wanting more things to build, more oddities that can occur, etc..  You start thinking "boy I wish there were more occupational buildings I could make!" and "I wish I could do something with this lake...it's just there taking up a ton of space".  On the other hand, you start encountering little gripes like "Why are my villagers so damn dumb?  Use the roads I built you fools!" or "Why are workers carrying stuff to the storages on the opposite end of the map when there none of the others are full?"  However, this is a great problem to have in general as it gives some indication of direction for later efforts (both by community and dev).
Very recommended for people like me who can spend an entire weekend day playing and even for those with busy daily lives who may not be able to dedicate more than maybe an hour in a sitting.  The really hard part for both types of players is prying yourself away from it to do things that are necessary...like eating and sleeping.

PROS: Napoleon: Total War is a very enjoyable game and has the advantage in both battle interactivity and historical interest. Multiple historical generals are available in battle mode for each side (such as Duke of Wellington for England, Napoleon for France, von Blucher for Prussia, etc.), and they all have their own experience levels (Napoleon has more stars and is able to inspire troops better than Soult). Plus, these generals are able to inspire nearby units and rally troops during the intense moments of battle. They also included special units in the limited edition (which I think is out now) such as the Black Watch and the 47th Czech Regiment. Even without the special units of the Limited Edition, there are more special units in Napoleon: Total War such as Silesian Shuetsen sharpshooters for Prussia and grenadiers. Napoleon Total War also allows you to give special orders to units for a limited time such as commanding cannons to barrage enemies or have increased accuracy. There are also more historical battles in Napoleon Total War, and they give you the option to either play the large, full-scale campaign, or play mini-campaigns of Napoleon's conquests. The campaigns are: Tutorial (this leads you through Napoleon's life story and teaches you how to play campaigns), Italy, Egypt, Europe, and I think the last one is Waterloo. There is also an expansion pack for the Peninsular Campaign. These campaigns have their own movies and so do the battles. If you're not a big Campaign player, they also included Napoleon's largest battles starting at Lodi and going to Waterloo. So, it gives a great historical feel. Plus, for naval encounters, Steamships and Ironclads are available.
CONS: Napoleon Total War is also lacking in some large areas: there are fewer playable nations (only allowing you to play as France, England, Prussia, Austria, Russia, and Spain with the expansion pack.), and the world map is significantly smaller, only including Europe and North Africa.

AN IMMERSIVE SPACE SURVIVAL EXPERIENCE
Into The Stars puts you in control of a spaceship and its crew as you lead the last vestiges of humanity from its destroyed planet in search of a new home. Faced with a series of tough survival decisions you'll constantly be on the run from the mass-murdering alien Skorn, you'll be fighting them off when you have no other option, and you'll be scrounging for every last resource you can get your hands on to survive and complete your journey.
I'll start the actual review by saying that I'm new to this genre. I've never played FTL, and quite a few of the negative reviews seem to be here because people are comparing Into The Stars to FTL. Sadly, ITS appears to be losing the intergalactic battle.
However, I have played almost 14 hours of Into The Stars in addition to the 5 or so I must have played at a friend's house on their Steam account before I rushed home to buy my own copy.
Even though I'm new to this type of game (feel free to decide for yourself how valid this review is) I can definitely recommend Into The Stars. Here's why:
PROS
- Good graphics, excellent sound effects, and wonderful ambient music that immerse you in  an outer space race for survival. Immersing the player in the game world is the most crucial aspect of a game, and Fugitive Games have definitely succeeded in this area.
- A constant pressuring feeling that you’re always fleeing from a mass-murdering, evil race of aliens due to your onboard AI alerts and the Skorn patrol ships you can see scouting the sectors of space.
- Excellent starting customisation options for your ship, your cargo, and your crew that can make a big difference to your survival success.
- A surprisingly fun mining mini-game.
- A good number of very interesting ship upgrades to be found by risking the completion of shuttle missions. Such upgrades could include a faster engine, stronger shields, or a module that increases the effiency of your life support system thus making your oxygen supplies last longer.
- Every decision you make could affect your survival. Staying on a planet a little while longer to mine for essential oxygen could allow the Skorn to find and destroy you. You have to weigh up every decision.
- Very polished for an early access title.
- Combat is simple but good fun and challenging.
CONS
- With a relatively small map, and no apparent randomisation of stars and planets, the replay value is good, but not great.
- The game does need more breadth and depth to create longer lasting appeal for players.
- Still has quite a few bugs, none that were game-breaking (at least not in my experience), but this is to be expected from early access.
On a final note, yes, the combat can be very hard and even very unfair - especially towards the start of the game. To get around this you need to train up your engineers so that their shooting becomes more accurate (I've had late game engineers who've almost never missed), and you need to avoid large fights. So in other words, flee an area as soon as you're given a yellow alert, and avoid Skorn patrol ships like the plague.
***18th December 2015 UPDATE***
-The devs have really listened to their fans and have now made it possible for the enemy ships to miss when shooting at your ship. Before, they had a 100% success rate of hitting you.
-The game now has an evade (dodge) feature that allows you to move out of the way of all incoming fire. This is especially useful if different Skorn ships are attacking you with different colour-coded weapons at the same time (your shields can block only one colour-code at a time).
-To offset these two new ways of making combat fairer on the player, Skorn ships have a new weapon. This is a very powerful charged laser attack for which you get plenty of warning. The only way to avoid taking damage from this devastating weapon is to use the game's new evade feature.
As always, leave any questions below and I'll get back to you.

Okay now it's been awhile since I've written a review (previously under the name The Gamer Gourmet) so bare with me.
Now this game has a bit of history with me.  I was one of the unfortunate ones who were getting stuck behind the Nebraska error. After some attempts I requested a refund. Then an update came out. Loving what I had been seeing, I chanced getting it again. Still prevented by the error :(.
Some time passed and a work-around came about involving an update to WMSIE. Viola it worked!!
I was beyond jazzed because everything I read, saw, heard was exactly the game I felt I needed to stave off the fiend until No Mans Sky comes out. time for the nitty gritty.
The game is as described. A combination of Bridge Commander, FTL, and several other space born titles. At first it can feel over whelming. LOTS of details.
"Like being on a date with a Librarian, who also is chocolate for the eyes"
The setup is a big deal as if effects the rest of your ability to survive in the vastness of space. Crew finding is relatively easy, able to sort them by highest rating in their fields and found the crew set up the easiest, although not quite sure of the necessity of a toughness trait, often ignoring it to double up on engineers.
The hardest (or I should say toughest choice) was the modules. While the urge to get modules that use the same resources, you will discover certain planets can only be mined for specific ones...in  other words, your Ark maybe based around a lot of CO2 usage but find a planet that contains none.
This is usually the first error I can see made during the first attempt at playing
The difficulties however are easily tempered through multiple plays....but still can seem overwhelming at first.
Once past the multiple set up screens you are greeted with a beautiful scenery of planets, asteroids, suns and all sorts of anomalies. The feeling of being able to go anywhere is amazing.  The controls are simple, up down left right roll.
The game is a graphical beast for sure. The suns have solar flares, the planets have rings of asteroids, there's even half cracked destroyed planets frozen in time.
Exploring and taking int eh sights is an easy thing to get lost in immediately in this game. The urge to push on is apparent right off the bat, JUST to see more space related eye candy.
But then comes the first 'break' from this joy. The constant pursuit by the main enemy race in the game. The Skorn. Now I understand the desire to have this element. It gives a constant urgency to keep mushing on. It did however leave me annoyed often when trying to explore a new area, just to find I am getting tracked before even finding anything. BUT its a minor issue and like I said, keeps the constant feeling of 'keep on pushing on', which does force a positive need to progress forward whether u want to or not.
The space battles are my biggest frown. Often the same battle consisting of 1-3 enemy ships which pretty much may vary in design, but still consist of the same. Now I haven't indulged the game 100% so I am unsure if any other enemy but the Skorn fight you, but have played enough to be able to say I'm pretty sure you don't. This leaves a bitter lack of creativity int he battles. You get into a battle, try to disable a ships weapons, finish them off repeat if more ships. Often battles being purely determined on the ability to be lucky, and your shots come in contact with their targets. However once 'experienced' these battles often become routine, and make little impact other than slowing you down some OR rarely sometimes the rewards from such giving a much needed resource boost. At first, a nice mechanic to the game but ultimately becoming a 'sigh' moment.
This would be, as the developer, my primary focus when it comes to altering, upgrading, altering the game. More alien vessels to combat, more options in combat, howabout the simple ability to flee would be nice sometimes, even a boarding ability. Often the battles fall on the same 3 basic principles. Phasers, torpedoes, shields. It becomes paper rock scissor type combat. It is attempted to be deeper through a color coordinated battle scheme (red shields absorb red weapons etc) but this falls kinda flat and small enhancement to a drab combat system. It needs to be deeper, enhanced someway, perhaps some form of mini-game to determine effectiveness, accuracy, rate of fire etc. It simply needs to be more in depth especially being 1/3 of the games entertainment.
Now aside form combat the games meat and potatoes come from surviving. Managing resources, and finding the methods to go from one end to the other in the galaxy. The sites again, are amazing. The aura, and feel of different parts and lighting effects give a sensed of dream like state, as you approach a sector of random marvel.
however with the grandness that comes with it, multiple plays lead to a 'almost cramped feeling'> the galaxy is universal, each play has the same layout. While it has TONS of sights, playing many play through's makes even this large galaxy seem small. BUT even so, the sights and number of anomalies leave more to discover even after my 15th play.
The galaxy is large and the limitations of randomness, are only enhanced by an obvious attention to detail. Random alien vessels litter the galaxy but often only provide a lackluster trading opportunity. This was quite disappointing as I was hoping to combat some of the other vessels and they end up being a minor 'mix' in the formula. Forgettable at worse, minor help at best. It would be nice if the event offered more, like a side mission or something.
Planetary exploration is descent distraction in the game. Especially when fighting to survive with moments when low on resources, like those that provide food or air, or fuel. Most the time these visits to planets involve drilling for resources which is based around a mini game of guiding a 2d drill into the ground going over the resource squares you need. A simple mechanic but often entertaining as when in a hurry find yourself eager to go fast but with haste often find yourself hitting the 'bad squares' that stop the drilling altogether. This can be frustrating when dealing with an impending patrol and a dire need for fuel/air/food necessity. BUT however is tempered with the simple mechanic the more u drill the easier the drilling becomes...with more risk comes greater reward. And after a few ship upgrades the battles become relatively easy so the desire to suck as much resources is an often tease....stockpile and fight, or get a quick fix and flee.....
Now throughout your travels you will often have ship born emergencies. Stuff from a random viral outbreak, to space raccoon's making a mess. These missions are relatively handled the same way. Assign a crew member to it, depending their level in the particular skill required depends on the rate they finish the objective. A past time event usually only causing issues when finding yourself with many on board ship issues at once and suddenly being attacked as each device needs a crew member to work (phasers, shields, missiles, medical). Not really a major feature but does keep you micro managing things.
For the price the game is worth it. There's many more features but not enough space to list them. You love space games, you will love this game. With its flaws, still is a gem that needs some more polish!

It was fun to get into despite the lack of info or interface that would explain how squad exp works or what career points are good for and so forth. Some silly things I noticed right away with the system and UI that are noticeable.
-Tooltips vanish right after you mouse over things and require you to click them over and over.
-You cant see soldier upgrades because the upgrade menu is obscured with text blocking its view.
-Creating a squad, you cant assume any position in your own squad except leader until you join a battle. It took until around 9 hours of gameplay before i was even able to try being a sniper without combing other squads for this reason.
The gameplay is simple and gritty, shots kill with 1 hit usually, as they should and there arnt any extra tasks or objectives except the all important trench.  There is nothing to interact with on the maps (you wont be digging your own trench or putting up sandbags) and you cant help people that are dying or injured so its all about taking that ground and moving forward. The guns are nice and the gameplay itself is what you should expect however the problems that start to present themselves after you get the feel for things take the fun out of it unless you learn to avoid/abuse the problems that seem persistent in every match or battlefield.
-Thrown grenades can glitch and go at different angle than where your looking/throwing.
-No ammo replenishment, what you spawn with is all you get, ever. 1/2 the time you cant tell if your shooting a helmet or a rock so with no way to replenish ammo it restricts your ability to give suppression fire or probe spots you suspect enemies might be.
-Falling through the ground into the abyss (you do not clip through teammates so its possible to get shoved into abyss).
-bullets hit around corners or seem to have some strange AoE where they hit. Shoot into empty space and score a hit.
-conversely bullets get stopped by invisible hitboxes that seem to stretch beyond the objects visual appearance and sure-shots are stopped by outstretched level geometry or a wire post nub.
Personally I could overlook all of that since the game itself feels good to play (if you like this kinda battle). The fun is diminished further however by the fact that there are few maps and the max battle size is only 32 or 16v16 at best. Once you become familiar with these linear maps, the battlefield becomes a turkey-shoot. This makes it possible to hide someplace where you cannot be observed but are able to kill with impunity by shooting through cover into areas without needing real visual contact with enemies. Too often matches will become a chore or a waiting simulator and that is still considering that the nature of this kinda game demands lots of deaths, possibly all at the hands of 1 machine gunner but it doesnt work well with only 32 and/or 16 per side max. I cant offer any clever solutions despite my criticism but I would have at least thrown in some fluffer ai soldiers to fight alongside or something if 16v16 is the best it gets.

This is an excellent game, defnitely one of the best single player action RPGs out there. There is SO MUCH content, too! It's not an open world/sandbox game, but rather sets the player on a specific path with the option of doing many side quests. It's old school in that it often requires intution, guessing and puzzle solving on the part of the player. It doesn't hold your hand like some games do, but does point you in the right direction and leave you to find the secrets for yourself.
What I like most about this game is that you have a completely open character build - you can put points in any tree at any time and create a hybrid class, though I find that picking a class and sticking with it is a highly effective playstyle.
What sets Divinity II apart from many other games of its ilk is that you gain the ability to transform into a Dragon and fly through the game world. It is great fun to fly around the valley battling airborne foes and destroying enemy structures, then turning back into a human to enjoy the fast paced action/rpg combat.
The game does have a handful of bugs and glitches that were never worked out. A handful of side quests are not possible to complete and others can accidentally be restarted, but it is not game-breaking. Given how good the rest of the game is, it is a minor issue at best.
This is defintely an underappreciated gem and I strongly recommend it to anyone who enjoys RPGs like Dragon Age, Mass Effect or Neverwinter Nights.

First of all, this is a very good game and at version 0.03 it is ready and complete. I can say many good things about it, but only thing I cannot do is recommend it. Why?
So let me explain a bit.
What I expected, what I believe I was promised, was a little bit of excitement and planning of FTL, little bit of unexpectedness of a roguelike, little bit of atmosphere of Mass Effect because of the style and of course Jack Wall, and a lot of space exploration, the wonder, the excitement, learning, danger, the New Stuff that science fiction brings, whats best in Star Trek, Mass Effect, or Star Control, or the even older classics like Starflight.
A journey.  But this is not a game of going where no man has gone before.
This is a hunting simulator and you are the fox chased by hounds. Everything else is just filling and fluff and sugarcoating. And as such its a great game. But its not what I want, or what I was promised. I dont want to pay for this.
If you like the feeling of rush and constant fleeing, its worth the money.
I really feel like I have been lied to and my money cheated from me. This game could have been worth two or three times the price, or even more.
The mining minigame in Mass Effect 2 is worth more than this and gives a better feeling of space exploration, and its mostly just a bouncing wave. Just closing my eyes and listening to Jack Wall´s New Worlds is better than this whole game. Not to say its bad. It might be good. It could become GREAT. But its wrong, just wrong made worse because of what it might have been.
If the "flee from A to B" is changed to "search for a new planet" and the "constantly being hunted" is changed to
" not especially hunted but attacked on sight" and the stupid, stupid idiotic limit of one planetary exporation per planet is removed, this could be much better. And an autopilot and a better map. And a bit of rework on the whole system.
Or just say its a hunting simulator, ok?

This game is certainly challenging like Dark Souls, and some people might find enjoyment in that but for the average person - you may have more frustration than actual fun.

If you want a good story and character building, then this is not your game. But what you have is a very good Action-RGP, with focus on action, it has one of the best combat systems in an ARPG, I have experienced. The draw back is a more arcade-style approach to character building, so there are no class-system, but you can change you skills and weapons of you character with different skills cards (Destiny Cards), so you one second can play with a big smashing hammer and the next a pulverising shotgun.
First you control your character with the wasd keys and mouse. You can also use a gamepad. You can also roll duck, jump and even wall jump, this make for a very interesting and fun gameplay although the dynamics wears off after a while as with other games . The atmosphere in the game is good, the graphics are very beautiful and there is a lot of areas. Every area has five challenges, if you complete can get more experince, and loot. The hunt for loot is one thing this game does well, and with the challenges is what keeps this game going. Not because there is a lot, but you appreciated more when you get it, and to find that piece you need to fit with your skill cards. You can also use the loot to transform already own equipment.
It might be more of a summer game, than a dark winter game but it is really fun playing this game.

Angvik is quite the annoying little platformer. Other reviewers compare it to Dark Souls because it's so difficult, but it's honestly nothing like Dark Souls at all. From what I understand there are no save points in this game at all. I've made it 8-9 screens through the game after 20 minutes. So yeah, kind of neat, it's only $3, but why so freaking hard for no reason other than to be the frustratingly kind of difficult? Instead of the challenging kind of difficult like Dark Souls is. Meh, not really for me.
