I made this
review well over a year ago now. Yes I was trying to be funny but, looking back, I did injustice to a game I have come to love so much so that it ranks highly on my own list of best games of all time. Time to right a wrong.
HoI3, as it is now well known, is a game of waging war at the operational level. The game is played out over a 2D global map, a classic trope of Paradox games (see Europa Universalis), and on it are represented all the world's major and minor countries at the beginning of the year 1936. You can select any one of these nations with the intention of controlling its diplomatic, economic and military development. The former two aspects are largely abstracted; you can select another nation to do business with but your options will usually be severely restricted unless you're playing multi-player or playing as a major power in single-player (Germany for instance). The latter aspect is much less so.
Building up your military forces requires direct involvement on your part and you will need to make the critical choices to decide the makeup of your military forces long before war arrives, due to the nature of building units. The smallest land unit you can build is the brigade or regiment: a tiny fighting force of around 3,000 troops. The equivalent air and sea units are squadrons and flotillas. When you have concrete ideas on what you want to do, you then need to check that you've got the technology to do it.
The technology tree in HoI3 is split into various areas of interest, including civilian technologies to assist in producing certain resources and doctrinal advancements concerned with improving the training and capabilities of your fighting forces. It follows a largely linear path, so to get to more advanced projects you will need to research the earlier versions. This process is based around game time, with inefficiency penalties for researching late-war techs earlier in the game. Trying to get to stage eight of Small Arms in 1938 for instance might present some issues.
Leadership plays a critical role in tech research. Each nation begins with a certain number of leadership points, which can be thrown into slider adjustments depending on how many technologies you want to research at any one time. This needs to be balanced with three other aspacts on the scales, again depending on what your strategic choices are, which I will leave you to discover.
People who play war-game board games will probably be quite familiar with HoI's primary resource pool: Industrial Capacity. This is literally what it says on the tin and decides basically everything in terms of strategic decisions. IC is used for such things as producing military units, delivering supplies to them and producing consumer goods to keep the common rabble happy at home. You will quickly learn that early game production is a balancing act, between keeping everything ship-shape and actually building the military forces that you want in quantity. You may often find that you don't have the necessary IC to build many different units at one time. The answer, of course, is to start a WAAARGGH!
Before you start salivating, you should know that this is not simple. Neutrality governs the vast majority of nations at the beginning of the game, and you will have to start getting rid of this very early on if you expect to start annexing the neighbours before 1939, when the global conflagration begins. This process is a good deal easier if you're playing an Axis-aligned nation, since members of that faction get the option to begin wars with other nations quite a bit before neutrality hits zero. It really is possible to "conquer the Bolsheviks as Hungary", provided that beforehand you can absorb the resources of several of the other central and eastern European states that surround you.
Which brings me back to combat. True to Paradoxian form, this aspect is also mostly abstracted: you drag a box over the military units you want to go on the attack and you right-click the enemy province(s) that you want them to hit. Control is still left up to you as to where you want those units to go however, and thus comes the pleasure of the operational nature of the game. Do you advance on a long front across Yugoslavia, taking each line of provinces slowly yet inexorably? Or do you punch through on three different sectors, in a miniature copy of Operation Barbarossa? Alternatively, do you concentrate your armies in one sector, smash through then expand outwards in a mushroom hoping you can cut off enemy forces heading for your undefended provinces? Such decisions rest solely with you.
HoI3 definitely requires a measure of patience and actual cerebral work. If you are an FPS player, or stick only to tactical-level games such as Company of Heroes and Wargame, then you might prefer to steer clear. But, and this goes double for military history buffs and fans of other operational-level games, there are few other titles out there which could quite so effectively satisfy the need for a wargasm as much as this one can. Buy it. Play it. Enjoy it.

They're giving it away for free right now, so you may as well give it a shot.
Got it on sale, I definitely wouldn't buy it for full price. Graphics are pretty good, car exterior detail and rain are especially attention grabbing. The car sounds are really weird and probably a weak point-it sounds like they were synthesized rather than recorded. The game world is huge and the detail is pretty good considering the size, but it feels a lot emptier than any of the competition. The driving physics are pretty good and beginner-friendly and you can turn off the assists if you want. Nothing on the level of say, Forza Horizon but much better than Need For Speed 2015. The tuning is probably the biggest advantage-there are a ton of parts for every car. Bodykits, interiors, wheels etc and many cars have widebody versions in the "Perf" tuning spec. That brings me to the car selection. There are about 60, I think, plus their various tuning kits. This would be fine but the selection is a bit dumb- we get a Cadillac Escalade but no CTSV for instance. Attention to detail is where a lot of the cars fall apart-cockpit gauges are often off, or in some cases don't even work. You also can't sell off unwanted cars either which I don't get. The money system is annoying but not horrible. The game doesn't nickel and dime you that bad and you can make a lot doing skills and just drifting around, but the system is definitely skewed to try and get you to buy stuff. Cars especially are super expensive but you can test drive them before you buy which is nice. Parts are cheap though and handed out for free for doing skills.
It's a fun game but the world feels a bit dead at times and a lot of car appearance and spec details are overlooked. You can get lost just driving around for a long time though, and you can turn off the road at any time. Pick it up while it's free or try the trial and wait for a sale.

You can summon birds and they will help you fight with enemies on your way. You can also collect and use oils to improve your attack abilities or just to repair your armor/weapons. Every item you have can be destroyed by using it (weapon) or when you take hits (armor). Each map has time limit and your character gets older very fast, so you can't just stand and waste seconds. You can't block incoming attacks, so the only one way to avoid is jumping like there's no tomorrow "mario-like-jumps". At all timing is a key and everytime you start game again your run will be better than before.
From graphic side game is fine - you'll not find a fireworks in here but everything is aesthetically made and will not hurt your eyes. Sounds are fine too - after 2 hours I still do not turned music off.
A game not for a long time and not for everyone, but with fair price adjusted to what it offers.

While the game is in early access, it suffers from flaws that I believe to be fatal.
Crises come in rapid-fire sequence beyond anything remotely believable, and your crew can't fix anything without a direct order. Combat mechanics are badly flawed; shields can't defend against more than one enemy at a time, and you usually face at least two. There is only one possible way to find repair parts, and it happens so rarely that you're not likely to be able to fix any damage you take before the next fight. You can't avoid combat because resource consumption is off the charts; you have to stop at every planet and gather, gather, gather until the bad guys catch up with you or you'll die from running out of fuel.
Also note, the game is pure iron-man mode. No normal save-restore; you can shut the game down and come back the next day, but you can only pick up right back where you left off. If you die, you start over. Period.
This game is suitable only for people who hate winning and can only take a game seriously if they lose every time. Hardcore masochists only.

Buying Divinity II ( or Ego Draconis, and the confusion revolving the fact it's the first game but somekind of spiritual successor to Divine Divinity) was a shot in the dark when it was released. It had been forced out of production too soon for the developer's taste due to lack of funds, I found out after I had played it.
What you actually recieved out of the box was a brilliantly written storyline that kept you engrossed pretty much from the start, a combat system with more depth and variation than it initially lets on and with graphics that could rival any AAA game on the market during the time of its release. I was shocked to hear the developers claim they were disappointed because it lacked so many things that they wanted to put into the game, but couldn't due to financial strains. The main rival to D2 was Dragon Age 2, and the fact Larian Studios, the developer, was disappointed in themselves meanwhile mopping the floor with every other RPG on the market, (in terms of game quality and not sales) says a little about their selfstandards. This is pretty obvious in Divinity: Original Sin if nothing else.
For a game that lacked half the content it was supposed to have, you'll wonder exactly what that content was when you come out an odd 40 hours of gametime later when you've finished one of the most engrossing and twisting storylines this side of a classic JRPG. As an example the Divinity Dragon Commander title is actually a byproduct of what was originally supposed to be an RTS part of Divinity II.
If you enjoy any rpg from Diablo to Skyrim, I would recommend trying this out. It is challenging in that the combat system is used to its' full extent throughout the game and there is no one tactic that would work on all enemies or situations. It is varying in that the scenery changes everywhere you go and not much is reused in terms of assets and nothing feels rushed or left out and it is, of course, engrossing thanks to wellwritten characters and a twisting storyline with many small pitfalls that you decide the outcome of in best D&D spirit.
If you've played Original Sin, or anything from Diablo to Skyrim, you would probably enjoy this game. If nothing else than to blast airships as a dragon.

(Important note: I am writing this from my impressions of closed pre-alpha state of this game)
Our heroes have grown and new adventures in Etheria awaits them!
Dungeon Defenders 2 is here and it's free (or at least it's going to be). Some time passed since the first, simple Unreal Engine 3 project came out to see the light of sun and people this single level, third person tower defense loved so much that we eventually got full relese of Dungeon Defenders, many DLCs followed the success of the game, making it that much more bigger and enjoyable. But development of the first Dungeon Defenders is over and that's where Dungeon Defenders 2 comes in place.
You can expect completly new game, while the core elements we all love stayed the same. You are still going to be building your towers to defend cristals and you are still allowed, heck you are suposted to run around and join the action yourself! You are still going to be picking up loot of different tiers as you go through the levels to make your heroes and therefore abilities and towers stronger so you can tackle harder locations.
But the game itself have been built from the ground up again.
The game looks gorgeous, everything is so pleasing to the eye, outdoor maps have never felt better, the unique graphics style works great and I especialy like the water in this game. There is amazing attension to details here. Only the UI is lacking some love, but that's confirmed to change. As you level up your towers, they change in appearance too. Enemies no longer change in colors when they are of highest tier. Insted you'll notice visual changes like they are suddenly wearing different armor.
The level design is great, but we all know that Trendy is capable of creating nice and challanging levels. Be it indoor maps or outdoor maps, they all are unique in their own way. Prepare to encounter new mechanics added to the mix. You can now set off traps, like a bunch of TNT or freeze your enemies with a gian ice cube cannon or maybe flush your enemies away with releasing the sewage valve, there's alot of crazy traps for you to utilize to thin out numbers of hordes of enemies. And you'll encounter new places to guard! If you let enemies destroy a strategic point, prepare for another path for them to unlock. Sometimes you may want to let them destroy it so you get more XP but be careful to not play with the fire too much!
Loot is a major part of this game, the same as in the first game. You'll notice 1 thing right away, the loot doesn't seem to pop up as often as it used to. Remember the maps filled with junk? That's pretty much no longer here, but it's not a bad thing, I've still been able to find upgrades along the way and it's not like you get 3 items per map, even on lower levels I could get 20+ items from 1 level and that's not too bad! You'll find new weapons, armor, totems and trinkets. Pets are not yet implemented at this stage of the game, but they will make their way in again. And just as in the first game, you can further upgrade your items, but it works differently here. There's an echanter lady in your tavern. You put your item in the middle of this magical wheel (of fortune), than you put items you don't need in the surrounding slots. The wheel will turn around while "infusing" all the items into the one you are enchanting. And based on the rarity of the items, your enchanted item gains certain ammount of XP and eventually levels. It's an interesting concept and I like it, at least thtere's a use for the items you don't need. and it cost you some gold too. You can also buy new items in the tavern from vendors.
There are currently 4 playable characters available, and if you played the first game, you'll know them already! You have your apprentice, monk, huntress and squire ready to roll right off the bat. Apprentice builds magical towers, monk can provide you with auras that damage enemies, boosts your character or towers, huntress is "trapmaster" planting many traps to take your enemies by surprise and of course squire to build durable baricades and some heavy towers. Combinign all of them is a key to success and if you can play with your friends, it's even better! You can switch to another character during build phase in any map, but you can only choose 3 of them that will be available to switch before entering any map. It's called "hero deck" and it's not going to let you put in all 4 of the heroes available so you have to think about who you are going to bring along!
So far Dungeon Defenders 2 delivers alot of fun! And that's only in pre-alpha, I can't wait for the flashed out release version! I'd love to talk about bussiness model, but there's nothing you can buy for real money yet. I am sure we'll have skins for heroes and for towers. From the looks of it, we'll be able to buy boosters (XP and Gold boosters at least) and maybe more inventory space. But I can't be sure about anything else.
This game is worth your time, even if you don't usually like tower defense games, because this one mixes in alot of other mechanics that you won't find in your clasic tower defense games. You could say it's Action RPG tower defense game and you wouldn't be wrong.
See you all in Etheria!

This is one of those times that I wished Steam offered a number or star rating rather than just a Yes/No.
I'll give my critiques in a Pro/Con format:
Pros:
* Graphics - It's a pretty game, pretty scenery, cool particle effects for weapon/power actions, effectful lighting
* Sound - Good voice acting, sound effects add to feel of the gameplay, nice music.
* Gameplay - Movement is tight and has an interesting jump mechanic
* Combat - (Lower level) is fun, lots (number) of mobs to kill, feels impactful
Cons:
* Combat - (Higher levels)
- Scaling is horrible once you start getting over level 20.
- Mobs scale up faster than you can upgrade your weapons and items.
- You get mobs that can hit through your gear and have so many hit points that it takes a lot to burn them down.
- Mobs start hitting so hard that they can effectively 1 or 2 shot you.
- They'll stun or slow you then throw down a power you can't get away from fast enough.
- These overall problems make combat needlessly hard with lots of deaths and generally not fun.
* Transmutation
- It takes 3 of the exact same type/level of item to transmute.
- These come mainly from random drops, the "store" rarely has what you need so that means more grinding and leveling up faster than you can transmute better items.
- For weapons, you have no control over attributes of newly transmuted items (random).  Legendary items are a random chance from transmuting epics
- Demonic powers transmute into a random other power.
It's a really close call, but, at the end of the day, I can't recommend the game because of the horrendous scaling that ends up making combat at higher levels just not fun.  I even bumped the level down to "casual", but the same issues of stun/slow kills were still there.

So this game is pretty old at this point, and most folks who want to play it have played it.  That said, it is a pretty good little sandbox game that takes on a setting outside of the usual American-urban (or even military fantasy) and actually pays some attention to it.  The setting is a southeast Asian island nation very similar to Indonesia and the aesthetic and factions of the game represent that.  The main character is there working for a US agency to overthrow the dictator who stopped following US orders and brutally terrorize the country for points and money along the way.  He does this with a wide array of conventional weaponry and a bionic commando arm thing that lets him grapple around the jungle environments. The writing is downright terrible, but is largely an optional experience.
It has some flaws, being kind of repetitive and by default also very grindy.  The game world is massive and they insist on travel cutscenes for locations you can go back to--but you have to get somewhere near where you're going first.  The vehicles drive...poorly, being extremely hard to maneuver.  Some of these issues can be resolved with mods, however, which is why the PC version is the best version.  I haven't finished the game, I play it slowly, but it has a lot of content if one just feels like tooling around the jungle highways and blowing up water towers then this is the right game.

Very new at the game but also very much enjoying it. Just completed the first boss of the game and have a few things to say.
First of all, graphics and voice acting are awesome, Victor's voice is just so right for his character, although "Voice" get's a little annoying from time to time, he's pretty funny (like calling me a cheater when I jumped in the maze.)
Gameplay's pretty smooth, a nice breath of air to most RPG's where it's point, click, wait, repeat. The active combat, move cancleing and dodging are all very well done, slight gripe to be had on the dodge's I-frames (if it has any) but I put that down to me being used to Devil May Cry games. The ability to switch between two equipped weapons on the fly is awsome as well, although I wish we had the option to exchange that second slot for Dual Weilding (hint hint)
Now for a couple of personal gripes. All of which have to do with the Wraith type enemies encountered, most noticibly, the blue one. Either I'm stupid and am missing a huge cue they're about to do their rush or you need freaking future-sight to dodge those things. Secondly, a certain kind of challange is begining to grate on my nerves a bit; the "slay X enemies without taking damage" challenge. By itself, it's a hard challenge of which I'd have no quaral if I didn't have to restart the entire area if I screw it up! I'm going to say this is also going to crop up in later dungeons with "Slay X without using potions" or "slay X without using Demon Powers". I'm not dissing the challenges, gotta have them their for the extra fun and bragging rights, but why can't the counter just reset upon failing the condition rather then forcing a complete restart if you want to get it? It doesn't help the the first time you get this challenge, you're very quickly greeted by one of the afformentioned Blue Wraiths who wiped out any chance of that on my first dodge. The "Slay without using potions or demon powers" in one of the later dungeons in zone 1 cut it close too, had to resort to some huge shotgun cheesing to complete the task without dying so I could use a potion.
I get the feeling these gripes of mine will dissappear as my skill at the game gets better, as said, played up until after killing the first boss of the game (who was a very fun fight by the way, only needed one statue although it got a bit dicey when he started summoning 3 totoms at once) and loved pretty much all of it bar those niggles, Looking forward to the DLC!

Played it like all the others many times on the console, buying each on the computer when they go on sale.
So I got into the game and my first thought was to see how many achievements I could log before dying and getting the death achievement. Then I died in the tutorial area because my character did a wide turn for no reason and flung themself off a ledge. That's a good summary of a significant part of these games, poor controls and the use of gravity to kill the player arbitrarily.
After that I decided to beat the boss in the Heide's Tower of Flame, a higher level but early accessible area; for kicks and because some armour sets found in the area I like. Then I rediscovered that it's one of the worst maps I've ever seen in a game. First off, half the enemies have constant one eighty degree swinging attacks and the other enemies have instanteous attacks with no telegraph. Second off, the main boss of the area is guarded by the drake. Here's the problem. If you try to approach the drake when it has woken up it will stunlock you with fire and kill you, so literally you can't progress to the boss. The drake wakes up while players are fighting a basic enemy placed near it, so fundamentally you can't progress to the boss if you fight that random enemy because the drake will wake up and then become impassable. You need to specifically run past that exact enemy, hope it doesn't hit you on the way past in which case you will not reach the drake before it burns you; and then you must fight the drake and the enemy at once. Or, you can lure the enemy far away from the drake and hope you luring it doesn't wake it up anyways. In either situation you need to kill over half the enemies in the map before you reach the last enemy before the drake otherwise they will all follow you and gank you. This entire process is one you need to learn basically by dying for however long until you figure out the exact way to make the map playable, because it isn't in its base state. By the way, the drakes fire breath phases through everything including solid walls.
That's these games. Obnoxious, unfair, and poorly designed. But that aside, here is that which many console play throughs has wrought.
The graphics are terrible, in only one or two areas of the entire game do the graphics look semi logical, in every other part of the game it looks like some kind of blurred cartoon hybrid. It is shaped like a blurry real object yet is it textured and lighted like some kind of obscure cartoon. Which looks worse then games from the early two thousands because at least they still were trying to look real, this game generally just looks stupid and is profoundly less interesting to look at then most other games.
The post written joke of a lore continues to deteriorate to the point where what little story there is, doesn't make sense. Why does the king of a nation marry a woman who shows up out of nowhere, then starts a war with a race of super powerful giants that live across the sea just because she tells him they are a threat even though they literally weren't until the king attacked them. Why are there magical sub-dimensions where all the additional purchasable content takes place, why is the king able to fuse the crowns of all the kings of the sub-dimension together into one that stops the curse. There's no logical basis to any of the fundamental plot points of this game, at least in the previous ones there are a semi-sensible generic fantasy system in place. In this one there's zero structure or logic. It doesn't matter since there technically is no plot, or story progression, or story telling, or any kind of cinematic design to the game at all just like the others. But the post written generic fantasy lore put in as flavour text to the item descriptions, makes less sense then it already did now. And the world design is hilariously bad, considering that the land is a bunch of completely different biomes all connected for no reason. And there's that one tower which teleports several hundred meters to different places in space based on which location you are looking at it from.
Of course the concept design also deteriorates as well, giant one eye hippopotamus creatures, giant versions of existing animals, slightly above average sized versions of existing animals. Most of the enemies in the game are just generic looking humanoids, and most of the maps are just generic looking locations with inconsistent climates.
Once more they continue recycling items, boss concepts, animations, all kinds of little things into the game from the previous ones. And once again they still did not balance or fix any of the previous issues and keep releasing overpowered or underpowered weapons and spells. The player versus player combat is even worse due to how much more the game depends on players just mashing the light attack button, making numerous weapons that support this, and so on. It's hard to actually list the amount of meta there is, because there is legitimately so much of it. And none of it ever got patched. The arena matchmaking for player versus player also constantly pits players against others who are not their own level. So players will have fights against others whose characters are blatantly stronger or weaker then theirs.
The game continues its legacy of artificial difficulty with giving enemies massive hitboxes, ganks, hyper tracking, massive attack chains, inconsistent attack elements, miniscule recovery animations, attacks with no telegraphs, jump tracking, so on and so forth. With the combat breaking down even more by the developers removing the poise mechanic while encouraging button spam and also giving more enemies the ability to spam their own attacks and giving enemies less resistance to being stunned by attacks. So players can just mash the button and it will often work. It only gets worse in the next game.
Like in the other games there are numerous computer character quest lines which players must complete to get access to exclusive content and achievements. These quests require highly arbitrary and fourth wall breaking amounts of knowledge to the game progression and it is extremely unlikely players will complete them without looking up a guide because of how tedious it is. The games aren't bad enough without having chores added into them apparently.
Most of the item pick ups and items in the game, aren't worth using. The armour is fashion and not armour, most weapons are inferior to other weapons in that same type, some weapons are straight up inferior or superior in general, most consumables are completely pointless, shields are overpowered and underpowered, parrying is a free win hinging on a quick time event, archery is pointless, backstabbing is a free win hinging on literally nothing but the players discretion, magic isn't a combat style it's free damage. Continue, continue.
And you have to level up to get a proper amount of invincibility frames from dodging. So for a significant chunk of the game your dodge will only have a fraction of a second of safe frames to it. And this is also the same game where early level shields had their effectiveness lowered.
Essentially this is a worse looking and even less structured recreation of the previous games, which has significantly less combat balance. The only improvements at all being that in this one backstabbing is not instant and the jump button is not attached to the run and dodge button. Both of which were abhorrent mechanics that shouldn't have existed in the first place.

Review written as of 0.01 Early Access.
The game has more than a few design issues.
-The pacing can be grueling as the ship just seems to move too slow, and watching your food and oxygen go down as you're closing on a possible encounter ship that might not even give you those resources just doesn't vibe.
- Given the fact that the setup you start the game with is the setup you will play the game with, with ship upgrades being more a matter of RNG than actual choice, and given that the initial setup is far from varied or giving any real variety to choose from, mixed with the fact that the map is static just points towards very little replayability. And since the game speed is so low.. let me touch on that.
- Game speed. Mixed with the pacing above but the game just has bad use of user interaction and timing. The 'command pause' is not always availble, including in moments where you'd want it by default on, like when interacting with planets. You're left at the mercy of shoddy animations that take too long to load up menus while you're on the clock. I have a vague feeling that using Mining Probes is a better choice than Mining Rigs in the long run specifically because the animations and time you spend  in sector is smaller, and you draw less of attention from the enemies. This is /not/ proper use of player agency within the context of game mechanics.
-Combat itself isn't horrible, but there is one single questionable design choice.. Misses. The enemy never misses, yet you do. Then again, i agree that so far what i've played your ship is quite a lot stronger, but the fact of SO many misses makes the initial weapon choice moot. Any long-charge, high-power-per-shot weapon is a ♥♥♥♥♥ier variant when compared to the higher rate of fire/charge ones just because of misses. The only choice is how much you want to micro the colors/frequency matching, but that shouldn't be a choice in itself.
Those aside, everything else can be chalked up to Early Access issues. Things like control, optimisation, animations and balance as well as placeholder names and unintuitive UI. If i want to play a great space roguelike with fantastic replayability, pacing and balance, i'll be playing FTL some more.
To note, i did Kickstart this, but i will be leaving this to stew for a good year or two until they sort it out, since for now, i wouldn't recommend it to anyone if they'd ask me for a single choice of a game to play.

It's E.A. and you notice it in small things that will probably be resolved. A lot of bugs mentioned in other reviews are already solved. As others have mentioned: it's FTL in 3D + a big Star Trek feel. The graphics are fantastic (I like the sperm-like things that fly around, have never seen that before but is much better than space debris). The user interface is ugly but that might change in the future.
Lots of people dislike the game for its lack of save/load functionality. They probably haven't played a lot of games in the 80's or early 90's where ironman mode was more common (or maybe more accurate: was expected to be normal). Although I dislike iron man modes in some games (they usually give a choice), I do like it in games like these. It's quite realistic that you will start your journey and that every decision you make is final. Loading a savegame to revert choices or even randoms would be cheating.

I thought this was an interesting idea, but it just isn't fun to play.  I know I had to click on things, but what is the point?  For combat, you basically have three buttons to push and spend most of the time waiting for them to charge, then click the button.  Events happen as you're travelling and you basically click on a crew member then click on the event to have them handle it and wait until they're done.
I know it's an early access game, but it seems to take a long time just to move between screens.  It would be nice to have hotkeys to put you at any screen you wanted.  I'd also dock the game for not having a load feature, you basically can only save the game when you quit and come back to the same game later.  It's easy to get around by quitting to the menu then copying your save file so the only effect is to frustrate people.  The best games let players decide how they want to play them, not have everything dictated to them by the developer.  You could always have a 'hard mode' that doesn't allow loading and 'insane' that won't even save if you quit the game.

Probably my most played Steam game to date. This game is a lot of fun for me, as resource management and builder games go - it's simple, but can also be very unforgiving. Don't expand too quickly, don't switch your focus too slowly, and don't put off necessities for too long.
Once you've mastered keeping your collection of people fed, clothed, and equipped with tools, the 30+ achievements can point you in a new direction. The challenges range from something as simple as building a long bridge, to something as specific as maintaining a certain population mark in really harsh conditions for "enough" years consecutively (one day, Mountain Men, one day!).
This is probably the only town builder game (other than SimCity) I've played that hasn't shoved combat down my throat. The world is frankly dangerous enough without the added complication of resource competition. Just one more reason I enjoy this game.

Foreword: I wish steam counted the time I played Victor Vran in offline mode... I should easily be over 12 hours and I own the game since a few days ago - and that is saying something...
What's Victor Vran?
Take the Diablo series (if you don't know what Diablo 1-2-3 is, you most likely don't like or care about isometric ARPGs, so you're better off closing this review now), remove its class system, and add the following: jumping and dodging; Guild Wars 2 style of combat (skills tied to the weapon type); way better voice actors (Doug Cockle, the Witcher 3's Geralt and Andrew Wincott as the Voice); good humor and easter eggs that break the leveling tedium, and last, but not least, just tell me in what other game you can do Gangnam Style in Kung Lao's Hat!? If it were only throwable too...
So, let's take a look at the good and the bad.
The GOOD:
1. Great artwork and level design - extremely well made locations ranging from city streets, labyrinths, caves, halls to various dungeons.
2. Great flashy combat animations - they really do justice to the title, even if the graphics are more reminiscent of a 2012 game than a 2015.
3. Great music - the soundtracks are very dark, sinister and thematic. Even during the Gangnam style easter egg scene.
4. Great voice actors - Doug Cockle, Andrew Wincott and Elena Saurel do an amazing job in this game. I also felt like Elena Saurel tries to immitate Triss at times and sound like her... Might just be me though. Too much Witcher 3, you know...
5. Great protagonist - Victor Vran, the bulky demon hunter with a husky voice, the worst pickup lines ever and a voice in his head that both helps and misleads, jokes and makes fun of him is just awesome. And about that...
6. There aren't many ARPGs that can put a smile on your face. This one does though - just when you start feeling bored with all the button mashing, either Victor Vran, the Voice, a monster, or a Boss shows up to crack a joke or do something funny.
7. Innovates the ARPG genre - you can jump, wall jump, and dodge roll to either reach an area, a secret, avoid damage, or strategically position yourself in a fight. It makes an AMAZING difference in comparison to other ARPGs. I am sure masters of the game will abuse this mechanic a lot to avoid damage and set up perfect combos.
8. Great weapon variety for both close, ranged, and mixed style-oriented "Vrans" - I was pleasantly surprised to discover that there is no obsolete weapon type in this game. 90% of the time you can easy build around the type of weapon you prefer (or want to run with) by improving on its strengths. The other 10% represent encounters where other weapon types work better than the one you currently predominantly use, or objectives that require you to complete some fights with a different weapon to get a reward.
9. Even without classes, builds are possible - there are plenty of options in the game that you can mix and match to create efficient builds. You have your weapon with various prefixes and suffixes, outfit (but no armor pieces), destiny cards, demonic powers and potions. You can opt to build for melee-tank, melee-dps, ranged with crits, big demon power usage, etc. There are plenty of variations to keep you occupied.
10. Set your own challenge - by selecting various hexes that affect you or the enemies upon entering an instance, you can increase the difficulty of an area and improve the awards gained from it - and of course, brag about your badassness.
11. Every area has a task-reward system to it - I wouldn't call it a quest, really. Upon entering an area, you will be given a number of tasks you can strive to complete (or completely skip) with rewards like gold, xp, items, destiny cards, and so on tied to them. I find this a very nice touch, as it makes me think about something else than the mindless button mashing or grinding.
12. Just like any ARPG, you can get your grind on in a major way - while you can absolutely do any instance just once or rush through the game, the completionist Vrans will endeavour to look under every nook and cranny, find all the secrets, do all the tasks, reap all the rewards, and redo areas as many times as it takes to complete everything.
13. Awesome controller scheme - while controller usage is not a commonplace in ARPGs, Victor Vran does a stellar job integrating it. I am an all-out keyboard-and-mouse pc gamer, and I have been playing this title for about 12 hours with the controller. That is indeed saying something, so if you're more used to the controller, you will absolutely love the fact that they implemented it to such great extent.
14. And mind you, this is purely subjective - I am personally done with grindy ARPGs and MMOS that take over 100 hours to complete. I am also over games that make me see the better way halfway through it, and because of the player that I am, I always restart to correct my mistakes... I did my fair share of them (over 2000 hours total in Diablo 1-2-3, over 1500 hours in Lineage 2 and over 2500 hours in Guild Wars 2) and I am all for 20-25 hour ARPGs right now, and this is why Victor Vran is the right game for me. Here you can just play - and fix the errors in your ways by swapping your builds on the fly.
15. 4 player co-op - always a great thing to see!
And now, let's take a look at the bad:
1. Passable story - while the story is serviceable, do not expect anything amazingly epic. Someone screws up, you go fix it. That simple. No more, no less.
2. Semi-RPG mechanics - while builds are an option based on mixing-matching the options given to you, the ARPG fans are used to way more in terms of min-maxing a character, with more skills, build options that make every class play differently and so on and so forth. Victor Vran does another serviceable, but by no means stellar job. It is nowhere near the likes of Diablo, Torchlight, Path of Exile, and Sacred 1&2 where you have tons of classes, you could shop, gamble, and grind for hours to make the best build. However, it is also not as pointless as the one in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows where you were leveling up without even realizing it...
3. Replayability - steam says I am about 6 hours in, it is incorrect. I am about 12 hours in and I still have plenty of things to do. So I would venture to say that a single run would take anywhere from 15 to 19 hours, and over 20 if you are more fastidious and like to clear every single monster from an area and complete every single objective. This might be a turn-off to some gamers, and while to me in isn't, it is a fair point that I also need to put out there.
4. A number of bosses so far really made me sweat and switch builds before tackling them... Boss battles in this game are hard, and yes, the one-hit-kill mechanic is present, and profoundly frustrating.
5. No armor customization - while the outfits in this game are awesome, ranging from Dapper Vrans to Savage Vrans, the customization there is barren, as it is a whole piece. Yeah... no gloves, boots, torso, hat, amulet, ring, etc.
CONCLUSION:
Victor Vran is the right game for me, so it gets an easy recomendation. If you like action packed ARPGs with good amount of loot, lots of stuff to kill (as you'll be tripping on enemies every second step you take) and a side serving of humor alongside it, this game is absolutely the right one for you. I also believe that by the time I am posting the review, it is still on sale, so it should be a great buy. Anything over 33% off the title makes it a must own. You will absolutely get the full value for your money, even moreso if you decide to try another playstyle. The satisfying combat, the loot system, the amount of achievements, challenges, easter eggs, and the funny narrator are very strong selling points to this game. It is only held back by its mediocre story and incomplete customization (i.e. no classes and armor pieces). If you can live with these flaws, this game is absolutely the right one for you.

text:
Back in the days of the Pentium and the PS1 there was a little company known as Shiny Entertainment. In addition to a bunch of well-animated games by a less than scrupulous fellow, they made a rather surreal third-person shooter called MDK. Starring a janitor named Kurt Hectic and his parachute-equipped Coilsuit, it went on to become a Cult Classic.
In 2000, a sequel came out for the PS2, Dreamcast and PC. This game, while written by a different team, still held up well in spite of feeling a bit different overall from the original. This change in writers came with a requisite change of tone - Whereas MDK1 was a very surreal game and derived much of it's humor from that, MDK2 loves it's refuge in audacity, and has a very action movie feel to it. For example, in few other games will you see a Robotic Dog with a Chain Smoking habit quad-wield miniguns? In spite of the different writing, MDK2 still was a good game simply by virtue of being fun as hell to play.
In 2011, Overhaul Games brought MDK2 up to speed. The new models and textures look very good and the game is solid as ever, and the System Requirements are modest as ever (Though you're still gonna need newer hardware to play the HD flavor). My only real gripe? Overhaul did not put much effort into making the game make bettr use of widescreen. Most UI elements (such as the zoom on Kurt's sniper rifle) are still in 4:3, causing a fair deal of letterboxing. This does not make the game any less playable, mind, but is more of a presentation nitpick than anything.

I won't try and say the definition of a hacker is easy to pinpoint, it means different things to different people, but this film runs on a outdated archtype. Credit where due, points for cinematography, in a way I found the grainy footage and cold/dark motifs oddly comforting... Probably because of a heatwave at the time of writing.
3/10 would only recommend to scared, sheltered people who feel the need for there leftover cold war paranoia to be validated.

Tentative recommendation. What Into the Stars does well, it does very well. For other things, it is merely functional.
The good:
Into the Stars offers an interesting take on the space ship adventure game. Ark 13 is big, slow and unweildy, exactly as you'd imagine such a big ship to be. there's no point in doing clever manoevers, you basically point and let her fly. But just because it's a slow ship, doesn't mean that as the captain you'll have nothing to do. There are constant little emergencies that require your attention, for which you need to apply your specially selected crew, and by the half way point of the mission you will know there characters quite well.
The bad: Unfortunately, when you do arrive at the planets that dot your path, the gameplay becomes mediocre. Exploring planets is little more than a menu selection, and mining for resources is a rather obnoxious mini-game.
The ugly: Combat is not optimised for PC play, and leads me to think that Into the Stars is being developed primarily for the mobile market. On its own, the act of selecting weapon frequencies and sheild frequencies is a novel idea and hearkens back to the Star Trek feel. But there are no short cuts for all the buttons, meaning you have to move the mouse, making the experience clunky and un-immersive. Secondly, the enemies float right in front of your ship, looking for all the world likethose JRPG menu based combat systems.
But I still l want to play more, and you are supposed to be avoiding conflict. I hope the developers make some changes.

Overall, I am really enjoying this game.
IMO this is a great JRPG. The turn based battle system is great and even makes the minimal amount of grinding seem enjoyable. There is not a lot of strategy in the battles, which I liked since some JRPGs can be quite complex. The character animations are quite nice as well ;)
For those looking for adult images, etc, this game may not be for you. The characters are all cute (in that anime way) and you can play as Neptune in a swimsuit if you wish (hehe), but that's as far as it goes.
The story initially is very good, but unfortunately starts to get a bit boring mid-way through the game with long run-on dialogue, some of which does not move the plot forward at all. The story strongly depends on Neptune who is constantly shaking things up (in a good way) and Iris Heart for her... umm... being herself? The dialogue is certainly humorous, but there seem to be a lot of references that I ended up not understanding (perhaps from my lack of knowledge of other Japanese games?), which was mildly frustrating, but they seem to not be vital to understanding the story, just side-notes.
The dialogue is voice acted nicely, but I found that only the main dialogue scenes are voice acted, while the rest is just text. Although I suppose this makes sense from a dev point of view (less work, money), I found it strange that one scene can be voice acted while in the next scene later on, I had to read the text. Imo this takes away from the immersiveness of the game.
But really, I was surprised I could play this game at all. With the min specs of 2.66GH CPU and 1GB GPU, my laptops specs were just a bit over half of this. And it was actually playable! Unfortunately, there is no option to turn down the graphics settings that I have found (possibly due to it being a port). As many have claimed, there are infrequent crashes that WILL occur, but in my case they are bearable, they just cause me to save more often than I normally would.
Overall, I would certainly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys JRPGs. It has that nice JRPG feel to it , despite the few flaws and bugs that are present. 9/10

70 hours into the game, I can say two things about the crew. One, pray to god you don't get any game breaking bugs, because more often than not, you will have to resort to community help rather than Ubisoft actually trying to mend their own mess. Two, play with friends. This game gets tiresome and tremendously boring if you are on your own.
The campaign is generic at best, really forgetable. Not much to say about it.
The physics tend to make no sense at times, especially in PvP.
Not a big choice in cars either, to add to that, most cars have two to tree specs available and that's it. Higher end cars such as the Agera R and LaFerrari only get performence specs.
Map size is good for an online multiplayer racing game. But most cities will feel very small aside from maybe NY and LA.
And finally, the bugs. In the last month or so, I have been experiencing game crashes at random. I have tried various different solutions (most submitted by the community), as Ubisoft tech support doesn't seem to care, which can ruin the entire experience.
Overall it is avarage at best, it's fun at first if you are alone and just want to finish the story missions. However if you play for longer and have no one to share in the experience with, the is a high probability that you will get tired of it in a short while.
EDIT
Following different Nvidia driver updates, the game can surprize you in many different ways. For me, it doesn't even want to start up anymore, right after I set the new drivers. Goes to show how much thought process was put in the optimization and support of this ''game''.
In all honesty, it is a waste of money and time. Ubisoft don't care about your experience, so why should you buy their product.

When I first heard of Victor Vran, I initially paid no attention to it. Even the name of the game sounded really generic and lackluster. My assumption was that it would be a Van Helsing clone, which I didn’t like, and as far as Action RPGs go, I already owned and was quite happy with Diablo III. However, one of my friends really got into the game. He talked about the voice acting, the ability to be able to jump, the co-op gameplay, and he also shared some of the humor that kept the game light-hearted and didn’t take itself too seriously. This intrigued me and I had to check it out for myself.
The story is set up with the player taking control of Victor Vran, a demon hunter trying to purge the fantasy kingdom of Zagoravia. An evil dwells within the walls of the kingdom, and in the surrounding areas as well. No one knows the origin point of this demon infestation, but I imagine we very well may find out. During the first couple of hours into my playthrough of Victor Vran, I was very intent on reading all the quests and talking with the denizens of the realm. I was really trying to soak in and absorb this fantasy world that the developer, Haemimont Games, took time to create. However, it got boring very quickly, and started to skip everything. The story ceased to exist with me and now, in my mind, this game was going to solely live or die based upon the gameplay experience. Also, you may recognize the name of the developer, which were responsible for creating the Tropico series. It is interesting to see a developer that is known for creating Real Time Strategy titles go into the Action RPG genre.

This is the best platformer released in the last decade. There's absolutely no fat. Mechanics are introduced, tested, refined, developed, plumbed, and discarded within 10 minutes, and it feels totally organic. The open world feels even better than Super Metroid, and the individual world-segments are beautifully self-contained. Every single platforming puzzle works. It doesn't overstay its welcome; it has about 3-4 hours worth of content, and that's exactly how long it'll take you. Every screen makes your grin wider as you realize that, yes, they did just pull that trick out of the bag. There's something to be said for perfectly executed modesty.
What's wonderful is that despite the handful of mechanics, they all descend from one base mechanic--you can flip from ceiling to floor or vice versa but can't change directions during a flip. That's it.
The crown jewel is an optional sequence called "Veni, Vidi, Vici" which is the one of the most challenging sequences I've played in a game in years and so so satisfying when you beat it. What's most poignant about the VVV sequence (and thus VVVVVV as a whole) is that the theme of being able to do these amazing space flips but not even make a little hop causes both thematic frustration--I can see that damn shiny trinket, why the hell can't I climb over this block and get there--and puzzle-related frustration. Wonderful.

Outlast is a game which suffers horribly from common horror tropes but redeems itself in its smooth, pretty gameplay, interesting environments, and occasional creeps. To be sure, it is an experience, and one you will not want to miss out on if you enjoy horror/mystery/adventure. It is a good adventure game in its own right, with mystery elements that you piece together by recording certain events with your camera, taking notes, finding documents et cetera. Where the game falls apart is its horror aspect. Surprisingly, Outlast does not rely on jump scares to "get you". Most of the time it relies on Amnesia-style horror where you have to run and hide, or navigate very creepy areas with even creepier music completely unarmed. It does this well. However it reuses some of its scares so much to the point that it gets annoying. One of the characters was so overused that I began to sigh in frustration everytime his entrance music would play (I literally ran into him five different times in the course of three hours). The innmates of the asylum are also so overdone that they are sadly comical. I found myself laughing at them or examining them more closely instead of fearing them. One thing the game does right though is that there is no way of knowing whether an inmate is a homicidal maniac or completely harmless. The game suffers in its second half where it feels as if the player is being strung along on the same mission to find the same person for over three hours. The objectives would literally change from "Find Father Martin outside", to "Find Father Martin in the Female Ward" to "Find Father Martin in the Admistrative Building" to finally "Find Father Martin on the third floor" in the last two hours of the game. Father Martin was quite an illusive man. The game is also very short; it took me a little under 7 hours to finish it and I by no means sped through the game. So while the game is burdened by overusing certain horror tropes, by stringing you along the last three hours, and with its somewhat weird and whacky ending - it does redeem itself through its gameplay, moments of horror, and the uniqueness of the camera aspect / piecing the story together yourself. 7/10

Getting rid of the wordy mess that was my previous review.
Banished, on the outset, seems very bare-bones and drab.  I wish I could go back and recreate the first few hours I spent on it, watching my townsfolk die within the first year because I had no idea how to accurately meet their needs.  Food was a nightmare, and the game will punish *heavily* any sort of wrong step the player might take.  Planning ahead is crucial, and the learning curve might be steep for some, but once you see your town exceed 200-300 people, thriving with plenty of resources to trade, you will feel a sense of major, satisfying accomplishment.  That never goes away.
Now that I've mastered it, I've found a plethora of additional content in the Workshop.  There's all sorts of cool things to do, some rather cheaty, some full-fledged overhauls, some adding to the difficulty.  I expect this to be a game I go to whenever I feel like I have "nothing to play".  Banished might look a little gray around the edges, but it is a beautiful, well-oiled machine.

This game is awesome, and yes while limited - and I'm not usually one to scream "Early Access! It's an understandable setback!" But really, it is. When you buy an Early Access game, you KNOW it isn't finished, you're supposed to be reviewing what has been made thus far. With Into the Stars, the progress made is amazing.
Pros -
Graphics are good, but runnable. There is a slight "graininess" to them ingame, but it is easily dismissable by the rest of the space around you.
Gameplay is fun, and though at times repetitive, it is certainly always different in terms of difficulty. Remember, this game is meant to be similar to FTL's genre of gameplay, and if you didn't like it, you probably won't like this.
The things you come across in space so far are always interesting, and you almost always have to make that tough decision of sending out one of your trusted shipmates and the possiblity of never seeing them again.
The difficulty is playable, but you will certainly need a few runs to get used to the learning curve. Like I said before, it's similar to FTL, so you'll need to get used to it.
The controls themselves are simple and easy to use w/ a good amount of fluidity to your ship, so even if it does move rather slowly, this makes sense.
Cons -
The amount of different events that you'll come across are decent enough but lacking the diversity to really immerse you in the game efficiently.
The amount of ships in the game is limited and while you certainly feel that the ship is at your command, it doesn't make you feel as though you're actually connected to the ship in any way other than it's now your responsibility.
The weapons in the game are your classic laser & torpedo duo and the effects are pretty, but after awhile you get used to it and it doesn't surprise you anymore as to the effects. The different "types" of weapons (damage and charge time differences) aren't really enough to fill the gap.
Glitches come into the game fairly often, but none of them are gamebreaking, more of just small nuisance that is easily fixable by player, but they can certainly be tedious. Though, this is expected, just something to be mindful of running into.
--------
If you're looking for a tutorial to play the game, there is a guide in the Guides section of the game's Steam page.
All in all, I'd definitely recommend the purchase as the game itself is very fun, but as of right now, the replay value isn't of significant importance to really come back more than once or twice. If you want to see this game become more diverse and enjoyable - though it already really is - BUY IT.

I loved Dungeon Defenders 1, I even loved the nightmare-gear gap that a lot of people struggled with.
This is my opinion about DD2 on Day1/2.
DD2, out of the box and eventhough it still is in early access, is a heavily gated experience. It forces you through an abyssmal grind while isolating you from the rest of the player base the higher you go. Personal skill isn't rewarded, but how many times you attempted a mission. You can win a campaign map but it doesn't unlock the next one - something I have never seen before - it's behind a ridiculous mechanic where you have to grind previous maps over and over for XP until the next one unlocks even if you wouldn't have any problems winning the next ones. You can't even attempt harder maps or harder difficulties. I know a fair deal of grinding, but I don't understand why a game won't let you progress even if you conquered all the maps you've previously played. The whole war table thing doesn't make any sense and should be abolished because a system where players are put into tiers is dumb.
A lot of my fun in DD1 was figuring out placements, but it seems it has been completely thrown out of the window here.
If you're too strong, the game just downscales all of your stats/towers and always attempts to put you on the verge of barely winning. It's good if you want that sort of challenge, but the game also forces you through this item progression grind. In DD1 you could perfectly well do maps below Nightmare if you knew how to play. You would also believe that finishing on normal would unlock harder difficulties for the map - it doesn't, you have to accumulate a ton of XP until the game decides you're up for 'hard' mode on specific maps. It doesn't make any sense, considering that the game limits your access of maps depending on your level. Most of the times you will not be able to even replay levels in the next tier. So the progression system actually regresses the options you should have available. WHY?
I think this is all an effort to stop people from twinking and powerleveling, because otherwise selling gold or other services isn't going to be profitable in the future if it wasn't obstructed. Which is probably going to be a big deal because even upgrading your gear requires a lot of gold to a point where you waste more gold on a level 1 upgrade than you possibly get from finishing a map. That's completely bonkers. Though there are a few silver linings.
The PC version is well done, as opposed to DD1 which struggled with a lot of port problems. Eventhough there are a lot of interface options, it's still lacking a way to disable ally health and enable that tower health is always being shown or at least if it's on low health. I like the concept of the chests at the end and that you don't have to complete all waves to still get a reward. Actually between finishing or failing a map there is very little incentive, aside from the possible higher rarity loot at the end and slightly more xp depending on the wave you were. All that matters in the end is that you've attempted it and you get your fair share of a reward. It turns everyone into a winner, behind a heavily grind/gated based mechanic.
I can't recommend this to anyone who loved DD1, as it is right now. Wait for it to come out in 1-2 years and hope that they didn't turn this into a game on-par with a mindless cow clicker and with more substance instead. Also be aware that this game can only be played if you are online, it's basically a mmo.

While playing Banished I came to a realization.  That it has been the first middle ground of city based management in a long time.  At the Tripple A side we have EA charging DLC for things that should have been apart of the main game, and on the indie side most indie managment games are either way to easy, or you need a calculator and a degree in mathmatics to enjoy it, and the community snubs you if you don't 'get it'.
Banished is the perfect balance, it is a compleate game, it doesn't take much to learn, the tutorials are very helpful and quick and it is as easy or as hard as you wish to make it from there.  The graphics are very nice for a one man team and gets across everything it needs to, there is little to no confusion on what is needed, everything is pretty straight foward and its a nice game.
If you enjoy management games, god games or building games, I highly recomend this one regardless of the price.  It is worth it any time and any price for you.
Although if you are an achivement hunter I highly recomend staying clear of this one, the achivements are earned and not given away so freely, even after plugging six hours into the game at the time of writing I have yet to achive anything.  Not a complaint in the least but, the game really isn't kind to achivement hunters.

I have not had this much fun with a fantasy RPG game in Years.
There isnt really a "class" in the game you being a Dragon Slayer/Dragon Knight you can mix and match however you want :D
There are Priest spells: Which is summoning different creatures and spells like Fear, Blind, Charm and others.
There are Mage Spells: Which are Magic Missiles, Fire Blast and I think there was Ice Lance as well oh and one of the most powerful ones later in the game is Firewall for when the enemy gets in your face ^^ and dont forget Heal :)
Priests and/or Mages usually do good with 1h maces because they mostly have intelligence stats on them and you can either dual wield them or find a shield that has spirit on it like I did.
There is also the Warrior way with Whirlwind, Rush Attack, Fatality (like Execute) and other attacks or Defensive Posture if your more a 1h and Shield kind of person :) Which also works nicely with Whirlwind :)
Warrriors can either dual wield 1h weapons like Swords or Axes or they can use big 2h Swords which are slower but of course do more damage :)
And of Course theres the Archer way of playing where there are skills Like Poison Arrows, Ranger Suprise(Lowering the enemies defences), Stun Arrows, Explosive Arrows and other attacks :)
Obviously Archers use a 2h Bow for their attacks :) and you dont need to worry about buying arrows because apparently you have a unlimited supply :) either that or they're magic ^^
Oh and you can Equip 3 sets of weapons at the same time and switch between them whenever you want :)
When I had things more or less figured out I had my main weapon set be Dual wielding maces with that intelligence on them and my second was a 1h sword with a nice shield and my third was at some points it was a bow which I never used but it was a just in case thing and at some points it was a awesome 2h sword near the end there which I actually used more then my dual wielding weapons.
There are also a couple Dragon Slayer abilties which 2 of the biggest ones  I think are Mindread and Lockpicking :)
But there are also skills like Wisdom (increases your xp gained by 1-2% per skill put in it. And Encumbrance which increases the capacity of your backpack. (I know it may not seem so usefull at first but if you loot everything you get your hands on to sell or use later you will most likely put all the points you can in to that skill ^^ that being 5) and of course the weapons expertise skills Single-Handed, Dual-Wielding, Two-Handed, Sword and Shield and theres even Unarmed expertise if you wanna try that out.
Im telling you this game got A Lot to do in it :)
I almost forgot, there is a quicksave in the game and I suggest you save often because your choices can change things, as they say in-game "Your Actions have Consequences"
May I just say one more thing that will guarantee you will be interested in trying this game.
After you get to a certain point in the game (Its pretty early in the game) you are able to turn into a fire breathing dragon at will! At the push of a button! (Default being Q) :D But you can only attacking flying enemies or Ballistas and other buildings that attack you. Oh and there are several DIfferent Armor Sets that gives bonuses to your Dragon Skills :) You get your first one after you get your dragon form if you check your Storage Chest in the tower :)
Only bad thing is at some point it got a bit repetitive, but that may just be because the way I played it with magic only. I leaned more towards using bigass swords near the end because I got them and it was way more fun at the end :)

It has dragons so how could I refuse. Having read some reviews and seeing it on sale I decided to give it a go. I see now that this is a big game and its going to take a while to complete so I may add to this review later. My first impressions are good having just finished what could be classed as the first area. There are similarities here to other RPG's in that you have a bunch of side quests and then the main one. Thats  where they stop as the rest of the game is quite original in that your character is a dragon slayer pretty much with an open book skills develoment tree. I like this because you can customise your path to be either a pure class or a hybrid. A kind of pick and mix of skills. I've varied my character up to this point and he seems ok in combat so at this stage there doesn't seem to be a penalty for being a mixed bag. That may not work for everyone though depending on your play style. There is a certain strategy when dealing with opponents and it is this that may make you think more about the skills you buy. For instance I found my survival chances went up when using a bow against certain opponents as opposed to just charging in. This is why I am warming to the game because its a thinking mans RPG. Skyrim it is not but at least you can be a dragon in this rather than just riding one. The story is also fascinating with lots of historical references which add meat to the world you explore. The decisions you make also have consequences from small to large depending on what you do. The graphics are quite nice with varied scenery and architecture. Monsters range from little kick them in the butt types up to larger more challenging ones. Often you will get mobbed so its wise to learn some aoe skills or face oblivion. Its a game of secrets as well and some are not easy to find. NPC voice acting is pretty good and adds to the atmosphere. I like all the different personalities you encounter on your journey.
As it stands if you are a hardcore RPG fan then give this one a try. If you are new to the genre you may find this one a bit difficult to get into due to its depth.

note: the time displayed is incorrect, as my computer isn't constantly connected to the internet. I've clocked over 35 hours in the game according to the save file.
So, a return to the Hyperdimension Series. Frankly, as far as i'm concerned, Compile Heart and Idea Factory (US)/Marvelous AQL (EU) can't pump out these games fast enough. Each is good in its own right.
Do note that if you're expecting a serious plot with high drama then this is not the game for you.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 3 returns to the universe first introduced by Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 2 and sees the characters of that universe once again battling the forces of piracy in abstract form. However, where Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 2 tackled this basic plot in a rather anvilicious manner, R3 is altogether a better game. This is largely because of the reinclusion of Neptune as the main character and the antics she brings to the table; the Hyperdimension Series has never been about the story itself, but about the interaction with the characters that the writers bring to the table, and their interactions with each other. As such, HDN: R3 improves upon the formula introduced by the first game in almost every way but one: combat.
Part of the fun, personally speaking, was being able in HDN: R1 to pull off insane attacks with little effort. R3 attempts to curb this "abuse" by making EXE attacks both unlockable via achievements and require most--if not all--of a character's SP. Until you get the "drill" disc modification in the latter stage of the game, this heavily limits tactical options, as maintaining one's SP in battle becomes a chore in its own right.
an additional criticism of mine would be the game's performance even on relatively new machines. While the game is advertised as being playable at 60fps on 1080p resolutions, the reality is that the game presently locks itself into certain framerates and resolutions. with 8 gigs of ram, a dual core i7 5500U, and an AMD Radeon R9 M275--capable of getting upwards of 40 frames on fallout 4 at 720p and 50 frames on Warthunder on high settings at 1080p, I get a measly 27-30 frames on HDN;R3 at a locked resolution of 1280x720. Either due to a function of bad drivers or poor port-programming, all of the games in the HDN: R series perform poorly on systems which are well above the listed specifications. This may in part due to the games running heavily off of the CPU and not really using the GPU at full capacity.
In sum:
Pros:
-more nep
-shinier prettier graphics
-more of the parody and cute girls doing cute things that the fans have come to expect.
-more replayability
cons
-poor performance graphics-wise
-combat system has been poorly revised, and fails to add tactical depth
-annoying achievements to unlock potentially crucial character abilities
-limited post main-plot-arc content; sequel hook seems like an afterthought
Overall Score:
8 neps out of 10.

Victor Vran is a rather dark but comical ARPG that isn't afraid about taking the mick out of itself. If you're reading this you probably already know what the game is. You're a demon hunter called to investigate a city overrun by demons.
While I'm writing this review I haven't finished the game yet. I'm playing this game with a friend of mine in coop. I have played a lot of its competitors like Diablo, Sacred, Torchlight and what not. I will refer to them frequently.
The game has quiet a lot to offer, hence while I would recommend it.
Graphics:
The graphics are slightly more demanding than Diablo 3, but the game runs fluid on a mediocre system. It looks pretty and I haven't had a single graphical glitch during my sessions.
Difficulty:
I played the game on normal and it's a fair difficulty. Just as a reminder I play multiplayer not solo. So the game might be a lot more difficult in single player. There're three difficulty levels: Casual, Normal and Hard. For an even further challenge you can even play Hardcore (perma-death). During my sessions I died quite a lot, but I'll come back to that later...
Audio:
The voice over is awesome. The narrator did an incredibly good job capturing the atmosphere of the game. Victor tends to talk to himself a lot, refering to the voice in his head as headman. Those monologues are brilliant sometimes. The downside is, that all the other characters fade a bit in his shadow.
The musical score is good, but nothing to write home about.
I noticed a crackling sound every now and then which is quite annoying. Haven't found a fix yet.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is quite different from what I was used to. There are no classes or races, just Victor Vran. But there is still room for some customization. You can choose from an arsenal of different weapons (e.g. Rapier, Sword, Hammer, Shotgun). Each weapon has a different skill set: a standard attack and two special abilities. You can equip up to two weapons simultaneously. Swapping weapons during a fight is just one click. There is no classic magic system. Instead you have a demon power item which you can equip two of. It's a little like Sacred 2, tho you cannot upgrade those "runes". Last but not least, there's armor which you can get by reaching a certain level.
You can carry around two different sets of items. One of which is usually occupied by the health pots. You can equip buff potions, bombs and medi kits as well.
Finally there are destiny cards which further enhances your stats (e.g. critical chance, critical damage, health).
Of all the equipment there're four different qualities. White, Green, Gold and Purple. So no real difference to all the other ARPGs out there. Only difference are the destiny cards. Some of them have a slightly glowing effect to them. Those are divine cards, which have some additional effects.
The maps are really great. Every map has a different medieval theme and they look gorgeous. There is no random map generation tho, so replay value is limited. Each map has five challenges, which give bonus XP, gold or items. Some want you to defeat champions, others to achieve a certain number of kills with one weapon. Later some need you to activate hexes, which either buff monsters or debuff you.
Also every map has a set number of secrets to find. Those are item or gold chests.
The number of different enemies seems a bit limited so far. Most share the same model and have just a few different animations. There're some hilarious gimmicks, but a few more different mobs wouldn't hurt the game at all.
Controls:
And here comes the big let down. The controls are abysmal at best. There're two different control sets. Normal and Mouse Movement. Normal is WASD movement control, which is... well... you might get used to it... I simply can't. I played every ARPG on god's planet with mouse movement... why you might think not in this game? Well... to be honest the mouse movement is totally broken. You might remember Diablo. You click with your left mouse button and the character moves to this position. You hold the left mouse button and the character moves in the direction your mouse cursor points. This totally holds true for this game, but... not really. The most distinct feature of Victor Vran, namely elevation and jumping, made a total mess of that. I have been in High Quarter yesterday. To reach a certain secret chest you have to jump up over a few balconies and down on a roof. Sounds easy... yeah... no! The game has a problem calculating the exact position of your movement order. I was walking on the roof. On the backside of the mansion was an alleyway. You can access it if you walk around the house. But while I was clicking on the roof, the game thought I clicked on the alleyway behind the house. So Victor moved in every direction instead of the one I was pointing at. Also jumping over fences or hedges can get frustrating if you're not at the right angle or distance. The only workaround is, to constantly rotate the camera in a position where there're no obstacles. As much as I love this game, this really makes me want to rage quit sometimes.
I really enjoy the game so far. But the controls need a serious overhaul.
