This game has a niche target audience so I'll do my best to outline it below. If i have to give a rating I would give it an 8/10 and reccomend getting it on sale. I'm very aware that while I enjoy these games reccomending them is a bit dodgy as alot of people simply will not like what this game is. It does what it tries to do but that wont appeal to ALOT of people.
REASONS NOT TO BUY THIS GAME:
This game is not mechanically deep, characters roles are pretty simple to figure, beyond buffs debuffs and manipulating the turn system theres not alot to learn, the last one is a nice touch but still not a good game for someone who wants to think hard about their strategy.
Story is pretty poor in general (though not even close to as bad as rebirth 2 imo) and it has alot of repetition in monsters, dungeons etc.
The game is rated 12+ and that age level seems appropriate so if you're looking for adult images, look elsewhere. Fanservice is tame and sporadic.
It has quite alot of post game content through the free dlcs but unfortunately there is pretty much no way to progress to the last 4 areas or higher level fights in a  natural way. To do these you simply turn on the "in-game power level hax" and grind levels for an hour or two. This means that to keep things fun post game you have to carefully balance your levels or else you will be annihilated/untouchable.
The difficulty is a bit low for alot of the games until you reach the ultra late-game at which point it reaches stupid levels and the only way to balance is essentially to be really careful about how you break the game (see above point)
The 4th wall gets SMASHED repeatedly here. All the games broke the 4th wall but this one just completely ignores to the point where even I got annoyed in later chapters and I'm normally immune to it.
REASONS TO BUY THIS GAME:
The games characters are the main draw. Its a mix of a visual novel with a turn based rpg and the characters keep the visual novel element highly entertaining for the most part. Having all the dlc characters active can make it a bit too much dialogue wise so I reccomend not using them for a first playthrough if you intend to do more than 1. Some of the characters might drive some people crazy and as obvious as it might sound, anime like characters and reactions are plentiful so if you like anime you probably have a higher chance of liking this though I'm sure its not necessary.
Is funny.... well I think so anyway :D
The battle system while simple is fun to play and the animations are really smooth. If you have played the other games you have a good idea whats going on but this one is a step up on this front, not anything massively different just little things that make game more fun to play. The entire interface is massively improved in this game too, it still has its flaws but the menu in this game alone is enough to make it the best of the three.
Theres a challenge system introduced where you get little bonuses by completing challenges and while some of them are a little painful and the higher targets in many are RIDICULOUS, its still a nice addition.
The game isnt too short at about 40-60 hours for a casual playthrough of true ending if you read everything, certainly not long by rpg standards but long enough that you wont feel ripped off.

Just finished this game on Nightmare.
Warning: Contains spoilers.
The game's story has a really great flow and won't let you feeling hang up when the game is over.
The game manages to take you through an asylum with all sorts of horrors and just when you think you've seen enough it gives you even more.
Though, I do feel that the big guy was introduced to the player (me) a bit too early and later on he felt a bit of a chore to deal with.
Also, the ending was quite interesting; Did not expect that turn of events. Though, it sort of strikes me as a bit weird that the ghost would hurt you so bad and then take over you.
The ai is a bit 'naive' when it comes to finding you while hiding and you can outrun most of your opponents so in many cases if you know where you are going you can just rush to it until you find a 'safezone'.
Regardless, it is still a thrill to deal with the ai and it is true that often the ai surprises you in ways that you did not expect.
Hiding spots are vast but a bit repetitive in the way that they are presented. There were some cases where I would run to a dead end without any hiding spots while being chased and the only thing that helped me through was luckily the way the ai was designed, where I would run from wall to wall until I'd find a way back whilst it would just stand there and watch me, while occasionally hitting me once, which allowed for a couple of mistakes on my end. I'd love to see more diverse and scattered hiding spots though (in a sequel perhaps).
The puzzles were a bit too simple and/or repetitive; That could maybe be a bit adjusted next time. At least when you are not in immediate danger, because then you can wander around a bit more and explore.
Even on Nightmare, I was never too careful about using my batteries and only once did I almost run out of batteries, only to find another seconds to a minute later, but maybe I was just lucky to be at the right spot the right time.
The graphics were stunning and the scenery was suprisingly diverse and big, certainly a one of a kind asylum (Just kidding).
The music and sound effects were really well done; Though I do wish the characters would have a bigger collection of one-liners for when they have lost you in a chase, for example. Moreover, in some cases I was certainly away from danger but the 'spooky' music would still keep playing, which then started to feel irritating.
Regardless of any small faults the game was extremely enjoyable to me.
I'd give it a 9/10 because it feels like there is some room for improvement.
Strongly recommend to anyone who likes horror adventure games.
PS. Please give us a sequel, or something along those lines!!

#Edited for the first launch day#
Having played this game for 50+ hours under different conditions, difficulties and scenarious, along with getting the very first A+ score, I can safely say the following: get it. It is a 3D Faster Than Light + a few more games mixed in it (most notably Star Trek Bridge Commander) + Ironman experience.  It is there to test the fans of the rogue-like hardcore genre who do not complain about losing stuff or people, getting destroyed, then learning and adapting as a result. There is no save and load function. You roll the roulette and you live with what you've gotten in a beautiful 3d FTL-Star Trek format.
FOREWORD:
If someone says that the game has no replay value, they have played it way too little. Look at my play time. I rarely did the same run twice, unless trying to beat my previous score or testing new stuff.
The game is out of early access as of today, the 04.03.2015. Sadly, it already received a number of negative reviews during the years of development, so you will be looking at mixed reviews for a while. Most of it was because the devs were trying to find the reasons for the game not launching for a number of people, and those were readily cranking out the negative reviews. FYI, before I start with the good and the bad.
As usual, I will start with the good and the bad.
The absolute BEST:
The game generates meaningful stories through its gameplay, the type that make you take to the forums and share, be it for a win or a loss. How you had a great playthrough until everything started falling apart, people started dying, enemies were swarming you in throves and eventually destroyed you. Or how everything was so bleak, you were out of resources but managed to find a solitary planet where you safely did 6+ probe runs, restocked like crazy and won the game? Or how you went all out berserk and punched your way through the enemy lines like a boss? Or how a single rash decision on an away mission lost you two of your most valuable crew members and it all went downhill OR you still won nevertheless? Yep, all of this is possible. I absolutely love this about a game.
The Good:
1. Beautiful backdrops - the space, the planets and the suns look beautiful. The space must be black by default, but you are playing a game right?
2. The ship is also a looker. I personally love the way it appears on my screen with all of its flashing blue red and metal stuff. Once you start building structures, they will also appear inside it, which adds a new level of immersion.
3. Resource Management - picking what you want, what you need, when you need it might be the difference between defeat and a victory. Shortages really punish you, and even if you win, it affects your score big time.
4. You get to pick your ship parts - this allows for huge customization. You may pick a nimble ship with fewer systems but tons of cargo space, or you can make yourself a juggernaut. with less storage space and better weapons, absorption, shuttle missions, etc. All up to you.
5. Last ditch effort - this type of play really reels you in as you see the last 10 000 people of the human race die from lack of food, oxygen, killed by enemies and random events. Speaking about random events...
6. Random events are either detrimental (e.g. Alien Flu) or beneficial (Training for crewmembers). This forces you to deal with situations even more strategically, because while fighting, people still die.
7. Ironman - no going back. I love this type of play for certain games and this one is certainly worth it, just like FTL.
8. You have a decent grid size and you need to pick your way through it till you reach the end goal, dealing with hostile encounters, resource shortages, planet and object exploration, etc.
9. The combat - in FTL the combat was minimalistic. Shoot something and it will either hit or miss. Here, you need to think on your feet, use different coloured weapons and shield harmonics, defend and fire when necessary, evade shots, pause, think, and do your best. If you wish you can opt to play completely without pausing - that makes the combat extremely dynamic, but you will most likely suffer way more hits.
10. Strategy wins the game - trust me, I felt that. Making rash decisions isn't the best thing. You really need to accept the position you are in and adapt to it. Playing to the strengths of your ship and crew is key.
11. Renaming crewmembers - are you a Star Trek, Star Wars, Farscape or another franchise's fan? Or you like to use the names of your closest friends or family members? You can!
12. Like FTL, there are multiple ways to victory - at present, I would split them into sneaky, semi-sneaky, bold and reckless types of wins.
13. The game lets you do stuff on the fly. You just need to learn the mechanics. I am not going to spoil those for you.
14. Runs vary. A faster engine will get you to the end goal quicker, but a battle-hardened combat crew getting you trough 1 vs 3 encounters is a joy to behold.
15. Flying through gorgeous space. If you dont like it, it is simply not your jam.
16. Play-throughs take about 2 hours, which I find good for these types of games.
17. Scoring system that allows you to check how well you did in comparison to the others.
18. Many new features added since EA - 3 difficulty settings, ship setups, civilian management, more away missions, etc.
19. Replayability has been improved a lot since alpha, so you will be looking at a lot of different runs. While the end goal is the same, just like FTL, nobody forces you to reach it - a full exploration run (mine was the first full exploration run to date) takes about 8 hours.
Ok. Here's THE BAD.
The ABSOLUTE WORST:
You will ragequit if you hate games that punish you. Many a time. Get used to it, or don't buy the game.
To continue...
1. Steep learning curve - you need to play with ship setups for a while, learn how they work, what resources to pick at start, how long to stay at a planet, which awaymissions are easier and which ones harder, and so on.
2. NO multiplayer, like FTL. Can't be fixed.
3. Some bugs are still present, but the devs are all over the community forum, listening to the people and taking notes. Always good to see.
4. Combat - while I praised it, one can still find it minimalistic.
5. Punishing away missions since alpha. While the death to success ratio has been curbed a bit, and more choices given to the player, one should still exercise extreme caution when taking on away missions..
6. Some players still can't launch the game. Best check the forums before buying this game. The devs are hard at work at it.
CONCLUSION:
The game is quite the looker, and has this FTL last ditch type of feeling. Up until now, the devs have been on the money with the updates, consistently adding more content - with the last patch enabling us to manage the civilian population by adding more buildings, with the option to upgrade them in the future to avoid the constant civilian problems. Whoever says this game is short... is right, but it can also be played is a plethora of ways, adding replayability. Fastest way to goal, explore the whole quadrant, go left side, go right side, be sneaky, fight a lot, try not to fight at all. Or plain handicap yourself if U R A PRO. Just try it! I know I did, with runs with as low as 575 credits. To me, this game is one huge sandbox - I get to pick my difficulty (and by that I don't mean the pre-set ones), my setup, my way to play the game and try to win. It is fun - whether you should choose to challenge yourself or just explore the vast quardant of space and enjoy the extremely atmospheric Into the Stars.

I really want to like this game as I've enjoyed all other Paradox games I've played, but this game is simply unplayable for me.  It takes an inordinately long time to load and then will crash within a few minutes of loading.  I was able to play it a bit better when I first bought it awhile back, but it crashed a lot then too though I got farther into the game then so I shelved it hoping that problem would be fixed, but alas it hasn't been.  In the meantime, I tried Supreme Ruler 1936 and liked that game much better, though very similar.  The main reason I like Supreme Ruler 1936 better is simply because I can play it!  I think Hearts of Iron III is much more complex which is nice, but can be confusing and overwhelming and the tutorial in-game is a joke, it doesn't tell you anything you couldn't figure out on your own in just a few minutes.  Luckily, I was able to find a good tutorial by Surray that helps a lot, but alas the problem still exists with the crashes!!  I think the graphics in this game are a bit drab and lacking (Supreme Ruler 1936 were better imo), though I'm not too concerned with graphics in a game like this, but it just helps with the feel of the game.  I thought Supreme Ruler 1936 played a lot better (a lot simpler, didn't have to manage so much, not so easy to make mistakes), though Supreme Ruler 1936 has a few flaws of it's own... namely that if you amass a large force and invade and take another country and keep them around too long you run out of resources too quickly and then you're screwed.  I think it is probably something I'm doing wrong, but still, I should be able to play like I wish to play... within reason.  Usually I have to quit game because units have become frozen and can't move because they can't be refueled and I can't repair facilities even though I had a surplus prior to the invasion and had a huge surplus I couldn't get my infrastructure to meet my demands once I invaded and became overextended.  I also think that the AI for SR 1936 is a bit inefficient at times, a lot of time units won't move at all even though they have supplies, fuel and everything.  Probably my fault, but still frustrating to get so far into game and have amassed such a huge army and done so well up to that point only to have to quit because you've become stranded and can't do anything.  Saying that though, SR 1936 is still playable (up to a point) while HOI3 isn't (at least not for me).
If I could play this game without it crashing I would probably enjoy it and it would probably get a recommendation.  I would say I would probably prefer Supreme Ruler 1936 or it's ilk over the HOI3 line and recommend those games more.
For those who can play this game they probably enjoy it, but I've seen quite a few that have problems with the game crashing so I would be leery about purchasing game unless a patch to address crashing is made available, which seems more unlikely since HOI4 is now in the works.  I would probably wait for HOI4 and hope the crashing issues are resolved.

So I bought this game day 1, when it came out on 360, and too be honest, it was dissappoining then. However, since then this game has become much better. There are still a few things that need to be addressed. Until the Cops vs Racers update, I'd give it a 7/10. Once the new update is here, depending on what gets fixed, it might go up.
1) Open world. And I mean OPEN WORLD. The map is immense, go any where you want to go. It literally takes almost an hour to drive at 150mph to get from NY to LA, and that's if you don't get distracted by something shiny.
2)Envornment. Might not make a difference in how your vehicle handles. However the change from forest to snowy mountains to desert adds life to the game. the addition of wildlife also adds a nice touch. challenging when your going 180mph in a McLaren and then DEER!!!!
3)AI. Ubisoft still has some work to do on this one. However, compared to what it was at the beginning, massivly better. The cities actually feel like their alive to a point. Its also neat when your in the countryside, theres no where near as much traffic as in the city.
4)DLC. I know most people don't like paying for extra game. However, the DLCs have brought much needed content to the game, and has greatly added to the depth of the game.
5)Graphics. They are just fantastic to look at, and i have a $50 low resolution TV, so imagine if a High-def TV is used. I can see the individual drops of rain on the windshield.
6)The cars. What car game can be complete  without the cars. I still felt that there were too few cars, maybe about 35 total with the DLC. They have been adding new cars for free however, so there's still hope for this one.
7)Cops. Ok so this is probably my biggest irritant. The cops are well, easy to beat. They don't really present a challange. However, they do set up roadblocks, PIT you, and they have even down the rolling box on me. However it is so easy to get away. On this one, Im waiting too see what happens with the new cops vs racers uodate in November.
8) Physics. Kindy goofy. For those looking for a simulator level of driving, go look elsewhere. Its got a arcady feel to it, which for me its fine. If I wanted simulater I'd go play Forza.
9)Always online. With good internet connection, you can still play and not deal with anyone else. They'll still be there, but it doesn't force you to interact with them. However it would be nice too have a offline option. Eventually Ubisoft will have to add it in. They cant keep the servers up forever.
10)Story. Really short. Feels kind of forced at times, and makes you go "wha" at times. But i didnt get tis game to watch cutscenes, i got it to take a sportscar off roading and launching it off cliffs, because why the F--- not.
Overall, I give this game 7/10. It is fun racing game that can make hours dissappear. Id wait til its on sale to get it. Get the one woth all the packs. It'll make the game that much better too play.

I've only played a couple hours
and I'd have to say this game
is just amazingly hilarious! It's
a simple platformer game
with the catch that all players
can add a part every turn to help
and/or hinder other players
(including themselves) while trying
to reach the goal alive for points.
Everyone living = no points,
Everyone Dieing = no points,
so the goal is to make the stage
hard enough that someone can fail
but easy enough that someone
(preferably yourself) can beat the
stage.
The controls are basic, move left,
right, jump, duck, run, with wall kicking.
The controls are quite responsive
so moving around really is simple.
What makes things really challenging
are the parts.
Parts range from simple blocks
(plain blocks), to moving objects
(moving platforms), to hazerds
(spikes, arrow traps, black holes),
which can have combo effects
that mix with other parts (arrow trap
+ black hole) to make insane
death machines. With up to four
players, the stages can be the
easiest platformer ever from the
start, to an absolute massacre by
the next turn!
This game can be played on one
computer as a crazy party game,
or if you don't haveany friends
available, there's online
multiplayer which can bring just
as much laughs just by the nature
of the game alone. There always
seems to be people playing, and
if all rooms are full, a couple
refreshes will usually show an
open one that usually fills up quite
quickly for max players. The only
downside to online are the
ragequiters. With a game like this
dieing alot is part of the fun, but
as usual, some people can't handle it.
If they're the host, they end the game,
when they leave, but even if they're
not the host, one less player = one
less part = less chaos, and the game
is the funnest when there's parts
flying all over.
Overall, this is a really great game
for laughs. Controls are good, you can
play with friends, there's always people
online, and even with rage quiters, you
most likley will get a laugh just by killing
yourself with a trap you thought you
could easily avoid, but than become the
first victim of. I know I do often :3

I've played similar games, Van Helsing 1 & 2, Diablo 3, Torchlight, and this is in the same vein. It's not anything new, in fact I feel like Van Helsing at least gave some replay value with different classes.
+ Weapons are tied in to skills and there are no permanent talent decisions.
+ Bounties for killing elites & Treasure hunts (finding "pieces") reward you with gold and chests/items.
+ Campaign took me 10 hours of playing, fairly straight through but taking a detour now and then to get a visible secret or complete a bounty.
+ You get access to all the inventory slots pretty quickly.
+ Transmute system for upgrading your equipment.
+ Seems to be an active community with build guides and such on Steam.
- No classes, you can change your armor to affect how your Special Ability (Demon Power) works, but that's it.
- I didn't know if there was enough replay value to make me continue playing.
- Switching to "casual" mode didn't really seem to dip the difficulty as much as I was expecting - but that is not really a plus or minus but I was hoping for it to be very casual because I just wanted to experience the story without having to worry about perfecting my gear or build.

Here is my Neptunia Re;Birth 3 review :)
I will start by saying the Nep and her friends are back in tossing 30-minute to hour-long chats which plays out like a visual novel with RPG elements.
The good :)
~Seeing more of this series coming over is a nice thing.
~Being able to have all the DLC at once instead of waiting for it in pieces is nice.
~Plutia and Neptune are amazing
~Scouts are gone, replaced with Stella's Dungeon.
~Battles are handled extremely fast.
The Bad :(
~The conversations and events can easilly last 30 minutes to an hour without seeing any actions.
~The dungeons are frequently reused with different sets of enemies.
~There is a lot of dialogue, but there is not as much voice acting as the first game...which is what I love to see.
~I would have loved to see dialogue which would poke fun at the fact that the characters are in a 'new game+'
~Battles are really about overpowering enemies and not truly using that many tactics.
~DLC Characters are extremely overpowered until around Chapter 6 - 8.
~GLITCH: Very rarely, if a player had played for many hours...sometimes the game would crash entering battle.
The truth when taking Global Steam Stats into account:
The game maintains an "Overwhelmingly Positive" review considering its a port and slight remake of the 2012 game Neptunia Victory. However at the time of this writing:
~Only 80% of the playerbase chose to start the game.
~Only 52% of the playerbase completed the prologue chapter.
~Only 47% of the playerbase completed the first chapter.
~Only 37% finished the second chapter.
~Less than 5% of the playerbase had the resolve and endurance to finish the game and actually see the ending(s).
If one knows a little bit of math, one can say that out of the people who actually have played the game (80%), of that total population....we can write 52/.8 = 65. Basically two thirds of those who started the game went through the prologue chapter at most. However, when the math is applied....by the end of Chapter 2, less than half of the people who actually started the game) actually remained playing the game passed the second chapter.
The game is really for the playerbase who actually likes a combination of Visual Novels mixed with RPG interfaces in its own game. I love the game for its humor in a time where most games are super-serious and humorless, but even I admit that when I started the game to show my fiancee how the game started...it took an hour to go through the prologue chapter because most of it were the two of us reading it.
I am currently going through the New Game+ attempting to get the TRUE ENDING after getting the Good Ending. :) I am one of the few who actually went through the entire game ;)
Get this game if you have the patience to read a ton for a lighthearted, lukewarm story :) This game reminds me of games like Xenogears that beat out final fantasy in acquiring the award for "most ridiculous amount of text" in a scene. :)

Highly recommend this game for fans of action role playing games like Diablo, Torchlight, Van Helsing. Initially this game felt and looked very similar to The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing. It was also a little hard to get used to the control mechanisms of WSAD for movement and the mouse controlling the camera and attacks. This was a change from the numerous ARPGs that use the click-to-move mechanic.
Anyway, after getting through the first few maps, attempting to complete some of the challenges and getting to level 15, the game really starts to take hold of you. Even moreso when I found the online multiplayer option and co-oped with a friend. This then really enabled us to have some great fun and 8 hours later we realised how cool this game is becoming. We're now level 22 and each play session we discover something new.
The mechanic of transmuting in this game is outstanding and couple this with completing map challenges gives alot of replayability to maps that you may have rushed through to progress the story. On top of this, i started to get some links to yellow items in the global chat. I ignored these initially as it looked like spam (weird named items) however learnt that these are treasure maps, bounties and other game challenges that get dropped in later levels. Not only do you get them when they drop in loot, you can right-click and share them to whomever is playing online in your particular game room and they can get it too. I had about 36 people in my game room, but only myself and my friend were playing co-op. Not entirely sure how the game rooms work as im sure there's more than 36 people playing in the world.
So far I'm absolutely hooked and looking forward to finding more of what this game has to offer. My OCD is also going in overdrive trying to finish all challenges on each map as i go through the game. Exciting fun times ahead!

Many undead have come to the lands in the game to do exactly what you are trying to do.  I won't get too into the little details as there is a lot to say and explain. Just take my word for it. Attention to detail is what makes Souls games great, and this might be the most poorly planned game in the entire series. With that said, It's still a souls game. Combat is excellent, new areas are tricky, the lore is still overall very good, and the aesthetic of the game is very pleasing. I completed the game on ps3 upon launch, but the PC port is very well optimized.

I nominated Banished for the Test of Time award.  It could be bigger, it could evolve further, but what it does it does so well it's hard to not keep coming back.
Winter Update:
I left Banished running overnight at 10x to take a run at the last 200 year achievement.  I figured I trained my peeps well, they'd survive without me for a night (errr, 20 years).  Recovering from the fallout is about the most fun I've had with this game, and that's saying something.  When I returned, tornadoes and fires had ravaged two major population centers.  Two markets were in ruins and 50 homes destroyed.  Half my farmers unassigned.  They were freezing with almost no stored food with twice as much consumed as produced in the last year.  500 people without tools.  But I've got 1400 stored iron, weirdly enough.  Even weirder, my population is not only within my designed parameters at about 950, it's actually been on a growth spurt for 10 years.  How did my town grow under these conditions?  I like to think they evolved the ability to digest iron while I was sleeping.  And that's why I love my people.

You've just gotta hate it when a game dev figures out that exact formula to completely overwhelm your good sense and trap you in a never-ending spiral of digital imprisonment.  It must be amusing to wield that kind of power over people.  I imagine the dev has a throne and a white cat and often spontaneously "mwahahahaha!"s while stroking the kitty.
I was half finished with the tutorial when I began to suspect that this game would suck up hundreds of hours over the next few years.  About 20 hours later, I know I was right.  I don't know how long it will take to build out the modest space I'm in now, but I know when I'm done I'm gonna want to try again, and again, and the modding possibilities are tantalizing.
Sure, the interface could be improved (suggestion: display recommended worker count alongside material requirements while laying down pastures/fields) in several places and there are some limitations to the A.I. and prioritization that require a somewhat restrained style of play, but all in all I haven't been this pleased with a purchase since I bought Defense Grid.  I actually feel a tiny bit guilty for having gotten Banished on sale.  Release some DLC, Shining Rock, and I'll do my penance.

Dark Souls II does not meet my expectation of a difficult and challenging game with a steep learning curve. I am aware that this game series all about trying to defeat overpowered bosses by repeated try-and-error-approaches and thus includes death after death after death.
What I found is a game that punishes you by replaying a whole section over and over again with worse conditions in each try. Every item gathered, every money earned just vanishes, and on top of it, overall health is reduced unless some rare item is sacrificed. Whereas I like challenging situations in games that are rewarding if finished, Dark Souls II just delivers unexpected deaths of which one half are due to environment (enemies and traps) and the other half are due to poor level design (edge next to an abyss, stones hindering dodging, walls hindering attacks).
The Scholar of the First Sin edition apparently makes things worse by placing common but very strong enemies right in the first few areas to be encountered after starting a new game.
This is neither difficult nor challenging, it is just frustrating and somewhat insulting. After all, this game does quite the opposite of rewarding you for playing it. Whereas I belong to those calling for more challenging games (a scarce resource in the last years), I will not join those defending games like this.
If you enjoy messing around with a game that earns its nimbus by flawed design, go for it. If you enjoy constantly switching to a walkthrough to avoid unnecessary instant deaths, go for it. If you do not mind accumulating played hours by playing a section over and over again, go for it. If you want to play a game that makes you analyze enemies' behaviour and develop tactics from that, gives a rewarding victory afterwards, and actually encourages you to retry over and over, avoid this game.

Being part of this game since it's beta on gface. I would've recommended it at the time when it was still in its haydays, but due to how far it has gone downhill since then, I can only recommend this game for those to try as something new.
So, let me break it down in the pros and cons:
This game is moderately fast paced, but not fast compared to other games I have played in my lifetime.
High quality models, textures, and fairly high quality sound.
A moderate selection of armor/weapons to match your playstyle, with whichever class you have chosen to play as your main class.
You have a choice to put attachments on your weapons on-the-fly using the C button (or whichever button you mapped it to).
Interesting maps to explore, pvp and pve.
A system similar to COD, where if you do certain achievements, you can unlock medals/patches/backrounds to have with your name/profile picture.
A series of interesting seasonal/event items.
The ability to slide, which I would have to see as this game being unique in that aspect, before other games started to adopt this feature into their games years later.
When you level to level 12, you find out that all of your weapons will not be able to dent an enemy, unless you learn to aim for the head all the time. You will need to unlock armor, and better weaponry stat, just so you can find any miniscule of chance to attempt to match against people higher then level 12. This makes the skill curve for this game in the levels of the downright stupid the second you hit that level.
The feature to repair your items that degrade through time. Since beta the struggle required a bit of grinding just to achieve enough money to repair your items, and another trick being buying the same item to increase its durability, which I saw a ton of people doing back then, just to attempt to save money. Nowadays, you need to do every single daily bonus just to have adequate money to repair your gear, with no extra money to really get you through to try a new weapon, unless you grind for hours on top of that.
The fact back in beta there were a ton of people who DID hack or boosted for their respective levels, by making private rooms and farming off of eachother for exp/money and whatnot.
The sole fact that back then, most of the "good" weapons like the karkov and such were capsule weapons, meaning YOU NEEDED TO USE CASH TO OBTAIN THE MOST BROKEN/OVERPOWERED WEAPONS IN THE GAME. Nowadays it is not as bad, due to rebalancing of most weapons, but the tradeoff is that there are a ton of weapons severely nerfed for no reason now. There are still a few weapons that are capsule weapons, however, but many of them aren't severely overpowered compared to their regular counterpart whatsoever.
The fact that even since back then, there hasn't been a server for SA, or proper optimization for NA server, so the people in the western part of the US aren't 1-2 bar like everyone else, but people in the east and in canada can have shining full bars.
The fact that the insane forms of harassment/racism/ and cheating that has been going on before, and after the transferring of publishers is apalling, and reporting/sending in a ticket/recordings/pictures do not seem to do a dent to these people, making it seem that me, or anyone else who have done the same thing feel that the staff are actually listening to the community, or investigating any problems or concerns people have had in the past/present/ and future.
To add insult to injury, most of these people are these said "p2w" people, who buy VIP on a regular basis to max, which is pretty much the whole sense that they have "immunity" if they throw any form of cash at you, the devs, just so they can get away with things such as this. The problem is that this isn't just an issue for just this game, but any other game that has a p2w feature to date, which is downright wrong in itself.
The removal of most maps during the transition from crytek to
. (Where is farm?)
The hit registration/hitmarkers. (You can shoot a person in the forehead, many times over, and it will not reg for the life of you, you have to literally shoot them right in the face, just to get that well-deserved headshot.) (There is also a bug/issue where you can shoot a person point blank, and the shot will just penetrate through them, with no registration at all, but it sure registered well on the wall/object behind them.)
The fact that the lack of community makes most game modes unplayable to begin with, and grinding for money is more of a daily chore, then anything, seeing how nowadays Co-op seems to be everyones staple to get money, and not a good ol' plant the bomb. (My personal favorite is TDM, but doing an hour for a measly 5k? Not worth the time.)
Anyways, as there may be more PROS or CONS I may have not have listed here, that I may wish to add in the future, my final verdict is that I cannot recommend the game in the state it is now.
This game had awesome potential, and I personally come on  it every few days for a run of shooting people, but it is not a game I can overall recommend to those that are looking for an FPS to actually call home, until a comback happens.
If you have any further questions of this game, do not hesitate to message me, also, this review may change depending on how the state of the game goes, but as for now, I can't recommend this game as a keeper, but as something to compare and contrast with my pros/cons, and every other person on the negative side of this list, as well as trying it to have first-hand view of the potential this game has.

I want to like this game. For a free to play co-op shooter, this game has a lot to offer. Consistent updates, an intense co-op experience, and adequate multiplayer almost make it worth it. However, lately, it's almost like this game wants me to hate it. With little to no matchmaking once you've put in 15 or so hours, you'll be in with the big dogs, who have the best weapons, best armor, best gadgets, and best attachments. The default equipment is sh*t. Good luck unless you want to put in another 20-40 hours to get to where they are, suffering the whole time. Or you can spend real money. Which I understand, as this is a free-to-play, but it is quite unbalanced after you hit Lvl 12 or so.
I like that you get consistent rewards each time you level up, because I feel like I'm always working towards something. Like a 24hr trial of a weapon/armor piece, but after that, unless you are high enough level (and for any of the good weapons, you have to be 30+), you can't just buy it outright with all your hard-earned cash. This infuriates me to no end.
With Clans feeling like a tack-on and playing with/adding friends getting to be a nightmare these days, this isn't worth your time in the long run. If you want to play in short bursts, this is your poor man's CoD.
Finally, the latency is what hurts the most. IT. IS. AWFUL. EVERYONE has 2 bars or less. Hit registration is so broken sometimes I refuse to continue playing.
Pros:
Variety of weapons
Variety of attachments
Variety of modes
Gameplay is relatively fun in PVP, until you hit Lvl 12
Enjoyable Co-op experience
Consistent rewards
Cons:
Want to play with people who are near your rank once you get past Lvl 12? Too bad
Want to try a mode other than Storm, TDM, or Plant the Bomb? Too bad
Want to play with friends who just picked up the game? Too bad
Want a good weapon? Either get a high enough rank or spend real money
Want the best attachments like grenade launchers? Either get a high enough rank or spend real money
Want good armor/skins? Either get a high enough rank or spend real money
Want a rewarding experience after 15 hours? Either get a high enough rank or spend real money
Overall, I'd give it a 6/10. Fun in short bursts, but don't expect to enjoy yourself after 15-20 hours unless you plan to spend plenty of real money and grind endlessly for the better weapons.

Update December 12, 2017.
Continue to avoid this game. Despite leaving early access the title has failed to find its way. If there was anything that emphasized this more it would be the player engagement over the last year. It has been in a death spiral. Anyone who takes the time to look over the SteamCharts data for this game can plainly see the PC community is near dead and has given up on the game.
The latest update does little to curb the lack of fun in the game. It is a thinny veiled treadmill designed to offer you a shallow reward system for grinding the same tired maps again and again. It a minor sense of progression in exchange for hours of repeating the same content again and again.
The mode attempts to mix things up with monster bonuses randomly applied to lanes, but this is countered by the 100% random mix of enemies in lanes. This continues Trendy's track record of forcing scenarios onto players that completly nullify the majority of hero towers. Rather than creating scenarios where all heroes get to shine, the onslaught maps reduce every build to one that successfully withstands Cyber Orcs and EMP Kobolts.
Update May 7, 2017.
Just avoid this title. The design team is hell bent on turning the once great tower defense series into a confused mess. Update after update the game gets more refined visually, and less fun. Bugs and hiccups aside, the gameplay focus of the team is so lost that there is very little to enjoy in this title anymore. A damn shame considering the source material and history of the Dungeon Defenders franchise.
Update October 10, 2016.
Current Play Time: 1,639+ hours of play time. This includes close pre-alpha, through public alpha, through pre release, through early acces.
tl;dr: Pass on this game until they deliver on the vision a quality successor to DD1 that is just as feature rich and improves upon the original formula. While the current content demonstrates the great potential for this title to elevate the original Dungeon Defenders experience to new heights, the lack of depth and simplified character kits and meaningless grind are insurmountable negatives.
Unfortunately, the game has not grown substantial for veteran players. While I continue to take an active role in the very limited community of the game, there is little longevity in the current build of the game.
The development path is all over the place and the development is quick to paint you a picture of an ideal future. "Down the line" and "it would be great" are common mantras on the developer streams, but these do not often reach fruition.
My initial impressions of the game are still valid (see original review), but the game has not grown enough to justify a positive rating in the last 1-2 years. The game looks great and is a visual upgrade when compared to its predecessor. Unforunately it lacks the depth of content that made DD1 a joy for fans of the series.
I pulled up the orignal Dungeon Defenders to take a look at some of the content that made that game so appealing. Many of those core features like surival mode, pure strategy, hardcore, or mixed modes are still missing. Gear progression and strategic diveristy have remained stagnant for quite some time and are rigid in comparison to DD1's universal loot. There has been little in the way of meaningful changes to the game to create challenging and diverse end game scenarios.
The utopian ideal for this game would be a huge step above DD1, but at the current development
pace there is little hope that it will be a worthy sequel to DD1 without another 2-3 years or work.
Free to Play or Pay to Win: I would like to dispell any notions that the game is pay to win. I do commend design team for maintaining the integrity of the game by avoiding selling power to users. There is nothing that cash purposes buy you that impacts your power level over other users.
Original Review:
Current Play Time: 360+ Hours participating in the closed pre-alpha.
tl;dr:
If you enjoyed Dungeon Defenders Eternia then picking up Trendy’s latest installment of the tower defense series is a no brainer. There are still a lot of improvements to come to the game, but in its current state it still shines as a tower defense title.
General
Despite being an Early Access title, Dungeon Defenders 2 is in a well polished state. There are 10 beautifully rendered maps to play on, with multiple levels of difficulty, and the loot system is fleshed out enough to offer hours of replayability.
There are 4 playable characters with their own unique set of towers and abilities. You will have to master each of their kits (or call in some friends) if you want to complete every map. The interplay between towers is rewarding and there are dozens of effective strategies for every map.
The difficulty on later levels does fall short. Once you reach end game equipment, none of the maps offer much of a challenge. That may change with the introduction of harder difficulties or other game modes, but keep that in mind if you expect to push your characters to their limits.
Multiplayer
The lobby system is still in its infancy, but you are able to participate in both public and private games. The game incentivizes playing with others as it provides you a bonus to your drop rate. Additionally, all item drops are instanced for each player. This means you will never have to fight anyway over who gets a legendary drop. Unfortunately, the game still lacks a trade feature so for now you are unable to share loot with friends.
Core multiplayer features like the ability to browse through a list of hosted games, kick players, and created player restrictions (level requires) are not currently available. If you choose to play in public games you will be playing with whatever other players are currently in the public realm for your chosen difficulty level.
The current pre-alpha community has so far been very helpful and pleasant. Your mileage may vary depending on the types of players who enter your game. This revision of the game does include a dynamic ping system that allows you to send simple messages about where defenses should go. This goes a long way towards aiding in communication when working with a team of strangers.
Overall
There is still a lot of work to be done to improve the player experience, but as far as Early Access titles go this is by far the most fleshed out and polished I have come across. The game will ultimately be free to play, but at the current price point the game offers enough content to justify the purchase for fans of tower defense games.

Well that was fast, the third installment in such a short period of time, Idea Factory must put a lot of changes into there games, or do they? Here's the run down, each area of Gamindustri has it's own CPU and CPU candidate that looks over each area. This time around however, you aren't going around collecting the mascots power or anything like that, instead (Spoiler warning) Neptune gets sent to an alternate dimension that is in the 80's (Y'know, when cassets where still a big thing for games) and must find her way back to her dimension while at the same time, helping that dimension with it's problems. As always, you can expect a lot of references to the actual game industry, videos games and anime while poking fun at them. It's a series that loves to reference everything it possibly can but if that's not your thing, you may find the comedy to be a bit dull or repetitive.
Similar to the other games, it feels very JRPG esc so there is little you won't be familiar with. It leads me to think if Idea Factory will ever do anything different from the other Neptunia games since almost every aspect of this game is identical to the others that are currently available on Steam. I sometimes like to think it's a "Stick to what you know and what you can do" situation but that can sometimes come off as being lazy or re-using assets, since there's hardly anything different about this game compared to the others, apart from new characters and story. Briefly onto the options menu, there's hardly one again but on the plus side, the game does run at a solid 60FPS.
Yet again, the dungeons themselves aren't anything to write home about since they're fairly small with some consisting of several floors. They're pretty standard dungeons, as far as JRPG's go and don't have much in the way of exploration, just a small amount of enemies littering the area and random items and material dotted around. You would think that they'd do something more with the dungeons, since many JRPG's do but you gradually grow bored of exploring them since there's hardly anything to explore.
Moving on to the combat, there's practically nothing different here except for one change. Previously, you had to fill a guage everytime you entered a dungeon to pull off an EX finisher at the end of your combos by fighting enemies and would empty the moment you left the dungeon. Now however, your EX finishers are tied to your overall SP guage which makes the combat more enjoyable, albiet a bit easy. The games focus is it's strategy elements while being fast passed at the same time. In each battle, each character and enemy takes there turn when it's there's (Duh) so both you and the enemy can move each of your characters around the battle arena and position them carefully to get the most out of the battle. During one characters turn, you have multiple options for what you can have her do but only specific characters can do one special thing. There's:
Attack,
EXE skills,
Defend,
SP skills,
HDD on/off,
Switch,
Item,
Flee.
Whichever one you pick (Apart from HDD) will consume the characters turn and move to the next one in line. If you choose attack (Which you'll do a lot of the time) you are given the option to choose between three attacks that are tide to one of three buttons. These allow you to do different attacks which will have different effect but once you pick one, it'll move onto the next attack tab. Break focuses on depleting the enemies guard which if you accomplish that, the enemy will take more damage till it's there turn. Power which focuses on dealing damage and rush focuses on filling your SP guage. It leads to you having to mix and match your attacks together to deal with an enemy faster and effectively. The rest are pretty self explanatory apart from HDD on. Characters who are CPU's or CPU candidates have the ability to transform in the middle of battle, which increases there states but use up 20% of the SP gauge. Since it doesn't have any downsides to using it, you'll more then likely use it a lot of the time. Also, characters who aren't CPU's can also do there own transformation called Awaken which does practically the same thing.
As I've previously stated many times before and the main part of these games that I love so much is the art style. I adore how the environments are done, as well as how the characters are designed. Each are just so gorgeous to look at, they're colorful, bright and the way the colors blend together is fantastic. Speaking of the characters, we are introduced to a new character who goes by the name Plutia and I have to say, I find to her to be quite enjoyable. Ultimate Chicken Horse is a multiplayer puzzle platformer-kind of game. At the start every player selects a block, trap, or other thing that is shuffled into the party box, and then places in on the level, then the level is played by the players and points are awarded for their performance. Then the next turn to select and place things comes, and then the players go again, repeat until somebody wins. That sounds very simple, but the devil is within the details.
The game has a great selection of stages, twelve (I believe) very different levels with various gimmicks and themes, all of them just as fun as the last one. There's enough varriety to endlessly rotate the map roster and never get bored with any stage.
On those stages you can place various things. They range from blocks and platforms of various shape and size, to moving and rotating objects (that you can attach other things to with glue!), and ending with a lot of traps ranging from simple crossbows and spikes, to black holes, cannons, and puck shooters. With some clever planning you can create very complicated trap setups, and make the stages as tricky and challenging as you want.
But, hands down, the most fun thing about the game is the interactions between the elements you place. That aspect of the game is INSANE! You can attach a crossbow to a rotating block to make a rotating crossbow, and then place a black hole to curve the arrows in a weird angle to catch players of guard and get points from killing them, and that's only one example!. There's so much to explore here, the combinations and different type of configurations you can do feels like it's limitless with enough imagination, and it makes the game a thousand times more interesting and fresh every time you play a map.
I was never into party games myself, but Ultimate Chicken Horse is just so very charmful and fun, I am totaly in love with it! I will definitely put more time into it if my friends will be up for it. The game premise is simple, but it executes it extremely well, everything is so well put together and thought out, the scoring makes the game not just about rushing to win the stage, there's much more strategy here than meets the eye. Even the soundtrack is great, it sets the mood for the level perfectly, but it also fits a party game with it's upbeat music perfectly. It's tons of fun to play with friends, so definitely pick this up if you're looking for a superb party game!

Despite the terrible name, the forgettable story, the bad dialogue and inconsistent voice overs, Victor Vran provides an incredibly active and fun fighting system and the ability to almost completely recreate your character on the fly, even mid-battle.
I turned the Voice track off about three hours into the game, so I had a few odd moments when the hackneyed gothsylvania storyline intruded on the otherwise excellent game play. This ammounted to a vendor disappearing until I'd completed a particular mission or enemies on a map spontaneously disappearing and then reappearing several seconds later. My point is, that you can mostly dodge the story, which is a blessing.
The mediocre voiceovers that I listened to were stereotypical old horror movie rejects and the two voices warring in Victor Vran's head, one deadly serious like Max Payne, and the other mocking and filled with odd, anarchronistic references. The two fall totally flat, in my opinion.
But the visuals are detailed and interesting, if a little too consistently on the darker side. Most of the animations look nice and some of the sounds, particularly the ambient track are quite nice. The weapon sound effects, however, are repetitive and tend toward thudding, percussive or tearing sounds that limit my interest in using weapons such as the shotgun and the rapier, at least with the volume up.
While we are unfortunately stuck playing as Victor Vran (or Vicki as the mocking voice insists on calling you... yes, it's THAT bad), there are several levels of customization available.
By eschewing character attributes or skill trees like you'd see in most ARPGs, your character's abilities are constructed from two weapons, an armor, several Destiny Cards, which add to current basic stats such as health or grant procs of many different flavors, and two Demonic Powers that act as nuke powers or big whammy spells.
By collecting, upgrading and strategic equipping, it is possible to come up with all sorts of ways to smash, slash, zap and explode Victor Vran's numerous, varied and fun baddies. Vran can be kitted out to just lay down Demonic Powers by selecting weapons, Destiny Cards and armor that all add to the Overdrive Meter (i.e. Mana). Or life-stealing and healing procs can be stacked with heal-on-hit weapons to make a tanky sort of vampire character. An obvious possibility is stacking the very many on-crit effects to create massive spikes. The possibilites go on....
The point is that, though you're always stuck looking like the same guy in one of six different okay looking costumes, you can make him wreak havoc in many different ways. More than just switching weapons on the fly, though, you can pause the game at any time and change out any or all of Vran's equipment; thus, totally respecing the character. The generous inventory space allows for a hoarder's delight of stuff to swap, should the mood strike.
The maps and environments are all hand-crafted, so the surprises they contain become less effective on repetition. While it would be tempting to expect a random map option, there is rather a lot of content that can be replayed under different rules by way of the game's Hex System. Hexes increase the difficulty, but grant bonus experience and extra loot drops. The game also contains 5 Basic Challenges and 5 Elite Challenges per map, which leads to all sorts of opportunities to revisit favorite fights and scenes and try to win under some pretty strict and arbitrary conditions (e.g. killing seven tough baddies with PBAOE bombs without using any potions and such).
Victor Vran serves up a fair variety of baddies, but often in mass quantities. This leads to some crazy, frenetic fights, which the game generally does well at. Some targeting issues, such as with the Hammer, seem to have been addressed. The developers have released a roadmap of mostly free content, and they continue to balance and patch the game.
I cannot stress how important the feel of the combat is in this game. It allows for several, meaningful strategic choices by way of the different attack effects of your two weapons, a multitude of Destiny Cards, several Demon Powers to choose from and a variety of triggered events, choke points and unexpected enemy ability combinations, because, seriously, if you don't like the fighting and the looting then there's little to recommend Victor Vran than some good, if murky looking, graphics and dialogue so awful that you'll be embarassed to be listening to it.
If you like Diablo 3, Torchlight or any other ARPG lootfest, then Victor Vran offers a slightly different approach that yields much the same fun of smashing the next big bad guy and grabbing fresh phat loot, along with great fireworks and some steampunk style.

Verdun is an amalgam of arcade and realism that mostly works. It's an immersive game that's a lot of fun to play, despite many annoying game mechanics.
The spawning system is chaotic at best. Most of the time you spawn with your squad, even if they're in the middle of a fight on the front lines. This means the player has the potential to experience non-stop action through the course of the battle. I have mixed feelings about this. Nonstop fighting wears me out and reduces my time alive, because people only last a few seconds on the front line before getting cut down. So the player waits from 1 to 30 seconds for their next spawn wave, and they last a few seconds on the front, and then they get cut down again. This can be quite repetitive and when the enemy team is kicking your♥♥♥♥♥ it can get pretty frustrating pretty quickly.
The small arms are mostly accurate, but firing from the hip gives you a ridiculous accuracy penalty. Hitting targets 5 feet away becomes a challenge. When scoped, however, weapons have pinpoint accuracy, giving a huge edge to snipers and long range fighters. Quickscopes are everything in Verdun. Machine guns also gain this magical ability, although that's balanced by their inability to fire without being set up first.
The player is very weak, dying instantly to a 7.62mm bullet impact anywhere, impact by a club, spade, or bayonet anywhere, or 1 second of exposure to fire from a flamethrower. This weakness is balanced by quick regen, but that takes away from the game's realism. I'd like more realistic injuries and healing supplies provided by medics back at the initial spawn area.
Artillery spam plagues the more populated battles, with a surfeit of officers targeting many people in a limited map area. Often it's impossible to stay alive for 5 seconds at the front line because of multiple enemy officers spamming artillery barrages, in addition to grenades. A more balanced system would see artillery squads manning cannons and bombarding the enemy from long range based on team guidance, instead of infantry officers calling down heaven's wrath every few seconds. But that's saying what I think the game should be, and not what the game is.
Hacking is a definite problem in Verdun. I'm not sure how many people use cheats, but they're easily available (E.g. here's a program that lets the player see enemies through the ground:
). I wish there was some kind of reporting system so that these people could be investigated and stopped. The community is non-toxic and most likely wouldn't abuse the system.
All quirks and annoyances aside, my favorite part about this game is the maps. The level designers obviously put their utmost into recreating these battlefields, and it shows. The battlegrounds are almost tangible, they're well-lit and atmospheric. My personal favorites are the Vosges, Picardie, and Flanders.
I recommend this game if you were interested enough to visit the store page. It runs well, has a good community, features lovingly crafted maps, weapons, and playermodels, and provides plenty of immersion, despite its flaws. There's also a companion game called Tannenberg on tap for release later this summer which you can follow here:
At the end of the day, Verdun attempts the nearly impossible. WW1 was not a war defined by its action, but a war defined by its inaction, its stagnation and decay. Verdun's high-octane mud-slogging sits awkwardly on the memory of a war made famous for its slowness and bitterness. But its representation of the war is good enough, probably the best one we'll see for the forseeable future.

I purchased Banished during the Steam Summer Sale due to the fact that I love simulation games and the price was right. This game is the most challenging simulation game that I have ever played. The other would be others either real or computer generated that you would battle against. I myself do not miss those two factors.
That being said what I do like about this game is it’s challenging factor. You have to balance your focus on many things at once and make smart decisions on where and when to build and or expand your city. Just one minor wrong decision could make the difference between having plenty of supplies or running out and having half to three quarters of your cities population starve or freeze to death.
Another great factor of the game is the pairing of people. If you building the community shelter not a lot of “Breeding” will go on and your cities population will not expand. You must build houses at the correct time and the correct amount in order for your citizens to move in and create children.
The graphics are acceptable and the terrain maps are okay but it is the game play that makes me spend so many hours trying and trying to build a huge city. My maximum population that I have achieved in my 50+ hours of game play is 149. I know and realize that I am doing something incorrect for any possible expansion.
I intend to play this game as long as it take in order to create a thriving city that is well balanced and expanding. I am glad that I purchased the game and I give it a 7 out 10. Thank you.

However, there are some people getting the word, who seem to be hackers, although they don't seem to be located in "Hackerville" and also might just be using tools written by other people to get access to servers and email accounts, which would go more in the script kiddie direction, than hacking - but since this "documentary" doesn't bring light in this matter either, they could be any of this.
Although it is a bit informative, like it's not really smart to use 123456 as a password, I give it a negative review because the title and description is misleading, and to make it worse, puts hackers on the same level as scammers which is like putting a Porsche GT3 on the same level as a Fiat Panda.. Update December 12, 2017.
Continue to avoid this game. Despite leaving early access the title has failed to find its way. If there was anything that emphasized this more it would be the player engagement over the last year. It has been in a death spiral. Anyone who takes the time to look over the SteamCharts data for this game can plainly see the PC community is near dead and has given up on the game.
The latest update does little to curb the lack of fun in the game. It is a thinny veiled treadmill designed to offer you a shallow reward system for grinding the same tired maps again and again. It a minor sense of progression in exchange for hours of repeating the same content again and again.
The mode attempts to mix things up with monster bonuses randomly applied to lanes, but this is countered by the 100% random mix of enemies in lanes. This continues Trendy's track record of forcing scenarios onto players that completly nullify the majority of hero towers. Rather than creating scenarios where all heroes get to shine, the onslaught maps reduce every build to one that successfully withstands Cyber Orcs and EMP Kobolts.
Update May 7, 2017.
Just avoid this title. The design team is hell bent on turning the once great tower defense series into a confused mess. Update after update the game gets more refined visually, and less fun. Bugs and hiccups aside, the gameplay focus of the team is so lost that there is very little to enjoy in this title anymore. A damn shame considering the source material and history of the Dungeon Defenders franchise.
Update October 10, 2016.
Current Play Time: 1,639+ hours of play time. This includes close pre-alpha, through public alpha, through pre release, through early acces.
tl;dr: Pass on this game until they deliver on the vision a quality successor to DD1 that is just as feature rich and improves upon the original formula. While the current content demonstrates the great potential for this title to elevate the original Dungeon Defenders experience to new heights, the lack of depth and simplified character kits and meaningless grind are insurmountable negatives.
Unfortunately, the game has not grown substantial for veteran players. While I continue to take an active role in the very limited community of the game, there is little longevity in the current build of the game.
The development path is all over the place and the development is quick to paint you a picture of an ideal future. "Down the line" and "it would be great" are common mantras on the developer streams, but these do not often reach fruition.
My initial impressions of the game are still valid (see original review), but the game has not grown enough to justify a positive rating in the last 1-2 years. The game looks great and is a visual upgrade when compared to its predecessor. Unforunately it lacks the depth of content that made DD1 a joy for fans of the series.
I pulled up the orignal Dungeon Defenders to take a look at some of the content that made that game so appealing. Many of those core features like surival mode, pure strategy, hardcore, or mixed modes are still missing. Gear progression and strategic diveristy have remained stagnant for quite some time and are rigid in comparison to DD1's universal loot. There has been little in the way of meaningful changes to the game to create challenging and diverse end game scenarios.
The utopian ideal for this game would be a huge step above DD1, but at the current development
pace there is little hope that it will be a worthy sequel to DD1 without another 2-3 years or work.
Free to Play or Pay to Win: I would like to dispell any notions that the game is pay to win. I do commend design team for maintaining the integrity of the game by avoiding selling power to users. There is nothing that cash purposes buy you that impacts your power level over other users.
Original Review:
Current Play Time: 360+ Hours participating in the closed pre-alpha.
tl;dr:
If you enjoyed Dungeon Defenders Eternia then picking up Trendy’s latest installment of the tower defense series is a no brainer. There are still a lot of improvements to come to the game, but in its current state it still shines as a tower defense title.
General
Despite being an Early Access title, Dungeon Defenders 2 is in a well polished state. There are 10 beautifully rendered maps to play on, with multiple levels of difficulty, and the loot system is fleshed out enough to offer hours of replayability.
There are 4 playable characters with their own unique set of towers and abilities. You will have to master each of their kits (or call in some friends) if you want to complete every map. The interplay between towers is rewarding and there are dozens of effective strategies for every map.
The difficulty on later levels does fall short. Once you reach end game equipment, none of the maps offer much of a challenge. That may change with the introduction of harder difficulties or other game modes, but keep that in mind if you expect to push your characters to their limits.
Multiplayer
The lobby system is still in its infancy, but you are able to participate in both public and private games. The game incentivizes playing with others as it provides you a bonus to your drop rate. Additionally, all item drops are instanced for each player. This means you will never have to fight anyway over who gets a legendary drop. Unfortunately, the game still lacks a trade feature so for now you are unable to share loot with friends.
Core multiplayer features like the ability to browse through a list of hosted games, kick players, and created player restrictions (level requires) are not currently available. If you choose to play in public games you will be playing with whatever other players are currently in the public realm for your chosen difficulty level.
The current pre-alpha community has so far been very helpful and pleasant. Your mileage may vary depending on the types of players who enter your game. This revision of the game does include a dynamic ping system that allows you to send simple messages about where defenses should go. This goes a long way towards aiding in communication when working with a team of strangers.
Overall
There is still a lot of work to be done to improve the player experience, but as far as Early Access titles go this is by far the most fleshed out and polished I have come across. The game will ultimately be free to play, but at the current price point the game offers enough content to justify the purchase for fans of tower defense games.

I'd like to like this game - I really would - but I just can't.  It's pretty, and at first getting to fly around manually instead of jumping from point to point like FTL had you doing was interesting, but it suffers from three major problems:  overly difficult battles, boring mining minigame and tedious alerts.  Aside from those three problems, there are some minor annoyances like an apparent lack of manual entry for resources (instead of clicking and holding on an arrow as the resource goes up or down at an accelerating rate, and then clicking repeatedly to fine tune it) or a 'take all' button for mining, and a rather clunky startup procedure.  It would be nice if they'd save your previous system selections so you could just hit 'continue' or tweak the build a little instead of doing it all over again each time, not to mention letting you see the stats of officers you've already selected and more easily compare those still waiting - say, a way to sort by a specific stat or some means of highlighting two officers so you can see how their respective stats look without picking them out from the list.
The combat is simple, but hard.  You select one of up to three (as far as I've seen) enemy ships, and then decide if you want to hit their shields, hull or weapons.  Weapons seems like the obvious choice, but to judge by the duration of the red glow and "our shot was deflected" announcements that appear to be tied to it, each of your opponents can hold their deflectors up twenty+ times as long as your ~50 command officer can.  That means that they can sit behind their apparently perfect protection while they hammer on your ship, so both shields and weapons are critically important to destroy - too bad your starting crew won't have the engineering to hit very often even if the target's shields are down.  On my second game I made avoiding combat a priority and got through four systems before they caught up to me, only to destroy me in a single two-ship combat; either the Skorn get better the farther you go, or there's some trick to combat aside from 'use weapons when available, use deflector when enemies appear to be charging weapons'.
The mining minigame is absolutely essential to your success.  You *can* send probes that bring back a small amount of each resource if you want, but you'll need to send the mining rig from time to time in order to concentrate on grabbing whatever your engines this run use as fuel.  Sadly, this minigame consists of the rig moving down at a steady rate while you control if it goes left or right to avoid obstacles (shown as flashing red or red with crosshatching, the latter being instantly fatal) and collect resources.  You have 40 seconds per deployment, at least with the rig I purchased, so expect to sit around waiting for the Skorn to catch up while sending it down three or four times in order to refuel and resupply.  Oh, and did I forget to mention that you apparently get a maximum of 200 of a resource, and have a return load capacity that you'll reach easily if you don't destroy the rig partway down?
Alerts could have been interesting.  Unfortunately, they always consist of the same thing - command alert, send the crew member with the best command skill to deal with it.  Engineering alert or medical alert, send engineering or medical staff.  They'll be busy for a while, but don't sit around waiting because the Skorn will track you down and make fights more frequent.  There isn't even much in the way of description, and unless you pause and hover your cursor over the alert you'll never know that this mysterious case of space rabies comes from raccoons in the supplies.  Yes, raccoons.
This is of course an Early Access game.  I hope that everything will be improved, especially making the mining minigame more enjoyable - but as it stands now, I can't recommend this game.

Yes, it's Early Access, so I knew what I was getting into.  There will be a couple of issues to raise, but mostly I like it so far.
First, this is a game where you will Die A Lot Figuring Things Out.  That's okay in a game where you can get right back in and learn from your errors.  Right now, however, you have to launch a brand new game from scratch every time --- including ship customization, crew selection, and initial supply loadout.
That gets tedious rather quickly.  The ability to save a template of your ship and resources, which you can then modify or run with as you like, would speed things up immensely without sacrificing the need to re-select from your randomized crew options.
Once in the actual game, however, it's FUN, if frenetic.  Days pass in the space of seconds, so you often feel rushed even though you really shouldn't.  Being able to scale time down somewhat, when not in combat, would let you savor more of what's going on rather than having to flit about like an ADD-afflicted squirrel.
That still doesn't detract from the feeling of discovery as you explore this immense star system and see what it has to offer, from the vantage point of your captain's chair overlooking a wide-open bridge.  Rarely have I gotten such a fresh "Star Trek" vibe from a game which has nothing to do with Star Trek (and frankly, Into The Stars does it better than most Trek games to date).
The core game engine also seems solid (from what little I've played so far).  I could not get it to run at all using the Epic settings (perhaps they're not implemented, I don't know), but even on High it was smooth as silk.  Your ship feels somewhat ponderous, as should any vessel which isn't a starfighter.  Mining was a rather interesting minigame, too.
I may come back to revise this as things develop, but these are my first impressions for now.  And I have to say: even with the things I don't like so far, I don't think my $20 has been wasted.
