The game set high expectations but fail to deliver in too many areas. The bottom line is the game is very complex, unfortunately although I took the time to learn the various mechanisms, what I found behind the complexity screen was very disapointing and a bit holow for a strategy game which such high claims. It is not a completely empty shell, but the ratio of complexity vs substance is really bad IMO. HoI2 had a better playability overall.
A major issue is also technical bug and glitches, just check the forums. it is a pity that after several expansions, and many patchs, that the game is still unstable.
The game piles features upon features, but that didn't add up to make neither a interesting nor fun experience. From HoI 2 to HoI 3, each sub-systems increased in complexity, but this feels really gratuitous, as despite the complexity, the un-modded game is a poor political and historical simulation.. What the point in making such a complex game if the game so quickly move into fantasy land. in one game as the Germans, while I was dealing with Poland, Italy invaded France through the Alps in early 1939. In the end Italy reachedd Paris by the south in July 1939, at the same time I reached it from the north by the historical path. It so badly fails to reproduce the historical course of events, I won't give him any credits for portraying "alternative history"
Worse for a WW2 game, the military operations are poorly implemented. Moving units is tedious, and combat feedback is very poor, you neither feel as a frontline commander, nor as a HQ staff officer planning operations. The idea of making a pseudo real time game (actually the game move in 1 hours increments), doesn't work so well with such a long and intense conflict. Micro managements is very high, but the tools and interface to give you orders are inferior to many 4X games.
You can delegate a number of functions to the AI, however the AI is just bad even for simple thing. In fact it doesn't work well because if you pursue a specific strategy the AI assistance won't go in the same direction as you. For example setting trade on AI automation, the AI sold critical ressources I was in short supply instead of buying them. Another exmaple setting part of my units under AI control, I had the surprise that he AI abandoned the French Frontier in 1940 to move to the Eastern front leaving the border vacant.
There is an important supply and command chain in the game: Division>Corps HQ>Army HQ>Army Group HQ>Theater HQ. However after a few days of battle your units can easily get messed aroundq the frontline as you react to enemy threats. Yet, tracking which units belong to which HQ is not easy as units and HQs are not color coded as in other games. Hence you spend hours unlinking and re-linking your units after every major operations. This is a real chore, and computer assistance is pathetic for such a mechanical task.
The game attempt to do too many things at once but the end result is a failure.

If you loved the first one, you will ABSOLUTELY LOVE this one. Maybe because the protag was Gear-chan (too serious), but rebirth2 lacked a lot of the humor of the first game for like 80% of the game. This game definitely takes the best of the first game's tone and adds on a revamped UI and even more fun and humor. I'm only into ch 1 but I'm already in love with the game already!
I don't know if I would recommend slogging through game 2 to get all the references here, but upon doing so you'll really feel the engine improvement between this and games 1 and 2.
**EDIT 1: Into chapter 3, and there's a LOT of translation freedom here. It's a little hard to tell sometimes whether some things were intentionally mispelled or not.
**EDIT 2: I finished the game, and to sum it up:
+ A TON of content and new stuff to play with, and more characters than you'll know what to do with (all the DLC are included with this game except the one for stella's dungeon I think, which you should definitely get)
+ You'll definitely get all the references Rebirth1 had to this game, making it feel like you travelled in time.
+ Neptune is best protag. Plutia is love. Plutia is Life.
+ The UI and battle system is vastly improved. Everyone gets "CPU form" in a sense. Equipping a backline makes sense.

In essence, V is a gamified version of the Stroop test. A simple task coated with progression mechanics and an interesting aesthetic motivates to challenge one's own reaction time.
Visually, the distortions and flickers of the simulated VGA TV screen are very well done and don't turn out to be disrupting the attentiveness. Surprisingly, the player is required to focus so much that the effects are mentally put into a blind spot and thus, at least in my case, don't cause nausea. Nevertheless, options to reduce the effects of some interferences and different colour-blind modes are available.
The music is dope but, depending on preference, maybe a little too boisterous compared to the activity it accompanies. Together with the driving beats, popping visuals and clean sound effects, V pressures the player to concentrate hard. After unlocking additional continents and playing these, new prompts that introduce alternative rules appear and intensify the synapse activity. One or two hours at a time are doable before attention slowly drifts away and mistakes become more frequent. Frustration over one's own stupidity sets in and brute force doesn't help, so taking a break every little while is vital.
V is a glorified reaction test with nice trappings.

Everyone is comparing this game to Van Helsing... I guess ill start with that too. Sooo both games are ARPG&Hack'nSlash (tho van helsing is more likely a clone of diablo, victor vran i wouldnt say so) Both games take place in some eastern-south european lands (Seriously Borgovia in VH and Zagrovia in VV  ^.^) ,there are vampires in both series. Also story of both games is all about saving the world, woo-hooo! (but i guess like 95% games of this kind is all about it, so...).
Now... There are 2 reasons why i bought the game imidiately after its full release..
1st: I really like hackn'slash genre. Plus this game looked really nice (i mean graphics and all)
2nd: The game looks like its meant to be played on gamepad. And its quite rare in this genre. It was always all about button mashing with your mouse. And gotta tell you... this game gets even greater and  better if u are playing on gamepad. The possibility to dodge attacks, roll over fireballs, and jump through pulse waves is just great. If you are skilled and fast enough you can basically dodge it all :) First time its not all about how beffed up your hero is...
Now lets talk something about hero development. Its not super great, but i find it pretty solid. If they polish it in some future paths it might get great :) There is no stats like strenght or agility, but instead you are getting destiny points, destiny card slots, or little max HP buffs. Destiny cards are passive bonuses. The more destiny points you have the more powerful cards you can equip. And there is plenty of them. Plus there are some legendary ones, that benefits you depends on weapon you are using at the time.
Item properties in this game are pretty standard for Hacknslash (extra damage, crit chance, life steal, etc.)
Devs mentions something about unique behaviour of enemies. I guess thats truth. Every single enemy has his own skills and moves (except the simplest ones). But... i would love to see more variety of enemies. Because in this state there is no many of them. Also the game is not that long. It would take less than 10 hours to complete if you rush through it.
I love challenges, and hexes in this game. (hex makes the game more difficult, f.e. monster hits harder, or runs faster) That will let this game to stay alive for long. It would take a lot of time to complete them all, and they are really diverse. Also the difficulty level of many of them varies a lot. The toughest of them, are very difficult. I mean it :)

Pretty great shooter. Sometimes it's a little frustrating. Not quite going to wet your Battlefield whistle, I think, because the scale isn't as grand. However, I think the charging, crawling, and clearing gameplay for most maps and classes is a lot more thrilling than anything I can recall in BF1.
Pretty nice community, very little drama or trash talk. It's kind of closenit and it didn't take long until people started recognizing me from other games. There's usually at least one full game on the US or EU servers, even in the dead of night.
Lots of weapons, lots of classes (though you have to play as a class that's open if the servers are at high capacity). Class changing works by clicking an empty position on the leaderboard or making a new platoon. It's been awhile since I've played a good PC FPS leaning more simulator than arcade.. but I think the gunplay feels very nice, and can often be satisfying. The sniping has some drop and drift, but it doesn't seem as detailed as BF1 or Battlegrounds, as far as I can tell. The sniper scope is pretty awful to my taste, it's a little blurry fisheye that's intended to work with a spotter (and even gives you a spotter class), but nobody ever plays that position as intended. Although, many snipers overcome what I consider a pretty terrible scope and lack of bionoculars, and rake in the kills. I've found that the machine gunner is just as good or better at sniping, with any weapon, as long as you get a good position.
And yes, you'll have those iconic "machine gunner mowing down human wave" moments.
My only real gripe right now is that artillery is too frequent, too lethal, and with some upgrades comes with too big a radius. You'll see people get 8-9 kills in a hit, then they wait 45 seconds and do it again.
All in all, I think anyone who likes a good FPS and is willing to learn to do things a bit different and have some patience is going to love it. Players of games like Mount and Blade Napoleon will also enjoy it, I would say, although there's certainly much less discipline and roleplay here. But the feeling of siege, chaos, and gritty battle is alive in Verdun.
Overall a very enjoyable game, mechanics are top notch and leave little to ask for.

You've got weapons, armor, demon spells, runes, cards, transmogs, uniforms...all of those things you need to keep a super close eye on and you've dozens of areas in which you need to spend your gold.  I personally haven't invested any time in keeping up with the runes or transmog parts of the game, but it could easily be where all of your gold goes, leaving you with zero spending cash when that awesome weapon arrives.
The online multiplayer lets you join anyone who has an open room, but will still only let you advance by how far YOU'VE gotten in the story (to avoid power leveling I assume).  But if I join a friends game and they are further in the story than me but 2 levels below me, then we're both making a sacrifice to play together.
The camera/point and click movement can be a pain often times as well. You'll want to click to go somewhere, but instead you click something that is in the foreground but was invisible (as to not obstruct the player's view) and you'll move in a different direction.
Overall, I enjoy this game. But I feel that very soon I am going to hit a spot in the game where I can't proceed because my character is too weak because I haven't invested the time into the cards or transmogging anything.

Summary of review:
Worth a whirl if it is available to you or on sale. Although it has its problems it is a fairly decent and challenging platform puzzler with childish (some would say charming) graphical design. However if you do not have a controller (Gamepad) i cannot reccommend this game to you as this game is near impossible to play on a keyboard due to very awkward key bindings i have been unable to change (heaven knows i've tried).
Pros:
- Increasing level of difficulty with each zone, and unlike most platformer games this one is actually challenging at times.
- Large variety of obstacles, or "enemies" in the game as every enemy gets (almost) completely replaced per new area.
- Different "levels" to each map as there is a challenge in each map, there is general completion with 100% lugnut pick-up and golden bolt pick-up, Golden bolts will unlock new areas. On top of that there is an overall completion score which will grade you (general school grades) based on how much time you used, Whether or not you fell off the platform, how many lugnuts and how many golden bolts you got etc. Giving each level a certain replayability as you try to obtain different goals.
- Very bright, but not so much so that I suffered from it. I tend to get severe headaches and nausea if a game is too bright or the contrast and fine detail of the game is too prominent. This game however was no problem at all. If you suffer with headaches from games, like me, this one will likely not give you any trouble graphic-vise.
Cons:
- Insanely annoying audio.
- Very childish graphic style. Considering how difficult the game can be the game then either becomes too difficult for its target child audience or too childish looking for its target adult audience. Either way you look at it there's a problem there.
- In game shop is both unnecessary and overpriced. When you earn up to 40 lugnuts - if you're lucky - and a single item in the shop will cost you approx. 1000 lugnuts the effort needed to put in to purchase a single item is just not worth it. Regardless the game shop mostly just offers different characters and various personal graphic choices. There is one side of boosters which are cheaoer (200-400 lugnuts) but still overpriced and just really not all that worth it as far as I see it.
Independent points:
- Much more difficult on keyboard, the key binding is off and it all just becomes really very awkward on the keyboard, so i would highly reccomment using a gamepad for this one.
Review: (for summary, look at top of review)
Albeit the game starts off very juvenile and crummy looking/sounding there is a certain sence of quality to the difficulty of the puzzles you will be faced with and a limited time to boot. Although being a timed puzzle-like platform game with challenging sections I have not at all stressed playing this game. It is difficult but enjoyable once you get past the childisness of the design of it along with the crude and, to be perfectly honest, incredibly annoying game sounds.
I tried playing this game with keyboard and mouse first and found it close to impossible and had destinct distate for hte game at the time because of how it did not integrate well with the keybord at all. However, after giving it a short with a gamepad I have found myself actually enjoying my game time and the difficulty of the levels as it is my own inabilit I have to fight with in order to fully finish maps, and not the awkwardness of poor key designation.
I recommended the game, although it is more of a so-so game in my book because it is worth a go if it is on sale, It is a good platform puzzler, but it has its downfalls, which, for me, includes the graphic style of choice along with the completely useless in-game shop. It seems more proof of poor planning and far too high expectations of the player rather than an atribute that brings any form of new level of involvement in the game.

Among the many Free-to-Play FPS Titles available on steam, WarFace stands out as one of my newly discovered favorites.
The game is Free to play, and like many free to play titles, there is an advantage to be had in shelling out real cash to beef up your arsenal or gear.
HOWEVER, that being said, I can myself say that I was able to get into the game quickly, and despite being new to the game and not having spent a single dime on it at first, you can ABSOLUTELY enjoy and be competetive in Multiplayer versus matches of any kind without spending a single dime. The obvious drawback here is that if you just play the game as provided, it will take you longer to unlock new weapon attachments, gear, and weapons for your character. I find that those who complain are those with the lower level of skill.
For the most part, everything is obtainable through the in game currency "WarFace Dollars" awarded for the completion of a match, which awards a bonus to the winning team, and a bonus for the first win of each game mode daily.
Make no mistake, Warface is a fast-paced action FPS I believe is most enjoyed by people used to small map, arena style game modes with quick, action, think on your feet, twitchy style gameplay.
Use of Tactics is not a huge concern in Warface as there are basically three types of players in any given game; The camper, The agressive hunter, and the reactive attacker/defender. That being said a minimal use of tactics and thinking on the run will help you be competetive here. I have also noticed that a player who is patient and can think on the run has the advantage in these arenas of death, though as I mentioned advanced tactics are not needed as there is typically no organized teamwork going on, with no VOIP option, and minimal communicaiton as far as the teamchat is concerned, you are lucky to get a few messages with short abbreviations as to enemies location and whatnot.
"Will I get matched against players who are much higher in rank than me?"
No, matchmaking up to a certain level will match you with people within a certain range of your level. So a level 1 newbie will not be matched against a level 30 1337 killing machine.
At the first 5 or so levels I believe, you will be matched with players of similar level to you, which is nice because you can learn the maps/environments, and feel out the gameplay style without getting immediately rekt by uber players.
Teamwork: In short, if you are seeking a team with amazing teamwork I would say Warface is not for you. But that is my opinion from experiences in games so far. I am sure some clans utilize teamspeak or similar programs, but I have never been invited to one so idk.
Teamwork in public matchmaking PVP games appears to be minimal. However, I have noticed that teamwork in matches with low level players only tends to be more commonplace. The reason for this is that as you advance in level and unlock more gear, your reliance on your team mates for their support abilities diminishes.
As this is a review and not a strategy guide I will give a simple overview of these support abilities, which are nice, but do not expect to receive them very often from your team mates.
Support Abilities:
---------------
Rifleman: Ammo Box- Resupply the Ammo of your team mates or yourself. (you RARELY* will have a team mate resupply you)
Medic: Medical bag/Shock Paddles - Medic bag heals you or team mate/Shock paddles revive team mates. (You will RARELY get healed, you MAY get revived on occasion but do not hold your breath.
Engineer: Armor Kit - Replenish your own or your team mates armor. (Again you will RARELY Receive this support from a team mate)
Sniper: No Special ability.
But Do not be expecting your team mates to provide anything of the sort, and just be pleasantly surprised when they ACTUALLY do.
Con: Many non english speakers ( if you are an english speaker that is)
Pro: The game forces you to play the Tutorials prior to playing as each class, you start out with the rifleman tutorial, then go from there until you have completed them all, upon completion of the tutorial, you are awarded with the basic weapons/gear for that class. You also will have to play some COOP Matches at first to familiarize you with the game, but its a fun way to get your feet wet in WarFace so no complaints here.  I also consider this a pro because it ensures everyone knows HOW to play their role, even if the only role people ACTUALLY end up playing is "Shoot the enemy and ignore everything else."
Pro: The Tutorials are very short, sweet, and to the point. They show you what you need to know and do not waste your time with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Overall I recommend it to any baller on a budget!

I decided to pick this game up since it was on a deal during the Christmas Sale, and I also enjoy playing the occasional horror game. Normally horror games don't usually give me many frights and I thought Outlast would be exactly the same as the rest. However, Outlast definitely made me eat my words.
You play as the male protagonist Miles Upshur who, according to the start of the game, is a wimp when it comes to fighting. All you're equipped with is a camcorder. No guns, no knives, no weapons whatsoever. You're an unarmed, athletic journalist. Throughout the game you have to accomplish multiple goals in an attempt to escape from the asylum. Most of the time you'll have to sneak around in order to not get brutally murdered, and trust me it sure is brutal. If you get seen, the tense music will kick in, the adrenaline will start rushing around your body, and you'll make your character sprint and jump over obstacles as you head towards the nearest point of safety, whether it's in a locker, under a bed, or hiding under a desk. You'll also try to make sure you have enough batteries for the nightvision feature on your camera, which you can only find lying around. Otherwise you may end up being in the dark, waist deep in sewage, trying to find the way out of the sewer while an enemy, who will rip you apart if he finds you, is hunting you. Trust me, you don't want to have that problem, otherwise dying is probably the best option since it's the quickest way to get your batteries back.
In my opinion, trying to sneak around enemies while also trying to complete objectives is the biggest fear factor present the game. i'm sure for most people who have played this game, it's quite nerve-racking when you're trying to see where the enemy is, the music is slowly building up, you move round a corner to get a better view and "BAM", the enemy is right in front of you. The panic will be there immediately, you'll turn around to go back into the room and attempt to duke the enemy in order to escape. As soon as you're safe, and the music has settled down, and there's a high chance that the above process may occur again, provoking the same response. There's also many jump scares present in the game, which adds to the fear factor already present when crouching around dark corridors with nightvision as the only light source present, with only your footsteps and breathing being the only sounds to accompany you.
I wouldn't say the story of the game is too complicated, but I wasn't really into the story that much. I did care for my character and for the events that caused this place to become what it is now, but the way to sort everything out, to "fix" everything, didn't grip me that much (which is the only negative thing I can think of, other than some framerate issues which I think is due to my PC having exactly the minimum system requirements). The documents you find throughout the game will help you understand the backstory, and the good thing about them is they're not a long read, and I've got the same opinion for the notes that you're character makes. Even though I had to run the game on the lowest settings, the enviroment and graphics are very well done and I was certainly impressed considering Red Barrels is a company I've personally never heard of.
Overall, the game is very well done and certainly a great horror game. If you're a fan of horror games, then I highly recommend to buy this game, even if it's not on sale. Also a personal thanks to Red Barrels for making a fantastic game, and I can't wait to see the future DLC for this game.

Absolutely thrilling ride. From the get go, the game sucks you in. As you start, its horror brings the best out of you. I found my heart beating so loud after I stopped playing and at times, it was too scary to continue playing it, let alone start playing it. You actually think you are in the game, thanks to the effort put into my player's sobbing and breathing.
In case I didn't point that put enough, the game is really, really scary.
As the story progresses, you get used to the enemies horror and you figure out the ways how to avoid them or survive the level. But what really starts to take over in the place of horror is the story. Not that the game stops being scary at any point, but story really sucks you in and you keep on playing because you want to complete just the next stage over and over again, just to see what is next.
Graphics are just wonderful. The blur, movements (except for enemies when they turn around) is very well created and the feeling playing this game is spot on. The game's gameplay gets repetitive at times, but thankfully story really takes over so you don't mind.
The game ends with dramatically, and you are either going to hate it or love it. Overall, the game feels like a very good horror movie with superb story (which you will not forget for a long time) and keeps your attention going all the time.
It is a game you will probably only play once (although highest difficulty sounds a great challenge), but you might want to bring a friend and enjoy watching him get scared over and over again. It is a no-brainer if you find it on Steam sale, otherwise it's still a great deal, if you don't mind playing it for only 7 hours.

Pretty great shooter. Sometimes it's a little frustrating. Not quite going to wet your Battlefield whistle, I think, because the scale isn't as grand. However, I think the charging, crawling, and clearing gameplay for most maps and classes is a lot more thrilling than anything I can recall in BF1.
Pretty nice community, very little drama or trash talk. It's kind of closenit and it didn't take long until people started recognizing me from other games. There's usually at least one full game on the US or EU servers, even in the dead of night.
Lots of weapons, lots of classes (though you have to play as a class that's open if the servers are at high capacity). Class changing works by clicking an empty position on the leaderboard or making a new platoon. It's been awhile since I've played a good PC FPS leaning more simulator than arcade.. but I think the gunplay feels very nice, and can often be satisfying. The sniping has some drop and drift, but it doesn't seem as detailed as BF1 or Battlegrounds, as far as I can tell. The sniper scope is pretty awful to my taste, it's a little blurry fisheye that's intended to work with a spotter (and even gives you a spotter class), but nobody ever plays that position as intended. Although, many snipers overcome what I consider a pretty terrible scope and lack of bionoculars, and rake in the kills. I've found that the machine gunner is just as good or better at sniping, with any weapon, as long as you get a good position.
And yes, you'll have those iconic "machine gunner mowing down human wave" moments.
My only real gripe right now is that artillery is too frequent, too lethal, and with some upgrades comes with too big a radius. You'll see people get 8-9 kills in a hit, then they wait 45 seconds and do it again.
All in all, I think anyone who likes a good FPS and is willing to learn to do things a bit different and have some patience is going to love it. Players of games like Mount and Blade Napoleon will also enjoy it, I would say, although there's certainly much less discipline and roleplay here. But the feeling of siege, chaos, and gritty battle is alive in Verdun.

At its heart, Banished is a low-tech version of SimCity. The best advice for handling the steep learning curve is to begin the game on "Hard" instead of "Easy." Unlike SimCity and similar simulations, the Easy mode actually offers far more responsibility and a greater chance of a horrendous outcome when winter comes and your citizens die off, whether one-by-one or in droves.
The premise of the game is that you are at the helm of a small population of banished peasants, struggling to make a new start in the wilderness. The map is generated at the start of the game, though again, consider choosing a fair climate at least, including a map without too many mountains. Flat land (whether cleared or forested) is your lifeblood, producing food that your villagers will harvest either year-round or during harvest season, in the hopes of surviving the winter. In addition to food, you must also provide tools (hand-made at the Blacksmith), clothing (Tailor), religious guidance (Chapel), education (School), and relaxation (Taverns which brew alcohol from a wide variety of foods). It's a lot to juggle, which is why it's best to start slow with a small population of about a dozen.
There is an active wiki community, though no amount of guidance teaches as well as a sudden smallpox epidemic, town-wide fires, or the dreaded mass-starvation in late winter.

Victor Vran looks and feels a lot like "Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing".
Its main new and fresh feature is the totally different leveling-system:
You gain XP and level up, but you don't have skills.
Instead there are different weapon-types (equip 2 at the same time), each have their own basic skills. So a Sword has always the same sword-skills but each sword you'll find has different stats.
Then you have 1 (later 2) "demon-powers". Which are nice special powers. But they drop as items. And they have come in different qualities and can be collected and transmuted into something even greater.
And then you "fate-cards". As the name implies, those are cards. Different types, boni, quality and stats. Again collect-able and transmutable.
The higher your level the more fate-cards you can equip.
What a true item-orgy!
So no more worries about choosing wrong skills and gimping your character. Just pause mid-fight and change the cards/demon-powers/weapons. Yay!
The story is...the story of an ARPG. You are a hunter and super mighty and blablabla. It's ok but nothing you would tell your grand kids at a campfire :)
(I have not tried the multiplayer-part, so no judging here)
If you like ARPG, you will like Victor Vran.
If you liked said "Incredible Van Helsing"-series, you would like it even more.

I really like car games, however, the crew does not have even remotely realistic physics. If you are looking for a game that is even slightly realistic, I urge you, go elsewhere. If you are looking for an openworld cruising/racing arcade style car game, this may be fun for you.
There are so many problems in this game that I am not going to list them all but here are some of them:
a)Cars feel like they are floating through corners, drifting is nearly impossible even with a drift kit (you have to buy one before you can drift for more than a few feet) due to the fact that the game doesnt rely on a realistic physics engine for drifting, i.e. loss of traction to the rear wheels (or all four for AWD) instead it chooses a 'brake to drift' style, simply turn and hope for the best.
b) Cars take forever to upgrade, and the process isnt exciting, you simply do a single jump over and over, 10s of 100s of times, untill you get what parts you want. This process is comepletely random, no matter how skilled you are at the game or how high of a score you get, you will get the same thing, at total random.
c) The Physics for offroading and jumps is absolutely trash. You can flip your car at the slightest provocation, and it is not consistent at all. One second, you can drive right over a large boulder with ease. The very next second, a tiny rock will somehow flip your whole car. Also, you cannot continue to roll back over while still in the air (barrel roll), so if the car flips it counts as a wreck, even if you would have landed correctly.
Honestly, if you like car games that give you control over your car, wait for Forza Horizon 3. Its just over a month and a half away. do yourself a favor here.

Hearts of Iron 3 explores the thrilling history of World War 2, from the onset of the infamous war, to Nazi Germany's demise (or victory). Although the game does usually follow the real-world timeline, what-if scenarios can occur at any time, such as Japan invading Siberia, or a communist revolution in France, or even... the fabled Axis victory. Being able to strategize is a MUST, in HOI3, giving minescule armies the ability to conquer a colossal military force. If handling the military isn't really your thing, you can delve straight into politics. From firing Stalin (and probably sending him to perish in Eastern Siberia), to giving the German people, the right to vote, and hate the Nazi party. The other main part of Hearts of Iron 3, is diplomacy. A neat chart, allows players to see where their nation is on the political spectrum, and which alliance (Allies, Axis, Comintern) they're drifting towards. And so much more. I highly recommend the third installation of the Hearts of Iron series, and would pay more than double the price for this legendary game.

Where to start. I got this game when it first came out on the Xbox: 360. I was kind of disapointed. I mean the game was quite buggy, laggy and just had it problems. Needless to say, I returned it and got something else.
Not I see it on sale and decide, why not give it another try. Well I did and I can say its not so laggy, or course I have a gaming machine now that can handle it. Anyways, the storyline isnt that bad, I'm not super far into it, but it's rather interesting. However, this game can be brutally hard. I recommend to save often. And when I say often, I mean before a battle, after a battle, and every other step. If you don't become a ranger/mage, and save up your money for a really powerful bow, your gonna have a hard time. The difficulty spikes in this game can be ridiculous.
I've always been a warrior type. Love to go in and battle my enemies toe-to-toe. But in this game, It's so hard to do that, especially when you get ganged up by 5+ people at once. Even with good armor, they can shread through your health like butter. But in this game, I had to do ranged just to get by. And some quests require you to go into some difficult areas, usually above your level.
However, this game does have its interesting bits. The story is interesting to say the least with your choices having an effect on the world around you and even what price people sell their goods for. Having the choice to decide peoples fates, or to have my actions matter is something I love about a game. The NPCs in the game are also quite welll done. Every NPC has it's own name, characteristics, and converstions. Each thinking something different that may help you in a quest, or with getting lower proces at shops.
The skill system I can say however is nicely done. You don't have to dwell in just your calss based stats. You can be a battle ready warrior shooting fireballs and summoning creatures, to an unarmed mage beating his enimies to a pulp.
All in all, with the crazy difficulty spikes, the somewhat "ok" story, and the just barely getting around, I can't recommend this game. The skill system was great, and the NPC's are wonderful, but the combat difficulty is what ruins it. It's an ok game, but not great. You can give it a try, and you may love it.

One of the best in the series in terms of story, some classic and touching 4th wall moments.   The Story continues off where MK2/Re;Birth 2 left off with Neptune being sucked into the UltraDimension and meets Plutia, the extreme Sadist CPU in the 16Bit Era.
The Good;
The main story is perhaps the best out of the series, its very well told and the voice actors do a great job as usual in bringing our favorite nepneps back.   Also Re;Birth 3 improves on several features such as an improved treasure hunting system so no longer spamming 'scan' in order to find those treasure, or reloading the same dungeon over and over to find rare or important items.
Also, I think its a positive change but others may disagree, they significantly changed how the SP system works, so now everything from healing spells, to the typical EX attacks use SP instead of previous games where special attacks/healing used mana and the EX had a seperate meter, its all combined now so some battles require a bit more strategy instead of just spamming the same attacks over and over.
Another good point is the awakening system, which gives a large stat boost to non-CPU characters, along the same lines as a HDD transform.
The Bad;
Now for the bad aspects,  unfortunately whilst the previous games mostly had limited bad points.  Victory//Re;Birth 3 does have several points which are quite negative and should be talked about, I will list these and explain them.
Ultra Extreme GrindFest (Worst in the Industry)
The developers incorporated new challenges into the game, by repeating the same process or achieving certain milestones, however they completely and honestly - went way over the top in terms of requirements for some of these,  such as jumping 10,000+ times... to unlock bonuses, I am not even kidding or lying how obnoxious some of these challenges can get,  luckily - no trophies are attached to them so for the most part, it unlocks stats/extra items or skills but still, it is way over the top considering these challenges are for each and every character in the game.
Another bad point is that the clothing has been priced far too high,  much much higher than the previous games so that all the unlockables and cute clothing are more or less a complete waste of time because by the time you've beaten the game, you'll still not be able to afford any of the clothing or accessories.  In fact,  getting money this time around is much harder than previous games.  In future games, I would like to see the clothing prices drastically reduced so that at least during the first cycle the player can at least purchase some clothing without skipping on upgraded gear.
Another minor point is a few boss fights, especially end of game have ultra cheap moves which can insta-kill and even immediately game over if your unlucky or not sufficiently levelled high enough to wipe her out in one turn.
Choosing the mean conversation options is the most fun way to play this game.

Synopsis:
Anime clichés, a story with plenty of humour related to the gaming industry, fourth wall breaking, grinding for crafting unlocks, cuteness, boobs and panties. Sound interesting? If yes, you'll probably LOVE this game. If not, you'd better stay waaaay over there! No, a few more steps backwards ... there!
Bigger and better, Rebirth 3 takes the series back where it belongs.
Pros:
* Very funny (unlike Rebirth 2)
* UI and mechanics improvements over previous titles
* Bigger
* Best story in the series (so far)
* Friendly to people new to the series
Cons:
* Easy
* Lack of new moves
* Some 3d cutscenes still as low-res as in the previous ones
To me, Rebirth 2 felt lackluster after the first game. The story wasn't as funny or as long, and dialogue dragged on with neverending pointless Chirper messages. Rebirth 3 feels like it goes back to what Rebirth 1 was: hilariously funny and full of protagonist wackiness and fourth wall breaking. The story continues after Rebirth 2. It feels more developed, and thanks to its nature and Nepgear's helpfulness it's easily understood by new people to the series. All old characters in the series return as playable characters although all of them don't participate in the main story. There are also some great new additions to the cast.
There are several mechanics improvements which make me happy. EX and SP point systems have been merged which makes skill management a bit more interesting. UI in the menus have improved. Stella's Dungeon now has a friendly drop list for dungeons and monsters. The map is bigger, with multiple layers and screens, providing space for more dungeons. No more search spam for hidden treasures; they have a new mechanic and are spotted visually. Visuals are also slightly better. The gallery is big, there are plans for changing BGMs and old scenes can be reviewed.
Unfortunately at the point where I'm at, the game feels a bit too easy. When I played Rebirth 1 I didn't feel bad about turning on Easier Enemies. Now I feel like I want to turn on Harder Enemies instead. The combat doesn't offer as much to old players as it could. The old characters all seem to use their familiar moves. The graphics in some 3d cutscenes are blurry and low-res, which can probably be blamed on the PS VITA original.
I'm thoroughly enjoying this one! Jury is still out, but possibly the best in the series. Thumbs up!

Note: I have FOSE installed so it doesn't log my play-time.

Fantastic little ARPG here.
It is very streamlined compared to most traditional rpgs, you wont be sorting through piles of loot to find marginally better pants or whatever. There are only a very few things that monsters drop and those are automatically picked up meaning that you dont ever have to stop killing monsters unless you want to.
The games class system (or lack thereof) is where it really shines though. Victor wont be slowly putting points into a skill tree and becoming a better mage/swordsman/archer or whatever. Oh no Mr Vran can use all weapons right away and can even swap between 2 at any time.
This makes for very dynamic gameplay as you can swap things out instantly mid combat, allowing for all sorts of awsome combos and gameplay variety.
Finally the setting/theme/voiceacting etc are all great. The narrator is particularly funny as he quips when you reach certain areas.

I don't always spent a lot of time playing a single game. Divinity II broke that rule. Although the story itself it's not the best, (It's a normal story for this kind of games) it got a couple of interesting plot twists that make it even more interesting.
Let's admit it, it's a game rather "old" by now. (Let's keep in mind that Ego Draconis went out in, I think, 2009). But, even if the graphics were upgraded with Dragon Knight Saga, (Yes, if you had "Dragon Knight Saga", the game upgraded itself to the "Developer's Cut"*) there are some textures that could be better and some minor bugs. I mean, I don't want to be disrespectful at all. I feel nothing but respect to Larian Studios. They proved that it doesn't take a worldwide company to make an awesome and unforgetable game.
One thing that I think the game lacked is better character customization. There're just a couple of options in hair and face. Nothing deep at all. And, other thing, (And, this is just personal) I'm, let's say, an achievement hunter. I find both entertaining and challenging to try to earn every single achievement every time I play a game. I am in two minds about this game. The gameplay itself is quite enjoyable, it's an arcadey racer much like Driver San Francisco. But there are far too many flaws for me to recommend this.
1) The grind! If you want a decent car you better be prepared to either grind tedious missions over and over or buy some in game credit. Most missions net you 2k, but top of the range cars come in at 700k not including the tuning which some will set you back 500k. That's a lot of grinding for little reward.
2) The story is abysmal, I didn't care at all about what was going on or who these people were. Which would be ok if it wasn't for;
3) The missions. The missions in this game is the same repetitive few types with different locations/cars. It will either be a race (by far the best), an escape from the cops mission, a checkpoint time trial or a Smugglers Run esque cargo smash. That is as deep as they get and you will soon get bored.
4) Little reward. I don't really consider this a spoiler and I think perspective buyers should be aware. There is no reward for completing the story. No car. No paint job and just the same diddly amount of cash as the rest of the missions.
5) Always online and Uplay. Not really an issue for me but understand this is important for people with limited internet connections
That being said there are some positive points to this game. The map is huge and full of landmarks, the Wild Run add on creates a bit more variety, and if you manage to get a crew cruising round the U.S.A can be fun.
I have played this with a Logitech Driving Force GT and it will work ok, but the arcade controls are far more suited to a controller, both controller types are supported well with mappable button configs.
All in all I can't really recommend this game, especially not at full price, but it may be worth a punt on sale if you are looking for an easy on the eye arcade racing sandbox. It is what it is, and is easilly worth getting on the cheap for the map and crew antics alone.

A magnificent sequel to an incredibly popular series or a horrible fan-pandering blunder? You decide in Dark Souls 2: Sins of the First Scholar, a combination of the original launch of Dark Souls 2 with all of its DLC included as well as additional challenges included.
For those who have played Dark Souls 1, the majority of the game’s combat and statistic systems have remained the same and the few differences come from “extracting” one stat from another. For example: Vitality, which used to be part of endurance (a stat that determined stamina and equipment load) now represents equipment load entirely on its own. Adaptability is another new statistic that determines speed of consumable items and most importantly invincibility frames during rolling or dodging. These new stats force the player to split their point load more evenly, encouraging a more versatile build instead of overly specialized builds seen in DaS1, though the latter are still possible.
Thematically, when compared to the first game, Dark souls 2 can be a bit of a mess. It almost seems like different teams worked on their own ideas for what the game should be and later glued them all together awkwardly presenting situations where your character moves up a long elevator only to end up in a lava filled castle in the sky or a desert area strangely shoehorned in between caverns and churches. It certainly lacks the overall flow of DaS1, which was more centered over an entire city with logical settings that all fit together neatly. This isn’t really much of an issue as far as gameplay is concerned, but for anyone wanting any sort of immersion, Dark Souls 2 has more of a theme park feel and this may be a turn-off for some.
Additionally, the game has the habit of throwing groups of enemies at you, sometimes even when you “pull” single enemies with a ranged weapon. As a result of the souls games’ poise system, where hits received can interrupt and eventually stagger your own attacks, a group fight will typically end in a quick death for the player. To be successful, you will often have to find ways to funnel enemies towards you in corridors or around choke points and quickly deal with them in series before you become overwhelmed. By the way, if you kill a particular enemy enough times (12-15 kills approx.) they disappear from the game world until you bring them back at a higher difficulty level by burning a bonfire aesthetic.
Soul Memory was another controversial update to this iteration in the Dark Souls franchise. With SM, every soul your character absorbs is counted, regardless of whether it’s spent or lost. This “score” is used when matching you against online players for PvP purposes. Ideally, it was supposed to be a means to prevent twinking, where players deliberately under-level themselves while using their souls on improving gear making for an unfair challenge when they faced new players. Unfortunately, all SM really results in is lower-skilled players being punished a different way by placing them against good players who die less, or use items like the agape ring to avoid taking in souls, and thus have a lower SM.
Dark Souls 2 SOTFS felt like a grand experiment to me the entire time I was playing it. All of the new systems, items, environments, and statistics have the feeling of a bunch of idea guys sitting on a board room throwing concepts at the wall to see what sticks. Some things worked really well like duel-style PvP (which tended to be more fair and fun) and a few of the PvP covenants like Bell Keepers and Rat King made certain areas of the game way more interesting than they would normally have been. On the other hand there was a lot of recycled content in the form of previous Dark Souls bosses, except with slightly different forms. This also made me think there was some sort of tug-of-war going on between the traditionalist types and idea men and the (lack of) consensus was the game we received here.
Regardless, Dark Souls 2 SOTFS remains fun to play and has all of the challenge of a proper Souls game, complete with invasions and jolly co-operation. It’s definitely still worth playing, just be prepared to make a few compromises and adjust your expectations beforehand.

Divinity 2 is a game where you can (at will) turn into a dragon, attack a flying fortress & its army of dragon riders, land on the courtyard, kill the guards with a mix of sword fighting and destructive spells, subdue the fortress’s commander and then read its mind to know his deepest secrets. All this 100% gameplay, no cutscenes involved. It has to be the goddamn best RPG ever made by man, right?
Sadly, not quite. Larian Studios was held back by time constrains, lack of resources and, worst of all, the focus on consoles and their limited hardware. While the game overflows with original ideas and Larian’s usual clever writing, the execution doesn’t deliver. It’s not a bad game by any measure; the gameplay is good, some quests are creative (and funny) to do, and it succeeds in giving players interesting mechanics to play with (like mind-reading). But sadly it lacks that “special something” in its execution, making the game somewhat repetitive and mediocre by the end. Still, is a great game that’s not afraid to break the mold and bring something new to the table.

I really just can't bring myself to enjoy it. It's just... Such a downgrade from DS1. Warning, lots of reading here.
Improvements from DS1:
Graphics
Hud seems alright
Voice acting
Downgrades from DS1:
Player versatility/options
Recycled plot (oh hurr-durr, everything is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ somehow, can't be worse, oh wait then there's DS3)
Less-interesting setting
Poorly handled item mechanics (Effigies mostly)
First off, the graphic upgrade is top-notch. The hud seems easier to navigate, and the voices are crisp and well-recorded, subtitles are no longer a necessity as they were in DS1.
But that's about all I can praise on this game.
Let's start with player versatility. In DS1, battling an opponent felt like a dance. The movement and interactions were smooth, and sure you died occasionally from locking yourself into a long animation, but picking up a new weapon/piece of equipment and swinging it a few times would get you used to which attacks would be useful when, and how you should be able to utilize them. DS2, every single weapon I've tried feels sluggish and disappointing, at least in the sword category. As someone who usually goes for Slash out of Slash/Bludgeon/Pierce, I can tell you that you will not be impressed moving from DS1 to DS2 in this regard. Nearly every attack is a long-winded, then with incredibly slow recovery/windup speeds around these slow animations to boot. I'm here for interesting battles with variations on how to complete the fight, rather than roll, slow slash, slow slash, roll away. I want to enjoy watching the un-life fade from a hollow's eyes as I interrupt his charge attack with a quick shank, instead of clicking as soon as I see he's winding up for a heavy hit, watching my character try to remember how a sword works, and then have my character complete a fast attack at the same time that the hollow brings down his heavy hit. I want BOTH sides of the system, Player and Non-Player, to punish eachother for launching into heavy attacks without first stunning/accounting for timing on them.
Recycled plot? It's pretty much the same. You're a random♥♥♥♥♥dead dude. This kingdom used to be great before the undead curse and everything somehow getting even ♥♥♥♥♥ier. There's some whole debacle with this lady being rude and corrupt, who was the original final boss, which would have not been so much recycling until SotFS, which then brings in this random tree-guy who thinks you can avoid restarting the age of fire. Which is where, we hit the exact same final plot point as DS1. You kindle, or you walk away. And no matter what you choose, the next game in the series is where things have just happened to get ♥♥♥♥♥ier while somehow previous stories existed but didn't exist at the same time.
Less-interesting setting. Honestly, we just took the magic school names and slapped new ones on there. We re-named a few characters and added some new ones. DS1, you take some time to look off into the horizon, you see some♥♥♥♥♥♥ You see architecture, you see buildings, structure, sometimes areas you can get to sometimes you can't. DS2? You're in valleys or along cliff edges with no discernable features, there was no "Let's make this look like a place" thoughts on this, it was, you're in this area and you see the areas you are in or will be in, or you will see walls or empty space (empty space could be referring to ocean, empty air). Occasionally you'll see some rubble thrown in front of an archway to the point that you couldn't even peer into it to think about why it exists, or see down a tunnel that might make you think, oh I bet that used to be a mine, or maybe they had a prison down there, instead it's just a blank archway, simply a wall made to look like an un-usable door.
Poorly handled item mechanics. Honestly, DS1 had FANTASTIC setups for bonfires/hallowing/etc. In DS2, if you die your max HP is reduced. That's... that's artificial difficulty at its finest. Sure, you just fought an enemy and learned how to maybe deal with one of their attacks, or their placement, or literally anything. Guess what. Now you're gonna have to sacrifice an item to get your max HP back, or hope that you can make it back through the level, pick up your dropped souls, and then not ♥♥♥♥-up on the path to the next part, where you will STILL have to expend an item to return to your max HP. Death, death is already a punishment in itself. It restricts the player from advancing, and wastes their time from continuing to experience the game. But at the same time, you learn from death, so there should be some other negative to add for that positive, right? That's where dropping souls comes in, not only are you reset back, but you will lose your recent progress if you don't fight through all the stuff you just fought not 30 seconds ago. So you're forced to put your new knowledge to the test to not lose progress on what you're trying to achieve. This is the receive punishment, gain knowledge, apply knowledge, reap rewards setup that DS brought as a fresh breath to the gaming  world, with the possibility of skipping any part of that four-step process as you encountered each new problem. In DS2, perhaps they were attempting to relive the praise they received for this, and instead added a new element, receive punishment, gain knowledge, force expenditure of item or receive additional punishment, apply knowledge, reap rewards, which throws the whole system out of whack. No matter what part of the process you achieve, it's downplayed. Finish the level without dying? No new knowledge. Die? Receive additional punishment. Use an item? If you haven't picked up on what you failed to do before, you'll just be wasting it. Apply your knowledge? Well if you didn't use the item or you ran out, you're less likely to succeed even with your new knowledge, and probably going to wind up back at the bonfire again, perhaps even tricking yourself into believing you never learned anything and continuing to attempt again and again with no luck due to your diminishing health bar with every new bit of information you gleem from your last death.
Truth be told, it's not a bad game. I know, I've seen people play it, I've played it. But it's not what I'm looking for. And if you find yourself agreeing with what I want to see/expect in DS a game, you're not going to enjoy it unless you've never been spoiled by DS1. Disregard everybody saying this takes 2-4 hours to beat. I did it in less than an hour in my first playthrough, and slowly cut time from there. There are 20 trinkets to collect and if you do that it will take longer, but most of them aren't too out of the way. There are two trinkets that together will take twice as long as it did to beat the game. It's worth it though. You may rage some but the game flows smoothly and constantly, so you can die 15 times in the span of a minute and still feel like you're making progress. Going by the achievement statistics, less than 10% of players managed to beat this game, which is in part a testification to its difficulty but honestly I think it's mostly that this is not everyone's game. If you like platformers, it doesn't get much better than this, but if you prefer 3D games that focus more on storyline than gameplay (nothing wrong with that), then you could pick a better game to start playing 2D again. Note: there are at times a lot of moving colors onscreen, but it's generally monochromatic - if you have epilepsy and are the photosensitive type you should be careful with this purchase, but know that it's not that bad and probably won't do anything (it's nothing at all like Super Hexagon).
tl;dr If you're bad at 2D platformers and want to get better, buy this game but be ready to rage. If you like platformers, this game is amazing.

I know its an old game, but I thought I would write this because Fallout 4 is coming out, which is why I bought this.  So this review is for two groups: those who want to know what the game is like in 2015, and those who are not typically into RPGs.  I fall into both catagories.  I don't play many RPGs, and I only played this because everyone is hyped for Fallout 4.
TLDR:  Fallout 3 is a fun experience, so long as you are willing to take it slow, and accept that it is old.  If you are new to fallout, or RGPs in general, but know how to manage an inventory, you will have a good experience.
Full review:
I came into fallout 3 not expecting anything in particular.  I only knew that it was reviewed well.  I also knew it was old, but I didn't expect it to be this old.  Its 7 years old but feels  like 10-12.  On ultra, I think it looks worse than half life 2.  It has it's moments, such as weapon and clothing textures, but its generally ugly and incosistent.  Performance was also poor.  Without any changes, it ran at 80-110 FPS indoors, but it suffer from extreme micro studder.  Locking it to 60 fps helped some, but microstutter was definately there.  On the plus side, I was able to use Nvidia DSR down from 4k (im using a gtx 970).  That made it look better, but not superb.  Draw distnace was ok, and FPS was inconsistent.  There were also two instances of crashes, but these were easily fixed with google.  Additionally, aiming felt akward and inconsistent.  Many weapons are inaccurate at more than 50 feet, but enemies can hit you from about that range, so I felt strangely forced to get up close and personal to kill most enemies.  Facial animations are stiff, (but the voice acting is generally good).  The whole thing made it feel old and clunky.  I would compare it to the first Bioshock, not very pretty, not very polished, and clunky.
However, despite all this, it only took me an hour or two to have a great time.  You spend about 5-10% of your time in dialog, which was off puting at first, but it allows you to create your own adventure, so to speak.  Its mostly all precreated senarios of course, but sometimes you get some great stuff.  One of my first adventures (spoiler free) involved trying to obtain some information.  I tracked down a guy who knew something, but wasn't giving me any help.  He asked for some cash, which I went to go retrieve, but upon returning he demanded three times the aranged amount.  Frustrated, and refusing to be cheated, I shot him, and hacked into his computor.  Next, I met a shady fell who asked me to do some questionable work.  I reported him to the local sheriff and accompanied the sheriff to the villian, who promptly kill the sheriff.  I then killed the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and went around town in his lovely business atire.
I beat the main game in less than a week, and played 23 hours.  I usually don't play that quickly, maybe 2 hours a day for a new story game, but I enjoyed it enough to play quickly.  I will probably stick around for another ten more hours to do some side quests.  Between managing inventroy, trading weapons, completing side quests (some of which are funny and a bit corny), and following the primary story I had a great time.  Maybe its only because I'm new to the experience, but this was a good first RPG for me, because I am used to the FPS model, and the transition was pretty quick.
I'd recommend this to anyone who wants to try fallout before the next one comes out.  Even if you are new to RPGs, you should have a good time.  Just be ready to take it slow, and put up with some glitches and old style flaws.

It's very easy to compare Banished to classic games we know and love. My first reaction was to say that it's "Like Age of Empires without the fighting". A range of other comparisons can be drawn to such games as SimCity and generally any other top-down RTS game, but it really is in a genre of its own, sitting somewhere between strategy and survival. You watch over a growing town and it is your job to prevent your citizens from dying of starvation, hypothermia and disease. You achieve this by ordering your citizens to build infastructure and choose which citizens work at which task. Food can be gathered in a number of ways, as can ways to ward off the cold or disease and eventually, when you can afford it, you can build a tavern so all your citizens are not just alive, but happy.
The game is fun, looks good, works well and if you work at it your town will grow into a bustling city. However, there is one niggling issue with this game that has the potential to undermine everything this game does so well.
The citizens are either extremely dumb, or absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
As a top-view RTS game, Banished strays from the normal protocol in preventing the player from directly controlling the citizens (i.e. you can't click on a citizen and right click their next destination) meaning the citizens have only their job and their survival instincts to rely on. By sacrificing this kind of control, there needs to be a decent AI to take its place. The AI is far from deecent, or intentionally cruel. I've had many people (farmers or woodcutters, vital to the survival of the town) die of starvation simply because they refuse to eat.
In my last session a child died of starvation because there was no food in the storage barn for her mother to take back to the house. This was because a man from a different house had already taken it. This man lived alone and his house was already full of food. Citizens who are starving will walk past farms full of crops, orchards full of fruit, fields of animals, wild mushrooms, and even people walking past holding baskets full of food and then die.
While the death of citizens shouldn't be a game-killer, the process of building a house for a family and waiting for them to have children and for those children to grow up is so slow that every able-bodied man or woman is necesssary to the survival of the every other man or woman. Three deaths in one summer - not because of bad management by the player - but just because of the idiocy of the AI is devestating for the town and is usually the reason I quit the game at the end of the session.
In conclusion, I recommend this game. It's still playable, despite th inability to direct a hungry person to food, or an idling builder to a construction site, but I hope this issue will be addressed in an update.

Sim City finally put on its big boy pants.
From a person who loves strategy building/management games, this one is stellar. The concept is simple: survive with what you're given. The game IS difficult and you will lose a few times. But the pacing and resource usage set a very peaceful, albeit deceptive tone. Even when the game is going well, you're always one disaster or rough winter away from destruction. Taming that feeling is one of the biggest accomplishments in the game.
The graphics are smooth and the scrolling frames harken to the classic "Caesar" franchise. Don't expect a lame military add-on; there is none and the mechanics work better that way. Be warned: this is not a good introduction to the management genre, and less experienced players will be in for a very steep learning curve. Individuals with a desire to play with an AI capable of providing exceptionally balanced conditions to survive should not hesitate to snatch this little gem up.

Set in the fictional land of Zagoravia, this action RPG adventure from Haemimont Games gets back to the genre's hack n' slash roots. Engaging combat and skill based gameplay are this title's cornerstone features in a crowded market. Utilise powerful aimed abilities, demonic magic and timed attacks as you jump, dodge and smash your way to victory.
Join Victor as he journeys deep into this monster infested kingdom in search of his lost friend and fellow hunter, Adrian. Along the way, encountering beautifully drawn and well voiced characters who help us uncover the truth about Zagoravia and the hideous beasts that plague it.
Victor Vran represents a departure from current trends in the genre, trading loot grinding for subtle, mechanic shifting gear choices that shape the way the player approaches the games many challenges. While it borrows much from esteemed contemporaries, such as Diablo, Torchlight and Path of Exile, Haemimont Games have managed to create their own unique take on the modern Action-RPG while also managing to invoke some of the spirit found in hack and slash classics like Blood Omen.
The graphics and art in the game are a real high point, perhaps eschewing the expense of fidelity for a dark and sombre, with a hint of the fantastic, style that is carried consistently throughout out the gameplay and story segments alike. The music is moody and subdued, matching the setting perfectly and complimenting the action with aplomb.
I highly recommend it and you can check out my Let's Play if you want to see the game in action:

A magnificent sequel to an incredibly popular series or a horrible fan-pandering blunder? You decide in Dark Souls 2: Sins of the First Scholar, a combination of the original launch of Dark Souls 2 with all of its DLC included as well as additional challenges included.
For those who have played Dark Souls 1, the majority of the game’s combat and statistic systems have remained the same and the few differences come from “extracting” one stat from another. For example: Vitality, which used to be part of endurance (a stat that determined stamina and equipment load) now represents equipment load entirely on its own. Adaptability is another new statistic that determines speed of consumable items and most importantly invincibility frames during rolling or dodging. These new stats force the player to split their point load more evenly, encouraging a more versatile build instead of overly specialized builds seen in DaS1, though the latter are still possible.
Thematically, when compared to the first game, Dark souls 2 can be a bit of a mess. It almost seems like different teams worked on their own ideas for what the game should be and later glued them all together awkwardly presenting situations where your character moves up a long elevator only to end up in a lava filled castle in the sky or a desert area strangely shoehorned in between caverns and churches. It certainly lacks the overall flow of DaS1, which was more centered over an entire city with logical settings that all fit together neatly. This isn’t really much of an issue as far as gameplay is concerned, but for anyone wanting any sort of immersion, Dark Souls 2 has more of a theme park feel and this may be a turn-off for some.
Additionally, the game has the habit of throwing groups of enemies at you, sometimes even when you “pull” single enemies with a ranged weapon. As a result of the souls games’ poise system, where hits received can interrupt and eventually stagger your own attacks, a group fight will typically end in a quick death for the player. To be successful, you will often have to find ways to funnel enemies towards you in corridors or around choke points and quickly deal with them in series before you become overwhelmed. By the way, if you kill a particular enemy enough times (12-15 kills approx.) they disappear from the game world until you bring them back at a higher difficulty level by burning a bonfire aesthetic.
Soul Memory was another controversial update to this iteration in the Dark Souls franchise. With SM, every soul your character absorbs is counted, regardless of whether it’s spent or lost. This “score” is used when matching you against online players for PvP purposes. Ideally, it was supposed to be a means to prevent twinking, where players deliberately under-level themselves while using their souls on improving gear making for an unfair challenge when they faced new players. Unfortunately, all SM really results in is lower-skilled players being punished a different way by placing them against good players who die less, or use items like the agape ring to avoid taking in souls, and thus have a lower SM.
Dark Souls 2 SOTFS felt like a grand experiment to me the entire time I was playing it. All of the new systems, items, environments, and statistics have the feeling of a bunch of idea guys sitting on a board room throwing concepts at the wall to see what sticks. Some things worked really well like duel-style PvP (which tended to be more fair and fun) and a few of the PvP covenants like Bell Keepers and Rat King made certain areas of the game way more interesting than they would normally have been. On the other hand there was a lot of recycled content in the form of previous Dark Souls bosses, except with slightly different forms. This also made me think there was some sort of tug-of-war going on between the traditionalist types and idea men and the (lack of) consensus was the game we received here.
Regardless, Dark Souls 2 SOTFS remains fun to play and has all of the challenge of a proper Souls game, complete with invasions and jolly co-operation. It’s definitely still worth playing, just be prepared to make a few compromises and adjust your expectations beforehand.

I know its an old game, but I thought I would write this because Fallout 4 is coming out, which is why I bought this.  So this review is for two groups: those who want to know what the game is like in 2015, and those who are not typically into RPGs.  I fall into both catagories.  I don't play many RPGs, and I only played this because everyone is hyped for Fallout 4.
TLDR:  Fallout 3 is a fun experience, so long as you are willing to take it slow, and accept that it is old.  If you are new to fallout, or RGPs in general, but know how to manage an inventory, you will have a good experience.
Full review:
I came into fallout 3 not expecting anything in particular.  I only knew that it was reviewed well.  I also knew it was old, but I didn't expect it to be this old.  Its 7 years old but feels  like 10-12.  On ultra, I think it looks worse than half life 2.  It has it's moments, such as weapon and clothing textures, but its generally ugly and incosistent.  Performance was also poor.  Without any changes, it ran at 80-110 FPS indoors, but it suffer from extreme micro studder.  Locking it to 60 fps helped some, but microstutter was definately there.  On the plus side, I was able to use Nvidia DSR down from 4k (im using a gtx 970).  That made it look better, but not superb.  Draw distnace was ok, and FPS was inconsistent.  There were also two instances of crashes, but these were easily fixed with google.  Additionally, aiming felt akward and inconsistent.  Many weapons are inaccurate at more than 50 feet, but enemies can hit you from about that range, so I felt strangely forced to get up close and personal to kill most enemies.  Facial animations are stiff, (but the voice acting is generally good).  The whole thing made it feel old and clunky.  I would compare it to the first Bioshock, not very pretty, not very polished, and clunky.
However, despite all this, it only took me an hour or two to have a great time.  You spend about 5-10% of your time in dialog, which was off puting at first, but it allows you to create your own adventure, so to speak.  Its mostly all precreated senarios of course, but sometimes you get some great stuff.  One of my first adventures (spoiler free) involved trying to obtain some information.  I tracked down a guy who knew something, but wasn't giving me any help.  He asked for some cash, which I went to go retrieve, but upon returning he demanded three times the aranged amount.  Frustrated, and refusing to be cheated, I shot him, and hacked into his computor.  Next, I met a shady fell who asked me to do some questionable work.  I reported him to the local sheriff and accompanied the sheriff to the villian, who promptly kill the sheriff.  I then killed the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and went around town in his lovely business atire.
I beat the main game in less than a week, and played 23 hours.  I usually don't play that quickly, maybe 2 hours a day for a new story game, but I enjoyed it enough to play quickly.  I will probably stick around for another ten more hours to do some side quests.  Between managing inventroy, trading weapons, completing side quests (some of which are funny and a bit corny), and following the primary story I had a great time.  Maybe its only because I'm new to the experience, but this was a good first RPG for me, because I am used to the FPS model, and the transition was pretty quick.
I'd recommend this to anyone who wants to try fallout before the next one comes out.  Even if you are new to RPGs, you should have a good time.  Just be ready to take it slow, and put up with some glitches and old style flaws.

Definitely one of the trickiest games I've played in a long time, but also one of the most enjoyable. VVVVVV has a surprisingly intriguing storyline and cast of characters as well as an awesome soundtrack (worth buying if you like chiptune). Its visuals and aforementioned music definitely appeal to the retro-gaming audience but could easily charm even the most modern of gamers. Also if you're a space fanatic like me, you'll be happy to know that that is where the entire story takes place (though not just in one dimension). Despite this, the difficulty of this game is undoubtedly something you should consider before buying it. While completing the story should not take more than a few hours, it will not be without a good deal of frustration and is just about impossible if you lack persistence. A knack for puzzle-solving and the willingness to take risks are also good things to have if you plan on playing this game. Outside of the main story, VVVVVV offers a quite a bit of bonus material and challenges for those who want to take its inherent difficulty to the next level. On that note, if you plan on completing this game 110% be sure to get plenty of rest and stay hydrated because doing so borders the humanly impossible.
Overall, VVVVVV is an excellent game that is both compelling and unique, but not a great choice for the more casual gamer who isn't looking for much of a challenge.   4/5
