Entertaining and realistic naval warfare simulator where the player acts as a commander of a whole fleet, which includes various ships (transporters, aircraft carriers, battleships), submarines, planes (fighters, bombers, scouting) and helicopters, along with all their instruments. That includes many different radars, missiles and torpedoes. The scenarios allow for creativity and tactics, as in most missions you are given the fleet to command, but how you use it is up to you. Usually the success depends on all units and instruments working together, but as even single missions are somewhat randomized (the same mission plays differently when playing second time because enemy units spawn in different locations and in different quantities etc.) and require adjusting tactics or adapting new ones. Did you use bombers in this mission and replay it? Now you might get surprised the AI has much more powerful air force, but perhaps at the cost of submarines? Moreover the game has a huge amount of vehicles and weaponry from various countries, South and Northern American, European, Middle Eastern and Asian. Missions also happen on different places of the world with many different sides. One time you sink Brazilians as Argentinians, the other you sink Chinese as Taiwanese, and so on (though it seems everybody speaks English). You can also choose single missions of different difficulty, beginning with the easiest and slowly getting into more and more challenging ones as a great way to learn the game and form tactics. This is probably the best and the most fun naval combat game I've ever played. In addition, if you are new to the genre, you can set to automatic many settings, which will make a bit more similar to more popular RTS genre and get you accustomed to use of various radars, weapons and vehicles.

I really, REALLY want this game. Or what this game should be. I have been trying to find a pseudo-simulator for grand scale battles in naval warfare, and this is it. Sadly, I can't recommend it for anyone. Too many things don't work well. It's hard to get working. It's no longer supported by the developer. And even once you get it working, little things break in gameplay that make it hard to enjoy. At some point, subs broke completely; now they go on autopilot and refuse to engage or come to the surface (yes, I'm aware of the setting that supposedly fixes this; it doesn't work for me). Missiles disappear on launch from destroyers or cruisers. Airplanes disappear on launch from carriers. It makes play kinda worthless.
Gameplay wise, you're a fleet commander and you have to tell everyone what to do. Literally you have to command a combat plane in the middle of a battle to take the mach 1.4 contact that's headed straight towards him. I'm pretty sure a combat pilot wouldn't be waiting for orders from HQ. Ditto subs: they do nothing even at close contacts. Planes avoid missiles only when they get super close, and you can set it so ships self defend (again, only when missiles close to within certain death distance). The level of micro-management necessary is far beyond what a...fleet commander would have to do.
It's also irritating that certain obvious non-moveable targets (enemy airports) are unidentified, and you have to get within range of SAMs to identify them. Enemy ships and planes can ID and shoot you from afar, but you have to close to within visual to ID them. You learn quickly to preemptively shoot at anything moving above mach 0.5. Shouldn't I be able to tell the nature of these enemies from their radar emissions? And forget about cruise missile strikes on those airports once you've figured out where they are. For some reason, SAMs have no problem seeing and killing them, even if you launch 50 at one airport none will land. Jam the SAM sites, kill all nearby planes and literally a plane will lift off, kill all your missiles and flip you the bird before you can do anything.  It's just too hard to kill land targets to be realistic. You run out of ammo instead.
A lot of the scenarios are interesting, but many of them fall into the 'gotcha' category: "you're a US carrier fleet, you have no early warning or combat planes in the air, and there are unidentified enemies within 10 miles of you (really, how exactly did I get in this position?). But they apparently know who you are because suddenly there are 200 missiles headed your way! Personally, more interesting to me is the feint, maneuver, initial contact and jabs of the conflict than struggling to defend (yes, you have to tell individual ships to shoot down every one of those missiles in real time unless you want them to get too close to defend properly).
TL;DR: the seed of a great game for those interested in the subject. Lot of little bugs and issues make it tedious and irritating that will never, unfortunately, be fixed.

This is the classic Modern Naval Strategy Sim, and no I don't mean Real Time Strategy. While support for the game has dried up, it still remains the last great theater-level realistic Naval Sim. Since it doesn't look like anybody will make any game like this again, this is the game to get if you've ever thought of being an Admiral. This isn’t a game where you collect resources and generate units, instead you play out missions designed to simulate real world situations. You’re tasked with using what you’re given to solve the mission. This ranges from Destroyers, Aircraft Carriers, and Land Based planes and missiles to solve the mission.  While the game was made in the late 90s and the content reflects that, at the time it featured an accurate collection of most of the world’s naval forces for simulation. There have been mods created to bring it up to date, (Most notably The Naval Warfare Project, or NWP), which I highly recommend finding because they add tons of additional depth.
One major criticism of the game is that it is too realistic at times. The game takes place in real time, meaning that one minute in game universe equals one minute in our time. With ships moving at 20 knots, that means for ships to move from one side of the map to the other it can take many hours of play for that to happen. The game does have a “speed up time” feature, but it doesn’t go anywhere near fast enough to make casual play of the missions possible. Expect to dedicate about 12-20 hours to some of the built in missions.  But there isn’t any newer game like this for die hard Naval Sim fans out there.

VVVVVV is a big pixel, open world platformer in which you switch gravity instead of jumping. Its design and mechanics are simple. Its 'levels' are anything but.
You, Captain Viridian, have found yourself stranded in an unstable dimension along with your ship and its crew. The first problem? You're not all in the same place. You have to locate your ship and then find your crew - this requires finding (it's an open map) and progressing through the 'levels'. The levels all have slightly different mechanics, from static screens to constantly moving floors/ceilings. The platforms may disappear beneath your feet, make you bounce or switch gravity. :)
Its simple mechanics make VVVVVV easy to approach and get into, but do expect to be challenged at times! If you like a challenge, then I highly recommend picking this one up. It isn't a long game, but you unlock modes and trials along the way if you do want to come back for more. It's good for short sessions (or you could spend an hour or so 'doing things the hard way' like me...). It also has a stellar soundtrack - a perfect fit for the game. So, what are you waiting for? Pick it up and begin VVVVVV!

I got this in a LazyGuys bundle. I would guess that I paid about 25 cents for it. The game took me 11 minutes to complete, with a walk to my kitchen to get some water adding an extra minute or so. As I filled my glass, I glanced over at the calendar and saw that today was "Pi Day". I didn't know that, and I learned something new... true, it's a fact of questionable worth, but still. So all in all, the time spent getting water was productive, hydrating and informative.
I'm sad to say that my trip to the kitchen was in every way a more enjoyable, valuable, moving, fulfilling and emotional experience than "The Interview". I really tried to be forgiving when I thought about what to put in this review... you know, points for uniqueness, the strange and disturbing images, the complete weird nothingness of it all. But in the end, no. The few generated thoughts I had while playing... i.e. maybe this is a government experiment on my character, how will it unfold?... none of those musings came to fruition. The ending felt contrived, the whole thing felt like it had an hour-long development period (and I mean from concept creation to finalized content), and it was ultimately just lame. There's potential for something interesting to come out of this mess, given more thought to the content and result, but as it is it's a wasted concept.
So.... 25 cents/11 minutes. Worth it, either money-wise or time-wise? No. But if you buy this "game" anyway, I must recommend getting a refreshing beverage while "playing"... it will likely be the highlight of your short experience.

I'm only some 4 hours in, but am really enjoying this game!
I am a huge ARPG fan, and basically will buy and play any ARPG that has even decent reviews.
Victor Vran did something I didn't believe I'd enjoy, and that is offering dodge / jump in an ARPG. Something we've seen before is the option to have two weapon sets (in this case just two weapons) equipped, and in Victor Vran due to the special move charge mechanics I find myself switching all the time. It's really fun, too! Nothing like jumping in the fray with the 2H Hammer leap slam, and then demolishing the rest with my sword or rapier.
Due to the somewhat peculiar (for an ARPG) mechanics, I now find myself trying to take down packs of mobs unscathed. Dodging here and there, using leap slams etc.
The voice acting is quite entertaining, especially the guy mocking you as you go. I once lol'd when I went back to find a secret I missed, to which the commentator remarked how Victor decided to go the wrong way. :D I mean, that's just awesome. :D Then when I went where I should, he made of of me by saying how I finally decided to go the right way. That's just brilliant coding imho.
I also enjoy the fact that very little in the character is locked, so you can switch out demon powers and destiny cards to change your play style. This is a nice casual change to having played Path of Exile recently.
In the beginning you choose class (actually an outfit) which determines what your character is like. Not sure if you can change it, I heard something about changing outfits later...
The map challenges are great as well, and some of them are actually quite hard.
Secrets are a nice addition too, having to wall jump to special locations etc.
There isn't much on the loot side, but I haven't missed that so far. Usually I love farming items and perfecting my gear, but in the case of Victor Vran the gameplay itself is just so fun I don't really care for the lack of itemization.
Regardless, can definitely recommend this game to ARPG fans! Easily, you will not regret it.

When I bought the Divinity Anthology, I was really just buying it for this game (but I still soldiered through Divine Divinity at least first before jumping to this one). It was worthwhile playing through Divine Divinity - there's a lot of little callbacks and references to the world and previous events that made the experience of Divinity 2 more enjoyable.
Divinity 2 is a 3rd person Action RPG with a skill tree and stat allocation - think like a combination of World of Warcraft and Diablo. My wife said it reminded her of Dark Souls (or at least watching me play it) and I can see the resemblance. Overall the system works well - it's got a nice skill basis such that you can dodge around projectiles and attacks and avoid using potions and even kite enemies around if you're ranged. The options for character customization are broad too.
The world is large and full of character, and they definitely improved the quality of voiceover from Beyond Divinity. The plot is solid with an interesting (but apparently controversial) ending. Unfortunately it does fall into the trap of 'throw dozens of enemies at them' again, with the endgame becoming a -bit- of a trudge. They do close it out with a solid final area though.
The expansion pack sold the game for me though. They took the enemy count, toned it down, and made the majority of it venturing through one town fixing problems, talking to people, solving puzzles. One giant series of side quests, essentially. It was executed really well - and then they nailed the final sequence out of the park.
Playing through the first two Divinity games to get to Divinity 2 was definitely worth the wait - and I'd even recommend picking it up outside of the anthology if you don't care about the world-building done by the previous two games.

I could never get into Fallout, but I MADE myself play it when it went on sale.
Wow.
I really enjoyed this game, and it definitely was a new experience for me!
Pros/Cons
Pros:
-Wonderful Main Plot, always making you want to keep pushing.
-Beautiful, open world to explore.
-The radio, felt nice to hear someone talk about my good deeds (/flex)
-The Pip Boy itself, nice menu to organize things, and never was confusing for me.
-I liked the stat system, was able to priortize what I needed and improve skills that were needed easily.
Cons:
-Plot was average, and the end seemed very abrupt and just slapped on quickly.
-While it was beautiful (2008) and open, it became a chore to walk to a new location you haven't been to that's across the map, even with metro stations.
-I personally felt limited on my armor, as most of the armor was trash save the few upper tier that you were able to choose from.
And finally, a Pro/Con, I wanted more. And, yes, that is a good thing, it's also bad imo. By the time I knocked out most of my sidequests and finished the game, I wanted more. Of course I could have just stayed in the wasteland, searching every nook and cranny, blowing mutants  apart. But I wanted more quests. Maybe that's telling me to move on to New Vegas, probably. I enjoy having a packed quest log. During this game, I had to hunt for more quests, and sometimes it was hard to find where some could be, I had to actually look some up.
Overall, this game was spectacular, first Fallout game I've played, and as a casual RPG'er I can approve it. Combat system was a little broken, but I managed to adapt. I'd give it an 8/10, with the only huge con being limitations. I enjoyed and loved what there was to offer, but I didn't feel as if it was enough in the very end. Plot was fine, wasn't anything special and the end was WTF. I would recommend this to anyone looking for a great RPG, but not one that will suck the life out of you.
TLDR; If this game was food, it would be like an amazing sandwich. They skimped on the cheese a little, but you'll be fine, you've had worries that you're lactose-intolerant anyways. As you're eating it, wonderful sensations fill your mouth. Your eyes light up as you've found a wonderful dish in this restuarant. And then all of a sudden, it's gone. You ate it all. You try to remember the sandwich in your mind, you realize that it wasn't as big as you thought it was. You aren't completely full, so you try to ask for another. Sadly, there are no more left, the chef is too busy preparing something else. So you look back to the menu to find a sandwich like it.

I had fun with this game, until about level 25. I'll point out some aspects of the game I liked first:
Pros
~Multiplayer that isn't a hassle.
~Full range of interesting weapons.
~Customizable builds based on style of play. For instance, if you want to tank, there is a setup for that.
~Said setup is made based on Destiny Cards. These aren't too hard to find (some given during level-ups).
~Diablo-style legendary items (no sets). The weapons I got that had legendary effects were fun to use and I tried my hardest to keep them in my inventory at all times.
~Able to change loadout on the fly.
~Large amount of inventory, even for those pesky low-level cards that you need to hoard.
~Boss fights that will keep you on your toes
Now this was my experience before around level 25. After this the gameplay changed, and so did the need for new ways of tackling the game.
Cons
~Getting certain items in multiplayer (esp. lightning guns) will kill your friends in a heartbeat if they are melee. Friendly fire should not have been included.
~Some legendary weapons are too OP to pass up.
~The game forces you to play at a harder difficulty to obtain said legendaries.
~The increased difficulty creates a huge gap from the original gameplay. It honestly felt like a completely different game. Not just a harder game, an impossible one. Here's why:
Enemies can have any Demonic skill in game, including a 5 second stun and pull. No build, even full defense, can handle this later in game. The monsters that can cast this ability are multiplied at this level. You will run into them, and they will murder you.
~Builds become cookie-cutter. Tanks are no longer viable, and the only build you can use includes certain OP legendary items with high-damage output/vamp.
~Money will always be a problem if you decide not to grind.
~You will decide to grind anyway because once you increase the difficulty (which some areas require to pass their achievements) you will run into problems.
~Upgrading cards to have Wicked/Divine stats becomes a larger grind than getting OP weapons.
~Last thing- every area in the game will scale it's difficulty to your level. Going back to old content won't mean easier content.

This review is coming from somebody who has never played any other souls game, I did attempt to play the atrocity which is Dark souls prepare to die edition for the PC, but imo it doesn't count, since I haven't patched it or done anything to it. From what I hear it's good, but I cannot pass judgement as of right now, however, this is about DS2. I have attempted to remove spoilers the best I can, some scenarios do mention bosses, and if you mind this then do not continue reading.
Dark souls 2 has some good spots and some very poor spots to it. The sense of accomplishment is there and personally I did feel good finally killing the bosses (I'm looking at you smelter demon, fume knight and persuer) but the road to get there was often the biggest issue I have. There are a LOT of "Where the hell am I supposed to go" and "I sure hope this is the right way" moments. With that also comes a road paved heavily with multiple enemies. In DS2 more than 2 enemies usually spells death simply because of how multiple enemies usually give you no respite when they attack. This may not be true for all but I had played as a knight, on my only (single) playthrough with no NG+ and did it solo with the broadsword I started the game with, long sword and butchers knife with a trusty shield. I did not partake in summons. OF course these weapons were upgraded.
So, the good parts: More than half (imo) of the bosses had good/great designs, and I feel as though some get a bum rap, such as the earlier bosses which are meant to be easy so newer players can get their bearings. I feel as if the estus flask animation is very good for this type of game, as it makes you choose to either heal or attack and to realize when you have time between enemy attacks to heal, it adds a depth to combat which is nice. I have just began darksouls 3 and the estus feels very fast in comparison.
The "overworld" if we can call it that has a great calming atmosphere, and it is a pleasure to go there after long journies and tough fights. It was very enjoyable every time I had stopped by and did truly feel like a haven.
The combat was decent enough to be a positive, however, I did not feel like much of a knight since dodging is the name of the game here. Sword and board only take you so far in this game and you must learn to dodge. Unfortunately this means that heroics are often out the window and staring down a baddie and man-mode is often off the table. This is ultimately also what makes the game fun, since you can't just hide behind your shield the entire time.
One other tidbit that was good was the fact that poison and bleed (poison in specific) were actual threats.  I did enjoy it being deadly, however I didn't enjoy it's gimmicky placements, it was also part of one of the worst boss fights I think i have ever witnessed in a game, and everybody knows which one that is. It was both good and bad imo but I can't say I didn't enjoy the threat.
Now for a short glimpse of the bad: This was not TERRIBLE but I had trouble with the level design... Oh good god did it have me running in circles most of the time. Pitfalls, traps, random ganking enemies, getting turned around, this is truly a where the HECK AM I GOING kind of game, especially at the start, you have no map, but this is also partially a fun element. I do admit that at some parts I grew impatient and look for where to go next since at points it is very irritating being lost.
The enemy types - for somebody who was pure melee this was a tad annoying at times, specifically ranged enemies. Namely mobs before the smelter demon, since you were fighting 1 or 2 swift enemies while taking fire from archers from a distance. You must conserve your healing items for this boss (although he is optional) and this part alone took me about 3 hours to complete, since permanent death does take hold at 15 kills (I think) of a mob, and boy did I kill those mobs... Over and over and over. This is not the only instance this had happened, but it is the most memorable one.
The DLC for the most part was good, I had killed every last boss in the game and had to skip the two dogs in the ivory king dlc, simply because the route to get to them was too silly for me, this was definitely the games weakest point (the worst part, for me, of the entire game, dlc and core). The frozen waste (I think that's what it's called) is a complete nightmare and atrocity. It is simply not fun. In the DLC I found myself running past many enemies, which I had not done a lot of in the core game. I found it silly that it was simpler to run past and that the developers couldn't have seen how their level design and enemy placement at points would influence the player to want to just skip their hard work. Seems like poor decision making to me.
All in all this game was fun, infuriating, but fun. It was fun enough for me to purchase the third installment (although with my very short time in the third game I have found to enjoy the combat in the third game more so far) I recommend giving this a try when it goes on sale. It is not a bad game, it is just different from the other dark souls games from what I can see right now, with my experience. Enjoy it and don't give up, skeleton!

After beating vanilla twice, my thoughts on this game are:
Excellent combat. When you first start playing, you think the devs are trolling you at every turn and it's BS. They are. You die. You die again. You die some more. You lose all your souls while trying to get back to where you died to reclaim them and you hate the game and the devs for what they've done to you. But you keep playing, because you'll be damned if you're going to let these troll ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s win! You learn the trick to defeating each enemy. You learn the tricks for getting through each area. You learn the timing for how to parry attacks and deliver devastating counter-attacks. You learn how to circle-strafe and you think "God, I wish I'd been doing this all along!"
Level design. You hate it at first. Seems like every place you go is either a tight corridor or a thin piece of ground over endless chasms on all sides. The terrain kills you more often than the enemies ever will. But then you realize it's done to make you think and plan and strategize. You learn to work with the limitations of the level design. Banished really does a great job of making a sandbox "city builder" by removing all the noise of warfare, barbarian raids, and annoying military-based requirements.  You start out with a small population of people and some land, and it's your job to make a self-sustaining community.  There are a LOT of buildings, commands, etc.  It's a very well designed game.  The graphics are nice, the atmosphere is soothing, and the game mechanics are straight forward, so why am I giving this a negative review?
... frankly, it's boring.  It's not boring because it's lacking in warfare elements, rather it's boring because to keep your city going you basically have to take a linear approach to creating it.  I'm a huge fan of city-builders as I've lost days/months of my life putting together intricate cities in the various Sim City games, creating large Roman centers of trade or war in the Caesar series, and even tossing my hat in the ring a few times with the Cities XL game...  These all allow different ways to make your city work... work being the operative word here.
To make my point clear, in each of these aforementioned series, there is a clearly defined path to get to a large city, but if you deviate from this path you get varying results, such as a city overrun by hooligans or covered in a blanket of pollution.  You can try and make the city completely dependent on a certain type of industry, etc.  Things may not function as efficiently as if you were to stick to the tried and true path, but they still work.  The point is deviating from the established path gives you a different outcome, but it varies based on the path you take.
In Banished, if you deviate from the established path, people die.  Run out of materials, people die.  Run out of food, people die.  Grow the wrong type of food or don't have a diverse enough set it, people die.  "Bad" choices result in one outcome: death.  Frankly, I give the human species more credit than this.  If you want to raise a community of vegetarians, you shouldn't have the entire populace die from exposure.  Having a community of hunters shouldn't result in a plague sweeping through the town because the food isn't diverse enough.  You should be able to create a city where they have a sole export and import all other items required.  You can start making towns with these different approaches, but over time you always end up at the same conclusion.  People just die, en masse, and it's frustrating.
I understand this is an Indie title, but once you waver from the beaten path, the game has one result, failure.  For this lack of flexibility, I cannot recommend Banished.  It is fun when you do things the right way, but the moment you have that "What happens if I try it this way?" question pop into your head, your time enjoying this game quickly starts counting down to zero.
Give it a try if it falls in the $5 range or they start to vary the outcomes of deviating from the established methods... until then though, I would recommend you try something else on for size.

I've scored many games in many bundles over the last year, and  I must say that I couldn't be happier with this one in particular. 'Ski Region Simulator' is exactly what you'd expect out of a simulation game. It's relaxing, it's not very challenging, it works perfectly with a controller, and it offers just enough variety and just enough incentive to keep itself interesting for a good four or five hours, at least. Giving you some money and a dream, 'Ski Region' gives you the tools and the talent to take a single trail and turn it into a massive ski empire. And I'm not sure about you, but personally, I've always wanted to build my very own highly successful virtual ski resort. I guess somebody out there was listening.
It's not an easy road though, as you scratch and claw your way to the very top of the premiere ski resort league, and many obstacles will surely get in your hair before the journey is through. Maintaining trails, transporting injured skiers, and other various tasks such as moving salt, and adjusting daily prices occur throughout a busy ski day and it's now your responsibility to take care of the minutia. Buy trails, hire help, and build businesses such as restaurants, schools, day-care centers, and more as you repay your loan to the bank and gain a reputation as a world class ski resort operator.
And let's not forget about the vehicles like snowmobiles, tractors, and other things that are fun to drive around in the snow, messing with the trails that you hope to own some day. So like I said, this game is pretty relaxing, and if you're not looking for a challenge, then it's easy to burn a few hours trying to build a successful resort. And ten dollars is a really fair price as well, considering how well the game works with a controller and the overall quality; although the graphics are somewhat dated. 'Ski Region Simulator' is easily one of the better simulation games that I have played on Steam.

That may seem hyperbolic, but the attention to detail put into this game really shows. I've always like retro videogame soundtracks, but Palsson's chiptune work is sublime here. The game is short, and the plot is sparse, but IMO it's exactly as long and detailed as it needs to be to accomplish what it's trying to here. It distills the essence of platformers down to an hour or three of madcap wall-bouncing with no apologies.
Segments of this game can be brutally hard, but never feel unfair. You can dive face first into the same set of spikes 5 times in a row, for the same reasons, but still feel like you're learning how to dodge it better on the 6th try. You're EXPECTED to dive face first into spikes... over and over... which is why there are checkpoints in basically every room (sometimes several in the SAME room!) to give you almost zero delay on death, like all the best torture-platformers. If you want to collect all of the Shiny Trinkets, there are some real gems of happy frustration to be found (one with an actual note laughing at those with the guts to try it). If you want a smooth, easy ride, or if your manual dexterity isn't what it used to be, then you may get overly frustrated here, but if not...
Overall, if you like platformers, and you like chiptune music, and you like supporting indie games, why don't you have this yet?

At first, you'll probably notice that the game is very easy. So easy you feel pretty silly playing it, or feel incredibly bored. However, things start to pick up, and you'll notice that you end up taking more damage. That of course comes with better loot. And more ways to customize your character and different ways to kill your enemies.
Each weapon type comes with their own satisfying skill set. Usually a basic attack, an AOE attack, and a high damage attack. For example, Rapiers attack quickly, have a satisfying lunge/charge attack, and a presice high damage attack. Hammers have a powerful single attack, a charge up AOE slam attack, and a powerful Jump/teleporty attack. Scythes allow you daze enemies, absorb life, and come with an effective Whirlwind attack.  This really makes killing enemies fun!
It's very fun learning to play with weapons, and you can equip two at a time, and can easilly swap between them to perform some really fun attack combinations.
With your first character, don't fret too much when the game asks you which type of "class" you want to be if you want to play on the normal difficulty. Even if you choose the "wrong" kind, you'll still be having a lot of fun and continue to be effective in battle.
As you progress, the game offers a bunch of different types of enemies to kill. All ranging from various levels of difficulty. The maps come with their own set of challanges that are fun, rewarding, and completely optional.
As you level, you'll be able to customize your character in a variety of ways, weapons being the first way, but there are cards and demonic powers that you can swap in and out at any time. If you found a weapon that offers a high crit chance, you can swap out your original health or melee damage cards for crit chance cards that increase or cast certain spells when you land a crit. You can also swap out your demonic power from a healing aura to a diamond shield or teleport spell on the fly.
They did a good job to not punish you for customizing your character, and offered a wide range of ways to do so.
Definately recommended.

I have lost count the amount of my life I have lost playing this game because its that good :-)
Although I wouldn't give it 10/10 because there are some major flaws that give this 10/10 but I would say 8/10 would be a fairer assesment.  The game has become more complex but in some ways better for it, the creation of armies has now come more structured so you can spread your specialisation abit more. For instance an army could have a corp dedicated to attack fortifications via their generals or brigades. Its lost some of its military accuracy and some of the pictures do not represent the item you can build, for instance a Tiger tank shows a British heavy instead.
However I will advise on what I think is wrong and why it looses 2 points.
1: Alliance features.
Wheather you decide to be the Allied powers or the Axis powers, they never seem to work together except use the ability to use friendly territory. A negative review below puts it correctlly, in this game they added the ability to create battleplans or use historical ones, but they do not work, the allies required do not follow though with the plan and do not offer units. An example of this would be Operation Torch and Husky. I played as the US yet the Brits did not help out in either operation. That being said if I was to counter argue this, one could say that because this game is unique that history never really plays out as it does historically, its possible that the Brits had all their transport ships sunk and are struggling to build more, also the fact that  they lost Africa doesn't help either. But that in its own way is a vilification that the game AI lacks the ability to think strategically and historically.
2: The airforce
I encountered this same problem in HoI2, were you could have top airforce training for your fighters and interceptors, and even good research, yet go up against anything, intercept bombers or even go fighter hunting, it seems to struggle to work correctly and always leaves me requiring to heal my fighters more often then anything else. Air attacks against ground forces is either hit or miss, either they do what there supposed to do or do nothing at all. I find the only really effective options is strategic bombing, which actually do damage to cities and cause some really nasty problems. But there is a negative there also, if you were to focus historically on WW2, Germany and Japan where on their knees near 1944 and 45 due to the effectiveness of stragegic bombing. New equipment could not be built quick enough and resources became low as factories became ineffective due to either lack of resources or their own destruction. Yet in HoI3 a country can overcome a bout of bombing very quickly and shake it off like a light bang on the head. This makes things a little boring and in the end you focus your efforts elsewhere.
Inspite these issues I love this game and always revert back to it when I am bored of other games which is becoming often. There is so much to do in this game that offers new challenges, and more uncertain outcomes. As HoI4 in well into its development I will eventually get that, hopefully it will improve the areas I have gripped about, but we will see.

This RPG is seriously like a underrated diamond in the RPG genre. In my opinion as a fan of the RPG-genre, Divinity II is a title that you should have played or tried for at least once.
Story + NPCs:
The story is kinda typical for a RPG with a medieval setting: Dragons, magic and war. The game itself focuses on exploring, completing quests and interacting with the huge number of NPCs.
The NPCs are really well and realistic written and each one of them shows a kind of own personality with a background - which is for me - the most interesting part of the game. The dialogues also get accompanied by a really good voice acting. It's fun to read and listen to what the NPCs are saying. The humor in this game shouldn't be ignored too.
What to say about the quests? The missing map-marker for target places makes them some kind of difficult and sometimes you have to choose the right option to finish a quest. But this doesn't have an influence on the story-line at all. (The worst thing that could happen is that you failed the quest and won't get a reward.)
Sadly, the setting doesn't make you believe anything what the story is actually telling: The story-line brings you in a sunny forest at first - more like an idyll. Nothing there reminds you about the war, the dark magic and the possible end of the world. The monsters mostly appear like totally out-of-place.. After all - the story is pretty weak.
Graphics + Technical aspect:
I personally think: The graphics are beautiful. The animations appear fluent and everything has the right atmosphere to create that kind of feeling that brings you even more into the game. Well, the textures could have a better quality and the environment appears blurry.
However. If you aren't the  "ULTRA-4k-1080p-I-NEED-3-NVIDIA-780TIS-TO-BE-PLEASED-WITH-THE-GRAPHICS"-type of person, you won't be bothered by it.
Ok, the character design could have been a little bit better like sometimes you get that feeling that all the soldiers were created in the same laboratory with the same genes (or everyone is just a product of incest).
Technically, Divinity II reminds me of a game from the early 2000s due the fact that you got no auto-save - which is awful (When you die, you have to load an older savegame and start everything from the beginning). So there is a reason why I am already over 25 hours in the game and haven't finished the first part yet. Another point is the missing map-marker. That's just soooo out-of-date.
Enjoyment:
Well, it's obvious that I really enjoy the game. But not only for its atmosphere or its great-written dialogues - I love it because it's actually pretty damn hard. I have never found myself dying so often or restarting a level than in any other game. It's indeed a challenge, but not frustrating. (I haven't played Dark Souls yet pssssh)
I got it for like 1 buck in a steam sale and I couldn't be happier. It's more worth than that!
Pros:
+ No rushing since all the monsters do not respawn
+ Cheap (It's on sale during every big steam sale and you even get the key for like 2-5€ online due a humblebundle)

+ THE ATMOSPHERE

+ Cinematic cutscenes
Cons:
- No Auto-Save (and even putting the 'auto-save' on a shortcut-key didn't work for me at all)
- Blurry graphics and low-quality textures
- Weak story
- No multiplayer

I'm a little disappointed in Ubisoft for taking the Heroes series in kind of a weird direction. If you enjoyed the prior "Heroes" games for things like the cityscapes, faction details, and down-to-earth plots, you won't find all that much of those things in "Heroes VI". What you will find is over-the-top unit designs and a lot of the current trend to make the bad guys seem not so bad after all. The Inferno Faction has really suffered in that regard - it's not so much evil and demons as it is a bunch of misunderstood guys with horns.
Gameplay, though - that's what's remained true to all the previous "Heroes" games, and the developers did a lot to expand on the options available to a Hero in terms of the skills and powers they can develop. The AI is a bit smarter, and the game can be very challenging if you don't stay on the ball in the early parts of missions. Some units are a lot more useful than others, and the factions have been homogenized a little bit, and there are only five...

As you can see, i played this game for about 22 hours. This is how long the game held my interest.
The game is a unique and original idea, something i have never seen before. First playing the game, i enjoyed grooming the slopes and buying snow plows that actually push around snow! I very much enjoyed these features of the game until i started to look farther into the game.
Slopes
Slopes require much maintenance from grooming to delievering snow to keep the slopes in good condition. I Love all the different tools and attachments that can be used to care for your slopes. The problem i have with this is core feature of the game is the ability to "hire a worker." If you have played GIANTS other popular series, farming simulator, you may ask, "why is hiring a worker so bad?" Because you are not really hiring a worker. You pay one flat cost and your slopes are instantly in perfect condition. This has ruined the core featue of the game for me. There is absolutely no point in buying or paying to maintain any equiptment for your slopes when you can have your slopes groomed instantly.
Parking Lots/Plows/Salt
Well when the core feature of the game has been ruined, there is still caring for your parking lots that no one parks on. Yes, you spend time clearing parking lots of snow that no ai traffic goes through to park, not even magicly appear in a parking spot. Well okay, clearing snow is still sort of fun.. Using snow plows i expected some monster of a plow that pushes away all the snow in its path mush like you see in real life, but in this game all it does is make one small path that would make clearing a parking lot take hours of real life time. Well when plows are horrible at their job what do you turn to? Salt. Salt is nothing special, we see it on the back of all snow plow trucks but in real life, tell me, do you instantly see it destroy all the snow it touches? No? well it does in this game. Salt is extremely overpowered and makes clearing parking lots too easy.
In the end, there is no real gameplay that is worth your time and turns this simulator into a micromanagment mini-game.

For the asking price though it’s great value for money and if you’re into Gothic games of this nature then it comes highly recommended despite being a little simplistic overall. Aside from a lack of local multiplayer, a camera that’s perhaps too far away at times and no other characters to choose from there’s little else to complain about here making Victor Vran well worth checking out.

Divinity 2 starts off like a lot of typical Western RPG’s with a seemingly standard introductory storytelling experience.  Just when you think the game is being too generic for its own good it suddenly gets epic, it actually takes you by surprise.  Welcome to the world of Divinity 2, Larian Studios most ambitious RPG title to date.
The land of Rivellon is a whimsical yet foreboding ecosystem filled with colourful characters and sinister creatures, all of which are surrounded by a gloriously thought out fantasy realm powered by the same Gamebryo engine used in Oblivion. It is a place where talking to obnoxious fruit and getting seduced by lascivious treasure chests is the norm.
This sort of fantastical absurdity makes Divinity 2 all the more engaging and places it in a class above the normal RPG fare.
Divinity 2 is real time action orientated Role playing experience with dense, yet slick old school RPG elements.  The character creation process is simple yet effective as your characters progress is shaped through the course of levelling up. Unlike some other games in this genre, enemies do not scale and level with you which is a refreshing change, if you fancy taking on a new area with low experience prepare to get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you – you will be slaughtered!   This element may initially force you to stay close to home, but it also allows you to flesh out your abilities, strengths and weakness and work towards the goal of combating these high level foes.  If you do manage to take out some high level enemies, the XP gained is truely worth the effort.
Throughout the realm there are tonnes of hidden caves, chambers and areas filled with all sorts of loot, all of which will help in your quest.  Weapons, garments and armour can also be charmed altering the statistic values based on the type of charms used as well as enhancing your own skills. Levelling up allows you to assign points to various skills, all of which are accompanied with an introductory video on what each skill does in the real world – a great touch.
Later on in the game you get the ability to transform into Dragon and be in command of your very own Battle Tower, I won’t go into any spoiler specifics with this but it presents the player with a completely new gaming mechanic in regards to both combat and fast travel.  Certain locations can only be accessible in Dragon form and populating your Tower is an excellent well thought addition to an already astounding RPG.
Pop culture references feature throughout Divinity 2 in humorous abundance adding to its charm and appeal.  NPC voice acting is fantastic, breathing life into a densely populated land.  The characters you meet all have there own motivations and needs which you can manipulate to your advantage with the Dragon Slayer power of Mindread – with often hilarious results.
Both Divinity 2 and the sequel Flames of Vengeance are excellent examples of the RPG genre that are definitely not dumbed down for the masses and will provide a richly rewarding experience for any player willing to invest some time in the land of Rivellon.
I can definitely recommend Divinity 2: The Dragon Knight Saga if you want an in-depth, charming and highly playable action RPG, I grabbed it on sale off Steam a while ago and have put well over 100hours into this game. Divinity 2 has all the popular RPG staples such as lore, books, thousands of weapons, items that can be “charmed”  and presents itself with golden age RPG sensibilities with no constant hand holding.

Divinity II has charm, I'll give it that. It has a beautifully realized fantasy universe, excellent writing with snappy dialogue, engaging characters, and a genre identity that seamlessly blends serious epic fantasy with satire and humor.
Despite these wonderful marks in its favor, however, the game itself is rife with flaws. Divinity II is a hard game, but not in the satisfying or rewarding way that many other RPGs claim to be. The gameplay is typically uninteresting at best and painfully difficult at worst, thanks to many random and often nonsensical difficulty spikes. The story, while incredibly well-told, is still typical fantasy tripe involving the monster-hunter becoming the monster, an evil megalomaniacal sorceror, plot-twisting betrayals that can be seen from a mile away, and more McGuffins than you can shake a stick at.
Transitioning between Dragon form and Human form is perhaps the worst offense that the game commits. While you can transform at will at almost any time, your enemies are tracked separately. Having trouble with a particularly tough pack of necromancers? Turn into a dragon and burn them to a crisp from above, you might say! Well, because of the way the game works, you can't. Those necromancers suddenly disappear along with every other enemy when you become a dragon, magically reappearing right in the same spot the moment you switch back to human form. This creates all sorts of other problems as well, like using dragon form to reach an otherwise impossible floating platform, only to be eviscerated by the sudden appearance of enemies as soon as you land. And don't get me started on how aggro is handled...
Despite its flaws, I couldn't help but enjoy Divinity. I enjoyed creating my character out of every skill imaginable. This wasn't just a fireball-spewing demon-summoning plate-armored dual-wielding berserker, it was MY fireball-spewing demon-summoning plate-armored dual-wielding berserker. As painful as the transformation process was, I couldn't help but get a gleam in my eye and a smirk on my face as I soared through the skies in dragon mode while epic fantasy music blasted in the background.
Divinity is a game that really wants you to like it. To be fair, it does fix most of its big issues by the second half of the game, Flames of Vengeance, but the first half of this 30 hour adventure can feel like a bitter ordeal up till then. The writing and charm, however, keep the game alive. It is truly a beautiful game, and one I did enjoy, personally, but it's not one that I could recommend in good faith. It is definitely a game that is worth borrowing or picking up in a sale, but unless the charm infects you, and it just "clicks" for you, there are definitely better options out there for you.

Here's the deal about this game:
If you're in it for the PvE, you're gonna have a great time. The raids can range for short to long, and the maps are well made-- a route for each person. Snipers? Ledge over there. Riflemen? Head out front! SMG user? There's a small corridor over there. Medics? Well, you're gonna have to do your job if you're a medic...
Anyway.
The PvP is more skillbased than pay to win.
For a game made with CryEngine, You can expect anything to be a 1-shot to the head, unless the enemy has a Pay to Win helmet. Even then, since the fire rate of some weapons are so fast, you've probably already shot it twice. The head hitboxes are rather large as well, so you'd be better off shooting them in the face.
People might cry out because of the Microtransaction aspects, but if You're willing to do the grind in PvE, you'll be able to get every gun in the game via credit-gambling.
The weapon customisation is also very nice as well-- as expected of a CryEngine game. The leveling system for said customisation is balanced as well. Early players are usually pitted with early players, and if anyone were to have an end-game attachment for their weapon... well, you'd probably know.
Overall, I think the game is fun if you're up for either PvE or PvP.

I bought this game due to my absolutel LOVE of ARPG's, even bad ones like the Van helsing series. I play ARPG's more than any genre, Torchlight series, Diablo series, Van helsing sereies, Grim Dawn, Path of Exile, etc. etc. This game had tons of great reviews, had new interesting game mechanics, so I gave it a shot.
First off, there is no real skill progressoin of any sort. Every ARPG i've ever played has a real solid RPG aspect, where you can really create your character how you want to. In Victor Vran, you equip a weapon, and the weapon gives you skills. You can equip "demon abilties" which are just charge up skills. Finally you get cards, these cards have some base passive stats for your character to give a minor customizable aspect to your character, but its very bland and doesnt feel like it changes anything. I can get past all of this for the most part, this im fine with.
What breaks the game is the controls. There three options for controls, and yet all feel clunky. When it comes to ARPG's, tight controls make a game, and clunky controls break them. This had weird hit boxes where I would be clicking on an enemy, yet I would be walking to them rather then attacking them. Also the fact that multiple of the skills are on keys (W, E, etc.) but don't automatically attack when pressed. So therefor you need to Shift + key to attack. It's minor but it makes no sense. Im well aware shift is used in many ARPG's if not all of them. But when Im surrounded by 30 spiders, and want to using my PBAOE skill, i cant just click it, and have it go off.
Secondly the map will randomly rotate your view and will be south after exiting a point. Im all for map control and camera rotation if its needed. The weird hit detection on things made it so I couldn't walk to area's and needed the camera rotation just to walk to the area i needed to go. So it's needed in this game, but it's needed because of bad mechanics. Map/camera rotation is something ARPG's simply dont need if the camera is implemented well, and can only sometimes confuse the player, there is no benefit to having it.
It's all these minor things like this that coupled with weird hit box detection that makes the combat feel bad and unsatifying. I really wanted to give this a chance for the simple fact that it was trying new things to broaden the ARPG horizons. It just wasn't implemented well, and thus I must give this a "No" recommendation.

This game was one that caught me by surprise. Upon reading great reviews about it, I had to pick it up.
Stylistically it's a lot like Diablo. The Isometric view, the art style, the environments, and even some of the enemies remind me a lot of that series.
Gameplay wise it's a lot like Diablo as well. The combat is very similar.
This is where the similarities end and where Victor Vran becomes it's own unique game.
For starters, after a brief tutorial you're told to pick your clothing. This clothing dictates what type of "class" (if you can call them that) you'll be playing. From the tutorial you enter the main hub and hang around (transmute, sell, buy, etc...) or go to the map and choose your destination. After you've chosen your destination you're met with a list of challenges. These range from "Kill x enemies" to "Find 3 secrets". Upon completion of said challenges you get new items, gold, and XP.
Secondly, each time you level up you're given the choice of 3 random items. You might want to pick a new card that gives you a health boost or maybe it offers you a weapon (let's hope for rare!). Did I mention the loot is all random as well?
Also, throughout the whole game you're aided and sometimes harassed by a snarky narrator. He's usually pretty funny and I've chuckled quite a bit while listening to him.
Overall, the game is very fun and I found myself saying quite a bit "Ok, just explore one more area and then head to bed." An hour later and I'm still not in bed.
PROS:
+ Sound (music is great!)
+ Lots of gameplay with more free dlc being added
+ Unique class system
+ Gothic and dark style
+ Narrator
+ Challenges
CONS:
- RNG hasn't really been on my side so far. Not really their fault just something I'd mention.
- The environments tend to repeat themselves sometimes

: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
From the makers of Tropico and Omerta: City of Gangsters, comes an isometric hack n' slash RPG! Victor Vran boasts a fun, intuitive combat system that can pump out some serious hurt on the hordes of enemies you'll be facing as you explore the game's world. Victor is a Hunter, and at first is on a mission to find his lost friend, Adrian, in a city plagued by monsters. With the city's defenses failing, it's up to Victor to save everyone during his quest to find Adrian. Let's take a closer look at Victor Vran.
==========
Taking the signature isometric angle that other games in this genre take, Victor Vran plays nearly exactly like games such as Diablo II or Torchlight. The difference is in the combat system. It is almost completing hack n' slash styled, and is really a blast to play once you have all your gear and abilities in order. Victor is able to jump off of walls to reach higher ground or avoid attacks. There are several different weapon types, including Swords, Rapiers, Shotguns, Scythes, and Hammers. Each weapon type excels at a certain aspect of combat. Swords are great all-purpose weapons, while Scythes and Hammers are great for tackling large groups. Shotguns and Rapiers handle single targets very well, although are a bit slower than the other types. Each weapons type also comes with a certain set of Skills. Learning how to most effectively use each weapon type and their abilities is key to survival. Oh, did I mention you can have 2 different weapons equipped at once, and switch between them on the fly at the press of a button? This allows you to chain together some pretty sick combos!
In addition to weapons, there are also Outfits, Demon Powers, and Destiny Cards. Outfits simply define your playstyle, offering different ways to fill your Overdrive Meter. If you've ever played Final Fantasy X and remember the different Overdrive Modes it had, you're on the right track. There are a total of 4 possible Outfits, and it is recommended that you take the one that most suits your style of play--ranged, melee, caster, or all-purpose. Once you have filled Victor's Overdrive meter, you can unleash a special Demon Power ability. These range from dealing damage to single or multiple targets, giving Victor special buffs, or placing debuffs on surrounding enemies. A great way to stack on damage is to tack on an area of effect Demon Power to your Weapon combos, such as Meteor. Destiny Cards are cards that you can equip to add small bonus stats to Victor. Demon Powers and Destiny Cards can be found via loot drops, or hidden in secret chests which are sparsely scattered about each map.
Speaking of secrets, each map has a set of challenges you can complete. These can be anything such as defeating a certain number of enemies in a certain time frame, breaking a certain number of urns, defeating specific special monsters, or finding a number of hidden 'secret' chests on each stage. Some of these challenges are very difficult, and can take some time to complete if you are going for 100% completion on each stage. Each challenge, when completed, instantly rewards you with items, gold, or experience points. As you gain experience points you level up, and upon level up you get to choose between 3 bonuses. These bonus can be extra stats (like +300 health), item chests (which contain random weapons/loot), Destiny Cards, Demon Powers, or weapons.
Victor Vran also offers co-op, with up to 4 players that can join a game and mow through hordes of enemies together. There are also a lot of neat little Easter Eggs and references scattered throughout, such as the infamous "Arrow to the Knee" Skyrim joke, and a small nod to The Stanley Parable.
==========
Victor Vran is a beautiful game. The angle at which the game is played helps to point out details in the environment. Everything is fully fleshed out and detailed. The buildings, the NPC models, the monsters...all of them look very good and are easily distinguishable. The game has a very dark feel to it, which is perfect for this style of game and its setting/concept. Each monster type is unique and can be identified on screen with ease. Champion monsters have a special aura that can't be missed.
==========
The very first thing you will notice about this game is that Victor is voice by Doug Cockle...the same guy who voices Geralt of Rivia in all of the Witcher games! This can be a selling point or a hindrance, depending on how you look at it. People who aren't big fans of the Witcher might be annoyed by it slightly, but those who are fans will realize that Doug's unique voice talents lend perfectly to bringing Victor and his persona to life.
Dreary and archaic are the two best words to describe the soundtrack. The music lends to the dark mood that the game has, accenting the action and locations perfectly. Weapon attacks sound great, although the shotgun is a bit louder than everything else. If you choose to go the ranged playstyle route, be prepared for that! Some enemies have unique sounds, and at times only make specific sounds when performing specific attacks. Along with their visual cues, if you listen closely you can learn to dodge monster attacks on the fly using the roll/dodge button. Dodging is key to survival when facing large groups, so paying attention to visual and audio cues can save your life!
==========
This game is very well optimized. I ran it at a nearly perfect 55-60 FPS on Medium settings with my low-mid tier custom PC. Lowering the settings made it run even better, at the expense of visual quality--which for this type of game isn't too big of a deal. I can see how some people might have issues running it, so lowering the quality of visuals will definitely boost your performance. Speaking of quality, there are a lot of options for it, video and audio.
I frequently use a Logitech F310 controller with whatever games support it, and Victor Vran played perfectly with it. I did not try mouse/keyboard controls because my controller worked so well!
==========
A great title that somehow stands out on it's on in the genre. With a great combat system and the potential for some amazing combos, Victor Vran is a great experience. The only downside is that it is a bit shorter than most other games in the genre, even more so if you play co-op with a friend or friends. It is still very much worth taking a look at, especially with some of the free planned DLC on the way!

Dark Souls 2 was made by different developers from Dark Souls 1, and it shows. They don't understand what made DS1 a good title; they got the impression that you merely have to make the game difficult and people will enjoy it. Nope. I'll have to explain what made Dark Souls 1 good in order to better elaborate why this game is not recommended.
Dark Souls 1 had a Metroidvania style map, in that there were many linear areas connected to one another creating a massive map. You would have forks in the road which would lead to other areas or lead you back to a previous area; in DS2 the map is fairly linear without the branching paths; it defeats the exploratory aspect of the game and the sense of no direction and cautionary exploration. Now it's just a fairly linear hack and slash.
Dark Souls 1 had enemies that were as weak and frail as the player character; just as you could die in two hits so could your enemies. Just as you could block attacks, so could they. With Dark Souls 2 the enemies always take a FAIR amount of hits to take down, even with surprisingly strong weaponry; I have to carry around a great sword just to even the odds. This isn't a complaint about the game being hard; I'm saying that the enemies have such a massive pool of HP that I have to carry around a slow, lumbering, massive weapon just to take them out efficiently because the weapons you can pick up are pitiful. Typically enemies with massive HP pools in DS1 were the larger type, and they didn't populate the entire map. These were the enemies you switched weapons for; here its as if everyone has the same massive HP pool so you'll always carry around great swords.
Matter of fact, most of the "mirages" I see of other players are also people with greatswords, which means there's a trend here that favors STR based weapons. But more importantly, the enemy placement itself can be..pathetic. Heide's tower of flame is literally lol giant knights every 5 feet. I'm like, "this is the laziest, most unprofessional♥♥♥♥♥♥design..."
And again, it's not that it's hard. Because I literally just lol ran past all of them. It's just....bad. "Let's place a massive knight every 5 steps" isn't "extreme" and "hardcore". It's just....really♥♥♥♥♥♥design. And that's all there is to an area that looks PRETTY COOL. It's a damn shame. It doesn't compare to Anor Londo (sp?) and it's varied enemy placement and challenges. Here its just, "keep running past them because you're too early in the game to fight them all".
Some of the map design is meh. Some of it is just trolly, like placing enemies with massive, swinging attacks near barrels of dynamite on small walkways you have to go through. It's sort of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it's nothing I will ♥♥♥♥♥ about, since you can bypass it. It's just, again, sort of stupid. But not difficult. The Boss fights, on the positive, are still entertaining and fairly fun. I won't complain about that.
They've adjusted game mechanics, some of which are sort of...weird. For one; rolling is no longer viable. Whereas in Dark Souls 1 you could time your rolls and take advantage of invincibility frames, here there are no invincibility frames at the start. This was a MASSIVE part of DS1 play and getting better; in DS2 it's still in the game, but much later in the game. As you level up agility, you gain a few more invincibility frames; you have to continously level up Agi to gain the invincibility frames once more.
What this means is that rolling isn't viable at the outset; you better get a shield quick and start blocking. You attack during enemy recovery, which makes combat slightly slower. The game also likes throwing hordes at you, which is never fun. Packing on massive amounts of armor isn't THAT big a deal anymore since rolling is trash anyway, and the mobility gained from rolls is offset by the fact that you can be damaged during them, so you're better off putting your shield up and slowly backing away anyway.
As a standalone game it's....fine. I personally think its badly designed in some aspects. But if you're a big DS fan go ahead and play it-if you want to play all the entry's in the series go for it. But if you're contemplating whether to play this as a stand alone title and have options, I'd say skip it.

To preface Fallout 3 has amazing gameplay and is one of my favorite recent RPGs.
However its total lack of writing skill makes it unworthy to bear the name fallout, especially glaring considering the importance of storytelling in Fallout 1&2.
The plot is garbled and shallow, characters are little better than props, dialogue is borderline fan fiction level bad and the larger Fallout universe is totally ignored at best, with the timeline totally botched up by the game at worst. (Examples: Harold, a rotting and elderly ghoul, travels from the west coast to the east coast on foot, then becomes a tree, the Enclave somehow exists as a strong and fully functional organization, despite having all of its leadership, equipment, resources and 80%  (further 15% slaughtered at Navarro, leaving only the 5% in FNV and scattered across the east coast) of its manpower destroyed with their de facto base of operations, Aliens are implied to be the cause of the Great War which completely and utterly defecates on the themes and morals of Fallout, the west coast (the primary target of the Great War due to the numerous FEV facilities) is somehow more developed in 150 years than the east despite the East Coast still being far more intact, the lack of microchips in the fallout universe makes a totally lifelike android impossible and despite the supposed technological brilliance of various west coast organizations most seem totally oblivious to everything going on in the East Coast.)
If it was reworked as an original franchise it might be one of my all time favorite games. Its not though, it claims to be a fallout game, which frankly it is not.
Go play 1&2 for a proper fallout game and New Vegas if you crave more.

The download was like... 170MB? I bet your average porn video would take longer to download... and would be way more exciting.
Anyways, I wasn't a fan of this game. Here's why:
When you launch the game, the settings screen appears, giving you options for the game. It's basic graphic stuff and keybindings, nothing special. The graphic settings range (and I'm not making this up) from Good, to Beautiful, all the way to Fantastic! And, of course, you can change the resolution too and which display you want the game on as well as if you want the game to be windowed or not.
At the start of this game (if you can even call it that... probably finished it in less than 15 minutes) you are greeted by a somewhat nice looking starting screen. You'll probably be thinking "Golly! The other reviews might just be wrong! Looks like a thrilling indie game ahead!" If this is what you think, then you might as well not play and save whatever is left of your hopes and dreams.
However, if you do decide to continue, you'll be greeted by a computer generated voice. But this isn't just any voice, this is that one british voice (Daniel... I think...?). And honestly, throughout the entire game I was expecting him to say "And this is the pro as heck guide to Master Yi". Unfortunately, he never does, and instead starts narrating something... as if it matters. He starts talking about how Adam (I assume this is your character) wants a job and he's going to an interview. After that little bit with him saying stuff, you finally end up in a hallway leading to an office and are given control of you player as well as a tiny black cursor.
Now here's the biggest part of the gameplay right here. What? The interview? No, silly! Battling the ♥♥♥♥♥iest mouse/control scheme in the history of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mouse/control scheming! They decided to say "Hey! ♥♥♥♥ the sensitivity or having individual conrtols for anything! Lets just combine everything and hope it works! The main camera (this is first person, if it wasn't already apparent) and the cursor are both controlled with the mouse, and to make it even better, they're both at different sensitivities. Like... extremely different. The main sensitivity on a scale from 1 to 10 would be somewhere far beyond 10, as to where the sensitivity for the cursor wouldn't even reach 1. It's great, too, because you're gonna be needing that cursor a whole bunch for when you actually start getting interviewed. Oh wait, there's more! If you cared the least bit about anything in the game you would soon realize that there is no menu! So good luck with that!
As for the actual gameplay: As I was stating earlier, you're in a hallway and then you go into an office where you are told by our Pro as Heck guy to sit in a red chair. Then, right from the get-go they're trying to push for some mystery in the game by presenting you choices, such as "Where are you? " (As the interviewer isn't in the room) and "Why the red chair?" It's as if this game doesn't know what subtlety is, or that it doesn't care about it, which would be alright, if this game was supposed to be ironic.
After some dumb answer to your question that makes it obvious that there's more to their answer than what they just said, you begin answering pointless questions. Over time, though, they slowly porgress from stupid questions to... slightly less stupid ones. And whenever you answer a question, usually, you'll hallucinate for a few seconds. By hallucinate, I mean you teleport to some weird lcd looking vision in a jump scare-esque fashion and return after some creepy music and sounds play. The interviewer will urge you to calm down and whatnot, further pushing the mystery that was never there.
After a bit of questioning and struggling with the damn controls, the next phase of the interview begins. And this is where some people probably would perfer a warning or a caution... or anything, really.The next part of the interview basically just rolls a video where you can see a person get assassinated, another person getting hit by a car, and animal cruelty. It didn't really bother me as much as it would other people, but regardless, the game should probably have some type of warning about that, whether it be ingame or in the description.
Once the video stops, you are then asked even more questions, and this time, nothing even happens for the most part. You are just simply asked questions for a while. That don't mean anyhting. At all. The story doesn't change depending on what you choose. They're really only asked so that that the questions can progress into more serious and "disturbing" ones.
Not wanting to spoil the "wondeful" mystery the game has to offer, I won't tell of what else happens, but I will give you an idea:
After the questioning ends, you get to have fun with the walking feature that the game never really let you have fun with until now. That means you get access to super slow walking! And super useful jumping! I hope you can feel the sarcasm, because it's there. However, the greatest part of this game has to be the ending.
After all of this mystery and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t they tried to throw your way they really get you with the ending. I might have been able to at least be somewhat remotely okay with this game if they could have done this ending right (but, of course, that could never take away from what a travesty this game is.), but no. They really ♥♥♥♥ed it up.
When you finally reach the end, after spending half of the playthrough walking, you are greeted with a black screen and some text.
Imagine you were reading a detective novel or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you were so into it, and on the last chapter you finally get to find out what's really going on and you read this:
Jones was the culprit. He stole the stuff. The detective found out because he stole something. He became a famous criminal because he stole that important thing. He was taken to jail. The end.
Well, that's not too far from the ending of this game. I mean, the fact that it's so hilariously blunt that you'll ♥♥♥♥ing laugh your face off, not that he stole something. I mean really, I think I read another review talking about this game's lack of subtlety, but damn, this took it to a whole new low.
I bought this game expecting a horrible product, and what I got in return was something to occupy at least an hour or so of my time (this review :D). I got a game that wanted to be an eerie indie horror(?) game, but instead ended up being clunky waste of data. It gave me a good laugh, though, and now I can tell all my friends that I've possibly encountered the biggest pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥in my entire life. That, or I can tell them it's a masterpiece and get them to waste 2 bucks on it.
So the bottom line? Where do I stand? Should you buy it?
Hell, buy it if you want. If anything, it'll give you a laugh. Just make sure you have a PC that can run it.

Ultimate Chicken Horse is, despite the name, one of the greatest games i've ever played. Couch Games in general are incredibly fun to play with friends, but this one takes couch multiplayer to new heights. With its devious dreadful and dangerous traps, you can stop your friends from completing the level. However, you must be warned; you also have to complete the level. If you make it impossible, it will hurt you as well as the other players. Playing online can be slightly slow, but if you don't take the game to seriously, the glitches and lag can be slightly amusing. This game is in Beta, so beware, it can have lots of glitches. Most of the time they are funny and ridiculous, although they can be irritating at times.
In short:
Pros
- Great to play with friends
- Funny traps, taunts, and player models
- Costumes allow you to personalize your character

I found the game to be great fun, but your mileage will vary depending on your thoughts about some very crucial characteristics this game puts out as selling points.
* As close to 100% historical accuracy as you're getting. Gun balance is reflective of the balance between firearms between nations. They're largely around equal, but everyone plays on different grounds where one nation might have specialized over another. Additionally, bullets of all sorts kill you very quickly 1-2 shots. Never more.
-A subpoint to this: this is taken to wonderful lengths, there is a very large amount of gun variety.
* Trench gunplay. Run and gunning can work, but only with players of much higher skill with those of lower, between equals of any sort you will, most assuredly, die. In order to succeed, you must move cautiously with sound, visibility, and map awareness in mind.
* Trench mode. The mainstay of the game and its strongest mode, in my opinion. Positioning is crucial and defending and attacking can be intense in games where both teams are active with good players, however negligence on a commander's or gunner's part can quickly turn what would be fun into a slog where one team just gets utterly trounced. It nominally is played well, but this is something that happens often enough for me to take note of. It follows a format of attack, counterack, attack, etc. where whoever secures the most ground wins.
* Consistently around 1-3 server's-worth of players, more with sales. The game is by no means massive; it's no CoD, so you should be ready in the event that nobody is on at certain times. The game isn't dead, that's not to say, it's just a reality of playing a hardcore indie shooter.
If those sound like your cup of tea, a hardcore shooter with a focus on realism and accuracy with cyclical gameplay where teams take turns, then this will be fun. But if you need constant action or are seeking a more competitive experience, this may not be the game. When the game is on sale for cheap, I'd advise even the hesitant to give it a chance.

Great city building games are few and far.  Banished is a very fresh take on the genre, and takes it a few steps futher than others.  This is an outstanding game, and any who are into builders should play it.
PROS
Easy to pick up the basics (the tutorials don't kill the mood and weigh the fun down), just the right amount of difficulty.  Once you understand what it takes to make it through the first winter or two, you get a great feeling of accomplishment.  That's when things start going wrong.  The game really makes you analyze what you did try different methods.  Never once was I disappointed when a town died out.
Introduced the idea of sustainability to a city building game.  Most games like this have either a single resource (money), or several that are used to build stuff.  Banished makes it much more real by consuming your resources the way they should be.  It's your job to make sure you don't expand too quickly, or remain stagnant and your villagers die of old age before a new generation comes in.
Many city builders are plagued by annoying micromanagement and not enough of the right kind of customization.  The way they designed how you can assigned different types or workers and change them on the fly is awesome.  Also, the idea of being able to limit your resources and how they are used adds a great layer to the game. You'll quickly learn that maybe it wasn't such a great idea to make a crapload of tools for your town.
CONS
The only thing I can really think of is some people may want more options of buildings, jobs, crops, tools, etc... While I think they did a good job, some may want a bigger variety.  I can understand some of the negative reviews about how it doesn't have a lot of content, but I believe the gameplay is good enough to play a long time.

A kinetic visual novel, curiously referred to by its developer as a "game". As a strong and frequent advocate of walking simulators and such, even I'd opine that a product in which you click through a linear story and never once make anything resembling a choice is not really a "game".
It is, however, a fairly interesting and by-and-largely well-written short story (though the end was a tad abrupt for my liking). So is the unorthodox audio-visual presentation of a visual novel justified? I would say so, yes. It arguably makes for a more immersive experience, though some literary purists would no doubt argue that the text should be doing that job for itself. Each to their own I'd say, and I certainly can't fault someone for trying something new in this artistically-saturated day and age.
This said, the otherwise excellent choice of music does go a little askew in the story's final act. There are also some...odd visual choices which I'll leave you to discover and ponder upon for yourself. They certainly increase the sense of enigma already inherent in the narrative. Whether I would have opted for these choices myself is another matter entirely.
I can certainly recommend this to anyone who enjoys a dark, slightly surrealistic story. Is it worth three dollars? Hmmm...I guess the question is whether or not you're the kind of person who would pay that much money to read a 5000 word short story written by an author you're unfamiliar with. I generally wouldn't, so I'd probably say wait for a sale.
Verdict: 6/10.
