First of all, this is a kinetic or visual novel, in the length of a short story. Not a game. Which is not to say that it isn’t good, but rather that it doesn't have any interactive elements aside from controlling when to advance to the next written phrase. In fact, when you start from that expectation, BAPTISM is really quite good. Both the story and writing are very well done, and the character design is distinct and striking, capturing the weight of the characters and their situations quite well.
For me, the tone reads much like an Esben and the Witch song - eerie, self-fulfilling, and prophetic in feel. Dark, sad, troubling, yet without feeling despondent - it instead just looms overpresent and discontent like an ancient mysterious god. And this is a tone that I enjoy, hinting towards those of Lovecraft, David Lynch, Portal, BioShock, and more. The writing is evocative, written in a future-perfect tense that captures the prophetic-horror-tragedy mood perfectly, and is full of great asides and phrasings that clue us in to what may come ahead without giving anything away. The music, though sparse outside of the ending, does its job well, expanding the mood created by the images and words to a satisfying end. As well, the serene yet off-putting character designs and beautiful background photographs fill the story with memorable images and imaginings that stick in the mind past completion of the game. A few non-character shots are also drawn by the artist, which capture more of the burbling emotion, darkness, and depth rumbling beneath the surface of this story than any of the photographs do, leaving me wanting more of these throughout.
However, where BAPTISM does suffer, and this is where my only drawbacks lie, is from a clear lack of budget, time, and resources. Where the writing draws you in with good suspense and evocative phrasing that perfects the horrific tone, it is also clear that it would have benefitted from having a professional editor in certain places, or more time to develop the story in deeper detail. This is a tragedy I wanted to spend much more time with and was disappointed I could not. Similarly, while the character art is striking and removed in an elegant and terrible (in the biblical sense) way, the budget or staff to have these animated or increased in number, at least for certain portions, would have improved the product further. And a voice cast or addition of any sound effects outside the music would have added further immersion and truly completed a couple of already great moments. Lastly, the story is only 30-55 minutes, depending on how slowly you read or want to stay with the panels, which leaves me aching for more story to see and read, and may seem too short for most. This clearly also came from time and budget restraints, which is unfortunate, as with more material it could have expanded the story further or offered differentiating narrative decision paths for the reader to choose between, much like other visual novels might.
However, overall, I truly enjoyed this story and was quite pleased with the material I got. It was an interesting, different sort of myth that kept my attention and kept me thinking about it some time past when I finished. I was satisfied with my experience and was left wanting to learn more about this tragedy and this setting. I can’t wait to see more from this creator and spend more time in this terrifying but serene world of horrifying beauty and pulchritudinous terror.

I don't many(or any at all) hours logged into the steam version yet, but I've put about 6 hours into the Gamersgate version, which doesn't come with a Steam Key. I had originally got the Hearts of Iron III Collection + Their Finest Hour DLC + 'Arsenal of Democracy: A Hearts of Iron Game' on sale on Gamersgate a couple weeks ago since it was so cheap and I've never tried a Grand Strategy before.
I was very impressed. While it loads a bit slowly on single state drives(at least I think that's the term), it was an amazing game. The Scale is huge. Each Continent and each Sea is made up of Provinces, which works much like the Hex Grid from Civilization V, but less uniform. But in Hearts of Iron III there are over 10,000 Provinces, and only a very small number of that is the seas. Like I said, the scale is huge.
It takes place during World War 2, and you can play any nation that existed at that time. And all the events that happened in real life during that time frame, also happen in the game, though you'll only see it if you're playing as the nation it happened too, or a nation also affected by it. But other than that, things can go any number of ways. Things tend to drift towards what happened in history, but other than UK always being Allies, Germany always being Axis, and the Soviets always being Consortium, any nation can join any faction potentially, or even remain neutral. Wanna play as Japan and seduce Mexico and Canada to the Axis and nail Murica'(♥♥♥♥ yeah!) in a 3-way? It might take a little while, but it's certainly possible.
There is a huge tech tree also, though I won't get into that.
There are also many unit types, and a very detailed military hierarchy, and an extremely large amount of room for tactics.
This game, and pretty much any other Paradox Interactive and/or Grand Strategy game, is very difficult to get into though, due to the steep learning curve. Even now I'm still getting the hang of the game, though I'm loving every moment. I recommend watching Michael Broschek's tutorial on the basics, which helped me immensely.
Also, this game is best played with all it's expansion packs, which are 'Semper Fi', 'For the Motherland', and 'Their Finest Hour', in that order of release. You also need the previous expansion to play the next. To clarify: You need the base game, Hearts of Iron III in order to play Semper Fi. You need Semper Fi in order to play For the Motherland. And finally, you need For the Motherland to play Their Finest Hour. All the other DLC's are mostly cosmetic, so you can have all armies have the appearance their real army had at that time period.
Anyway, I recommend this to any Grand Strategy fan, Paradox Interactive fan, or a Strategy fan looking for something much, MUCH deeper.

It's hard to fully describe the charms in The Crew. It's a driving game more than a racing game, it's a broken MMO, it's a semi functional Diabloesque Car-RPG, It's a run of the mill single player game.
And then again, it's a work of art, with one of the most fully realised open worlds ever built, featuring the entire USA, with it's most recognizable cities, mountains, forests, with every square inch drivable, with dynamic weather and day-night cycles, where you can feel the pleasure of driving with a small but ecletic selection of vehicles, in beautifully rendered cockpits, every vehicle completely customizable, and travel anywhere you want in this huge map right from the start.
With the possibility for friends to join you in these roadtrips, and in the campaign mode, the pleasure is amped the amount of friends you manage to play with.
Word of the advice: the default steering settings are too floaty and unintuitive for some people, me included, but with every driving setting available for you to tweak at your leisure, the game will certainly fit every racing enthusiast's preferences wit a bit of fiddling and pacience.
-to sum up: this is one of the most ambitious games out there, beautiful graphics, and a huge and atmospheric world where you can give wings to your driving fantasies, certainly one of the most underrated titles of recent years, and indeed deserving of a chance and a closer look from everyone who enjoys the simple pleasure of driving.

When you unlock guns from crates/supply drops or whatever they are called, you only get access to that gun for a certain  amount of time, Eg. 4 days or 7 days. To permanantly unlock a weapon you must buy it from the shop, or go to the vendor and choose your next unlock, when you choose it you must earn a certain amount of XP in-game to unlock it. When you do - you can keep it permanantly.
When you try to buy weapons from the shop, you can use some regular in-game cash that you earn from playing to unlock the gun, but, it is usually only for a certian amount of days. Most guns in the shop can only be permantly bought with another in-game currency called 'Kredits', the only way to get Kredits are to buy them with real money. That is a problem for people who don't want to spend any money on the game, only a small selection of weapons are availabe to be permanantly unlocked from the shop. Which makes the game slightly pay to win.
You can also customise your soldier with new armour peices that have diferent traits, luckily, you can buy most armour peices with standard in-game cash permanantly. There are different types of grenades you can buy, but those all need to be bought with Kredits, Eg. 10 Kredits for 30 grenades. If you do not use kredits,  you are stuck with the standard frag-grenade.
I hope this was helpful to you, I recommend the game because you can get some fun out of it if you enjoy FPS games.

This is basically the middle part of older 3D GTA games, Saints Row, or Far Cry - you know, when you've done some story parts, and now it's time to just look at the map and remove all the little dots from it. But that's where you start in Just Cause 2.
I'll admit, I never played the first one. But from what I can gather, there's this organization called "The Agency", which I work for. And I have to go to this Asian island and kill some dude. But I have to befriend the three rival gangs to help me find this guy.
Oh, and I'm basically invincible, have a grappling hook strapped to my arm, and an infinitely reusable parachute that never needs to be packed.
What can I say, this is really up my alley. I personally love open-world games when I'm given free reign to do what I want. But there are some downsides - most notably, everything related to the controls. Everything just feels "backwards", and I'm not really interested in spending a few minutes to map my controller.
Will I keep playing?
Maybe. I like the formula, but something is causing me to get crash-to-desktop errors during heavy action scenes. I can't really stand two or three more of these.

Great city building games are few and far.  Banished is a very fresh take on the genre, and takes it a few steps futher than others.  This is an outstanding game, and any who are into builders should play it.
PROS
Easy to pick up the basics (the tutorials don't kill the mood and weigh the fun down), just the right amount of difficulty.  Once you understand what it takes to make it through the first winter or two, you get a great feeling of accomplishment.  That's when things start going wrong.  The game really makes you analyze what you did try different methods.  Never once was I disappointed when a town died out.
Introduced the idea of sustainability to a city building game.  Most games like this have either a single resource (money), or several that are used to build stuff.  Banished makes it much more real by consuming your resources the way they should be.  It's your job to make sure you don't expand too quickly, or remain stagnant and your villagers die of old age before a new generation comes in.
Many city builders are plagued by annoying micromanagement and not enough of the right kind of customization.  The way they designed how you can assigned different types or workers and change them on the fly is awesome.  Also, the idea of being able to limit your resources and how they are used adds a great layer to the game. You'll quickly learn that maybe it wasn't such a great idea to make a crapload of tools for your town.
CONS
The only thing I can really think of is some people may want more options of buildings, jobs, crops, tools, etc... While I think they did a good job, some may want a bigger variety.  I can understand some of the negative reviews about how it doesn't have a lot of content, but I believe the gameplay is good enough to play a long time.

Victor Vran sports deceptively enticing gameplay at the outset, but as a whole, the game slowly but surely devolves into tedium over the hours.
Anyone who has played Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance or its sequel will find familiarity in the setup of Victor Vran. You have a dodge button, a jump button, 3 weapon attacks, and a powerful ability called an Overdrive that gradually charges as you deal or take damage. Movement and abilities are responsive and fluid, there's even a wall jump mechanic. Areas offer secrets to be found, and challenges to be completed. And you will of course level up, gain new abilities, acquire powerful equipment, what's not to like?
As it turns out, quite a bit. Because apart from the relatively polished gameplay, there are cut corners on nearly every other aspect of the game. Victor Vran had such POTENTIAL, which was unfortunately squandered by either a limited budget or a lack of vision.
To begin, when you go to your home base the first time, it's pretty sparse, but still you think: "Wow, this is probably going to get a whole bunch of other people offering cool items, crafting and spells over the course of the game!" But then 10 hours later, you've nearly beaten the game and none of that ever happened. Transmutation(oooh!) unlocks at Level 16, and then you discover Transmutation is just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ crafting system to increase damage or critical chance on your weapons. Or you can forget about it entirely and just wait a few levels and get a better weapon from drops. That works too.
The combat is great fun at first. It's awesome blasting skeletons with a shotgun for the first hour or so, but then you expect the combat to evolve in some way, but it never does. 7 weapons in the game, each with 3 moves. The same 3 moves you use when you get your first Scythe are the same 3 moves you'll be using at Level 50.
Areas offer secrets to be found, but those secrets are merely gold or a random weapon.
Monster variety is limited. Spiders, skeletons, wraiths, rifle skeletons, hammer skeletons, elementals are the majority of what you fight. Areas consist of gardens, caves, crypts, cemeteries, city streets, and houses. Mix and match area and enemy types as you see fit! Perhaps a garden with spiders, skeletons and wraiths. Or a cave with spiders. Or a house with gargoyles, skeletons and wraiths. Or an open plain with skeletons, spiders and elementals.
The theme of this game is literally: What you see is what you get. Nothing of substance ever changes in this game to keep you truly interested. You level up at first and can use 2 weapons. Cool. Then you level up and can use 2 potions.  Ok. Then you level up and can use 2 Overdrives. And that's the extent of the leveling system. Every time you level up after that you get more health or Destiny Points so you can equip Destiny Cards, which are just more stat padding. There is no real, meaty customization to be found here.
The characters are lifeless. The story is forgettable. On a better note, Victor has a voice inside his head who makes wise cracks about things from time to time, and he was funny enough to make me laugh several times.
If I were to express my biggest issue with this game, it's that we should be playing its sequel right now. Victor Vran has laid down a decent foundation which could be massively improved to great success. Unfortunately, that is not the case. As it is, Victor Vran is not worth more than 2 hours of your time, and no more than $5 of your money.

"I'll start off by saying that this isn't a bad game, it's just a bad game for someone like me.
If Battlefield 1's lack of realism bothered you to an unplayable extent, this is probably the game for you. Verdun clings to its source material, almost to a fault, by providing a much slower paced experience than most other shooters where you'll be spending plenty of time trying to stay alive. Running wildly around No Man's Land will certainly get you killed, while taking cover in trenches and craters will keep you alive, at least for a little bit. True to history, most of the weapons are bolt action rifles, so be prepared for a slower rate of killing, but for shots that pack a lot more lethality (getting shot once will kill you 95% of the time).
The shooting mechanics feel rough and somewhat unrefined, but I think that's intentional. You're playing a soldier who's just been drafted--you're not a highly skilled professional soldier who is capable of surviving the average CoD or BF firefight. You are mortal and slow. This is probably where some of the biggest gameplay divides come from: whereas games like Battlefield 1 sacrifice realism for more casual playability, Verdun holds to it. Reload times are long (and can be fatal if poorly timed), and aiming can be tricky to nail down across the lifeless battlefield.
Unfortunately for me, that dedication to realism is what turned me off of the game. I want to say that none of the elements I mentioned are inherently bad, they just didn't provide the experience I was looking for. While the people I was playing with certainly appreciated the slow methodical pace of the game, I would often find myself looking at the timer to see when the round would end so I could safely quit to save my progress.
To put it briefly: if you value refined shooting mechanics over realism, you'll probably enjoy Battlefield 1 better. But if realism is the clincher for you, this is, by far, the better experience."

TL,DR: A relaxing game that however lacks depth and has you fighting against the controls.
Banished is a city-builder game designed to be small in scope, concerning population sizes smaller than 300 people, who have to be micro-managed by hand. For that, the game provides you with tools that more often than not end up working against you.
The game itself seems very simple compared to other city-builders, as you villagers only require you to keep them fed, warm, equipped, healthy and happy, with little care for details. The solutions are also very simple, thanks to the shallow tech-tree of the game: From fishing to hunting to farming, there are many solutions of providing food, warmth is provided by houses with fuel and clothes, tools are made of iron and wood. Health and happyness usually happen by themselves, assuming the other things are taken care of.
Simple, except for when the mechanics start working against you. A lack in any of those areas can quickly cause shortages in another, resulting in disaster dominoes that wipe out your village. No firewood might result in your fishermen dying of cold on the way to the lake, adding a famine to the problem.
And it's not just those intentional desasters that can spell doom, there are several things which probably weren't meant to be this frustrating, but can end your village nonetheless. Farms aren't harvested in time if there aren't enough workers on it, resulting in the loss of the entire crop. Dying workers are only replaced if there is somebody unemployed right now, not when somebody becomes available later. The weather, which can spell bounty or doom for your crops, is only displayed in a tiny line and there are no warnings of extreme conditions like an early frost. Storage can't be specialised, and everything is just stuffed into the closest, even if that is already overflowing (workers only check for capacity at time of pickup, not dropoff, no matter how far they walk). Production limits are usually useless as they can't be specified exactly enough. The storage of your trader ends up getting filled first, instead of last, and you'd have to tweak by hand a lot if you really wanted to store surpluses. Traders appear randomly, offer nothing you can't produce locally (except seeds), and only accept goods they'd sell themselves, making them worthless for actual, well, exchange.
There is also no way to win, and not much of a drive forward. You could build a working village with maybe 15 people, and except for the regular labourer-reassignment, it would keep on going forever without your input. As there is no higher technology or culture, things that would actually make you want to build a larger city to support it, there is no point in going further. The map is also very uniform, since procedurally generated, and except for looking for a handy mountain to put your mines in, there it little that warrants expansion.
The good points? Well, the graphics are fine. They don't overflow with polygons or texture details, but the houses and scurrying villagers are pleasant to look at, and the progression of the seasons, from green trees in summer to snowstorms in winter, looks very good. Any troubles in production or supply are displayed prominently, so you can counter them easily if needed.
The UI, as annoying as it might be in what it tells you and allows you to control, can be adjusted freely. It only consists of a bar in the lower right, and every other information window you want, like a message log, minimap or worker overview, can be opened and placed manually. So you can have the UI that works best for you.
The game is also nicely moddable, and many mods exist to clear up gripes that you may have with the gameplay. There are even large overhaul mods like for example Colonial Charter that give the game actual tech progression and variety. While this is commendable, a game should be able to stand without its mods, and Banished fails in that regard. The Steam Workshop is also poorly kept, consisting of hundreds of duplicate mods, while the actual modding community silently migrated to the Banished website.
It is, however, a very relaxing experience to play, assuming things go smoothly, and you can spend hours pottering about, improving your village here, expanding there, waiting for the babies to be born. But this doesn't change the fact that for those looking for progression, there is close to none to be found, and thus my final verdict has to be that it is not worth the money. In the previous version of the review, I wrote that it might be better to wait for later, as the game was still in development then. Now it's later, and nothing happened, so negative it stays.

Paradox returns again with their newest WW2 Clunky Interface Simulators, bringing you the latest in paying money for minor graphical changes to the game.
I have not gotten into the depths of this game quite yet (Though I have more than my fair share in Darkest Hour multiplayer matches), but from what I have seen it is not too bad. A graphical update from Hearts of Iron II, Oil needs to be converted to Fuel, diplomacy affects trade, and automation out the wazoo.
The biggest change that this automation brings around is your theatres. You create a hierarchy of troops, and can give each part of the hierarchy a goal to accomplish, and the AI goes about doing it. The AI isn't too bad at this, but if you feel like you could do better, you can still manually select and control any divisions. My biggest problem with this system is how damn clunky it is to create the hierarchy. However, once you have spent half your day organizing your armies, its pretty fun to manage. It makes it feel a lot more like you are a general of some form, assigning officers and giving them generic orders, and letting them do the micromanagement. But because its not required, you can still take care of any details you want and just let the AI deal with the rest.
Overall, I would definitely reccomend this game to someone who is interested in hearts of iron in general, and especially if you liked Hearts of Iron 2. However, if you feel like you are completely burnt out on Hoi2, this may not be for you. The way you manage government, technology, and diplomacy has changed a bit for the better, but the base game is still very similar.
Note: I have not played enough to say anything definitive about the AI.

Dark Souls 2 was made by different developers from Dark Souls 1, and it shows. They don't understand what made DS1 a good title; they got the impression that you merely have to make the game difficult and people will enjoy it. Nope. I'll have to explain what made Dark Souls 1 good in order to better elaborate why this game is not recommended.
Dark Souls 1 had a Metroidvania style map, in that there were many linear areas connected to one another creating a massive map. You would have forks in the road which would lead to other areas or lead you back to a previous area; in DS2 the map is fairly linear without the branching paths; it defeats the exploratory aspect of the game and the sense of no direction and cautionary exploration. Now it's just a fairly linear hack and slash.
Dark Souls 1 had enemies that were as weak and frail as the player character; just as you could die in two hits so could your enemies. Just as you could block attacks, so could they. With Dark Souls 2 the enemies always take a FAIR amount of hits to take down, even with surprisingly strong weaponry; I have to carry around a great sword just to even the odds. This isn't a complaint about the game being hard; I'm saying that the enemies have such a massive pool of HP that I have to carry around a slow, lumbering, massive weapon just to take them out efficiently because the weapons you can pick up are pitiful. Typically enemies with massive HP pools in DS1 were the larger type, and they didn't populate the entire map. These were the enemies you switched weapons for; here its as if everyone has the same massive HP pool so you'll always carry around great swords.
Matter of fact, most of the "mirages" I see of other players are also people with greatswords, which means there's a trend here that favors STR based weapons. But more importantly, the enemy placement itself can be..pathetic. Heide's tower of flame is literally lol giant knights every 5 feet. I'm like, "this is the laziest, most unprofessional♥♥♥♥♥♥design..."
And again, it's not that it's hard. Because I literally just lol ran past all of them. It's just....bad. "Let's place a massive knight every 5 steps" isn't "extreme" and "hardcore". It's just....really♥♥♥♥♥♥design. And that's all there is to an area that looks PRETTY COOL. It's a damn shame. It doesn't compare to Anor Londo (sp?) and it's varied enemy placement and challenges. Here its just, "keep running past them because you're too early in the game to fight them all".
Some of the map design is meh. Some of it is just trolly, like placing enemies with massive, swinging attacks near barrels of dynamite on small walkways you have to go through. It's sort of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it's nothing I will ♥♥♥♥♥ about, since you can bypass it. It's just, again, sort of stupid. But not difficult. The Boss fights, on the positive, are still entertaining and fairly fun. I won't complain about that.
They've adjusted game mechanics, some of which are sort of...weird. For one; rolling is no longer viable. Whereas in Dark Souls 1 you could time your rolls and take advantage of invincibility frames, here there are no invincibility frames at the start. This was a MASSIVE part of DS1 play and getting better; in DS2 it's still in the game, but much later in the game. As you level up agility, you gain a few more invincibility frames; you have to continously level up Agi to gain the invincibility frames once more.
What this means is that rolling isn't viable at the outset; you better get a shield quick and start blocking. You attack during enemy recovery, which makes combat slightly slower. The game also likes throwing hordes at you, which is never fun. Packing on massive amounts of armor isn't THAT big a deal anymore since rolling is trash anyway, and the mobility gained from rolls is offset by the fact that you can be damaged during them, so you're better off putting your shield up and slowly backing away anyway.
As a standalone game it's....fine. I personally think its badly designed in some aspects. But if you're a big DS fan go ahead and play it-if you want to play all the entry's in the series go for it. But if you're contemplating whether to play this as a stand alone title and have options, I'd say skip it.

If you only like sim games, I wouldn't recommend this unless perhaps you tune your car a certain way. Otherwise this one of the best arcade racing games for PC at the moment.

Being a big fan of Giants Software's Farming Simulator series, I was very curious about Ski Region Simulator when I first saw it.  Being Canadian, you just have to love snow, or at least like it, if you're to remain sane living here.  A love of skiing might be something you'd think of useful of this game, but you won't be snapping your boots into those bindings and shred the slopes in Whistler or Blackcomb.  You get to manage a ski resort with some pretty detailed aspects of the whole business.
You start off with just 2 stations which are connected by a ski slope, and you need to ensure there's enough powder there and that it's groomed just right, which is a bit hard packed for my taste, but it's not back-country heli skiing in deep powder.
There are helicopters flying around, the rescue kind, but you don't get to fly them, only bring the 'injured' skiers from some of the missions to the helipad for medivac.
You get to buy more ski stations, from small to very large ones, which cost more based on their size.  Own the stations at either end of a ski slope and you own it.
Then you get to build small to large support buildings all over the mountain, and these include from a simple Tourist Information outlet, to full size Conference Halls, Spa Retreats, Movie Theaters, and so on.
You get to choose what kind of service is offered in each building, which have a few selections for each one.  The trick is to cover all demographics of your guests/clients, and the game has some nice statistical breakdowns to help you manage your resort.  Young, Adult, Young Senior, Family, Single, Couple, Romantic, Party, Business, poor, middle-class, rich, and so on.  Lots of info and details to manage day to day, even hour to hour.
And of coure, the best part!  You get to drive all kinds of heavy machinery and 'play' in the snow.
All in all I'm really enjoying this Giants title, and the Gold edition includes both DLC packs.  Also, there's some mods available, but not many. Game: Just Cause 2
Platform: PC (Steam)
Sponsored by: infyrnos
Gifted on: July 21st, 2013
TL;DR Review:
Bionic Commando, as an FPS, meets Saints Row and Far Cry 3
Slightly longer, grappling hook fueled review:
I blame one of the latest GWJ podcasts, where Just Cause 2 came up a few times when talking about "games borrowing from other games". And after 2 hours of game play, I can 100% agree. This is basically the middle part of older 3D GTA games, Saints Row, or Far Cry - you know, when you've done some story parts, and now it's time to just look at the map and remove all the little dots from it. But that's where you start in Just Cause 2.
I'll admit, I never played the first one. But from what I can gather, there's this organization called "The Agency", which I work for. And I have to go to this Asian island and kill some dude. But I have to befriend the three rival gangs to help me find this guy.
Oh, and I'm basically invincible, have a grappling hook strapped to my arm, and an infinitely reusable parachute that never needs to be packed.
What can I say, this is really up my alley. I personally love open-world games when I'm given free reign to do what I want. But there are some downsides - most notably, everything related to the controls. Everything just feels "backwards", and I'm not really interested in spending a few minutes to map my controller.
Will I keep playing?
Maybe. I like the formula, but something is causing me to get crash-to-desktop errors during heavy action scenes. I can't really stand two or three more of these.

Looks pretty but plays horribly.
The most unresponsive combat I've seen in a long time, character gets stuck facing one direction and ignores prompts to switch. Hit boxes make no sense, you get stun locked and juggled without any tells.
Can't re-bind keys or see what keys are outside tutorial pop ups.
Also is buggy as all hell and many of the programming decisions are amateuristic at best, like the loading at the start, the checkpoint system constantly popping up, the half working upgrade menu, etc.
Feels like a student project where they didn't think the program structure correctly from the start ending up in a stiched up mess of game that barely does what's intended...

Okay, this game is a mixed bag. Let's get the good in first: It's hard, creative, and pretty fun. Both the normal game and expansion (not really, see below) are included, which is paramount for one reason I shall share.
For off, gameplay: it doesn't hold your hand and SOME builds do NOT work. I ended up becoming melee/magic with summoner abilities. Unfortunately, the gameplay has a few downsides. Quests EXPECT you to have taken notes (aka put notes on the map) for characters and places. Otherwise, you'll end up Googling a lot. THis was a nice touch since the game expected you to use your brain and not follow the waypoint. It's like this in both parts.
The premise of the game is that you can become a Dragon. Of course if I tell you how that happen, it's a spoiler. Anyway, it took me about 10 hours in to get said Dragon power and then at about 20 hours in Divinity II: Ego Draconis ends. This is where the game got serious: The ending for Ego Draconis is downright evil. It puts you into a mindset, THEN Flames of Vengeance begins! NOW YOU'RE READY TO KICK♥♥♥♥♥
Not really. Here's a minor spoiler: The ending boss is NOT Damien. In fact, the game ends on a happy note with Flames of Vengeance and.... LOOSE END Damien is still alive. Plus, in the expansion, all you do is run around a city, not really exploring exotic places like in Ego Draconis. Flames of Vengeance is notoriously easier too since you're already super leveled and have epic gear.
But yeah, if you see this game for $20 or below I'd recommend it.

For this review to work it's crucial that you don't touch anything for the next three minutes, but allow the words to load into your brain.
For those that have already purchased and played this game will understand the in-house joke. Yes, when you start this game you are asked not to touch anything or else. The else comes in the form of massive white obtrusive blocks blocking your way, a schizoid flickering screen, and objects that phase in and out when they feel like it. However those patient enough to run the game as Administrator and NOT PRESS BUTTONS will be delighted to eventually see the game working 'maybe'. Anyone up for Russian roulette?
Im one of those that were lucky to get it to work and immediately became enthralled by a beautifully hand drawn pixelated side scrolling platformer. The imaginative landscapes dazzling my eyes with an alien world of concepts and Norse Mythology bizarre.
You play the part of a ‘Ravager’ someone who is told that they cannot die, but who longs for a death in battle so that they can get to Valhalla (a door that moves you on). Like me you should therefore be surprised when you start this game and meet the first boss, that you will actually die a lot. After vanquishing the first boss after many cries and pounded computer keys you are again confirmed as the ‘Ravager’ someone who is immortal and cannot die. This is because around the littered landscapes are safe zones and if you die you simply respawn at the last safe zone you have visited. This technically makes you immortal.
Your goal is to simply ravage the lands of trolls and crows and all things not nice. Show the 7 bosses that your male appendage is bigger than there's and collect 12 characters each with their own 4 special abilities which you can turn into to help you to defeat those big baddies. The first two bosses gave me some grief, but as you begin to develop the various characters, the rest become somewhat a picnic and the last boss was as painful to deal with as stubbing a toe.
In final the curse of immortality and the blessing of mortality was an interesting concept to ponder in a story that was brazenly basic. The games immortality is its beauty and artistic license in the form of imaginative and colourful levels that will stay in your mind and last forever. However the games mortality is the developer’s inexperience in coding which makes the game somewhat temperamental. Hopefully however if you ravage the game as administrator and don't touch anything gaming opportunities will open to you and you'll get to play and feel like you’re in Valhalla for the next 3 hrs.

great game, great surprise. I was bored and wanted to play something new, so i bought it, expecting it to maybe bridge the gap till i find something better. I was presently surprised that this game was better. What makes it great is A: the actual quality of the game, and B: the fact that it was quite scary. The atmosphere is amazing, and amazingly creepy. Lighting and sound are stellar, and i found textures to be above my expectations (although not the best). The setting alone is enough to keep you on edge. You are defensless in an abandoned lunatic asylum. Blood and gore are everywhere, along with crazy people (kind of wild cards, some are trying to murder you, others stand still....not hostile, but suceeding in making you paranoid of them). Jump out scares are spread well throughout the game, but arent over used. There are a few "find three keys to proceed" segments. They arent that bad, and as tedious as they can be, the scare factor persists as the enemy stalks through the corridors, waiting and watching. The story is.... well lets just say that it isn't as bad as it could have been, ive seen many worse. To get most of it, you're gonna have to read found documents and scrawled notes. Its decently consistent, not to interesting... putting myself in the shoes of Miles Upshur (the journalist that the game is played through the perspective of), I dont think i would care much about the story anymore either, id be to worried about staying alive. That objective of "staying alive", i think is meant to be the focus and this game succeeds at making that a hardship, which is the point.

How to best describe the Black Sheep of the Souls franchise?
Unfair. Yeah, that sums it up. This game is just unfair to the player. Let me elaborate by comparing it directly to its predecessor, Dark Souls 1.
Dark Souls 1 challenges the player with each encounter, but there's a fair chance you'll survive each encounter if you approach each one with respect and caution. Dark Souls 2 thinks that challenge is you running up a beam because there's an item at the top of it, and having 4 guys drop down from a platform you can't see and ganking your♥♥♥♥♥is a challenge. Expect this trope to repeat itself over and over, several times each area.
Dark Souls 1 is consistent. Each roll has a set amount of I-frames, each parry has a specific window. Dark Souls 2... consistently ♥♥♥♥s you because your I-frames are tied to a stat you have to level of all things. In Dark Souls 1, you will play an area over and over until you get good enough to overcome its enemies. In Dark Souls 2, just fail 12 times, and all the enemies disappear.
When you encounter a boss in Dark Souls 1, its a moment of both excitement and dread, because bosses in Dark Souls 1 are generally harder than the area enemies running up to them. In Dark Souls 2, when you encounter a boss, its a moment of relief, because this game's bosses are pathetically easy, but the areas they reside in are gank filled ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that surprise kill you constantly until you finally learn all the surprises, sprint through, and then slaughter the boss with little to no effort. Even fans of Dark Souls 2 admit this game has the worst bosses in the series, no contest. Bed of Chaos is a better boss than probably 30% of this game's bosses.
Lets talk animations in this game, because this is what pisses me off more than anything else. This game is floaty. Super floaty. Parry's are god awful terrible. Trying to execute a standing riposte after a parry is more likely to just hit the enemy with a normal attack than riposte them, so you wait for them to fall so you can do a ground riposte, which does less damage, and has a longer animation. While you're getting ganked. Also, there's this weird confirm hit before you actually execute a riposte, which makes no sense. Dark Souls 1 literally had this system perfect, I don't know why the B-Team at Fromsoft messed with it at all.
Now, having said all that, let me praise Dark Souls 2 for some heavily improved aspects.
Magic. God is magic fun in this game. Everything I said above only really applies to melee characters who have to invest in Vitality, Vigor, Endurance, Strength/Dex, Adaptability.  Magic? EZPZ. Level Intelligence and Attunement, some Adapability, a little vitality here and there and you're good. Maybe get enough base stats to wield a rapier. The casting animations and speed are so fast and fluid, and magic does such decent damage its basically cheating. But hey, Dark Souls 2 deserves to be cheated. If you must play this game, be a Sorcerer and save yourself some heartache.
Leveling: Each Stat is good for the most part, no Resistance Dump Stat.
Majula. God Majula is beautiful, and just a wonderful hub area in general. Its my favorite area, by far.
Having said all this, I do plan on beating Dark Souls 2. Its not a terrible game, its just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Dark Souls. I'm trying my best to love it, but it keeps ♥♥♥♥ing me and wearing on my patience.

Somewhat complicated to get into, but totally worth it, once you understood everything.
It's the only game that really deserves to be called "global strategy".
You can play every nation during the begin of and throughout the Second World War. (And by that I really mean EVERY nation. It doesn't matter whether or not you want to play as Panama, Australia, USA, Germany, Argentina, France and so on and so forth. You can really play every nation.)
As stated before, however, it doesn't give you a tutorial of what to do. You have to figure all of that out by yourself. There are a lot of Tutorials or some Let's Plays online though, where you can see how the game is played.
From politics, diplomacy and trading over research and espionage to strategic planning, fighting and maybe even couping a country, you can do everything. (Or you can decide to let one thing be controlled by an AI, where you can decide which policy it should follow, so that you can focus on the other things more efficiently.)
It's also quite open to modding and a lot of mods exist already. (You can also rather easily script your own events to make the game more historically accurate or to give it a complete alternative history twist.)
I highly recommend it, as long as you are looking for a good strategy game that is really pushing you to the limits in terms of strategy. (Not in terms of mechanics though, as games like StarCraft2 are doing, for example. That simply wouldn't work out well in this game. It's not competetively oriented.)

DSII seems to have forgotten what made Dark Souls great. It lacks many of the things that defined the first game; everything from its world design to its weighty combat. It feels like this game is a straight downgrade in almost every way compaired to the original.
The biggest thing that defined DS1 for me was it's amazing world design. The feeling of looping back around to a place you have already been is just amazing. It grounded the world and made it feel like a real place. Being able to walk from one end of the map to the other allows you to immerse yourself in its world. DSII just forgets all that. You are given warps between bonfires right from the beginning. This was done because walking back through an area you have already been through is pointless. The world design means most of the levels are just dead ends. To compensate for this, they alowed teleportation between any bonfire at any point. It completely breaks the imersion of the game simply because the game was not disgned as a consistant world. If the level design was better, the warps would not have been necessary.
The combat is much worse in DSII. The first game had a weight to it that was addictive and had a great feeling to it. DSII tries to replicate that feeling, but falls short. There are improvements to the movement system, but they are let down by the animations. Everything feels like it was smoothed out quite a bit, but in that process, the weight was removed. Because of this the controls feel less precise without a tangible benefit. It feels like the animation system has the same problem as the world design, not enough time was put into development. Had more time been put into tightening up the animations everything would have great. Besides the considerably different feel to the combat, there is another glareing issue; the aim tracking. There are many enemies that will spin in place to track you as you move to dodge their attack. This wouldn't be a big issue, but they continue to track you as they attack, meaning that you either have to dodge by rolling or by a shield. it feels incredibly cheep to have an enemy with effectively an aim-bot, they don't miss. Even if the enemy times their attack incorrectly, they can still easily land a shot. DS1 allowed enemies to track you up until the point they attacked which would allow you to punish an inorrectly timed attack.
The graphics are also worse in DSII. The game engine did recieve many technical upgrades, but they are not used properly. DSII has the ability to outshine its predecessor on a technical level, but falls short on execution. DS1 realized what it's capabilityies were and worked around them. They put time into making sure all of the textures and models worked together. They were consistant and had great art direction which greatly contributed to it's great world design. DSII wanted to show off what it's engine could do, but it lacked any real effort. Many of the areas and levels lack any lighting at all. There are little to now shadows or actual light sources. The lighting comes off very flat, as if they wanted to leave all of it to the engine to take care of. This also brings out another issue. Because of the lack of lighting, the uninteresting textures become more and more noticeable. They lack the same consistancy that the first game had. It's not all bad though. There are several areas that look like time was put into making sure it was perfect. Majula is beautiful and has a great warmth from the bright sun. However, that quickly devolves as you proceede to the next level through a tunnel that unexplainably bright despite the lack of any real light source. It seems that the ambient light level was set very high in many areas to compensate for that lack of lighting.
Maybe I'm being harsh on the game, but I legitimately did not enjoy much of the time I spent with this game. I went back and played DS1 again and realized that DSII just doesn't hold up. There are so many things that go wrong with this game that it's hard to see the things it does right.

Best First World War game I have ever played. Fun, fast paced, realistic to a degree that doesnt interfere but still is obviously not rewriting history or making things up, and very polished.
Pros:
- Excellent gunplay. Bolt actions clack in a very realistic fashion. Sounds are crisp and sharp. Machine guns are quite mobile for how heavy they are in real life, but I suppose unless you gave the gunners two thousand rounds on a belt and let them chirp away all day theres no way to change that for game reasons. Pistols are actually useful in this game. Grenades are scary, and artillery is terrifying. Guns are as accurate in this game as they are in real life, not the laughable blunderbusses of Battlefield or Call of Duty.
- Balance is actually quite good. Each squad has a role they specialize in, and each member has a function to fulfill that role. Some squads have overall better guns than others, but the less armed units might make up for it in grenades or abilities.
- A bayonet is not a fashion statement, its a very real weapon.
- Very polished and refined. Game effects are tasteful and dramatic. Layout of the HUD and markers are noticeable but not distracting. The maps are very large and detailed, but due to how the gamemodes work you are almost never going to get lost.
- Gamemodes are awesome. The squad based attack and defend is obscenely popular for a reason. You get to battle it out trench to trench across the whole map, and it makes it terrifyingly obvious how hundreds can die for a few meters of dirt.
Cons:
- The leveling system. There are 2 of them. One for your player and one for the squad. The player based system is for guns and upgrades primarily, whereas the squad one is for squad abilities and new uniforms. What this means is that you will forever be in an early 1914 uniform and have the most basic squad abilities unless you get those once in a blue moon nights where all the friends you have that play verdun are on. Playing with randos in a squad resets you to level 1. It remembers each person you play with and how much you level up the squad with that person. There are something like 14 different squads. I almost never see another unit at a high enough squad level to change uniforms. It doesnt seem like that big of a deal, but you unlock guns very quickly and within a few hours the only real reason to keep playing will be for enjoyment as the squad leveling system effectively doesnt exist. It could have been done much better.

I wish I could elaborate more on whether I recommend it or not, rather than a simple "yes" or "no", but in a nutshell, this is good if you want to get into the horror genre, but it's lackluster at best if you've already played several horror games. It begins to build up a nice atmosphere in the beginning with generic but effective tools like eerie sounds and mood lighting, but any concept of subtetly gets thrown out the window when in the first 15 minutes you experience multiple jump scares and any concept of pacing and subtlety are thrown out the window.
It feels like the designers wanted to make an "action horror" game, like Dead Space, using the engine that would be better suited to make a horror game like Amnesia: The Dark Descent. The lack of combat just seems weird when enemies are thrown at us with abandon, because in a game like Amnesia the lack of combat works well since enemies are hinted at and glimpsed for half an hour before you actually see them. In Outlast the constant barrage of threats just makes me frustrated that my only recourse is to run and hide, because it feels like I've been staring at the inside of a locker for half of my playtime. Basically it goes back to the developers not seeming to understand pacing. There's about 3 minutes of tension and buildup, then it shoves horror down your throat for the rest of the game.
Basically what I'm trying to say is that it's not scary. The enemies cease to be threatening and the whole "horror" aspect of it falls apart. Blood and guts are strewn everywhere to the point where it becomes meaningless and there are so many dead guards that seeing a body is about as effective as seeing a chair.
That being said, it has its strong points. The graphics are amazing, and it would be great for someone who wants to get into the horror genre or someone who can't handle horror very well. It's a very high-quality game and the storyline is intriguing enough to make me finish the game. If I had played this as my first horror game ever, I probably would have been satisfied and left with a desire for more of the genre. The problem is that I played Amnesia: The Dark Descent first, and when they're both survival horror games with no combat it's hard not to compare them.
I think the biggest issue is that there's no pacing or world building. The developers didn't seem to worry about making us feel like the enemies are menacing, they just assumed we would already feel that way. Amnesia emphasizes the fact that you're alone and helpless in a place that you don't understand with enemies that are more eldritch abomination than human, and Outlast fails to do that.
Outlast is a good game, it just fails to stand up to other, scarier horror games in the horror department.
I apologize for relentlessly fanboying Amnesia throughout this review.

For easily driving around with all freedom in the world, this is it. For a realistic game get NFS.
What I just said I did not just say lightly. I like this game, I do. But in the 5 hours I have played this game so far (In one sitting) I have been so insanely upset and happy at the same time, I still don't know what to feel.
You might ask now: What? How's that possible? Should I buy this now or na?
Well, let me get to that for you
:
If the game is on sale,
. Get it.

If not, then don't waste your money.
The first thing I can tell you is the handling is something you will HAVE to get used to. I played Need For Speed 2016 before this, so I was used to something more accurate. But the Handling in this game feels so heavy. Too heavy.
But taking curves is fairiyl easy and makes fun.
Offroad it is really easy to slide around corner and get overtaken by AI in every single race, but on the street it's much more difficult to steer. Irony, right?
The handling in this game isn't great, that's obvious. But it's not the worst, either. After 5h I have gotten used to it and no longer get upset because of it. I'm sure if you get into the game even more you won't even notice it. It sure as hell doesn't make the whole game bad though.
Depending on what vehicle you use, the handling should change, but it doesn't really. Even lighter cars still feel heavy. Bikes on the other hand feel much more comfortable and I actually prefer riding them.
The drifting is great though, offroad and on the street. No arguments.
Like I said, I played NFS2016 before this, and I can tell you something now.
If you want a realistic racing game, that challenges you in every turn, is accurate with every car and requires skill and thought, get NFS. It's not just the realistic graphics and models, but the insanely good handling and difference with every car. It requires you to sit down and study it. It's Need for Speed. There's not much more to say, I loved it.
The Crew on the other hand is different.
It's not as realistic, the graphics are lower and the handling is a lot different.
So, why should I even consider The Crew over NFS? Both MP and SP and both racing games.
Well, no.
NFS is good, really good. But like I said, it needs time and liking and skill. It's not something for everyone.
While with The Crew you don't need to worry about your Computer Specs or low framerate. No need to study the game and learn how to drive every corner. Also; you can specialize on off-Road or Dragrace or whatever.
In NFS, you can't.
I like the Crew because it's a game for everyone. You can costumize your cars to whatever your prefered style is:
Dragrace, Drifting, Performance, Street, Offroad, Monster Trucks, etc. In NFS, it's just street racing. But it's perfect.
You see?
Need for Speed is the ultimate Racing game because all you do is Race.
In The Crew you do much more. You can specialize your vehicles and try different kinds of races, different spcialized enemies and upgrade them accordingly.
The little challenges on your way help you improve your Parts and even get your amazing stuff for finishing it. Whenever you ride a road with a challenge twice, you always do the challenge. No matter what.
NFS's tuning is detailed and thought through. You gotta see what parts fit and earn them.
In The Crew you literally get them thrown in behind you. They fit your vehicle.
And this is great. You can level easily and get good parts without having to win any races.
Now, Pro's and Con's:
Pro:
- Huge World
- Specialized Vehicle Costumization
- A lot of Vehicles
- Bikes
- Easy to get into
- A lot of small & big things to do
- The sounds are actually good and don't cause earcancer
Con's:
- Not too good graphics
- The god damn handling
- AI
- AI
- AI
- Did I mention AI?
Now, AI. Yes, yes, yes. I HATE IT. Why? let me explain to you, my friend.
So, in the beginning I chose wisely what veicle I chose and what parts, coming from NFS and all. I was always high in points than my opponents. My car was much more advanced. I did so to win easily, of course.
But the AI didn't care. My car: 210 Street level. Theirs: 150. AND YET I ATE THEIR DUST. Seriously, at level 20 you can have the best gear, the AI can be low, you will have to play multiple times a single god damn race because the AI just takes off, and you start with no Nitro and they do.
Plus, the traffic AI seems to be out for you, always stopping for the enemy AI, but never for you.
There is this one Offroad race that I had to play 7 times, because the Mini copper had infinite Nitro and just blasted away. Had to hit him into a tree to win. #Tactics.
And that shouldn't happen. The game can be so frustrating, it's annoying. It doesn't happen often, but when it does, it really gets on your nerve.
Oh, you need to hunt down a car? Here, let me change lanes from the left to the right without indicators, so I drive right into you. Aw, that car is almost down with 20sec to go? Let me give it infinite nitro so you won't be able to catch up.
I had to learn their route to get them. #TacticsNr.2
But despite all of that, I worked through it and I have to say: This game is
.
Not the "YOU GOTTA GET THEM ALL"-kinda good, but it's good. You can play it.
Getting the entire game, plus Season Pass + ALL DLC' for 30€ was a really good deal. But I wouldn't pay more for this game.
Ending:
This is a good racing game with specialized cars and certain terrainracing for everyone. It's simple to mod and easy to get parts. The graphics are alright, but at least it works smooth on medium PC's. MultiPlayer is great, but no worries, Singleplayer is a lot of fun, too.
For a -once-in-a-while-online-racing-game where you don't have to put a lot of time in, it is amazing.
For a NFS-like racing game, it's not.
If you see something challenging and realistic, not annoying, buy NFS 2016.
If you just wanna drive around, offroad, drag, drifting, get this. The Crew.
And watch out for that grey van. It's always standing around corners or on streets. It doesn't move. It will find you and kill you.
Apparently this is the easiest entry in the series.

How to best describe the Black Sheep of the Souls franchise?
Unfair. Yeah, that sums it up. This game is just unfair to the player. Let me elaborate by comparing it directly to its predecessor, Dark Souls 1.
Dark Souls 1 challenges the player with each encounter, but there's a fair chance you'll survive each encounter if you approach each one with respect and caution. Dark Souls 2 thinks that challenge is you running up a beam because there's an item at the top of it, and having 4 guys drop down from a platform you can't see and ganking your♥♥♥♥♥is a challenge. Expect this trope to repeat itself over and over, several times each area.
Dark Souls 1 is consistent. Each roll has a set amount of I-frames, each parry has a specific window. Dark Souls 2... consistently ♥♥♥♥s you because your I-frames are tied to a stat you have to level of all things. In Dark Souls 1, you will play an area over and over until you get good enough to overcome its enemies. In Dark Souls 2, just fail 12 times, and all the enemies disappear.
When you encounter a boss in Dark Souls 1, its a moment of both excitement and dread, because bosses in Dark Souls 1 are generally harder than the area enemies running up to them. In Dark Souls 2, when you encounter a boss, its a moment of relief, because this game's bosses are pathetically easy, but the areas they reside in are gank filled ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that surprise kill you constantly until you finally learn all the surprises, sprint through, and then slaughter the boss with little to no effort. Even fans of Dark Souls 2 admit this game has the worst bosses in the series, no contest. Bed of Chaos is a better boss than probably 30% of this game's bosses.
Lets talk animations in this game, because this is what pisses me off more than anything else. This game is floaty. Super floaty. Parry's are god awful terrible. Trying to execute a standing riposte after a parry is more likely to just hit the enemy with a normal attack than riposte them, so you wait for them to fall so you can do a ground riposte, which does less damage, and has a longer animation. While you're getting ganked. Also, there's this weird confirm hit before you actually execute a riposte, which makes no sense. Dark Souls 1 literally had this system perfect, I don't know why the B-Team at Fromsoft messed with it at all.
Now, having said all that, let me praise Dark Souls 2 for some heavily improved aspects.

Best First World War game I have ever played. Fun, fast paced, realistic to a degree that doesnt interfere but still is obviously not rewriting history or making things up, and very polished.
Pros:
- Excellent gunplay. Bolt actions clack in a very realistic fashion. Sounds are crisp and sharp. Machine guns are quite mobile for how heavy they are in real life, but I suppose unless you gave the gunners two thousand rounds on a belt and let them chirp away all day theres no way to change that for game reasons. Pistols are actually useful in this game. Grenades are scary, and artillery is terrifying. Guns are as accurate in this game as they are in real life, not the laughable blunderbusses of Battlefield or Call of Duty.
- Balance is actually quite good. Each squad has a role they specialize in, and each member has a function to fulfill that role. Some squads have overall better guns than others, but the less armed units might make up for it in grenades or abilities.
- A bayonet is not a fashion statement, its a very real weapon.
- Very polished and refined. Game effects are tasteful and dramatic. Layout of the HUD and markers are noticeable but not distracting. The maps are very large and detailed, but due to how the gamemodes work you are almost never going to get lost.
- Gamemodes are awesome. The squad based attack and defend is obscenely popular for a reason. You get to battle it out trench to trench across the whole map, and it makes it terrifyingly obvious how hundreds can die for a few meters of dirt.
Cons:
- The leveling system. There are 2 of them. One for your player and one for the squad. The player based system is for guns and upgrades primarily, whereas the squad one is for squad abilities and new uniforms. What this means is that you will forever be in an early 1914 uniform and have the most basic squad abilities unless you get those once in a blue moon nights where all the friends you have that play verdun are on. Playing with randos in a squad resets you to level 1. It remembers each person you play with and how much you level up the squad with that person. There are something like 14 different squads. I almost never see another unit at a high enough squad level to change uniforms. It doesnt seem like that big of a deal, but you unlock guns very quickly and within a few hours the only real reason to keep playing will be for enjoyment as the squad leveling system effectively doesnt exist. It could have been done much better.

DSII seems to have forgotten what made Dark Souls great. It lacks many of the things that defined the first game; everything from its world design to its weighty combat. It feels like this game is a straight downgrade in almost every way compaired to the original.
The biggest thing that defined DS1 for me was it's amazing world design. The feeling of looping back around to a place you have already been is just amazing. It grounded the world and made it feel like a real place. Being able to walk from one end of the map to the other allows you to immerse yourself in its world. DSII just forgets all that. You are given warps between bonfires right from the beginning. This was done because walking back through an area you have already been through is pointless. The world design means most of the levels are just dead ends. To compensate for this, they alowed teleportation between any bonfire at any point. It completely breaks the imersion of the game simply because the game was not disgned as a consistant world. If the level design was better, the warps would not have been necessary.
The combat is much worse in DSII. The first game had a weight to it that was addictive and had a great feeling to it. DSII tries to replicate that feeling, but falls short. There are improvements to the movement system, but they are let down by the animations. Everything feels like it was smoothed out quite a bit, but in that process, the weight was removed. Because of this the controls feel less precise without a tangible benefit. It feels like the animation system has the same problem as the world design, not enough time was put into development. Had more time been put into tightening up the animations everything would have great. Besides the considerably different feel to the combat, there is another glareing issue; the aim tracking. There are many enemies that will spin in place to track you as you move to dodge their attack. This wouldn't be a big issue, but they continue to track you as they attack, meaning that you either have to dodge by rolling or by a shield. it feels incredibly cheep to have an enemy with effectively an aim-bot, they don't miss. Even if the enemy times their attack incorrectly, they can still easily land a shot. DS1 allowed enemies to track you up until the point they attacked which would allow you to punish an inorrectly timed attack.
The graphics are also worse in DSII. The game engine did recieve many technical upgrades, but they are not used properly. DSII has the ability to outshine its predecessor on a technical level, but falls short on execution. DS1 realized what it's capabilityies were and worked around them. They put time into making sure all of the textures and models worked together. They were consistant and had great art direction which greatly contributed to it's great world design. DSII wanted to show off what it's engine could do, but it lacked any real effort. Many of the areas and levels lack any lighting at all. There are little to now shadows or actual light sources. The lighting comes off very flat, as if they wanted to leave all of it to the engine to take care of. This also brings out another issue. Because of the lack of lighting, the uninteresting textures become more and more noticeable. They lack the same consistancy that the first game had. It's not all bad though. There are several areas that look like time was put into making sure it was perfect. Majula is beautiful and has a great warmth from the bright sun. However, that quickly devolves as you proceede to the next level through a tunnel that unexplainably bright despite the lack of any real light source. It seems that the ambient light level was set very high in many areas to compensate for that lack of lighting.
Maybe I'm being harsh on the game, but I legitimately did not enjoy much of the time I spent with this game. I went back and played DS1 again and realized that DSII just doesn't hold up. There are so many things that go wrong with this game that it's hard to see the things it does right.

Many of you are wondering if this game is worth playing if you've played Rebirth 1 and is it different. And I'm here to tell you...
Short version- YES!
Long version-
First off, the story focuses on just the CPUs. While the side characters can still be there, they're included as dlc when you download the game, so you can choose whether to have them in the game or not!
Second, there's changes to the gameplay. While the core gameplay exists (rush, power, and break attacks), it's a lot more different that 1&2. Now, instead of an exe drive, you know use the sp bar for exe related attacks. Meaning you can't spam the exe attacks like you use to, and you also have to plan how you use your other sp attacks. Meaning the game is a lot more strategic!
Third, grinding is a lot more fun now thanks to some additions. Each character can level up by doing certain tasks. For ex. Neptune finding 10 items as a lead character can level up her luck. And this goes for EVERY character, giving you a reason to swich who you leader is. (Oh, and btw, there's leader skills too!)
And even though there's much more, the last thing I'll say is that THIS ISN'T A BAD PORT! If you ran rebirth 1, you'll have no trouble running rebirth 3. :D
So what are you waiting for, get the game!

This is the Diablo style game you've wanted since 2. It's more action oriented with multi-level dungeons that allow you to wall jump to new locations, a solid dodge system and skills automatically generated by the weapon you're weilding (similar to GW2).

My wife and I only turned on the Tyrant/Champion hex and the difficulty felt perfect.  Nice thing is it isn't just a blind increase in difficulty, you get increased experience/items appropriately.
The game also has an objective/optional objective based star system that honestly reminds me of Mario 64 when you look at the world map.  The nice thing is every time you complete an objective you either get a boost of experience or money.  And because you can see the total stars you're encouraged to always try and and get full stars.

Short version: This game is well worth the money. It's an action packed Co-Op which will make you question the reasoning behind the prices of other ARPGs out there.
Pros:
Price - yes really, you're getting a LOT of game for this price. It could easily charge £20+/32$ for what it is. Being so cheap is definitely a BIG plus.
The physics behind all the level jumping involved are executed very well.
Theme: I suspect the studio is based in Easter Europe, and we're lucky that they decided to go with native culture for the characters in V.V. I have never been happier to see an orthodox priest!
Humour - Lots of referencing and joking. It's a light hearted title that doesn't take itself too seriously.
Mechanics - a new, refreshing take on how to "customise" your character via the Tarot cards.
Fully voiced narrative! - I can forgive the small budget "rogue-like" games out there that you have to read through a lot. However every decent RPG should be at least 90% voiced. I find reading from a screen, often in a 'thematic' font, to be tedious work.
Good Guy developers - yes this is a pro, I would mention it again if I could. The devs have promised to release several DLC's for FREE. For a game this cheap?! Take a look at Tropico 5 page if you want to see what the opposite of that is.
Treasure hunting - occassionally you'd get a map that requires you to revisit some place to fight a more beefed up boss. It's a nice touch.
Cons:
Content: At this stage there's too little depth in the actual customisation. After 6 or so hours you're likely to have found most if not all the range of weapons (not find all uniques, but find all variants).
I would really like to see a new item slot with the same depth as the stuff we've been getting for guns or Tarot cards.
Story & characters - I have to admit they're all pretty forgettable and insignifficant, except for You and the secret voice in your head. I feel like it's worth mentioning as a con, but what is also worth mentioning that an original story is almost impossible at this stage, certainly if you pick a classic theme.
Difficulty - Simply the game is too easy! "Hard" mode  is what I would call default. It can be very challenging, sure, but I wish it was kicking my♥♥♥♥♥ You can respawn in the same dungeon without losing progress, exp, or money. That's not very hard is it?
My verdict:
For the price you can't beat it. This is a game made by people who love to make games, not money. For that reason alone and if it sounds like something you'd enjoy, You should buy it!
For the game to be a "must buy" I would suggest it should include either:
More weapons/item customisation. You can't really call it a co-op without there being some sort of healing class, can you?
OR
More creative boss fights. If the devs read this review take note of RIFT. That game changed the MMO genre the way DAoC did. But what I'm talking about is that every boss fight in Rift from the very first dungeon was: 1. voiced and 2. required a unique strategy to defeat.
Promice me #2 in a DLC or expansion, devs and you will become legendary.

Upkeep of your weapons and armor is now exceding the amount you earn from missions. Divinity 2 is a massive fantasy RPG spanning a huge world and hours of your time. You play as a Dragon Slayer; a soldier of an order dedicated to wiping the last of the dragons off the face of the world. Early in the story, a wounded dragon mind-melds with you giving you the soul/powers of a dragon as well as a Dragon Slayer. You also learn of a much bigger threat facing the world previously only known to the dragons. Unfortunately, as a dragon you are now an enemy of your former order. With no allies you set off on an epic quest to save the world!
Combat is set in third person with basic attacks coming from mouse clicks and spells/special moves triggered by the 1-8 keys. The style is similar to World of Warcraft and its ilk. Overall, it feels solid and satisfying and the animations are well executed. The other part of combat is in dragon form which plays more like a flight game. You mainly fight other flying enemies and ground anti-air defences by burning everything with fiery breath! Unfortunately, the dragon form feels much weaker than it should and could have been better.
Character progression is your standard Diablo-style RPG; with stat points, skill trees and hundreds of pieces of randomly generated loot as well as sets and uniques. Further customization comes from enchanting, alchemy and necromancy (for your summons). There is lots to play around with and no two people will play it exactly the same.
In closing, the game is well worth your time if you enjoy this kind of RPG and it should last you 100+ hours if you like to do lots of side quests and exploring.

Outlast was a pretty nice little game while it lasted. Sadly, its final half couldn't meet the quality of its first half, and the ending took a nosedive into an ill-advised paranormal/scifi area that ultimately kind of squandered the potentially harrowing, and personal finale the game could have had. That said, it was pretty unsettling throughout, helped in no small part to several flashes of brilliant level design that worked wonderfully with the mechanics. Not many horror games have been able to creep me out just from the actual level design itself, disregarding environment and atmosphere, but several parts in Outlast sure did.
It had some problems that kept it from being a great game, but it never outstayed its welcome, nor did the weirdness of the ending really ruin the enjoyment I had earlier. The biggest issue is pretty much the repetitious encounters. By the halfway mark everything sort of repeats, and by the end some encounters can feel a bit like a chore. The first half is great, and the second half is okay. Overall it's a good game though, and worth the money.

Refunct gives you a simple goal, navigate the environment to reach buttons that'll make more zones appear: every block you touch turns from gray stone to grass and, as you move towards your objective, you're basically restoring the game world.
It's fun, pretty relaxing and parkouring around can feel downright exhilarating: sadly it's a very short lived experience.
-nice graphics and art style
-relaxing electronic soundtrack
-pleasant dreamlike atmosphere
-simple yet effective gameplay featuring parkour moves like sliding/ walljumping and objects like elevators, tubes and springboards
-having to find out what you can do (and how) by yourself might frustrate some players
-very short, it'll probably take you half an hour to complete
Playing Refunct provides a good mix between pleasant calmness and exciting moments: it's easy to just stop for a few moments and contemplate the view while listening to the soundtrack before starting to run trying to pull off a few jumps between pillars. It's a simple affair and, apart from a few possibly tricky sections, you can easily move seamlessly between blocks thanks to the tight controls: the actual gameplay is good enough to be fun while its simplicity and atmosphere easily make this a relaxing game to play.
Depending on how easily you discover your abilities you might find certain parts a bit awkward to navigate but trial and error will generally solve things quickly: even if you find a jump a bit hard the lack of timers and the fact you don't necessarily have to 100% complete the game to get to its ending make Refunct an experience free of frustration. Sadly it's short, very short and once you're done there's no extra levels or anything else to do unless you want to go through it again: more levels or a way to randomize the area you play in'd have been a great addition.
Even as things stand Refunct is a game worth playing for the experience it's able to provide, it's good, fun and easily accessible by people of all ages and skill: just be mindful of its short length and get it on sale if possible.
