I wish I could elaborate more on whether I recommend it or not, rather than a simple "yes" or "no", but in a nutshell, this is good if you want to get into the horror genre, but it's lackluster at best if you've already played several horror games. It begins to build up a nice atmosphere in the beginning with generic but effective tools like eerie sounds and mood lighting, but any concept of subtetly gets thrown out the window when in the first 15 minutes you experience multiple jump scares and any concept of pacing and subtlety are thrown out the window.
It feels like the designers wanted to make an "action horror" game, like Dead Space, using the engine that would be better suited to make a horror game like Amnesia: The Dark Descent. The lack of combat just seems weird when enemies are thrown at us with abandon, because in a game like Amnesia the lack of combat works well since enemies are hinted at and glimpsed for half an hour before you actually see them. In Outlast the constant barrage of threats just makes me frustrated that my only recourse is to run and hide, because it feels like I've been staring at the inside of a locker for half of my playtime. Basically it goes back to the developers not seeming to understand pacing. There's about 3 minutes of tension and buildup, then it shoves horror down your throat for the rest of the game.
Basically what I'm trying to say is that it's not scary. The enemies cease to be threatening and the whole "horror" aspect of it falls apart. Blood and guts are strewn everywhere to the point where it becomes meaningless and there are so many dead guards that seeing a body is about as effective as seeing a chair.
That being said, it has its strong points. The graphics are amazing, and it would be great for someone who wants to get into the horror genre or someone who can't handle horror very well. It's a very high-quality game and the storyline is intriguing enough to make me finish the game. If I had played this as my first horror game ever, I probably would have been satisfied and left with a desire for more of the genre. The problem is that I played Amnesia: The Dark Descent first, and when they're both survival horror games with no combat it's hard not to compare them.
I think the biggest issue is that there's no pacing or world building. The developers didn't seem to worry about making us feel like the enemies are menacing, they just assumed we would already feel that way. Amnesia emphasizes the fact that you're alone and helpless in a place that you don't understand with enemies that are more eldritch abomination than human, and Outlast fails to do that.
Outlast is a good game, it just fails to stand up to other, scarier horror games in the horror department.
I apologize for relentlessly fanboying Amnesia throughout this review.

You're a cargo collecting guy, and you live in a large space box.  Your box is also a electromagnet. A smaller portion of the game is collecting every unique loot item found in the levels.  Collecting more unique loot gives you a higher rank and some starting bonuses at the beginning of each level.  Extra cash, bullets, etc.
Anyway it's fun and I recommend it.

Brick Rigs is essentially a mash-up of Lego Digital Designer and Lego Creator (from 1998). I don't say that as a negative thing, however! The ability to not only build whatever vehicle you want and then drive and destroy it in an open world was and still is extremely appealing to me, and that was what the old Lego Creator game was all about. However, the '98 game had its limits. Due to the technology of the time, the graphics and lighting sucked, and playing it in the early 2k, more and more Lego bricks were not available in the game due to it being distributed on a CD with no updates.
Jumping to today with Brick Rigs, it has that same build-em' and break-em' mentality that I loved as a kid, and it has a spectacular graphics and lighting engine. I even dare to say that it's Creator on steroids. BUT, the one thing that I am not too happy about is the lack of variety of bricks. It makes recreating some Lego models extremely difficult, either trying to find a substitute or ditching a part of it completely. But, since BR is still Early Access, I hope to see that this problem is eliminated. (Or maybe some genius will find a way to import their own bricks into the game... Much like Blockland.) I'm also not too big of a fan of how some vehicles handle. I know from reading past reviews and developer updates that sliding has been an issue, but at least it doesn't make the game unplayable. There's also no AI in the single-player sandbox. No other vehicles driving around (except for the train in the city map), no AI minifigs, it's just you. Hopefully that'll change.
Overall, this is a great time waster that I've enjoyed thus far, and I'm excited to see what kind of updates the developers will release in the future.
TL;DR:
Pros:
Great graphics and lighting engine
Build-em' and break-em' mentality that feels slightly childish yet oddly refreshing
Open world maps, quite a bit to explore
Cons:
Lack of variety of bricks to build with
Vehicles occasionally 'slide'
No AI in single-player sandbox mode

The Crew is a love/hate relationship. The gameplay is good enough, the cars are beautiful, the graphics are great but the developers are insane. If you've read other reviews you know why I dislike them. If you haven't:
The Crew launched back at 2014 with massive hype leading up to it. It supposedly had the map of the entire USA, hundreds of cars and the bestest multiplayer. At launch it costed 60€ and the season pass at 25€. After turning out to be a letdown, the game still had a community and the developers were still developing. So 2015 comes and The Wild Run is released which adds a graphical overhaul, new weather effects and The Summit. Also, new cars were added every month with each new summit which was nice.  The Wild Run was a nice feature to have and was welcomed. For The price it was good with me. Now, we get to the juicy part. Calling All Units. That currently costs 25€ and adds a new gamemode and 11 skins for old cars. Now the problem is that if you bought the 25€ season pass you didn't get Wild Run or Calling All Units. And if you had The Wild Run you didn't get Calling All Units. But if you buy Calling All units you do get The Wild Run. So Ivory Tower or Ubisoft or whoever, is making old fans and players pay for new and useless stuff while new players get everything.

A peaceful life in exile, where you fantasize about starting over from the roots with just a hand full of comrades. This is what Banished offers as a town building simulation. Those disasters include weather, the dangerous work of mining, and the great risks of fire, starvation, and disease. You'll likely abandon a few towns before you get this game right, but it's interesting to watch life unfold and it feels rewarding to succeed. It's a perfect game to sit down with a hot drink in the evenings and just mellow out to the calm rhythms of rustic life.

As a long time fan of the action RPG (ARPG) I'm always on the lookout for new entries in the genre that Diablo made famous. With some glaring exceptions, the ARPG over the last few years has not disappointed with games like Torchlight 2, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing, and Diablo III (post auction house). I'm happy to report that Victor Vran is another excellent example of ARPG done right.
Graphics: Let's start off with the least important (and least impressive) thing in this game. ARPGs rely on visual indicators to tell you what kind of attacks you are being subjected to and they can't clutter the screen with tons of words and icons like a MMO or traditional RPG. Victor Vran's art style is clean and fits the dark tone of the game, it's not visually amazing even with everything cranked to the max, but the information the game and its user interface delivers to the player is streamlined and I never had trouble figuring out what I was looking at or what exactly an attack was.
Sound: Fittingly spooky music, good voice acting (the main character sounds remarkably like Geralt of Rivia), and some really "meta" lines from the narrator (which you will either love or despise, believe me). The weapon attacks sound great from the boom of the shotgun to the weighty thumps of the hammer.
Gameplay: Ok, let's get down to what really counts here. What makes this game worth playing amongst its peers? The action it puts back in ARPG. Victor can run and jump, roll deftly, and leap down from ledges to explore lower areas. The gameplay feels great and the controller interface is nice and smooth without taking away from mouse-driven staples like clicking away frantically at monsters. The skills are weapon based, but the game really encourages you to switch weapons often and doesn't use a skill tree so you're always going to be very efficient with every skill in the game (more or less depending on your other gear synergy, of course). Fans of the genre may lament the lack of a sprawling skill tree with tons of customization options, but this game places skill above build and you will need to actually learn how each skill interacts to clear all the "kill monsters with x weapon" challenges.
Victor can also equip potions and bombs (on cooldowns, no spamming) as well as two magic spells called Demonic Powers. These powers range from beneficial auras to meteors that fall from the sky. The destiny cards you find or get at level-up grant your passives and can be swapped on the fly to mess with your build. There are also outfits that change how your demon power is restored (amongst other bonuses) so there is plenty to tinker with even without the skill tree.
The most interesting thing for me about the gameplay was the challenge system. Each map has a few challenges to complete that really direct your gameplay. The effect of these challenges cannot be understated because their presence keeps the game from feeling repetitive. On one map you may be trying not to take a single hit and on the next you may need to use a weapon that you haven't mastered yet. Past level 12 you pick up "hexes" which are similar to Bastion's gods or Transistor's limiters in that they reward you with greater prizes for suffering buffs to your foes and debuffs to you. The rewards are so amazing that I was tempted to leave them on, and they even have a leveling mechanic of their own to intice completionists.
Victor Vran is a lot of fun. I don't know how long the game will remain fresh without different classes and skill trees, but for the money to time ratio, it's a definite "buy".

Victor Vran is an excellently crafted hack and slash RPG that does things a bit differently than your typical diablo like game and in a good way that shouldn't be missed.
The story is, ok let's get real nobody ever plays a hack and slash for the story, there are demons and such and it has good voice acting that paints a compelling enough backdrop for which to murder to your hearts content - that's all that really matters in that department.
The combat and mechanics around it are where it shines. There are a few different weapon archetypes (around 8) that all share movesets with one another - so if you find a sword, it will have the same moves as another sword you find, a rapier will have the same as a rapier, etc.  You can have 2 held weapons at once and most of the skills have a cooldown so you will dance between both weapons triggering cooldowns while dodging enemy attacks and unleashing demonic super moves.
You can equip yourself with:
Cards -Apply a passive bonus to you stats or cause things like explosions when you overkill an enemy
Demonic Ability - Active skills used after charging a meter, can do things from rain damage, shield, slow time and others.
Weapons - The various weapons all have different moves that feel very different when switching between styles.
Armor - The armor you choose can change heavily the focus of how you play causing you to either gain demon powers faster, give you more armor and others.
Everything that you can equip can also be modified via the transmuation (crafting) system allowing you to upgrade most things you find.
The game also boasts a challenge system that unlocks fairly early on (level 13) that you can turn on various bonuses for the enemies to increase the experience and drops you get from them but also increase the difficulty for you.
Each of the areas within the game has set challenges tied to it as well allowing you to try and do various challenges every stage for rewards - they may be things like kill this boss without using a potion, find 3 secret chests, kill so many enemies with a hammer and so on - these make the trek the each area all the more interesting and provide you with gold, experience and items should you choose to pursue them.
The game also has online capabilities but I have not played that so I can't weigh in on that particular aspect of the game.
Anyone who likes action games, diablo clones or RPG's should really probably give this game a look - and it even has a indie game price to make it all the more inticing (<20$ at launch)

VVVVVV is a great little platformer built around a single unique mechanic: instead of jumping, you have the ability to switch gravity up and down. This mechanic leads to some of the most inventive and challenging platforming gameplay I've ever encountered. Every single room becomes a platforming puzzle as you try to figure out how to use gravity to move through hostile environments without dying, which you will do often. Luckily, the game wastes no time respawning you at the nearest checkpoint, which are liberally sprinkled throughout the environment. VVVVVV also thankfully leaves lives and game overs out of the equation. The result is a game with a high challenge but that never feels punishing or impossible and moves forward at lightning speed.
Also welcome is the open world game design that makes VVVVVV feel Metroidvania-esque. Different areas of the map have different sorts of obstacles and challenges, allowing you to explore and progress at your own pace.
Another interesting aspect is the game's story, which does not feature a villain or enemies of any kind. The story feels like a small side quest happening in a larger world, which is a refreshing change from a typical platformer where you need to save the world/princess.
It also has one of the best chiptune tracks that you will ever hear and features simple but effective graphics inspired by C64 games.
Overall, VVVVVV is an immensely satisfying experience for anyone up to the challenge and I highly recommend it.

Let me say up front that I'm not good at Dark Souls. I love Dark Souls 1 to (un)death, but I'm not good at it, even more so because I'm a heinous klutz, whether on controller or keyboard (I've tried both). Even so, I have a lot of fun playing Dark Souls 1 while it eviscerates my characters; the subtler form of storytelling is enjoyable, and I get a sense of heart-pounding exhilaration from Dark Souls 1's combat that makes the frustrating aspects of it more than worthwhile.
I don't get that out of Dark Souls 2. At all. I've had far more time playing it than shows on the clock (I'm not interested in the PVP side of these games, so I play offline), although a lot of it was spent doing the same bits over and over for the practice with a handful of different character builds. And it still FEELS like Day 1 Hour 1 Oh God Why Did I Buy This Game. This in turn has made me rather numb to a lot of whatever storytelling it's trying to do.
That's strange, because Dark Souls 2 runs more smoothly than 1 on my system (partly due to the fact it actually HAS a reasonable selection of game and graphics settings, looking pointedly at you here Dark Souls 1), and I hoped that would make it even better than Dark Souls 1 where I get brutal slowdown in places where it's really bad to get brutal slowdown.
Unfortunately, Dark Souls 2 seems to have gone nuts with the features of Dark Souls 1 I most dislike, and has added a mechanic I venomously hate:
- You're Cut Off, Mate: Estus flasks are more limited. Better hope you get enough expendable life gems to compensate. Thanks to the life gems, this is more of a pet peeve than a full-blown gripe, but it annoys me.
- We'll Have That Fixed For You Next Thursday: I dislike gear breakage in games, for which I forgave Dark Souls 1, but it's markedly worse in Dark Souls 2.
- Have A Nice Trip, See You Next Fall: Navigating narrow footing over insteadeath drops in 3-D games with janky controls, sucks, and if you thought Dark Souls 1 liked that stuff, well, Dark Souls 2 evidently wants to marry it. I swear it's even clumsier than in Dark Souls 1, and that was no picnic. Now, I'm not afraid of "hard" in a game even if I'm bad at it, but killing me because my character is a bag of elbows to control while doing something is just cheating, Dark Souls 2.
- I Swear It Was Right Here A Minute Ago: Here's where that hatred I mentioned comes into play. The measure of an 'instadeath drop', like the leeway you have to get hit in combat now and again, gets shorter and shorter the more you die in Dark Souls 2, as it lops off some of your MAXIMUM health with each death. While you can recover your max health when you revert to human, the items for doing so aren't exactly something you can casually burn through if you have a bad run. [SPOILERISH] There's a piece of gear in the game that limits this to removing up to 25% [[Edit: 20%,rather]] of your max health bar, but, bluntly, the mechanic is BS in my book and this doesn't save it. [End]
This also means that if a particular fight was already ruining you, it will get worse health-wise possibly faster than it gets better with practice and awareness of where things are and how they attack. You can look up walkthroughs in videos or on the wiki, sure. But I want to be doing that because I have absolutely had enough of trying to figure it out for myself, and NOT because a game mechanic has gradually destroyed all likelihood that I will do so.
- Hey, Where'd Everybody Go?:  Limited 'trash mob' respawns... This is a mixed bag, for me. On one hand, you can eventually clear a path and not have everything come back when you rest at a bonfire, which is good, and with the ability to teleport between bonfires from the start to level up and (from not quite the start) to repair (something I wish Dark Souls 1 hadn't kept for so late in the game), it's even better.
On the other hand, it's bad enough deciding I don't need to homeward bone in Dark Souls 1 after a boss fight, and then having a series of screw-ups or clumsy missteps cost me a pile of 40,000 souls, when I know I can grind all those souls back with a bit of patience. I still occasionally mutter '40,000 souls! 40,000 souls! Aaahh!" in anguish for the next two or three hours after it happens, but while it stings like mad and leaves me kicking myself for a while, it doesn't make me angry at the game. Much.
With limited trash mob respawns, getting souls back if I lose my bloodstain in Dark Souls 2 goes from "anguished scream and then slowly recover as I play on" to "ragequit swearing and feel my level of hatred for this game permanently increase by another notch".
Yeah, yeah, Dark Souls 2, I get that you're trying to penalize death to make me avoid dying, and the Dark Souls 1 version I'm fine with. But this is more like playing D&D with a gamemaster who's so rabidly eager to show off how awesome his dungeon is by repeatedly killing the party, that he doesn't care that the players aren't having any fun. It might be fun for him, but I'm walking away from the table once I catch on.
- Was It Good For You?: And then there's that thing I mentioned at the start. The combat. Dark Souls 1, for all its jank, gives me such a charge out of its engaging combat that it's worth everything I don't like to keep playing for the stuff that I do like. It did this from the very beginning, and it has yet to show signs of fading.
Dark Souls 2 doesn't do that for me. Not even a little bit. Oh, it did at the start, when I was anticipating it being like Dark Souls 1 combat, but that faded in the first hour as the Dark Souls 1 goggles fell off. I'm not even sure I can fully explain why, although the limited mob respawns and the max health penalty per death aspects certainly contribute a lot to this issue. Maybe those are enough to suck all the fun out of Dark Souls 2's combat by themselves.
Whatever it is, there's no charge here for me, no excitement, just frustration, annoyance, and a tiring sense of futility each time I engage a monster, even when I do well. All of this  builds until I feel exhausted and fed up and quit out of the game, usually with a headache from clenching my teeth.
I do keep trying, because Dark Souls 1 beat the buttons out of me and took quite some time for me to get not-entirely-horrid at the game (part of that was the controls, but a lot of it was me) and be able to combine that exhilaration of the combat with actual progress through the game.  I'm trying to cut Dark Souls 2 the same slack, but I've uninstalled it twice already, come back later and tried again, to no noticeable improvement of my impression of the game even though I've gotten better at playing it.
[Warning: As far as I can tell, and unlike Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 2 seems to NOT have Steam Cloud support. I hope I'm wrong, but the little cloud icon's not there for me, so.... Back stuff up before you reset your drive or change computers, etc.]
But anyhow, the longer this goes on, the more I feel it might not be worth it for me to continue trying to "git gud" at Dark Souls 2. I'm still trying, but probably only until I've got Dark Souls 3, which I will be buying eventually because of Dark Souls 1, but which I'm not putting at the top of my buy list anytime soon because of Dark Souls 2. Since I missed getting 3 in the Summer Sale, it will probably be a while. Right now, I wish I'd bought 3 instead of 2, because I doubt I could dislike 3 more than I do 2. Hopefully Dark Souls 3 won't one day prove me wrong.
I'll revise this should I change my mind, but at this point I can't recommend it, and suggest that you go buy Dark Souls 1 instead. And a controller, too, probably; I'm not a fan of controllers and even I prefer one for these games.
Lots of people seem to like Dark Souls 2, though, so no need to take my word for it.
[Edited for clarity and a couple of additional observations.]

Divinity 2 is a remastered version of Ego Draconis featuring new content with an enhanced engine packaged with an add-on Flames of Vengeance (FOV). The 2 games form a complete story when played together.
Personally it took me 45 hours to finish the 2 games, and this is taking into account that i had skipped alot of side quests and even referred to a walkthrough for some of the puzzles. If you were to do everything and experience all the game had to offer, it will probably take you close to 80 to 90 hours or even more.
The first starting village you entered had a surprisingly huge amount of sidequests. The problem is, most of them just aren't very interesting, and most of the time, instead enjoying the story in the sidequest, alot of them felt more like merely items in a checklist that has to be finished off just for the rewards.
The main problem i feel though, the whole game just doesn't take itself very seriously. It tries to tell an epic story but the execution just feels amatuerish. (Was it really necessary to re-introduce the player character in FOV via a parody of the movie "The Terminator"?)
The character animations are very rough and almost all characters you talk to tend to like to flail their arms wildly in the air in a very exaggerated style. Its as if they were thinking if they make the NPCs move their arms more, they would look more alive lol. Its really funny to see an esteemed Knight Commander talking to you and flailing his arms wildly in the air like a mad loon. Alot of the NPC faces are also re-used and you will see quite alot of similar looking faces everywhere.
Voice acting is noticeably bad, and alot of them either sound bored, over-enthusiastic, or just plain silly. Music is a mixed bag, with some tunes feeling suitably atmospheric, and some tunes that won't sound out of place in a James Bond movie lol.
The main selling point of the game is to be able to turn into a dragon and fly anywhere. But this concept isn't as exciting as it sounds. For one thing, the world is not truly open-world and fully explorable. There are alot of invisible walls everywhere. And you will not have the pleasure of morphing into a dragon and burning down all the enemies on the ground. They just magically disappear when you morph into dragon mode which i suppose was to not imbalance the gameplay. Still it would have been nicer if they were able to combine the 2 into a seamless experience instead of the current system that they had.
One particular feature that i enjoyed was Mindreading, which basically lets you listen to the thoughts of NPCs. Its a very nice idea, as you can sometimes get extra rewards or even new quests with it. But again, they had to put a silly penalty of requiring EXP to actually do mind reading. Personally i felt that it was really unnecessary to do this, to punish the player's level progress while he checks out something cool with an NPC.
The ending of Ego Draconis is also very controversial and suffice to say, basically undermines everything you have done, and is one of the worst endings IMO in an RPG. The add-on Flames of Vengeance(FOV) corrects this however, and provides better closure. I am aware that FOV came 11 months after the Ego Draconis, and i have a gut feeling that it was crafted to pacify the players who have been crying foul of the original ending.
It may look like i am bashing the game, but i really am not. There is an interesting game in there somewhere, but only if you are willing to endure the amatuerish style it is presented. Maybe thats the way this RPG is meant to be enjoyed, a funny little game with some movie parodies that doesn't take itself very seriously.
Overall Rating: 6.0 / 10

I'm surprised I hadn't heard more about this game earlier; it was fun, funny, and featured a pretty compelling story.
The graphics are a touch dated looking but nothing so antiquated that you can't look past, just something that would have been pretty cutting edge a few years ago. The art direction was a fairly typical high-fantasy look without going too wild. As 'real' a world as you're likely to see in this genre.
The music was extremely well done. Not much more to say about that. It was very good.
Gameplay was mostly smooth, there seemed to be some issues with jumping and it became advisable to always jump just a little ahead of what you thought you'd need. There were also some issues with clipping on objects but didn't occur often enough for me to get frustrated by it.
Levelling was very smooth - each level actually made you feel more powerful but never took you to a point where there was no challenge at all. Different builds (Can't really call them classes, it's a classless system, you just choose the talents that you want and level them up as far as you want) may get different mileage but by the time I was near the end of the game the only thing I really had to watch out for were large groups of ranged or magic users since my health was tightly tied to hurting things.
Overall it felt like a slightly more primitive version of Dragon Age in many ways. Certainly preferable to what they did to DA2! Also, no spoilers, but you WILL feel like you've been kicked in the neck at the end of the game, don't worry, the expansion makes up for it.
Yeah... the expansion. I should mention that you don't import your character and you don't start with any of the gear you had, or indeed any at all, just enough gold to help buy things to get you back on your feet. Also, it takes away your shape-shifting ability until right at the end, that felt a bit dickish. So, while the 'world' was smaller and the play more limited, it did still have a reasonably engaging story to help get you through it.
Made me all the more eager for the studios upcoming Original Sin game set in the far past of the same world.

- Decent wheel support for an "arcade driving" title. At least with a Logitech G27.
- OK car physics and handling. Hardcore "petroheads" are probably going to laugh at this but from my experience, car handling is fun AND challenging.
- Huge and very diverse environment. Driving game with huge environment are not exactly common so...
- Nice graphics during sunrise and sunset: Very impressive lightning.
- Extremely poor support of TrackIR. Cannot even look behind with it while you can with the mouse!
- Glitches: All over the place. Floating cars, "cars inside" the road, floating rocks, slight but constant stuttering when loading assets. Heck, during a cut-scene, my car literally went through a prop in the scene!
- Intense network rubber banding/teleportation of other players cars.
- Washed out, ugly lightning effect during storm and raining... Nights are also very dark. Lightning is not consistent: Range from superb sunrise/sunset to WTF moments at night and during cloudy weather.
- The game use some sort of "instancing" where players are not necessarily going to encounter each other, even when exactly at the same spot on the map.
- Lots of DLC exclusive content and "buyable with real currency" cars. Not a fan of the latest.
- Of course, UPlay, which totally sucks. Add another layer of unneeded complexity to the whole experience.
So, if I could, I would give a "maybe" rating. But I can't so, I have to rate it negatively.
If you like sand box, non-hardcore driving game, you might find it interesting. Exploring the map is a blast... but expect glitches. Get it during a sale at 50%-80% rebate.

For me, Dark Souls 2 is just no action RPG that I would recommend (I would rather tell people to play DS1 and DS2). I played and loved Dark Souls 1 but DS2 just didn't understand what made the first game good. The first game was hard because it didn't explain much and you would die in a few hits. But so did most enemies. The normal enemies were similar to you. Only 2-3 hits to kill and similar rules regarding stamina and blocking. E.g. blocking an enemy blow with a shield led to an opening that could be abused. For both sides. Enemy patterns could be learned and nearly all traps could be foreseen if you watched closely enough. And of course the amazing level design.
I don't mind that the level design is worse than in Dark Souls 1 but what really bothers me is that the game is in many places just hard to be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Many enemies that drop behind you that you cannot see before and you fight against at least 2 enemies at the same time most of the time. And that's one of my big issues with DS2. Fighting in DS is not made for more than 1 enemy. The 1on1 combat is even better than before with many nuances. But you usually get swarmed by enemies and than you have to use magic (which is the easy mode for DS2) or cheese the enemies. But many times you get hit from the sides or in the back just because the camera and lock on system (which are basically the same as the one from DS1) are not made for groups. And even if you see the enemies, you don't have enough stamina to effectively fight groups without hit and run tactics (which gets boring and takes time). This combined with the following makes DS2 a hard game but not in the fair way DS1 challenged you but in a unfair way that just wants to be difficult because DS1 was difficult:
-In DS1 you could level up at each bonfire. Now you have to travel to the starting area (one loading screen), talk to an NPC, listen to the same two lines every single time, level up, travel back to the bonfire you were before (another loading screen). This serves no purpose whatsoever. It's just annoying.
-Weapons in this game break way too fast. They get repaired every time you use a bonfire but be prepared to have at least 2 of your favourite weapons (even more if you are dual wielding) because if you fight every enemy between two bonfires, 1 weapon won't make it in many areas (and switching them while fighting is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you don't have them already equipped which again costs weight).
-Enemies don't follow the same rules as you. Like I wrote above, DS1 was fair because you and your enemies had a level playground. Not so in DS2. Enemies have much higher poise, stamina and stamina regeneration. The NPC red phantoms that invade you were introduced in DS1 to get used to player invasions or at least have a similar offline experience. So these phantoms were basically other players. But in DS2, they have way more health than a normal player. And the enemies are also not affected by attacks from other enemies (like in DS1). They just hack and shoot at you but are invulnerable to everything but your attacks and fall damage.
-Unclear roll invulnerability: They reduced the invulnerability frames you have per roll. Which in itself is not the problem. But now you can be hit while still rolling. So there is no clear visual indicator when you are invulnerable during a roll and when not. Yes, you get used to that and learn it, but Dark Souls was always about clear visual indicators.
The DLCs that were so praised also have the same issues. While especially the second DLC has an nice end fight, the rest is just groups of enemies attacking you over and over again.
TL/DR: The game wants to be difficult by being unfair and that's why I can't recommend Dark Souls 2. Is it a bad game? No. But not a good one either. Play DS1 or DS3. You can easily skip this one. After playing through most of this game, there isn't a single memorable moment (like e.g. Sif). Just random areas (altough very pretty at times) mashed loosely together with hordes of enemies and some nice boss fights (when it's finally 1vs1 again).
Edit: After finishing the game, I also find the end of the game very underwhelming and lacking some coherence. You travel up to a certain NPC/boss (cool fight though) that gives you an item. With that item you have to find a place you were before but nothing happened there, fight a very easy boss, then go the final area to fight the final boss there (did it in the first attempt). Without reading the wiki, I had no idea who exactly I'm fighting there and why that mattered. Yes, most DS lore was always hidden but still, DS1 made very clear what and why you are doing even if you missed the nuances in the lore. DS2 surely had some good bosses. Like I wrote, 1on1 is where Dark Souls 2 shines, but the final boss(es) were rather "meh".
Still: It took me 63 hrs for one playthrough so there is definitely enough game for your money. For me, a large part of this game was just not that enoyable.

Yes, I know, city building games are my weak spot. Somehow, it is the only genre of games that can keep me at the computer for any number of hours.
Banished is a very nice sandbox city-building game. At first it seems rather simplistic: in normal mode you start with just around 10 adults (and some children, who can't work anyway). Their main concerns are, unsurprisingly, food and warmth.
After just 6 or 7 hours of game time your town has grown to 30 or 40 adults and you've built all the available types of building. It may seem that the game is almost over: after all, you've overcome the harshest year, in which you had to manually rotate the single individual free from gathering food between building, blacksmithing and tailoring. But it turns out, that the game just turns into the next phase: the scaling of your settlement. You no longer can rely on all your citizens getting what they need from just one barn. You have to deal with exponential growth of population, and besides that have to house and feed the random groups of nomads coming to live with you. The game turns from survival to logistics.
The game lacks any kind of levels of scenarios, and to be honest, it remains fun even without them. You can easily spend tens of hours on just one map. The amount of micromanagement scales very nicely. In the first years you carefully weigh the efforts of every single individual. When your storage of warm clothes is full, you send your tailor to do some other useful job. When I first started to grow crops, every year during winter time I re-assigned all my farmers to other jobs, to get things done while there's no work in the fields. But as the time goes, you have to spend less and less time on the details and more on the general economy: having just right amount of everything.
Finally, about a few things that could make the game better. Firstly, it could gain from having various scenarios, that favor different ways to playing, like, for instance Tropico. This includes better generator of more diverse maps. Currently there are just two modes: mountains/plains. The plains map has 2 or 3 almost round lakes and 1 or 2 rivers.
P.S. And one more thing. Kudos for having achievements that one has to, you know, achieve. The easiest one involves a town with the population of 100, which requires at least 10 hours of game time.

For a game that came out before EA went balls deep with WWI, Verdun really embraces it's source material. It takes the concept of the bolt-action rifleman, and makes it an integral part of the game, as opposed to BF1's emphasis on submachineguns and early machineguns. Trench warfare is surprisingly hectic, and you are quickly discouraged from playing "fast and loose" with cover as you would in, say Call of Duty, and I often found myself crouching and crawling prone more often than walking. But by far the most exhilarating part of the game is going "over the top" and rushing across no man's land with three or four squadmates on your side, only to see them cut down by machinegun fire, and diving into the enemy trench, and skewering the nearest kraut on your bayonet.
An aspect of the game that I think may often go unappreciated is the way in which characters die. Yes, they scream as their limbs are blown off or they're shot in the chest, but it doesn't stop. Standing near a recently killed player, you can hear either more screaming of pain, moaning, or simply gurgling as some poor sod chokes on his own blood.
My internet connection is okay, but I found myself often automatically kicked from servers when my ping temporarily goes a bit high. The respawn times are a real drag; far too long for a game in which you just have to accept that you will die quite often.

This little contraption is the main highlight of the game, and I had so much fun with it I can't belive it wasn't using in other games. What I don't like about this game: The main problem with this game was it was to empty. Sure, there were enemy bases to blow up, and things to do, but they are so little of them. Swords & Crossbones was a very interesting game for me to play. It's basically a "Tactics" game, following the Final Fantasy Tactics combat-style, which is essentially taking a normal JRPG and adding terrain to its combat. Now, units actually move around, have AOE abilities, etc. etc. which adds quite a lot of depth to the more traditional JRPG combat, with a few new interesting possibilities.
I have not played any of the tactics game, but I remember one of my friends playing it. This game made me want to go back to those games (which I'll do, sooner or later, now) in a very unexpected way.
The ideas of the game are cool, and I really had a blast in the beginning. Unfortunately, and perhaps due to the mobile roots of the developing team, the game ends up falling apart after a couple of hours. It's full of potential, though! Especially since it's a genre that I don't think I've ever seen on PC (not often, at the very least).
I won't write a long review, just focusing on a couple of points that I feel were very relevant when I was playing.
Going against some other reviewers, who claimed the game to be both "deep" and "casual"... well, I wouldn't call it depth, as much as
. The game does a lot of different stuff. Not only does it have the Tactics combat, but it also has a city-builder element, where you must manage resources in order to build a growing island, to construct buildings that provide resources or upgrade possibilities for your characters.
It also has some exploration element, where you sail to find new islands (unfortunately purely linear, going along with the story), and some other repeatable quests.
I disagree with the "depth" because of a single, yet huge problem with the game: the combat is too easy. I've spent most of the game without even knowing there were abilities (the game explains everything in the first 30 minutes, while some of the things are unlocked hours after the fact... later), and even then, the combat provided no difficulty at all.
This is mostly a problem when you realize that the whole upgrade/skill system is rendered pointless. Which, in turn, renders most of the city building system pointless as well.
It lacks depth in the sense that you'll never have to think about the combat situations you're in. The game is also very much extended by repetition (again, mobile roots), keeping you stuck in the gameplay loop of discovering islands to unlock more upgrades, to discover more islands, to get more upgrades, ad infinitum.
Well, not again infinitely, but for far longer than it should.
So, except a lot of the same battlefields, enemies, etc. while at the same time requiring no thought to get through it.
It has an interesting button: auto-combat. The AI isn't very good, but it works. 5 hours in, I stopped playing most battles. There was no point. I just hit the little button, and very sub-optimal AI would do the obligatory grind for me!
This is not enough, since the UI requires you to still click quite a lot of times to get the auto combat started.
There are a bunch of problems created by the previous one. Random encounters during exploration, some obligatory battles while you're doing the main quest, etc. etc.
If the combat was well tuned, it might have been good.
Unfortunately, the game is mostly a skinner box. It would almost work better as a clicker game.
And this is all very unfortunate, but it's a useful example to have, I guess.
The game seems very cool. The visuals are pleasant, the writing was actually good (I was laughing at the start of the game! And I rarely appreciate the writings in videogames), and the various system had incredible potential. The combat system and skills may have even been good, if the enemy encounters were balanced. As they're not, the game turns into a huge, huge grind... There's no point.
I apologize for just hitting the same point over and over and... But that is the single problem that ruined the whole game, for me. If it was shorter, I would have enjoyed it, as I would not have experience much down town. While I was learning the systems, it was cool! After that, the game couldn't keep up and still extended itself (rather artificially) for a good 10+ hours.
You have a bunch of characters, equipment upgrades, etc. You never get to explore any of it.
With all this said, I look forward for the developers' next game. This was so close to being great... hopefully, they'll take similar concepts, but with a larger focus on the game's core, instead of all systems that are mostly skinner boxes.

A gentleman's game for gentlemen. Possibly the most criminally unapreciated game to come out in recent years.
Soundtrack's still great, writing's still extraordinary, humor and self-awareness are still fully-intact, combat still ends with either you or the rude dudes dying within five seconds, and it still runs Gamebryo. Sorry about the last point, but it's still better than most of the things Bethesda's done with that engine in spite of having giant piles of money.
So far as I can tell, the Developer's Cut adds some pretty neat design documents and artwork, along with a copy of aforementioned kickin' rad soundtrack and a mode that lets you mess around with the dev console. Not quite a full remaster (which would have been GOTY material) but a bit of extra gravy never hurt.

TLDR: A must buy game.
I have played Diablos 1 through 3, Torchlight 1 and 2, Path of Exile, Marvel Heroes and Divinity... Having said that, I think Victor Vran has reached peak perfection on the ARPG genre. This is the game you should not think twice of picking up. I was hesistant at first since I wasn't an early access buyer and just decided to buy the game based on all of the good reviews on Steam (and youtube gameplay videos). I bought one for myself and for my brother and we have never looked back.
PROS:
- Very fluid gameplay and great graphics. Keeping things fascinating is the ability to jump, and dodge, and so on
- Can downscale graphics to be playable on low-end desktops/laptops
- Decent story with great voice acting (much much much better story than Diablo 3/Torchlight 2)
- A bit steampunk (enough to please fans of the genre, but not too much to turn off non-fans of steampunk).
- The setting and ambiance of the story and game - old eastern European "Transylvannia" - is very much on point
- You can change your difficulty almost on the fly with hexes - plus the difficulty setting is so innovatively done (again, not like D3 where higher difficulty settings just give more health, toughness and power to mobs)
- The outfit you wear essentially determines majority of your playstyle. However, the system is easy to understand but at the same time is intricate and deep. No skill trees here - but how they implemented choice is wonderfully done. Your outfit, weapons, demon powers, and destiny cards determine your "class", and there are possibly a billion combination of these
- A lot of people seemingly hate "The Voice" character but I love him. A lot of el-oh-el references and funny quips abound
CONS:
- still some bugs that need to be ironed out. Some champion mobs don't reset from rage mode when you die even though their hitpoints goes back to full. Also there are areas where when you make the mistake of stepping on them the whole screen freezes (but the UI is still active, strangely). happens rarely though.
- online coop mode works but can be confusing. It turns out that you can only be friends in-game with folk you are Steam friends with. Also, the UI needs to be worked on to show you if you are already in a party or night as there is no confirmation if you want to join a friend's party when he/she invites you. The game should immediately port you to your friends' instance when you join
MINOR GRIPES:
- no playable female characters (which doesn't matter to me as I'm a guy and I like playing guy characters but putting it here for gender equality - they should make an Irene costume or skin)
- should have a costume/skin system
- more addicting than crack :(

I was a big fan of HOI2 and played it a lot.  It had a good balance of playability and realism and there were some issues which needed fixing, such as convoys and the occasionally flaky AI but it was a good game.
HOI3, sadly, is not.  It has taken me a while to work out why, but I think it's because, in trying to make it a complete war simulation, the developers have failed to either make it accurate or make it fun.  The accuracy claim sounds harsh, so let me explain.
1 - Research.  There's no logic to it.  One has to seperately research the gun carriages and weapons for anti-tank guns, for anti-aircraft guns, and artillery.  That's six separate thingies to research.  Then there's a seventh bit for heavy AA for your provinces.
Now in reality, what happened was that the best anti-tank weapons (British 17pdr, German 88, American 3") all started life as AA guns.  It would make far more sense to have a 'foundry' option where guns could be researched and then applied to different areas.
Why even force people to research three lots of gun carriages?  It makes absolutely no sense.
The same applies to separate research for cavalry weapons, militia weapons, and infantry weapons.  What, we're all using different rifles now?
As a minor aside let me come on to the logic behind the naming of each progressive unit.  For example, the British medium tank starts as the A9 cruiser, then when you research 1940 tanks it becomes the A15 Crusader (skipping the A13), then for 1942 tanks it becomes the Sherman Firefly.  What?  No Cromwell?  Why the Firefly?  This isn't the only case of a total lack of logic in the choice of naming. The naming doesn't affect the game but for a game which boasts of its realistic nature it is totally out of place.
IMO the complexity of the research tree does NOT add anything to the game.  I think it could have been halved in size and been far more enjoyable to use without losing any gameplay.
2 - Convoys.  The problem with convoys is that there is no mechanism to manage their routes.  This was a problem in HOI2 where the German AI could sink the entire British convoy fleet by hanging around in a few areas of the North Sea and continually sinking ships.  The very least HOI3 should have had is a convoy management system.  The player should be able to tell the convoy routing system NOT TO SAIL through certain areas.  Instead I have to watch convoys being sunk in the middle of the North Sea and around the English Channel, instead of rerouting all my convoys to the NW coast of Scotland or Liverpool and Belfast (as was done historically).  It's a huge oversight and it is one of the primary problems with playing as the British.  One of the other problems is that the cost of both convoys and escorts is fixed and does not fall over time (as it did historically with Liberty Ships and corvettes).  It's almost as though the game is written solely with land combat in mind and about 3/4 of the way through someone said "Hey, wasn't there someone else in WW2 beside Germany and Russia?"
It's a real problem and affects playability and the prospect of a historical outcome to WW2.
3.  Naval AI.  While I'm on the subject, the AI doesn't seem to know what to do with its ships.  The Germans send their battleships out unescorted to hang around the west coast of England and get sunk.  Which they do.  A lot.  It makes me suspect that the major emphasis for the game was on land combat and naval was not addressed properly.
4.  Allies.  In HOI2 getting allies to fight for or with you was easy.  They often sent you units, and there was an option for you to take over their entire armed forces.  In HOI3 that option doesn't exist.  And they don't send you units.   You have to 'set objectives' to get the allies to work with you.  These objectives don't really work.  So, when playing as Britain, Canada keeps its air force and navy and army in Canada.  When you urgently need Canadian fighters to defend your airspace and Canadian destroyers to patrol the Atlantic, they won't budge.  There is no way to unify command, so you don't fight as allies but merely as participants in a global war where you aren't fighting each other.  It's poor.
5.  Crashes.  Oh my goodness, the game's unreliability is terrible.  It crashes to desktop the whole time.   To minimise the inconvenience of losing my game progress I set it to autosave every game week, which is the most frequent autosave setting.  However, if you are in the middle of a huge amount of preparation for your forces (reorganising your divisions for example) the game might crash.  This has happened a couple of times to me, where I've been playing as Soviets and have been engaged in a major reorganisation of my 300+ divisions, and the game has just crashed to the desktop, and of course the autosave hasn't kicked in because I'm not progressing time through the game.  HOI2 never did this, and it's by far the most infuriating feature of the game.
6.  Graphics and Interface.  It's cluttered and it's illogical and it's poorly laid out and it's not designed to work on higher resolution settings.  It's a bloody mess.  And let's talk about the little pictures for each unit that appears in the research window and the production window.  Apparently it was too much effort for the devs to dig out the pictures of the units that they used in HOI2.  As a result far too many units, which had the correct photo in the previous game, have a 'stock' photo in this game.
There are historical oddities, too, ones which ought to have stood out like a sore thumb.  It is now possible to build (assuming you have the IC) lots of provincial AA without expending any manpower.  Who's manning all those guns?  Historically Nazi Germany had to commit a million men to defending their homeland from bombers, and that was a drain on manpower.  In HOI3, they don't have to.  They had to in HOI2.
I could live with the game if it was new.  If it had been out for a couple of months I'd say "Well, every game ships with bugs so I can live with it for now."  But this isn't a new game, it's been out for years, and instead of fixing the very serious reliability bugs, and instead of sticking in a few dozen stock photos, Paradox decided that an urgent priority was some 3D counters which they could charge extra money for.  It's not good enough.
I can't recommend this game.  If it was claiming to be a beer-and-crisps wargame I could overlook its historical inaccuracy.  It's claiming to be a very accurate game, and it isn't.  It's not accurate enough for a historical wargame, it's not fun enough for a 'quick dip in and have some fun' wargame.  It's too unreliable to be any kind of game at all.

I only played this for a little bit before I had to stop, which is unfortunate, as it has some nice elements to it.
This game has your standard breakout/arkanoid mechanics - move the paddle, bounce the ball back and forth until all the blocks are broken.  What's a little different with this the ball comes out of your liquid metal reserve in your paddle, meaning the length of the paddle is directly proportional to how many balls you have left.    When you run out of liquid metal, you lose a life.  There are also three different sizes of balls you can have in play, which change how many bricks you can break before the ball will bounce.  As you break the blocks, drops of liquid metal drop down and, if you catch them, they cause your paddle to grow.  Catch too much without using it (you can have multiple balls in play), and the paddle will start ejecting the liquid metal all over the place.
...I'm probably making this sound a lot dirtier than it is, but I don't really know how else to describe this without getting really silly.
Anyway, the game has power ups, all of them deal with how the ball destroys the bricks.  Some make you punch through them in a line, others take out a large group at once, others shoot off electricity and hit others randomly.  Their usefulness can be situational.  Finally, there is an area on the stage that, if you get three of your balls into it (it doesn't need to be all in one stage; they seem to carry over), you can create a REAXXION, meaning the balls turn from silver to gold, go from three to five, grow in size, and then shoot out everywhere.
Anyway, while all of that sounds neat (and indeed, it is pretty neat), it has some flaws which made the game unplayable for me.  If you're playing in windowed mode, it doesn't take much for the mouse to travel out of window, causing the paddle to stop moving.  And if you're playing full screen... it still kind of seem to do that.  The other problem is the paddle seemed to stutter quite a bit, which is aggravating when you're trying to bounce the ball back.
So yeah.  Good concept, but those issues make it a poor execution.

One of the worst things a brick-breaker can do is fail to be exciting. I've played some where I spent too much time staring at the screen, waiting for the ball to make its slow way back down so I could painstakingly aim for another brick. There are very few of those moments in Reaxxion; power-ups and unique mechanics keep things pleasantly hectic. The game's graphics are a bit dated, but they still have style. The neon colors are appropriate for an arcade game, and the shapes fashioned out of obstacles are often surprisingly cute.
There are plenty of levels to play through (165), and it took me nearly 6 hours to beat the game on normal difficulty. I enjoyed myself enough that I'm going to play through again. If you're good at this type of game, you should probably play on hard. I finished the game with about 15 lives left and didn't get a "game over" once. I'm not bragging; this says more about the game's easiness than it does about my ability! If you like arcade games, there's plenty to enjoy here. If you're still not sure, wait for it to go on sale.

This was a good looking game, with a well executed minimalistic atmosphere, but it really wasn't worth the price of admission. While I do feel it has redeeming qualities and the format has potential the experience it offered was extremely underwhelming. The game does not change enough or do anyhing particularly interesting with its' mechanics and you have already done almost everything you will do in the game within the first three minutes of playing. On completion, I was launched into the sky and saw that the island I had created resembled a heart with the words 'THANK YOU'  written under it. I was perplexed by how unsatisfying and silly this whole sequence was and I legitimately believed that this was a red herring so I continued onwards collecting all the red cubes and activating all the panels. This is a superb arcade racing sim. Besides the wonderful graphics, and cheeky easter eggs that can be found everywhere, the immensity of the map makes freedriving a pleasure. I've racked up far more time just driving around than actually doing missions and pvp. There is a very large array of the finest cars in the world, which need to be tuned to perfection; although that doesn't necessarily mean that when you max out your car's parts you will have an unbeatable car. PVP is where that definition is put to the test.
I don't really like multiplayer games, as they often bring out the worst in people, but I do like playing PVP in The Crew because if you can handle your car, then you have an equal chance of beating any player. Ubisoft should be congratulated for resisting the pay-to-win agenda many publishers turn to, to make a quick buck. Indeed, there are cash cars in the game, but again, they aren't supercars that can destroy all unpaying comers. They are just treats. Like the McLaren F1, which is a beautiful car, but that's it. Put it against the Zonda, and it will run very close; it's a shame they didn't put the Bugatti Veyron in, as then I could relive one of my favourite Top Gear episodes:
The only problem is a major bug; and I mean major. About 90% of the time when I enter the garage to tune a vehicle, the game will crash. This is maddening, and really screws up the enjoyment of the game, as you often try to avoid going to the garage at all. It's a pretty critical part of the game, as the parts you collect for your car are very delicately weighted against every other part. I'm trying to work out if you can build a much better car by slow grinding from lower levels, rather than just pay for a level 50 part. This takes time and concentration, so when you're analysing your parts and the game crashes, then you reload and can't be bothered, or too scared, to go back into the HQ. I've found if you go into the HQ when you first load the game, the game does not crash with such frequency. But who wants to go to the HQ when you've just loaded the game? Rather you go the garage after racking up a load of parts and then want to compare one against the other. Maybe if Ubisoft patched the game so you could tune your vehicle outside the HQ; the system is technically there in options, but you can't compare parts outside of the HQ.
Although this is a massive negative for the game, it does not spoil the enjoyment of the game itself, as there's so much to do. Hone your skills against your friends. Play missions, PVE, Factions Missions, and the PVP arenas of course. Again, I usually shy away from PVP, as this often brings out the worst in people, and if you leave collisions on, then you will quickly run into those people. There is also a trend of people's to harass drivers they encounter by ramming them continually, but, if you can handle your car, then you will not have a problem escaping from these morons; and I think this is just loser rage. In other games this would be a good reason to rage-quit, but I don't mind it so much in The Crew, because if you want the best, you have to beat the worst; and I usually always get the better of them on a circuit track with collisions turned off; and believe me, that's a satisfying feeling, especially if they rage-quit after the race XD

Yes, I know, city building games are my weak spot. Somehow, it is the only genre of games that can keep me at the computer for any number of hours.
Banished is a very nice sandbox city-building game. At first it seems rather simplistic: in normal mode you start with just around 10 adults (and some children, who can't work anyway). Their main concerns are, unsurprisingly, food and warmth.
After just 6 or 7 hours of game time your town has grown to 30 or 40 adults and you've built all the available types of building. It may seem that the game is almost over: after all, you've overcome the harshest year, in which you had to manually rotate the single individual free from gathering food between building, blacksmithing and tailoring. But it turns out, that the game just turns into the next phase: the scaling of your settlement. You no longer can rely on all your citizens getting what they need from just one barn. You have to deal with exponential growth of population, and besides that have to house and feed the random groups of nomads coming to live with you. The game turns from survival to logistics.
The game lacks any kind of levels of scenarios, and to be honest, it remains fun even without them. You can easily spend tens of hours on just one map. The amount of micromanagement scales very nicely. In the first years you carefully weigh the efforts of every single individual. When your storage of warm clothes is full, you send your tailor to do some other useful job. When I first started to grow crops, every year during winter time I re-assigned all my farmers to other jobs, to get things done while there's no work in the fields. But as the time goes, you have to spend less and less time on the details and more on the general economy: having just right amount of everything.
Finally, about a few things that could make the game better. Firstly, it could gain from having various scenarios, that favor different ways to playing, like, for instance Tropico. This includes better generator of more diverse maps. Currently there are just two modes: mountains/plains. The plains map has 2 or 3 almost round lakes and 1 or 2 rivers.
P.S. And one more thing. Kudos for having achievements that one has to, you know, achieve. The easiest one involves a town with the population of 100, which requires at least 10 hours of game time.

What an interesting little game!
For the last year or so I've been constantly whining at my partner, and my friends, that there's simply no good settlement building game on general release. I know Tropico 5 will be awesome (I'm a long time fan of the Tropico series, but I'm on a tight budget). We all may choose to argue the merits of Cities XL, Sim City, and the various Empire building games in the Roman-esque genre (started by Sierra back in the 1990s with their title Caesar), but this game offers something a little different.
I read many reviews before buying 'Banished', some of which complain about various little mechanics, others praise the 'mature' nature of the game. Granted, this title won't suit everyone; for there are no enemies advancing on your settlement ready to remove you from power, nor are there any options to build up a military and slaughter some AI controlled foe (as you would in the Stronghold series). Instead, what Banished delivers is a settlement building game in which you battle the elements and the tight restrictions imposed by gathering the resources needed to build and thrive in your randomly generated landscape - before the cold winter sets in, or you run out of food. This may sound a little dull on paper, but it really is very difficult to master.
Attempt number 1 resulted in my population dying from starvation. So I restarted and placed emphasis on food stocks.
Attempt number 2 resulted in my nourished population freezing to death during a harsh winter.
Attempt number 3 resulted in an outbreak of the mumps, which without proper medical facilities became deadly.
Attempt number 4... Well, I'll let you know. The previous three attempts took me six hours (hours that simply flew by!)
I guess the TL:DR of this review is; if you want a settlement builder that's really quite intelligent, beautifully charming to play, and that doesn't cost a fortune, buy Banished.

I bought this when it came out as Early Access sometime in February 2015. I was looking for a good ARPG at that time to replace Diablo 3 and Path of Exile, as I had played them till utter boredom. Several games, indie and professional alike, had disappointed me, however, Victor Vran did not.
You play as Victor Vran, the titular demon hunter, on his quest to free the city of Zagoravia from a demon invasion. You don't need much more story in an ARPG, and the first versions of Early Access didn't even have that - the quest givers were basically the developers talking to you. The current version has the fill story, which is fine by ARPG standards, but nothing to write home about otherwise.
You can play with gamepad or different keyboard/mouse configurations, I personally like the gamepad controls the best - they are fluent and support the action-oriented gameplay with dodging and a fully-rotatable camera.
To kill stuff (which after all is the prime activity in any good ARPG), you can pick form a variety of melee and ranged weapons (swords, hammers, rapiers, shotguns, mortars and lightning guns at this time). Each weapon time has one basic and two special attacks, which males for interesting synergies in combination with magical properties (up to two per weapon).
Character development does NOT work with a skill tree, but by choosing weapons, demon powers (spells you can cast once your overdrive meter is full; it fills by dealing damage) and Destiny Cards. The latter are items you put in slots that are awarded by leveling up and grant various buffs.
The graphics are fine for on ARPG (don't expect photorealism) and a bit on the bright side palette-wise. The music sounds nice, I think it's a bit above the average ambient "music" of many current RPGs.
Is it fun? Hell yeah, it is! If you're looking for some fun, fast-paced monster-slaying, grab it. However,  if you're looking for an "MMO" ARPG in the line of Diablo 3 and PoE, with trading and ladders, check out some videos before, it might not be what you crave.

The game runs at locked 60 FPS in all areas.  Can't remember what the Vita version ran at, but my awful memory doesn't remember it being as smooth as this version--and even if it was, you're probably still better off playing it on the PC for the larger resolution/display potential.
Some stuff you might want to know.
- All the free DLC found in the PSN store for this game is included automatically.  You don't have an option to not download it as far as I can tell.  That said, there is no DLC like the 2nd game that gives you a massively overpowered sword, so you won't have to worry about that.  The oracles are kind of strong, but the best characters are found in the base game, anyway.
- There appears to be DLC (included for free) that wasn't in the PSN, or at least wasn't in the PSN when I originally bought the game there, and I haven't gone back to check to see if it was added later.  Appears to have some minor amounts of new content.
- The game still does not good resolution support.  I have a 1920x1200 monitor which is not a supported resolution (max appears to be 1920x1080, although I do not know if a 1440p monitor unlocks a configuration option unavailble to me).  This forces me to play the game windowed or stretch/distort the game when playing in fullscreen.  This is not really a huge deal, but given that they've had 3 games to address this issue and still haven't bothered to, I feel it's worth mentioning at this point.
- Going off the basis that everything else is the same as the Vita version, I'm going to go on and say that this is definitely the best game in the series so far.  It dramatically improves the system for ranged attacks, now allowing you to make ranged attacks at point blank range.  Every character has their own SP bar, so now you can't basically spam the hell out of EX Techniques to faceroll everything in the game (you actually can, but only with an extremely specific party composition).
- Instead of tying everything to level, now, there are "achievements" per character that do things like unlock their EX move, leader skills, and other things.
- The Chirper spam is significantly reduced.
- Dungeon upgrades are more streamlines, you no longer have to worry about changing items, adding enemies, or changing dungeons.
- Stella's dungeon is more interesting fun.  I recommend the DLC since some monsters apparently inflict 9999 damage if Stella can't kill them quickly enough (like an unlucky string of misses) even if she's otherwise invulnerable and easily capapble of clearing the area.  There is a way to get the DLC bonuses normally sort of, but it requires equipping/partnering with specific people for the dungeon.  The DLC allows you to get those bonuses while using completely different set ups.  It's also only 99 cents.  That's less than what most of you probably pay for garbage shovelware on Humble Bundle that you will never play.

This game is a light hearted pirate themed game with turn based grid combat and island management/base building. Sounds great so far? TLDR it is indeed great.
Light hearted Pirates - the theme in this game works really well. The jokes are constant and mostly pretty funny. Lots of call backs and clever developments building on other previous things. You build boats and sail around raiding and looting and making jokes about it, it's great.
Turn based grid combat - Each member of your pirate crew is essentially a unique class. Enemies are also of these classes, but you only get one of each. The move and act system is very forgiving, letting you move around as much as you want before confirming. The tactical combat is pretty fun and varied.
Island management - every member of your crew, every craftsman and every resource gatherer needs a house, and then with beauty objects you can upgrade each building from level 1 to 3.  Your island draws tourists and produces resources and gold as well as being able to craft equipment.
I would say that each element of the game is simmilar: the story, combat and building are all well implemented and enjoyable but not super deep.  I find myself opening this game up very often, if only to play a couple fights while I wait for something. For $5 (or below) it's a very well done game with a lot more depth and length than you might expect.
Only negative note: SAVE OFTEN because sometimes it will just crash to the desktop out of nowhere.

Let me start by saying I enjoyed this game more than I expected. What follows is a somewhat spur-of-the-moment
wall of text since I had just completed the game. Don't pay any attention to my game time though as I did a lot of idling. Still I probably got a good 20 hours out of the game.
Swords & Crossbones: An Epic Pirate Story is tactical battle rpg with city sim and exploration elements, packaged in a casual wrapping. The pixel aesthetic is easy on the eyes and works, and the character design unique, if somewhat unusual.
First, the RPG parts. The combat system in this game is an old-school turn-based grid-based system reminiscent of Final Fantasy Tactics or Disgaea or any of a multitude of N64/NES/Gameboy tactics RPGs that used to be so common. Characters can move anywhere within their move radius, no matter how many steps they have to walk around to get there, and vertical layers can be traversed by jumping based on the character's jump stat. Since this is a pirate-themed game most maps include substatial amounts of water tiles -- these can be traversed freely but restrict using actions. On actions, each character can move and act in a turn, and actions include regular attacks, skills/spells/abilities, using items, or even swapping places with an enemy corpse that's blocking the character's passage. There are lots of skills and abilities to choose from and each character is themed slightly differently.
Enemies are a mixed bag -- story enemies are mirrors of player characers so make for decent combat, but these encounters are limited to some two dozen or so boss battles. The majority of combat is in random encounters and generic battles, and those enemies only come in limited archetypes and some pallette-swaps so eventually fighting them becomes a grind. Thankfully there are ways of avoiding the random encounters so only island liberation battles against pirates are obligatory. If taken in small chunks the grind is manageable enough though.
Story is cheesy and fun, an epic rescue and pursuit of revenge. It works well with the varied characters and original graphics design. I won't say much else because anything else will pretty much spoil what little of the story there is. It goes well with the game though.
Aside from the combat the game has elements of city building/management. It comes in the form of building up a pirate island to provide houses for the crew, collect resources, craft better equipment, and build bigger ships. Eventually players can expand into tourism to entertain residents of liberated islands and provide a level of gold income to fund further expansion and upgrades. Needless to say, plans for each building have to be obtained by defeating enemies and clearing islands. Resources and items can also be found while exploring the seas and recovering sinking wrecks.
It's all casual though, so no deadlines no rush. Time can be sped up at will up to x16 speed to simply wait for more resources when needed. Battles can be re-tried however many times needed -- getting the whole team knocked out simply sends the team back to the pirate island to train up and upgrade equipment.
That pretty much sums up the game, in way too many words.
