NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
GiAnt is a first-person ant simulator from a new solo indie developer.
You play Adam, an ant who is unfortunately miscategorised as a girl and given the job of a worker ant. The game starts with you attending a brief session at ant school before "The Captain" sends you out into the world to collect candy. Outside of the nest you need to avoid other insects and spiders while you explore and collect enough candy to be allowed back into the nest.
Unfortunately I'm not sure what happens after that, as in over an hour of play I didn't manage to collect any more than two pieces of candy before the game crashed or I fell afoul of the aforementioned other insects and spiders.
Graphics - Graphics are a very mixed bag. Ant models are nice and have a bit of character, and the nest is sort of good in a cute way. Once you venture outside, though, you'll see the graphics really start to shine, with a great blurry effect put to fantastic effect on everything beyond a certain distance away. When you stop and look at it, it's really very impressive.
Unfortunately, when you move there are some weird texture distortions and flickering, and shadows tend to flicker in and out in some areas as well. Couple that with some variable-quality close-up models and scenery, and a general lack of activity and feeling of emptiness in the game world, and after the first "Wow!" moment, I rapidly found myself much less impressed. The sprinkler, too, is terrible, and I still can't work out how a blowfly is hurting me! The cubist reflections in the kitchen cupboards are pretty weird as well (see the screenshot in my profile).
The UI is mostly good, although the use of a default Unity UI font for the candy and lives counters looks very out of place. Loading screens, too, are pretty terrible: just a plain black background and two-tone grey bar in the middle of it that fills up as the next area loads. It's disappointing and quite jarring, taking away from the immersion of the game.
Graphics options are fairly straightforward and offer a fair bit of choice for optimisation for lower-power systems.
Sound - Sound is fairly minimal, but okay. The lack of any consistent background music or audible environmental sounds makes the world feel even more empty sometimes, but triggers for music and some world interactions kick off some interesting changes.
The game includes voice for the ants. This is mostly well done, although the "Ow!" sounds get a bit painful to listen to over and over again. Similarly, the annoying high-pitched spider sounds and buzzing of the flies when they're near are too loud and grating.
There are no sound options to adjust volume of music, environmental sounds, and voices, and the mix is a little off, making it impossible to get the right volume all the time. I missed a fair bit of the speech due to nearby insect sounds or a sudden musical trigger, and environmental sounds (except for other insects) would be good if they were a bit louder. These should all be separately adjustable for user preference.
Gameplay - The game plays like any other first-person game: WASD for movement, space to jump, and mouse to look around. You're unable to attack or defend yourself, or even interact with the environment, though, so you'll not be needing mouse buttons any time soon.
The aim of the game is to wander around collecting candy, which you locate on the minimap (sorry, "Antdar") in the bottom right. It's not always reliable, though, as the map is in 2D, whereas the candy can be above or below you as well.
As you explore you'll encounter (overly) aggressive flying insects (that look like blowflies) and spiders, as well as other creatures on occasion as well. Other ants will talk to you, while environmental creatures will just ignore your passing.
The game also includes powerups, but these aren't explained and they don't seem to do anything except to add some green misty stuff to the area directly around them for a short time. When I collected one once it seemed to scare a hostile insect away, but the next time it did no such thing and I was killed while walking into and out of the powerup trigger.
Hostile spiders and insects are annoying and have extremely poor AI: they just make a bee line (haha) for you all the time and keep following around until they've killed you. There's no way to fight them off or escape, especially since the powerups seem to do nothing the majority of the time.
To make matters worse, the game plays like a typical gravity-based FPS, completely ignoring the fact that you're an ant and should be able to climb pretty much anything. The best example of this is probably the candy that's 'hidden' at the top of the tree under which your nest is located. Rather than just running up the tree, you have to find a weird walkway that seems to be made of timber boards running up and around the tree like a corkscrew, but even that is on an angle and you'll find yourself getting stuck between it and the tree as your ant insists on staying perfectly horizontal. It's a real shame and is probably the biggest problem with the game, as it completely ruins the suspension of disbelief.
It's very easy to become stuck on the terrain, and there are some crazy clipping issues as well, making it possible for you to walk through some stones and then become stuck between them and other terrain.
Finally, there are a number of little niggling problems:
- poor writing in the small amount of text that's included (the wrong 'their', 'occational')
- the game often crashes if you minimise it while playing
- there are no visual damage indicators when you're being attacked, so if you've turned down the annoying sound when insects are chasing you, you'll often be killed before you realise it
- sometimes the game doesn't realise when you've died, so you have to quit to the main menu and restart to try again
- the ant bridge mentioned as a cool feature is really just a static part of the map (see my screenshot), rather than a cool dynamic feature of ants helping you
- the Steam page says it has achievements, but it doesn't seem to (at least not yet)
Pros:
+ very impressive 'long range' graphical effects (esp. outside)
+ creative use of size differences
+ mostly entertaining voices
+ an interesting idea, by a solo developer
Cons (see above for more):
- you're an ant, but you're stuck on the ground and can't climb anything
- poor enemy AI that just doesn't give up
- a lot of terrain and graphics problems
- some annoying sounds and no volume options
- a very empty-feeling world that's just not much fun to explore
I'm sad that I can't bring myself to recommend GiAnt. I wanted to love it, and for the first few minutes I did. But after that all of the game's faults started to appear, and there are many.
With a little bit of work, GiAnt could be a great game, and if it were in Early Access I would probably recommend it. But it's now been released and it shouldn't have been; it's unfinished and it needs a fair bit of work to reach its potential.

A delightfully different platformer about retrieving lost cargo in space and fighting monsters. Addictive and infinitely replayable.
In this game you endure waves of containers. They crash into your home container one by one, and you must float through space and drill your way inside. Each container has its own center of gravity, which is cool. In the containers you'll find monsters, guns and varied loot. Loot comes in all shapes and sizes, from sweaters to old donuts to alien sex toys - some are rarer than others. You must collect enough loot to advance the story.
There's a pretty cool system called sectors. Basically, a sector is a series of containers generated based on a name. Each sector has a Sector Pass that lets you unlock a new one, either by typing in a name or selecting one from a list of the most popular names. There's no RNG in generating a sector, it's all based on the name so each sector will be the same for everyone. Different sectors also have different loot so exploring new sectors is very rewarding. I like it.
There is an online aspect of this game, but it's not as direct as you might think. You find postcards in containers-- sometimes blank ones you can write and send into the vast reaches of space to be discovered by some other player, mostly written ones another player wrote at some point in space and time. You'll also find the corpses of other players that died in that very container. In fact, I've come across my own corpse plenty of times. Postcards and corpses really contribute to the feeling of loneliness.
If you press F your guy will yell "♥♥♥♥ YOU!" which bumps this game up to a 11/10.

Hearts of Iron III is an excellent game. One of Paradox's best strategy games, in my opinion, it allows the player to control any nation in the lead-up to WW2, or during it if you prefer. These range from Nazi Germany, of course, to the Dominican Republic, which gives you an idea of the level of choice on offer. The game essentially drops you into the world as head-of-state of one of these many nations, and it's entirely up to you what to do from there: will you align with the Axis in Europe to gain your share of the economic gains in the upcoming war? Or will you side with Stalin's Russia and work to undermine Fascism and the Allies, in an attempt to dominate the world with Communism?
However, the level of historical accuracy in HOI3 is astounding, despite the player's ability to make independent and alternate choices. For example, there is a system of "decisions" in the game which often provide some sort of benefit, one of which is the historical Anschluss of Austria for Germany. As well as this, there are literally thousands of officers, with their own traits and skill levels (which can be improved with combat), to assign to command your divisions or brigades. These are just two examples in an intricate web of historical detail. WW2 history buffs like myself will be elated at the opportunity to not only, for example, command Rommel's Afrika Korps, but lead it to complete victory in the Middle East! Again, this is just an example that popped into my head, the level of possibility is insane.
Aside from the military aspect of the game, which is the focus, there are various other sectors of your nation that you can alter control. There is the politics tab, where you select your ministers and make policies, as well as administer the areas that have come under your occupation through war. There is the diplomacy tab, where, if you are a leader of a faction, such as the Axis, you can influence nations to join you in alliance, and make trade deals, sell equipment, declare war, ETC. Other tabs include research, production, intelligence. I won't go into detail on these, but all are as important as each other.
Anyway, pros and cons:
PROS
- Insanely high level of historical detail (accurate divisional names, commanders, ministers in governments, literally tens of thousands of provinces)
- Ability to relive or rewrite history, in your own unique way.
- Greatly immersive, you get to the point where hours just slip away in what feels like minutes!
- Huge scale wars, on land sea, and air, where you are the commander in chief.
CONS
- Not recommended if the player is looking for amazing graphics- the gameplay is what sells HOI3, not the visuals.
- A tad buggy. The game crashes relatively frequently, especially if tinkering around in console commands.
- Steep learning curve, but once you get the full hang of it, you'll realise it was well worth the time put into it.
9/10 The cons do not affect my opinion of the game significantly in any way, and I hope that you too will be persuaded by this long-winded review to buy this awesome game too!

Interestingly, the story takes place right after Street Fighter II ended. Chronologically, the game can be put between the 2nd and 3rd episode. Bison's Shadaloo organisation still exists and organises another tournament to gather the best fighters in the world - this time, however, instead of Bison you have Seth as the final boss. Seth combines the best moves of all the players out there - he has a lot of counter special attacks, very agile and overall a pain on harder difficulty settings.
Gradually, you can learn to fight with each SF character and can continue to play online. You need a lot of time and effort to master these fighters. You can unlock many more as you progress through the game.
Overall, this is a really good game. When I was young my parents bought me Street Fighter II for the Super NES so for me this game was instantly captivating.

A short, minimalistic game, the freerunning counterpart to a walking simulator. A classic example of a game that is short enough not to overstay its welcome - brief, but enjoyable for the whole of its length. Definitely worth the $2.99 asking price.

The visual are simple, but serviceable. Lighting and shadows are sharp. I feel like there could be more variety here, but I wouldn't say it felt like anything was lacking during my playthrough. The pillars were not overly “blocky”, with textured edges and corners helping to escape the usual polygonal look of some titles in this genre.
The music is appropriate, providing a mellow, vaguely uplifting atmosphere. Since the experience is short, the soundtrack never becomes tiresome, at least through the first couple playthroughs, whereupon you can up on your own progressive trace or whathaveyou. Sound effects were nothing to write home about - would have been nice to have some variety in footfalls, since that's essentially what you are listening to for most of the experience, and diversity here would offer some gameplay feedback. Atmospheric effects would be welcome as well, though perhaps that would have run contrary to the aesthetic.
Controls are a little floaty, as to be expected from a first-person platformer. There's plenty of assistance with edge-detection - I would have liked to see more in-game feedback to have a better idea about my motion, though it’s more of a personal preference. The slide ability seems a bit stunted to be of any use, and could have been better integrated into the gameplay.
Speaking of which, gameplay is solidly implemented – the tiling is both instructive and encourages novel use of the mechanics. Difficulty is minimal, and there doesn’t appear to be any kind of a failure state, so it isn’t particularly challenging – this could probably be resolved by community content. Despite its design, Refunct is still a little too short. This is as mentioned above probably a good thing, given the narrow variety of content, but they could probably have done more with the concept if they increased the length of the game. I’m guessing the idea was to limit the resource requirements so the game will be compatible with VR, something we’ve seen quite a bit as of late. Nonetheless, even at its current length, the game is a complete experience.

This might not be a thorough review, but after 16 hours of playing this game, I do feel I have enough to share about Banished.
If I wanted to describe "Banished" using a single phrase, I guess that phrase would be "Colony Management". All you do in this game, is manage your colony. You are responsible for the lives and the well-being of your colonists, sometimes very literally. For example, if during the summer you neglect an important aspect, such as producing food, your colonists will probably starve and not survive the cold winter. Or, for another example, you don't make sure your colonists have enough wood and the ability to use it to warm their houses during the winter, they'll just die of hypothermia. So far, the game's formula seems simple, yet deep and complex enough to make it interesting and carry the weight of an entertaining game.
Visually, Banished looks really well. There's nothing too fancy about the game's graphics, as it seems the developers were smart enough to focus their efforts and resources on other aspects of the game, but they obviously did enough to make everything really polished and smooth. I really liked the weather effects, they really sell the seasonal theme of the game. I raised the game's settings to the maximum and it runs very smoothly. Up until now I haven't encountered any bugs or problems. No crashes, no slowdowns, nothing - pure gameplay experience! While I do have a decent computer (Quad-Core i7, 12GB RAM, Geforce GTX465), it seems like this game could handle itself well enough with much cheaper hardware.
The only aspect I'm a litthe disappointed of, is the audio. There are important sounds effects, but the music is so insignificant, that after 15 minutes I decided to turn the game music off, so I could listen to popular music while playing.
If you like colony management games, you should definitely try Banished. While it might not be an incredible AAA game or a pure city-builder, it's easily better than the broken and buggy Simcity and Cities XL.

Victor Vran Is the Greatest Action RPG Since Diablo 2
This is an Early Access preview, which I published on TechZwn.
I sometimes wonder whether any action-RPG could replace the mythical spot held by Diablo 2. There were only a couple that came close (in my opinion Bastion, Torchlight 2, and Path of Exile), and I’d say the rest were just fillers.
But a new game is has joined these ranks, and while I can’t say it manages to out-do Diablo 2, it certainly comes close.
I nearly wrote off Victor Vran before trying it. It looked too much like a copy of Van Helsing (which is decent), but after giving it a shot, I was surprised to find a game that takes the monster-slaying mayhem of Diablo 2, combines it with the narration of Bastion, and brings in some of the skill-based combat of The Witcher series.
The developers at Haemimont Games seem to take many lessons from The Witcher 3. First and foremost, the main character (Victor Vran) sounds exactly like Geralt from The Witcher games. In Victor Vran, you’re a monster slayer, and you get called into a city that has been overrun with more horrible creatures than you could shake a boom-stick at. Your character comments on what he finds, comments on the smell and feeling of the places you take him. And he reminds you here and there of his role in this world, and the brother-like bond that exists between him and his fellow hunters (who you may come across alive or dead in this fallen city).
Also like in The Witcher, the combat makes you consider which tools would be best for a given area. Fighting spiders? Maybe the scythe would be best. Skeletons? Grab a warhammer or shotgun. Taking on a vampire? My choice is the rapier.
The combat is also built in a way that allows you to basically not get hit, if you’re good enough. You can roll out of danger, you can jump over enemies or projectiles, there are only a handful of skills and buffs you can use at once, and potions can only be used sparingly.
Taking a few lessons from Bastion, you have a mysterious narrator who comments on your actions. And also like in Bastion, every weapon type in Victor Vran brings a significantly different combat experience. Playing with the warhammer feels slow and powerful. The sword feels devestating and puts you in harms way. The rapier is fast and agile. The shotgun makes you feel like an old-West gunslinger with a special attack that instantly recharges if you manage to kill the enemy.
You can choose between the Diablo-style controls, where the mouse controls your attacks and movement. Or you can go with the default action controls (which I chose), which lets you control movement with the keyboard, and attack with the mouse. The action control makes it feel a lot more like a skill-based combat game than it does a random click-fest.
The voice acting is very well done. Characters are convincing, and the actual dialogue is just as good. You don’t roll your eyes when an NPC speaks, and I found myself taking time to listen to the characters even if I could finish reading the dialogue before they could finish saying it.
There are a few features that some gamers might not like, but that seeem to be done intentionally by the developers. Victor Vran is simple. You only get a few spells. There isn’t a skill tree or a sheet of attributes you level up. And it basically doesn’t have any character classes.
There is only one hero in Victor Vran, with a choice of three different looks that give different buffs. Every time you level up, you’re given a new feature (like being able to wield two weapons, or being able to carry a new skill) and you’re given a choice between three items (typically cards that give you buffs, a spell, a weapon, or a mystery chest).
Instead of having classes, it adapts to your playstyle. As you pick your perks, you slowly build the type of character you want to play. And you’re not locked into these choices. If you chose a card that gives more health for melee combat and you want to play ranged, you can just switch it out for another.
It seems the developers also expect you to swap weapons depending on what you’re up against. You could probably use the same weapon the whole game, but you’ll quickly see that some weapons work better against different enemies. This makes the combat feel more varied. If combat is starting to feel monotonous, you can just switch it up.
What really makes Victor Vran shien, however, is that it’s deeply immersive. This is a culmination of everything it does well.
You feel like a monster slayer, Victor Vran describes his feeling or sensing, the narrator teases and comments on your actions, characters have personalities, the combat makes you stop and consider the best approach for each situation, and the story makes sense of why you’re basically one-manning a city overrun with monsters.

While on Steam, the game gets an overwhelmingly postive review, I have to say, I mostly concur with them. It's a paradox of a game, well made, with flaws that almost seem to make it better.
Pros:
- The physics are amazing. Flying around in a parachute, pulling yourself along with a grappling hook, or tying vehicles and people together is just so satisfying.
- Blowing up buildings, military installations, and just generally causing chaos is hilarious and fulfilling. Too bad it doesn't actually affect the enemy's ability to fight you.
- The weapons, vehicles, and people are many, immense, and hilarious.
- The graphics, while dated by now, still pass the test of time.
- The voice acting (see cons), and sound quality is great. I can still hear the chord play in my ears, you know, the one that it plays when you blow something up and get caught doing it.
- The Story (see cons) is hilarious.
Cons:
- The voice acting (see pros) is really bad. Hilariously bad. It's like listening to an audio book, written by Silvester Stallone, and acted out by the Arnold. The guy who plays Tom Sheldon gets REALLY annoying after awhile.
- The story (see pros) is similarly idiotic. There really is not 'plot' per se. It's literally a video game-incarnation of a terrible 80's movie. And you kind of have to accept that for the game to be fun.
- The AI is both stupid as all hell, and WAY too smart. As in, they're fighting ability is terrible, but somehow have omnipotence and can know what you did, where you are, and where you are going in order to hunt you down and get killed by you.
- (Just personal) There are not enough armored vehicles, so it's sometimes tough fighting off waves of enemies, vehicles, and air support.
This is a great game, though it has its flaws. Definitely worth your money, and the at least 50 hours of time you're going to put into it blowing things up, and just causing chaos.

I like open world games for the freedom and a chance to do whatever whenever. I’m not into online racing and while I do complete a lot of the single player content it’s only as means to an end. Namely opening new cars and locations. The Crew is an open world sandbox with whole North America as the playground. On paper that sounds like the best thing ever.
One big problem I have with the complete edition is the DLC. As a bonus you get for free some of the fastest cars in the game and they are unlocked from the beginning. You can’t take these to beginner races and dominate everything but it does kill the need to progress. It takes hours upon hours of gameplay to earn enough to buy some of the fastest cars but since I already had a Ferrari and couple of McLarens there really was no need. It’s nice to get a Lamborghini but it’s not that different.
Even with the DLC the biggest complaint I have though is the car list. There just isn’t anything fun here! Most of it is just new supercars or American muscle cars and even those are new models from recent years.
Do you want to drive a red convertible into Las Vegas as in Fear and Loathing? Sorry the game doesn’t have convertibles. Do you want to be James Bond in one of his iconic cars? None of those are in the game. Fast and Furious it up with Mitsubishi Eclipse? Isn’t in the game. Maybe a hippie road trip in an old VW bus to San Francisco? Nope, can’t do that. Tofu delivery in the mountains with AE86? No. Herbie? No.
The open world in the Crew is absolutely humongous and it basically has no loading times. You can fast travel to any point on the map and it takes about a second. It’s insane how fast everything is loaded. The map isn’t to scale (obviously) but comparing cities like New York into the versions seen in other open world games and the cities in the Crew are much bigger. Plus there is almost an endless amount of wilderness to explore. There is no other game that comes even close. When you do jump somewhere though, the roads are empty for a while before any traffic starts to show up. Even in its fullest the streets are quite empty. You can’t get stuck in traffic at New York because there never is enough vehicles. While the scenery changes a lot and cities look different everything feels a bit devoid of life. It feels like the map was created by algorithm, not hand crafted by actual humans. There aren’t any funny little details or anything like that. While understandable in a game this big it does take something away from exploration.
Handling is arcade but I think it’s a good kind of arcade. Stock and street cars have nice feel to them. There are different variants and their behaviour is almost cartoonish. A performance car sticks to road like on rails while drift car just slides everywhere. Sense of speed isn’t very good at speeds under 100kph but going more than 200kph is really exiting. Collisions have some visual damage but it doesn’t have effect on handling and is repaired automatically after some time. Also respawning back to track is so fast that the dust from previous try hasn’t settled before you are back. It’s a really forgiving system.
Personally I didn’t feel like there was annoying amounts of rubber banding AI. For example: The cars have levels depending on their handling, speed etc. All races have minimum level and at that level you can win with good driving. If you join an AI car level 70 race with a car that is level 140 the AI will still give a suspiciously good challenge. If you join with a car that is at level 250 though you will absolutely destroy them. So the AI doesn’t scale up indefinitely. Cops and other chase related activities is a whole another story with spawning roadblocks and such usual open world stuff.
For someone who plays single player content the Crew is and open world playground without the “play” or an amusement park without “amusement”. The parks are and ground are on a technical level really worth seeing but the game lacks any soul. It’s sterile. The game runs fine and looks really good at times (The screenshots on the Steam page are bullshots). I had some issues with registering the keys to Uplay but few restarts did the trick. Without registering the game acts as trial which seems to have caused a lot of confusion but is not really an issue.
I Recommend the free trial version. It is basically full version with a time limit so do test before you buy! Many of the things i found irritating are subjective and maybe someone else who is in for the multiplayer side of things can get a vastly different experience. One thing to note is that your trial profile is the same as in full game so choose carefully which car you buy! You can’t start over.

Victor Vran is the isometric action-RPG (ARPG) published by EuroVideo Medien and developed by Haemimont Games. Haemimont Games are best known for their work on the Tropico series however they have also developed games such as: Celtic Kings, Imperium Romanum/ Grand Ages: Rome, the Tzar series and Omerta – City of Gangsters as well as a few others. Haemimont Games have as this list suggests primarily focused on RTS and city building games, it’s nice to see a developer try something new, but not without its risks, does the risk pay off? Read on to find out.
You are a demon hunter with a secret, you made a pact some years ago in order to wield Demon powers. A message arrives from your friend Adrian in the land of Zagoravia, a land that succumbed to a Demon invasion one year earlier, telling you he’s found the thing that you seek (what this is, is yet to be discovered).
You do not know much about the land of Zagoravia only that many Demon Hunters travelled to the land only to never return including your friend Adrian. The travel to Zagoravia in order to find out what happened to your friend and also in the hopes of finding this secret that your friend discovered. Perhaps you may find out what exactly happened in the mystery of the Demon incursion into Zagoravia. Upon arrival you start hearing a character calling himself “the voice” that resides apparently in your head.
Victor Vran is an action-RPG that focuses on customisation as opposed to classes as there are no specific classes to speak of, essentially you can customise your character to play in a class of your own design. You can choose to wield up to two weapons consisting of mortars, swords, scythes, lightning guns hammers and rapiers (there may be perhaps others I have yet to discover) you also have a choice of outfits and can even customise its colour if you so desire. Additionally you have a choice of multiple Demon powers and can wield up to two of them there is also a choice of what is called “destiny cards” which you collect and they provide you with various buffs. Each of these items have various levels and/or rarity.
There is also a variety of consumables that can be used from the basic health potion to the more advanced leech bomb. Upon reaching level 16 you have access to the “transmutation” facility which allows you to combine all of your pickups except potions into either a generally improved item, an item of higher rarity or if you so choose a random item.
In Victor Vran you are extremely mobile and have the ability to jump or dodge to avoid incoming damage. You can also wall jump in order to reach otherwise inaccessible areas, and can also use the mortars special jump ability to reach even more inaccessible areas. Each of the levels have various different optional challenges that you can attempt completion of, which will provide a reward of some description from money, XP to a reward chest that can contain a random item of the same level as the chest.
In addition to the normal and hard modes players can also add further levels of difficulty with the addition of “hexes” which add certain buffs to the enemies granting a further challenge and higher reward. Players can also join in multiplayer with up to 3 other people for Co-op action or even venture into the PVP arena to find out who is the better hunter.
Mechanically speaking the additional mobility of the character provides an extra layer of skill which helps with the overall immersion of the game. The loot, items and challenges/rewards system all work really well together. The only issue I found was a slight graphical glitch which occurred under certain circumstances I have however alerted the developer to this.
However this is very minor and is to be expected of an early access title. Graphically speaking the game has a dark Gothic theme which suits the era and overall aesthetic. As for sound the soundtrack is suitably Gothic and dark, the music and sound assets all work well, the combination of which adds to the overall immersion of the game.
Overall I found this game to be an absolute joy to play, it of course has similarities with Diablo 3 however I found that I lost interest with Diablo whereas with Victor Vran I thoroughly enjoyed it and find myself itching to play some more. This can be attributed to the customisation of the character, the hilarious movie quotes (Monty Python and the Holy Grail and Star Wars to name but two) and other equally hilarious abuse received from “The Voice (inside your head)” or perhaps it’s the hilarity that ensued from meeting the “Gangnam Style” dancing skeletons. Sufficive to say this new direction for Haemimont Games paid off with dividends, and I for one can’t wait to see both what additions they make to the game and of course the next game they work on.

Developed by Serious Brew and published by Missing Link Games, Cargo Commander is a rather unique 3D platform game that borrows heavily from other succesful genres. The very fact that all the levels are randomly generated, can give you a first clue that this won’t be a repetitive experience. Also the destruction you can cause in this title is more prevalent than in regular side-scrollers.

Cargo Commander features an upgrade system for the weapons and tools in the game, giving us a sense of moving forward. Some hefty  looting of the crates is required but I never felt bored once while playing and the destructible enviroment is a nice bonus to an already fun title. A text-based story is included and it does present us with rare moments of comic relief. Not many platformers attempt that and also succeed. This is entirely a single player experience but the level diversity and well scaled difficulty ladder offer a balanced gameplay. It wasn’t too short and it didn’t drag on either. My main gripe with the game however, was the inconsistence of the loading times which are a bit unexpected. I guess some glitches can’t be fixed by further updates.

It has beautiful 3D graphics with just a touch of cel-shading in the mix. It never looked bland or out of place. Few things to comment as far as the looks go. It carries plenty of diversity in both enemy selection and the titular cargo crates which form an integral part of the gameplay.

The game’s second flaw has to be sound department. You have a limited selection of sounds that play on a loop. It gets boring fast even with the entertaining gameplay, encouraging you to press on. We’re already used to the fact that platformers seldomly feature any noteworthy soundtrack, but this game deserved more in that regard.
+ Pleasant graphics
+ Excellent gameplay with incentives to try different aproaches
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements

- Inconsistent loading times
- Repetitive sounds

Cargo Commander is a very nice addition to any game collection since it has both Trading Cards and Achievements. Fans of the platformer genre will not be disappointed as the gameplay brings to table both classic and novel features. I most certainly enjoyed it and I do hope for a sequel even if this title was released in 2012 and the dev team haven’t released anything else in the meantime. Even by 2016’s standards, this game is a worthy choice and overall fun experience.

Let me tell you what you need to make a doll instead.
Plan: Doll
1 doll template (take Nep)
2 washable fabric, at least 12x12sqin if not more
10 sqin of cotton Jersey

Pins
Polyester batting
A rod

floss
1. Cut fabric after printing the doll template. Talk to Anonydeath about Noire pattern

3. Stitch fabric with 1/4 seam allowance or less, snip away fabric with scisssor
4. Roll the batting. Use wool as that's highly Nepable.
5. Make the head, hands and feet. Make neck by tying a thread around the batting ball, stitch bottom to close the stubs.
6. Stuff the body. Make the head firmer than the body. Whipstich the head to body with double lengthed threading. Repeat for hands and feet.
7. Make hair by using pins to mark placement on head and then sew on yarn or better yet, real CPU hair. Keep in place, make tiny stitching each loop, insert needed threaded with embroidery floss through back of the head and out at a pin, and the stitch features.
8. Complete the hair on the head by snip looping the hair.
9. (optional) Using the same doll template, design suitable clothing. You don't want your doll to be naked, even if the doll's quite Nepable as she is.
10. Proceed to Nep with the doll. Refer to the Steam guide: How to Nep a Nep Nep for more detail.

A short, minimalistic game, the freerunning counterpart to a walking simulator. A classic example of a game that is short enough not to overstay its welcome - brief, but enjoyable for the whole of its length. Definitely worth the $2.99 asking price.

The visual are simple, but serviceable. Lighting and shadows are sharp. I feel like there could be more variety here, but I wouldn't say it felt like anything was lacking during my playthrough. The pillars were not overly “blocky”, with textured edges and corners helping to escape the usual polygonal look of some titles in this genre.
The music is appropriate, providing a mellow, vaguely uplifting atmosphere. Since the experience is short, the soundtrack never becomes tiresome, at least through the first couple playthroughs, whereupon you can up on your own progressive trace or whathaveyou. Sound effects were nothing to write home about - would have been nice to have some variety in footfalls, since that's essentially what you are listening to for most of the experience, and diversity here would offer some gameplay feedback. Atmospheric effects would be welcome as well, though perhaps that would have run contrary to the aesthetic.
Controls are a little floaty, as to be expected from a first-person platformer. There's plenty of assistance with edge-detection - I would have liked to see more in-game feedback to have a better idea about my motion, though it’s more of a personal preference. The slide ability seems a bit stunted to be of any use, and could have been better integrated into the gameplay.
Speaking of which, gameplay is solidly implemented – the tiling is both instructive and encourages novel use of the mechanics. Difficulty is minimal, and there doesn’t appear to be any kind of a failure state, so it isn’t particularly challenging – this could probably be resolved by community content. Despite its design, Refunct is still a little too short. This is as mentioned above probably a good thing, given the narrow variety of content, but they could probably have done more with the concept if they increased the length of the game. I’m guessing the idea was to limit the resource requirements so the game will be compatible with VR, something we’ve seen quite a bit as of late. Nonetheless, even at its current length, the game is a complete experience.

Ultimate Chicken Horse is a very funny party game that can be played together with friends or online against strangers.
Since none of my (real life) friends own the game, I have only played online so far but it has been alot of fun nonetheless. I can imagine that playing it with your friends would be even better!
I mainly used my keyboard to play the game and I don't have any complaints about the controls. I have tried playing it with controller once but after ~50 hours of getting used to the keyboard, it was too much of a change for me so I decided to keep playing it the way I have always been.
It won't take too long to learn the controls but people who have experience with platformers (like me) have a significant advantage and if this is your first time playing this kind of game, it won't be easy (unless you only play against players of the same skill level of course)! That said, more skilled players can give themselves a handycap to make it a little more fair so in general this is not a problem.
There are a few bugs and sometimes the game will crash or freeze but that happens rather rarely so it's nothing to worry about too much.
The games can range from mere 5 minutes to over 20 minutes in length depending on the settings the admin of a lobby chooses. This means that it can very well be played to kill some time when you're bored but also for much longer durations. It will certainly not get boring too fast since every game is significantly different from the last one. There are many many kinds of placeable objects and maps.
The graphics are good, very cute art style. Same goes for the sound design and the music is very catchy. It fits the game's feeling perfectly.
You may meet annoying or rude players if you play online but that's just how some people are, I guess. It's not like the playerbase is small so don't worry about this. And you can of course also always just leave or kick the trolls if you want.
Overall, the game is a great way to kill some time and get a quick laugh out of simultaneously. It has certainly been worth it's price for me.

This might not be a thorough review, but after 16 hours of playing this game, I do feel I have enough to share about Banished.
If I wanted to describe "Banished" using a single phrase, I guess that phrase would be "Colony Management". All you do in this game, is manage your colony. You are responsible for the lives and the well-being of your colonists, sometimes very literally. For example, if during the summer you neglect an important aspect, such as producing food, your colonists will probably starve and not survive the cold winter. Or, for another example, you don't make sure your colonists have enough wood and the ability to use it to warm their houses during the winter, they'll just die of hypothermia. So far, the game's formula seems simple, yet deep and complex enough to make it interesting and carry the weight of an entertaining game.
Visually, Banished looks really well. There's nothing too fancy about the game's graphics, as it seems the developers were smart enough to focus their efforts and resources on other aspects of the game, but they obviously did enough to make everything really polished and smooth. I really liked the weather effects, they really sell the seasonal theme of the game. I raised the game's settings to the maximum and it runs very smoothly. Up until now I haven't encountered any bugs or problems. No crashes, no slowdowns, nothing - pure gameplay experience! While I do have a decent computer (Quad-Core i7, 12GB RAM, Geforce GTX465), it seems like this game could handle itself well enough with much cheaper hardware.
The only aspect I'm a litthe disappointed of, is the audio. There are important sounds effects, but the music is so insignificant, that after 15 minutes I decided to turn the game music off, so I could listen to popular music while playing.
If you like colony management games, you should definitely try Banished. While it might not be an incredible AAA game or a pure city-builder, it's easily better than the broken and buggy Simcity and Cities XL.

Although there are no direct conflicts and no hostile forces, this is amazingly well designed, well coded, and beautifully crafted. If Caesar II and Age of Empires made a baby in peace time, this would be it. I have a few slight beefs for those who want more in depth issues to the current features...
Point one. The town can entirely survive on firewood and food indefinitely as long as supplied. There is no reason to develop much further, nor is it required. This ruins the whole concept of progression and expansion and vise verse.
Stone and Iron are incredibly difficult to amass, then again, not really needed as to point one. No need to send child labor into the mines and quarries to gather the resources needed for their headstone in the graveyard outside the incredibly expensive chapel.
Citizens choose the shortest path, regardless of roads when transversing long distances. When I say well coded in the first part, I mean algorithmic and procedural, not intelligently. The path finding will set you off guard should you accidentally indicate a collection of resource across a river or mountain, and then wonder why your people are freezing to death. Then again, that is some of the best path finding I have seen in any game, if only AoE2-HD could take some notes. The procedural map creation is astounding, though the coder inside me thinks using dome punchers for lakes is a bit cheap and fuzzy, and makes it look like crap. If the same person knew how to implement great path-finding, at least turn to the next page in the epic-code manual to find noise generation and applications, it's right next to river and mountain generation, how can you be missing just one page? Of all things to make look cheap, it had to be lakes. Which brings to next point...
You cannot flatten land... this makes children in your town cry because their new house can't be built on a slightly elevated hill. Also about buildings...
Area bounded buildings are size limited. If I wanted a huge farm that sprawls, I can't. Even at small scale, to fill in some 'gaps' of layout planning it is restricted by a draconian width and length limit. Why can't the nice old lady in the last wooden house have her own 1x4 cherry garden before she dies?
Speaking of age, one world year is 4 citizen years, I know, difficult for me to grasp to when I saw a one year old going to pick up stone at the local quarry. It was a different time back then, or when ever, better question where ever? I think I now know the reason these folks were banished, they age incredibly fast, navigate the wilds with ease, AND can crush rocks, cut trees without tools all at the age of three. Hell, I'd cast them out too, freaks.
In the greater scheme of things, difficulty is up to you and you alone when progressing the town, how long can you keep the town alive is the real goal. You'll be rage flipping tables as soon as your food and firewood hit zero and little 12 year old Timmy the harvester is the only one left with his more 'experienced' wife expecting. He gets crushed by a tree, and she dies at age 37 in childbirth. Population: 0

A friend of mine convinced me to restart my dark souls 1 playthrough after I gave up in the undead parish and I finally relented, playing through the entire game and DLC over the course of about 3 weeks. I very quickly realised why they love the game so much.
The combat was fluid and reactive, the fights felt challenging but overcomeable and the bosses were devistating - till you learnt how to hold your own against them. Each level and enemy felt very carefully crafted to test different aspects of the game, be it dealing with multiple enemies, hard hitting attacks in tight spaces with deadly drops, navigating intricate maps with what feels like an endless horde of enemies chasing you, the list goes on. The combat felt beautiful, each attack had a solid impact and every block, roll and turn felt extremely responsive.
As for the difficulty, yes it was hard, challenging for certain but it never really felt punishing. There were a few moments that made me grit my teeth, capra demon being one of them, but after some exploration of other areas and getting some better gear I was able to overcome it.
Dark souls 2 on the other hand feels like a mess.
The first thing I said to my friend after an hour of playing was "this feels more like a dark souls clone than a dark souls game"
The combat is substantially less reactive, every attack feels like im having to slog through knee deep water and the movement controls are fickle at best. And then theres rolling. Whoever's idea it was to halve the number of invincibility frames to make DS2 starter rolling worse than fatrolling in DS1 needs to be fired, if they havent been already. It almost forces you to bring a shield early game and horribly reduces the effectiveness of dodge based tactics till you have a much higher agility score. The joy of DS1 is that even from the start you have so many options for playstyles, this game just feels like im being crammed down one specific path till I reach high enough level to branch out and actually enjoy the game
And to top it off (Oh im gonna get so much crap for this), the max health drain. Its the single worst design decision in the entire game and i hate it.
Its the perfect example of challenging vs punishing. A challenging game (like DS1) has a difficulty level that is highly tuned so that you need to play very well, if not sometimes perfectly, in order to succeed. No matter how many times you smash your head against it, you're just as likely to succeed and through time, dedication and learning you generally take the boss down.
A punishing game can share a lot of these qualities but have one horrible thing on top. Every time you fail you get put at a disadvantage the next time you try. This actively discorages exploratory gameplay and forces me to decide between taking risks and possibly losing my souls (oh no how terrible) or being able to progress without having to deal with my health being gimped because i dared to try something new. As an example: After getting a little bored with dying in the forest/castle area near the start I decided to go and check out another route in the starting town. I found myself against a huge great big enemy with a ton of health and some really strong attacks. Naturally they killed me and I was sent back to town. After a few attempts, I gave up.
You're probably thinking "pshh yeah you just gave up because you're a noob and cant deal with losing"
No. I gave up because I was annoyed that I had to burn through what for my char is a fairly expensive item just to continue having an acceptable chance against this guy. The health drain actively discoraged challenging gameplay and instead made me want to go play something else.
All in all, the game, while visually gorgeous, feels like a very stale sequel to what is now one of my favourite games. If you play this without playing any other dark souls game, you may enjoy it but honestly I'd just point you towards DS1, its far more of a satisfying package and still has a lot of life for such an old game.

You are proberbly wondering if Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is worth your time and money.
Well, here are my reason why it is, in fact, worth it.
Dark Souls 2 is a linear game that focuses more on game mechanics and well done, good looking, challenging ´levels`.
From all the games in the Dark Souls series, this is one is the most beloved in terms of PVP and DLC´s.
I´ll talk about the DLC´s(The Ivorny, Sunken and Iron Crown´s) later.
The game introduces you slowly to the Souls franchise, giving you hints and not punishing you too hard for mistakes. In SOFTS(short for - Scholar of the First Sin) it teaches you how enemies agro work and how to avoid traps/notice them and will reward you for learning to use these techniques.
Compared to Dark Souls 1(I´m not gonna use Dark Souls 3/Bloodborne for examples) this game is less punishing in general, where in DKS 1 you had to use humanity(if you dont know, a very useful item in terms of health) to get all your Estus Flasks(basically Healing Potions) back from Bonfires, SOFTS gives you them back without doing anything of that sort. For some Players this was a major turnoff but I think it´s fine, especially if you are new to the franchise.
Graphics look pretty good even for today´s standards and you don´t need a Godtier PC for it.
And the music? Some OST´s are really good while others tend to be ´meh´-ish and forgettalbe, this is because most of the tracks are just a chor playing music or singing not in our languages understandalbe words. Doesn´t mean that every song like this is easily forgettalbe and bad, but in DKS 2´s  case, it is.
As for the DLC, that is in my opinion the best example of good DLC that you will get in the entire Soulsseries to play.
Everything that was accused of being bad, or lacking content was proberbly fixed in those good 3 pieces of DLC content. Good enemy designs, shortcuts, good boss design´s(exception being like 2, one who is re-used from the main game and another who is kinda boring), they encourage you to explore more than the main game did and are really breathtaking in both graphical and gameplay terms. All three DLC`s add alot of additonal content, more armors, weapons and all that good stuff.
So my conclusion: Dark Souls 2 SOFTS is not at all a bad game. It´s fun, looks good and is proberbly in terms of gameplay the best one yet in the Souls Series. The main game is ok, nothing to incredible except some locations and boss´es. The DLC is the best content in it and also most likely the best in the Series. PVP is fun and amazingly done with good arenas to fight your enemy´s.  IF you are a newcomer to the Series, this is proberbly your best bet.

I was really surprised when I heard Haemimont was making an action RPG. I loved their Tropico series of games, but the action RPG genre isn't something you just dive into when all you're known for are sim games. I'm a huge fan of the Diablo series, I've played quite a bit of Marvel Heroes and Path of Exile as well as both Torchlight games. Victor Vran is like a breath of fresh air in the genre, and it's not just because you can jump and roll around - the game does a good job making all drops feel valuable, something that very few action RPGs succeed in doing. The story and voice acting is average, but the combat is really solid, the idea of switching weapons and having no classes is pretty unique and well done.
In Victor Vran you can switch between two weapons at any time, giving you access to a total of four weapon skills (plus regular attacks for each weapon). You can then equip two different Demon Powers, which are essentially spells, giving you access to six skills total. Then there's two slots for consumables and trinkets, like potions or a lucky rabbit's foot that gives you 100% critical hit chance for five seconds. To further customize your character, you gain access to Destiny Cards and that's when Victor Vran gets really awesome, because you can switch how your character players pretty easily. If you want to be able to live longer, you can put on a bunch of life steal and armor Destiny Cards to make your character tanky. Or if you like playing ranged, you do use the Archer card for increased range damage and stack critical hit chance and critical hit damage. Be able to switch up how your character is at anytime is pretty rad, especially when you can upgrade nearly everything in the game through the transmutation system.
I wrote a longer and more detailed review here:
but really, if you're a fan of action RPGs, you should definitely check out Victor Vran. The end game is pretty solid right now, and Haemimont has been adding a ton of content, so I expect it to get much better in the coming months.

Very fun game. Has a great combat system, good customization, and very nice online play. Italso has impressive camera work, making seeing where you need to see possible in all areas of the game.
The combat system is very action-filled and allows for a variety of combos. Speaking of variety there are quite a few different types of weapons of which you can equip two of them (after reaching an early level) and can freely switch between them at any time. Each weapon comes with it's basic attack and two skills. It may not seem like much at first, but then you realize that you can combo different weapon skills together and the possibilities are pretty much endless. There are a few different classes of enemies with their own subclasses, each with varying levels of style. There could b more IMO, but what is currently in the game is more than sufficient.
I really like the customization in this game. It allows a person to "build a class" so to speak. While it's possible to stick to the usual , it's also possible to go and make something whacky. There are 2 slots for weapons, 2 for potions, 1 for your suit(armor), 2 for overdrive(super) skills, and up to 5(one suit gives a 6th) Destiny card slots. The suit serves as a foundation for your build, as it not only influences tankiness, but how you gain overdrive. The Destiny cards serve to tweak the foundation. The potions and powers augment your style while the weapons help determine your offense. It's very well done and offers many combinations.
Have you ever had that moment where you can't see something but if the camera were 5 degrees to the left you would be able to see it? Well fear not, those days are over in this game. The camera can *gasp* BE ROTATED. This feature wil spoil you. You may even spin it around for no reason. Don't worry, these are just symptoms Acute Visual Rotary Obsession Disorder. They may (or may not) wear off over time. With that said, Objects will smoothly vanish so you can see behind them as you travel behind them according to your perception if you forget to rotate the camera. It doesn't look weird and is very well done.
There is many more things good about this game, but these hit me the most. There are still a few minor bugs but the get squashed quickly with the hammer of debugging (I wish this were an actual weapon lol)
overall 10/10, did not get 11/10 cause no hammer of debugging weapon.

Luxuria Superbia is a lovely gardening game that will truly challenge your green fingers.
You start the game with a sterile white garden, 11 empty flowerbeds and one with a single pink flower.
As the master gardener it is your job to take care of that flower and make it happy so you can harvest seeds, and to unlock the flower of the next flowerbed.
This is of course easier said than done.
The flower has a bronze, a silver and a gold stage of happines and an extasy stage where it's really REALLY happy.
Pacing is crucial, a beginner gardener might try to rush the flower to extasy in the bronze stage but the flower will become overstimulated and you'll have to try again.
Once you've made the flower happy enough (though not too happy) to clear the bronze stage you can bring the flower to extasy whenever you want, straight away or later, for example after clearing the silver stage.
Clearing the bronze stage also unlocks the next flower.
After the extasy stage you can harvest the flower's seeds to bring colour to your garden and move on to the next flower to make that one happy as well.
It might be a bit embarrassing (or something like that) at first because even as a master gardener you've probably never had flowers like this before, but they're really encouraging while you're trying, forgiving when you get it wrong and grateful when you get it right.
15/10 for a unique experience

As a strategy game, it's wondrous; as a piece of software, I'm finding it to be problematic. The gameplay is deep; running through a year of wartime often requires dropping the speed several steps. Taking care to keep forces equipped with the latest weaponry and in supply range is difficult, but nowhere near impossible; if anything, it's almost pleasing to be both general and logistician.
The real issue, however, is stability. It's rare to be able to complete a whole game in one sitting, even as a neutral power that never gets involved in a war. Particularly when playing a major power, the game is unstable and prone to crashing. Monthly autosaves alleviate some of the frustration, but long load-times compound the problem and rob it of some of the entertainment value. The fun is bulletproof, but only so long as it remains stable.
Crusader Kings II might prove to be a better option for someone looking for a general strategy game; Hearts of Iron IV is listed as in-development, so I might consider that a better option if it turns out to be stable.

Ultimate Chicken Horse is a very funny party game that can be played together with friends or online against strangers.
Since none of my (real life) friends own the game, I have only played online so far but it has been alot of fun nonetheless. I can imagine that playing it with your friends would be even better!
I mainly used my keyboard to play the game and I don't have any complaints about the controls. I have tried playing it with controller once but after ~50 hours of getting used to the keyboard, it was too much of a change for me so I decided to keep playing it the way I have always been.
It won't take too long to learn the controls but people who have experience with platformers (like me) have a significant advantage and if this is your first time playing this kind of game, it won't be easy (unless you only play against players of the same skill level of course)! That said, more skilled players can give themselves a handycap to make it a little more fair so in general this is not a problem.
There are a few bugs and sometimes the game will crash or freeze but that happens rather rarely so it's nothing to worry about too much.
The games can range from mere 5 minutes to over 20 minutes in length depending on the settings the admin of a lobby chooses. This means that it can very well be played to kill some time when you're bored but also for much longer durations. It will certainly not get boring too fast since every game is significantly different from the last one. There are many many kinds of placeable objects and maps.
The graphics are good, very cute art style. Same goes for the sound design and the music is very catchy. It fits the game's feeling perfectly.
You may meet annoying or rude players if you play online but that's just how some people are, I guess. It's not like the playerbase is small so don't worry about this. And you can of course also always just leave or kick the trolls if you want.
Overall, the game is a great way to kill some time and get a quick laugh out of simultaneously. It has certainly been worth it's price for me.

This was an interesting one.   Not a very deep game, this rogue-like platformer puts you at the helm of your space-house slash cargo collection headquarters.  The game plays out like this: Your ship sits in a space-junkyard of abandoned cargo containers.  You activate a magnet that attract a random container which slams into your ship, temporarily joining the two.
Your job is to then explore the newly adjacent container, looting all the valuables you can find.  Enemies along the way will attempt to stop you from taking the contents, but you’re armed with several different weapons to help dispatch your opponents.
Also fortunately, ammunition and weapon upgrades are plentiful and easy to find along your journey.
The main obstacle to your mission is time; shortly after you begin looting the containers, a wormhole will begin to open in space near your container, ripping it to shreds.  If you happen to be inside the container when it disintegrates, you’ll find yourself floating along, gasping for air.  You then have a very limited time to get into another container and find breathable air, or make it all the way back to your ship.
If you don’t make it home in time, you’ll find yourself a permanent resident of the space-junkyard, drifting along with the cargo containers forever.  Bummer.
Assuming you do make it back to your ship while you’re still breathing, your onboard computer will evaluate your loot and tell you if anything you found is of any value.  Accumulate enough loot, and you’ll begin to earn levels and gain the ability to permanently upgrade your gear, armor, and weapons.
What I liked: The premise of the game is cute.  It’s a fun game.  The graphics are playful, the sound effects were well done, and the controls were well configurable.
What I didn’t like: I got really tired of dying.  I know that dying is a regular part of a game like this, but I always felt like my deaths were slightly unfair.  Maybe I just need more practice.
This game was heavily discounted when I picked it up; I think that selling Steam Cards paid for this one.  So if you see it on sale, and looking for a little game without a lot of thinking involved, you could do worse.
Thanks for reading.

You’re broke and your family is going get evicted unless you do something drastic. So of course you decide to fly off into space and become a Cargo Commander, probably one of the most dangerous jobs that never existed, and then prey that you can make it home before mutants eat your face off. Oh and you have to collect every single type of cargo that exists or the corporation won’t give you the coordinated for Earth.
Yep, sounds like a great idea for a game to me and you know what? I’m absolutely right; it’s a great little game. Your job is to float from one cargo container to another as they smash into each other and gather as many crates as you can all the while dodging attacks from glowing mutant death beasts and making it back to your home base before the whole hulk of mangled metal that now surrounds you disintegrates into a worm hole and blasts you into the void to suffocate.
There are bunch of upgrades and weapons that can be unlocked through progression, getting every type of cargo, and the collection the baseball caps from fallen cargo commanders who have themselves been mutated. The game plays so well and is a ton of fun as you run, gun and smash through everything with your drill arm equipped with its various weapons, a shotgun or mine launcher for example. The story is always a driving force in background with emails and drawings from your son giving you brief glimpses into the happenings back on Earth and how your family needs you.
It’s a deceptively addictive game that is very easy to play but difficult to master.  Each level is randomly generated when you give it a name and you can play the levels other people have made by entering them on the level select screen. There is a world-wide scoreboard that you can partake in or not, but if you are the best person at a certain level you get to wear a crown. Also with the journeyman mode unlocked you can play a level forever and get a higher and higher score.
The game doesn’t look the best but it plays so well that I can recommend it all day. You can play it casually for a good time or if you want to complete it you will be at it for a long time.

Not every game has to be fun and jolly, and there's a tremendous amount to be said for the sort of thing this game does, but frustration was a more prevalent emotion for me than poignance, and that just can't work.
The bottom line is that the game isn't fun, and it's too frustrating to carry itself off without being fun. I don't regret buying it, but I still wouldn't recommend it to others.

The concept is like a dream come true for me personally. KSP-ish building style in a completely destructible lego environment?  Sounds great on paper but in its current state, doesn't play well in practice... yet.
Definitely gonna remain hopeful for this one but some major issues need to be addressed first that I was able to assess in just a few minutes, such as...
-Physics: Tires just don't have nearly enough contact on surfaces and therefore create a nearly uncontrollable "ice like" driving situation at just about any speed with any vehicle. Helicopter control is almost non-existent due to current control scheme the game is stuck with and honestly couldn't tell what aerodynamic physics were like because the heli was flipping instantly at take off with zero input.
-Options: Crucial showstopping issues not yet implemented like key mapping (at least none that I could find), reasonable controller support, etc
-Stability: What can I say? It's got to stay running without crashing for at least a few minutes in order for me to test reasonably and provide legitimate feedback.
It's funny and quite a lot of fun to watch how bricks behave when bashing around, no doubt it. But to put your creations to legitimate "use" for lack of a better term, is just as, if not more important than just tearing it up or running around destroying the environment.
Here's to hoping I need to return and change this to a thumbs up!

A friend of mine convinced me to restart my dark souls 1 playthrough after I gave up in the undead parish and I finally relented, playing through the entire game and DLC over the course of about 3 weeks. I very quickly realised why they love the game so much.
The combat was fluid and reactive, the fights felt challenging but overcomeable and the bosses were devistating - till you learnt how to hold your own against them. Each level and enemy felt very carefully crafted to test different aspects of the game, be it dealing with multiple enemies, hard hitting attacks in tight spaces with deadly drops, navigating intricate maps with what feels like an endless horde of enemies chasing you, the list goes on. The combat felt beautiful, each attack had a solid impact and every block, roll and turn felt extremely responsive.
As for the difficulty, yes it was hard, challenging for certain but it never really felt punishing. There were a few moments that made me grit my teeth, capra demon being one of them, but after some exploration of other areas and getting some better gear I was able to overcome it.
Dark souls 2 on the other hand feels like a mess.
The first thing I said to my friend after an hour of playing was "this feels more like a dark souls clone than a dark souls game"
The combat is substantially less reactive, every attack feels like im having to slog through knee deep water and the movement controls are fickle at best. And then theres rolling. Whoever's idea it was to halve the number of invincibility frames to make DS2 starter rolling worse than fatrolling in DS1 needs to be fired, if they havent been already. It almost forces you to bring a shield early game and horribly reduces the effectiveness of dodge based tactics till you have a much higher agility score. The joy of DS1 is that even from the start you have so many options for playstyles, this game just feels like im being crammed down one specific path till I reach high enough level to branch out and actually enjoy the game
And to top it off (Oh im gonna get so much crap for this), the max health drain. Its the single worst design decision in the entire game and i hate it.
Its the perfect example of challenging vs punishing. A challenging game (like DS1) has a difficulty level that is highly tuned so that you need to play very well, if not sometimes perfectly, in order to succeed. No matter how many times you smash your head against it, you're just as likely to succeed and through time, dedication and learning you generally take the boss down.
A punishing game can share a lot of these qualities but have one horrible thing on top. Every time you fail you get put at a disadvantage the next time you try. This actively discorages exploratory gameplay and forces me to decide between taking risks and possibly losing my souls (oh no how terrible) or being able to progress without having to deal with my health being gimped because i dared to try something new. As an example: After getting a little bored with dying in the forest/castle area near the start I decided to go and check out another route in the starting town. I found myself against a huge great big enemy with a ton of health and some really strong attacks. Naturally they killed me and I was sent back to town. After a few attempts, I gave up.
You're probably thinking "pshh yeah you just gave up because you're a noob and cant deal with losing"
No. I gave up because I was annoyed that I had to burn through what for my char is a fairly expensive item just to continue having an acceptable chance against this guy. The health drain actively discoraged challenging gameplay and instead made me want to go play something else.
All in all, the game, while visually gorgeous, feels like a very stale sequel to what is now one of my favourite games. Victor Vran is an aRPG with some twists.
It has a rotating camera, which is extremely helpful. It also has a dodge system which makes combat quick, addictive, and enjoyable.
The way you play the game is very immersive, there are no skill trees and stat selections upon leveling up, instead you're given bonuses and upgrades, you get to select one of 3.
There are no classes, your playstyle is based on your outfit (which determines the way you gain overdrive, which is used to activate demon powers), your cards (which grant specific buffs and abilities, you can select multiple), and your demon powers (powerful skills aquired from killing enemies with demonic powers, you can equip two of these.)
Now, one thing to point out, all the items in the game can be upgraded. Everything can be transmuted and made stronger. Weapons can have power stones, which add stat buffs. Outfits can be upgraded to gain traits from legendary cards. Cards have regular versions, and the more powerful wicked and divine versions which have useful passives and buffs.
The game also has plenty of MMO like challenges minus the trivial part of actually acquiring the quest and going back to the person for your reward. There is also multiplayer, a PvE arena, basic fighting pit PvP, and probably more things that I still havent found.
This game has been very active and the devs seem to be putting all of their effort into this game. Overall its a beautiful game, I have had no bugs or errors, the game runs perfectly. More content is added weekly.
To sum it up; if you like aRPGs but you're looking for something different, refreshing, enjoyable, and challenging, just buy this game and stop looking. Seriously, this game is amazing. Easily the best aRPG since D2.
Buy Victor Vran, buy it now.

Not only in how it looks, but in how it
.  It hits that all-too-uncommon sweet-spot of video-games: it remains challenging enough to be rewarding, but not so difficult as to be discouraging.   It is a lovingly realized, flawlessly crafted, deeply immersive experience.
The controls are quick and responsive on both K & M and gamepad.   The animations, are elegant without being laborious and don't get in the way of the action.   Combat is straightforward carnage that demands as much tactical consideration as quick reflexes.   I can't get away with just button mashing because I'll die.   Instead of combos, there are three types of attacks unique to each weapon class: a quick attack, something involving range, and some sort of massive attack.  Large melees take on the look and feel kaleidoscopic saloon brawls –- colorful crashing motion.
Everything about the character of Victor Vran is customizable.  The game has taken a fresh approach to skills/perks, allowing me to shape Victor's fighting style through the nuanced interplay of perks, powers, weapons and potions.  I've personally settled on a handful of favorite weapons I rotate through, depending upon the situation.   I'm forever tweaking and re-working my perks and powers, ever refining and improving them.
Weapons (and everything else) and their powers are upgradeable through the process of "transmutation.", over the course of the game I've upgraded my favorite sword from it's original green (uncommon) state, through a gold (rare) state, to its present almighty purple (legendary) state.   Like the rest of the game, upgrading and modifying items meticulously well balanced without resorting to arbitrary level limits.   Upgrading items is a matter of money and other items, which are consumed in the process.   Both money and items drop from enemies and environment alike but never so abundantly that upgrading is ever quick or easy.
Comparisons to
seem natural.  Both games excell at visceral, flowing, dynamic combat.   But I find combat in Victor Vran delightfully more challenging than
.   And if I want to make
even more challenging, instead of the age-worn “Easy,” “Normal,”  “Difficult” settings, I can choose to use so-called "Hexes."   Each Hex adds a different kind of buff to the enemies (or debuff to Victor), so by using some, none, or all of the Hexes, I can modify the flavor of difficulty, the form it will take.  In return for the added difficulty (and fun) each Hex also significantly increases the amount of XP earned.
The devs are productive, responsive, and communicative.  This game is a well made gem.

One of the most addicting games I've played this year!
Endless Dream is an odd game. It's a mix of roguelike with tower defense game, and packed with cute (and funny) story bits with anime-looking characters. At first, it plays like a more clunky Binding of Isaac, but won't take you long to notice the differences. This game is NOT about the action, but creative thinking! And it's not just about surviving, you also have to protect Mimi, a (at first) stationary character that sits in the first room. To do this, you can built towers that shoot enemies, towers that heel you, etc. But the resources to build them are scarce, and knowing where and how to build them is VERY important, specially in the escort mission at the end of the level.
Yes, escort mission, and that's another difference from similar games. You have to to to each room, kill enemies, install towers and un-curse rooms, but do all that to reach the final objective in each level: escort Mimi transporter room. The game is not evil though: you can start the escort mission whenever you want (and have found the transporter room), so feel free to prepare the way with towers and stuff. I mentioned "un-curse rooms" before, and that's a very important thing to notice: cursed rooms WILL produce enemies whenever you open a new door OR when you start you escort mission. So it's IMPERATIVE that you un-curse them. But you will NOT have enough resources to un-curse every room, so knowing which room to un-curse is part of the strategy.
The game is way more complex than it looks, BTW:  a good strategy is REQUIRED to succeed, even at low levels. The action is not very important: knowing where to install towers and what rooms to open (and un-curse) is the core of the game. It's like a game of chess: you CAN play if you just know how to move the pieces, but don't expect to win if you don't use your brain.
Lastly, the game is packed with random events (and they are usually dialogues between the cute main characters. And are usually funny!) and tutorial classes, but the best thing is that you don't HAVE to see them. After the first few introductory events, the "New Game" option is enabled, and you don't have to worry about tutorials and story events, if you don't feel like it. They start in a separate screen, so you just look at them IF you feel like it.
There are LOTS of options before starting the game, BTW. From multiple characters to multiple classes (and one of the characters can be any class), multiple difficulty and parameters, and even multiple supporting passive skills (in form of some fairy-like thingies. And they are cute!).
The graphics are simplistic and kinda repetitive, but the character sprites are very cute and well animated, and the characters' faces in the dialogues are very well drawn and full of funny expressions. And while the action of the game is indeed a bit cluncky, it's like I said before: the action is NOT the focus of the game.
tl;dr:
This game is not perfect, but it surely is WAY better than I was anticipating it. I'm addicted to it, and HIGHLY recommend it if you feel like playing a tower-defense-rogue-lite game with anime characters, optional story segments and a deep and VERY challenging gameplay.
