I dont normally write reviews this early on, but I believe I understand the game enough at this point to do so, particularly with it's similarities to a certain other game.  Plus, reviews help games like this get more attention (something Steam's storefront fails to do, every time).   And I think this one deserves it.
The game I refer to, that inspires this one, is Dungeon of the Endless, an absolute favorite of mine.  Like that game, this combines a couple of genres, tower defense, and roguelike.  Also like DotE, it is both turn-based and real-time, at the same time.  On top of this goes a layer of RPG-style character stats and similar things, adding more complexity to an already complicated game.
Chances are, going into this one for the first time, you're likely to be a bit confused.  Few other games work quite like this one... actually, only one works like this one, which again is DotE.  The game uses tower defense concepts as the core of the gameplay, but unlike most TD games, a battle is not just constant waves while you struggle to keep up.  Instead, there are two phases:  Preparation, and combat.   The preparation phase is when there are no enemies present.  You are free to move from room to room, construct towers, and interact with various NPCs to do different things such as buy items or research new towers.  When you feel that you're ready, you go and open a door, revealing a new room.  Opening a door effectively means the beginning of the next "turn", and advances a number of things.  For example, this is when your resource production happens, and when tower research also goes forward.  But more importantly, it begins the combat phase.  Enemies spawn in every room that is still cursed, and make their way towards Mimi, who serves as the "core" that you must protect.  Your towers will do their best to destroy these monsters, but they cant do it alone.  You have to join the fray yourself, adding a very active element to a genre that often consists mostly of waiting.
Unlike DotE, you do not have a full team of characters to manage here.  Instead, you have just your one character who you play as (though there are multiple characters to choose from when you start a new game).  You have various attacks and skills/spells with which to attack the marauding robot monsters, doing everything you can to prevent them from winning.  If Mimi goes down, or if you yourself are defeated, that's it, the run is over.  Like any roguelike/lite/whatever, this uses permadeath, so loss means starting over from the beginning.   Combat is often difficult, as your enemies are outright overwhelming much of the time, and they vary in their functions.  Some enemies will make a beeline for the room that Mimi is in.  Others will hound you endlessly, trying to crush you.  And some will even target your various towers and other gizmos, trying to wreck them.  This means alot of chaos, and it will really test the strategy you have been setting up.  All that preparation you do before each combat phase is very important, and involves alot of careful decision making.
Add to this the random nature of roguelikes.  For example, when you go to research new towers, generators, or whatever, you do not know just which ones will be available (another idea carried from DotE).  When buying items, you never know what the shop will have.  And then there's the Sakuras, a variety of girls with crazy powers who can be contracted to help you; they dont make direct appearances in combat, but you can assign them to be either supporters or operators, to go along with whatever tactics you are using.  Like anything else though, you do not know which Sakuras you will encounter in the dungeon.  Victory in this game is all about taking what the RNG gives you, and finding a way to make it fit.  In my experience, there is always a way to make it work, even though it will seem tremendously difficult.  You're going to have to really use your head to get through this one.
Which brings up the one problem I think it has:  the learning curve.  Chances are, when you start up a run, you are going to be annihilated by robot bees.  You're not going to be quite sure how you could possibly deal with such opposition.  I've heard of players not even being able to pass the first floor (of many).  I recall that DotE had this exact problem, which I call "deceptive difficulty".  The learning curve creates the perception that the game is harder than it truly is, because you will find yourself struggling to figure out how you can possibly deal with everything.  You may start to think that things are imbalanced or even broken, or unfair, or... whatever.  Again, same exact problem DotE had.  But once you truly learn the game, you find that seemingly unfair situations actually arent.  You find ways in which you can alter your tactics, new things you can try, new approaches to different situations.  As your understanding increases, so will your progress.  But reaching that point is difficult, and I suspect this will push away many players. Tower defense games can be more than a bit obtuse when it comes to the sorts of ways you can strategize in them, and not only is this no exception, but it takes it a few steps further.
Which is a shame, because like DotE, the game really is lots of fun.  Tons of depth and challenge to be had here.  And there's more that I havent gone into, for example the shop that allows you to unlock more Sakuras between runs (and power them up a bit).  Or the fact that there are actual story sequences, something which DotE didnt really bother with.   The story has issues, but the dialogue and characters are entertaining and the art is well done.  Even when you're dying horribly in each run, new bits of story and such will still open up to you.
But it's the gameplay that really makes this one what it is.  And I'm glad that it exists.  I absolutely adored DotE, and wished there could be more games like it, but nope, there really wasnt.  Until this comes along.  Many similarities, yet still this one does enough to make it stand out as it's own unique thing.  The learning curve is absolutely brutal, and the difficulty only increases the further you get into each dungeon, so expect many losses before you start to get anywhere.  This is not a game for those who are easily discouraged.  But if you can persist with it, you'll find something really nice here that will offer many hours of challenge and fun.

"If you press the attack button you'll attack" was the first one.

This program is not a game - it is an interactive story.  From a user perspective the flow is very linear. The story is set in the United Kingdom in the months leading up to the first world war.  The main character is Richard Hannay, whom you follow  as he gets caught up trying to thwart an attempt to assassinate a Greek politician in London.  Events take Richard to Scotland and various other locations in the south of England.
I really liked this digital media story and I do recommend it to others.  The artwork for the locations, especially the Scottish countryside was very well done.  The voice acting is excellent.  The music and sound effects are very good.  It takes about four hours to play through the 19 events.  For your time you are awarded with a Steam achievement for each event and one more for completing the entire story.
I give this interactive story 8 out of 10.  I bought it on sale for 2 dollars and it was worth the money for sure.

Cargo Commander caught me totally off-guard. I was expecting something more traditional, with set levels and power-ups and some goofy story. That's usually a safe bet with indie platformers, which makes the ones that break the mold all the more pleasing to behold. And that's exactly what I got here, a deceptively clever roguelike that started eating hours of my time, at least once I got over some rough patches.
You play an employee of Cargo Corp, sent off to the♥♥♥♥♥end of space in a boxy little junker of a ship to salvage equally junky boxes. Your ship is equipped with a magnet that, when activated, draws in a random assortment of giant space containers to smash into your ship and each other. Within these containers are the random bits of space junk Cargo Corp wants, along with enemies, hazards, and weapons to handle them. Connected containers usually have gaps to pass through where they collide, forming a rudimentary platforming level, but you can also drill through walls or spacewalk (as long as you can hold your breath) to get where you want to go.
Surviving enough waves of salvage gets you a container with a sector pass, which lets you travel to another area of space with different containers and salvage. Sectors are random based on their name, and the navigation system shows you popular systems, unpopular systems, systems your friends play, random systems, and even let you enter your own name to create a new one. It's a neat bit of continuity between players, further bolstered by the player corpses you can find and loot in heavily-trafficked sectors, and postcards from other players you can find randomly, or fill out and shoot into space if you find a blank one.
As far as gameplay goes, that's it. You call in waves of containers, loot them for cargo and resources to upgrade your dude (which reset for each sector), and get back to your ship before the "level" gets sucked back into space. There are basically two kinds of enemies in the game, melee monsters of varying size in the containers, and aggravating drill-squid things in space. You can find and upgrade a handful of weapons to deal with them, but combat is pretty thin and it's easy to get overwhelmed. The platforming isn't much better, with the random containers sometimes making regular exploring impossible and forcing you to drill out tons of walls or spacewalk around obnoxious areas.
With each sector essentially the same aside from items to find and container layouts, the game risks getting repetitive very quickly. I was about ready to punch out after 90 minutes or so... until I started paying attention to the story. Cargo Commander has a surprisingly dark, dystopian plot propping up the platforming, told through darkly funny emails from corporate and charming letters and packages from your family. As you tick off the the 88 different kinds of cargo to find, you rank up with the company, getting you new tools to speed up the process and maybe making progress towards getting home someday.
The whole package is far more compelling than I first thought, and I find myself returning to it whenever I have a free moment. The graphics are pretty basic indie 3D and the sound design works well enough, but it's the unique roguelike format married to an interesting world and story that keep it fresh. Every level is a mash-up of space debris crammed full of goodies, and those goodies get you more tantalizing bits of the story. On top of all that there are leaderboards for each sector and an endless mode to challenge if you need more variety, but even without those details Cargo Commander is well worth digging into.

Game is fun, and definitely emulates the feel of the first world war.
Pros:
Historical realism is pretty decent
Maps look decent
Gore effects and body wriggling is good
Guns *mostly* handle well enough.
Diversity in factions is great
Small details like uniforms and the unique level up system is pretty cool.
Melee is neat.
Limited gear is a nice challenge.
Cons:
Skill disparity and balancing of teams can really be off putting.
Aimbotters aren't nearly filtered enough.
Game has a few map exploits where one can shoot through some parts of the terrain.

No facial animations.
Flamethrower spray graphics looks really subpar.
Voice Acting could've been expanded upon, more ingame shouts, more commands for players to do, like sharing ammo or asking for reinforcements, and just more overall coordination would've been nice.
No ability to pick up and use weapons.
Overall, Verdun is a neat little game that focuses on squad combat taking over trenchlines on a map, and there's a few other modes as well but the trench taking is the most common. It certainly feels like the grindy and horrifying situation the Western Front definitely was, and it does justice to the brutality and at points, sheer pointlessness of the conflict in terms of how it was fought, the ineptitude of the strategems used and it does immerse you well enough into a First World War battlefield.
I recommend it, just be prepared to die a lot.

Verdun is an engaging historical shooter that makes good use of its World War 1 setting. The central game mode sees each team starting in their own trench with one team attacking and one defending. If the attackers can't get a foothold in three minutes, they go on the offense while the other team switches to defense. If the attacking team get a foothold in the enemy trench, the time is extended. If the attackers capture the enemy trench, they must defend against a counter-attack before attacking the next enemy trench line.
This is a great game mode that feels historically accurate and also means that if one team is struggling on the offense, after a few minutes they will go on the defense so it never turns into a frustrating meat-grinder for either team. Trying to get across No Mans Land as the attackers is absolutely terrifying, while fighting in the trenches is tense and exciting. Several historically pertinent mechanics like Gas attacks that force you to put on a view-limiting gas-mask, or barbed wire you can get tangled in instead of just being a wall, add to the atmosphere and the gameplay in a meaningful way.
The squad system means that you are given access to a good variety of weapons and abilities, although you will need to enjoy bolt-action rifles to have fun with this game. Some rifles feel all-around better than others, which while historically accurate can lead to some frustrating gameplay if you get stuck with a class that uses one of the lesser rifles.
While the game in its current state is totally playable, it would benefit greatly from some spit-and-polish. Ragdolls are jittery and can break immersion. Hit detection leaves much to be desired. The current system for joining servers has you picking a squad instead of a server, and you can't see what the ping is when doing this. However I seem to have exactly the same ping no matter what server I join, which makes me think all of the servers are centralized which is not ideal.
Overall if you enjoy games like Red Orchestra 2 or Insurgency and are interested in the WW I setting, Verdun is a game I would highly recommend. The central game mode is excellent and the maps are generally well designed with one or two exceptions that have huge no-mans land zones that are impossible to make it across in the given time as the attackers.

A game that is similar to Dungeon of the Endless, but with a different playstyle and anime waifus.
Few main differences are:
You only have one playable character at a time, so you only have one life throughout your playthrough.
You pick and recruit Sakuras who each have different stat bonuses, and can be assigned to either directly help you or your towers.
Has an element system in which some are stronger/weaker to the other ones.
Items have an element affinity which have bonuses correlating to your Sakura's element, so you have to select which ones are worth owning or getting.
A sadistic bunnygirl who gives you a minor/major debuff in exchange for a item/tech/skill.
The enemy spawning system is more brutal in this game, you can't unlight/recurse a room, it's set in stone. You have to be careful where you want allocate uncurse. Those cursed rooms, they will always spawn enemies, always.
Escorting the WaifuCore, is harder, depending on amount and location of cursed rooms. You have to not only escort her safely to the exit, but have to power up two engines (In the exit room) and wait for the exit to open up. During this, you try to defend the WaifuCore from the waves of enemies.
When you get a skill, it's purely RNG. You can't select what type of skill you get or where it goes, so you can either get lucky or don't.
Tower research takes two doors, but can only go one at a time.
Turret Towers miss a lot of times, sometimes struggles from all the enemies on room since it shoots towards their current walk location rather than their path, so you end up with core-target enemies passing by the room.
Risk and reward with opening doors was a bit more ambiguous in DotE, which is good. In here, you can expect what will happen when you decide to open a door or not. Especially since each dark room will always spawn enemies.
Game has waifus, and game is harder than DotE with good and bad reasons (At its current stage). Sadly no plans for co-op, but still worth the try.

This game is fun! I gotta admit, I was hesitant because my experience with Tropico 5 wasn't good, but I chanced my money because of the fantastic art style in the game and I was very pleasantly surprised.

Everything is put together in this nice package that compels me to explore and try different tactics. There are a few things that could be better for multiplayer (separate loot instances are not my cup of tea), but nothing that would keep me from playing online. It's still a blast to complete the different quests and missions with your friends.

Victor Vran:
~~~~~~~~~~
You play Victor Vran in this Action RPG set in the fantasy world of Zagoravia.  As this game is currently on sale in early access version, it shows so far enormous potential.
If you enjoyed playing Diablo and Van Helsing, Victor Vran is a must try. Big variety of monsters to slash either with melee weapons such as swords, rapiers, hammers and scythes or you can use shotguns and mortars for your distance arsenal.  It goes without saying that all weapons have their own characteristics and level of damage they can inflict to your adversaries.
Stacks of potions and powers to help you go through each level and one of my favourite powers is the Boomerang, a massive purple boomerang that hits your enemies twice on the way out and back. Absolutely marvellous stuff!!
You will also pick up destiny cards; these cards are very useful as you will be able to add or modify your character attributes.
Different ways to level up your character, of which the obvious one is every time you kill an enemy you get experience points, but you will be able to get higher value points if you achieve challenges within the levels.
The available playing levels are well designed and quite challenging as far as you progress. Make sure you collect as many items as possible, including gold coins so you can upgrade your arsenal with the traders.
Graphically, Victor Vran looks good, runs smoothly and I have not encountered issues so far.
The only negative is if you are using the keyboard and mouse as your controls, it is a bit sluggish.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Fairly large and well designed levels with interesting monsters
-	Plenty of weapons and other goodies at your disposal
-	Online mode
-	Challenging
-	Achievements
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~~
-	  Controls need to be twigged a bit especially if you are using the keyboard and mouse
I really enjoyed this game so far and thoroughly recommend it. I am looking forward to the final version.

If you're looking for a very solid ARPG with a superb combat system look no further, this is the game.
The feature that makes this game fun is its combat, it is very refreshing to see something like this in a ARPG.  You actively dodge and jump around to avoid damage.  Basically the movements and attacks is like an MMO, but in a top-down view like traditional ARPG's.
The character customization isn't super deep like other ARPG's, there are no specific classes.  The customization comes in weapons, destiny cards, and demon powers.  There are different weapons that you can use and each weapon has their own special skills to use.  There are no rings or accessorie slots, but there are items called "destiny cards" which are similar to those.  These cards give passive bonus' to your character, asyou level up you can equip more and powerful cards.  Also demon powers are special spells that you can equip to use against the enemy and there is a variety of them that you can use for different situations.
With all of this said, each of these items have different rarity tiers and also you can upgrade the stats on these items as well.  So all in all, customization is not that deep, but there is enough depth to keep you occupied in obtaining the best stats in the game.
Final thoughts:  I have been searching for a game that will give me that "new game" feeling I had as a kid.  It has been a long and expensive search as you can tell from my library, but I think I have found it with Victor Vran.  Every time I open the game I get excited, planning what I want to do that day, be it slaying monsters for fun, finding legendary weapons, or just crafting.  Usually these days I can only play games for about 1 hour before I get bored, but with this game I can go on for hours and that is rare for a game nowadays to do.
So if you're looking for an epic combat system and have fun for hours on end, get this game, you will NOT regret it.  Trust me :)

The reason why I don't recommend Hearts of Iron III is because of its various limitations which I do not think are overcome by its many features.
The game is set between 1936-1948.  That is, this is a World War II game.  If you enjoy WW2 lore and strategy games, this is not a bad game - the strengths of the game include technological advancements; the use of era-specific units; actual historical events that influence the overall experience (to make it more realistic in terms of both chronology and "what are you going to do about that?"); and hardy diplomatic and espionage systems.  There are also levels of customization in terms of unit names, province names, and other minor details.
Hearts of Iron III would be a totally awesome game if you could play it for much longer than just thirteen game years.  That is, the combat, economic, diplomatic, and province construction elements of the game are very, very cool.  But how cool can they be if you can't ever use them fully?
The biggest limitation, in my view (besides being limited to only thirteen game years), is that you MUST play as one of the great (or at least most significant) world powers of this era if you would like to do anything significant in this game.  If you simply want to develop, say, South Africa into an industrial or military or nuclear powerhouse - just to give the big boys a run - then you won't be able to do it (without significant modification to the game; you cannot accomplish this regularly).  The game is set up too historically accurate and plausible; so because a country like, say, South Africa never did anything so huge on a global scale, then you will not be able to make South Africa do anything globally significant in this game.  For those of us who like to play an underdog and build them up and alter world history, this game is not for us.  We are pigeonholed into the "realism" of the actual chronology and cannot do much to escape it.  So this limitation is probably ideal for WW2 enthusiasts, but it is certainly not ideal for us strategy gamers in general.
For me, the two limitations listed above are what kill the game for me.  I am not a WW2 buff, though I do appreciate the historical accuracy in terms of units, events, and other things.  Nevertheless, as a strategy gamer, Hearts of Iron III makes it essentially impossible to play the ways that I want to.  So that is why I do not recommend it.  I could only recommend this game to people who are thorough enthusiasts of the period and only if you bought the full, complete game for $6 or less.  That is, if you just want to buy "another WW2 game," then this one can give you some fun.  If you want to use the strategy elements of the game, then consider a different title from Paradox (like Europe Universalis III or IV or Crusader Kings II).  Even then, many of the strategic elements of Hearts of Iron III are not available in other Paradox titles except for other limited titles such as Victoria II.  Again, Paradox limits strategy players with period-specific games that do not allow for breaking from the mold and doing anything too free-form and significant (except when leading to a quick demise if you go too radical).
Just as a side note, the Hearts of Iron series (all three titles) is entirely limited to the World War II era.  Hearts of Iron II, however, had an interesting expansion pack that enabled a time frame into the 1950s where the USSR provided a fictional threat to the USA (similar to the storyline of Indiana Jones IV with the pseudo-history of fictional Cold War events or possibilities).  Hearts of Iron III, however, will stop you at 1948 - either you played as one of the major Axis Powers and took over Europe, or you played as one of the Allied Powers and prevented that.  Period.
--------
I wanted to provide some more technical or more specific reasons for why I would not recommend Hearts of Iron III to the general strategy gamer.
1)  Some technologies have twelve tiers to them.  That is, you will research one technology twelve times in order to cap it at Level 12/12.  Some technologies will require something like at least Level 3 of one technology in order to research a different technology.  This is really cool, of course.  However, you will find that unless you are either the United States or Germany, you will not be able to cap nearly any of these.  (As the USA or Germany, you might be able to cap just a few, even though there are several you'd probably like to.)  This is all fine if you just want to play a period-specific, relatively historically accurate game.  If you love strategy games in general, then this is a major let-down.
2)  If you want to modify Hearts of Iron III, then you probably should be (or will get to be) familiar with tweaking certain values in the text file of your savegame.  However, unlike Europa Universalis III or IV, Hearts of Iron III is not so simple to figure out.  And once you do, you will notice that there is not much you can significantly do to change your lot in the game world besides cheating to full capacity.  In all, it is ridiculous how limited this game is if you simply appreciate its strategic elements and also don't give a crap about historical accuracy.  But, of course, if you are a WW2 nut and just want historical accuracy above all else, then modifying the game should not be important to you, as this game definitely limits itself to that period faithfully!

I Pre-Ordered this game (complete with DLC Season Pass), thinking it would be the "killer app" for NFS. I also had the opportunity to get access to a weeklong beta preview (which I did a few videos on). The first three days of its release, I streamed all my gameplay on Twitch - that later got ported over to Youtube. I thought this game was awesome, the sh!t, the bomb, whatever.
I was wrong.
Three days of gaming, and I had already beaten the campaign, made it to Level 50 (which is the maximum level you can reach), and complained like a motherf*cker about how bad it was. Police chases were impossible (they used to be easy in the beta, they turned into brick walls in the release), the handling was so off that you're forced to use AWD vehicles to win (looking at you, mountain missions!), and so many classes for cars were missing (back then, the Nissan Skyline R34 GT-R just had Street, Dirt and Performance specs), and the rubberbanding was stupidly ridiculous. Oh, and don't get me started on the fact that Perf-Spec Hummers could wipe the floor with most other cars.
And then...Wild Run came out.
And made everything worse.
Getting Platinum no longer meant that you had a random chance of getting parts from Lv. 40-50, but now you had a chance to get visuals from Platinum wins, too. This means bumpers, spoilers, car colours, vinyls, stickers, rims, and more - all battling against a performance part that's just 1 level above what you currently have.
Car physics went even more awry than before - I used to be able to drift on the mountains fine with my Perf-Spec R34, but now I can do it with my Circuit-Spec R34, instead.
Wild Run brought specs to vehicles that have no right for them - I mean, who even wants a Monster Truck version of a Skyline R34? Or any sedan/coupe? Isn't that spec supposed to be for, y'know, trucks?
And then the Bikes - basically everyone uses them in PvP. And with smaller hitboxes and more torque than even supercars, they're guaranteed to win every match. It's not fun anymore.
I don't hop on the game anymore, and I wonder why I keep it installed. I guess some part of me holds a small bit of hope that the right people will come along, and make the game what it was meant to be, instead of this crazy clusterf*ck that it currently is.
All in all, I would not recommend this game to anyone, regardless of sale price. Just don't bother.

It doesn't take much to make a good Diablo-Clone.  Just take what made Diablo great and expand on it.  Simple right?  If you know anything about these games, you know more times than not, it's either Hit or Miss...Hit meaning classics like Titan Quest, Torchlight, and Grim Dawn...or Miss meaning pieces of trash like Blood Knights, Sacred 3, or The Incredibly Impossible Adventures of Van Helsing.
Anyway, Victor Vran takes the ARPG formula and makes it real simple and functional.  Firstly, you get to choose your controls - WSAD to move & click to attack, Click to Move/Attack, or gamepad.  You read that correctly...all three are options, as well as key mapping for either keyboard option you choose.  Why other dungeon crawlers don't attempt to adopt this kind of setup is beyond me.
That said, there's a reason more people enjoy playing Diablo III on a console..using a controller feels so excellent for this type of game, and it's actually very responsive.  Your attacks are quick, but weighty, and you actually get experience points for doing more damage to an enemy than needed.
They've added a jump button, which at first seems stupid, but combined with the ability to wall jump, it actually allows you to get to secret areas and get away from enemies.  They've also included a dodge button, taking a page out of the Dungeon Siege III book.  There's no cooldown or stamina bar for dodge rolls like there is in Risk of Rain or Dark Souls, respectively. You can do it as many times as you want and it really comes in handy.
Sound is great, voice acting is pretty spot on as well.  From time to time it DOES sound like the voice actor is reading his lines..because he is...but it's still well done.  Looting is par for the course, and you'll be able to upgrade your weapons, transmute, etc.  Since there's no skill tree or even any classes so-to-speak,  your skills and based on your outfit and the weapons you use.  It sounds strange, but it really does work.  That goddamn skill tree in PoE turned a lot of people off, myself included, so to have things simplified so I can concentrate on killing stuff is a breath of fresh air.
Each dungeon actually gives you 5 tasks to complete, each one giving you a star for completion.  Some of them require you to take no damage, use no potions, or slay a certain number of beasts in a certain amount of time.  If things get hectic and you can only accomplish 4 out of the five, no biggie.  Just leave, get your mind right, go back later and get that 5th star.  It's pretty linear gameplay, but if you're a fan of this genre, then you've come to expect that.
So far the game's a lot of fun, and it's only gonna get better.  Grab it now while it's in Early Access or wait til the 26th when it gets a full release.  Either way, it's worth owning.  Hands down one of the best ARPGs I've ever played.

Cargo Commander is a fun little indie game that combines the art of scavenging and platforming. You play as a "cargo commander", who lives in a floating home in the depths of space. You pull cargo containers up to your base via gravity generator, and it is your job to search these containers to find what else, cargo. The rarer the cargo is, the more unique items you add to your database. The more cargo, the higher your score in the sector you reside. You really feel the lonliness of space while isolated alone with no communication, but you still feel compelled to adventure and discover more of the void. It can have some glitches at times, such as being stuck between two containers and forcing you to die and end the mission as well as random texture issues, but the overall game functions pretty well. Cargo Commander is a fun, pick-up-and-play game that is extremely easy to play and learn.

The 39 Steps is a nice electronic adaption of John Buchans espionage thriller published in 1915.
The story is told accurately in a attractive mix of changing narratives.
The artwork is very artistic and impressive. Especially the short shadow-playing films are awesome.
The voices of the speakers are adequate and partly in Scottish dialect (dialects can switched off in the main menu).
All in all more an interactive movie than a game (the action is fixed) it offers very nice entertainment for 5 to 8 hours with very lovingly implemented action. For somebody who likes classic literature themes nice and slowly adapted it is surely an insiders tip.
I hope there will be more of such games in the future.

Addicting and challenging "city" builder. The term "city builder" is used loosely here as even at the largest, the towns created in here aspire to "large medieval hamlet". This game distinguishes itself from other city builders in two respects.
First, it is difficult; almost punishingly difficult. This is especially true if you are used to more forgiving city builder sims, where the tide of the game can be shifted with an ordinance, a building, or a tax hike. There are no such instruments in Banished. Build too many houses, a season later there are hungry mouths to feed with not enough workers to provide food. Build too slowly, and the aging population is unable to replace workers fast enough. Each decision needs to be made with the consequences of the future in mind, as the impact of a single building can have a ripple effect seasons later.
Second, unlike many other city builders there are not a plethora of buildings, and no direction towards the "You Win" building. All buildings and upgrades are available from the word go. The exercise of Banished is one of a balancing act, rather than a sprint. The player must keep food, population, and resources in perfect balance or a death spiral can very rapidly occur.
It can lead to some frustration early on, but the best advice that can be given is not to get too attached to the first town that one builds. However, as the mechanics become more and more apparent, a rhythm to the gameplay will emerge and that is when Banished truly hooks the player.
The game gets a recommendation for players who long for a city builder with some serious depth despite the bucolic exterior. If someone is looking for a game with a campaign to lead them through a series of missions and hand hold through each step of the way, look elsewhere. While there is a tutorial, it only covers the very basic mechanics, it leaves the rest to the player.

Refunct is an awesome platformer, where you have to jump on various platforms to unlock more platforms. That is done by getting to the highest point and push a button, which unlocks more. The graphics are minimalistic and it works for what is is. It has vibriant colors, which seems to draw a lot of inspiration from the Super Mario Games.  An overall beautiful game.
Soundtrack is made by Singto "Kristofferson" Conley, which did an amazing job with the soundtrack. The soundtrack is very pieceful and relaxing.
The game is a lot of fun and an excellent time filler. It has a lot of potential, but the game is too short to really explore this. It is a very mediocre game and for the price of 3€ you can find better games out there.

Make no mistake, this is not Diablo.  Nor is this Torchlight.  And, not even Van Helsing.  But, it is a decent ARPG, if not a little bit on the casual side.  What I mean by casual is, fighting is pretty much set on easymode.  Early on, you just hold 1 button to attack, literally the whole time.  As the game goes along, you begin mix it up with 2 other attacks.  I wouldn't expect much build variation, as I said, this isn't any of the above named ARPG's.  There 2 weapon slots and card slots (which act as a sort of replacement for skills).  That's right, there's no skill tree.  Gameplay is pretty arcade-like.  It does however, seems more story driven.  Hey, it's even got the Witcher's Geralt voice actor.  Though the static portraits seem a bit cheap.
What did I like?
Dodging - yes, I like my dodging (hello Guild Wars 2)
Jumping - while not absolutely necessary (well, to access some areas it is), it's always nice to find shortcuts
Precise controls
Smooth gameplay
Appears to be plenty of maps - though with 4 players i'm not sure how loot distribution is done, nor do I know if the size is big enough.
What I didn't like?
It feels pretty empty - After more play, I feel the sound is missing some big effects.  I kinda wish it had some of the annoying Diablo 3 Crusader grunts...
Combat feels a bit bland and simplistic - needs some on-screen oomph (more effects I suppose)
Jumping and attacking is pointless - add in the regular attacks and that might add a bit
Can't rotate images (e.g. weapons and portraits) - You get a cool weapon, but you only get a 2D image of it.
Navigating the menus can be confusing - especiallly when using a controller.
Too much of the 'other' voice (not sure if he's trying to be the narrator) - kind of ruins the brooding mood (I guess they wanted some comedy)
You can still get hit while dodging
While the graphics are ok, there really is a lack of detail.
Keep in mind I've only played a few hours now.  So, maybe some of the 'didn't likes' get improved upon.  And, while it may seem like there's more to dislike than to like, it's actually a pretty decent game.  To me, it's just OKAY (though, it grows on me more and more).  If I had to give it a score, i'd give it a 7/10.

I'm becomming better acquainted with this game and I'm finding that as Victor Vran nears completion, it's really taking its own shape and bringing its own flavor to the genre. It fills a niche and provides an experience unlike my other favorites like Path of Exile, Grim Dawn, and Torchlight 2.  The "Tony Hawk-Style Goals" for each map are a fun change, and I really like Victor Vran's take on the /player system (the /player system is a reference to Diablo 2, where a player could type /player 8 and the game would treat the map as if it had 8 players on it, being very difficult, but giving high rewards).
The Controls can be touchy if you're not using a controller, and I hope they improve with each patch. They have seemed to considerably thus far.  It's not the most in depth arpg, but I highly recommend it regardless.

Addicting and challenging "city" builder. The term "city builder" is used loosely here as even at the largest, the towns created in here aspire to "large medieval hamlet". This game distinguishes itself from other city builders in two respects.
First, it is difficult; almost punishingly difficult. This is especially true if you are used to more forgiving city builder sims, where the tide of the game can be shifted with an ordinance, a building, or a tax hike. There are no such instruments in Banished. Build too many houses, a season later there are hungry mouths to feed with not enough workers to provide food. Build too slowly, and the aging population is unable to replace workers fast enough. Each decision needs to be made with the consequences of the future in mind, as the impact of a single building can have a ripple effect seasons later.
Second, unlike many other city builders there are not a plethora of buildings, and no direction towards the "You Win" building. All buildings and upgrades are available from the word go. The exercise of Banished is one of a balancing act, rather than a sprint. The player must keep food, population, and resources in perfect balance or a death spiral can very rapidly occur.
It can lead to some frustration early on, but the best advice that can be given is not to get too attached to the first town that one builds. However, as the mechanics become more and more apparent, a rhythm to the gameplay will emerge and that is when Banished truly hooks the player.
The game gets a recommendation for players who long for a city builder with some serious depth despite the bucolic exterior. If someone is looking for a game with a campaign to lead them through a series of missions and hand hold through each step of the way, look elsewhere. While there is a tutorial, it only covers the very basic mechanics, it leaves the rest to the player.

Now, Don't get the vote wrong.
I love the game and it's one with the most potential I've ever seen of its own style. I could put the good parts but it would be just spoiling.
However, there are some TERRIBLE flaws.
Firstly, most minimally:
You can't change controls. I'm used to using arrows on the PC VERSION (You'll see why it's uppercase). Second, the control buttons switch from PC to console, even if you're not on console, so if you're new, you won't remember how to, say, put turrets and it's gonna be terribly bad for doing things such as Last Stand, where turrets are VITAL.
You can't force to find items, so if you skim over the easier levels, you'll never find basic level items, therefore never finish your collections. The bonuses are almost useless, but still very nice.
Now, for the HUGE flaw that wrecks the entire system:
I need you to follow me here:
SAS4 is available on both
and as mobile app.
Of course, the website version is on PC.
So, do you think they ported the PC version for a PC game?
Nah. Pc game, mobile port.
When they could have used the PC version.
Now, one could just say: "Oh, but it's just uncomfortable for you! Many can just play it the same!"
No, the two games are very different.
I haven't gone deep in PC game, but there is another currency called "Alloy", which gets somewhat more useful in the Black Strongbox part of the game, if I remember. It also helps doing some kind of augments, but I've wrote enough that going back would be a waste. I will maybe update this part if I go further.
Also, the entire view of the game is different, done to be just clicks apart, while the mobile version is based on "scrolling", which is obviously more practical on mobile.
Oh, let's not forget the entire other set of missions on another planet that is on the pc version.
Honestly? The game itself is wondrous. Perfectly sculpted missions, the virus has some originality and goes beyond that would be considered "realistic", becoming even a DIGITAL virus, infecting many tough bosses.
The scaling is perfect, inventing many augments and upgrades to bosses, not just making "levels" for zombies.
The missions are one more unique than the last and they are all equally entertaining and unique. The bosses themselves are very fun and balanced. An example: The first boss found (And easiest to defeat) is the Regurgitator. High melee damage, an ability to vomit acid and a kind of very fast worms supposed to distract you from the main threat. The Regurgitator is then followed by the Wicker. The wicker is able to summon fireballs from far away to incendiate the player. It is faster, multiplicatively stronger than the Regurgitator and shoots meteors upon death, discouraging close-up fighting with wickers.
Devastators, oh now we're having fun.
Devastators are incredibly more resistant than the wicker. Faster, deals destructingly high damage and goes into a berserk at around 15-20% health and deals ungodly, one-shotting tier damage and becomes practically the fastest unit in the game.
They don't come together, no. There's a huge difference from them.
The scaling's beautifully balanced, once again.
Infact, if we're considering the game itself, i'd give it like a 8-9/10, maybe 10/10 when I will get into Nightmare mode and Black Strongboxes, but they chose to make it a mobile port.
If they choose to modify or change it back to be a PC port, then I'd switch back to recommending it, because it's beautiful.
We need more story development though, I share it with many.

Time for a controversial review. I’ve played this game on and off for the past 5 years, and I’ve gradually come to realize it's not that great. I’ll try to explain why.
To get one thing out of the way, the music is fantastic. The chiptune album “PPPPPP” is a true modern classic, catchy and energetic and well-produced. The game sells for $5, but I’d be willing to pay $20 for the soundtrack alone. It’s that good. Even after hearing these tunes for 5 years, most of them still haven’t gotten old to me. But chances are you’ve already heard the music and know this for yourself.
To get another thing out of the way, I think the visuals are awesome. The minimalistic art throws back to a time older than the NES, and the ever-changing neon colors are strange and mysterious in their simplicity, and demand to be explored. In a way, the game itself is a fitting music video to one of the greatest chiptune albums there is.
So, what do I dislike about this game? Well, where do I start…?
The game is built around a novel idea – flipping the gravity of your character instead of jumping – and then spends an hour or two trying to pretend this mechanic has no crippling limitations before just giving up.  And I’m not exaggerating here: the entire game can be consistently beaten in about 30 minutes. The first time I played it, it took me about 50. Finding all the hidden trinkets can take about an hour more, depending on how many tries it takes you on the “Prize for the Reckless” and “Veni, Vidi, Vici” challenges.
Most games which are built around a central gimmick will try to expand it with additional game mechanics.
comes up with about four new mechanics to complement its gravity-flipping gimmick: conveyer belts, automatic-flip lasers, auto-scrolling rooms, and rooms that wrap around the edges. It then uses each of these mechanics in a tiny dungeon area and almost nowhere else. Two of the game’s areas use a somewhat irritating mechanic where you have to lead a friend around, with the level design poking fun at the fact that your friend has no common sense and you have to do everything for them. As far as new ideas are concerned, that’s pretty much it.
The central hub area, which comprises the majority of the map, is mostly just empty space: no enemies, no platforming puzzles, nothing but a few spikes here and there and a few of the collectable trinkets hidden away in corners. Even the interesting mazes are scarce. The hopelessly catchy track “Passion for Exploring” plays in the central hub, but in this case, “exploration” means just repeatedly falling through dozens of empty screens and searching for the next dungeon entrance. The overworld is also littered with dozens of checkpoints and teleporters which you will never use because there’s just nothing out there. They could have removed it entirely, replacing the hub with a series of teleporters to the dungeons, and the game hardly would have lost anything.
The game is touted as a “super hard” and “tough as nails” platformer. If that’s the case, it’s the easiest “super hard” platformer I’ve ever played.
parts are hard, but there’s no steady sense of progression; the difficulty is mostly just limited to a few problem rooms which may take hundreds of deaths each, but otherwise the whole game is smooth sailing. If you want real difficulty, you can try no-death mode or the time trials, but it just amounts to repeatedly playing the same ridiculously short game until you get it perfect. In this case, the difficulty is mostly just self-imposed rather than the work of a level designer. Personally, I’ve spent the most amount of time on the Super Gravitron, a fearsomely difficult mini-game that was probably the spiritual precursor to
.
The game’s story might as well not be there. I can summarize the story as follows: “You are some kind of captain of some kind of crew piloting some kind of ship, which crash-lands on some kind of planet due to some kind of disturbance. In order to escape, you need to deactivate some kind of device located in some kind of alternate dimension.” I’m not exaggerating. Nothing is explained. This story could have been mysterious and compelling, but instead it chooses to go the “self-referential humor” route by having the characters poke fun at checkpoints and the level design, while they’re not busy talking about nothing.
And for those who say “Why would you play this game for the story?” I propose that you consider this: the game’s story could have been
if you removed all of the dialogue. The story is told perfectly through the visuals. The explosions, lost crew members, and alternate dimensions are all self-explanatory, and it would have left all the details up to the imagination. Captain Viridian would have made a great silent protagonist that you could have projected your own motivation into. Instead, the characters are all given completely needless speaking lines which don’t convey anything, and I’m just left wondering why anyone bothered to write dialogue.
Aside from the superb music and the visuals,
feels like a game that was hastily thrown together. The difficulty is schizophrenic, rather than a fine-tuned progression curve. The overworld map is mostly empty space, as though the level designer had tried filling it with enemies and mazes but finally said “screw it, nothing works” and deleted everything. The story had no effort behind it. Interesting game mechanics are few and far between, and are only used for a few rooms each. The bonus game modes are needless masochism that are far too great of a difficulty jump from the main game. Overall, it feels more like an hour-long proof of concept than a full-fledged game exploring the possibilities and implications of its main gravity-flipping gimmick.
Yes, it was influential. Yes, it rode the very first wave of indie games back when Steam was gaining steam. Yes, the music is crazy good. All things considered, I
this game. But after five years of playing and reflecting on it, I can’t help but see it as a short, pointless waste of time with no interesting gameplay statements to make (even for its time) and no heart put into it. It’s style-over-substance. But hey, it’s got a great style, so I can’t quite fault it for that. I know a lot of people love this game. I loved it for a while, but now that I've noticed its flaws I can't shake the sour taste this game leaves me with.
I know that few will agree with my sentiment, but hopefully I’ve explained my thoughts adequately.

quick preliminary review:
- This is a Great game!!

I really need to start making consistent reviews because it's games like this that go 'under the radar' while total trash garbage takes over the gaming world today..
Why is this game so good?
Because it still has some semblance of an actual 'real living breathing open world' to it,  with free-form combat and somewhat non-rail gameplay..  All in a graphics format that allows you to look around and see the sky etc.
(Please note this is a very early review but that's the sense I got from it so far (I could be wrong about the 'non-rail gameplay' ))
Again VR is around the corner yet still most games have a top-down view or 'stylized' graphics setup that just feels warped..  this actually has a realistic, vibrant graphics feel realistic enough to feel 'alive' yet not so heavily textured you feel like you're staring at people's pores..

Games seem to have lost that 'fine-line' between reality and fantasy but this is one of those games that has it.
This feels like one of those games you would play all day on a Saturday/Sunday growing up and enjoying every minute of it, exploring a fantasy world that felt compelling and non-stressful, not like todays games that are either a chore, grind, or stuffed with over-the-top vulgarity, political agendas, scantily clad girls, robots and freaks  etc etc
By the way, why only 2 hours?
Because this is one of those games I want to play while actually devoting my time and effort into it, nowadays it's hard to do that so have it on the side waiting for me when I want to experience it fully...
So - ..  no, it's not perfect, but if the above means something to you try it out, games like this are getting harder and harder to find..

7 Wonders of the Ancient World is an old looking match 3 game. Basically you need to destroy the blocks behind each block by matching 3 or more of the similar block (gem, or whatever you even call it in this game). Each level I played was timed and as long as you beat it before the time ends, you can move on to the next level. The game gets more and more challenging as you play, but it never gets too challenging (I never lost a timed level so far).
The game is very similar to other match 3 games, but the way they do their 4 match and 5 match is different than most other match 3 games. A 4 match gives you a row destruction block which the moment you swap it with anything comes into effect. A 5 matches gives you the same thing except it also destroys the column. Additionally, every now and then you get this random block destroying thingy, which somehow always destroys blocks I want it to destroy. These things actually made the game pretty easy.
Overall, not a bad game, but a bit dated and repetitive. I would recommend this game to play if you are bored and need something to pass time.

Numen is a game that I respect greatly. It may not be the greatest game in its field, but it truly shines in its ambition to try something unique.
The idea of creating a competition based system between other characters who favor specific gods, and trying to reach an ultimate goal is what grabbed me in the beginning. What stops it from being the best it can be is the inability to weave this narrative into the story in a solid. There will be points of conversation you will have between other characters during your travels, but they do not mean much, and do not carry weight, as the overall mechanic of favor does not influence your character meaningfully.
I think making this a single player adventure is a strange choice, too. It screams for multiplayer functionality, or long-term co-op adventures, but may not have been able to be done by the developer.
On that note, the developer has been amazing in communication and support for their game (at the time of release). Implementing additional challenges and puzzles for players to solve within the world (treasure hunting), gave more of a connection of the world, inspired by the islands of the Aegean Sea.
I wish the story was better. You are able to follow a young child through their life, from humble beginnings to completing an epic quest, but there is something that gets in the way of my investment. Maybe it is the confusing connection between your character's level and their respective age, or maybe it is connection the game has to wanting to be an MMO, because it certainly wants to be one of them.
I only recommend this to those who wish to learn from other's experiences, and how games are made, and who ask critical questions about development. This game is a great example of the potential games can have to be fantastic experiences, but fall short for one reason or another. It is certainly a mixed game, and demands patience from its players (especially when the game crashes and corrupts your save file).

is a third-person hack & slash RPG. Having demonstrated enormous courage as a child, you are selected by a Greek God to be its hero and must compete against those of other Gods in order to find the Sickle of Kronos first.
: You get to pick from a boy or a girl, although can't actually customize your appearance. When beginning the game, you are given the option of using different weapons, and your class is determined by the type you used the most. Your mastery of any weapon comes from using it. Each of the three classes allows you to pick from three different Gods to be the champion of, so the game offers a total of nine sets of spells and powers. There is a large variety of equipment you can find (common, enchanted, rare and unique) and may equip up to 16 at a given time. Some of the items you find are only good for one gender, but can be refitted to your character. Rather than being class-specific, items are attribute-specific, meaning a mage that works strongly enough on its Strength will be able to use that badass sword usually meant for Warriors. Graphics are ok, most textures are pretty good, and each piece of equipment have a different look on your character.
: The writing is bad: sure, I spotted several typos and even apparent missing words, but the bland story itself is badly written with many mistakes about Greek mythology (example: Neptune is NOT a Greek God), you never actually feel like you're playing in Greece. The game lags and drops in frame rate when looking too far away. Combat is uninteresting, you click on the opponent once and look at the character fight, this game should've been an isometric hack & slash, but that would probably make the tiny size of the maps too obvious, or the comparison to
(a much better Greek mythology RPG) too easy. There is little to no development, interactions with other champions are very limited and fighting them in arena battles is lackluster. The game is short, very few main or side quests, no branching paths, save a few short class-specific quests in the early game. The game itself would be over quickly if you didn't spend that much time grinding for levels, the first few hours of which is so tedious that I almost stopped playing (although the grinding got less annoying a few hours in).

is a 2D game where you have to collect cargo to upgrade your character, to level up by new cargo types and to prove your cargo company that you are the best of the best - a real cargo commander.
TL;DR. ^^ You are a male protagonist working for a cargo company. You have to deliver cargo, which you collect in the levels called sectors, for your company. You are able to upgrade your character with a better suite, a better drill and so on. To upgrade your stuff you need to collect caps. Caps are hidden in cargo or dropped by enemies. There are three enemy types: small, intermediate, big. You can find better weapons in the sectors at certain points to kill the bigger enemies much faster. You start with a nail gun and you can carry two weapons. Every weapon can be upgraded with things like an autofire option or faster reloading. At the start of the game you have three terminals (nagivator, console, magnet) at your spaceship which looks like a cargo crate. With the navigation console you can travel to other sectors. You can travel to popular sectors, unpopular sectors, random sectors or sectors which you are naming. Every progress of every player will be traced and save for the leaderboards.
You can find in each sector a new sector pass to unlock new sectors and each sector has it's own type of cargo. Every new type of cargo found will level your rank at you company. At each new rank your company will deliver you a permanent bonus like a cup of coffee (faster run), a terminal to repair your ship, ammunition supply, a better drill, etc. If you die and you have collected the sector pass it won't be lost, but all your upgrades will be lost. Yes - death, travel to another sector or going to sleep will reset your upgrades - they are all temporary except the upgrades from your company. Story ... is available but only as text by reading e-Mails at the console. You have a wife and a kid who will send you parcels or drawings from time to time. The e-Mails from the company have some kind of humor, so it's not only text to skip - it makes you smiling, if you died the tenth time and reading an e-Mail from your company, that they are proud of their new all-time-dying-employee. ^^
Something missed? Ah yes; it's created like a tower-defense. You start your spaceship magnet to pull up a new wave of cargo. The cargo containers will crash into your spaceship and then you are able to enter these containers. The ship's side and all the platforms can be bored with your drill (except one type of platform) to make your way through, because your way will be blocked by walls. Every container has it's own gravity field, in some of them you can toggle the gravity via a terminal. You can exit always into the space to move directly back to your ship or to other containers. You will move faster in space by using the recoil of your weapon. You have to hurry within each wave, because after all containers have been arrived you have only a short period of time left until a warp hole is opening and one after another container will be released/destroyed.

An action-platformer game with rogue-like elements. Nothing too special but it does become addictive after learning the simple mechanics.
Your job is to gather crates from different mini levels that come in waves and return them to your home space cubicle before a wormhole sucks everything up and finishes the wave. Each new procedurally generated sector (which is based on the names given to them) has 6 new items to hunt for based on rarity and you level up your character by gathering the materials from each sector. This is your main character level that stays persistent throughout your gameplay.
On the other hand, you can upgrade your weapons, life and other criteria as perks for the sector you're in. You die or leave the sector and your upgrades are nullified and reset to zero.
You can also unlock Journey Mode which removes the time limit of the normal mode but also your home cubicle is destroyed and you're forced to travel through continuous waves of containers.
I don't think the game handles the rogue elements very nicely as the sense of progression is usually gone as soon as you find the 6 items in each sector. The only reason to keep playing that sector is high scores which I don't really care about.
Cargo Commander has a very nice atmosphere to it that truly immerses you in the vast loneliness of space and the horrors of running out of oxygen while drifting between containers. Your enemies are the mutated space zombies of other cargo commanders who have lost their lives (killing them gives you "Caps", the currency used to upgrade your character's arsenal) and while your home base has a cheerful vibe to it, everything becomes dark and forboding as soon as you leave it behind.
There are only 2 music tracks for the game that despite being pretty cool, become grating and repetitive after a couple of hours in. Thankfully you can play your own music (.WAV and .OGG only) by copying them into the game's playlist folder.
The precedural levels do start to look and feel the same with only shuffled platforms and enemy placements. Also, as long as you're in a sector, the levels will remain the same until you generate another sector.
Technically, the game can be a mess. It's frozen on me more than a couple of times and there's a lot of stuttering to be found in some areas. Nothing too dramatic but also very off-putting when you're surrounded by enemies and can't aim right because the framerate is all over the place. UI design for in-game menus are pretty poor.
Cargo Commander is a cool game marred by technical problems, very shallow overall game mechanics and a sense of utilizing but a fraction of the great innovations it has (drifting like crazy between space containers as a wormhole is sucking up everything while your oxygen is rapidly running out is a pretty exciting experience).
But I'll still give it a thumbs up because it was really fun while it lasted. It just didn't give me a strong enough reason to push on and continue playing after the first hours.

The definition of a Rogue-Lite states that it needs to have two key features; perma-death, randomized levels and a turn-based combat system. Therefore, Cargo Commander is actually a dungeon crawler. As such, it could be compared to a variety of titles which don't have randomisation since in reality the random nature of Cargo Commander is actually based upon the seed of the galaxy you are visiting. As such, each galaxy can be played multiple times with exactly the same containers appearing.
As a game, CC is certainly fun. But only as much as it has that - one more try - aspect absolutely nailed. If you are looking for a challenge it is fair to say you will find that here to some degree and the endless array of potential zones means that you can always find something new. But it would probably be something I'd only suggest you pick up on discount because the novelty of the multi-directional gravity does wear off and there is a clear ceiling for skill which impacts your enjoyment when you reach it. The difficulty curve however is fierce, which can work for or against the chance you will enjoy the game. Depending upon the person.
If you have some disposable income and want to try a dunegon crawler which offers something different to the fantasy theme. I would certainly recommend Cargo Commander. Just be aware that it is best enjoyed in short bursts.

I think the way “death” is handled in the game is perfect.  It is not the kind of game where one mistake and death means the past two hours of gameplay meant nothing.  You still keep all the
you collected— and since the whole meta-game revolves around collecting

you must reach at least a certain point without dying so you can retrieve the “

The gameplay is also quite simple and unvaried; the first hour of gameplay will be basically the same as the tenth.  But it is also this simplicity that makes the game enjoyable and addictive.
Put simply,

Let me preface by saying the last great city builder game I played was Sim City 4. That game was released over a decade ago and not a single city builder game released since then has been able to capture the same level of addictivness, replayability, and enjoyment as SC4. Untill now. I expected to like Banished but I didn't expect to truly enjoy it as much as I have. It is surprisingly well balanced in its gameplay once you get past the learning curve. Between building up a village, micromanaging trade, gathering resources, controlling population, and dealing with disasters it can take a bit of stratagy to not somehow kill off your town.
This is a great game in my opinion, and coming from such a small developer it is a pleasant surprise to see so much thought and detail go into the gameplay. That being said, there are a few things that I would like to see added in the future. More buildings, different styles, maybe even more technology and building choices as time goes by and prerequisits are met. Making population control a bit easier to understand would be a nice addition. I can say with full confidence that this is the best city builder out there right now, but it is not quite as extensive as others.
tl;dr
This is worth your time and money. Get it!

Luxuria Superbia is a game in which you must tease, tickle, and stimulate the sensuous concavities of several flowers, engorging them with color and causing them to experience untold delights as you make them burst forth with fertility. It is a thin, laughing veneer of gardening on top of a Beginner's Female ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Instructional Video, and it is gorgeous and rich and every 13 year old should be given a copy as part of a solemn adulthood how-not-to-suck-at-this ritual.
As you pleasure the petals, they will go from pale white to rich with color - the more brightly colored they are, the more pleasure the flower derives, the more fertile it becomes when it experiences its final climactic rush, and the faster your score piles up. Delivering too much pleasure too quickly, however, causes the flower to burst early, resulting in a failure; ideally, you'll attend to every spot equally, tapping lightly and driving the flower to greater and greater heights of ecstasy before the eventual plunder. Along the way, the flower will goad you on, dropping euphemisms ranging from the charming and playful to the uncomfortably surreal. While each flower plays roughly the same, they each come with their own surreal visuals, their own beat-heavy background music, and their own sensual banter, all of which combines to give each of them a memorable personality and an image uniquely their own.
In the end, the game ends up feeling a little short and a little meaningless, but it's an exhilarating and unique rush along the way. Top marks to Tale of Tales for attempting something as unorthodox and unconventional as this; even if the game's appeal vanishes the minute you finish, it's certainly something you can look back on fondly. If you like boundary-pushing weirdness, definitely give it a go.
For the records, the touch controls of the tablet version are far, far superior to the gamepad controls of the computer version, but you should get a pretty solid experience regardless.

I've played this game for hundreds of hours, alternatively loving and hating it, and I must say that you'd be better off not giving it a try. I'll lay out the pros and cons of it and why I can't recommend it.
Pros:
-Nice graphics. Some map look better than others, but overall it looks good, especially for a free to play game.
-It is decently optimized. I can get over 100 fps on max settings on my laptop, and it doesn't take that good of a computer to play.
-The coop is decently fun, with several different missions to play. It can be hard to find a game, however.
-When things are working properly and playing with good players, the game can be genuinely fun.
Cons:
-The company behind it is greedy. In the game's shop, there are random boxes that might give you special guns that you have to pay real money for. They expect you to pay real money for a CHANCE to get a virtual gun.
-The game has HORRIBLE lag issues. In any given game, half or more of the player will have a game ruiningly large ping. This leads to bad hit recognition, teleporting players, and other problems. There are many videos showing this.
-The sniper rifles are infuriatingly overpowered, with half of them killing you in ONE shot unless you have a vest that takes a long time to unlock. This leads to games that are overpopulated with snipers, destroying the balance.
-Hackers are frequent. The game's anticheat system isn't nearly as advanced as it needs to be, so you'll see obvious hackers pretty often.
-Teams are frequently improperly balanced with one team having several more players than the other. Very annoying.
-The rewards system needs to be reworked, because the cost to repair weapons and equipment is frequently MORE than the amount given when a game ends. You lose in game money by playing the game.
-There's a good chane you'll be kicked for cheating even if you don't cheat.
Overall, I have to say that the issues with the game outweigh the promision aspects of it and that there are simply many better shooters out there. I really expect a better product from the people who developed Crysis.

Fair warning, this review might get weird. But that's sort of hard to do when you're talking about a game that is a giant metaphor for sex. Luxuria Superbia is a game about making love, thinly disguised behind the notion of making flowers "bloom", placing you in the "role" of a hypothetical♥♥♥♥♥♥♥flying through an infinite ♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's both incredibly strange yet oddly alluring, like something you know you shouldn't enjoy but can't quite pull yourself away from it. All the same, it fails entirely at being anything more than a very unusual art project; hyper sexualized (though not at all pornographic) and occasionally even beautiful, but shallow and tedious as an actual game.
Though I'm hesitant to say you actually "play" Luxuria, interaction comes in the form of you flowing through colorful tunnels, with burst to life as you touch petals that come along the path, with the goal being to keep as much color showing without entirely filling up every side and "finishing" the flower too soon (which results in a disappointed message on screen asking you "what went wrong"). The longer you can stay in a flower the more points you get (which are gained faster when more color is on screen), and the happier the "flower" will be at the end. That's really all there is to the "game", which straddles the line between interactive entertainment, and something you'd find on a perverted corner of the internet. Every moment is tinged with a highly suggestive undertone, though I wouldn't call it subtle, for as soon as you begin to get deeper into a flower much of any pretense is abandoned as the developer makes sure you know exactly what they are symbolizing.
Playing Luxuria Superbia made me feel dirty, like I was a kid stumbling upon his father's secret magazines and proceeding to throw away my innocence. It's awkward and maybe a little uncomfortable to sit through, but at the very least I can't knock it for being anything but unique and artistic. Once you get past the erotic outer layers though, you are still left with an incredibly boring and ultimately pointless experience that grows tiresome before you bring your first flower to completion. I couldn't say quite how I feel about the analogies the game presents, but my opinion of the portion that makes it a game at all is very clear, that being one which I couldn't wait to abandon and really have no explanation for why I started in the first place.
Let's just say Luxuria Superia is weird, and you would probably be best to leave it by the wayside in favor of more traditional forms of pleasure.

For the most part, you can get through most levels on your first try as long as you keep your eyes open for good opportunities. But Wonder 7 is where the game gets CHEAP. I've been trying really hard to like this game from the moment that I started playing. With each passing encounter, with each newly introduced event, with each new NPC speaking and each logic flaw in either narrative or combat; my task grew to become harder and harder. Finally, I give up. This is the day that I'll leave an RPG unfinished.
As the curtain opens, we watch a cinematic about a legendary artifact; the Sickle of Chronos being stolen. Then, we choose between two 12 year old siblings - one male and one female - to take as our character, and begin playing a pesteringly long, somewhat illogical and predictable prequel story. By the end of the prequel, our "hero" is given the "choice" of becoming the champion of one of the 9 Olympian Gods to compete in a contest. If she/he prevails, her/his one wish will be granted by the gods. To accomplish this deed, our hero is sent to the Island of Machantar to the main temple of his/her deity. After that point, our hero will venture out on an unending journey of hack & slash to acquire that accursed sickle.
is a single player 3D RPG in a run on the mill MMO model - which is based on fetch quests or killing a certain amount of monsters to get a certain drop - with the skill bar, mobs to kill and levels to gain. You slay monsters, gain level and loot, travel to new areas with tougher monsters and so on and on... which would be quite alright if it wouldn't be for a couple of downers. To begin with, the storyline is botched, with you always ending up aimlessly wandering around to try and discover "what to do next". Quest indicators fail to present pointers or direct towards locations. Any and all areas of the game are open, so it wouldn't differ whether you are level 20 or 80, you can always find a mob to get yourself killed by accidentally.
There is a monstrous imbalance between classes; warrior being overpowering, mage being somewhat decent and archer being completely pointless. Skill and item usage are completely laggy; you end up pushing a hot key 2-3 times before the game decides to cast that spell and by then - guess what? - You are usually dead. There is no actual lore to gods or no differentiating factor between gods, so your choice of whomever you decided to follow there is somewhat irrelevant. The game fails to deliver any kind of authentic lore: there are Greek names and figures thrown around, bravo. As if that would be enough for a setting. Aside the main scenario - and a vague one at that - side quests are not many, and they end up popping around in completely imbalanced levels. Dialogue is forced, unimaginative and usually contains a couple of typos anyhow. Arena battles or tournaments rely on luck and how laggy your casting would be instead of actual skill and reflexes. Oh, and as far as atmosphere goes: graphics and textures are okay - with no facial or physical customization option for your character, and the soundtrack decides to take long pauses of silence as you play for no apparent reason.
Phew, sorry. I hate being thoroughly this negative, but
would be a somewhat acceptable MMORPG. As a single player RPG, it fails to deliver either interest in story, any character or scenario involvement, decent game or combat mechanics or basically any good time. I remember having better time with
. That was multiplayer at least. When I bought this game, it was on sale for 99 cents so it's not a big loss, but if you are interested in an Action RPG in a Greek Setting,
is most definitely a better choice. Good day.
