Cargo Commander is a very interesting game, to me. It has some more serious aspects in its setting and story, but it covers it all up with tongue-in-cheek humour. It also has a very slow and game-y progression system, seemingly in place to justify the 10€ price tag.
If you look at the top reviews (both positive and negative), you'll see that the negative ones have considerably more playtime than the positives. There's a reason for that. The game gets very monotonous, completely desynchronized with its progressions pacing. It's one of those games that uses procedural generation and rare items to collect to extend its playtime in a ridiculous way. Reprisal Universe is a game that did something similar: the content is so sparse that the game loses a lot as a result.
Anyway, this review will not be of much use to most people. If you want to know if the game is mechanically good, or whatever, you can check all the other reviews. I mostly agree.
I liked the game, the execution is well done! Aside from the progression, anyway. The game has some little tricks that you have to learn, and it's a nice thing to pass time with. For a while.
What is this review about, then? It's about how the game explores the darker themes.
In this game, you're stranded in space. You accepted a job of collecting cargo from containers lost deep in space. You're away from you family, with them not knowing what your job actually is. To top that, you're also victim of a big corporation, who has little to no regard of its employees, and uses a gamification system to keep them working, ranking up and give the illusion of progress. All that while doing the very menial work of collecting cargo.
There's a lot to think, with this premise. The game takes a humorous approach to it, though, which, in my opinion, leaves a big part of the game unexplored. It's a very mechanically oriented game: you're constantly trying to achieve something
, which doesn't leave much space for thought.
How does the game explore its themes, though? Well, there are mainly 2 aspects that I noticed. First, is how you encounter other cargo commanders -- players -- dead in some containers. You loot them for ammo, caps (upgrade currency), and the like.
The enemies also seem like mutated players. Confirming that you're not the only one out in deep space, and also that the company simply abandons its employees after death.
The other aspect is the mailing system. Every so often, you'll receive emails. Some are tutorials for a newly introduced system, some are from your family, and others are from the company, congratulating you on ranking up. Apparently, you'll also receive an e-mail from a lost employee asking for help -- but this one is very deep into the game, and I didn't get to that. Which goes to show how sparse the content is...
The most interesting aspect of these e-mails are SPOILERS
It can be a really dark game, at times. And that's awesome!
While I do really like these aspects of the game, I don't think it takes a big advantage of them. For once, as I've mentioned several times already, the content is veeery sparse. Most players will probably not even get to that point, for the simple reason that the game doesn't really evolve much. It's interesting and new during the first couple of hours (perhaps a bit longer), but then it gets really stale. And getting an email every couple of hours really isn't enough to keep the interest high -- especially since the actual game, while random, gets a bit too formulaic.
Then, there's the fact that these aspects are very disconnected from the action. It's a side thing, and players will treat as that. It's too game-y for it not to be like that, I guess.
Also, the fact that death is meaningless, kind of defeats the whole point, although this is a very feeble subject, for the time. I've seen a game called The Flock a few days ago -- apparently, it's a multiplayer game with actual perma-death. If you die, you can't play anymore. If everyone dies, the game closes.
It seems like a bigger game, so I people were very skeptical of paying for it. I'm assuming the skepticism would translate to small indie games as well. It's also a horror game, so that choice ends up influencing the game in a different manner... ANYWAY, I'm rambling.
I'd like to see actual permadeath in some games. That would certainly make the player far more conscious of his choices, and hopefully enhance the experience, overall.
In this game, it doesn't happen, although it would have been a cool approach. Then again, not at all marketeable, so I understand why the game is like this.
Yeah, this was not a review at all. It was me rambling about some aspects that aren't even about the main game. On the positive side, I think I highlighted something that other reviews mostly fail to mention, so yeah.
P.S.: I was experimenting with this idea of perma-death and multiplayer used as a "history"/mark, instead of competitive/cooperational play -- you know, finding dead players, sharing tips -- or traps -- like in Dark Souls...
If you're reading this,
. Permadeath is risky, but I'd say it's worth it, if the game is explained accordingly -- and priced, I guess.

I'll update this review after I play more, but this game is really well done. It's an action RPG, but it's not. It's fast. You move with WASD. You can jump (and double jump off walls). The abilities are aimed by the mouse (which is never used for movement). All of the levels have challenges to do (like completing them without taking damage). When you get to level 12 you start to unlock hexes that make the game harder but give benefits like increased XP. You customize your character through various types of items (weapons, spells, and "cards" - all of which can be swapped out whenever you want - so if you're looking to grind a "build" that's not what this game is). You'll find yourself swapping around weapon types a lot and trying out a lot of things, or if you're like me always using whatever item gives you the best item/gold find bonuses.
I've been playing 3 or 4 hours now, and intend to continue. How many of the abilities and customization options have I already seen? I honestly don't know. Will this game be worth playing for weeks or months to come? I don't know. I have no idea if the multiplayer works well because I haven't tried it yet. What I do know is that with the 40% off sale this is an $11 very well spent.
The negatives? Mostly that it's not complete yet. What I've seen so far is really good, but there are various things currently missing (like difficulties above "normal"). I believe the missing things are supposed to be added soon, but even without them there's plenty of fun to be had.

A thinker's dream.
Banished is built around the concept of XXXS. Explore, Expand, Exploit, SURVIVE. There are no enemy towns, no armies, no diplomacy and no barbarians. Only the cold army of winter.
This game pushes you to redfine your previously held notions of how to play and win strategy/sim games.
The mechanics of defining labor are different from your usual cast of characters: Civ, Starcraft, AOE, etc. Instead of focusing on the individual laborer, you focus on his place within the greater economy. As such, it forces you to think more broadly and differently than the games I just mentioned. For instance, in the winter, you need firewood. You can't just click on a peon then right click on a tree. You must first build a woodcutter then assign a citizen to that woodcuttery. This along with other unique gameplay mechanics make this game incredibly interesting and challenging to learn.
The graphics are not the "best". But there's a real aesthetic the developer went for and knocked out of the park. It reminds you of what Jamestown might've looked like. The soundtrack can be repetative and it would probably be the only thing I would change about this game as it stands.
Overall, if you like city building and strategy games, buy this game. If you like your gaming status quo to be upset, buy this game. If you're expecting another run of the mill RTS game, don't buy this game.

The 39 Steps
The 39 Steps is a beautiful visual novel, with very subtle game play elements. It is based off a paper back novel so needless to say it has a great story. I started playing The 39 steps for something to relax with. A bedtime story that I would read my self. By the second chapter I realized I would not be going to bed until I finished this story.
Talk about amazing screen shots, the 39 Steps provides them. Page after page of jaw dropping visual stills, newspaper clipping and old timely photos will keep your eyes entertained. The presentation of the story its self intrigues me, you have the option to be as involved or not in the actual interpretation of the story as you want. Some parts are voice acted others fade onto the screen in the form of text and lastly you can dig around for newspaper clipping and note pads that contain even more information. It is up to you if you read any of it, listen to the story, or just aimlessly click through.
That being said there is some game play mechanics, like moving your mouse in circles to open doors, or up and down to search a box. Most your thoughts will go into reading and listening. It is not a CSGO  trainer that is for sure.
I have not previously read this story, as I mentioned above I intended to put my self to sleep with The 39 Steps. Well here we are 2hours and some coffee breaks later, writing a review because it was that great. I  shame my self for not having read it before, and deep down makes me ask, what is it about video games that keep me entertained for hours while the thought of reading a short 300 page novel makes me dread life? As another user mentioned in there review, there should be more books converted into “games” like this.
I know this one is not for everyone, but for those of you who like to read, like history or epic screen shots I recommend this one for you.
P.S I got this in haste thinking it was The Running Man by Richard Bachman a.k.a Stephen King. It seems I mixed the characters name and the authors to read Richard Bachman.  The 39 Steps is just as good. I am still happy with the purchase. FYI this is not the Running Man.

Where to start.
This is a puzzle game, with the added story mechanic of finishing levels in order to 'build' the seven wonders of the ancient world. Thus the title.
How this is achieved is by playing your typical gem-switching puzzle (Not sure what I mean? Replace 'Gem' with 'Candy' - that help at all?) - when you switch gems into appropriate groups of three or more, they disintegrate, and the gems above it fall into place. The 'background' of each gem is smashed, and the pieces fall to the bottom of the screen as bricks, which are picked up by tiny minions, who cart them off - supposedly to create the various parts of each Wonder. The premise of each level is to smash all of the bricks, by disintegrating gems on every square on the grid.
Et cetera et cetera. There are other mechanics, but none which really make this anything other than a puzzle game similar to many many other puzzle games. It's definitely good fun for a time, but not £5-worth of fun.
As usual - if you can grab it in a sale or a bundle, definitely go for it. You'll be entertained for a while, but when better alternatives spring up regularly on mobiles and tablets for 99p - it kind of makes this seem stuck in the stone age.
As always - a video accompanies my review.

7 Wonders of the Ancient World is a casual tile matching game where in you "build" the 7 wonders of the world by matching lines of 3 or more of the same shape. Doing so breaks the tiles behind them. Break all the tiles on the board to proceed to the next board. There are 7 levels in the game, each consisting of several sub levels. In total, the main game took me about 3 hours to play through.
: The story in this game is pretty flimsy, but in a nutshell, you supervise the building of the 7 wonders of the ancient world. You do this by creating blocks (done by breaking tiles on the board) and moving cornerstones down the board (done by matching shapes) for the workers to collect.
: The graphics are pretty standard fare for a casual matching game. They're simple and, with the exception of the workers, fairly static.
: By far, the best part of this game, in my humble opinion, is the music. It's rather catchy, and despite it playing in a constant loop, it didn't get tiring or turn me homicidal (always a good thing).
: I was able to get through all 7 wonders in about 3 hours, managing to get the second highest title reward in the game. For £5, this is a bit short for my liking.
: Carrying on from above, 3 hours isn't really a good length for the cost of the game. The game does allow you to go back to previously completed levels to try to get a better score, so it is slightly replayable.

Hearts of Iron 3 is without a doubt, the most in-depth WAR game ever made. If you've never played a paradox before, you'll be in for a major surprise. It took me roughly a month of every day play to "master" all of the basics. The tutorials are woefully inadequate and a complete waste of time, but the strategy guide is a gem and the paradox forum is an excellent resource. To ease your learning, parts of the game can be automated. Anything you have to do can be assigned to a highly sophisticated AI; it is possible to delegate every task to the AI, or just the ones you aren't yet familiar with so you can take things one step at a time.
The breadth and scope of HOI3 is enormous. You can pick any country in the world from Germany to Tannu Tava (I never heard of it before, either) and the developers have done an excellent job modelling historical limitations, while not restricting flexibility. HOI3 is essentially a war game, unlike other paradox games. Its focus is just that, with only the minimum necessary attention to the homefront. Battle, however, is beautiful. There are so many different brigade considerations, such as toughness (how many casualties does it take?), soft attack (infantry attack), hard attack (tank battles basically), defensiveness, organization (how much damage a brigade can take before retreating), strength (how much damage can it inflict), etc. You have the ability to craft each brigade and assign its leaders, all the way through the chain. A well-organized army enjoys significant benefits over one without proper leadership. The bread-and-butter of any army are infantry, and I highly advise tacking on an artillery brigade to each infantry division. Each unit draws supplies, and fuel in the case of mechanical ones, from your base. The supply system has serious flaws, however, but recent patches and independent fixes remedy this issue. In addition, Paradox has added an arcade version that ignores supply routes. What fun is that, though? All it takes to turn the tide of war is to bomb your enemy's choke points, and bam! -50% battle penalty and no reinforcement to the front lines. Indeed, supply lines/routes will make or break you, especially when playing as a sea-faring nation, such as Japan.
Battle itself is effected by the values I mentioned before, plus many others. What's the weather in the province? A wise man doesn't invade India in the middle of a monsoon. Combat width determines the space of your battle, and frontage determines how much space each unit takes. The more space it occupies, the more it attacks in a round but the less each attack does. A unit with small frontage and high combat is ideal, though armored units operate oppositely. Tanks rely on a high frontage to rush enemy lines. There are "events" in battle, like "Ambush!" or "Breakthrough!" that give benefits to one of the belligerents. You can increase your chance of getting a beneficial event through researching doctrines, which are highly useful because they improve your army without using your IC (Industrial Capacity, each country's industrial output). Battle lasts until one side runs out of organization or strength, though the former comes first 95% of the time. Air/naval battles are represented well. Planes play a huge role, despite costing an arm-and-a-leg to produce. Smaller countries often can't afford to field a division of tactical bombers, but for bigger ones when you already have enough infantry, it will determine the course of many battles. Navies are optional for land-based countries, such as the Soviet Union, but absolutely critical to survival for the UK or Japan, the latter of which is forced to fight a multi-front war with a small manpower pool, few resources, and no nearby allies and a vulnerable homeland.
The world is divided into factions: Allies, Axis, Comintern, although one can be unallied. Each has its perks, but Axis are the easiest (and imo, most fun) to play. On top of that, each country poses unique challenges that model history. The Soviet Union has a gigantic manpower pool, but a disorganized army and a stalling industrial base. Germany enjoys significant boosts from '36 to '39 in its industrial output to prepare for the war ahead, yet becomes very strained in the east. The USA is the powerhouse of the game, yet can barely build a proper guard army until '42. Whatever country you pick, know your strengths and weaknesses. Building a major tank force with Argentina, for example, would be foolish. Tanks aren't well-suited to the jungles, and that money could go toward building a decent infantry base. Similarly, research only the techs you need. The basic infantry ones require only 4 research points, but planes require vastly more. Some countries just can't catch up to the giants like the US or Germany. That isn't a fault of the game, it's just history (although you can expand significantly; I have played a game with The Netherlands where I conquered over 10x my original area).
Whatever path you choose in HOI3, you're in for the most thought-provoking game you have ever played.

Cargo Commander was definitely fun, though not a masterpiece. CG was the second Rogue-like game I played, the first being Dungeon of the Endless.
Pros:
-Fun gameplay
-Acceptable and fitting graphics, albeit not awesome
-The types of cargo and their descriptions provide a bunch of laughs
-Since the sectors are procedurally generated, but the name is the seed, you can both play places others visited (including discovering and looting their corpses) as well as creating entirely new sectors
-While unfortunate impossible encounters are probably possible, they're extremely unlikely, so dying is at least your fault
-If played strategically it should be possible to discover every type of cargo (with help of the scanner for the last pieces) without needing a walkthrough (I only needed a hint for 1 cargo type, because I spent my scanners too early)
-Journey allows to infinitely travel a sector without pesky scroungers (those annoying flying space drills)
-Weekly Struggle gives one random sector each week which can be played only ONCE, so it's nice for competitiveness (though there don't seem to be many players left)
Cons:
-Short life span: The game can be finished with every achievement and trying out everything there is in less than 30 hours
-Low replay value. Since you can't spend the cargo you find on anything after you received parcels, the replay value drops drastically down to Journey and Weekly Struggle
-While at first it seemed rather polished I manged to find quite a few bugs in the end
-At times the gravitational orientations can create annoying circumstances, requiring unconventional paths to circumvent
-Supbar music (in my opinion at least, I'm sure others can like it more than I do)
Bugs:
-Game breaking after playing Journey: After I played a Journey round I couldn't play another, and the game didn't exit properly so I had to manually kill the process
-Red Cargo Commander: Sometimes when being hit your character turns red, but doesn't turn back normal anymore
-Bad clipping: Occasionally enemies and other stuff can glitch through walls
All in all I think playing this game was worth it. Maybe I'll come back for another Struggle or some Journeys, but due to the low replay value I guess that's mostly it for me.
If there ever would be a Cargo Commander 2 though, the potential for a masterpiece is definitely there.

Hearts of Iron III is the best yet in the series. The political options are far more immersive, allowing realistic options to be made. You can play ANY country in the world at different periods of time before or during World War II. You have freedom to do anything at anytime, to anybody. Heck, I played as the U.S and conquered Mexico and South America. The U.S now makes the Soviet Union look small in my save game :D The customization options for each and every individual division you train, is just legendary. I can conscript a division and choose between 4 or 5 different brigade types to put in it. Perhaps you want this division to participate in the frontlines most major offensives. So you put an infantry brigade, maybe an armored brigade, a paratrooper brigade, a self-propelled artillery brigade, and maybe an engineer brigade or motorized infantry brigade. It doesn't matter, because there are tens of other different brigades. And you also research new technology to choose what model weapon they are equipped with. It's just absolutely amazing. You can also use aggressive action by one country to justify aggressive action of your own. Let's say, I'm the Soviet Union. Germany declares war on Poland. I can now justify mobilizing my entire army (this will bring all reserve units to full strength, and brings your normal divisions to full combat alert) because Poland is next to me. Let's say by chance, the U.S invades Cuba for no reason. I now declare an embargo on the U.S. All of a sudden, Canada may declare an embargo on me (not likely unless the U.S are their allies) It's a very realistic economical, industrial, military, political strategy game that anybody like myself can grow to love.
P.S I also chose to be Brazil on a different save game, and I conquered and annexed all of South America, and I'm currently engaging in thermonuclear war with the U.S. Such fun :D at least 50 million people have died, and Germany and the Soviet Union are still going at it. (It's so fun!)
I usually choose the time period of 1936, because it allows me to bring what country I lead up to full war preparations. Otherwise if I start during the war as belgium, I most likely am going to be turned upside down and gang banged to death by hundreds of German soldiers, and I won't have anything to stop them. However if I start two years earlier, I can annex the Netherlands and maybe Denmark, and then have so much fortifications and troops ready, that the German invasion won't go anywhere, even though it's highly unlikely it would be possible without cheats. But at any rate, I highly recommend this to anyone. The first hour or so of figuring everything out, might be depressing because it seems like alot to learn, but the wait is worth it. Buy this, and I'll give you a cookie. :) But then I'll declare war on your country in this game, and specifically nuke your hometown for the heck of it, cuz.... why not? :D

I have pretty much exclusively played sniper classes in shooters where I can for the past few years and Verdun was no exception, so this review is going to be from the point of view of a sniper!

Basically: it's great. It's a challenging yet very rewarding game that is incredibly simple with a very minimalist approach to the interface, engine and general playability. It is a very modest game; it knows what it does and it does it well. It does not try to cover too many areas, and even considering the stripped-down approach it still manages to generate a wonderful WW1 atmosphere far better than Battlefield 1 ever will, in my own personal opinion.
The most striking factor about the game is simply how rewarding it is. There is no spotting system and no effort made to mark enemy troops with some form of label so, as with games like ARMA, you are forced to actually look for your enemy. Most of the weapons available are either heavy machine guns that must be mounted on a bipod while prone or bolt-action rifles, lending the sniper's old ethos of 'one shot, one kill' to the game. This base level of accuracy and skill required makes it challenging from the get-go, and seeing your foe crumple to the ground after you lined up a shot with nothing but your iron sights from 50m is as thrilling as watching the neighbour's cat undress through the window.
Sniping, too, is very rewarding and feels crucial to gameplay. In Battlefield 4, snipers often get a lot of flak for sitting somewhere uselessly in the middle of nowhere lending no tactical advantage besides netting perhaps two or three kills in an entire round of Rush. In Verdun, snipers are essential for clearing machine guns and heavily nested areas in preparation for an attack. Snipers also do a great job of thinning out the attacking force on more open maps like Artois, and the ability to switch easily between scope and iron sights (with the challenging drawback of having the scope still covering half your screen) makes the rifles with sniper scopes equally viable on CQB maps like Champagne.
Overall, the game is great. Just great. It's polished, it does what it sets out to do, and the community and developers do a great job.

The 39 Steps
The 39 Steps is a beautiful visual novel, with very subtle game play elements. It is based off a paper back novel so needless to say it has a great story. I started playing The 39 steps for something to relax with. A bedtime story that I would read my self. By the second chapter I realized I would not be going to bed until I finished this story.
Talk about amazing screen shots, the 39 Steps provides them. Page after page of jaw dropping visual stills, newspaper clipping and old timely photos will keep your eyes entertained. The presentation of the story its self intrigues me, you have the option to be as involved or not in the actual interpretation of the story as you want. Some parts are voice acted others fade onto the screen in the form of text and lastly you can dig around for newspaper clipping and note pads that contain even more information. It is up to you if you read any of it, listen to the story, or just aimlessly click through.
That being said there is some game play mechanics, like moving your mouse in circles to open doors, or up and down to search a box. Most your thoughts will go into reading and listening. It is not a CSGO  trainer that is for sure.
I have not previously read this story, as I mentioned above I intended to put my self to sleep with The 39 Steps. Well here we are 2hours and some coffee breaks later, writing a review because it was that great. I  shame my self for not having read it before, and deep down makes me ask, what is it about video games that keep me entertained for hours while the thought of reading a short 300 page novel makes me dread life? As another user mentioned in there review, there should be more books converted into “games” like this.
I know this one is not for everyone, but for those of you who like to read, like history or epic screen shots I recommend this one for you.
P.S I got this in haste thinking it was The Running Man by Richard Bachman a.k.a Stephen King. It seems I mixed the characters name and the authors to read Richard Bachman.  The 39 Steps is just as good. I am still happy with the purchase. FYI this is not the Running Man.

It's important because that's the day I played the best game ever in my opinion. The game is basically a Post-Apocalyptic, Post-Nuclear RPG FPS, which sounds amazing, and luckily, that is the case with Fallout 3.
Most times with games, the first game in the series is the best and any others are usually inferior. However, Not with Fallout 3. While Fallout and Fallout 2 are basically masterpieces, Fallout Tactics: Brotherhood of Steel was okay, Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel was awful, having mixed reactions with many critics. While Fallout 2 offered a more variety of things and Fallout: Tactics: Brotherhood of Steel was the first and only (On PC at least) Fallout to have multiplayer, Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel wasn't good and should of never existed. Go to the year 2004, where Bethesda owns the entire Fallout franchise. A teaser is shown in 2007 for the game known as  Fallout 3. 1 year later, Bethesda releases Fallout 3. The game is given high reviews, named best RPG, best PC game, best Xbox 360 game, and of course, THE BEST GAME OF THE YEAR.
Fallout 3 is amazing and I highly recommend it to anybody who likes the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series or any of the other Fallout games, you won't be disappointed. Sadly, this game is given a 85% on Steam because Bethesda won't fix it and people are too lazy to look up how to fix it. However, I would recommend getting "Fallout 3: Game of the Year Edition" because you get all of the DLC, and if you were to buy all the DLC seperate, it would cost more than the actual GOTY edition (GOTY: $19.99; All DLC combined: $24.95) Please, get this game.

I consider myself relatively new to city builders, so I guess I have an objective view of the genre... That being said, there was something seemed very interesting about Banished. The visuals looked nice, and it looked easy enough. I had seen a not-so-serious YouTube series on it, and decided I wanted to give it a try.
Once you start playing, it instantly draws you in. It is simple to pick up, and at first, it seems laughably so: "No currency? No levels to limit your building availability? This should be easy... I'll get every building, then there will be nothing left to do." If you are thinking this (and I have to admit I did have a bit of doubt, even after seeing gameplay), I can tell you that you are completely and utterly wrong. Keeping your citizens happy, healthy, and far away from starving or freezing to death requires careful management and planning ahead. Since there is no currency, resources are bartered in the trading system. Being able to determine what you can feasibly trade away takes a keen eye and the ablilty to think ahead. Every action has a consequence. At best, it can help grow your population; at worse, it can leave them out to starve, freeze, or die by some other means. This is not a game where you can afk for 20 minutes...
If you were able to successfully keep your citizens sort of fed, housed, and, well, alive, you may eventually find that your town is home to every building available (at least at the moment). Don't fret! You will soon find that you have developed the insatiable urge to keep building and growing your population. There is always the feeling that there is something to do, whether it's build more homes to help increase your population, or build more resource collectors to keep your current population better supplied. Basically, it is quite addicting, especially if it's your goal to try to see how far your town can expand or how large the population can get.
The fundamentals aside, the game is beautiful. Textures are detailed and bright, but not muddy nor unrealistic. The towns feel genuine and alive. The bustling little villages are filled with chatter, animals making noises, and tools pounding (albeit being close to a quarry at 10x speed can be a little annoying after a while). Whatever sounds begin to wear on you, though, are made up for by the peaceful acoustic soundtrack which fits the theme perfectly. The UI is simple, easy to read, yet provides plenty of information. That information is greatly expanded once you get a town hall built, where you can see graphs and stats throughout the history of the town, which is always interesting. It runs smoothly, though slower when the speed is increased to 5x and 10x, which is understandable (I usually play on 5x and find it fine).
Overall, it is a decievingly simple game, with pleasant visuals, and an overall peaceful atmosphere (which can change very fast). I was at first hesitant to buy it at $20, and I did end up getting it on sale for $10, though after playing it, I would now not hesitate to buy it at full price.

Initial Good/bad Comparison by a new player of Banished.(1st week of play)
Good:
+Fun game, decently short tutorials, after all, nobody likes playing those little snippets of restricted gameplay where you do as your told...and only as you are told...because why be curious...nobody likes that! and the nail that sticks up gets pounded ;P
+Graphics are decent, nothing too amazing but nothing too horribly detailed unless you zoom in really really close anyway.
+Great variety of tools and perspective can be adjusted just about any position you please, very convenient.
+Full key mapping capablities, if you want to freeze time or make it fly by with one click...all up to you.
+Variety of ways to play a game and complete any objectives you set yourself.
+Very rarely do you experience disasters, easily avoided with careful planning of wells and building spacing in case part of your town gets wiped out.
+Balance, you can get away with focusing your resource production in various ways to produce the most from your city/town, but the traders come in their own time, so its best not to rely too heavily on them for time sensitive items.
+Huge maps, great potential for building any size city if you so please.
+No hostile forces to ruin your fun, just build to your resources limitations, then build more to expand the limits of your resource capacity/generation.
+infinite timeline so long as you can keep your village and NPCs operating within set parameters.
+Every villager has a name gender age and even inventory listing available to view.
Bad:
-Audio will initially begin playing the game soundtrack then eventually stop looping the wordless melody so all you hear is game sounds. (Suggest playing your own music on repeat all/shuffle in the background with music volume to zero.)
-No indicators as to where a followed character is going to exactly, usually just a vague description of "collecting materials" or "____ is working" while hes five miles away from the tailor or blacksmith shop you may have assigned them to.
-Strange things happen in this game, sometimes you find coal or uncut lumber inside NPC houses for some reason instead of the area you designated as a resource pile. Occasionally you will see mines or other resource generating locations with stacks of resources outside the generation location with resource gathering points right next to them...odd.
-Variety of upgrades are scarce, you get a few select options for upgrades but they are overall few and sometimes provide less noticeable variation than initially thought, most are only noticed when you see the exact statistics in your town hall statistics page.
-No direct control of NPC characters, maybe this is a city builder no no, but personally i'd like to smack my villager upside the head when they go running off to go collect resources from the middle of the woods when you need them to be doing the job they were designated to do, not the job the laborers job.
-Item consumption/creation amounts are only found by careful observation of the action in question, not listed at any work stations/characters/homes/etc.
-No backstory....at all, you simply control the expantion of the town full of NPCs with an aversion to last names.

What is the difference betwen:
A. Killing enemies that obstruct a forward path that leads to things that make you stronger to become stronger and
B. Killing enemies to get souls and collecting those souls, so you can go back to the bonfire away from the area you intend to beat, then go to the hub area so you can speak to the NPC and use the souls to level up.
Answer: Four Hours of Tedium
I fondly call these series of games Tedious Souls for a reason, because it seems that everything that is good about this game is lost to tedium. The meat of the game truly is the boss fights that involved calculated combat maneuvers (blocking, dodging, when to attack, how to do it, and how many times you do it before defending), and the bits of lore that are strewn about all over the place with nary a care about cohesion (which isn't necessarily bad, mind you, given that it's all flavor text and dialogue). For the most part, these bossfights range from passable to interesting with plenty of middle ground to be had. I particularly like fighting Vendrick and the Demon of Song. Exploration is still a strong point in the game, although Drangleic doesn't feel as organic a world as Dark Souls 1. These areas area also experienced with consistent 60fps even when your PC's specs aren't so high end. The enemies that are strewn about all over the place are often a variant of dude in armor, humanoid figure, or four-legged mammal, which makes for a lack of variety. Though in a game that's already filled with many things to manage like a juggler with arthritis, this lack of variety means less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to deal with.
Speaking of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to deal with:
1. Adaptability - Wow. Just when you thought Dark Souls couldn't get more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, they added adaptability. Why they decided to make it so that the I-frames a roll gets is based on a stat (and therefore annoying to learn because it's inconsistent) boggles my mind to this day. Geez! Way to incentivize, Dark Souls 2.
2. Item Discovery - Ahh, the token stat is still here. As it is aptly named, the stat dictates how much chance an enemy drops a rare item when killed. In a game with good exploration, this is perhaps the worst mechanic to put as it devalues the things you discover. Oh wow! I found a "Soul of A Hero" in this small passage, my goodness! Oh wait, it gives me souls. Just like the monsters that I've been killing over and over for the longest time." "Oh wow I found a cool Heavy Crossbow! Oh wait, there's a guy that sells it for souls."
Don't get me started on, "Oh these soul items are needed by those that do an SL1 run so they can have resources at easy access," because that wouldn't have been an issue had the levelling system been scrapped altogether.
3. PVP and Multiplayer - Sigh. Look, I do get it. These "builds" and these "versions of swords" that do "slight variations of slashing" are there because there's a pvp system that's honestly rich and to the people that love them it is very fulfilling. The nuances that each of these weapons bring can add so much flavor to PVP combat. Sadly, not every player that comes into the game is going to want to do PVP. Binding the humanity status to multiplayer and informing them that it merely "establishes links to other worlds" (as if to say the first time player is going to understand that it's alluding to multiplayer) is as much a diservice as it is an annoyance. "But wait, you only ever need to play offline to do that," my butt. One shouldn't have to pull plugs or set steam offline in the first place. Remember the last game that tried to allow other players to influence your experience? That was Mindjack. That game sucked, and it sucked for a reason. There's no incentive to helping a player in Dark Souls other than getting humanity and souls. What's that, you said? You can farm souls and human effigies in the second bonfire of the Shrine of Amana? Greeeaaaat.
Oh, and the Sunbros covenant! People looooooove to bloody use that as an argument that players are incentivized to help others as sunbros because of the rewards you get when you go up the covenant. Well, I ask you, how would a first time player know that working at a covenant will net them rewards to begin with? Oh, and if you do somehow figure out that there's a reward, is that going to guarantee that someone wants to join the covenant? What's that you said? The rewards aren't useful to the way you built your character. Well...
Coop is its own headache. Sure, you now have a ring that allows you to easily connect with people and the soapstone is easily found at the early parts of the game. Except... trying to summon specific friends is still a headache. You could quite literally spend more time trying to get a summon sign to be visible for another person than than trying to play the freaking game. The reason for that is because you have to make sure that you've collected approximately similar amounts of souls in your playthrough as the person you are trying to play with in a mechanic called...
4. Soul Level - which can GTFO
5. NPCs - Was I supposed to care? Each person in the game is connected with via A. multiple "talk" instances until you exhaust the dialogue and B. summoning them in a bossfight without dying. This ultimately means it's hard to care about them. They don't say anything particularly interesting, and they only ever serve to help you kill the next boss. Geez, the lack of creativity in how to interact with a freaking NPC is hilarious here. The only exception is the woman that sells pyromancies whose name is also hard to remember because she's only ever involved in passing. I can't care about these people and I can't be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to complete their "storylines" because the only involvement I've ever had with them prior to a fight is "talking". Y'know, at least allow me to make meaningful choices that involve them please. They did a better job with Lautrec, than the nonsense they have here.
6. Tedious Iteration Time - Sigh. Look, I have zero problem with having to go back to the bonfire and travel all the way to the boss area if I lose. That's alright, even if the mob killing on the way is menial at best. What isn't alright, however, is having to watch someone perform a long winded animation to rest at a bonfire, fog up the screen, press buttons to exit the bonfire menu, watch an animation of him stand up again and be allowed to stat freaking moving. It's TEDIOUS. Just like it's tedious to have to travel back to Majula or McDuffs and upgrade your weapon or level up when in the first game you can do this at the bonfire. It doesn't take skill to press multiple buttons and wait. It doesn't contribute to the challenge. It's just tedious. Just like it is tedious to have to freaking get a boss soul, and travel aaaaaalll the way to the bonfire and alll the way to Straid's cell or Ornifex' workshop just to turn it into a weapon. It requires ZERO SKILL. It's just tedious.
7. Behavior-stuck AI and Anticlimactic Boss Fights - OOOOH I'm NASHANDRA and I HAVE A BIG♥♥♥♥♥SCYTHE and I can totally die real fast because I swing so slow and I only ever prefer to attack via my extremely telegraphed laser as the enemy swipes at my ankles.
8. Item Fragility - Sigh. Why is this even a thing? Look, I get that the game has to have stakes and consequences. Just ask yourself if these consequences are fun when you play next time, or if it just adds more tedium.
9. Forced Platforming - It didn't belong in this game.
It's honestly a glorified hassle. Sure, you MIGHT get some enjoyment from beating a boss with your accumulated skill. However, the rest of the game quickly soils that enjoyment with the stuff above. In the end, you don't get a sense of accomplishment. You get the feeling that you don't want to have to deal with it again, instead.
Get it on sale, and if you want to test how much you can stretch your patience in a game then by all means try it out. That being said, there are better games out there.

Well, it's a "match-3" as they were made a decade ago. Graphics are crude/cheap when compared to today's standards. Still the genre may appeal to some players, like it does to me.
As the title says, the goal is to contruct wonders by retrieving stones from background you have to break. There are 7 wonders and each wonder has 7 levels. Each level must be cleared. At wonder 4 or 5, some background tile are doubled. As bonus blocks, it is the usual : 4 block align, 5 block align and every 4 bonus used, another bonus appears, this one destroying several tiles+backgound at random.
That's the extend of this game, which I finished in two hours. Once done, you can do a rerun, but with (unselectable) harder difficulty.
Oh, and expect a lot of "no more move" in this one. Thankfully, it's not at your expense as it redraws the screen freely when that happens. On a playability note, once you move a tile, you can't move any other until the screen has settled. That means that all raws cleared because of your move must happen and you cannot do anything until it's done.
I rank this as a difficult one, mainly because of the few varied bonuses. Some tiles are really hard to reach.
Last, I installed this on Win7 and it ran without problem. Although, mind the resized screen for any other app that may run in the background :)

Beautiful in it's simplicity, exceptional in its execution. From the moment my girlfriend and I first loaded this game we fell in love with its energetic music, the chefs we'd juggle each day we set down to play who we'd affectionately give names and background stories, and the intuitive controls that gave me - the hardcore gamer - and my companion - the happy casual - an experience perfect for both of us. She held the controller and acted as our frontline, the server, taking the orders and I was the crazy chef cursing over my keyboard whenever I typoed or screwed up a memorized recipe.
You play as a start up restaurant manager, owner and chef working their way up the culinary ladder and gaining mroe and more acclaim within the downtown skyscraper you're located in: the SherriSoda Tower.
You play through 'five levels' of many days of serving customers, upgrading your food items and crafting the perfect menu. You can buy equipment to improve many aspects of your restaurant as well as take bets and take on other challenges to gain much needed cash. We reached a five star level. I wanted to shoot for platinum but seeing CSD:2 on sale we decided to skip the pursuit of full completion and get onto the sequel.
This is where the love affair ends.
Cook, Serve, Delicious 2 is a
and should be avoided like the plague until the developers bring back many of the aesthetics that made the original so charming (the email inbox, not mentioned before, aided in crafting in more of a storyline and made the game feel more intimate) was scrubbed away. It seems the developers had the mind to focus on the manic experience of kicking out orders versus further expanding on the many factors that made the game, to me, so great in the first place.
Where are the 'buzz factors' that contributed to you choosing the perfect items for your food? Why is it that you can no longer just memorize recipes but must now flip the pages of your recipes instead of simply feeling a sense of mastery?
Nevertheless, this is about CSD - the first game, and I cannot recommend it more. As for its sequel, even while it's on sale, I would avoid it like an anchovie mushroom pizza.

I really like this game.
It looked to me like an arena fighting game at first glance so I always ignored it. I bought it on sale for 79 cents on a whim and I'm sure glad I did.
It looks like Titans Quest, but It plays very much like an MMO. Tab targeting, auto-attack, skills hotbar, camps of mobs you have to carefully pull, etc. If you aren't in to MMO-style combat, you may not like this. The combat reminds me of Vanguard and several others. Fights are quicker though, mobs your level usually die in 10-15 seconds.
The leveling is relatively fast so far. I've been playing about 6 hours and am level 31. I did grind out a couple of levels once to make an area easier, but it only took about 10 minutes.
A big plus for me is that there are 16 item slots, including four ring slots. I prefer many slots and slower upgrades rather than constant upgrades to 6 or 8 slots.
One of the things I didn't like about it are the slow walking speed when you first start the game as a child. But once you leave the tutorial island and become an adult, the walking speed is very good.
Another thing I don't care for is the day/night system. You have to find a campfire to rest, with the option of resting to restore stamina only, or until morning or evening. It seemed like I had to rest until night time to make one quest mob appear but there was no indication of this that I saw so I roamed around looking for him before trying to wait until night time. So far, this was the only time day or night mattered, other than picking some flowers on the tutorial island, and you are told to do that at night.
The last thing is the save system. You can only save at one of the campfires. There are plenty of them around so this is not a big issue for me, but a "save anywhere" would be nice.
I only went to the arena for a few minutes and it was kind of weird and not all that fun, so hopefully it'll be mostly optional.
The graphics are on par with most MMO graphics and the sound is adequate but there is not a lot of music.
Having finished all other RPG's that interest me, and being between MMO's at the moment, I'm having a lot of fun with this. I would have easily paid the full $7.99 for it had I realized what it actually was.
Edit:
1) I finished the game in 13 hours at level 80.
2) The arena is optional. I never went there again and only lost a little favor with the gods for missing a tournament.
3) The night/day thing was not a big deal. There are 3-4 times someone or something will only appear at night.
4) A couple of the quests are a bit vague. I consulted a walkthrough a few times.
5) It did crash on me twice, both times after saving and entering a new zone.
It was still probably the most fun I've ever had for 79 cents, and is well worth even full price, imo, if you can overlook a few minor issues.

This game was a dissapointment. The premise of platforming in space seemed like it would be fun and explorative; I was amped about the randomization. But instead of atmospheric looting, it's just a frantic dash through frequently inaccessible levels. The automatic gravity reorientation in particular was frustrating. I never reached the point where the random items collected seemed in any way meaningful; the promised upgrades simply didn't factor into what quickly became a tedious exercise in racing through boring stages. Overall, the design seems lazy and there just isn't much game here, and I am unwilling to slog any deeper into the mud looking for a nugget of entertainment. I had higher hopes for this one, despite some earlier poor reviews. Perhaps it will find a home with folks who enjoy repetition, randomization and quick turnover. But if you enjoy having more than a minute or so to explore a stage, the early part of this game are not for you. I have better things to do than wait for things to pick up.

There are not many games that are set in the eve of WW1, this game is one of those.
The story is set in 1914, at England, at the eve of WW1 where the main protagonist, Richard Hannay, has gotten himself involved in a plot to start a war between Germany and Russia.
The story itself very intriguing and the artwork is beautiful...but this game is a missed opportunity.
The game could be more: it could use more animation, free movement to explore the different locations, read more interesting texts from the era, interact with items that where unique to the time and get more info about them (interesting trivia, who invented them and what were they commonly used for).
The game lacks player interaction with the world and what it is in the end is just a regular book with pretty pictures that could have been on a PDF file.
I get it that they wanted to tell just the story but you could also add some more freedom to the player, more interactivity with the world like another game called The Last Express did.
This game is unique since not many games cover the colonial/pre-WW1 era and I would still recommend this game for the story but not at 15$, it's just too much,  maybe if it was 2$ or lower then I would say get it.

Updated 7/8/2015
My review was at the character limit already, so with this update I had to delete what I had written previously.
Rather than doing a long, in depth review of the game as I had done previously I will keep this short and sweet and try to justify changing my recommendation.
While I still feel that the shallow character progression and the lack of skill progression is a huge drawback, the recent updates including itemization changes, the addition of an item transmutation system, the addition of voiceover content and other small changes have matured this game into what the developers had envisioned.  The transmutation system did a surprisingly good job of making the itemization feel deeper and more established as well.
Having Doug Cockle (Geralt of The Witcher) voice the main protagonist was certainly a point in the game's favor.  I honestly never expected such talent to lend their voice to the cast.  Rather than limiting the voiceover work to cutscenes and active dialogue alone, as I had thought they would, Victor Vran and other characters routinely spout out lines during gameplay.  This has the effect of making the general hum-drum of monster bashing a little bit more interesting and even humorous in at least one case.
I have to admit that when I restarted the game with the sole purpose of re-evaluating my review, I never expected to change my recommendation.  I started with a new save slot and played to where I had left off before my last review.
The game as a whole seems to gel better than it had previously.  The voiceover work did a surprisingly good job of making the experience more engaging.  The combat is still excellent.  Don't get me wrong here, the combat is far, far from deep and intricate, but it's fast paced and feels impactful.  I like it.
I only experienced one bug which forced me to turn off reverb in my sound options.  With the option turned on character voices were accompanied by an incredibly annoying scratchy hum.  Other than that, I played with every option on ultra and had an enjoyable, smooth experience.  I also have to mention that I play on an ultra-widescreen monitor and had no stretching or UI issues at 21:9 aspect ratio.  Definitely a plus in my book.
I now feel that despite it's flaws this game is worth the cost of entry.  It has become the game the devs meant for it to be.

If you want to try Dark Souls 2 (it's a good idea), then this is the version to go for.
One HUGE tip though: DO NOT go with sorcery. It WILL do lots of damage to vanilla enemies after a few hours of work. But it WILL NOT do damage to the very tough DLC enemies you'll meet 50ish+ hours into the game, after putting LOTS of effort into your build. For all the DLC enemies, the only weakness is a regular, raw damage weapon. Their strongest resistances are Magic (sorcery), Dark (hex), and Fire (pyromancy) for all DLC enemies across the board :|
I went with a heavy melee build in the original DS2, so I figured I'd do Sorcery for SotFS... unfortunately I found out 60 hours into my sorcery character that sorcery is absolutely useless in the endgame DLCs, where every single enemy (not to mention bosses) has super inflated magic/dark/fire resistance. RIP 60 hour save.

Banished is just
game I had been waiting for. I like strategy games, but I am not good in combat as would be the case in Age of Empires and Civilization. I enjoyed making building plans and shaping the economies way more than building an army and beat the opponent. On top of that, the opponent ended up destroying my town I liked so much!
In Banished, there is no combat involved. It really focuses on building, gathering resources and -
- shaping an economy. The combat however has been replaced for survival. And trust me: this could be even more unforgiving than combat in certain ways. One mistake could kill the entire population. And even when you do not make mistakes, a disease could still damage your people without a warning. If you are too worried about losing your town because of that, there is an option to disable it. This game can be very challenging.
Another reason why I enjoy Banished so much is because of its pace: you decide whether you want to fastforward or just sit back and see your villagers gathering and building. The music is relaxing and the sounds gives the game a nice ambience. I prefer wearing headphones playing as it just sounds better. And if you really just want to build that thriving city, you can do that in your own pace. That is, if you are gathering your resources efficiently and keeping your villagers healthy and happy.
I think Banished is a great game for people who enjoy both the survival / strategy side of building a civilization, as for people that just like to be creative and design their own city.
A small note about the development of this game: it has been made by one person. He does all the coding, artwork and music composition by himself. I think that is really impressive, especially as the result is a very nice game.
This is my vision on the game and why I think it is a great game. I hope we share that same vision when you are playing this game.

Banished is... clean. Too clean, really. A city-building and resource management game reminiscent of Dwarf Fortress with a pretty GUI and a heavy antibacterial wipedown, Banished puts you in charge of a band of serfs, throws you into the wilderness, and tasks you with gathering resources from the environment in order to build a functioning settlement. Wood, stone, and iron are necessary for building structures. Tools and education keep your peons productive, food and clothing and shelter keep them healthy, and liquor, church, and corpse disposal keep them sane. Provide all of the above and your population will grow into a happy, healthy ant farm.
The problems lie in how basic and generic the game is. There are only a couple dozen structures to build, and with no options or upgrades for any of them, there's very little strategy to it; simply build everything as you can afford it, and make sure it's all densely packed with easy road access and ample wells around in case a fire breaks out. The environment consists of water, ground, and mountain tiles, with no unique resources or features to break up the monotony. Your citizens have no personalities, few unique traits, and cannot even be differentiated by skill - they can be Educated or Uneducated (which provides a slight penalty to all job performances), and everyone wields the same omnitools for all jobs. If the game provided the player with some concrete goals to aspire to, or made the world a bit more antagonizing, and made the losses from the few disasters it offers a bit more devastating, then maybe there'd be some fun here, but it's a pure sandbox game whose only goals are the Steam achievements, all of which involve playing for obscene amounts of time and stockpiling useless luxuries. It could be improved immensely with the addition of silly cosmetic buildings and structures, or some kind of lore or storyline to add flavor, but there's nothing of the sort.
I can appreciate what Shining Rock Software was trying to do here, but Banished just doesn't take any chances and isn't anywhere near being feature-ful enough to maintain interest. It's a nice demo, but let me know when you've got the rest of the game ready.

Conditional recommendation, see below for why.
Cargo Commander is a simple game where you play as a character who's trying to recover space junk. You are armed with a mechanical arm that has a drill, nailgun, and other things can be installed into it. It can also be used to flail away at enemies or containers.  The idea is that you live in a recovery module that can become a giant magnet to attract other modules. Those modules contain spare parts and other goodies that you collect. To enter those other modules requires a quick jump through airless space. These modules are attracted in random numbers and you have a limited timeframe to search them before a wormhole destroys all the freefloating modules. These modules can also contain aliens that will whittle away your health and distract you. You can also use up your limited ammo attacking them. You need to balance your time by figuring out the quickest way to collect things before you find yourself flailing in space while the modules you were in become destroyed. All in all the gameplay is quick, light, and fun.
My only gripe is that this game seems like it would be a good fit for kids, but if you tap a key/button (it has full controller support) too many times or hit a certain key, your character suddenly starts spouting profanities (which are also flashed around your character). While it could be funny if that's your slant, it otherwise feels out of place, and a cry to try to get a certain demographic to play the game. I think the gameplay could stand on it's own without the strange humor, but I think it could potentially limit younger audiences, and polite society, from playing it. I give this game a conditional recommendation based on that premise.

Victor Vran is an ARPG that has combat and twitch based action at the forefront. It has some interesting systems in play, such as your main skills are attached to your weapons. Since you can take 2 weapons into combat at any given time, it basically allows the player to take 2 sets of skills into combat, switching to maximize DPS and cool downs. Couple this with the ability to dodge we have an ARPG that's very much focused on the A part of ARPG.
Victor Vran has a lot going for it. It has great visuals and audio, a stream lined build system where it still allows for a great degree of customization, and an action focused, and very enjoyable combat. But since the game is in early access, all of it's current flaws lay with this fact. There's no narrative or a proper campaign currently, a lot of models, items, and mobs are reused, and the progression of the game is excruciatingly dragged out. I attribute all of these flaws to it being in early access. I feel the biggest flaw is the slow progression. I have over 7 hours pumped into Victor Vran and barely leveled above level 10. It almost feels like the developers artificially inflated the amount of gold and xp needed to progress in order to hide the lack of content the game current suffers from. It just doesn't feel rewarding and I stopped out of boredom.
Sure I have my complaints but almost all of them are tied into it being in early access. The fantastic combat and how polished every thing feels is my best indication that Victor Vran isn't a lost cause. In fact I highly recommend people to keep an eye on this one. I'm hoping that once it's fully released it'll be something really special. As mentioned before, the game has a lot going for it. The Combat and character build systems in place already are very strong and very enjoyable. The presentation is eye catching and polished, it just needs to be done. There simply just needs to be a lot more of these things.
Overall Victor Vran is an interesting ARPG that has a lot of promise, but in it's current state there simply just not enough of it. Keep an eye on this one.

Banished is... clean. Too clean, really. A city-building and resource management game reminiscent of Dwarf Fortress with a pretty GUI and a heavy antibacterial wipedown, Banished puts you in charge of a band of serfs, throws you into the wilderness, and tasks you with gathering resources from the environment in order to build a functioning settlement. Wood, stone, and iron are necessary for building structures. Tools and education keep your peons productive, food and clothing and shelter keep them healthy, and liquor, church, and corpse disposal keep them sane. Provide all of the above and your population will grow into a happy, healthy ant farm.
The problems lie in how basic and generic the game is. There are only a couple dozen structures to build, and with no options or upgrades for any of them, there's very little strategy to it; simply build everything as you can afford it, and make sure it's all densely packed with easy road access and ample wells around in case a fire breaks out. The environment consists of water, ground, and mountain tiles, with no unique resources or features to break up the monotony. Your citizens have no personalities, few unique traits, and cannot even be differentiated by skill - they can be Educated or Uneducated (which provides a slight penalty to all job performances), and everyone wields the same omnitools for all jobs. If the game provided the player with some concrete goals to aspire to, or made the world a bit more antagonizing, and made the losses from the few disasters it offers a bit more devastating, then maybe there'd be some fun here, but it's a pure sandbox game whose only goals are the Steam achievements, all of which involve playing for obscene amounts of time and stockpiling useless luxuries. It could be improved immensely with the addition of silly cosmetic buildings and structures, or some kind of lore or storyline to add flavor, but there's nothing of the sort.
I can appreciate what Shining Rock Software was trying to do here, but Banished just doesn't take any chances and isn't anywhere near being feature-ful enough to maintain interest. It's a nice demo, but let me know when you've got the rest of the game ready.

Victory Vran is a top-down isometric action-RPG where you play as a man with a fidora whom probably gets asked if he can lift, and although I wanted to be a different fedora man to play as in my adventure of killing a lot of cool looking dancing skeletons and getting to be Aladin, this game is a hidden gem I never expected to love.
The graphics are good with a nice art style to it, especially the handful of character art in the game along side its description, which does look great, and what give the game that awesome graphical touch aside from its general look, is that you can rotate your camera around, giving you the control of looking wherever you want to see the games world and beauty from multiple sides, adding to the immersion and connection you'd have to the world.
The sound design is good too, but the soundtrack is just great to listen to. Although there isn't voice acting at the moment, it would definitely help if there will be, adding to the overall great production of a game.
The gameplay is great with a lot of weapons to play around with, different armor/clothes types to wear, a lot of variety and fun in its different mechanics like simply jumping, which most if not all games in its genre does not use, wall-jumping which is extremely satisfying (as well as normal jumping) to access new areas, and finding secret nicely hidden areas which is awesome to find and rewarding.
Also, when going into a dungeon, or any level, you would have a nice little preview of that dungeon/level before going in. The game is moderately challenging, with boss fights being unique and extremely challenging, even with a coop friend. Mentioning coop, it's really nice with no complications to come along with it, as you just invite and your friend is in your world to slay monsters with you.
What I want from the game is voice acting as I mentioned above, and the ability to tilt the camera up and down as it sometimes feel weird not being able to do so. Another thing that's more to spice and mix things up a bit, is having a different character other than the main one, or at least having the opposite gender, not that important but would definitely add more value to its variety and somewhat to its overall enjoyment factor.
I was reluctant of trying this game out, but after my friend pushed me to give it a go, I was extremely surprised of how good it is and how it's adding features to its gameplay that no other in its genre is doing, and those features are blowing my satisfaction of the game and its genre sky high, more so than the top dog which at the moment which is Diablo 3. Definitely give this game a look as it deserves your attention, as it did mine.

I have never felt quite so awkward and uncomfortable while playing a game before.
The game does have a semi-entertaining mindless coloring aspect to it though. Essentially, you use your mouse to try to add color to the "flower" that doesn't really look all that terribly much like a flower, while some levels have other leaves growing on the petals that take away the color on that petal if you hit them with your mouse. There's really no real challenge of any kind involved, nor is any real concentration required. Basically, keeping your mouse moving and watching the color grow is all that there is to it.
Beyond that, there is also nothing that you're really working for at all, except to maybe take a longer amount of time coloring in the flower next time in order to score higher. Even when the game is "beaten," there's nothing special that happens. You just are given the same screen from which to choose a level to play. From what I've read, if it was accurate information, this was developed as a game for touch-screen tablets and such, and that would make perfect sense. Unfortunately, it's the right kind of game for that, but not really for standard computers.
As for the awkwardness, well, let's just say that this game is about as sexual as it could get without showing any skin, as it urges you to hit the right spot and make it feel so good while you kiss it slowly, and so on. I'm still not quite sure if it's really some x-rated simulator masking as a flower game or not, but needless to say, playing it with family in the room made me feel really weirded out.
So, for all the reasons detailed here, I really can't recommend it. For my part, I'm just glad that I got it in a bundle, because the  small amount of positives come nowhere near approaching the negatives as far as this game is concerned. The only reason I even found myself continuing to play it at all is that it took so little time that I was willing to hold out and see if there was more to it later on. Now I kind of regret that, but at least I can delete it knowing for sure that I didn't miss anything.

For simplicity's sake, I'm just going to call this 6-V for the rest of this review.
6-V is probably one of the best old-school reminiscent platformers on Steam. It certainly stands to hold the top place against FEZ. The chief reason being that while it has graphics like a 2nd Generation game, and plays like a 3rd-Generation game, it has none of the flaws of the two console generations' game problems.
The problem with the Atari games, was that they were too arcade-y. Nothing wrong with an arcade game, but I want something with a more clearcut beginning and end. And my biggest qualms with the original NES library would be the lack of story, life system, and respawn points at the beginning of levels. 6-V has a clearcut beginning and end, with a set goal in mind. It's got a concept similar to that Metroid-vania formula, wherein you explore a larger world to find specific V's lost in said world. But the game's ability to add context and give you a simple one-hit death with plenty of well-spaced Checkpoints to keep the gameplay well-paced and very fast. You can die from trying to solve a puzzle and then go right back to solving it, just like that!
And, much like the NES games of old, you will die. A lot. It's pretty much guaranteed. But what I like so much about 6-V, is that the gravity controls and movement are so tight that everytime you do mess up, you can count it as your own mistake for messing up, not the game's.
It does have it's handful of flaws. The story isn't dazzling. It just is there to serve a purpose, as are the relatively uninteresting crew members you save (And the levels you have to guide them through can be incredibly excruciating), and you can sometimes get a little lost in the overworld. But that isn't such a large problem, since you move fast enough to get from where you are to wherever you need to go pretty fast, with the help of the Captain's fast movement and plentiful teleporters. And, another thing, what was up with that elephant? Can anyone tell me what the hell it was doing there?
Long story short, if you're like me and weren't particularly dazzled by the NES library (after plenty of old-school nerds praised them for the complexity and fantastic nature they obviously don't possess), and just want a fun, simple indie game to keep your attention for a few hours, and challenge your skills with gravity, then 6-V is just the game for you.

As time-management games go, this is one of the best because it really connects you to food preparation -- not just running around the kitchen matching courses, or clicking on chefs to do the work for you. I love that the controls are so complex that you can map them to a keyboard. I also like that they've miraculously mapped them to controllers, too. This is primarily a game about the satisfaction of perfect runs, and the building of muscle memory required to perform them.
So what's it about? You're a cook. You must prepare food for hordes of endlessly starving and irritated people. They come in waves, notably at lunch and dinner a horde of orc-like customers stream into the place requesting sodas, fries, salad, fried chicken, pizza, pasta... it's a good variety. You get to pick your menu, which is regularly updated as you make process, and the game forces you to mix it up so it doesn't get too old.
When I first started playing this game, there was a problem with my laptop's hybrid video card, so it ran at about half the speed. If you find yourself waiting minutes between customers, make sure you're assigning the game to the right video card. Don't be an idiot like me and assume the game is awful.
Also, what's up with all the exhausted professionals coming into my establishment at 9am requesting a large frosty mug of beer? I mean, I'm not going to turn them away, they make their own choices, but hair of the dog at a cafeteria-style buffet, in front of your co-workers?
Not worth full price, controls are clunky, speed is blown out of proportion. Essentially a cash grab by Ubisoft.

TL;DR: Most reviews is negative besause first release was unpolished alpha-version. Now it's got version >1.0 and all problems from reviews has been fixed. Also game have entertaining minigames.
"Harvest Life" is a simple farming game. It somewhat looks like "Harvest Moon" and "Stardew valley", inherited (in simplified form) some stuff like RPG-elements and overall mechanic.
Idea is simple - player have a decadent farm and a lot of free time. Harvest and animal products can be sold for cash, cash can be used for buy farm upgrades.
Unfortunately game was released earlier than it should be, so in first pair of days (when fix-update was creating) it got some negative reviews, mostly about incompleteness of content, bugged game controls and disabled mechanics. All those problems has been fixed (no, if you can't walk where you can see a walkpath between edges of tiles - it's not a bug, it's a feature of tiling system, also as if you want to interact with something you need to stay in tile next to in, not in same), added new features and polished overall. Unfortunately I'm not a big fan of that genre due to my lack of perseverance, but my score:
. Game have some intresting moments. Also it's not only in english, so it's a fair +1 to points.

Краткая суть: Средняя оценка обусловлена тем фактом, что первая выпущенная версия игры была сырой. Сейчас игра в версии >1.0 и все проблемы, указанные в обзорах, решены. А ещё тут миниигры прикольные.
"Harvest Life" - достаточно простой симулятор фермы. В какой-то степени игра схожа с серией игр "Harvest Moon" и "Stardew valley", переняв в несколько упрощённом виде RPG-элементы и общую механику.
Идея проста - у игрока есть ферма, пришедшая в упадок, а так же много свободного времени. Урожай и продукты можно продавать, получая деньги, на которые можно улучшать состояние фермы.
К сожалению игра была выпущена немного раньше, чем стоило бы, поэтому в первые пару дней (пока готовился фикс) она получила несколько отрицательных оценок, в основном связанных с неполнотой контента, багами управления и отключёнными механиками. К счастью все эти проблемы уже исправлены (нет, невозможность пройти там, где глаз видит проход между углами - это не баг, это особенность тайлового размещения всех предметов в игре, равно как и то, что игрок взаимодействует со всеми предметами только если стоит в соседнем тайле, а не в том же), добавлены новые фичи и отполированы неровности. К сожалению я не являюсь большим фанатом жанра подобных игр, ибо не хватает усидчивости, но личная оценка:
. Есть хорошие моменты и интересные находки. К тому же игра не только на английском, что автоматически даёт +1 к счёту.

Numen: Contest of Heroes  basically plays like a single player MMO, complete with hotkey bar, ability cooldowns, and combat that doesn't feel like it's quite connecting.   It isn't a great game, but it's at least a decent one, and well worth the huge sale prices I've seen it (currently $0.99 as I write this review.)  I myself picked it up for $7.50 soon after release, and don't really regret it, though $5 or less is the sweet spot here IMO.
The introductory / tutorial section is pretty boring, but persevere and the game becomes more enjoyable later.  You start out as a kid, and through a few quests learn the basics of the three primary classes - Warrior, Archer and Mage.  At the end of the tutorial you get to pick which of the three classes you want to become, and appear as a leveled up adult with only the abilities of the chosen class.  At the same time you also pick which God to worship, granting you additional abilities and bonuses, which increase as you make your God more proud of you through your actions.
Then it's standard fantasy RPG fare.  You go on quests, trigger events which advance the plotline, unlock new areas and make more quests available, kill monsters to level up and get better loot, and eventually kill the final boss and beat the game.  You encounter other heroes along the way and choose whether to help, hinder or ignore them.  And there's an Arena tournament event where you can fight these heroes as well.
The balance seems a bit off in some areas.  A couple times you can be thrown into a new area severely underlevelled for the enemies, and have to grind before you can take on more than one of them at a time.  Then 3/4 of the way through you find that 90% of your attacks are critical hits and enemies don't stand a chance as long as you don't get careless.
Overall I'd recommend the game when it's on sale, though not at the base $9.99 price.

Verdun is a realistic shooter set in the first world war. It's events play from 1914 to 1918.

If you decide you don't want to get a new tier it doesn't automatically mean that you're at a disadvantage. Most weapons are one-hit kills anyway. The exceptions are weapons at longer ranges.
