Really a 3.5 star review, I agree with other commenters who assert that the game is a quick fix that fails to live up to its full potential. Initially maddeningly addictive, Cargo Commander quickly becomes repetitive and its lack of depth apparent. This could have been remedied with more imagination from the developers and the input of a professional game writer.
The idea, the game mechanics and the environment are great. With every activation of the magnet on your drifting home in space, massive crates from interstellar junkyards smash into the wall. You must search these, uncover valuable cargo, find better weapons, destroy enemy critters. After collecting enough cargo a crate will arrive with a sector pass. Only with this can you travel to another region, with the possibility of looting rarer cargo.
This is really fun initially, but it is easy to get bogged down on one sector that has a particularly difficult sector pass crate. If you fail to collect the sector pass or die, you have to redo another round of crates until it comes again. This quickly sucks the fun out of playing. With more weapons, more enemies and more direction in the form of a stronger storyline, what is a solid romp in the park could have been a great game.

As of v1.02 (although I'm sure most of the points will remain true even after the game's released):
Victor Vran is an Action RPG with isometric camera. If you’ve played Diablo, you know exactly how it will go.
The game plays equally good with both mouse + keyboard and a gamepad too.
I’d even go as far as to say that Victor Vran plays very similar to Diablo 3 on consoles. Which in my opinion is a very good thing, since Blizz loves to polish their games.
But Victor Vran has enough things that’s different to make you play it.
First of all, there’s no traditional classes in game. Which means that pretty much at any moment you can decide to switch to a different play style. In fact, I did that right in the middle of the dungeons, worked out pretty well!
The way that you customize your play style comes down to four things: weapons, demon powers, destiny cards and outfits.
Each weapon type you’ll use, in addition to traditional ARPG stats, has it’s own set of skills. So, with shotgun you’ll have AOE blast, while with lightning gun you’ll have an attack that kinda chains mobs that are close enough together. You can have two weapons equipped at a time with a convenient switch button for them. But some weapons work better on different monsters, so it’s generally a good idea to carry your best ones for all types in inventory.
Demon powers are sort of magic spells. And buffs, and auras, and lots of other things. It can be damage dealing power, buff that increases your stats temporarily, debuff that makes enemies simpler to kill, etc, etc. This stuff is actually pretty straightforward, you get the idea.
You can use demon powers when you have enough overdrive (something like barbarian rage in Diablo - increases on attacks). And you can as well only have two powers equipped at a time. And again - it’s a good idea to carry good ones with you as you might need to switch them for next boss (or mini-boss).
Destiny cards are passive buffs (e.g. +% dmg or +% life steal) that you can equip at will in several available slots. Equipping them costs destiny points and you have a limited number of those. If you’d played Warframe - they feel a lot like mods in there.
And the last one is outfits. I haven’t yet seen too many of those, but they do seem to alter the gameplay quite a lot (e.g. my first outfit made me gain overdrive over time instead of for attacking).
You can as well use variety of potions that’ll either do damage, apply debuffs to your enemies or buff you.
The enemy variety is quite large - almost every zone has some unique type of enemies that will make you sweat. And enemies can be pretty tough as well - almost all have different attack patterns, and when they are combined, you have to be pretty careful, or you’ll die.
The bosses are pretty fun too. I’d only beaten two so far, but they wasn’t easy and had quite a lot of tricks up their sleeve. Not quite Diablo 3 level, but very very close!
On top of all that the game has a very cool Van Helsing-like aesthetic which I personally enjoy quite a lot.
Downsides right now:
- No proper campaign (but that’s coming, just wait a bit)
- Only 6 weapon types (again - more is coming in next patches)
And that’s about it. Everything else is more or less perfect.

The 39 Steps is more of an interactive novel than an actual game, but it's nevertheless entertaining. It has incredible soundtrack and voice-acting, the art is, as well, brilliant.
The only con I can think of is the fact that the in-game achievements aren't appearing on Steam even after completing a playthrough. It's rather frustrating, but otherwise there really isn't anything unfavorable about The 39 Steps.  Like any great novel that's worth re-reading, The 39 Steps is an interactive novel worth replaying.

Finally i feel that i've tried out enough to have an idea about this game.
First time i played this game i went into a dungeon, saw 8 undead dancers do Gangnam style and recieved a shotgun.
Thats about the summary of the game.
Now for the serious part :D
First read this:
FIrst lets get rid of the cons so we have that done and over with:
- Optimisation isnt yet where it fully should be probably. Regardless it still runs well enough to show off some sweet graphics. I myself can't play it on that high settings due to the fact that msaa costs a idiotic high amount of performance, while at he highest settings you do need it to compensate some of the sharpness of textures that might overdo it if you dont have msaa turned on. However this is as said just a small thing, it looks and plays fin on medium settings so ill just do that. Most of the optimisation is planned in 1.05
- Though the amount of content certainly isnt scarce (havent done all content yet and probably will take a while more), i would guess like around 10 hours just for the normal exploring.. add running dungeons with curses (negative buffs etc. see it as hardmode)/all challenges will add alot more hours. There isnt any story added yet. This is only the areas for chapter 1 unlocked and challenges added to the areas, thats it for now. (still.. not that bad for this early into early acces release) More is coming as EA progresses
Now.. those 2 things are rid off our minds, lets start with the pro's
- Controls... wether you want a controller, wasd controls or mouse-driven.. its all there.
- online co-op.. got added!
- Graphics... yep.. they are available and not disappointing at all XD
- Difficulty... While playing normally and having some potions with you, its reasonable doable... not really hard. The further you get, the harder it gets but still within reasonable limits. Then you start doing dungeons with curses active on you.. getting more difficult and then yo end up doing the highest level dungeons with curses on and suddenly you have to watch your toes because those monsters will come and kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you dont pay attention for a splitsecond :D
- Skills...  It works like this. you have 2 weapons you can switch between. Each weapon has a basic attack and 2 skills. Aside from that you can also equip 2 skills (demon powers)(you start off with 1 slot). The weaponskills depend on the kind of weapon.. atm there are several kinds of weapons including hammers, lightning guns and more :D
- Stats.. the usual kind of stats ....health, damage etc. etc. and the normal sidestats.. lifesteal, armor pen etc. etc.
- Tactics and movement.. now we come to the part where it takes a surprising route.. there are several impressive features. One is the very nice dodgesystem, allowing you to dodge the more painfull attacks .. the other is the jump/walljump system. Yes.. you can jump.. you can jump over bushes and small walls.. but you can even go as far  as walljumping between walls to get to higher places or secret stashes.
- Gameplay ... the game feels very responsive and enjoyable. It feels a bit like a Diablo game except in the fact that it doesnt really on only spamming stuff but also well-timed dodges and skill-uses :P
- Talents ... there arent really any talents. What you have is 3 slots wherein you can store certain cards that give spcially additions. (explosions on overkill, extra lifesteal, frostblasts on crit etc. etc. etc.)
- Early acces risk... this is a new part ill add to any review i make for early acces games. By this i do some research after the developers, the intention and the way they have set up the Early Acces.
Looking at the games developed by this developer company, you will see alot of positive well-recieved games with high ratings. Overall this is a good rep-sheet. The developers do not seem to have much experience with a-rpg's yet.
Their roadmap seems very solid and actually achievable... i am happy to see some developers that aren't laying the bar 50 miles higher then they will ever get.
Seeing what is available atm, how the developers respond to feedback, what they gave planned and what they have done before.. only con i would find is that i hope that if thy ever in any possible future release paid DLC for it... it did better be good since it seems that at some of their tropico dlc they really missed the plank.
Overall i would give this Early Acces the risk-rating of 10/100 meaning the risk of these developers not adding all promised features, abandoning the game or ruining the game-experience in any possible way is really small.
(0= a promised no risk, no chance on any negative feedback .. 100 = .. dont even think about buying it .. example.. War-Z would have gotten a 100 from me instantly if i would have been able to review without owning the game at the time, while Divinity: Original Sin would have recieved a score of 5 due to the amount of non-promised content added upon the promised content during their early acces)
Overall it looks, feels and breathes the word "action-rpg". My experience with action-rpg's isnt THAT extensive so i will never be able to describe this game as extensive as some of the real Diablo/Torchlight/Baldurs gate etc. players...
Still the game is fun to play, gets difficult later in the game, controls work perfect and very responsive and it has that Diablo-type sense of pride when you destroy a group of skeletons and it sets of a chainreaction of explosions.

Washington D.C. is a radioactive pit, a charred shadow of what it used to be. The survivors either survive through shear luck, close knit societies, by raiding others, or in underground shelters called vaults that closed when the bombs fell. You, you are told that your were born in your vault, and you are told you will die here. A false promise shown by your father's escape, one that you quickly follow. Stepping out into the world reveals the wasteland of the capital of the former United States. This land has no masters, only factions that conflict with each other trying to gain more control. Searching for your father you get entangled into the middle of a battle for control of this wasteland, truly a war for dust.  As you find your father, you learn of his goals to purify the irradiated water, and this is where your story truly begins. As a lone wanderer, you are able to freely explore the wasteland and get caught up in any challenges you wish, whether it be utilizing a nuclear bomb to destroy a city or helping a tree die, there's a huge variety of quests and people to work with. The variety of quests and people also provides a unique arsenal of weapons for you to dispatch your enemies or people you don't like the look of, however, kill too many good people and you'll have a pretty bad reputation around. While the game can be fairly short if you just rush through, there are a million and one things to do if your restart your game making it easy to replay and have a completely different outcome. Fallout has many interesting functions that I still haven't discovered all of, or studied them thoroughly, but they all are very interesting, such as the perks you can take each level-up that give you various skills that aid you in your conquests. Fallout 3 was an interesting revival in the Fallout series I cannot wait to see how Fallout 4 delivers.

I thoroughly enjoy this game. It's different from the other soulsborne games, no doubt, and for lots of reasons that other people discuss ad nauseum---the chief issue being the game's markedly slower combat in comparison to the other games: warm-up and cooldown periods are longer, stamina regenerates slower, and hits/rolls use more stamina anyway. I would recommend that the best way to enjoy the game is to just realize that the combat is just different, and not necessarily better or worse.
The best thing it did for me to help my game is break my habit of spamming R1 attacks. You can get away with that a whole lot in DS1 and DS3 especially if you have a sufficiently overpowered weapon. In DS2 though, forget it. You'll run out of stamina and get stuck in the middle of an enemy's attack without actually doing enough damage to take them down. With my tank build, my goal was to wait for the enemy to complete its attack animation, and then do a massive one-shot kill. Learning this style of play has helped in playing the other games of the series.
There are a few other things this game does better than the others. For one thing there are more scripted invasions. I enjoy these, though i wish dark spirits dropped items once in a while. In any case, it's a good way to get a free Human Effigy. Another thing about PvP that I thoroughly enjoy is the Small White Soapstone mechanic. This is great for getting some extra souls, getting your humanity back, and clearing out an area without having to go all the way to the boss with someone or bail on them after you got what you want. I'm not sure why they didn't add this into 3 but i think it's a great mechanic.
Another thing I liked about the game is just how many items there are. It feels like there are so many more than there are in DS3, and I now find myself in DS3 looking around every corner where I'd expect to find an item in DS2 and being disappointed. Granted the items aren't always great, but still it adds something to the game.
Finally, the SOTFS version is gorgeous and runs smooth as butter on my GTX970.
That being said, I have a few gripes:
In the first place, I used my bow more than I have in any other souls game. Previously, it was possible to just use the bow to pull enemies one at a time and beat them up with your combat of choice. In this game, I found myself doing a disappointing amount of sniping from a distance, especially in the endgame. Often the format of a room would be one or more caster or archer enemies sniping you from a distance while numerous melee enemies went to town on you. And often the range on these enemies is truly ridiculous. What made this extra frustrating is just how easily enemies aggro, and how they tend to do in groups. That is, if you hit one enemy with an arrow, multiple will probably aggro. At any rate I spent lots of time trading hits with sniper/caster enemies (who do a ton of damage too). There might be a play style that can avoid this, but I haven't found it yet.
Also, on the same topic, I've found the hitboxes around walls to be especially aggravating. Lots of my arrows got caught mid-air forcing me into the line of enemy sight when I really should have been able to shoot around a corner.
Another especially aggravating and potentially game-breaking issue is the way that weapons track your joystick rather than the enemy once you start swinging. I once read that this is supposed to be a feature that makes pvp a bit less predictable. Furthermore, it really does add an element of challenge since often I find the hit-tracking in DS3 to be way too forgiving. That said, I probably landed two plunging attacks for my entire playthrough of DS2 since the hitbox is small and locking on doesn't guarantee anything.
Where this really sucked though was when I would try to back away from an enemy and start swinging but end up swinging behind me instead. I don't know how many times I died that way but it sure was a lot. I don't know how this could be fixed but at any rate, if you play a strength character especially where you're only able to get one or two swings per encounter with an enemy because of how stamina-heavy your weapon is, get into the habit of hitting the swing button and taking your thumb off the joystick.
Overall I love this game for what it is and will likely return to it once DS3 gets stale for me. It's different from other souls games sure, but I think the generally slower speed forces you to develop good combat habits---with the exception of sniping enemies from across the stage for hours on end.

Ever wondered what it would feel like if you read a novel with accompanying artwork, plus, each conversation was acted out by voice actors? This is what "The 39 Steps" feels like - the so-called "digital adaptation" of a Scottish novel by the same name.
The "game" shows us texts telling us the story of Richard Hannay. One picture follows another one; when watching these we hear the corresponding sound effects: horse carriages moving in front of Richard's house or the sound of a stream just under the bridge where he's having a conversation with a stranger. This is an interesting genre - I do not know what to make of it but 39 Steps was a good example to give it a try for the first time.
The plot revolves around an expatriate who returns to London and meets a strange fellow who starts babbling about a plan to assassinate the prime minister of Greece. Apparently, getting rid of this person can result in such a chaos that may bring World War I forward (historically, we are just before when the actual war broke out, in the spring of 1914). Richard takes in Scudder who is later found dead in his room. This comes as a surprise as Scudder explained it to Richard in detail how he actually arranged his death a while ago so that nobody would come looking for him (since he already knew too much of this plan to create anarchy).
So, Richard is on the run and while doing so he meets quite some people and uses a couple of aliases in order to hide. As mentioned, you essentially read texts to follow his story - these do not appear all at once but as you move your mouse clockwise you receive your next batch of sentences on the screen. As you complete certain sections (the game calls these events) you earn achievements; this is an easy way to get 100% since you just need to complete the game.
Occasionally, Richard finds himself in a room that he can investigate. This simply means that some objects are highlighted and once clicking on them the corresponding (explanatory) text appears. Diamond symbols in the lower-right or -left corner of the screen indicate how many items we can find and interact with. I do not know if they are a must for the achievement but since you rarely get more than 3 or 4 it is really easy to find everything.
If I remember correctly there are 19 chapters altogether and bookmarking any section within a chapter is possible so that you can pick up right where you left it off. There's some great voice acting done here and also I liked the accompanying music. The story was also interesting - mainly because I was eager to find out what exactly the 39 steps meant.
Like I said this is an interesting genre to pick - some might say it's best to just pick up a book and read it. Since I like the concept and the execution (casual gameplay and simplistic, but great looking menus and beautiful artwork) I give this one a thumbs-up. Unfortunately, upon checking if there were more from this developer I did not find any but this novel was already released 4 years ago.

Dark Souls is so close to being good at so many things but always falls short providing more frustration via poor controls, bad camera controls, claustrophobic size entrances remaniscent of early 3D games that twist like hidden rat holes, dark ambiance overpowering clarity, and little sense of direction.  Just getting to the Co-OP will prove too difficult for most players, and frustrating nonetheless with little payoff.  One might as well go play a stable, well built MMORPG instead of this odd hybrid.  The story is great but it's held down by a cumbersome system that will only appeal to sadists and masochists.  I also hate Left for Dead so, take it as you will.  The platform jumping is stupid and annoying as it's vital but shotty and difficult to aim.  Instead of making a character feel free, one feels weighed down and child could jump higher.  It just blows my mind that a small rock or log passes for a barrier in these guided, closed-world games.  It instantly destroys any sense of illusion the game might of had over you.  This is hell... but games should be fun.  This is punishing:  Only fun for those quite advanced in archaic controls and odd camera movements.  Poisonous Co-Op communities that mock the new players and troll them relentlessly are not my idea of a good time.  Dark Souls just doesn't seem finished.  It would be a better book ultimately.  The graphics just don't do death justice.  It's dark, sure, but not deathly.  More macabre camp horror that likes to laugh at you for dying by making a very strange environment.  It is nice that you can randomly kill NPCs.  There just needs to be so much more like all of the games in this genre:  too much action, not enough playability.

Where the game is lacking the charm with refinement of the details, it wins it back with the overall complexity of the game process, making you believe what you're really get into US Pacific fleet operations... Even closer than the participants themselves - due to all the variety of battle functions, aspects of interactions between all kinds of ships, planes and other units.
War never changes, you know. We may agree on the point it is disgusting, and brings all kinds of bad things (especially if you've witnessed some of them closely). But, on the other end, wars usually tends to remain the main shows for the whole life of the people who was there. Nothing comes close enough in reflecting this, neither the books, nor the films about it... But complex war games such as Battlestations - now, that's a huge step to get the feeling of the gross events your grand and grand-grand parents (could probably) saw with their own eyes. Next step closer will be addition of smells and constant feeling of fear for your life, and one more - real bombardment of your neighbourhood with artillery and strategic aviation. Which is too extreme, I assume.
So! So far we don't use hardware with the simulated outcomes of the real presence, with smells, pain, bleeding and starvation effects - games like Battlestations are as close as we can get.
Sure, the thing is dated, unpolished and all that. The battle formations, with the need to plan the warfare, moving various "units", sometimes even carriers into or out of enemy lines, issuing orders in the real time and control many vessels by yourself - all that can be Really Frustrating. I, personally, very much dislike of the realization of air combats and overall planes control in the game - and that is one of the two most needed aspects! But, again, if you'll get used to it - the overall complexity of the operations will change your look at the things. At least, if you weren't in the actual service, and see WW2 mostly from the barrel of the gun point of view (like Battlefront, CoD and other franchises we all know about).
How do I mark it? Well, it's gonna be 6.5/10, but with the regard for exclusive gameplay which you'll not get even from modern titles like War Thunder or World of Warships. The thing is - you gotta be ready to be multitasked and seld-collected in the one. And you gonna need some (maybe plenty) of time to master it. Without any casual "motivating" stuff like achievements etc.

I would say I absolutely do recommend this game if you like games like Test Drive Unlimited, and Need For Speed, that being said, there are some MAJOR downsides to this game but overall I find it a rather good game.
Let's start with the cons to get that out of the way.

-Hard to Start Out
As in it's rather hard to get money for actual good vehicles. I feel as you progress more, it'll be easier but when you have to go and get performance vehicles.... be prepared to spend lots of your time grinding for money if you want an actual decent car.

-Ranked
I feel as though they let you go into ranked WAY too early as I went into it (Not at all knowing what I was doing...) and was matched with the top of the top players (Platinum, Gold, Etc.). While they had level 1499 Vehicles, i sat there with a puny level 300..... As that may be my own fault for rushing it, I just recommend if you play to wait a LONG time before playing ranked.
-Street Challenges
As this may just be my own personal opinion, I find as you're driving down the road, the excessive amount of Street Challenges are way too much. They typically cover the entire road, and frankly try to force you to do them. You literally have to swerve off the side of the road to avoid them... Players begin their career as a Cargo Commander in a perfectly square space station that functions as their home for the game's duration. The space station contains all the necessary tools for a successful career, including a computer for checking email and changing levels (known as sectors in the game), an upgrade bench for buying new equipment and upgrading the commander's armor and weapons, magnet control for attaching additional cargo containers for exploration, and even a coffee machine when in need of that extra boost of caffeine.
As players begin each day in space, they are given a defined number of loot items to gain and eventually a key that rewards access to additional sectors. If players die in the process of collecting the loot, they begin a new day and try again to acquire the specified loot. As cargo containers are brought crashing into the space station through use of the magnet, their exteriors are covered, requiring players to drill into them before seeing what treasure or trap is waiting inside. Once players enter inside a container, the 2D platforming aspect of the game takes control and tasks players with collecting loot items and dodging the attacks of enemies while fleeing for safety.
Each container houses loot items that vary in rarity and value in addition to hostile alien creatures that complicate the process. After a short time, the cargo containers start to break apart as a result of violent wormholes which require players to grab the loot and rush back to the space station before their supply of oxygen is depleted. The entire process of drilling into cargo containers, frantically searching for loot, battling violent alien creatures, and finally rushing back to the space station is both a thrilling and extremely-gratifying experience.
Loot and other forms of currency in the containers can, in turn, be spent on upgrades for the commander character that range from reinforced armor to extended oxygen while in space. The catch is that the upgrades are reset upon each day or after your character meets their fate, which creates a roguelike atmosphere of gameplay. As players advance in levels, which is determined by the amount and rarity of loot earned, they are rewarded with upgrade points that are replenished each day. More advanced upgrades include improvements to the space station, one of which is that it can auto-repair itself after losing walls from crashing containers.
Beyond collecting loot, players can travel to other sectors that are simply just different leaderboards based on their given names. The only interaction that players have online is the competition of leaderboard scores and the discovery of other dead commanders within containers. It's unfortunate that the game did not include an actual multiplayer component as cooperative loot collecting would have been an absolute blast. After awhile, the leveling system and loot collection become repetitive as the gameplay, never evolving beyond the core mechanics. Day after day, players continue with the same menial task as aliens become stronger and loot more difficult to acquire. Without convincing a couple of friends to compete for the highest score of loot collection, the platforming entertainment of Cargo Commander becomes more mundane than engaging.
The presentation of Cargo Commander shines in nearly all of its aspects, from the pixel-shaded visual appearance, or the outstanding sound effects, to the lack of any sound while floating about in space. The most impressive graphical element is the destructible environments of both the commander's space station and cargo containers. Either using his drill or planted explosives, it's a thrill to tear apart any surface that is between the commander and his hunger for more space loot. In regards to the game's sound, details like the volume of the station's radio music becoming dimmer as the player floats further into space is a brilliant touch. The only downside with the presentation is that the game's environments of cargo containers never vary that greatly and after awhile can become just as mundane as the gameplay.
The elements of a 2D platformer, space, zero-gravity, destructive environments, and loot collection combine for an experience that is both entertaining and addictive for the beginning hours. As additional levels are gained and higher scores earned, the gameplay experience never quite evolves beyond its initial premise. Players that have a group of friends for online leaderboard competition will undoubtedly discover more value with the end game. 2D platformer and space enthusiasts are sure to find something they'll enjoy in Cargo Commander, while those seeking a more varied game will have to look elsewhere among the stars.

Washington D.C. is a radioactive pit, a charred shadow of what it used to be. The survivors either survive through shear luck, close knit societies, by raiding others, or in underground shelters called vaults that closed when the bombs fell. You, you are told that your were born in your vault, and you are told you will die here. A false promise shown by your father's escape, one that you quickly follow. Stepping out into the world reveals the wasteland of the capital of the former United States. This land has no masters, only factions that conflict with each other trying to gain more control. Searching for your father you get entangled into the middle of a battle for control of this wasteland, truly a war for dust.  As you find your father, you learn of his goals to purify the irradiated water, and this is where your story truly begins. As a lone wanderer, you are able to freely explore the wasteland and get caught up in any challenges you wish, whether it be utilizing a nuclear bomb to destroy a city or helping a tree die, there's a huge variety of quests and people to work with. The variety of quests and people also provides a unique arsenal of weapons for you to dispatch your enemies or people you don't like the look of, however, kill too many good people and you'll have a pretty bad reputation around. While the game can be fairly short if you just rush through, there are a million and one things to do if your restart your game making it easy to replay and have a completely different outcome. Fallout has many interesting functions that I still haven't discovered all of, or studied them thoroughly, but they all are very interesting, such as the perks you can take each level-up that give you various skills that aid you in your conquests. Fallout 3 was an interesting revival in the Fallout series I cannot wait to see how Fallout 4 delivers.

The general gameplay itself is also quite rewarding, especially to those who are persistent enough while also learning some "advanced" platforming-skill (couple of moves I've dubbed as "Slim-wall-edge-climbing" & "Floor-pile-ascend").
One fair warning is that since you're able to carry only two guns at the same, the "weapon-locker"-micromanagement can become an annoyance with the ammo-spawner, which is one of the "Promotion" / Permament-upgrades to make future-runs a slightly bit easier.
The game also is surprisingly atmospheric especially due the small details that can be easily missed out in bigger-images.
Many complain of "lack of variety"; I personally say the content (enemy-types, etc) is just-right to make this game possible.
Some also complain about game being a "online-single-player"-game. In reality it's the needed "evil" to allow the possibility of "sharing" the maps alongside the postcard-messaging-system, which is yet another interesting addition to this game.
All in all, if you're looking for a rather simple, easy-to-learn-game, this is well worth the asking price.

THIS GAME IS AMAZING. this is the most comprehensive, most complete game I've seen in any gernre. It's definitely the type of game you need to invest time into learning. There is a deep learning curve but once you get a feel for the game, it makes sense why its so difficult to learn, because it basically lets you control almost anything. The game dynamics are amazing and very complicated but then again, so is global warfare. There is a great community of devoted HOI3 players who have answered literally every question related to this game so if you get it and find yourself not understanding the game dynamics, such as the supply situation, you can easily go online and read up on it. The supply dynamics, while sometimes buggy, is one of my favorite aspects of the game. If you're invading Western france, make sure to get large ports and not to outpace your supplies, less you fall victim to an axis counter attack that finds your front undersupplied and pushes them back in chaos. I like how the game manages the organization of the troops, both in terms of command structure and in terms of the org of the specifc unit. If they're under supplied or disorganized, they'll fail in an attack and soon you'll find the enemy routing you across the continent. It really takes a great deal of practice and patience to mount the correct offensive. You get a sense for how underprepared offensives can go awry in a second, especially when playing as Germany and trying to raise through the Soviet Union. You might get within 2 provinces of Moscow before you realize that you're supply lines havent caught up (because you didnt research the techs you needed) and then the Soviets counter attack with inferior forces and you have to scramble to recover. Thats the fun of the game though. You can prepare all you want but if things dont work out the way you planned, you often have to plan on the fly.
I played as the Soviet Union and thought I was perfectly set up to protect the mother land against the germans but got my but handed to me three ways to leningrad. It was the game of my life, reorganizing and launching desperate and doomed counter attacks to slow down the germans while I get more troops ready. It's very interesting because when you play as the Soviets you get the impression that the germans better conquer you within a year, because if they dont, you can create about 10 infantry divisions a month and thats a pace the Germans can't ever sustain.
Anyways, this game is amazing. You can play as anyone, Brazil for example, and work just to contribute a tiny amount to the war effort. Or you can play as the US and let Europe be while you focus on hunting and eliminating Japanese carrier groups that you know they can't replace the way the US can. Nimitz, Halsey and Spruance to the rescue!
If you like strategy and grand warfare, give this game a try, If you take the time to learn it and you understand what kind of game you are buying, you will not be disappointed!

A lot of people compare this game to BF1. I personally find this hilarious. This game tries to capture the WW1 atmosphere, and balances the realistic-fun elements. But it's not perfect. So here's the Goods and the Bads.
The Good:
This game nails the sight mechanics, you move even at the slowest pace and your sight gets ruined, absolutely love this feature.
The guns actually do feel like they have a barrel, most games feel like the gun isn't even there after the iron sight.
Why is it perfect on that aspect? Because if you try to expose your head as little as you can, your gun would shoot just underneath you, which would provoke you to find a better position for your view, with the sacrifice of protection.
Speaking of protection, you can't escape from grenades just by hiding behind a thin metal sheet like in many other games. Grenades have a pretty realistic radius and that radius extends behind the cover.
The Bad:
Hit registration can be unreliable sometimes, mainly due to ping. (eg. 80 vs 89ms)
It would be awesome to have 64 player matches, It would mimic WW1 atmosphere perfectly. (Upcoming in the next title)
Gameplay is so straightforward, It's just "attack them" or "oh no we failed get back" over and over again until the match ends either in a draw or win/loss.
The animations need polishing.
I'm really happy to see most of the negatives are being fixed in the next game,Tannenburg. That being said, I definetly recommend this game.

I bought this game orginally without any previous experience of any other Paradox game, riding the wave of dissapointed and betrayed feelings after Rome 2:Total War's very rocky launch. I admired the fact that this apperaed to be nearest thing to actually commanding the conflict that one can ever hope to achieve, save for the people who actually fought in it. A very daunting, and perhaps even unfriendly game to beginners, it took me,  a realtively seasoned Strategy player of nearly all the Total War franchise, Company of Heroes and the even older Populous games, a very long time to figure out the games extraordinary complicity, and even today, I have only scratched the surface, after well over 200 hours of playtime. It is a flawed masterpiece however. The games AI, can be rather strange, commiting entire Heersgruppe's to deal with Norway, or in one instance, USA joining the Cominterm due to a pre-existing lend-lease treaty with Soviet Union. Also, those who have had their fill with singleplayer and dare venture forth to Multiplayer, will discover an ardous process of checking checksums, arranging private servers, and endless re-hosts,as Paradox did away with the Meta-server. As far as mechanics go, this game contains one of the most intelligent character build systems I've encountered in years.
It manages to actually solve the problem most hack and slash RPGs founder upon: how little impact skilled play (that is, the player's manual dexterity) has on the player's success. I'm racking my brain, and I simply can't come up with another game of any genre that manages to balance the importance of itemization and player skill so well.
By off-loading some of the mechanical depth onto skilled play, the game is able to keep the build systems remarkably straightforward, tight and responsive. At the same time, because the manual skill depth ceiling is meaningfully high, investment can be found beyond just getting all the best gear you can find. This also means items appropriate to the player's skills and playstyle are more valuable than just what is "best".
An example of Victor Vran's elegant design: the game's Destiny cards. These are akin to the "perk" systems found in many games, and the player is allotted a certain amount of points with which to equip them. More powerful cards require more points, and yet the cards are balanced enough that low level cards retain their value at high levels, particularly as the player is able to stack them together. Again, the end effect is that build choices have more to do with enhancing the player's skills than they do with defining them.
On top of all this, the ability to switch out cards and equipment on the fly (no visiting town to respec, or cumbersome cool downs in-between) makes this game's build system more flexible, player friendly, and open to systems exploration than is usually found in games such as these (Note to Devs: Please keep this going forward!). And this comes around to skilled play once again--Victor Vran is able to do this because it doesn't need to rely on enforcing player choice, sub-optimal or no, to inflate investment time requirements.
All that said, it should be noted that how the end game will work remains to be seen. I've managed to hit the current level cap twice now in the 9 hours I've played this game as of this review, and if the level cap at release remains a low 20 (as per the Devs' roadmap post), much will rely on just how high the player skill depth ceiling will turn out to be at that point. Worst case scenario: end game gear that requires the player to skill-grind prohibitive amounts of challenges to unlock. And, of course, nothing is known about what the content will be like in terms of story, characterization, etc.
In summary: smart mechanics, meaningful skilled play in an aRPG package. If you like substantial build choices packaged with challenging top-down action a la Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light or Dungeon Siege 3, you'll probably enjoy this game.

Luxuria Superbia is a colorful, musical journey made to fill you with joy. Exciting designs explode from your touch as you glide through playful stylized flowers. It’s all about the experience and the interaction.
There’s twelve flower-like tunnels and a garden with a temple.
In the garden, you select a flower by turning the dial.
When you complete a flower the next one is unlocked.
A flower always starts out colorless.
But when you touch it, color fills the tunnel.
Stay in the glowing flower as long as possible!
Play slowly and gently to get a high score.
Just pushing through as fast as you can will result in failure.
The game wants you to take it easy and be playful.
The blush you cause to a flower imbues the garden too.
For each flower, there’s a column in the temple.
Time spent in a blooming flower makes its column grow.
The garden starts blank, just like the tunnels.
But over several journeys, it flourishes with color.
Bring color to the flowers, bring joy and beauty to the garden

Something like a casual rhythm game but not based on musical timing. You will need to master the hotkeys in order to fill orders accurately and quickly. Game is simplistic but fun and can offer a compelling challenge. The only real weakness in gameplay is that food selection is easy to minmax.  The difficult time-consuming recipes aren't rewarding enough, and once you have the most efficient foods unlocked you'll find yourself constantly rotating between the same dishes unless you're forced to pick something else.
Graphical presentation is largely 2D and static, with a colorful, polished art style that makes the food look appetizing. The game seems well-optimized and has a snappy response to user input even on older hardware. A gem of indie design, it showcases that even when you have a small budget you can still make a good game by prioritizing tight gameplay and focused production values over pure aesthetics.

It's 10 minutes to closing time when he walks in.
"A pizza with everything on it, please."
I stare at him. I stare at the clock above the door to the back room. Can't he see that I've already put most of the dishes into the dishwasher? Why did he have to walk into my restaurant at such a late hour?
"I.." I start, before I lock my eyes into his and see a pain in them I haven't seen since I looked myself in the mirror this morning. I can't just tell him to leave, just because I want to get back home to my empty apartment, so I can watch re-runs of shows I don't even like. Alone. Just like he looks. I have to do my duty.
"..Sure, it'll be done in 15 minutes."
I make the pizza and I put on the salami, the olives, the freshly cut oregano, all the rest of the ingredients he wants on it. I'm sure this will be the best pizza he'll ever have, I even put a little extra cheese on it, just to give the guy some more to live for. Who doesn't love cheese, ya know?
Finally when the pizza is done and in its take-away box I hand it to him. He looks at it and opens the lid.
"There's too much cheese on this."
He leaves and doesn't even give me a tip.
I stand there and look at the door that he's already walked out through. All I can do is stare in disbelief. What has the world become?

CARGO COMMANDER is a really fun creative randomly generated Jump'n'Run. Imagine you live alone in space on a small ship. Imagine that your job would be to fly around with your ship untill you find a flying cargo and collect the lost items in that container. Got that? Yeah? Because that'S all there is in CARGO COMMANDER. You treverse those containers by runnning jumping and using your tools to get some items.  Those tools are a drill which is used to drill through walls and other objects and you've got a weapon which is used to fight the monsters that inhabit the abandoned containers. The more items you collect in the containers the more points you get. But you only have a certain amount of time to explore a wave of containers because after a few minutes a black hole opens which sucks the containers inside. There are randomly generated sectors which consist of endless waves of containers. On the fith wave or so you can find a sector pass which can be used to unlock a new sector. Becuase of the fact that every sector is randomly generated the game could be played endlessly but for me it got boring rather quickly, What I've played was a hell of fun . Try CARGO COMMENDER out if you search for a game that is played in short sessions.

Most of you who visit the shop-page for
probably already know what this game is all about. It's a hardcore (as hardcore as it can get, actually!) Grand Strategy Game by Paradox Interactive. That one sentence really says it all.
This review is intended for those who don't yet know what Grand Strategy (the capitals are there with a purpose!) is all about. Simply put: Grand Strategy games are the best, but also the most complex,  pc gaming has to offer. They are immersive, complex, and very addictive. They are not for everyone, that's for sure. You don't play them for the graphics, nor for the sounds or some great level-design, but only for the gameplay, which can also be very, very difficult to master. There are tons of stats, of units and/or provinces to be controlled and only one person who has the power to control them: you.
Let's take
as an example. Untill less than a year ago, I was convinced that this kind of games was nothing for me. Too difficult, too one-sided, yoo much of an effort to learn playing it; I had lots of reasons not to delve into them. That's untill my son convinved me to at least have shot at this one. I gave it a try, but stopped playing after an hour of so. I couldn't make anything out of all the numbers and stats on the screen, and the static map where nothing seemed to happen except for the slow advancing of the time. Then I read a superb guide made by the famous HOI3-community. It took me over a month to study guide and game (and it was really
, not even really playing), but then I was hooked. You see: it literally takes effort and even study to get into this game, but once you've done that, the effort more than pays off, and you can start guiding your nation to victory, survival or downright defeat during the crucial period 1936-1948.
HOI3 lets you play ANY of the nations in the world, starting on 1/1/1936 and going into World War II (or avoiding it by following a more peaceful path). It's a tough challenge because you have to manage all aspects of government, economics, technological research and military, but once you see your nation flourishing, the reward is enthralling. The amount of management needed to succeed is staggering: you'll spend most of your time playing HOI3 by looking at screens full of statistics, numbers and tech trees, but once you realize that you can really have an influence on how all of these evolve by making the right decisions, it feels like being in command of something very complex.
Just give it a try if you feel it's ok to have to study a game in order to be able to enjoy it; the rewards will be there for sure. Very important: do get the expansion packs
,
and
as well (all three needed). They really improve upon game mechanics and are needed if you decide to give one of the many, many available mods a try.
Gameplay: 28/30
Graphics: 14/20 (they do the job more than decently, but could have been a bit more engrossing)
Sound: 7/10 (playlist is great!)
Gameplay for your money: 18/20 (multiplayer is a technical disaster, but SP can keep you going for years)
Technical/stability: 8/10 (after lots of bug-problems, it's now fairly stable, but MP is really difficult to set up)
Personal feel: 10/10 (just love this one)
Overall: 85/100

This is a great game. There are two items of note about this game: it is both incredibly complex and deeply satisfying. With all the detail about World War Two that the game provides, nothing is more enjoyable than defying history. Maybe France won't fall to Germany in 1940, maybe Nationalist China can fight off the invasion from Japan (not so difficult actually), or maybe the Axis will emerge victorious. Some of those ideas may be more difficult than others, but regardless, after you understand this complex game, most of those ideas are possible to achieve.
Europa tries to model peace a bit too much, and thus there is less detail in war. Hearts of Iron is all about war. If you enjoy the great tactical and strategic battles of the second World War, this game is for you.

I really wish I had read a few reviews before jumping into this game immediately. I had fond memories of the previous games in the series on a few websites which made this more disappointing in hindsight.
I had fun with the game when I first started, which quickly started to run out for several reasons: 1) There were only 7 missions to choose from during my playtime, not counting contracts which are much smaller in scale (not sure if they will add any more missions, or have already). 2) This game jumps onto the lootbox bandwagon that has spread throughout the game industry this year. Sure the game is free, but it pesters you into buying lootboxes after each mission if you didn't open any yet, which makes it look even worse than it already did to begin with. 3) This is a mobile port, not even based on the browser version, and it certainly shows with its UI layout, barebones options, and the aforementioned lootboxes and overall microtransaction system.

I really, really like this game; most steam users will not (hence the thumbs down).   Why?
It is colorful, highly sexual without having any actualy pornographic images (though the text leaves little to the imagination), has an unusual, electronic and reactive soundtrack, and is less a game than an experience.  I happened to think it was a somewhat snide concept, innovative for it's genre, and immersive in an artistic way, and I took it on that level.  I like it.
On the other hand, it is not a game built for the PC, but a touch screen, and as I understand it, it hasn't been altered in any way to improve gameplay for a PC.  It has no plots, no really deep puzzles, isn't really a simulation (unless you count stimulation), and is graphically on par with a nicely done flash game.  It also has little replay value (unless it happens to fulfill some other needs in your life), and can be played through in under an hour.  In other words, it was built for casual gamers, and it is casual gamers who shall play it.  Because of this, while I like it, I can't in good conscience recommend it to the Steam community, which prides itself on technologically and graphically superior games and/or immersive, story-driven games.
Great for:  people who really like experimental games, colorful and design-heavy images, and simple gameplay (and innuendo).
Not great for:  Most computer gamers (I.E., if you want at least an hour of gameplay, to make use of your graphics card, and/or some kind of plot to your diversions).

Some people don't think DS2 is a good game for reasons that I find to be rather... insane. Just quickly throwing my review hat in the ring because of this, even if I'm just a TAD late in doing so.
I can understand not liking DS2 as much as DS1 or DS3 for that matter, but outright thinking DS2 as a bad game is an opinion I will always find baffling. I actually started with DS2, then played DS1, then played DS3 (acronyms galore). I found them all to be great. Sure DS1 is very open ended relative to DS2, but for people who are new to the series, DS2 (or maybe DS3) may potentially be a better starter point.
DS2 is less convoluted than DS1 and in some respects is easier not including the DLC sections. That's not to say the world design of DS1 is bad, I do think the open world esque design is probably better, but that doesn't make the way DS2 does things not good just because it didn't build the world in a similar way. It's still open ended, just in a much more simplified fashion.
The game's combat is still skill-based and I rarely feel like a death isn't my fault, it's the same deal as Dark Souls 1. Adapting, mastery of the mechanics, reaction time and so on.
The bosses are still well-designed for the most part. Not EVERY boss is going to be spectacular, but the majority of them were still pretty unique and different from one another. The DLC bosses and the DLC in general which is the end game content is arguably the best part of the game. All but maybe one of the DLC bosses were very challenging and really brought out the joy in mastery of souls combat. (Looking at you Fume Knight)
Some of the areas in the game MAY feel like a chore or just be a tad annoying. But there's a plethora of areas in DS1 that people also hate or areas that were rushed (Lost Izalith/Demons Ruins for example), and yet the game still shines greatly.
It's still Dark Souls. If you played any Dark Souls games you should I feel you should still play this. Just don't go into it expecting the world design to be the same. It's a different game: different world design, different area design, different bosses, etc. But it's not different enough to warrant overruling it.
I found the game to be great, and I don't find it overly worse or better than DS1, it's different. Whether those differences make a huge impact on you is up to you I suppose. Most of the criticisms are people taking nitpicks to an extreme, or the usual of the game being too hard for them.

I must start off by saying that VVVVVV is undeniably one of the greatest platform games of all time.
Its unique gameplay mechanics, simple but memorable graphics inspired by that of the Commodore 64, interesting level design, and Positively AMAZING soundtrack all contribute to making this game just how good it is. No one should ever hesitate to try it out.
You’ll be controlling Captain Viridian, a short, blue 8-bit man who’s somehow managed to have his spaceship’s teleporter malfunction, trapping him and the other 5 members of his crew in Dimension VVVVVV! The goal is simple: finish the levels, and rescue a crew member at the end (don’t forget the shiny trinkets along the way!) so you can repair your ship and go back home.
What sets VVVVVV apart from other platformers is, as I mentioned, its unique gameplay mechanics. Captain Viridian cannot jump – instead he switches gravity to stick to ceilings and fly up long chasms. This is simple in nature, and you might think there’s a limit to how creative the game can get with it, but the levels take this mechanic to extreme heights and do some very wacky and interesting things with it. You’ll find out when you try the game yourself =)
The best part about VVVVVV, however, is its music. It, like the game’s visuals, is presented in a chiptune style, and perfectly suits the environments you explore. Some tracks are happy (including Positive Force, my personal favorite =D), and some are mysterious, leaving you wondering what might happen next (Predestined Fate). It’s hard to describe, but you understand very well once you hear it.
Unfortunately, there is one drawback to the game: its high difficulty level. VVVVVV is not at all a game for those who have little patience for repeated deaths and inconvenient object placement. The game can, at times, become very frustrating. But the feeling of reward you get when you finally finish a level is so good that it more than makes up for the over-the-top difficulty.
In conclusion, I cannot recommend VVVVVV enough. Although the high difficulty may turn you away at first, you will surely see that the game’s amazing music, unique mechanics, and great level design all contribute to making the game what it is. It is very much worth the $4.99 price tag.

VVVVVV (Steam) (Humble) strips away all the superfluous stuff that fills our games and boils platforming down to a single question: Are you good enough?
Your spaceship has been stranded in a strange dimension and your crew has become separated.  As Captain Viridian, you must find them and figure out how to escape!  This looks like a standard platformer at first, but there is one key twist: you can’t jump.  Your only way to get over (or under) obstacles is to reverse gravity and walk on the ceiling.  The way this game utilizes this conceit is masterful, and also evil.  This game is extremely difficult.
The world is “open” in a sense, you can attack any of the five main challenge courses in any order you find them.  Each course has an interesting twist on the very basic formula.  One level is full of beams that reverse gravity when you touch them. On another, the screen wraps around itself selectively, making mazes of simple-seeming screens.  There are some secret collectables scattered around in hard-to-reach places, but they are completely optional.
You will die a lot in this game.  A LOT. I beat the game in a little under two hours, and I died 779 times.  A majority of those deaths occurred in the infamous Veni Vidi Vici (Doing Things The Hard Way) level.  This single challenge encapsulates what makes this game so great.  Death is temporary in VVVVVV, lasting less than a second before you respawn at the last checkpoint to try again.  Checkpoints are plentiful, never more than a few seconds away.  This makes failure almost painless, and allows for some fiendishly difficult rooms that you will try to navigate over and over again.  You won’t measure your own progress in stages completed or items collected.  No, you’ll become astutely aware of how many PIXELS further you went on that last run.  And you’ll yearn to get just one dot further on the next.
The retro aesthetic to VVVVVV is not unique by any means, but it is charming.  Simple, bright colors, a pounding and pulsing chiptune soundtrack, and adorable characters make this one stand out amongst the 8-bit crowd.  Viridian and his mates have only two facial expressions, but they are so genuine and funny.
Terry Cavanaugh did an amazing job taking a single mechanic (gravity reversal) and building an entire game around it.  The rules are simple, but the play space built on top of them is enormous and satisfying.  I wouldn’t hesitate to call it one of the greatest games of all time, simply for its masterful design.  VVVVVV is one of the best games to really exploit Flow State where you become so focused on the task at hand through sheer repetition and muscle memory, that you gain expertise in the task without even realizing it.  I love this sentence from Chris Breault’s discussion of VVVVVV: “For all the posturing by elitists in the gaming community, there’s no skill to games but patience.”
VVVVVV is not for everybody. If you’re easily frustrated or don’t want your games to stress you out, then avoid this one.  But if you are able to reach the flow state and rise above the challenges presented, you will experience the most euphoric feeling of victory in gaming.

I bought this game when it was on the Steam weeklong deal, and was really happy to have had a chance to try it out.
If you are interested in rogue-likes, action platformers, space themes, and loads of loot collecting, then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are nice - the detail in the enemies and different cargo containers you encounter is well-done. The sound effects and music are decent, however, the radio can get annoying fairly quickly. I like how the music volume is proportionate to how close you are to the home container. Once you gain a few (persistent) levels, you will unlock a music player, allowing you to use your own music. Keep in mind, however, that you must use audio files in .wave or .ogg format (never seen the latter before).
The controls are easy to familiarize yourself with, and the initial tutorial is quick and very helpful. The learning curve is minimal to moderate, depending on your experience with action platformers and/or rogue-likes. One of the most difficult aspects of the game is balancing your risk (going deeper into containers further away from the home base) and upgrade path - failure to achieve a proper balance will result in you getting quickly steamrolled by enemies that get progressively stronger with each new wave.
The main idea behind Cargo Commander is to amass as much loot as possible. Each sector you are in will yield a total of 4 higher-tier loot, forcing you to travel to different sectors if you wish to collect all possible loot (and also advance in levels, because more unique loot = more experience gain). After completing a few waves, a cargo container with a sector key will appear, and if you collect it you will be able to use it to unlock a new sector. Unlocking new sectors allow you to either select a pre-existing one (all user-generated), or create your own. You can move to and from unlocked sectors for free. Dying will end your "run," bringing you to the score distribution screen.
If you manage to be the top scorer in your sector, your character will spawn with a golden crown. Besides the scoring competition, you cannot directly interact with other players. During your playthroughs, you will eventually come across postcards. If they are empty, you can leave a message on them for others to find. The pictures on the front are randomized, and you can write whatever you want on the back.
As you progress through the game and level up your character, you will gain new perks - like starting with 10 currency and an upgrade bench. Using the upgrade bench is essential to surviving, and you can tailor your upgrade path to suit your playstyle. For example, levelling up your armor (health) and weapons versus levelling up your oxygen capacity and speed.
You will periodically receive parcels from your family back on Earth, and you can purchase these by using any of the loot you have already found (until the total cost has been satisfied).
Enemies spawn from crystals, which will keep spawning creeps until you destroy them (if you choose to). You can drill through most walls, and opening a container to hard vacuum to suck out your enemies is always fun. You can fly (or even skip) from container to container, however, the longer you stay in space, the higher the chance of scavengers spawning. This enemy type is weak, but very annoying - if enough of them spawn, you may have trouble staying alive.
After a set amount of time, a wormhole will appear, pulling apart all of the containers violently. You must balance and risk moving further away from your home base in order to find more loot. A challenging part of this game is your character automatically orienting to match the plane of each container. Due to this, trying to move from one container to another can be difficult at first - you will eventually learn to use this to your advantage (ex: hurling yourself toward your home base by jumping out of a container at the right angle).
The rogue-like elements come in the form of procedurally-generated, randomized cargo container spawns for each wave and permadeath. The "main" loot (4 for each sector) is specific for each sector you play in, but all other loot types are randomized as well. There is a small, shiny, blue container that is typically a "treasure" container with at least 1 piece of main loot, however, it can also sometimes have useless items. As you level up (through loot acquisition), you will gain more bonuses like extra starting cash, an upgrade bench, etc. Using the upgrade bench provides bonuses exclusive to your run, and are lost when you restart. The difficulty progression also ramps up with a fairly relentless pace - if you skip too many containers per wave, expect to die very early.
Overall, the game is very fun and challenging - and any rogue-like and/or action platformer enthusiasts should definitely give Cargo Commander a try.
Highly recommend!

To my mind, the worst mistake made by the Western powers was letting Republican Spain be conquered by the Fascists. If France, UK, and US had gauranteed Republican Spain's soverignty, they could never have been driven out of Europe in 1940. Worst case scenario, they could have retreated to Spain, and continued the war from there. Should the US joine the Allies early? No. Even if they have to support Spain alone, it is very important for the US to preserve it's freedom of action. In a game that I played as the US, Spain actually drifted to the Fascists BECAUSE the UK was bombing Spainish infrastructure. Defeat the Nationalists in Spain:yes. SAS: Zombie Assault 4 is an aged top-down shooter where you play as a marine fulfilling different objectives and finishing missions. It offers both single player and multiplayer game modes.
There is no serious story behind this game, but in my opinion you also dont need a deep story just to clarify why you are shooting tons of zombies down. Sometimes there is an intro when you start different missions, somewhat explaining what you have to do. The gameplay consists of 1) killing few hundred zombies 2) running to another player 3) killing another few hundred of zombies 4) looking for an objective (if there is one, since not all missions have it) and finally 5) killing few more hundred zombies including mostly a boss. As you can imagine this gets grindy and repetative quite quickly. Since there are only 7 missions, there is not much variation. People who enjoy repetative and grindy gameplay, might enjoy it though.
The combat is quite simple - place your turret and hold your left mouse button down. There were barely missions up to level 20  where i had to position myself right. Mostly zombies die so quick, it doesnt even matter what weapon you are using or where you stand. Sadly, it offers no challenge at all and having playing the game multiple hours I had not a single mission that I would call hard. What kills the combat feeling for me though is the old engine this game runs on - it starts to "lag" or "slow everything down" when there are too many zombies on the map (yes, not on the screen but on the map overall!). That means if your buddy is fighting a wave of zombies in the next room, it might take you a while to get there since the game engine slows everything down since it cant handle the mass of zombies.
The graphic is really aged in SAS:ZA4. It definetely is not an eye candy, most characters look the same or at least very similar. The interface consists mostly of simple buttons and strangely you can buy ammunition while on a mission. Once everyone throws their turret and grenades around, the screen feels with laggy stottering spam and with that old graphic it definetely is not enjoyable.
There are no mini-games besides if you count gathering and opening the loot boxes. The progress is consisting of grinding same missions over and over again. Since there are only 7 different + 2/3 different timely available contracts, it gets boring rather quick. Some harder missions and difficulties are locked behind character level, so if you want to get to the end game, you have to grind those zombies for hours, no skill envolved.
The audio and music was fine until I started playing with friends and saw, there is no volume adjusting. Its either on or off and sadly, the music is far too loud. So you either turn it completely off or adjust it in windows. Few missions were fine with same music, but then it not only repetetive, but also at some point of the game broken since the engine slowed down due to mass of zombies, so did the sound. You only can hear broken pieces of shots and explosions in the later game.
SAS: Zombie Assault 4 is fun for the first few hours, but once you get into later game and the engine cant handle it, the game starts to turn broken, laggy and very repetetive. The cash shop offering heavy pieces of gear instead of cosmetic items can be refered as P2W and kills any competetive elements this game has (ladderboards). If you up for a casual top-down zombie shooting with some friends, you might enjoy SAS:ZA4 for a short time, but besides that I cant recommend this game.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth playing this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

This game is based off of the 1915 novel by John Buchan. The novel is also named "The 39 Steps" and is an intriguing story about espionage, crime, adventure, and action. It is quite a rollercoaster of a story! As someone who has read the original novel, I was very pleased with this game. Also, this isn't really a game, per se. This is an immersive story that relies heavily on text and imagery to draw you into the plot. Thus, if you get bored reading books, then, this definitely won't be up your alley. You cannot change the outcome of the ending, you don't really have choices, and you aren't really playing anything. You are merely (for the most part) reading a lot of text and going along for the ride. However, the artwork in this game is STUNNING. Absolutely stunning. I have rarely ever seen such rich and vibrant artwork in games. Also, the voice acting in this game is superb. It's essentially a visual novel with voice acting, more or less. The voice acting, as I've mentioned, is very well done. The scenes also change often, and, each new scene offers more beautiful art to look at. It was overall an extremely satisfying experience. Book lovers will adore this game. Art lovers will, too. I was captivated with it from start to finish. However, if you are the type who doesn't like to read or gets bored easily with games where there's "not much to do", then, this may not be your cup of tea. It was most certainly my cup of tea, though, and I adored every second of this beautiful game! I only hope that the developers bring more works of classic literature to life. They did a splendid job here and the makers of this game should definitely make more of these literature-based games. 10/10 from me, without a doubt.

Think back to the medieval days, okay, just remember the
ecomomics gameplay where resources were created by a villager and then reworked into a variety of other objects and buildings for your town. Though micro-managing your village/town/city is what might bring you to play
and
and other games like it (
and
to name a few more) each game is slightly different in implementing basic tasks like gathering resources and completing projects.
unlike the other city building games does not rely on your ability to task individual villagers (game depending - still no one knows how work gets done in
) to a job that needs doing, rather the city determines who works where. You, the despotic mayor controls how many people can work a profession and how many workers each work site can accept. The key concepts for
is population control through resources (including housing) and resource control through professions. Understanding your city's needs will help you determine how you can grow and what big civil plans your city can support. Since I don't want to spoil much of the leraning curve that is essential to feeling the pain of poor intuitive sense, I will just explain the pleasurable parts of this game and then discuss the bothersome parts.
What I enjoyed:
Trading - this is cool that you can pool resources into a building that you can trade for outside goods to sustain your economy (especially stone). I might cahnge what goods come into the town by trade to reflect what the city might want to buy. For example, a city rolling in 2000 logs will not want to buy more logs - that's just silly. Instead, a more scarce resource should be brought instead to reflect that a trader works on simple economics.
City Planning - some buildings complement each other and some don't. It's always fun to enhance a building's output by careful proximal placement to another building with the same resource needs.
City Hall - this is a high investment high reward building. Unlike most of the game where only your current level of resorces is known, the city hall maintains records of resource production over the years (up to 100). It also acts as a professions panel to control where your workers work, has records of population and nice graphs for ease of use, and keeps track of what seeds and stock you can grow (provided that you have animals of which to breed).
What I did not enjoy and found frustrating to the point of laughing at:
Worker designation - the game is not that smart. It designates certain named villagers to tasks, if you change something on the professions page, then someone with an old job will change change to a new job. This might not necessarily be the person right next to the job you want him to have (unfortunately, this is most often the case). When you task workers using the building's task worker interface, in order to get the worker to work specifically at that building, you must make sure conditions are right for the auto-place worker to put the villager where you want them.
Quarries and mines - these useful but resource intensive production buildings are great as huge stockpiles of resources that take a while to get out of the ground. The drawback is that they permenantly use your land - no refilling for farms or trees. This sucks because quarries need lots of space
flat land, both of which cannot be spared for your megatropolis. It phases itself out of the meta and should be reworked so that it can be more useful in the long-run.
Mountains, hills, and those damn snakey tributaries - the terrain is a bother. There can be really weird mountain shapes that prevent you from mining on them due to the static mine model placement characteristcs. One red square due to terrain mislocation and no dice. This holds true for those rolling hills that look fine, but actually prevent you from putting anything from a mine on them. And lastly, the small little bumps in the ground that you flatten with stockpiles, but even when flat (viewed from all angles) remember that they were once a hill and prevent you from building anything on them.
needs to implement a remove elevation feature for these pesky situations.
All in all I would rate this game a 7.5/10, somewhat better than I expected but still needs improvement.

---
First of all, I love the setting, and if I remember correctly isnt there also some connection with the MOTÖRHEAD game? I've read something about that. At least, the setting reminds of something that I have read on the official facebook page.
Anyway, back to the game:
First off: Yes, this game is very early Beta (If not even Alpha).

But you can be anything you like, as long you find the cards for it and the right weapon.
---

Alright, so after putting 10 hours into Victor Vran and completing ALL of the content that this Early Access had to offer, here is my review:
The game takes a bit of a casual approach to the ARPG genre, pretty close to that of Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance. The enemies in this version of EA have good AI, varied skills, and different means in which you should go about defeating them if you want to be efficient. Rather than having classes, in VV (Victor Vran) there is only one hero, that's why his name is the same as the game. Instead the game's focus is on making every piece of equipment so vastly different that gives the game a very unique feel. Each weapon has a different attacks, effects and skills/abilities associated with them. There are also powerful spells that require you to build up energy through various means to perform for great effect, and potions/elixirs to quickly change the flow of battle in your favor.
The game offers a challenge to the more experienced players pretty early on in the form of Hexes. When activated, they will continiously reward you so long as they are on, but also make the enemies far more dangerous. As a veteran of ARPGs, I felt far more entertained with two of them on the entire time that I played, turning on a couple more every now and then to make the game more difficult when I went back to clear lower level areas. Speaking of which, every area has a set of five challenges that you can complete for immediate rewards. While this is cool and all, I sincerely hope that is not their idea of "end-game content."
The graphics in VV are good for an ARPG, no complaints there and the animations feel very fluid. Aesthetically, the game reminds me a lot of Torchlight which I miss quite a bit, so this game is hitting a lot of the right places for me. Sound-wise, so far the game has had a few bugs like a sound effect getting stuck on a loop but I am sure it's already being fixed, or will be. Now the controls... They are not your typical ARPG like Diablo or Path of Exile where it is mouse-based movement, instead VV goes for a WASD movement style with a panning camera which a lot of people are not too excited about. Honestly, after about an hour or two of gameplay and rebinding the keys to my liking, the gameplay felt very smooth. There are times when their acrobatics system is a bit tedious and being a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥with wall-climbing... It is a nice system that just takes a little getting used to but gives so many new options to how you approach the environment.
Currently, my only problem is... What will this game's content be like? What about it's end-game? Many ARPGs use procedurally generated content because it makes every playthrough a little different and makes repeating areas a whole lot less tedious. Victor Vran does not take after this idea and uses hand crafted terrain with preplaced enemy spawns. Now while I didn't really feel this was a big problem, it does take a bit of the magic away. This leads me to wonder about what will happen once you clear all of the areas and challenges, then what? Is that it? Path of Exile has semiannual races/leagues, maps, and a permadeath alternative. Diablo has levels of torment, bounties, and a pemadeath option as well. What will Victor Vran have? What will make me want to keep coming back to this game? Or is that really it, just a campaign with Hexes and Challenges to spice it up?
So in the end, my answer is Yes, I recommend this game as it stands now. I had a fun 10 hours of gameplay and feel the game has already been worth the $15 USD that I paid for it.
