Very torn on this one. It's a "digital adaptation" of Buchan's espionage story
and it's about as well-made as a visual novel can get. The voice acting is superb (performed by a real theater company, I believe), the gorgeous hand-drawn artwork really makes you feel like you're in pre-WWI Britain, and the overall interface is sleek without betraying the lovingly-rendered throwback aesthetic.
Unfortunately, the story itself is the main thing holding me back from giving this a more enthusiastic thumbs-up. It's essentially an innocent-man-on-the-run thriller, and the middle 3/5ths or so of the game basically have the main character escaping one sticky situation after another, with little in the way of actual plot or character development taking place. Because this is a straightforward novel with no player choice involved, this middle section really dragged for me as chapter after chapter of near-misses began to give me deja vu. The story picks up some momentum towards the end as the main plot finally begins to unfold (there's a global conpsiracy involved, which is always fun), but don't expect much in the way of action or suspense; the climax felt appropriately genteel for this most old-timey of British thrillers. (The original novel was written in 1915, so what do you expect).
With those caveats, I do recommend this game to visual novel fans, both for its production value and because the story does ultimately maintain some interest even during its repetitive middle chapters.
This was the first project of a development team called The Story Mechanics, and it looks like their intention was to produce "digital adaptations" (their term) of various literary works, beginning with this one. I went looking for them online and was sorry to see that they appear to be defunct, which is really a shame given the amount of skill and obvious enthusiasm they brought into making this game. Hopefully they'll return in another form?
I've never actually read the novel this is based on, but I have seen the Alfred Hitchcock movie version, which is fantastic and you should definitely watch it regardless of whether you get this game. (Though I was confused why the main character in this game didn't have a woman handcuffed to him while he was on the run... only to realize that Hitch probably threw that in there just to spice things up. Not a bad call, really)

Hmm,
This game received a
of criticism at launch, and its not like it didn't deserve it; the game was lacking in a lot of aspects and had so much potential to be more than what it was.
Fast forward to now when the Wild Run expansion has released and brought a slew of changes to the game visually and gameplay wise. I would actually recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the Test Drive Unlimited series which were also made by some of the developers of this game! If a huge map, exotic vehicles + customisation, and the freedom to drive around is what you want then this game has it all and plenty.
I mostly played The Crew prior to the Wild Run update. It was actually a lot of fun going through the to be honest meh storyline, but that isn't what anyone bought this game for. The selling point was obviously the fact that the map is a scaled version of the United States, and good grief is it amazing.
For what it is, it has plenty of detail (and now looks stunning as well thanks to the update) and nothing will beat the road trips you take solo or with friends, perhaps strangers on the road also playing their own game (so to speak because its a quick drop in/out lobby system for lack of a better phrase) between the various states. Putting my phone on a speaker dock next to me, setting up my Logitech DFGT, turning off the HUD, going to cockpit view and cruising along the freeways at night is just so wonderful I can't even describe it. And it's not short road trips either, getting across the states will take an actual hour or 2, maybe more, depending on the route. Super easy to lose time in this game like that.
Speaking of, car physics. It's pretty arcadey, but everyone expected that (right?). They've definitely improved it since launch and its fine to play now for the most part IMHO.
is handled pretty well. The UI could with quality-of-life tweaks but the modding of each vehicle it self is pretty well fleshed out (looking at you, NFS 2015). Should be noted, that all the vehicles do not have all the specs available to them. You can imagine my disappointment to the lack of a raid Murcielago :( still, Fiat 500 Monster Truck.
Music selection in this game is nice, didn't agree with a few songs but hey, I just play my own while playing now so. Car selection is also pretty good.
I cannot speak much for the events and the Wild Run exclusive "Summit", but I hear good things. PVP races are prone to being glitchy occasionally (maybe they fixed this now, can't tell for sure) but they have definitely balanced the vehicles you can use for the races now as compared to pre-Wild Run (the LaFerrari was the go to car if you wanted any chance at winning for example in the Perf-spec), so thank you devs!
So there you go, my thoughts on The Crew. Would 100% recommend if you love cruising around the USA.

This game could be so great, but unfortunately I can't recommend this game in its current state.
- They still haven't fixed performance problems that many systems have since the Wild Run update (it included some major graphical changes), despite those systems fulfilling more than the recommended specs. Sudden FPS drops for no apparent reason make it impossible to stay on the road sometimes. Really frustrating.
- PVP is not fun anymore for me personally. So there are the 5 different specs in the base game, which drive completely different. For example I love the circuit spec, which drives much like a real racing car would (even though it's far from realistic). You used to be able to select, which spec you prefer and play that one. Now they let people vote before the start of the race. Most people enjoy the street spec, which is much more arcade style. So if you like any of the other specs, you have to join a lot of races you don't really like, just to maybe win the vote one time and have a race you can enjoy.
- The previous point gets amplified by the fact that there really is no endgame content besides PVP unless you buy the Wild Run DLC. Though, I'm refusing to put more money into the game until they fix what I described in my first point.
- Thousands of players play this game. Yet the world feels completely empty, because of the their bad phasing system, where you see just a hand full of players at any give time, which are usually 5-20km away from you, meaning you basically never meet someone else just randomly on the street.
- The game world is definately very pretty and detailed, there's no arguing that. The USA are just not very racer-friendly in my opinion. In free play mode you spend a lot of time on highways that are not really interesting to drive on. You have to actively search for roads that are fun to drive on. Even though the world is huge, this makes it seem like there are only a few "good" roads that get boring after a while.
- Too many micro-transactions for a (former) full-price title. They are not mandatory, but it still bothers me when you paid for a game and have to pay extra for more content.
I had so much fun with this game, especially right after release. But it keeps getting worse and worse, because the developers don't seem to understand what is good for the game. Instead they try to milk as much cash out of the customers before the title completely dies out. It's really sad, because it could have been a long-term successful title, with just some minor adjustments and bug fixes..

The basic concept is kinda fun, but you will quickly realize that the game plays exactly the same way during the first 10 minutes of the game as it does in the next 10 hours of the game. Basically no new concepts, enemies, weapons, abilities, etc. are added.
There's basically 5 or so different types of enemies that mostly vary based on size (this guy is the same as the last one except a big larger, with more health and more damage!). The cargo you collect has no meaning or purpose other than "collect them all because you can!"
The upgrade system can almost trick you into playing more, until you realize that the number of upgrades are tiny and they reset at the end of every day, so the only sense of progression comes from ranking up, which gives tiny, boring advantages (often something like "you start with this small upgrade without having to buy it!"
The general concept is "you activate a big magnet on your ship, then rectangular cargo containers crash into your ship and you run from container to container collecting items, ammo, killing enemies, etc." Except the enemies are limited, there's 4 weapons, and the building layouts quickly repeat themselves. It's vaguely amusing for the first hour or so, and then you quickly get tired of it. I got all of the achievements because I'm a terrible person with a terrible problem, but I wouldn't recommend getting it for any other reason.

Outlast is a relatively well done survival-horror game which efficiently blends the thrills and chills in equal measure. However, while Outlast delivers an effective experience with the genre norm, it doesn't deviate from the set path for anything creative and unique. One can expect the usual set pieces, the usual enemies, and the overly used jump scares.
Now, to be fair... I certainly had my fair share of scares throughout the game (most of which were creatively placed), but towards adventures end I had found myself becoming slightly frustrated and annoyed with the lack of creativity. It was the same set path, over and over. Find this, hide from one enemy, run away, repeat. Outlast's biggest issue is the lack of enemy unpredictability, as essentially every encounter is scripted and therefore predictable.
That aside, Outlast is an extremely polished video game. The visuals are gorgous, realistic, and smooth. The audio is clear, crisp, and efficient at setting the mood. The use of the video recorder as night vision isn't anything new (and was a tad over-used), but was implemented and designed extremely well, and was definitely one of the games strongest aspects. Unfortunately Outlast is a short game, with limited (if at all), replayability.
I would only recommend a purchase of the game if it is on sale and you're itching for a quick horror fix.

SAS: Zombie Assault 4 is just a classic flash game based on zombie killing. Well designed, fun to play and can be really challenging. Steam version is probably some kind of old version, however graphic looks even better. Also there's a few issues:

City-building strategy. Plays like a RTS (aside from being able to speed-up and pause) but instead of fighting against npcs or players you fight the elements and the goal is to survive. To avoid perishing you'll need shelter, resources (stone/logs/iron) but also tools to use them with, and hey, don't forget your clothing or you'll freeze in winter. Oh, what's that? You built a tailor and blacksmith early on? Now you'll have to starve because you don't have enough gatherers or fishermen. Sorry.
But when you finally manage to juggle professions and birthrate (yes, if you don't increase population you'll end up with a village of 70-80 year olds that wont reproduce and eventually die. That was attempt 3.) it's immensely satisfying.

The goal is simple: build your settlement into a successful town. You'll manage resources such as food and building materials, as well as the mental, physical, and even spiritual wellbeing of your citizens. Oh yeah - and you'll need to try to prepare them to survive inevitable disasters such as various plague-type illness or severe weather that completely decimates their food supply without warning.
This is a very easy game to learn to play, and very, very difficult to master. I highly recommend that you play through the voluntary tutorial: it doesn't take long and doing so will save you a lot of hair-tearing your first few times trying to keep your people alive. Don't get me wrong, you're still going to facepalm and scream in frustration more often than not - but as strange as it may sound, that's why you'll keep playing! Nothing is more addictive than getting just that liiiiittle bit further along than you did last time, and that is exactly how this game keeps you hooked: just when you think you've figured everything out, along comes a tidy mess to decimate the population and make you rethink your entire strategy. It's a bit like Othello (the game) in that regard.
You have to be creative, detail-oriented, flexible, strategic AND resilient to really enjoy this amazingly indepth and detailed game. It truly is worth every penny you pay to play. I *highly* recommend it.

A challenging multitasking simulator where the individual tasks involve filling customers' restaurant orders or performing other daily restaurant chores.  The interface can, at times, feel like you are interacting with a rhythm game, trying to clear the queue of keys or clicks as quickly and accurately as possible.  The progression curve is relatively forgiving on the normal setting, introducing a simple concept or mechanic on each "day" (i.e. each game round).  As you develop a familiarity with the various steps required to prepare the dishes or perform the cleanup chores, you will be better equipped to customize the active menu.  You will also be more informed about where your precious seconds are being gobbled up by interfering events and chores.
The art style and sound elements are complementary, informing the player that preparing and serving food in the game is not such a graceful ballet.  The assets reflect this meal prep as a slapdash affair, successful when you haphazrdly jam the elements together as quickly and accurately as possible, the overall goal to churn the customers through.  The frantic key-pressing and inevitable screw-ups lend an element of humor to the experience.

What an interesting little game.
It's a Team Online-Multiplayer game with several game modes, all of which are classics. Team Death Match, Capture the Flag, and King of the Hill, with a few variations of these.
Everyone plays a bot, and there are a few to choose from. Each with their own little stats and weapons, although sadly customisation is very very minimal. You can select some active skills ( 2 ), and 4 passives. That's it.
I would have liked if you could actually customise your bot's look and weapons more as it seems rather funky that the smallest one with smallest looking weapons is actually the heaviest with the largest rocket launchers around.
The game is entirely meant to be played online, which could be very very problematic as so few people are online. Then again the game is only Just out, so it might pick up online.
It would have been better if there was even a small little single player campaign, even if only for the tutorial; which at the moment is just text and some animations of bots and a generator.
It's not bad, and it gets the point across but I feel it could do with more there.
In regards to single player, at the moment all it is, is the online matches played against bots. Similar to games of old, if there aren't enough people online the teams get filled with Bots. Their A.I can be lacking at times, and I've seen my team flag runner often getting stuck on another friendly bot.
Gameplay wise it's rather fun, and I do like the music. It's not hard to pick up at all and that's partially due to familiar game modes, controls and limited customisation. You simply quickly select your perks and get in there blasting.
At any time during the match you can simply press T, which brings up the original Bot menu. Here you can select a new bot or change your actives and passives.
That's it really. It's kinda fun, but nothing stellar. Although like most online focused games will be substantially improved when playing with and against friends over Voice Comms.

A simple, relaxing and short experience.
Refunct is very easy to play. Due to that, the game doesn't need to explain stuff to you with text on the screen, which keeps to the relaxing nature of the game.
Your objective is to bring the minimalist world back to life, by pressing buttons scattered around. As you do this, more parts of the world rise out of the water, and are available to traverse. The cool thing is the entire game takes place in this one area, there is no level select.
Throughout the environment there are some objects which create for a bit more interesting gameplay. Springs that throw you up into the air, or pipes you need to slide through. You also need to wall jump to get to some places.
Although the game is very short, I had an enjoyable little journey. The mechanics are simple enough and fun that it's actually a good game to replay if you feel like just taking it easy a bit and running through a nice looking world.
Overall, fun little game.

**DISCLAIMER**
I received a review key from the dev.  I also have some gifs of the game on my website if you want to take a look at them.
Overview:
First person platforming games are making a comeback, and parkour-style games look they’re starting to come back in full force. Refunct is a short and sweet platformer, featuring a minimalistic art style, light elements of parkour, an engaging musical track and flowing gameplay.  Discover the world and create your own path as you jump, slide, climb and swim around a beautifully crafted world.
Graphics:
The graphics in Refunct are simple, minimalistic perfection.  Refunct embraces the simplicity of it’s graphics and makes excellent use of its setting and environment to generate beauty from simplicity.  Refunct’s world features a day and night system, with the world gracefully changing from a blinding morning as the sun rises, to a cool evening as the sun slowly dips below the horizon as stars dot the sky.  The various blocks the make up the environment start off gray,  and regain their color as you bound across the world, as you revitalize the world and bring life to your surroundings.  For all of it’s beauty, Refunct does run into a common stumbling block that is seen often in minimalistic design, repetitiveness.  As beautiful as the world looks, the revitalized blocks look identical to each other, the same brown and green platforms dot the landscape, and while at first aesthetically pleasing, different color schemes would break up the monotony of the world.  Another small complaint about the graphics, is how the “grass” that appears after you revitalize a block, is just the top of the block colored green, not actual grass.  All things considered, the graphics for Refunct are gorgeous, with only a few minor details that take away from the experience.
Sound:
Refunct’s gameplay emphasizes peaceful exploration, and the soundtrack does a wonderful job in creating a relaxing, almost dream-like atmosphere to complement the gameplay.  The music is never intrusive and helps push the gameplay along, allowing you to feel like it’s okay to take your time and explore all the nooks and crannies the world has to offer.  The sound effects that accompany your actions are functional, they help emphasize your movement and feel organic to the game.
Gameplay:
First person platforming has never been a popular genre, with Mirror’s Edge being the only AAA game in recent memory that fits the genre.  With the recent resurgence of indie games, we’re now seeing a wider variety of games, covering genres that have largely gone untouched by some of the bigger studios.  Refunct has tossed its hat into the first person platforming ring, where it joins recent recent indie newcomers such as Deadcore and Lemma.
With exploration being the main focus of Refunct, tight controls and solid movement mechanics are going to be foundational to enjoyable gameplay. At first glance, Refunct doesn’t seem to innovate or push the envelope for first person platformers.  The basic movement mechanics are all there, you’re able to jump, climb up ledges, swim, slide and wall jump.  These mechanics aren’t particularly new or different and don’t seem to make the game stand out at all, but that’s exactly why the game shines.  The mechanics are implemented wonderfully, all of these mechanics feel organic and natural extension of your character.  There aren’t outstanding bugs, or quirks about these movement options, which allow you to become fully immersed in the game.  When these mechanics are combined with tight and responsive controls, any mistakes that are made, fall on you.  Refunct is a game about exploration, about forging new paths and discovering different avenues to reach your goal.  The controls and movement options are solidly implemented and augment the atmosphere that the game is trying to convey.
The actual gameplay for Refunct is simple, you spawn on a cluster of grey blocks that make up a tiny island and there’s a big red button that’s begging to be pressed, once you press the button more islands will rise out of the ocean with more big red buttons that you’ll need to press.  As you hop from island to island, you’ll revitalize the world around you, as grey blocks burst into color as soon as you step onto them.  The game isn’t particularly challenging, with only the last couple of buttons providing an actual challenge on how to reach them, but the point of this game isn’t to provide a challenge.  Refunct provides an unique experience that’s not common in indie games nor AAA games.  It manages to meld the atmosphere and purposefulness of walking simulators, with the joy and mechanics of a well polished platformer.
Conclusion/Notes:
For all of its strong points, Refunct does have one glaring flaw, length.  Refunct took me about half an hour to complete to 100 percent, and that’s with a lot of exploration(diving into the water is an amazing experience) and trying to find alternate routes to get to a button.  As much as I did enjoy my time with Refunct, the time was woefully short and left me wanting more.  The more challenging platforming came near the end and I would have loved an additional hour to spend roaming the world and completing more platforming challenges.   At times, Refunct feels like the engine for a much larger and more ambitious game, as the mechanics and controls polished to perfection.  Even given the length of the game, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Refunct and would recommend it to those that are looking for something a little bit different.
I do want to spend some time giving out a shout out to the developer for the game, Dominique Grieshofer.  Not only is the game akin to a pleasant stroll in the park, he manages to fully immerse the player in the world.  He seems to have an inherent ability to speak to the player and direct the player towards an objective without explicitly telling the player what to do and where to go.
If you’re on the fence about whether or not the game is for you, hopefully the gifs do an adequate job on relating the atmosphere and tranquility that the game offers.  The game sits at $3 on Steam and I believe it’s well worth the money.

The goal is simple: build your settlement into a successful town. You'll manage resources such as food and building materials, as well as the mental, physical, and even spiritual wellbeing of your citizens. Oh yeah - and you'll need to try to prepare them to survive inevitable disasters such as various plague-type illness or severe weather that completely decimates their food supply without warning.
This is a very easy game to learn to play, and very, very difficult to master. I highly recommend that you play through the voluntary tutorial: it doesn't take long and doing so will save you a lot of hair-tearing your first few times trying to keep your people alive. Don't get me wrong, you're still going to facepalm and scream in frustration more often than not - but as strange as it may sound, that's why you'll keep playing! Nothing is more addictive than getting just that liiiiittle bit further along than you did last time, and that is exactly how this game keeps you hooked: just when you think you've figured everything out, along comes a tidy mess to decimate the population and make you rethink your entire strategy. It's a bit like Othello (the game) in that regard.
You have to be creative, detail-oriented, flexible, strategic AND resilient to really enjoy this amazingly indepth and detailed game. It truly is worth every penny you pay to play. I *highly* recommend it.

I don’t think I’ve ever played a game on Steam before, that could be considered as pointless as Jumping Tank. I never even rated a game before with 1 out of 10 or 10/100, because even the worst title played to date had at least one redeeming point to its abysmal gameplay. Not this one though. The two hours clocked by Steam are not accurate. Its Trading Cards were idled, since they are by far the only thing of value to an otherwise useless package. I didn’t endure this “masterpiece” for more than 15 minutes of real time. Normally I would encourage a dev team at its debut to keep trying and perhaps their second attempt would be enjoyable, but I’m willing to use developer Maximus.ez as a clear example of just how wrong and lenient, the Steam Greenlight program has been and why it has to be shut down as soon as possible.
Where to begin? I’ve played smartphone games (and I’m far from a fan of the mobile gaming platforms) that were superior to Jumping Tank in all regards. You have a 2D environment and sprites made in one of the laziest examples of Unity Engine asset use, which not only have limited diversity, but the level itself is the same despite the illusion of in-game progress. Instead of at least several levels to unlock, you have basically, the same one with minor obstacle rearrangement. You control a cartoonishly drawn tank that cannot fire its turret nor does it have any targets to shoot at. So why did they use a tank as a game protagonist? Mystery. Anyways, the game’s objective is equally simplistic: reach a lever that will unlock the pathway to a blue duct through which you must enter. That’s it. No foes or challenge. You jump with the tank until you reach the lever while avoiding the hedgehog heads that will result in instant death. So much fun!
Avoid this “game” like the plague. I’m still debating if it would be a worthy acquisition as part of a cheap bundle or when bought for 10 cents during a Steam Sale. If those Trading Cards are worth it to you, perhaps. I was disappointed when I missed the chance to receive Jumping Tank on Orlygift but looking back on it now, I had no reason to be sad. Wasting 30 minutes to play & write about it is the real tragedy here.

"Souls" is a weird series because with each new edition there seems to be steps taken forward and steps taken backwards on successfully previously established components.
I found this game being the most re-playable. 600hours on the original and nearing 200hr on this version. I will say It does the most important things the others fail to do, or just does them outright better.
Dark Souls 2 never drops frames anywhere, at all. Stutter/slowdowns are nonexistent. This is easily the best optimized game released by From Software. It runs on a completely different engine then any of the other souls games do. This gives it a different feel. Where It shines the most is with its implented features that make PvP more/the most balanced. It has the widest variety of weapon types and combinations (actual weapon to weapon combo links are possible). Crossover movesets that 1 and 3 just dont have and being able to dual weild almost anything. Of course there are those weapons that are outright stronger but the meta in the game allows for anything to be viable. It also still remains the most technical (even with the release of Dark Souls 3) Unlocked play opens up a skillful spacing game that takes a very very long time to master.  Dark Souls 1 PvP is also skillful but very linear and revolves around backstab tech. Dark Souls 2 has far much more technical mechanics, these are just a few examples : Animation cancels, Inverted backsteps, Quicker quick Rolls, Pivot Backstabs, Recovery cancels, Quicker quick attacks, Stanceswap run/roll attacks, Movement freedom in any direction/tracking.
One of the most frustrating things about the previous game was punishing a healer. This is reduced hugely due to how long estus takes to drink and that it replenishes health very slowly as opposed to instantly. Dark Souls 2 does take a few steps back on world design, lore (who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥about this? lol), and bosses.The DLC included being the complete opposite, nonlinear and explorative, jam packed with a tone of new content for more replayability. It almost feels like the core of this games design was the multiplayer and it's always populated and fast.

Combat, Weapons, and Abilities:
The combat mechanics are smooth and support both keyboard/mouse and Controller. Being able to dodge and roll adds the feeling of complete control over the encounter situation. Though, it is a hack and slash ARPG, you still have the flexibility to choose how to go about an encounter.
Weapons determine which set of abilities you have. Each weapon comes with a basic attack and 2 specials attacks. Each unique within themselves, pressing you to be more tactful in your decisions. You can equip 2 weapons at one time. For example, you can carry a Shotgun with a Rapier. Allowing you begin the encounter ranged and then dashing in to strike quick and devasting blows. Switching between weapons is situation dependant and personal choice. It is, however, needed in order to progress with harder difficulty settings.
The four weapon choices are: Sword, Hammer, Shotgun, and Rapier.
Demon Power is nothing new to ARPG MMOs, in this game you will eventually (once you increase in level) be able to equip 2 separate demon powers.
Maps and Difficulties:
The maps range in size, just as any other ARPG. Where this game separates itself most from others like it, is the ability to jump. Jumping allows for you to reach heights where secret treasures await you. The current available maps environments range from inside a castle of Skeletons, outside in a spider infested courtyard, to deep into the bowels of an earth encrusted dungeon. Each sharing similar mobs as well as having their own unique sets of encounters.
The difficulty of the game is set by you at anytime. The hex system is quite enjoyable, you control a packs buffs and if you want more champions or less. Maybe you are farming for gold, so turn on the hex for gold drop increased. If you are farming for gear, turn on the appropriate hexes and start hacking away on any map you choose. Too hard, then turn off a hex or two until you find your comfort zone.
Character progression, gear, and cards:
As you level your character to level 10 (current max level) you will unlock more weapon, cards, and demon power slots. This is where the customization comes into play.
Cards boost your stats and more importantly can cripple or complement your build. So, choose wisely as a bad setup could leave you crippled on the battlefield.
Farming is part of any ARPG just as much as this one, this game is not for everyone. In order to progress to be able to stack your Hexes, you will need to farm for better gear, cards, weapons, and demon powers. Its a question of will you enjoy it.
Maps Challenges:
Each map has its own set of challenges. So, when you are 68/70 mobs killed without taking any damage and you get hit, you will have to start that challenge over. The positive side is that there are several challenges per map, so if you lose one, you may gain another. Allowing for you to complete that map and come back at a later time, better equipped and with a vengance.
Overall Opinion:
Victor Van.... Van Helsing.... not sure if its a ripoff or a parody of the other. Probably should have given a different name to the game, something more genarlized and not focused on a characters name. This would allow for the choice of Female or Male character.
Positives:
Gameplay is smooth and combat is enjoyable. The various amount of maps are fun to play and with the challenges and hex system, there are hours of gameplay to be had.
The background of the game is colorful and easy on the eyes. Making for some good scenery along your adventures.
Negatives:
The storyline dialogue and voice over is not yet in game, which puts me in a position where I am unable to play for countless hours on end. Not having the storyline, the only thing to do from start to finish is complete the challenges and the first set of quests. Do not expect to get lost in a story when it is not there yet.
The multiplayer is not yet active, so dont be fooled by the advertisement. It is content yet to come.
Should I buy it?
I would suggest buying the early access, since it is currently on sale. Some will get exactly what they pay for while the others will get more out of it. If you want something else to play that is new and inexpensive, buy it.

Disclaimer/TLDR: The game is a Visual Novel based on a novel from 1915, featuring harder-than-everyday's English, strong Scottish accent, and is about as interesting as it would be to read the book - keep these things in mind when purchasing. The story itself is really nice, but it's not presented in a way that it's easy to digest.
39 Steps is one of the worst good-games I played. The story is great, but because how the story, the era, the book is, the story is not the most pleasant to be experienced as a game. The story rather features classes, than real personalities, and focuses on the present - not even a hint what will happen, barely any reflection to the past than remembering the chasers makes the game enjoyable only if you're actively progressing in it - either the story lost parts when it got implemented as a game, or it's not exactly a type of story that works greatly as a game.
The language is a potential problem for a lot of non-native English speakers: the game features a really heavy load of English expressions, as the book of origin is from 1915, featuring well... a lot of fancy-talk between gentlemen and quite some part with really, really strong scottish accent. If anyone has trouble understanding a today's series without subtitles, I'm almost sure that they'll have problem with understanding this game.
The story of the game is interesting, the controls are easy (Click to progress, and mouse-gestures in some scenes) and the voice acting is phenomenal - but with all of this,  I think the story's pacing is off, the text can't really be urged to progress, and it's just slow. There is 19 chapters, and each chapter's title is on screen for 5+ seconds, then the location and date is on screen for 15+ seconds. The game has a lot of audio cues about what's currently happening - sounds of the city, a mass of people, car being cranked up and such, all with outstanding quality, but the majority of the game has no notable background music, or not at all. This turns the game somewhat tedious, as the story is action and progress-oriented. Just as a comparison: a good visual novel has good characters, interaction between them, and an interaction with the setting. In this story the protagonist is fleeing, and he's just states what's happening, whom he is meeting instead of reflecting to them. This is a storytelling VN-like story that focuses of what's happening currently and there are barely any reoccuring characters, and most of them have only a role, a rank, a class instead of a personality.  So in short: there is something happening, but there's barely anything to think about in the game, BUT the thing that's happening. And for me, this is the reason the game took me 3 + 11 hours to finish, while it's around 4h long. It's a really interesting piece, but the presentation's way and VN interpretation makes the game harder to be enjoyed, than the book would be.

When I first looked at this, I was worried that it would disappoint me. I'm glad I was wrong. This has become one of my favorite indie games now.
You play as a cargo commander; a worker for the company known as Cargo Corp. You travel to many sectors collecting cargo from storage units that have flown about in space. From what I've seen just about every sector is user made... at least the names are. This is a rouge-like game where the sectors are formed depending on the name, and I've seen some "interesting" names.
As I said before, you enter the sector and the first thing you do is activate the magnet inside your home unit, which will pull in storage units for you to explore. From there you search these units for cargo, which is indicated by glowing blue boxes with a "C" on them. You can drill through most of the walls inside and outside the container (and your home unit) to get around faster or to make a route to better deal with or escape from enemies. I always loved the drill since it opened new ways to move around the area. It also saved my butt multiple times.
Oh yeah, you though it would be easy to get that cargo huh? Well most of the time you'll find mutants that only want to kill you. You also have to worry about not running out of oxygen when floating outside of containers. Lucky for you you have the weapons to do the job. A personal favorite og mine is the magnabomb launcher. Why put holes in them when you can just blow them up into pieces? Either way all the weapons work wonders and feel great to use.
As you go through these waves of containers, you'll notice that you've been collecting caps. This is the currency of the game, and it allows you to buy upgrades for yourself. Very useful since things get very rough in later waves. Also, if you want to go to other sectors, you need to have a sector pass to unlock one. You simply get them from one of the early containers of the current sector you're in, but you can only get one pass in each sector, which is nice since it encourages people to try other sectors and not stay on one grinding for passes.
The work day ends when you either hit "End Day" in your home unit or when you die. After that you get to see how well you scored compared to others that played the sector... and it made me remember that I didn't talk about the online player involvement in this. While you won't be seeing others playing at th esame time with you, you can at least see their dead corpses from their demise in the sector if they did die. You can even loot the bodies! You'll also find postcards written by others, which is always interesting what I'll get to read as I blow through a ton of mutants.
Ehhhh, back to end of the work day stuff, the next screen you'll see is the cargo you've collected and your current rank. As you find new cargo, your rank meter will go up, and once it fills up, you rank up and get an award that sticks with you for the rest of the game. Some of the really useful ones is the upgrade workbench, a terminal that lets you repair your home unit and lets you use your own playlist for the music that plays inside it, and upgrades.
The game controls really well, and it does make you pay attention to what's going on around you, as a container can slam outside and push you around a lot. I do recommend putting in your own music playlist for your home unit when you get the chance, otherwise you'll only have the two home unit songs that it provides. Oh yeah, there's also a taunt button where all he says is "♥♥♥♥ YOU!", so yeah... take that DMC.
That aside, I highly recommend this game to everyone that's looking for a good rouge-like game. this one does not disappoint.

Warning: Buying this game will get you the most raw depiction of trench warfare.
That being said, it's also got plenty of kinks and oddities left in it after all these years.
But it's still more fun than battlefield 1. TTK is almost non-existant, melees are one hit kill, weapons are locked to their respective squads and nations and a weapon sound update is in the works.
The reason I bought this game however, is for the teamwork.
Verdun rewards you for playing with friends in a squad by linking the squad progression (seperate from player progression) to who you play with, squad xp is retained with each group you play with. It also takes a lot of effort to get from one trench to another, making squad coordination all the more important. Finally, you are issued your kits and classes based on which nation and which regiment you play as, the french wield french rifles, germans have Machine-gewhers, etc.
So grab some friends or buddy up with the squad you get stuck with, just do some research beforehand, watch someone else play it and learn how the classes work.

Cargo Commander is a great platformer and the embodiment of a good indie game--a term which has unfortunately been made meaningless by games _unlike_ this one. CC has a simple premise and simple mechanics: cargo containers crash into your ship, and you must go inside to collect loot and kill monsters. In doing so, you transition in between areas with and without gravity, which leads to interesting cavorting and shifts in view. After a limited amount of time, the containers break apart and you must race back to your ship before suffocating in the vacuum of space.
Where CC goes above and beyond is in delivering value beyond the basic game. The cargo you collect gives you credits to retrieve the mail sent to you by your family. Emails periodically appear in your inbox from various people as well. Through them, you learn the story of why you are a cargo commander. It's the kind of bare and yet tastefully presented story that you can only find in a game which is lovingly made. The various weapons and upgrades form an intelligent strategic layer which varies based on your playstyle. And as the game goes on, you start to get an idea of why there are so many monsters in those containers too. "Multiplayer" leaderboards for persistent levels were also a damn smart idea. What else do you need to find out in a review? It's a bloody well-made game, and it's probably on sale for $0.99. Buy it.

This game is fantastic, playing as a submarine online and trying to stay hidden in the depths while firing torpedos at your enemies is pretty intense.
There are a wide variety of ships, planes and submersibles all manually controllable for you to sink, kamikaze or stay too long under water with (thus suffocating due to lack of oxygen or getting crushed due to the pressure of the depths if you go too low) and many different ways of taking them out.
The game uses things like sonar, amount of munitions, level of depth and crew management to keep you constantly on your toes as you fight to dodge incoming artillery/torpedos/depth charges, sink and destroy enemy ships, bases, planes and submarines and ponder the worth of flying your plane directly into the enemy or risking heading back to the airfield/carrier to restock on explosives.
In short, it's a wonderful game that was ahead of its time and still holds up well to this day. True there are other games like World of Warships that try to do something similar, but they still come off as shallow imitations (albeit a little prettier in the graphics department).
If you're looking for the ultimate navy/aircraft battle simulator, then look no further, for this is it.
Added Bonus - For extra fun in multiplayer, grab control of the little 3 man boats (that can be destroyed by something as tiny as flak from a ship) and try to pull off successful torpedo runs on enemy BBs (heavy battleships), it is a difficult and perilous task, but if you can master it then you can be the nautical equivalent of David and Golliath.

So after about the 10th time of starting a new game due to complete failure, I finally stumbled upon the secret of success.  You see, the difficulty you pick in the beginning of the game basically (from what I understand) determines what your starting inventory balances and structures are going to be.  So when I started the game I figured the normal mode would suffice and I did do the tutorials and I have my fair share of SimCity type games under my belt so off I went.
In games 1-10, a combination of either 1) all of my people died from the cold, 2) all of my people starved to death, or 3) my village no longer produced offspring - meant a hard return to the main menu.  So I developed a few tactics which helped me overcome and expand very quickly... because if you're not expanding you're already out of business!
I start with nothing and immediately build into 4 wood houses, 1 fishing dock, 1 storage barn, 2 (2x7) stockpiles, all of which are extremely condensed.  I add a road both east and west where I build an 'outpost' - forester hut, hunters lodge, forest food scavenger people (whatever they are called).  OF COURSE - you have to build the 1 single outpost first, then build the good old woodmaker (firewood maker) and blacksmith before building the second outpost or you are just going to be up a river and back to the menu real quick.  Once that is done its a matter of well.... build some more (very limited) buildings.  The deal is that while I can store 25000 food and keep the levels sufficient for a large population.  Of course, what is the point then?  It just seems that - UNLIKE other city building games - the continuation of expansion is, well, not fun.  Expanding beyond a certain point is just a chore that drains the fun out of the entire game.
So basically for me, the game went - 1) figure out how to get past the first winter, 2) figuring out if I take the success of 1 and multiply it 10 more times I can have a big village, 3) why am I playing this over being in bed asleep?.
--------------------
Specific complaints
--------------------
WTF is with the builders who insist on building the damn roads instead of the houses sitting there with all the raw materials just waiting to be hammered together?  How about an order of precedence for the AI builders PLEASE!  This alone brought me to a point of failure on multiple games before the first winter.
What is the point of having a traditional 'town'?  It is much better for the game mechanics to keep housing available right next to their job site.  I mean, in the real world towns/cities were created due to people needing both protection and a craving to be social / apart of a community.  There is no reason to have a 'city' in this game.  You can still reach a VERY large population by using the 'outpost' method.
-----------
Conclusion
-----------
Great idea, great concept, great execution.  The community for whatever sick and twisted reason 'hype' this game to be amazing, when it is actually down right shallow and has a complete lack of content in order for you to continue playing once you have gotten past say year 25.  There literally becomes no point in playing the same city at all.  Unless you want to experience the thrill of raising cows and wheat (which you can only get animals and seeds by trade on the river) and you were unable to purchase seeds earlier.  I am sorry to report that waiting on seeds is not enough reason for me to continue playing - although from other reviewers it does seem to be enough for some - is it for you?

There are few games that continue to be divisive as Dark Souls 2, and the fact that people have changed their minds in cycle of love/hate is something I don’t believe one review can explain. In my experience with DS2, Scholar of the First Sin is not the definitive edition because of the graphical update as well as the added DLC; all the big and small touches have created a game that is more confident with its changes.
Before you continue, it’s important that to read my review of DS1 to better understand where I’m coming from as I will not focus on what makes DS2 better/worse than one entry. Instead, I want to discuss what elevates it into a unique experience from the SoulsBorne name.
Perhaps the most misunderstood mechanic is the overreliance on the camera-lock. These games have never explained when you should and shouldn’t rely on this crutch in crowd-control encounters and boss-fights. Enemies rely on tracking your movements when you are locked-on as well as being able to keep an eye on the whole battle are subliminal hints telling you to lower your reliance much like the shield. Once you have broken this habit you will begin to see the merits behind group encounters despite people believing the combat is made for one-on-one duels.
DS2 is perhaps the first to capitalize this idea before Bloodborne, and it’s also the source of most complaints that additional enemies are a design of difficulty, not challenge. The best way I can explain why crowd control works is with a less serious example. In Serious Sam, where arguably the camera inhibits you more, the chaos is mastered through enemy prioritization. You learn weapon counters as well as knowing how to select threats from their proximity, and the satisfaction is attributed to these unspoken rules rather than making every enemy a challenge.
This is why bosses like the Three Sentinels have you fight one to learn the enemy's manuevers shortly before you are taxed to encounter two at once; the skill isn’t knowing your enemy’s openings but knowing how to exploit them. Shortly afterwards there is fight with six gargoyles that continues this concept, adding time-to-kill vs. the risk to prevent the player from being overwhelmed. Enemy encounters throughout DS2 operate similarly because however great you are at duels your mastery is based on how to apply what you know to new situations.

There is one expectation I do agree with fans; if the changes of DS2 were applied to DS1 it wouldn’t be as effective because of the changes made to the level-design and health system.
As I described in my DS1 review, the strength of the new health system is in the recovery period being an option for difficulty. Instead of making the attrition about maximizing your resources, DS2 lets players use health for various reasons. If you’re intimidated, the slow regeneration gives you more time to study opponents while risking more damage; if you’re confident, you can use the regen as an aggressive tactic. Even for PVP, it keeps battles from overstaying their welcome. Instead of scarcity, player choice is the challenge.
DS2 also compensates these changes in its enemy placement and level-design. Here is where SOTFS earns its name as the relocated enemy and item placements add more character to each biome. The ogre in the forest is a unique stealth obstacle; the dragon before its rider makes sense. Not all changes were improvements like the petrified statues; however, most of the changes adds not only more lore but also level-specific obstacles. Funny enough, this version could make a case for how DS2 has become an Easy Mode.
What DS, not DeS, veterans will find harder to accept are changes in world and level-design. Instead of having one interconnected world both lore-friendly and visually, DS2 feels otherworldly with impossible transitions and a clearer sense of direction. The former issue is something I can understand why people find it “video-gamey”; however, it adds both surprise and interpretation into the fabric of Drangleic in time and space with its illogical design. As for the having better direction, this image shows how segmented the world is designed with pathways leading to ends to return to Majula:
As I argued in DS1, the lack of direction was counter-intuitive as it added tedium to a game designed to be repetitive to learn from your failures as well as being confusing to know where you’re intended to go. Furthermore, the misleading sense of freedom from DS whereas DeS is enjoyable because of its non-linearity is addressed in DS2 by having branching paths as well as player-choices to improve replayability as well as circumventing pathways all together. Where DS1 would prevent you from going after the Four Lord Souls and the intended pathway was both easier and faster, DS2 has branching paths of varying levels of difficulty with no abrupt spikes and if you find yourself up against a challenge beyond you there is always the option to go elsewhere and return later. You can even avoid a majority of the game if you choose to use Bonfire Ascetics to farm souls to reach the final route to Drangleic Castle.
Ultimately there is so much agency added from its gameplay, especially with build combinations not restricted by level design, to its variable means of difficulty that nullify the complaints of these games without compromising the Souls’ name. In addition to all these options, there is the best feature of replayability to DS2, the modified NG+ that adds even more challenge for bearers of the curse who seek it lest they remain hollow.

What also deserves praise is the humanization of the lore isn’t reliant on DS1 but tells a deceptively player-driven storyline. Until Bloodborne, these games never have engaged me in atmosphere as the player without being invested in the lore first.
This deception begins from the introduction that appears without significance to the rest of the game about Drangleic. You came here to find a cure. Whether you were the hooded man reaching out or the fading woman, your past becomes eroded the further you explore the plights of Drangleic, shifting the focus from the player to the world that mimics the effects of hollowing in seeking a purpose to retain what humanity is left much like the tragedy of Lucatiel. This isn’t a stunning revelation I am making; however, it showcases how DS2 puts the player into the storyline subtly.
It’s somewhat ironic then that the “Dude in Armor” problem is indicative of how the story’s significance is communicated through the humanized NPCs. The constant usage of enemy knights as fodder and bosses reminds you of the humanity wasted in the cycle of Drangleic. Bosses such as Aldria, Vendrick and the other Kings, the Dark Queens as well as indirect connections to creatures like Frejia and the Rat King relate the storyline about humanity. Even creatures with no ability to speak like the Giants and the Reincarnated Lord Vessels are given humanized features with as little as you can learn about them. NPC companions are given more chances to bond with the player as they further their storyline if you summon them in fights. Even the lands you only hear mentioned by name and the frugal information you know about the war with the giants through interacting with their memories, carries more weight because by having it visually, audibly and mechanically expressed to the player. Eventually the player must confront the Cycle, an abstract manifestation of the First Sin against humanity’s nature, resolved by confronting the souls of man.
As much praise DS1 and DS3 gets, DS2 is something with no clear answers; it’s a sequel that truly stands on its own brilliance and consternation among its shadows of past glories. Such is its fate.

"The 39 Steps" is, down to its core, a slightly-interactive-novel. That being said - it's not "bad" by any means. For what it is, it's incredibly well done, and a means in which I would love to continue consume various forms of classical fiction.
Based on the original espionage thriller "The 39 Steps" by John Buchan, you can definitely see where modern day spy stories came from - predating popular fictional characters like James Bond by at least 30 years. This story takes place on the verge of WWI and introduces a character named Richard Hanny, a man on the run after a young American spy divulges sensitive information to him. The game is presented mostly in beautifully painted backdrops, fuzzy silhouettes and the occasional shadow puppet show (of which are quite entertaining). These backgrounds take you from inner-city London, to the moors of Scotland and back again. There isn't much gameplay to be had (to my slight disappointment), but what is present is likened to that of a game like "TRAUMA" - drawing shapes and clicking on things to carry through the cutscene-like chapters.
Simply put - the game is awesome for what it is - but it really needs a bit more interactivity. There is one part that involves the character decoding a notebook. I got really excited, thinking that I'd at least have a mini-game or a puzzle to figure out the code, but alas - the game just carries on like the book. They allow you to zoom in and out on objects you see in the environments - here I am, thinking that I'll have to do some Sherlock Holmes work and pick out clues from the zoomed-in objects, but alas - there isn't much to discover but a few timeline-appropriate advertisements and newspaper articles.
I would love to digest all sorts of fiction this way. From Sherlock Holmes to H.P. Lovecraft to Franz Kafka - I would love to have this sort of artwork and voice acting and sound effects, mood, pacing, attention to detail, and the ease of taking it in via separate chapters (just incase I need to leave and come back to it) - albeit, more interactivity would be preferred

A fun, frenetic little restaurant game that's a little deeper than it looks.
Premise: You take over a garbage pit of a diner with the intention of making it a five-star restaurant. You do this by selecting a menu for maximum profitability and "buzz", and then prepping the food via a series of typing mini-games.
The Good: There is a lot of stuff to do in this game; 30-ish unique dishes to prepare, each with their own mini-game with (generally) unique mechanics. The difficulty of serving these foods varys from holding a single button for two seconds then hitting another button (fried chicken) to curating complex sequences of patterns with harsh failure conditions (kebabs) and the brilliant part is, the difficulty is largely self-directed as you can feel free to keep your menu as simple or as complex as you believe you can handle. The game throws a series of ever-varying challenges at you in the meanwhile (safety inspections, betting on your own performance, stopping crime, and a very bizarre dating sim) which keeps it from feeling like you're doing the same thing every day even if you are. When I got to the endgame I still enjoyed the act of filling orders in and of itself, which is a pretty impressive statement considering I'd done so for something on the order of 15 hours. The balance between being frantic enough to be interesting and being zen enough to be pleasant is incredibly well-struck in my opinion. Also, the game has custom key rebinding on all mini-games which is an awesome feature.
The Bad: There is almost literally no consequence for failure. You could bungle half your orders and the only thing that would happen is a loss of buzz for the next day, which is exactly the same as saying an automatic reduction in difficulty. I suppose this is a good thing when you are first learning the game, but after about day 7 I stopped feeling any remorse for my mistakes because the game wouldn't really let me. Feel free to meta-game by running your buzz up high, loading your menu up with your most difficult and expensive items, and then rapidly serving out rushed and error-filled orders for more profit than you ever could have obtained by actually attempting to be good at the game.
Conclusion: This game is excellent for killing a bit of time and despite its occasionally manic rush hours I find it very relaxing. It's hard to get bored by it!

I love reading, I love reading physical books. The 39 Steps is a book, and it's one of my favourites... so there
The 39 Steps is a digital adaption (visual novel) of John Buchan's classic of the same name. Developed by The Story Mechanics and published by KISS Ltd. This game has gotten a lot of mixed reception with gamers, however the game has gained critical acclaim with reviewers and critics across the board and I can understand both sides of the picture
The 39 Steps is a very faithful adaption of the book, you experience the story through beautifully designed landscapes and good voice acting with very little interaction
It can get boring and yes the length of the game is extremely short (I finished it in over three to four hours and in one whole sitting) and the asking price is a bit too steep, however, The 39 Steps' story, although not originally written by the developers, and visual recreation of the novel are nailed perfectly in the game
I can understand the mixed responses from gamers about The 39 Steps and I can also understand why critics and reviewers gave this game a near perfect score and to me personally I really enjoyed playing through The 39 Steps. Yes, I have read the novel before and yes it is one of my favourite books but that does not effect the way I play the game. True, the length of the game is ridiculously short and you hardly do anything just listen to a story, however, John Duchan's novel is so well written that I just wanted to continue playing it to the end
The 39 Steps will and has mixed reception but if you are reading this review, then you are dying to know my recommendation. The 39 Steps is a game everyone should try and play and finish in one whole sitting even if you don't like reading books (which you should!) and would like another way of seeing this interesting story, then the game is the other option, however, for the retail price it is offering, I would not recommend it at its full price and rather wait for a price drop or a sale
The 39 Steps is not the game for everyone, but a majority of gamers should at least give it a try and see John Bucahn's vision come to life
I cannot wait to see what other digital adaptations The Story Mechanics have in store!

The Crew tries to be a driving game with something for everyone. You can team up with a group of friends for an epic road trip filled with fast-paced illegal activities, and seamlessly explore a massive map of the U.S., from the tip of Maine, all the way down to Miami, over to Los Angeles and back again, passing through other iconic cities along the way. Though it's true that all of this is possible, the experience isn't all that it's made out to be. The Crew tries to do a lot, and while it technically delivers the features it promises, it frequently stumbles over itself. There are brief moments of joy within, but just when you start to think the game's turned a corner, a bump in the road sends your joyride careening off course. When the best thing a racing game has going for it is the variety of environments it has to offer, you know something's amiss.
You start off in the streets of Detroit, but it's not long before you're rolling through mountains, everglades, and forests. The huge maps and its colossal number of activities is intimidating at first, but that's great: the more places to go and things to do, the merrier. Story missions, which take you through a trope-filled campaign that plays out like a Fast & Furious sequel, send you from one region of the country to the next, and missions emerge out of the blue along the way. You street race, smuggle contraband, take down competing criminals, and tackle bite-sized emergent challenges that test your abilities behind the wheel while you're on the go. There are hundreds of things to do, but only some are truly fun. The problem? With so much ground to cover, The Crew feels and looks like it's stretched too thin, and it's evident from the start. The Crew's world may be massive and varied, but it's not good-looking. It's constantly plagued by texture and geometry pop-in, and looks generally outdated. People, buildings, the environment, and most importantly, the cars, are represented by disappointing models that suffer from an unsightly amount of aliasing.
Keep in mind that if UPlay, PSN, or Xbox Live is down, you can't play The Crew, even if you just want to go solo. During my time with the game, I was booted due to server or connection issues on a daily basis, which was very frustrating. The most enjoyment you get out of the game's connected world comes from player-vs-player competitions, but even they have issues.

Cargo Commander's the kind of game you really want to love but the longer you're around it the more flaws you see.
There's loads of things to upgrade, different playstyles, great atmosphere and soundtrack, challenging environments, nearly limitless worlds to explore, leaderboards, lots of collectables, and a button you can press to swear up a storm! Really if you're playing Cargo Commander for a few hours it's an awesome fun game with a slightly competitive atmosphere to it. The problems start rolling in when you actually attempt to COMPLETE this game.
There are 88 pieces of cargo scattered throughout the game world. You have about 20 scanners to help you find some of the harder to find ones, but once you attach them to a piece of cargo they don't come off. If you want to complete the game and return to your home, you need to collect every. single. one. This is where you NEED those scanners or help from friends in order to actually FIND those last few pieces. All the while you're replaying worlds and completing them to your best attempt, draining the desire to actually go around and explore the near limitless space available to you. On top of that, if you desire to compete in the leaderboards, each sector is only 12 waves long, effectively installing a top level cap on the sector. It isn't terribly difficult to complete all 12 waves either, as time goes on you'll find yourself getting through sectors with ease, often times holding onto a surplus of caps because you installed every upgrade along the way.
The absolute worst thing about this game is that it's mostly online only. There's a local game but that's a different save file altogether (for some reason). Online mode adds the leaderboards, the hundreds of thousands of sectors, and the random corpses of your failed fellow Cargo Commanders which hold stuff on them. Oh, and if you lose connection at ANY TIME while you're playing, then the game will freeze. If you don't get your connection back within ten seconds, you get instantly kicked back to the main menu. Everything you were doing during that in-game day will be lost as the game only saves after the results screen. So if you have spotty internet - like me - you'll lose fifteen minutes every now and again. Let's not get started on some of the bugs either.
But again, it aspires to be something great and for the most part pulls it off. Cargo Commander's fun, interesting, and packed with adrenaline, but the moment you start digging into it to see all it has to offer, you'll begin seeing a lot of the same, and just like its catchy theme, it'll begin getting on your nerves.
Play to experience, not to complete.

"Banished" is a sick, twisted game. You play as a town of exiles who must work together to survive harsh winters, famine, and natural disaster. While the premise sounds simple, the game throws a lot of really complex mechanics at you from the get-go.
The gameplay takes the Simulation genre to the next level. It's realistic enough that you must wait as the children in your town grow to working age, or until your orchards begin to yield crop. Unlike other simulation games, "Banished" also takes a very personal approach, going as far as to name each and every townsperson--and tell you when they die.
Each map is randomly seeded, so you must constantly adapt to the environment. For example, if there are no nearby animals to pasture, it is hard to collect wool for clothing. As a result, you might want to rely more on firewood early on. The key is always to go slow, but steady! Expanding too quickly will burn out your resources, but going too slowly is a death sentence when you run out of tools or have no access to medicine a few years in.
...There's really a lot to say about this game and not enough space to say it. The art style is perfect, the UI is minimal, gameplay is balanced. Get this game if you're into simulations. It's a true masterpiece. Not much for fans of action gaming, but it might be worth a try.

Midway is a serious game that allows you to just do anything you like: fly a plane into dogfights, order a battleship to pound your enemies or sneak around with a sub. The game doesn't do much handholding because it is probably made for a time when a game came with an instruction manual as part of the package, so you either need to go to the internet or just figure out the controls for yourself and pray you get used to them before you get gunned down by a Zero or broadsided by the Yamato.
The game leads to silly moments, like I am still unable to figure out how to dive bomb a ship, so I find myself often smashing into it Kamikaze style. One hilarious moment was when I got the control over a destroyer and was told to sail to the other end of a canal. While I got attacked by planes, a battery and torpedo boats I thought, geez, lets just bomb the Japanese base to smithereens, which I proceeded to do. After returning with an seriously busted ship to the end of the canal feeling smug for wrecking the Japanese base and everything in it, I got the message that I was about to be engaged by a destroyer.  The fight that ensued was totally awesome as I managed to outmanouver the enemy so it got stuck between me and the coast, forcing it to slow down and thus giving me the opportunity to give it a full load of torpedos, most of which missed, but enough hit home to sink it.
Fun game if you don't take it seriously.

- World Cohesion
- Some hitboxes

A: Yes! It's a great game, just not the best souls game.

Not really a game but rather a "digital adaptation" (as the developers put it) of a novel. It's narrated by the protagonist, whose shoes you step into when you play. There are no choices to be made; only simple mouse gestures (e.g. clockwise movement to unlock doors, left-right movement to run, etc) which are non-time sensitive, and some clicking on objects in certain scenes to examine them more closely. The story is split into numerous chapters, and you progress linearly through them. Any completed chapter may be replayed at any point of time.
- Intriguing story about a man involved in a WWI conspiracy
- Gorgeous artwork:
- Highly immersive (mainly due to the beautiful art & excellent audio)
- Convincingly voiced
- Nicely presented
- Historical setting is effectively conveyed
- Good mix of various media (text, voice, illustration, photos)
- The story takes you through a variety of different landscapes, from urban to rural to coastal
- Clicking to backtrack text requires an anti-clockwise mouse rotation. Why not just right-click or some simpler action, ffs?
- Cannot fast-forward voiced parts, therefore painfully slow at points
- Game intro very tedious to sit through (please, let's just
already, ok?)
- Language subpar on occasion (e.g. bad spelling, grammar, etc)
A pretty good VN to accompany a meal or snack, since you don't have to do much except sit back, relax, and click to progress through the story. The mouse gestures and game system take a while at first to settle into, but once you know what's expected of you, getting through the game is a fairly smooth and fuss-free process. The sound and music are immaculate. A large part of the story takes place in - and therefore features - the Scottish countryside and its folk. If this is something you enjoy or would like to experience, then I highly recommend this title.

This is the farming simulator of cooking games.
What if I told you that you could become a five star chef with a waggle of an analog stick and a few button presses? Well, in this game you can live out that fantasy. CSD is nothing if not an oversimplified QTE fest.
But that's why you play games, right? You want something to pass some time with. It's pretty entertaining either way. I can say I had some fun with this one. This is a game built entirely upon muscle memory, and I had realized this after picking this game up after a long hiatus. Instantly, all of my xiaolin-like culinary training flowed back into my fingertips. Apply the dressing, the cheese, two scoops of vanilla with nuts; jumbo water cup with ice and flavor blast, pounding on chicken exactly six times with some dangerous fury. I recommend playing this game with music blasting. Preferably k-pop or something you can sway back and forth with. That's the optimal cooking setting, obviously.
So what else? The music gets repetitive. The visuals aren't that exciting or interesting. After you've seen all the possible patrons, and you've baked them all lasagna 20x over, what is there to do? Where does the ultimate QTE chef go? To the real kitchen, my friends. Waggle that analog to flay that fish, and hold down on that analog to pour that beer to foamy muffin top perfection.
This game is a huge waste of time. That could be a good thing or a bad thing. I don't find it as particularly satisfying as others. But hey, it was fun while it was on my radar. It's an alright way to spend some otherwise potentially productive time. Thumbs up.

Rejoice, the cure for insomnia is found!  I'm not against visual novels, but the 39 Steps isn't quite one of those, it seems to be unsure of what it wants to be.   As a result, the gameplay, such as it is, is a confused muddle, distracting you from advancing the story, which is the primary focus of this game.
The graphics are quite good, a lot of attention has been put into the imagery which complements the story well.  Thematically it's excellent.  Unfortunately that's all there is to it.
Gameplay is a real let down - of course in a visual novel, the objective is to move from one "page" to the next but they picked a really convoluted and confusing set of interfaces for this which serve to distract rather than enhance or engage the "player".   In some stages you have to swirl the mouse around hopefully, in others you have to point and click, in others you're making bizarre silly mouse gestures.   That really doesn't fit with the visual novel theme.
Technical - no graphics scaling, you're stuck with the resolution they give you, and you have mouse cursor windowing control problems which doesn't help considering the gameplay is mouse driven - and they  hide the pointer deliberately so you can't be sure if you're advancing the game or if your mouse pointer has fallen off the edge of the poorly scaled game fullscreen window.
A dry story and a distracting and annoying control scheme makes this game too hard to recommend for gamers or visual novel fans.

Outlast.......... I still cant believe I beat this game. I cant bring myself to uninstall it, it is literallty a tool that will break the non believers. Refunct is a simple little 3D platformer that just wants you to have fun. You begin by rising from the sea along with a small island of square platforms. The map expands as you find buttons to bring more platforms up from the water. It's sort of like a growing playground of angular islands and towers and it's rather cool to see the world form around you. You can even dive below the surface to see all the islands lying in wait. Along with the buttons, you can try to color all the platforms by touching them or find scattered pickups to boost your completion percentage. The controls are fairly basic. You can jump, climb, crouch, and slide.  The climbing mechanic is very welcome, since it eliminates those frustrating, barely-missed jumps by allowing you to pull yourself up onto a plaform. Wall-jumping also becomes important later, but the slide maneuver is rarely used.
The graphics are refreshing and minimal,  crisp and colorful with some nice lighting effects. Unfortunately, some of the effects can be blurry and inconsistent since you'll be whipping the camera around a lot. The music is pretty upbeat and sometimes ethereal. It's very well done, probably worth a soundtrack purchase. Refunct is certainly nice to look at and listen to.
The platforming is, for better or worse, generally simple and easy. There are some tricky jumps, but they usually spare you the trial and error. Refunct is fast-paced and won't take you long to complete, but you could do multiple playthroughs or just run around for fun. The game is also very polished. I barely encountered any bugs or gameplay issues. The experience is modestly priced and easily enjoyable. Give it a go if you want to lay back and have some casual jumping fun.

-- from piloting planes in air-to-air and air-to-ground combat, from single small PT boats to destroyers with artillery and anti-aircraft flak, to commanding entire fleets!
Missions are varied well so you do a variety of tasks with both planes and ships.  Despite not doing the "Naval Academy" missions as I didn't know that was the tutorial missions in the game, I picked up on the controls and the way to play the game easy enough; though I do wish I had done the Tutorial as there's a ship repair screen I still don't really understand.  The game actually has a lot to do in it and is pretty well done!
You can take command of individual pieces in the war (a specific plane, ship, etc) or more manage the war from the map and just tell the pieces where to go.  It's fabulous what you can do.
+ Great missions with a good variety of goals
+ You can take control of many individual pieces:  planes (in air-to-air, air-to-ground, and air-to-ship combat), and ships (using AA guns, torpedos, depth charges, and artillery)
+ You can manage the entire fleet from the map and let the computer control the individual pieces
+ The game offers 3 skill levels for the missions and the "Regular" offered a good challenge.  I had to redo several missions a number of times.
+ It's a good length of a game.  My campaign lasted 10 hours (and that's not counting the various training missions, or the other 11 challenge missions)
+ The graphics.  Even factoring in the release date of the game, I think the game (gameplay) looks pretty good; better than I was expecting given its age.  The videos, granted, are terrible on a variety of levels.
+ Has multiplayer, but hadn't tried it at all, but it's nice they put MP in the game.
~ Story.  The settings and missions themselves were great, but the videos between the missions where they tell the story of your character; that was borderline at best.
~ Some missions are a little long, and being new at the game and a good challenge, if you loose, that was almost an hour you have to redo.  (Ahem, a couple more times in my case cuz I didn't want to go down to Easy!)
~ I had to change the controls from the defaults on a few different pieces (eg: planes controls seem to be inverted for mouse anyway); but the game does allow you to change them to whatever.
~ Planes don't seem all that manouverable when flying manually.  It was a challenge for me just to fly the plane and even SEE the enemy at times.  :-D
~ Some control screens just aren't intuitive such as the ship repair screen.  Granted there's a tutorial, but it's a single screen; you'd think I could figure it out, but ... I'm not really sure what effect my changes are having.
~ The UI isn't the most intuitive either.  Again, it may have been covered in the tutorial, but the red/green circles by the targeting crosshairs; that took a bit to figure out.  (Number of circles = how many turrets/torpedos you have.  Red Circle = a particular turret/torpedo can't fire in the direction aiming, Green Circle means the turret/torpedo is ready to fire.  Red Flashing Circle means that turret/torpedo is reloading.)
- The videos.  You really have to get past your plastic looking people in the animations and just enjoy the missions themselves.  Thankfully the videos and the gameplay are completely and totally different.
