Welcome to my review of We Need To Go Deeper!
In A Nutshell:

-Excellent Multiplayer (1-4 Players)!
-Fantastic, Comical Art Style.
-Hilarious Objects.
-Object/Item Mall.
-Wearables/Customization.
-Lots of Action.
-Frequent (Free) Updates.

-Early Access (So Some Bugs).
-Slightly Unstable At Times (But Frequent Fixes).
-Levels No-Longer Randomized?
-Random-Item/Level/Events Can Pwn You (Chaos Pro?).

We Need To Go Deeper (WNTGD) is a fast-paced, Action style Multiplayer adventure in which a crew of teammates dive deeper and deeper into the treacherous oceans. A recent update added Bots, allowing for a single-player experience, but it’s still way more fun with a living crew. The art style is whimsical and fun, as are the items you can discover/unlock in the item mall. Running around, stabbing your friends with a syringe to
help them? Yes, please! The Devs do frequent updates (and apparently seasonal events as well), and are super responsive in the community.
There’s the added appeal of exploring caves to look for loot, though the newer, larger caves can be a bit tedious or overwhelming at times. Multiple types of ships allow for different crew formations, and it’s important to decide what equipment you start with to ensure a balanced crew. Tip: Don’t skip a wrench at the beginning of your voyage! If you like funny, genuinely exciting Multiplayer titles this one is a must-play, must-own kind of deal, even in Early Access. I have no doubt the Devs will continue to bring their A-game. Highly recommended.

At the time of writing, I've played 8 hours, and so far, it's pretty damn good.
I picked up the game in a flash sale, being very wary of whether it'd actually be good or not, and I can safely say, money well spent.  I'd even go to say it'd be well spent at full price.  The game's graphics are done excellently, with their only slight fault being when zoomed in fully (at which point they're still better than most 'city' builders).  So far I've only played the game on it's easiest difficulty, and so I can't say how well the game plays on harder settings, however I hope to move up soon, as I've pretty much mastered the game at the moment.
How does the game function as a 'city' builder?  It doesn't, but it is a good village or small-ish town sim.  The main challenge is to stay alive, being able to produce food and firewood before it's too late.  My main problem with my first 3 attempts (which lasted 30 mins maximum) was that I was running before I could walk.  I tried to get more houses so that I could produce more, but this in turn meant I needed to produce even more, but it's easy to find your mistakes.
After you finally have a 'town' that won't trip over after it's just left the front door, you're free to expand at your own will.  You could stay as a town with only 30 inhabitants building up a stockpile, however eventually the town will become too productive.  And I don't mean with resources.  From time to time you'll accidentally♥♥♥♥♥♥something up and about 10-20 people will die, rapidly and without warning, but if you play your cards right, you'll recover pretty quickly.
Only problem?  Once you have sovled your seemingly unsolvable but then easily solvable crisis, you can build exciting buildings such as the town hall (which seeminly just produces graphs, because why not), or a brewery.  There's little to expand to after you've mastered your town, except pencil pushing, booze and possibly religion (in my case as overlord govenor, there is no such thing as religion, unless there's and option to add satanism simply for a laugh, which I haven't found so far).

This game is absolutely amazing, I'd love to get my own input on this game too as I feel it would make Polywings more enjoyable to certain fans.
1. Multiplayer Dog Fights. (Steam, not Port Forwarding.)
The physics and weapons are perfect for Dog Fights (Two or more planes go up, but only one will stay up.)
I've never seen a good game where Dog Fights have been perfected, except the old Star Fox 64 Multiplayer mode, this game is right up there with the classics!
2. Terrain and Plane degrading/destruction.
Another thing from SF64, if you strike your wing, it will become damaged, eventually breaking off and resulting it extreme tilting, or in a regular plane, it would cause you to spiral out of control, and your only option is to try and find something to heal your broken wing, adding a powerup system would be perfect for that.
You can also break your propeller, forcing you to glide and land as best you can, since you can't slow down normally, you need to use your knowledge of wind resistance to slow down.
3. Dog Fight exclusive: Lock-On missiles.
Weak homing missiles designed to home in on your enemy in the sky, easy to dodge, unless you're not very good at combat games.
4. Workshop.
Allow players to build their own planes, customize their character and create stories and maps to go with them, giving Polywings an infinite replayability rating, because as of now once you're done, it's done. (Until the new updates, but still it's not endless.)
5. Land and get out of the plane.
Adding houses, pit stops, garages for the planes and other interactable environments would work great if you could get OUT of your plane, and hop into another one, or grab gasoline, or find hidden unlockables inside of places too small for your plane to enter.
6. (Ties with #5) Parachute.
If you're in trouble, or just want to have fun, or test your freefalling skills, hop out of your plane mid-flight and open your parachute! You must be high enough though or else you won't have enough drag on your parachute for it to open and save you, or you'll hit the ground hard...
7. Cyclops boulder physics.
As of now, when the little guy tosses his boulders they go straight, maybe adding an arch to it would make it seem more realistic, and add a challenge to it since players can't go down to dodge it, only left, right or up.
8. (Ties with #6) Freefalling battles.
Once you're out of the plane and falling to uncertain doom, you'll also have a pistol to assist you, if you and your enemy both are forced to abandon your planes, you can parachute down while shooting at them, trying to poke holes in their chute, or killing them in mid-air.
9. Don't abandon your game like other devs, you'll miss out on great opportunities and only kill your game, which I for one would hate to see happen.
Keep up the great work and I hope one or more of my ideas has been taken to heart, and hopefully I'll see it in the game one day!

Heroes In The Sky has been around for some years now. There's a lot of things that have changed since when I last played it. Today I returned to it after 4 years and my first thought "Wow. This game has changed so much." I can't really say that all of the changes have been good and there's a lot of things that need improving.
First of all the language.
It appears to me that a Japanease company have taken over the game. This isn't a bad thing however the translations are somewhat sloppy and the text boxes need a big overhaul. The text is scattered all across the interface. In missions the text can be a bit urghh.. It needs sorting out.. And there's a lot to do.
Interface
Things are scattered around everywhere and it's a little overwhelming, especially to new players. It takes a lot of getting used to as well, even for returning players. It may be a wise idea help give the inerface a cleaner look and appeal - everwhere
Graphics
The graphical quality remains the same as it did years ago. This doesn't matter too much but they could do with being updated - higher resolution and quality of images rather than just settling with a lazy 2D look to various npcs that are found in the game. The game could do with 'Borderless Fullscreen' and a 'automatic resolution' detection option for optimal resolution settings.
Sound
My only problem with the sound is that there's this HORRIBLE buzzing noise when airplanes get very close. Please remove it. It's not a 'problem' as such but it's uncomfortable to listen to.
Trading
Oh my word... This is more of a community thing but if you're really into trading then you may find yourself facepalming repeatidly when trading with other players... Expect lots of skyhigh prices for easy to get items... By 'skyhigh' I mean 450,000,000 ghems for simple items... To point out.. you get maybe 5,000 ghems per mission if you're lucky... So yeah... If you want money quickly then pick a specialisation/skill and hone it. Make rare items and sell them. Doing so then allows you to buy expensive items.. In a nutshell people don't know how to trade.
Premium Items
I think this is what is going to get the attention of a lot of people so i'll try to add extra detail where possible.
To summerise: The game is not pay to win from what I can tell so far. You can use premium currency to aid you in levelling up but there's still quite a bit of work you have to do. You can buy boosters and so forth. Premium planes which can be purchased with premium currency can help you a lot. There's no need in spending loads of money on the game though.
$10 or around £6.75 can give you a premium membership which should be more than enough to stablize you and to give you a decent shot at getting your hands on a premium plane. If the premium membership is exactly as stated then It would be something that I suggest everyone gets, however I am unsure how long the premium lasts for, this is something that needs clarification. Premium currency will get you places though however you can get to the same places without it. It is definately not a 'need'.
Summary:
The game has been around for years, it's about time it was added to steam. I personally had to start from scratch but that's no matter. The game itself hasn't changed too much and there are several issues that need addressing. The game should run very smoothly on a lot of machines are it is not too graphically demanding. However lower fps may be expected on the more advanced mission due to the high npc count in missions.
Membership is entirely your choice, I do have a feeling that it is perminant as well. The game itself isn't too bad, however there are plenty of areas for improvement. It's fun to play casually but there's not a whole lot for hardcore players, and those players in particular may be disappointed.
Overall I recommend this game because it's fun to play and is a little different compared to other games around. It's enjoyable and with a bit of work from the developers and a bit of community growth then the game will become very fun. For now the game and the community is sleeping like a lot of old games.

The game is quite slow paced but not as slow as Arma. It is mainly trench warfare but there is a map with a fort and another one with a forest. If you blindly charge the enemy down the middle you will die. Simple as that. Use artillery craters, small hills, vehicle wrecks, half built trenches, corpses and whatever you can find to advance. Guns feel powerful killing in 1 or 2 shots. This is not a power fantasy. You can't carry an assault rifle, rocket launcher, pistol, knife, drive a tank, fly a plane and be Rambo on steroids. Some classes only have a pistol to fight back, yes, ONLY A ♥♥♥♥ING PISTOL. You do have MGs, sniper rifles, flame throwers, artillery strikes, gas strikes and all the good stuff from WW1.

The latest Midweek Madness gave players the chance to play at the theatres of World War 1.
Many brave men fell at the meatgrinding trench warfare and it can be frustrating to get shot across the map without even noticing where the shot came from or to get obliterated by some unseen artillery. Due to the medical conditions and the lack of armored vests most times one shot will kill you. Considering this many survivors of this atrocious war had heroic deeds to tell. Amongst them is the story of the The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen. As a player you get the chance to grasp a bit of their glory and fame. The only thing you need to do this is to pick a Canadian squad and rename them The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen. But beware of the burden you load upon yourself and your mates by doing this. In the following i will show you why.
When in 1917 the US army advances were held back by some infamous Mittelmächte units like the 1.-3. Elsässer Türkenjägerkompanie, 83. Zigeunerstrafbatallion, 2. Wiener Barackenhengst Division or the Bayerischen Freiwilligenkorps "Zipfelbuben" (which are all playable if you want to side with the Mittelmächte) president Wilson called the Canadians for help. His call for help would be answered and Canada sent The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen.
These men were the best Canada could muster. They were Veterans of the nowadays nearly forgotten Great Marple War (March 12, 1911- November 8, 1911) when the Canadian Confederation fought the secessionistic Caliphate of Hudson Bay. Shipping the yaks across the sea was no small task but the fear of an endless war in Europe demanded radical measures.
Landing in France in the late 1917 many Entente Cordial warriors smiled at the grim looking Canadians and their sturdy mounts. Could they really be their saviors?
The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen got their first taste of battle when the Germans launched an attack near a small Belgian village. When the Landser witnessed the yaks for the first time they mistook them for extra sturdy and well-bred cows that would be used as workhorses pulling artillery, ammunition and so on.... a fatal mistake. Due to the yaks natural immunity to gas, their  hard to penetrate wool and their ability to climb they were the ideal mounts for the ravaged crater landscape. This combined with the fearless and determined Canadian veteran Riders fighting from top of the yaks had a devastating effect on the German attack. It shattered like a dry twig under a hoove. Using the momentum The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen led a furious counter-charge deep into the German line.
The few German survivors told their comrades about the unbelievable new weapon the Entente forces used against them but most times their story would be seen as exaggeration mixed with post-traumatic stress disorder. As The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen fought and won more and more battles the number of German battle reports mentioning unstoppable behemoths rose until they finally reached the Generalfeldmarschall himself and his command echelon. Acknowledging the danger of rumours spreading across the Western Front they decided to use "Anti-Yak-Propaganda".
They told the soldiers that The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen were just some fanatical soldiers. They would scream: "Sirup für den Ahorngott! (Sirup for the Marplegod!)" and that they would feed captured soldiers to their yaks. In this way they tried to make sure that running was not an option against the fearsome new enemy. All research capacities were bundled to develope a new "Anti-Yak-Gewehr" (also a playable weapon in the game).
The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen rode from victory to victory being used in squads of four (like in Verdun).
The British felt ashamed by the numerous heroic victories of The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen and decided to develope some similiar effective weaponry. British engineers tried to mimic the way of the feral and majestic animals in a metallic construct  they called tank. A machine gun one each side should make up for the horns the yaks wield. The first test on the battlefield showed the inferiority of the tanks as they often had problems with the terrain. Something that never was a problem for The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen and their mighty yaks. Furthermore they decided to use Horsepower and not Yakpower engines which were utterly unfit to bring the power of a yak to the battlefield. Most of these problems would eventually be solved in the following decades but not before The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen had won the First World War.
Germany would sign the Treaty of Versailles with the only secret obligation to the Entente that they would forbid the use of yaks in wars (something every fighting faction has obeyed since then). Mostly because of the embarrassed British and French troops most of the documents talking about the yaks were changed. Renaming the yaks as tanks and the "Anti-Yak-Gewehr" which mostly failed was renamed Antitankgewehr (thats the in-game name as well and it still kind of sucks). Thus The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen have a slight contempt against the crude steel yaks called tanks as they took their well-earned place in the history books. In the end The Venerable Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen lost their faith in humanity (something this game can teach you aswell). Because honor they had earned although they never asked for it. They simply answered the call.
Yet their anthem survived all the years and should be played and sung before each battle you want to play as The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen. In the end all the enemy soldiers they faced admitted: "These are some damn fine warriors/yaks." Should you face The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen as your enemy in Verdun you should admit this too via chat. Thats the only way The Royal Canadian Kilted Yaksmen will be commemorated as the lost heroes of World War 1.

This is what visual novels should be, not borderline hentai anime ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
The 39 Steps is a very very very very very good digital adaptation of John Buchan's 1915 novel of the same name. I remember reading these early 20th century novels such as The Great Gatsby in highschool english class and thoroughly hating every word in them. The 100 year difference between then and now simply just does not translate well in text form due to changes to speech and culture this past century.
This game however was able to keep me hooked in a novel from this time period, I was engrossed in this thriller about pre-World War One conspiracy. The voice acting (despite using the same old english dialogue that I usually have trouble understanding in the book)  and art are both top notch and really helps to sell the immersion. Also the game mechanics, while simple (this is a book after all, there are no alternate paths in the story and there is no fail state) are enough to keep the player engaged with what is going on. Whether it be reading an authentic looking newspaper that tells more about the world or even just simulating the opening of a door knob with the mouse.
For anyone interested in a casual yet suspenseful story The 39 Steps is well worth checking out.

With 400 square miles of rugged terrain and hundreds of weapons and vehicles, Just Cause 2 defies gravity and belief.
UNIQUE VERTICAL GAMEPLAY - Take to the air like no other game. Experience total aerial freedom with the unique parachute and dual grapple
UNBELIEVABLE ADRENALINE-FUELLED STUNTS - Free fall, base jump, vehicle surf, para sail, skydive, grapple, slingshot, leap between vehicles, hang from helicopters, scale buildings. The impossible is within your grasp.
UPGRADED DUAL GRAPPLE - Your best tool is now a weapon. Fire two shots with the grapple hook and attach unwilling enemies to high-speed vehicles, hang them upside down from buildings, tether objects in mid air. The possibilities are as vast as your imagination.
DISCOVER THE SECRETS OF PANAU - Explore the island paradise; from sprawling cities, secluded beaches and towering mountain peaks – more than 400 square miles of your own personal playground.
EXPERIENCE TRUE FREEDOM - Hundreds of objectives can be completed in any way or order that you choose. When it’s time for a break from Agency business, kick back and enjoy all the attractions that Panau has to offer.
MASSIVE SELECTION OF VEHICLES - Catch air on a high-speed dirt bike, race across the sea in a power boat, or fire a spread of rockets from an attack chopper – more than 100 land, sea and air vehicles are yours for the taking.
System Requirements

where does one start with a game as conceptually hugamungus as this? Playing Hearts of Iron can be mentally taxing, intimidating, and utterly compelling all at the same time, and there’s no easy way to ‘sum it up’. But for want of a better topic, we’ll focus on what’s new, the most obvious being the graphics. Using an entirely new engine, Hearst of Iron III has been brought visually more in line with Paradox’s other flagship title, Europa Universalis III, making a shift from 2D to 3D. Counters, whilst still present at a certain level of magnification, have been replaced by generic 3D sprites to represent the different kinds of military units. The world map itself has been giving colour and life, with the different land types been visually represented. The only flaw to be had here is that the developers seem to have gotten rid of a lot of the urbanised areas, which is a shame because urban fighting was a major hallmark of this conflict.
Not only are the graphics better, but the game ‘world’ has gotten bigger. Just as Empire: Total War shrunk the number of land provinces available to conquer, so have Paradox increased them, to the tune of around 14,000. That, coupled with the 100 + playable nations, means that this game is clearly the largest yet.
The other ‘big’ changes are mainly to do with the AI and player interface. With a new streamlined military organisation system in the form of official ‘headquarter’ units, it’s possible to ‘assign’ the AI to various parts of your army. Whilst useless in combat, HQ units provide structure to sometimes unmanageably huge armies, and posse’s different levels, the top being the ‘Theatre’ command. Let’s say you’re playing as Germany, and World War II is about to start. Don’t fancy managing both the Easter and Western fronts? Simply tell the AI to control one of them. Assign it overall goals and objectives, and you can pretty much leave it be. Whilst the AI seems to get slightly dumber the lower down the command chain you go, it nevertheless proves to be a decently made system, and is definitely one of the games strong points.
Indeed, this idea of AI control is a subtle theme running through the game, as you can assign pretty much everything to the AI, with minimal input. Reminiscent of Nintendo’s up-coming ‘Demo play’ feature, it begs to question why anyone would want to simply watch the game being played, but sectioning off certain areas to the AI’s commands can certainly make things easier on players who find the level of depth intimidating. There are a whole host of other minor improvements as well, such as the ability to customize divisions (the basic military unit of a game) mixing and matching the various brigades to form dynamic and diverse armies. However, most of these you will have to find out for yourself.

Cargo Commander is an Action Platformer where you're an employee for a corporation that salvages cargo containers that are drifting owner-less in space. You're floating through space in your own corporation given Home Container, waiting to start the day. You activate a Magnet that attracts these owner-less containers, which you then loot and return to the Home Container. After activating the Magnet a wormhole will appear after a certain amount of time, depending on how many containers were pulled in, and the suck in all these containers which you're hopefully not in. Don't worry, you receive a decent amount of warning. Eventually one of the containers will have a Sector Pass in it, which you will use to travel to another sector.
There's 88 different types of cargo, and the more different cargo you have, the more you'll rank up.  You'll get different things for ranking up, like new features/upgrades for you Home Container, or more starting cash for each workday, etc. However, each sector has only a small handful of different cargo types, so to collect all of them, therefore ranking up, you'll have to visit other sectors.
There's an Upgrade Bench you'll unlock very quickly in the Home Container. This bench lets you upgrade your drill speed, health, run speed, oxygen, etc., but these upgrades only last for that work day. You find the cash, called Caps, to upgrade in the different containers you'll be exploring, either through enemy drops or searching dead corpses. However, some ranks will increase your starting Caps, meaning you'll be able to upgrade some things as soon as you start a sector later on. By the way, Caps brightly glow red and white when dropped. I initially didn't pay attention to these glowing items, as I assumed they were part of the scenery.
The Sector Pass will let you unlock another sector. You'll see different categories in the Navigator, such as Popular Sectors, Unpopular Sectors, Friends Sectors, Random Sectors, and Find Sector. When you use Find Sector, it asks you to enter the name. If it doesn't exist, then it is created. If you didn't notice, this sector creating feature is the reason behind the Popular/Unpopular/Friends Sector categories. Once you unlock a Sector, you can freely travel to that sector at anytime, just remember that you'll have to end the workday before you do so.
Some final things I forgot to expand upon during my review. This is a semi-roguelike/roguelite. Each wave of containers gets bigger and tougher as the workday goes on, and that each container has a random layout. If you die, all cargo, found weapons, purchased upgrades, and score is lost, and the day is ended. Each wave gets progressively tougher, so you'll need to know when to end the work day, or you'll lose that hard earned score. Final thing to bring up is that each Sector has it's own Leaderboard, which is why creating a sector is a good way to compete with friends!
Oh, I forgot to mention, there's a "♥♥♥♥ You" Button. By pressing the 'F', your character will scream "♥♥♥♥ YOU" at the top of his lungs, and swing his arm up in what is obviously Middle Finger gesture. It's childish, but I thought it was funny(probably a link there). Plus, sometimes you run into a extremely annoying enemy or container, and you just can't help but feel happy that there's a button that will perfectly express what you're thinking.
Conclusion: This is a fun game, and if on sale, it's a must get. I'd get it off sale too. This game CAN get repetitive, but it's still fun, especially when challenging friends to beat your score, or vice versa.
Edit: This review underwent a pretty large re-haul, since I have a bad habit of rambling incoherently and needed to make it shorter and clearer. While I'm pretty sure I covered everything as the previous one, I may have left something out or forgot to explain something I mentioned. If you notice this, please feel free to alert me and I can fix it. :D

This review won't do Cargo Command justice.  It looks like a simple 2d platformer/shooter with some low gravity physics fun... and it is, but it's also much more.  Cargo Commander is impressive in it's ability to draw you in despite being a 2d 3rd person game.  You will freak out when hordes of aliens start to overwhelm you, you'll panic as you coast through the void of space as your oxygen rockets toward empty, the black hole ripping apart everything around you as you scramble to find a way into a pressurized container.  You'll feel the sense of isolation and frustration of being alone in space, away from your family.  The game is drenched in a purposeful pervading sense of loneliness.  It's a wonderful immersive game, and despite losses and defeat the game is designed where each trip adds up to some progress, making you stronger and more able to take on challenges next time.
A note about the story elements of the game (spoiler?- speculation mostly):
I have a theory about the enemies that litter the random cargo containers are actually mutated versions of your player character from alternate timelines.  There's some major weirdness going on with the black holes and the fact that you can continue playing where you left off after death.  Additionally the enemies drop Caps, the games currency which is also a literal baseball cap, identical to the one you wear.
Summary: Pick up Cargo Commander.

First off, ♥♥♥♥ this game.
Now that is out of the way, let me explain. VVVVVV is made by Terry Cavanagh, the same insane genius behind Super Hexagon, and this game is hard as balls. You play as Captain Viridian, who was separated from his crew when a teleporter went haywire. You and the various members of the crew are trapped in a different dimension, and it is the Captain's job to rescue them.
This game has an element that was praised, the flipping mechanism. Need to get past those spikes? Can't jump? That's cool, just flip onto the roof! This adds to the difficulty, and is pretty neat.
I have to admit, the story isn't all that, however the level design is fantastically difficult (Look up Doing Things The Hard Way). Frequently resisting the urge to punch the screen was a issue, and death is mostly always imminent. Spikes and moving enemies are the main threats, with some variations to level movement. Only to be expected from the creator of Super Hexagon.
Of course like most games I play, there are some things that don't go well. Like the companion mission, in which one of your crew follows you, but only follows when you are on the ground. It took me about 2 hours just to get past one certain level, and I hated every single goddamn minute of it. Or the fact the game is ridiculously short. And to be honest those are the only things wrong about this game. The rest is A-OK.
So this game is a forced recommend. Buy this game, I urge you. You won't regret it.
Oh, and completionists beware, the achievements are hard as hell to get.

Banished has a strange appeal to it that is difficult to describe. It's graphics are very dated for a 2014 game, and the animations are very canned; possibly because it's making room for actively simulating hundreds of individual villagers simultaneously. Its gameplay isn't quite as complicated as its UI lets on. It's not a very exciting or eventful game. I've played the same village for 8 in-game years and nothing significant has really happened. Yet, there's something soothing and satisfying about watching the little village I designed go through day-to-day life. On the other hand, the game has no real life to it. All the villagers seem like mindless drones walking around, even the children.
I'd recommend the game to simulation enthusiasts, just to experience the different dynamics of this game, if it's on sale. For everybody else, it will probably bore you to tears, with 15 year old geometry and animation.

Pros: Setting, Graphics, Music, Controls
Cons: Gameplay
Cargo Commander creates a deep sense of loneliness in outer space.  The visuals and sound only serve to enhance this feeling.  Realists may use the "silent space" option, but the ability to use your own music aboard the ship is outstanding.  The controls are excellent, and they should be, for a relatively simple platform game.
Unfortunately, the gameplay matches too well the drudgery of space salvaging.  Sectors may be randomly generated but offer little challenge.  With over eighty cargo types and only six types per sector, the game is an exercise in patience rather than skill.  Completionists will find themselves weary-eyed searching for ultra rare cargos.
Salvage the fun by playing in short sittings.

this is the most effort i've ever had to put into reading a book — a very pretty book with great voice acting, mind, but the "game mechanics" included are both so simple and sparsely utilized the whole project probably would have been better off as an animated comic book or video of some sort.
the text itself, over a century old at this point, is hard to say has aged favorably either. those who appreciate highbrow literary concepts such as "character arcs" and "themes" will not find much to be engaged with here — this is pure thriller fiction, focused solely on the protagonist staying one step ahead of those dastardly germans whilst conceiving a way to stop their nefarious plot. it honestly wouldn't feel out of place in today's AAA video game market.
for something that's supposed to be suspenseful, the meat of the story falls into a sort of trite cycle as well, mostly consisting of the protagonist putting on disguises just clever enough to fool his would-be captors and/or chancing upon the most trusting and kindhearted people he could possibly meet to aid him at the exact right moment, only for him to be discovered again and forced to repeat the process. perhaps back in the day the suspension of disbelief was a little easier to uphold, but as of today i'd hesitate to call the haphazard feats of the protagonist anything but hilariously miraculous.
allies regularly pop up for a scene or two before never being seen again, and i honestly can't even remember if the villains have names or not, because they barely had presence outside of being bad and scary. events that feel like they should be shocking revelations fall flat because i have little to no investment in any of the characters or their motivations. even the final confrontation, which should have been climactic, was over and done with within seconds, the epilogue equally as rushed.
i was actually going to give this a positive recommendation at first, but looking over what i've written, yeah, the only compliments i could give this book are to its art and voiceovers. so in the end, i guess the biggest twist of all, was myself. dang. the end.

For a 2007 game it looks great, all the little details from the crewmen walking around a ship your zooming in on to the little bubbles your depth charges make to just the way your ships move through the water and the smoothness of seeing planes in the distance dive bombing a target and landing on a carrier, to the way a ship you've just either torpedoed or hit with a volley of guns slowly sinks.  It has a really nice look to at and I'll admit I'm one of those graphics make a game better kinda people.  I'm an artist and I love to see computer art just to see what has been done.  This may be old but I am really impressed and I haven't even started with the gameplay.
This is a simulation and a great one at that.  Everything is just how I would ask it to be done if you asked me how I would like this type of thing be done.  You can take control of everything and it is just seamless and just works right and when your not in control you can count on the AI not to go full Ben Stiller in that one movie, which is a huge point if your gonna do this kind of set up.
This is just a neat great find of a game that I had never even heard of until I saw it while looking for something cheap to get.  I got the Midway and Pacific bundle and can't wait to see what Pacific is like as it is 2 years later, I hope it's even better looking/playing.
In other words if you want a good SIMULATION experience with just the right amount of hands on action don't even hesitate like I almost did because of the price and obscurity (to me anyway).  I capitalize simulation because before I purchased I looked up a gamespot review (I know) and though they liked the game they kinda complained about long times between action or some such.  GOOD!  I'm sorry but WWII didn't happen in a way that fit in snuggly with your COD expectations and being a simulation I want things to play out how they would naturally and if that means I lie in wait for what might be an entire level in another game so be it.  I love fast games myself but when I want strategy I don't want punches pulled for the whiners out there and they didn't.  Not to say nothing happens far from it. As a fan of visual novels, I really enjoyed The 39 Steps, as that's basically what this game is. There's not much to do but read along, occasionally clicking a few things for some extra information, and as such the game may not appeal to traditional adventure-game lovers. However, the casual interactivity is more than made up for with the excellent story; I wasn't aware of John Buchan's novel previously, as I'm normally not one for espionage tales, but I was thoroughly engaged by this on-the-run spy thriller. The game follows the story of restless gentleman Richard Hannay, who forges a new friendship which rapidly plunges him into a world of deception, cover-ups and murder. The artwork throughout the game is attractive, with decent music and ambience, and great voice acting (including a cameo from Greg Hemphill of TVs Chewin' The Fat fame.) While the theme of the story is dark in nature, there are some amusingly light-hearted quips well-delivered by the cast, and in the form of a few shadow-puppet style scenes.
Pros:
- Consistently good art style and sound
- Excellent pacing, it neither drags nor feels rushed at any point
- Has the old-timey feel of a classic book, without feeling dated
- Decent playtime (over 5 hours for me)
Cons:
- It's a few pounds more expensive than I would expect for this sort of game
Overall:
The achievements are almost entirely unmissable, presenting a lack of challenge in that department, but it does make for a relaxed, enjoyable experience where you can really focus on the story-telling. I would personally consider around £3 cheaper to be a fairer price, but I have no faults with the gameplay itself, and highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a strong story-driven experience.

Why city.
Why?
A question as simple as it is deep.
A question we together will explore, but not before laying a framewrok from which we can understand this piece.
For to understand VCB: Why City, we must ourselves be proto historians of the genre in which it inhabits. A genre that spans from the Grand Theft Auto series, to Driver. From the Mafia series, to True Crime. A genre both full of innovation and, alas, repetition. Yet despite it's competition, it's successes, it's numerous failures, this is the genre in which VCB exists. This is the genre VCB calls it's home. A genre which ecompassing both the cadavers of lesser productions, and the flowing buds that sprout from the rich ground.
A disclaimer then in fore. This reviewer, though making every effort to be impartial, is an unashamed fan of the Grant Theft Auto series.
VCB: Why City drops the player straight into the deep end, leaving them to discover the workings of the world via direct exploration. In fact, the first mission extends to nothing more than this. A mission which has the player learn each and every feature of the host city through a series of seemlessly ending checkpoints; rom the barren ubranized locale of the local Kebab vendor, to the barren urbanized locale of the local cam♥♥♥♥♥'s apartment. It is a world both familiar and foreign. A world so real, yet so bizarre. A world teeming with rich narrative arcs begging to be rendered.
And that is what VCB delivers.
Despite a slow and somewhat ardous start,t hese locales quickly reveal themselves to be the generators of rich and diverse gameplay. Against the clock driving? Tick. ... Shooting? Against the clock driving while intoxicated? Tick.Tick. This game has it all. A few hours playing this feels like an etenity.
VCB: Why city rides an intricate line between GTA4 and GTA5, borrowing the best from the former whilst eschewing the regressions from the latter. In it's own way, VCB IS the successor to GTA4. But as much as it follows from the Rockstar franchise, it also breaks from it. Instead of an Americentric view of the world, VCB opts for a more idiosyncratic slav perspective on things. A switch that, whilst initially jarring, bears ample fruit.
So then what is a GTA fanboy to think of this title? Well, let's put it simly...

Much like Elder Scrolls games, though, it does often feel like you're way too anonymous, and therefore not as involved with the world as you'd like for an RPG. However, this is not a game that can possibly be missed. The storyline, world and detailed quests make it an incredibly enjoyable experience. Do not expect anything groundbreaking combat wise though, as Fallout 3 uses VATS, which involves zooming into an enemy, pausing, and then selecting which part of their body you want to shoot at based on which percentage will do the most damage. Not the most challenging nor rewarding.

This game is one of those crazy little games that you look at and think "What the hell could his game possibly do that's any good?" The answer is simple. It has excellent level design that use the gravity flipping mechanic brilliantly. It's a good game because in spite of the simplicity, it's great fun to play with amazing depth in the challenges presented.
Graphically, though very simple, are very lively and well presented. Yes, it may be primitive but it does work.
The music is also bloody awesome. Raw chip tune which sounds like it uses the Commodore 64 chip set. Makes the game feel very authentic which I personally love.
Another thing I like about the game is unlike many games that use 8-bit styling, this one looks like it might have actually be possible to make on a C64. I'm curious if it could fit on a tape but functionally, this does look pretty authentic.
Does it have a negative? Eh, questionable ones. The story is total rubbish, which fits in well with the overwhelming vast majority of retro games, let alone Commodore games and honesly, I don't see it as a negative because the story doesn't get in the way of my gaming. But some could find issue with it.
It's a damn hard game, but very doable with some persistence. Some, again, may find this off putting but I didn't. Compared to many retro games this is actually very forgiving.
It's also less than 4 quid. Take a chance on it.

Needs a lot of work
Graphics are a good place to start, they look silly. The game uses an approach of sprites stitched together to make a human. It used to be a common technique in flash games, nothing wrong with it. But here he's used too few, so arms and legs don't bend. Your character crouches by attaching their legs to their shoulders (legs which look like turkey drumsticks),  arms are always bent at a slight angle, face is permanantly locked into one stern expression (with unremovable goggles). In general its just really awkward to look at and visually disappointing
Controls are awkward. Interacting with anything is a game of carefully positioning yourself into the right spot so it glows and can be interacted with. Mildly annoying for treasure, but a serious liability when you're trying to use consoles in the heat of battle. Consoles themselves are painful to manage, interacting with them locks your movement keys. The chatbar is also a huge pain, as well as being very buggy. The button to close the chatbar (tab) also opens the scoreboard, which you have to hit tab again to close.
Neither your personal weapons, nor the submarine itself, can be properly aimed up or down. You get about 45 degrees of inclination and declination, which is a huge pain in a gameworld that is so heavy on verticality. It makes combat and steering awkward.
Combat, at least initially, is highly repetitive. Which is bad because it's the core of the game. Leftclick to attack, or more likely, hold leftclick to spam swings. That's literally it, attacks can't be aimed, there's no stamina, no timing, no heavy strikes or dodges. You just click and hold until something dies.
It gets a bit better when you unlock some ranged weapons, i was fond of hurling dynamite. But at that point the game's camera becomes your main enemy. It's zoomed in way too far, and you can't pan around. So anything more than a couple feet infront is offscreen. You practically have to get into melee range to use ranged weapons, or else fire blindly offscreen and pray. The close camera is an issue for submarine combat too.
If you die in any manner, you can be revived at the cost of a permanant loss of 20% max health. According to the wiki there's no way to undo this. Dying is already pretty easy, yyour tiny health pool forces you to sprint back to the sub to rest every 30 seconds. one mistake and you're screwed
Right now, combat on foot seems to be the main meat of the gameplay, you land in a cave and explore it. But it's just awkward and repetitive.
Submarine combat is a bit better. One person steers the sub, one mans the guns. The turret turns terribly slowly, but that's a fitting choice for the nature of the game. However it doesn't mesh well with some other choices. For example every early enemy is melee based.  Generally giant sharks, squids, etc. They charge at your sub and just hug you, chewing away. The biggest issue is that enemies can pass through you, so they can go from one side of you to another in half a second, while your turret takes several painful seconds to rotate.
The best you can really do is guess which direction they're going to go, and rotate the turret in advance to point there. it really is guesswork, since enemies stop for a couple seconds and charge suddenly, there's not much prediction.
There doesn't seem to be much story or context to speak of. There are some interesting events - like a ghost ship crashing into you, or a time traveller appearing on your ship. But these have very little narrative and seem to exist as a framework for more of the awful foot combat, by dropping intruders onto your sub. Everything comes back to the combat and it can't carry the game
It's also full of bugs, probably par for the course in early access, but bears mentioning. The scoreboard and chatbar are both buggy, you frequently end up halfway through floor, arms get stuck in odd poses, and whenever you're close to another player you seem to take control of their head and it looks at your cursor, instead of showing you where they're looking.
Last, but not least, crewing problems.
This is advertised as a game for 2-4 players. I have two - myself and a friend. There's also a small ship which specifically states it's intended for a crew of two.
But frankly, this game is not fit for two people.  There are three critical roles on a ship.
The pilot has to steer. This is emphasised by the rather baffling design that the pilot can't stop the ship. The sub can only be stopped or started by altering power in the engine room. So the pilot is glued to the steering wheel at all times, lest you crash
A gunner has to shoot. this is pretty important in combat if you want to not die. the shield wont last long, and you can die very fast once its down. The two ship weapons available (machinegun and torpedoes) can only be switched between by altering power in the engine room. If she leaves the guns, nobody is shooting and fights will never end.
And an engineer is needed to repair breaches, adjust power levels for the above two, and fight off boarders.
Given there was only two of us, we try our best to be pilot and gunner without a dedicated engineer, but it fails badly. Something is always left undone if one of us has to leave their console. The ship simply cannot be crewed effectively by less than three people
This could be ameliorated by adding a brake for the pilot, so they could at least pull over in order to go fix things
In summary, the game has a lot of issues, some in design, some bugs, and a great many sharp edges that need smoothed out. Since combat is the core gameplay, it needs a lot more depth, skill and complexity. The exploration needs some purpose to it. And if the game is seriously meant for 2-4 people, then some work needs to be done on making sure its properly playable at both extremes.
4.5/10, in need of a lot of work yet.

VVVVVV is a delightful, charmingly retro and infuriatingly evil platformer that will beat you down and make you its ♥♥♥♥♥. In a nutshell, it's about switching gravity (or "flipping") instead of jumping. It's a pretty short game, but it offers quite a lot extra in the form of its higher difficulties, prepackaged additional levels and time attack modes. After the introductory level, the game throws you into a freely navigable, almost open world map where individual levels must be found to be played, with each one toying with increasingly mind-numbing tricks to challenge you in ways you never knew were possible.
VVVVVV also has the benefit of a marvelous 8-bit soundtrack that continues uninterrupted when you die (and you WILL die), which compounded on its instant respawn and regular checkpoints makes making progress and beating challenges much, much less of a headache. For the supreme masochists, there is the Super Gravitron. Squirreled away in the "secret lab" portion of the game, it offers a timed survival mode where you bounce between an oncoming rush of deadly obstacles. Go ahead and add about 30 hours to my playtime- I have heavily played my non-Steam copy- and still I have never gotten farther than 15 seconds in the Gravitron.
So in short if you love dying, fun 8-bit graphics and crying bitter tears of defeat and rage, get this game. You'll learn to love the suffering.

Cargo Commander is a sort of mini "roguelike-like" in space. The levels ("sectors") are randomly generated, and it's up to you to rush into theses containers to get as much loot as possible before your inevitable demise.
On the one hand, the game will immediatly grab you. It's fast, it's fun to get loot, and there is a fair bits of tactics to get the most out of each container, without taking too much risk.
The game also has lot of dark humor. You had to provide for your family so you decided to take what is probably the worst job of the Universe. Your company doesn't care at all about its workers and their safety, they only care about their profit, and will pay as low as they can, while charging as much as they can for basic equipment. To not worry your wife about all this, you lied to her and she now write you thinking you're just a basic warehouse worker giving a very surreal feeling to her messages.
On the other hand, "finishing" the game, ie getting all the different type of loot feel more like a chore than anything. Each sector has only 5 or 6 different types of loot, and you have almost no way of knowing what you will get (you get some "scanners" that help you, but they are limited). So you go through a level, hoping to get the loot you're looking for, and if you're lucky, you will get maybe one new type of loot. But they are more than 80 to get ! That's a lot of sectors to explore, and the game doesn't have enough variety to make that grind really fun.
It tooks me 11H to get 2/3 of the items, but it felt twice as long and i stopped. Then a year later it took me another 13h to get the final third of the loot. That was pure grind, very repetititve and not fun. It's only my usual urge to complete games that made me finish that one.
Given the price of the game, it might still be worth it. It's fun for a while, you don't feel cheated. However, it's sad that it doesn't have lasting appeal. There are definitely better games out there.

After Dark Souls, most of the conversation was about how hard the game is, as if that was its only quality. It took some time, critical thinking, and noteworthy voices to bring new concepts into the discussion, like how fair the difficulty is (overall), the variety of playstyles, the great storytelling and world-building, the unique online functionality, etc. FromSoftware made DS2 with only difficulty in mind.
The story has been set aside. The intro tells you nothing and leaves you with nothing to think about other than that you're the cursed undead. Many bloodstains have been placed by the devs in an attempt to create atmosphere and tell mini-stories rather than clue the player into where and how people died, like in the first game. Messages left by other players don't appear like they should. Useful info that has been upvoted hundreds of times won't appear until well after you needed the information.
From there, DS2 throws giant spongey enemies at you, and lots of them. Or there will be hordes of enemies to fight, and the only way to handle them is to pull them out one at a time. That happened in DS1, but it was occasional; in DS2, it's constant. And when you die, you lose part of your maximum health, making the part that you had trouble with before even harder. Some enemies have grabs that will kill you in one hit. Enemies that used to be mid-late game foes, like phantoms, will now appear much earlier.
Level design is more confusing; at first, I couldn't even find the first level and went straight to later stages because that's what I thought the first level was. Most of deaths have been environmental. DS2 has a lot of narrow paths and falls that will kill you. Apparently, bad platforming was a highlight of the last game, so FromSoftware upped the ante by giving you more bad platforming.
I really want to like DS2, and I keep playing in the hopes of finding what I loved in the first game. But the first few hours were spent frustrated and confused rather than compelled. DS2 is more like a 3D version of "I Wanna Be the Guy" than a sequel to DS1.

There are few games I actually like enough to write reviews about (and they mostly suck in quality too) but this game desereves an honest review.
Ofcourse a lot of people are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about the season pass not including the Wild Run DLC but I never bought a season pass or the wild run, I just bought this game on sale because I wanted to play an good looking open world racing game and this one was worth the 14 euros I spend on it in a sale.
So lets start with the story
Many racing games lack a story entirely or just have a basic one.
This game is no difference, although the game has a lot more effort in giving a race an purpose, every race has a few lines of voice acting giving the context why you do it. so its not just "why did I just ram some random car off the road" in which the game responds "because OH HEY LOOK REWARDS!"
The story itself to spoil the least, Alex Taylor is a racer that wants to join the 5-10's but on the day he would get his ink his brother gets shot by Shiv and then you pretty much try to raise yourself in the 5-10 ranks to get revenge. (again im pretty much just explaining it bare bones there is a lot more to it).
For a racing game story i'll give it a: 7/10
For a general game story its a: 5/10 characters dont get any in-depth story
Graphics
The Graphics in this game are really good. shadows look great. cars super detailed. first person driving looks great too. Rain is stunning.
Night time is a little bright if you aren't in a shadow or if it' s raining. the world itself is detailed and there are people on the streets just walking around, some carrying stuff. (i even hit some hobo with a shopping trolley once) there is also wildlife running around from squirrels to moose. (Ofcourse it being a ubisoft game there is no senseless killing so you cant actually hit the people or animals) The forests feel dense and real.
There is even an in-game photo mode which allows you to take your own pictures in a higher resolution then you actually run the game. I have made a ton of screenshots using it and I even have a few new Computer backgrounds thanks to it.
There are a few pre-rendered cutscenes. Which im actually still trying to figure out if they are real recordings with the character models 3d rendered into them or if they are actually modelled so well that they look photo realistic.
The bad few things include:
A few floating rocks and tree's in forest areas off track.
Character faces in game up close are really ugly compared to the rest of the game.
short draw distance on cars (detailing like spoilers dissapear if they go a little far away even on ultra). wheel tracks also do not stay long, in the ending cutscene the camera pans into the distance following your car which is outside of the draw distance so it isent visible. Dust trails are really small (so small that if you look behind yourself in first person you dont see any dirt/dust kick up)
Mirror's have no real time reflection. (only like GTA V does. reflects low res world but no cars or anything) No option to enable a HUD rear view mirror.
AI cars in photo-mode dissapear after a short while due to the fact that the game is online and the cars drive on going beyond draw distance and de-spawning.

Graphically for a racing game this is the prettiest game I have played. 9/10 (compared to other racing games like Need for speed)
The Gameplay
First the biggest thing I like is the fact that there are more then 2 cars on the road. on highways in major cities you can actually end up just rushing past a continous row of cars. so driving on roads feel actually used instead of the ghost roads you drive on in games like Need For Speed.
Cars handle pretty good, feel heavy and in control. I barely drove any other cars then the forced cars and the starting car you pick though. (yes you can easily complete the whole game with the starting car), I've only had 3 occasions of physics doing weird and getting launched at crazy speeds. a few AI cars also glitch sometimes but there is nothing massive as far as i noticed.
The special thing about this game is the always online world.
So far as i noticed the map is devided in section servers. Major cities have a special server and the country around those cities have seperate servers. I personally have a good internet connection and the server crossings have been seamless. no lag, no freezes, no "connecting to server" stuff.
Ofcourse if you are like me you coulden't care less about the online stuff and rather don't have any online stuff.
there sadly isen't a offline mode. but the game plays pretty much single player, nothing online is forced on you, you could play it as if it were a single player game. Every race can be done solo (meaning you and AI).
The AI is easy. As far as I noticed there is no difficulty curve (but this could also be because racing might be one of the game types im decently skilled at) The difficulty is addaptive to your cars level. so if a mission says its hard it's most likely easy if you actually know how to drive well. I even ended up having a 10 second split time on a hard mission.
I should also not forget to mention that this game is not your generic "buy parts in the shop to upgrade" type. you unlock the parts after every race depending on how well you did. so being first doesent mean a gold part.
There are also on road skill challenges a few are:
Speed: drive on the road as fast and far as possible
Jump: Jump over a ramp into a landing zone
Precision: squeeze through gates that become smaller and smaller
Slalom: drive around posts
These also use the bronze, silver, gold loot system.
The Bad
This game also features Cops. Which are no threat at all and barely worth mentioning except for in the "escape from the cops" missions.
They barely do anything. you can speed past them at 300 Kmp/h and then wont do a thing.
The only few times i've gotten in a chase was when I purposely rammed the cop car or rammed a bunch of AI cars and objects.
If you do manage to get into a chase. well they arent that good either. if you want to have a good chase your better off playing Need for Speed Carbon or Most Wanted 2005.
You can get 6 stars which only changes how many cars chase you. at 4 you get a helicopter after you (which is the only hard enemy to lose) Road blocks are mostly 1 car and a police sign or on highways like 3 cars and a sign so easily avoided and they will not use Spike Strips or anything like that.
You can't disable the road skills meaning you either have to go around or start it and then close it via your phone.
I still rate gameplay an 8/10 due to how good the cars felt
Soundtrack
Not so much to say about the soundtrack. most missions have a special soundtrack which is mostly dramatic orchestral and a bit electric.
The in-game radio stations aren't that great either. I mainly listened to 2 of them, Koda boom for in the city and Sine wave digital for the countryside.
There is a "custom" playlist option which means "pick songs from our radio stations!" and no importing of your own music.
(a huge thing that bugged me was how the power glove songs (from Far cry 3 blood dragon) still had the in game sound effects in them. You made the game how do you not have a clean version!)
In races where there was no special soundtrack I would open my steam overlay and just look up some other music.
So the music in this game gets a 4/10 you might like the tracks in the game though. It's just a matter of taste.
Story. Graphics. Gameplay. sountrack. that's about everything I think, and im running out of Review space.

Verdun is the first multiplayer FPS set in a realistic World War One setting. The merciless trench warfare offers a unique battlefield experience, immersing you and your squad into intense battles of attack and defense. Verdun is part of in the 1914-1918 WW1 Game Series, with the second entry Tannenberg taking players to the Eastern Front.
The game takes place on the Western Front between 1914 and 1918, in one of the bloodiest conflicts in world history. The developers were inspired by the infamous Battle of Verdun in 1916. The game offers 4 distinct game-modes with many historically accurate features such as realistic WW1 weaponry, authentic uniforms, horrendous gore, and maps based on the real battlefields of France and Belgium.
Verdun key features include:
- Realistic World War 1 gameplay: Authentic weaponry with realistic bullet physics, skill based weapon handling, poisonous gas with a claustrophobic gas mask experience, horrendous gore effects, and artillery barrages
- Tactical squad-based FPS: Unique squad leveling system with distinct squad types and roles
- True trench warfare: Real-time dynamic frontline with momentum-based attack and counter-attack gameplay
- Authentic World War 1 setting: Typical WW1 music and style, historical battlefields representing the key theaters on the Western Front
- Challenging game modes: Team-based Frontline, tactical Attrition, skill-based Rifle Deathmatch and desperate survival in Squad Defense

If I could give this game a totally mixed review, I would. I have therefore decided to recommend this game, but only when it's on sale half price, like when I got it.
In my experience, the story is forgettable, the missions can get repetitive (and often very difficult) and the 'RPG elements' including car upgrades are severely lacking. I would have loved to see actual individual upgrade purchases, like in the forza games, rather than meaningless stats. I completed the story missions in around 20 hours, playing entirely single player (the game includes worryingly few other players btw), which is feel is a more than acceptable gameplay time.
The thing that redeems the game though (mostly) is the map and the cars... Firstly, i'll talk about the map. Ignore all of the criticism of it being too small, or not very detailed, its amazing. There are enough areas to carry on exploring after the story is completed and driving around is very fun on its own! If free roaming is your thing, then you will love this. The cars, as i've mentioned before, have limited customization when it comes to performance, which is a shame. HOWEVER, you can customize the looks of your cars, from decals, to alloys, to bumpers as much as you want. Also, you can customize a car for each spec you have it tuned to, so effectivley having multiple versions of each car! You can build your favourite cars and then use the in-game photography mode (which is very in-depth) to take pictures wherever you want, with filters, lighting, weather effects etc. This part of the game, however small, can eat up hours if you like getting the perfect screenshot!
Overall, this game is somewhat disappointing, when you consider the marketing and what it claims to be.. a driving MMO! If you want a simulation game, or something with hardcore racing, it's definatley not for you. If however, you are a fan of more 'arcadey' racing games, or just want something different to play, I would give it a try. I wouldn't however say it's worth the full price, especially when its plagued with DLC and microtransactions!

When I got The 39 Steps, I was expecting a visual novel adapted into a point and click type adventure game. What I got was various blocks of text I had to click with small bits of "click here to read this" and "do this to open that" type gameplay. Needless to say I became bored VERY quickly. I like casual games, and I like to do things at my own pace, but this snail's crawl was too slow and uneventful for my liking. I actually fell asleep at my keyboard twice during a 1 hour session.
The sound design is mediocre and the voices are too similar - it's overall very disjointed and not cohesive as a whole.
Adjust expectations before starting this game and I think anyone who just wants to read a story in small bits will enjoy The 39 Steps. If you expect any sort of action, you will likely be disappointed!
If The 39 Steps would have had a narrator instead of the player needing to click for each paragraph, I may have enjoyed it more. I feel like they should have chosen to go 100% visual novel instead of 90% visual novel and 10% gameplay. It makes the whole experience unsatisfying. I will simply read the original book when I feel like it. I will not revisit or complete this "game"

'Just Cause 2' may not exactly be my cup of tea, but I'm going to recommend it to those who like third-person sandbox action games. It is a game that doesn't take itself too seriously, evidenced by the cheesy dialogue reminiscent of those in outlandish action movies of the 80s and 90s, laughable voice acting, and the floaty jump mechanics and fall physics.
While its contemporary, 'Grand Theft Auto IV', features a tight, engaging story that guides you through its world and introduces you to various side missions and minigames, 'JC2' forgoes that in lieu of a truly open world that you can explore right from the get-go. The grappling hook, unlimited parachutes, and superior flight controls allow for more interesting ways to explore your surroundings. 'JC2', therefore, offers a refreshing, yet somewhat unfocused gaming experience at the same time.
While the above features may open up ways to approach a combat situation, the combat mechanics in 'JC2' (released in 2010) somehow feels antiquated compared to 'GTA4' (released in 2008) and it could have used a bit of tightening up. Even the mayhem you can cause in 'GTA4' feels more satisfying and visually stunning. The gameplay camera also lacks refinement, especially the tilting that happens when you ride a motorcycle. Say what you will about the driving in 'GTA4' at launch, but it is superior to that in 'JC2' to this day.
Despite its shortcomings and my personal preference, 'JC2' is an action game that is better suited to players who prefer a genre parody/homage over a satire, and one that makes exploration priority over a tightly knitted narrative. It's worth checking out at the very least given the game's price point at the time of this review.

I am going to start this review with controversy. Of the Fallout series I think Fallout 3 is the best of them. Now before you start flaming me over the fact your prefer Fallout: New Vegas or Fallout 1 for instance, let me try and explain this.
Fallout 1 & 2 remain good classics, that must be played by any fan of the later Fallouts, if only for the feel of it for the moment. The first Fallouts had the best incentive to go away from the safety of community, because either your vault or your tribe was in danger - both of them showing much of Fallout world. However, that said although I enjoy pixelated games... they are pixalated games and some of the tactic options are for the time excellent, but now outdated.
Fallout 3's incentive to travel is a bit odd. You must basically because you are thrown out and you are supposed to set out on your family member that walked out on you (before you go 'What?!', sorry I won't spoil more). This incentive is rather... odd. However, than comes Fallout 3 itself. Although opinions aside about the radio jockey - a controversy in the community - the added old school music and now stunning graphics make the Fallout world come to live. Although some errors in cannon can be found, most quests are excellent and tie into the world itself. Also allowing free roaming like the old game, but now the road itself is just as interresting - something Fallout 1 & 2 were less able do due to technical reasons (random encounters based on luck (or unluck)).
The main quest can be ended in much shorter time than I played in it, heck I have several lives, but I also have but one expansion. Still if you focus on only the mainquest than you are doing it wrong. Go out and explore and feel like an adventurer in a dismal post-apocolyptic world.

After Dark Souls, most of the conversation was about how hard the game is, as if that was its only quality. It took some time, critical thinking, and noteworthy voices to bring new concepts into the discussion, like how fair the difficulty is (overall), the variety of playstyles, the great storytelling and world-building, the unique online functionality, etc. FromSoftware made DS2 with only difficulty in mind.
The story has been set aside. The intro tells you nothing and leaves you with nothing to think about other than that you're the cursed undead. Many bloodstains have been placed by the devs in an attempt to create atmosphere and tell mini-stories rather than clue the player into where and how people died, like in the first game. Messages left by other players don't appear like they should. Useful info that has been upvoted hundreds of times won't appear until well after you needed the information.
From there, DS2 throws giant spongey enemies at you, and lots of them. Or there will be hordes of enemies to fight, and the only way to handle them is to pull them out one at a time. That happened in DS1, but it was occasional; in DS2, it's constant. And when you die, you lose part of your maximum health, making the part that you had trouble with before even harder. Some enemies have grabs that will kill you in one hit. Enemies that used to be mid-late game foes, like phantoms, will now appear much earlier.
Level design is more confusing; at first, I couldn't even find the first level and went straight to later stages because that's what I thought the first level was. Most of deaths have been environmental. DS2 has a lot of narrow paths and falls that will kill you. Apparently, bad platforming was a highlight of the last game, so FromSoftware upped the ante by giving you more bad platforming.
I really want to like DS2, and I keep playing in the hopes of finding what I loved in the first game. But the first few hours were spent frustrated and confused rather than compelled. DS2 is more like a 3D version of "I Wanna Be the Guy" than a sequel to DS1.

Tomb Raider Angel of Darkness is a strange game. In many ways it's the greatest Tomb Raider game that Core design ever developed, while also being the most broken. Even this port is basically incompatible with Windows 8 and 10, the controls are a waking nightmare, and the game is full of bugs and glitches that existed from launch that make it practically unplayable in certain area's.
That's where the fans comes in. Over time fans have developed patches designed to not only fix bugs, but to fix the controls, among other things. They are not difficult to find, and once you do, you'll have easily one of the best Tomb Raiders ever released. DIfficult? Yes. Painfully irratating? Yes. This is not the autosaving, hold your hand, action game we have now. This is true OG Tomb Raider. You will fall to your death randomly, be constantly frustrated, and completely lost. Just like the good old days. If you don't mind finding and installing player mods, and spending an entire day getting a game to run, then TR:AoD is certainly worth your time.
Original Review: "TR:AOD is an amazing game, though rough around the edges, however Eidos abandoned this port immediatly after launch and it is not compatible with Windows 10. Even if you get it to launch, you won't be able to save. Some community patches exist, but none seem to be able to fix all the problems at the same time. I bought it for .97 cents and still feel ripped off."

While indeed this game is fantastic, there are a few glaring issues that are here. First off, it's barebones. The content of this game is the absolute minnimum. Same as mobile. The one on the web browser has more to offer with a crafting system and more missions. The next issue is the options menu. There's no volume control. It's either off or on. I was in a call with my friend, and couldnt hear him over the sound of gunfire and zombies. This is a pc game. can't even make volume control? The third problem is with the HUD. It's much to big and easy to click on. I've tried shooting a zombie in the bottom of my screen, and instead bought over 400 rounds of HD ammo, money I did not want to spend. This would be fine, if i had to click again to confirm, or even to buy a new stack, but if you hold left click, youll buy them as fast as possible. In game currency that needed to be spent elsewhere. I did notice the controller support...I guess thats okay, the only thing is, is that this game is NOT a twinstick shooter. aiming sucked on mobile, it will suck with a controller. In terms of actually gameplay, what else is there to say? Its pretty damn fun. The fact that its on steam, means that now, you wont suffer from insane lag found on the flash version of this game. Not to mention, it's a lot easier to play with ONLY my friends. Just invite them on steam. Not to mention the microtransactions can come right through your steam account. always a bonus. The game is fair in the fact that you never need to spend a dime to get good loot, but it does help the process of grinding. My friend bought some nantonium strongboxes, and good fantastic loot...for his level. It didnt completely outshine me, who was a good 3-5 levels ahead of him. To fix some of the issues above, why not reduce the size of the HUD's buy options, and update the game to the standards that the flash game has? Because it's on steam, I assume you have some communication to the developers. Something new to go with this release would be nice too. New maps, New weapons, New bosses, all would be fantastic. If you don’t mind a game with almost no gameplay elements and you are looking for something diferent to relax in the cold winter, 39 Steps might be the game you are looking for. Sit back, get warm and grab a cup of tea or coffee because you will only need to move your mouse every now and then. You play as Richard Hannay, a man from London during 1914 with a boring life whose fate changed after a certain event. Now, he’s being chased by a crime he didn’t commit. And that’s when the story gets interesting.
The game reads like a book, and you won’t have any choices to make like, say, a Telltale game. You just explore your surroundings, read some descriptions, and move on with the story. The game does not lie about this, their premise is really honest and you should know what you are getting into, you will be reading a digital book with some clicks here and there. As the story goes, tension will go up as things may get troublesome in the road making Hannay finding different means to get what he want weather by escaping, stealing or using his wits and words with strangers. The visuals of the game are calm with vibrant colors. They are hand painted with minor movements like the wind and it will remind you of some old point & click adventure games. During your play through you will also find some collectibles by explorations. These are very hard to miss, especially if you are playing the game carefully and take your time to look at the scenario before being done with it.
After 4 hours I finished the game and I do not find any reason to play it again. It’s a different experience and it was something I rather enjoyed. The final chapters make the conclusion satisfying and I was engaged in the game from start to finish. When I finished a chapter I just had to go to the next one as I was too curious to know what was going to happen or how Hanney is going to find a solution for his current problem. Because there’s almost no gameplay mechanics involved this games ended being quite relaxing. You can be very tired after a long day at work sipping your hot beverage while playing 39 Steps and it’s going to be a nice experience.

The 39 Steps é um jogo que conta uma história de um conto policial, com um engenheiro que quase se tornou um detetive (com a sorte e ajuda de outrem) e com um pouco de  mistério. Este jogo tem um quê de Sherlock Holmes (inclusive faz referência ao personagem, à saga e ao autor Arthur Conan Doyle). A história é bem interessante, mas demonstra faltar alguns pontos chaves com elementos não tão detalhados e simplificados (subjetivos).
Sobre a jogabilidade em si, você não precisa fazer muita coisa. Basta ler tudo o que o narrador-personagem vai contar (que é o protagonista) e clicar em coisas brilhantes que te chamam a atenção e que o personagem vai notar e usar junto aos seus conhecimentos para dar continuidade à história (semelhante a um Hidden Object). As cutscenes do jogo mostram ambientes bonitos e bem feitos (que parecem telas pintadas ou fotos antigas de lugares a céu aberto ou ambientes bem mobilhados). Você ainda tem a possibilidade de fazer desenhos com o mouse (nos momentos em que o personagem vai abrir portas - normalmente, nada de arrombar - ou abrir janelas, garrafas. O jogo indica no canto da dela a quantidade de coisas que você pode encontrar no ambiente para ajudar seu personagem e a quantidade de parágrafos que você também vai passar por . Além disso, a história contada pelo personagem só dá continuidade quando você dá um clique com um mouse para ela passar ao próximo texto narrado. No mais, a história segue seu curso e você não faz muitas interferências (no máximo pular as cutscenes e entender nada da história e perder conquistas do jogo por causa disso).
A OST do jogo, apesar de não ser tão diversa nos diferentes momentos da história é boa. Acho que se encaixa bem no que o jogo propõe e os sons utilizados também.
Por fim, eu gostei do jogo, porém acho que ele foi pouco explorado. Ele tem uma proposta muito boa (pelo menos para mim) e poderia ter sido mais legal ainda com poucas mudanças. Mas entendo que a proposta talvez tenha sido essa desde o início, e é um modo de contar uma história.
