This is a tough one because I can definitely see the ambition here to create a story which tackles a couple of themes that are a bit meatier than the average horror game (i.e. drug abuse and mental illness), but as it stands, it doesn't really flesh out those themes at all.
In the game, you start out tied up in the back of someone's van where a brief control tutorial occurs and then the screen goes white and you suddenly wake up to find the van is off the road and the back doors are open. You then wander into a nearby town that seems to have been recently abandoned and try to figure out who you are and whate exactly is going on.
Now, as starting premises go, amnesiac protagonist is a fairly reliable one for keeping the player in the dark about the game world they are in, but in exchange, you have to spend a lot more time giving the player reasons to invest in the character they're playing as, and within the hour or so this game takes to complete, it fails to find space for that extra time.
The hallucination sequences which make up the bulk of the storytelling are cool and well done, but awkward controls and inconsistent collision detection make even navigating the town difficult, which becomes even more of an issue when you're escaping a building that is suddenly (at least from your character's perspective) engulfed in flames. These sequences are also frustrating because they frequently include loud ambient noise, but the game lacks a subtitle function, which makes it hard to hear any of the game's dialogue, even above the constant drone of rain that permeates the entire experience.
The flow of the game is also incredibly hard to follow. You visit various locations marked on a map where you are faced with some sort of puzzle which then gives you access to either a newspaper clipping, some form of audio, or both. However, there's never any indication given that you've gotten everything you can from an area, and in the last location, you can end up walking straight into the ending while missing over half of the final bits of story. Furthermore, you can visit these locations in any order, which destroys some of the tension of the slow reveal the story is trying to pull off since important details are revealed to you before you even know what their significance is if you visit the locations in the wrong order.
If the developer is serious in saying that they intend to flesh this out and create a more polished final product, I will definitely say this has a lot of potential, but as it stands, it needs a lot of work in how it builds tension and invests the player, otherwise it just feels like a sparse walking simulator with a horror theme, rather than an actualy horror game.

I first picked it up because it was free, and because it was not a top-down, or a side-scroller. In that sense, there are few games like it.
I saw a lot of negative reviews on it. I wanted to like it. I figured the other people reviewing it just didn't understand what it was, basically a demo by young developers and gave it bad reviews when compared to games made by larger studios like 'Gone Home' or 'Fire Watch'. Like I said, I wanted to like it.
But I couldn't. I can look past many of the bad graphics and janky model designs (they're students!), but some things I couldn't look past. The game was unplayable. There is no menu when you hit escape, so I had to CTRL-ALT-DELETE close it. Also if you hit the 'J' button a menu for Journals pops up, and cannot be closed. I gave this game the old 'college try', but the first building I walked into in the city, I became trapped, and the game wouldn't allow me to leave. That combined with the Journal menu in the middle of my screen, and not being able to exit out of it... after about 15 minutes I hung this game up for good.
Games made by young developers or small teams can still be good. They can still have heart, they can still have soul, they can be playable; unfortunately, this was not. The spooky city could have been cool but alas, I'll never know because I was stuck in the first building I entered.
That being said, if the developers read this, I want them to know I respect them for the amount of work they put in. Even a game like this, broken and a bit primitive still took a massive amount of work. I wouldn't say this game is hopeless, or to never make another game again, but this version, where it is, just isn't 'it'.
If you enjoy a good 2-3 hour challenge than this game is for you. 7/10

An undisputable work of genius and another gem from Terry Cavanagh; this game completely changed my view not just of games with minimalist graphics, but of all indie games in general.
Don't be fooled by the ordinary looking visuals of the game, the developer has distilled the core essence of smooth and satisfying platformer gameplay into a flawless work of art. As you move around this platformer you'll be in constant awe of the level design to the point where you'll find yourself muttering "this is pure genius!" under your breath section after section of the levels.
The absurdly simple controls (left, right and a toggle for up/down) allow you to focus on the smooth level design and beyond a point it feels like you've relegated the notion of mechanical "game controls" to a far corner of the mind and you're simply reading the developer's mind as fast as you can think. I wish I had the time to complete all the achievements this game has as it is very rewarding. Note:- I have more hours logged on this game than Steam displays, much of it was offline I believe.
If you're on the fence, just download the demo and give this game a shot. Chances are you'll love it!

Cross-media experiments are always risky, and this unique adaptation of ‘The 39 Steps’ is a good example to show it. There was a lot of thought and care put into it, but in the end it just didn't succeed. It’s a shame, really.
If you didn’t know already, ‘The 39 Steps’ was originally a serialised pulp novel published in 1915. Its protagonist, an involuntary adventurer, Hannay, gets caught in a web of German conspiracy against the power structures of Europe, only to be chased through half of Scotland, eluding his pursuers only by his quick wits and a few friendly locals. It was sort of a forefather of the spy thriller genre that was so popular in the 1970s.
This adaptation tried to do something other than the numerous others by being a cross between a visual novel and an audiobook. Sadly, it fell between the two stools.
For a radio drama, it is good, and the actors are especially adept at portraying all the various British dialects, but there are so few recorded sections that you sometimes forget that these characters have voices.
For a visual novel, it is just dull. Everything is a still image background with an occasional grey silhouette. The drawings look spectacular, but their stillness completely fails to capture the supposedly fast pace of this century-old action thriller.
I wish I could give a better rating, because the amount of work put into this adaptation is more than admirable. But in the end, I must say that if you are interested in ‘The 39 Steps’, just buy the book instead.

- covenants system still a mistery in game

- easier crafting system
- lots of resources for upgrade

Tomb Raider VI: The Angel of Darkness meant the end for the classic Lara Croft and the splitting of Eidos Interactive and Core Design. It was unfortunate, as Angel of Darkness brought a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack composed by the London Symphony Orchestra, and a thrilling and intriguing story by Murti Schofield. It may have lost fans and money, but it gained something else: A cult fandom, and a team of people united across the world to revision the unfinished sequel that is Tomb Raider: The Lost Dominion. It won hearts and inspired writers and artists alike, including myself.
Tomb Raider VI: The Angel of Darkness is the sixth adventure for Lara Croft, but it is not her last. I highly recommend this memorable tale of endurance and strife. It holds a deep story that has provoked hundreds if not thousands, and has built a community who admire the effort behind the flimsy controls. There is something to be found in every tomb; there is a story for every lost artifact. This is one of them.

The Angel of Darkness (AoD) was released before it was really finished. As a result, there are one or two minor plot holes and the game doesn't always feel as polished as it should. That being said, the game has been patched extensively and it's not actually buggy. Many people complain about the controls and, while they may not be the most responsive controls ever and will probably take some getting used to, if you're familiar with the controls of Tomb Raiders 1-5, you should have no problems with AoD's. And for all its flaws, AoD has many strengths, too: an incredible story with engaging characters and an amazingly deep backstory, a mostly elegant mix of adventure, RPG, puzzle and platforming mechanics, one of the best video game soundtracks ever made and levels oozing with atmosphere. If I had to describe AoD in one sentence, it would probably be "Tomb Raider meets The Da Vinci Code" and if that sounds at all interesting to you, you should check it out. It is still one of my favourite games of all time despite, or maybe even because of, its flaws and I wholeheartedly recommend it.

VVVVVV is a very simple platformer that runs with one simple idea. You can change gravity instead of jumping. Right into the review.
This game is filled with frustrating design concepts that force you to replay the same situation over and over. Not to mention the sometimes-overly sensitive-sometimes not movement. One pixel hitting a spike? Dead. Pressed on the arrow key for a fraction of a second too long? You will go flying off the platform right into death. Most of the situations in the game aren't actually that hard. But they are just set up in such a way that you will fail over and over until you finally get lucky enough and you can fall down a pit pixel by exact pixel not hitting any spikes on the way down. It would be like trying to drop a quarter into a slot machine from 10 feet up. Its not challenging, just repititive and tedious. Its not enjoyable, its frustrating.
This game is not imaginative. The concepts and level designs have all been done before. This game isn't revolutionary, its not Braid, and it is certaintly no Fez. The concept of changing gravity to move around the world has a lot of potential. But the designer was either a lazy designer or a bad puzzle maker. Instead of making a thoughtful puzzle game that requires much head scratching and brain storming. They went for a cheap "avoid the red spikes" route. The levels are all mapped out, sure there is an over world. But its laughable compared to what gamers in this day and age are used to. Avoid the spikes, run to the end, rescue the person. Boring.
Now most of that I could live with. Its unimaginative sure, but at least it wasn't too frustrating. But the one thing that did it for me, the one thing that just killed the game for me, was the escort mission. Yeah you heard me, there is an escort mission. I can just imagine the developer sitting around thinking to himself. "You know what this platformer needs? An escort mission. I bet the player would enjoy that." Its completely surreal that anyone would even put an escort mission into a platformer. The NPC that you are escorting follows you from a couple feet behind you. So now, not only do you have to make it through the extremely accurate maze riddled with spikes, but you also have to guide this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ NPC through it as well. It got frustrating, fast.
So, even though I love platformers and really wanted to like this game. I can't, I just can't. Don't get me wrong, its fun, for awhile. But then all the bad design choices just leap out at you as you play through the game. Honestly the quality of this game is something I would expect in a common flash game that I played online when I was in middle school. Now if I had recieved the game in that setting, I would have loved it. But that fact that someone is asking money for a game of this quality astounds me.

Retaliation... another mislabeled, short, Unity Personal Edition indie game that is nowhere close to the "horror" genre as tags would suggest. The game is littered with problems that will most likely never be fixed, but hey, at least it went from the dollar bin to free in May 2016, right?
The store page for this game doesn't really give much of an indication as to what the game is about, so to put it clear and to the point: drugs. Teenagers and young adults taking drugs, to be more exact without spoiling anything. You're a nameless guy who has been kidnapped, and you wind up in a "strangely familiar" town. You basically go around in a large circle, visiting all of the locations marked on the map, and solving small puzzles at each one. After each puzzle, more of the story is revealed. Though I believe that you can complete the game without even visiting any of the locations except for the last one. The entire experience lasts roughly an hour, but that's only due to the fact that it takes ages to get from one spot to the next.
The voice acting is awful, but that aspect is the least of the troubles that Retaliation hosts. Aside from jumping framerates, there are terrible texture flickers, popping textures, some of the worst mechanics imaginable, and controls that make it feel like you're moving a ten ton boulder instead of a human being. Climbing stairs is a monumental task, nearly impossible really, and you have to jump up any set of stairs in order to make it to the top; like this guy cannot even climb one single stair, I'm serious. One of the puzzles in the game is bugged. You footsteps keep going even when you stop.
Short and simple, Retaliation is another Unity Personal Edition indie disaster that tries to pass itself off as horror even though it has literally no horror elements whatsoever. I did enjoy the Bioshock reference on one of the posters, though. The game Morphine comes to mind actually, it has the same basic premise, bad assets, and hazy graphics, but even that paid-for mountain of garbage is better than this title; they're both bad, however, so don't go buying Morphine because "The Horror Network said it was good". Anyway... just avoid this one in lieu of an actual horror title. If you're looking for a free, good, horror game, check out Cry of Fear.

I must say, The 39 Steps really impressed me. It presents the perfect blend between video games and books. The game is essentially a visual novel, but a rather special one. It's a digital adaptation of a espionage thriller, where the main character is Richard Hannay, someone who is put on the run due to certain events to which I won't spoil for you. The story is engaging, and the way it's told is creative and original. Besides the beautiful hand drawn art design, the sounds effect are splendidly united with the phrases you'll be reading throughout the main events. The progression is linear, something expected. Simple actions are executed by dragging your mouse in certain directions (such as trimming Hannay's beard, for example), and those end up adding immersion to the game. The voice acting is remarkable and the only problem I had with it was due to the not understandable scottish accents, but that was easily fixed by turning on the lyrics. Various objects can be explored and viewed from different angles, and The 39 Steps, at times, even is educative in a way that it provides information on the history at that particular time, around 1910. The achievements are easily obtainable, as they are completed by finishing event after event, which function like a chapter in a book.

Below I will list the things that - personally for me - were a bit of a turn off from this installment:
- poor lore and story compared to DS1 (so far I cannot say anything about DS3). And not because it was not connected to DS2, the story was in general not interesting, as a player I havent felt any bounding with the world or the characters in it
- poor boss fights - if you exclude 3-4 of the boss fights you get poor mechanic, repeating patterns, easy bosses in general. The fight simply did not fell interesting, compared to DS1
- healing gems - the fact that you can buy infinite amount of them is just staggering
- cheap dying from unpredictable...things in general - left a sence of unfairness. Souls games are hard, but fair in general. This was not the case with this one.
- strange hitboxes - quite often you can die in a strange way, because an impossible hit landed on you
- inconveinient level design - lack of shortcuts, illogical placing of bonfires, some areas are a real pain because they were made artificially hard - constant sniping, ambushes, fighting in boggy areas, etc. (Shrine of Amana, Black gulch, Dragon Aerie)

- covenants system still a mistery in game

- easier crafting system
- lots of resources for upgrade
- Pharos lockctones
- very good graphics
- Smelter demon :D
- good fighting system
- better pvp gameplay
- warping between bonefires from the start
- more interesting messaging system
Buy it already.

I will talk about few things here but I will first say, that I use the control fix mod, HD graphics mod (only for first few levels) and some other mods. So I had a better gaming experience than it was at the release.
Story
One of the best in the series. I love how it's not a typical "Search for artifact without even have a clue why she is searching for it". The game was rushed and that's why it wasn't finished. The beta documents are in the internet so the story wouls've been better than it was already. But for now it's also great. I enjoyed the story and very well cutscenes. Also playing as Kurtis was also cool and that they put a second playable character in this game was something new, which I liked.
Graphic
The game turns 13 years old this year, so of course it's old graphic engine. I like the style about it and that it's not trying to look realistic (like nowadays), instead it's kinda of a comic style. I prefer this style over the games who came after AOD.
Gameplay
We all know that the controls weren't the best but before I used the control fix, I never had problems with the controls so I don't really have nothing against them. The only things I didn't liked were that she does 2 slow moves and then starts running. The second thing was the control on stairs sometimes. That was annoying. The grip thing was interesting and maked it more realistic but climbing under time pressure wasn't so good. The rest of the controls were good. They were kinda like the old controls so.
Music
The soundtrack is also one of the best in the series. I love the theme song the most and also the others. If you want to listen to it, search it on youtube and listen to the beautiful soundtrack :)
Overall
This game is one of my faves for some reasons (Really good story, the style of the Levels and good cutscenes for example). Many people dislike the controls or some bugs in this game but if you put them aside, you have a good game. I think it would've been the best TR, if it was finished and not rushed and released in an unfinished state. I recommend this game if you don't really care for bugs and the controls and just want to experience a good story with interesting game design than it's the perfect game for you :) This game deserved better-

Automatic weapons are few, cumbersome beasts that eat bullets and will rip your sorry body several new structurally superfluous orifices. While outside of the trenches, people will be shooting at your team mates, your squad mates, the dirt all around you, and your sorry body, while artillery rains down on you like money at Valve during the Summer Sales. Inside the trenches, you can go upwards of two minutes without seeing an enemy, but at soon as there is one, there is all of the enemies. Artillery will continue to rain on you, but luckily it's friendly so it is less likely to kill you. Half of a second can make the difference between life and death, where who ever can land the first shot wins. The accuracy of the weapons can be a bit of a hindrance, as hip firing allows greater movement but has little accuracy while aiming means you can hit something while not able to react so well due to slower movement. All in all, it is an enjoyable game if you like having your legs go in one direction and your body in a different direction, all though I had this game before it was on Steam, so I can say that it looks and acts nicer now that it did before.

Just Cause 2 is an amazing open world third person shooter set in the fictional country of Panau. Let me first start off with the map, which is absolutely MASSIVE. It takes an incredible amount of hours just to explore the island. The entire game is like a B-list action movie filled with explosions, car chases, missle launches, shootouts, and drugs. I mean B-list action movie in the best way possible because the game doesn't take itself seriously, from the absolutely ridiculous plot, to the riding atop airplanes in midair. The game uses the cliches of action movies to highlight the absurdity of the plot.
Gameplay wise, the game has left a good bit to be desired. The AI is terrible and have the minds of blind 12 year olds, fixing the AI would make the game much better. The game also fails to make the world feel "alive". An open world game should make the player feel as if they in another world that is alive and breathing, which Just Cause 2 failed to do. The gun play was nothing special, solid, but nothing we have not seen before. The thing that really made the gameplay enjoyable was the grapple hook. The grapple hook made lots of normal things diffrent and unique. The combination of the grapple hook and the parachute made getting around the island fun and different. The vehicles were also great, although the cars at times felt a little too "arcade-y", but overall the panes helicopters and boats all felt amazing. The Map design was also something that stood out exceptionally well. The island's geography made it seem as an actual place, in the sense that mountains and roads and lakes all seemed realistic. The design of high structures such as towers and mountain coupled with the parachute and the grapple hook made you feel like a dardevil jumping off and grabbing onto things. The short side missions all were basically the same and I think a variety in the missions would have positively impacted the game.

Outlast (4 Spooky 2 Me)
I was first exposed to Outlast when watching youtuber PewDiePie play the beta. I was very interested in this game, but I'm not a fan (and by that I mean a huge wuss) of the horror genre. Outlast was a whole $20 I didn't want to spend yet, so I thought it might go on sale. I managed to buy it for $6.49 during the Steam autumn sale 2013 and loved it to death. This game gave me chills and is my vote for GAME OF THE YEAR. (9.5/10)
1. Ambience (+8)
Whoa. A +8? Yes. This game had me so immersed that when I would make too loud of a noise in game I felt my heart pounding and yelled "NO NO NO WHY SO MUCH NOISE, QUIET DOWN!!!!". This game made me think I was actually in an insane asylum and made me see some strange things afterwards. Incredible ambience and enviroment.
2. Graphics (+1.5)
This game has some of the best graphics I've seen. Im running then on an old Sapphire 6970 at 60FPS just fine and it honestly, looks better than Crysis 2 (Not 3, but 2 yes.)
3. Old style Gameplay (+ or - .5 depends)
If you're used to tutorials, and things being obvious and blatent in games nowadays, like most are, then this game might now be for you. I'm a fairly old school gamer, used to titles like Legend of Zelda and Paper Mario in which puzzles weren't explained to you in any way. This game does a great job blending old with new.

As a game, I thoroughly enjoyed what the (base) game has to offer. I only have the base game so I will write my review based on that.
PROS :
+ Fast paced, arcade racing
+ Enormous map to travel around (If you love driving around for hours on end for no apparent reason like me)
+ Off-road racing
+ Graphics are pretty good. Dirt, snow, rain effects are present on top of car scratching and crumpling due to impacts.
+ Day/night cycle
HOWEVER the many things preventing me from recommending this game to anyone are as follows :
CONS :
- Multiplayer PvP is not balanced (i.e. Going into a Perf spec race with a Lvl 680 BMW M3 facing off against a Lamborghini and two other hyper cars beyond Lvl 1000)
- Physics engine is not good at handling bumps and jumps, making most Dirt and Raid spec related events frustrating.
- Wild Run advertisment EVERYWHERE. Main menu, Wild Run. Look for crew, Wild Run. Summit events on map, Wild Run. Don't want it, don't need it, don't intend to get it. (Get a hint from Dying Light developers, please.)
- Locked to Uplay. The bloody Uplay.
- Free roam doesn't allow me to race other players at will. (Even GTA:O has this feature and it isn't even a racing game.)
- The game instantly forces you back into the main menu when you lose connection to the servers, even when you're playing a Solo mission. I was doing a 100KM faction race and got forced back to the main menu when I just passed the 55KM mark. COME ON. At least put me on a temporary offline mode and reattempt connection while I continue my race you lazy twa ts.
And the last point which angers me the most :
- - - EULA Restrictions. I am currently studying in Sarawak, Malaysia and a friend helped me buy this game while it was on discount, but I can't even access the game in my home in Brunei just 2 hours drive away from where I am? Asia region my as s.
TL;DR = Great game, even greater flaws. If you would really like to try this game I'd suggest getting it on a 60% or above sale.

I deffinitely am reccomending this game - its Souls game and brings in a way that specific vibe.
However, for me this is the worst game of all three in the series - I have played DS 1&2 and currently started DS3 - 10h of gameplay so far.
Below I will list the things that - personally for me - were a bit of a turn off from this installment:
- poor lore and story compared to DS1 (so far I cannot say anything about DS3). And not because it was not connected to DS2, the story was in general not interesting, as a player I havent felt any bounding with the world or the characters in it
- poor boss fights - if you exclude 3-4 of the boss fights you get poor mechanic, repeating patterns, easy bosses in general. The fight simply did not fell interesting, compared to DS1
- healing gems - the fact that you can buy infinite amount of them is just staggering
- cheap dying from unpredictable...things in general - left a sence of unfairness. Souls games are hard, but fair in general. This was not the case with this one.
- strange hitboxes - quite often you can die in a strange way, because an impossible hit landed on you
- inconveinient level design - lack of shortcuts, illogical placing of bonfires, some areas are a real pain because they were made artificially hard - constant sniping, ambushes, fighting in boggy areas, etc. (Shrine of Amana, Black gulch, Dragon Aerie)
- somewhat poor choice of weapons and armor at the beginning
- covenants system still a mistery in game
Good points:
- easier crafting system
- lots of resources for upgrade
- Pharos lockctones
- very good graphics
- Smelter demon :D
- good fighting system
- better pvp gameplay
- warping between bonefires from the start
- more interesting messaging system

The sequel to Dark Souls is often regarded as the weakest of the series. I disagree and I think it's as great as the first one. Different, yes; Worse, no.
I recently finished the game and its DLC. It was great for most part and I can't avoid including this series of games on my best games I ever played list.
Many say that DS2 is the inferior game of the series. I, however, don't see it this way. It's a different game than all the others and it's fantastic on its way, don't let that fool you.
I can't stress enough on how great I think the PVP is in this game. There are some really great ideas that were implemented that you need to see for yourself and experience them.
I wasn't a fan of how some bosses and enemies of the DLC have such a large HP pool. I find that increase of difficulty a bit cheap and don't make said bosses interesting but there are some really, really amazing boss fights on the DLC that feel just right.
Talking about the DLC there is an area I trully despise. It was actually the last area I visited in the game and the last boss I didn't kill at the time. Unfortunately, since it was the last area, it left me a bit of a sour taste as I found it trully uninspiring, bland and rushed. It's an optional area, yes, but the quality of the other areas is simply not there.
All and all, DS2 is a magnificent game. Different than the first one, some things are better, some are worst. Great PVP and some fantastic boss fights, I love it as much as the first one.

- Crates can be gained while playing

That's about it, If I think of anything else, I'll be sure to add it! Overall, really fun game with three classes that can be all built in the way you'd like them to be built! Be sure to check it out, you won't regret it!

In the 39 Steps you play a bored UK citizen who gets involved in a complicated conspiracy right before the beginning of WWI. The game will get you hooked really fast because of it's great story (it's an adaptation from an actual novel), beautifully painted scenarios and awesome voice acting.
It's not an actual GAME, though, it's more of an experience, a new way of storytelling. There's not a lot of interaction - you just have to use your mouse every now and then to keep the story going, and that's pretty much it. However, the game manages to never get you bored by delivering the story in different ways: sometimes you get dialogues, sometimes you have to explore around a scenario, look at a newspaper, watch a small movie (I loved those!), etc. The BEAUTIFUL landscapes, accompanied by great music and sound effects will do the rest to keep you in the right mood.
I finished the game within a weekend, and it really felt like reading a good book. Whenever I wasn't playing, I was thinking of it, wanting to get lost again in the lovely Scottish glens. I believe that videogames are the future of storytelling, and this is a brilliant example. Very much recommended!

I enjoyed this game experience!
At first I was a little put off by the clunky controls (rotate mouse counterclockwise...), but this turned out to be easily mitigated.
Its an interactive novel, of sorts...
With that I mean that while its you, as a player/reader, that control the pace of the story, you have no influence over what will happen, you simply uncover the next step.
This means that game has no replayability, that is unless you have a somewhat bad memory or are very fond of the artwork in the game. Because the art work is at times very pleasing to the eye, several of them (a monoplane at sunset springs to mind) would have been nice to have had as backgrounds, but alas.
I thought the voice acting was more than decent too.
So, if you are looking for a good story, don't mind games that are good for one playthrough, and you don't demand action every minute to be entertained, I'd recommend this game. I got mine very cheaply indeed (thanks Indiegala), but its worth a few £/$/€.
Oh, not to forget, do stay till the end of the credits :)

You can align yourself towards a faction (Axis, Allies or Comintern) and once you join that faction you no longer control your own diplomacy. So if you want to be a rogue state and follow your own rules, keep yourself away from joining any of the three factions. Be aware though, that a lot of the major nations guarantee the lesser nation's independence and you can end up in deep trouble if you get an entire faction on your tail. However as a rogue faction, you can potentially exploit the world war by grabbing territories from unaligned factions creating yourself an Empire, or you can join a faction and fight for victory in the world war.
I gotta say, the game is surprisingly good. Once you jump into a session it's very hard to quit, like today I played as Brazil and I ended up sitting for 7 hours straight because it felt so satisfying when accomplishing stuff such as liberating countries, annexing neighbors and researching new technologies. This is my first paradox game and after playing this for only 15 hours I already feel like I have to buy the expansions in the future and perhaps other paradox games such as Victoria 2.
A great strategy game if you like to micro-manage an entire nation's economy, diplomacy, military, technology, politics etc.

This is a fast-paced single-player loot-until-you-die game, and its setting gives you the option of creative solutions for impassable areas. Is a container full of undefeatable mutants blocking you from valuable cargo? Then drill a hole in the hull, fly to the other side, and completely bypass your oblivious foes! Outwit mindless hordes, outlast deteriorating containers, and bring cargo back to satisfy yourself and benefit your uncaring corporate overlords! There is also a slower-paced "Journey mode" that is unlocked after a while, if you want to spend a more thoughtful and less frantic experience.
The main aim of the game is collecting all the different types of cargo, a blue-collar version of Pokemon. You won't have the option of knowing what cargo is in a level, not until midway through the game. If this is frustrating to you and you don't mind spoilers, there is a pdf walkthrough for this game with recommended level names out on the internet. A steam user called Catprog has also compiled a list of items on various level names on his personal website as well. Google these at your leisure.
Honestly though, the main goal of rounding out your cargo collection is tiring. Focus instead on the fun in the levels, leapfrogging mutants while structures break down around you. For me, everytime I brave the dangers of space and poor working conditions and get back safe with my working-man hands full of loot, that sends a spark of satisfaction through me, making this game all worthwhile.
Give it a go and try for a high score!

I'm definitely feeling some sympathy for the dev of this game.  First of all, through possibly no fault of his own, the game didn't seem to work for anyone when first put up on Steam.  Apparently there's STILL issues going on there, as the dev has now suggested to anyone who purchased his game to do a temporary "fix", which basically means you're playing a "beta" version of the game.  Having now played said "beta", all I can say is:  I sincerely hope the "fixed" version, once it's up and running, has far less technical and design problems, 'cause the version I played has an awful lot of 'em...

Firstly, almost straight off I noticed a bug in which the sound of my footsteps continued, even when I stopped walking or running.  Secondly, there are bits where your character has to JUMP to step up onto a sidewalk, despite said sidewalk only being a couple of inches off the ground, and you similarly can't traverse an ordinary set of stairs without LEAPING up them!  Thirdly, it's hard to tell which objects and doors you can and can't interact with, and even when you can, said interaction can be pedantic and hit-and-miss at best.  Fourthly, the map of a town that you pick up isn't that much help considering it doesn't show where you are as you move about, and fifthly said map disappears from your "inventory" and has to be picked up again if you start a chapter/section again.  Which sixthly, I ended up doing purely by accident, when I pressed the ESC button to pause for a second, and when I "continued", found myself at the beginning of an area which I'd already half-completed.  Oh, and seventhly, you do have a lighter, brought up by pressing "F", though I don't recall the game ever telling me this, and it kind of lights up ♥♥♥♥-all when you've got it out anyway.

All of this pales in comparison, however, next to the game's hands-down number one fault, which is the time-honoured "what the ♥♥♥♥ am I supposed to do next?" syndrome inherent in an awful lot of "independent" game-making.  For all their frequent lack of genuinely inspired ideas and slave-like adherence to established formulas and what-not, it's very rare to find a big-budget, mega-mainstream game in which you are left genuinely perplexed as to what your current objective is.  Now, I'm sure some would come to the dev's defense and say that it's all a bit "open" and you're supposed to uncover the town's secrets for yourself, etc etc, but that doesn't explain why I went into a building, searched around a tonne, found the numbers to a keypad by a door, entered the room in question and read a note and listened to an answering machine and THAT'S IT.  Not even some indication that I SHOULD go back outside and start looking elsewhere, just a complete confusion on my behalf as to whether I had missed something in the room or..?
In any case, the next building I explored was a high school, and a pair of what I take to be game-breaking bugs basically signalled the end for me.  Firstly, there was a room (with a very visible note on a desk) which I simply COULD NOT ENTER, despite the doorway being wide open.  Secondly, after collecting a bunch of jigsaw puzzle pieces I was instructed to go to a girls' bathroom, and sure enough found some "drugs" on the floor therein.  But again, there was no signal whatsoever that any "change" had occurred in the game, and this time 'round I couldn't even leave the building the way I came in.  Oh, and I should add...I had already managed to find and pick up the drugs earlier, BEFORE solving the jigsaw puzzle, but they still decided to respawn a second time.  Game over for me one way or another, I'm afraid.
Now, as to whether any of these issues are actually dealt with in the game proper I can't say, but given that the dev himself is suggesting that people play this beta, I can only assume that there won't be a dramatic improvement.  I can see what he's trying to achieve here, story-wise and so forth, and I won't deny that there's potential, for the game and/or himself as a designer.  But in its present state the game is eminently unplayable, and generally suggests a failed-but-interesting demo which should have been chalked up to valuable game-making experience, rather than released to Steam (even for a measly dollar).
By all means, should we get the word from the dev that:  a. the official game is now playable, and b. said official release is quite a bit more refined than the beta which I just attempted to play, I would be more than happy to give this another go.  For now, though, I cannot in all good conscience give it a recommendation.  You know there's something seriously wrong when you see the words "horror game" and "very short" all over a Steam page, and even YOURS TRULY doesn't bother to see it through to the end!  Here's hoping we get to turn that thumb the right way around some time...
Verdict: 4/10.

Cook, serve, delicious is one of those games that are easy to learn, but hard to master. You play as a restaurant owner that serves a line of waiting customers. You have to prepare each individual order by pressing the right button for each ingredient on your keyboard (you can also play with mouse or controller), and while it is pretty simple, it gets frantic very fast. You get to pick your own menu and upgrade your kitchen and recipes, which most of the time also makes them more complex to make but also more rewarding.
The game never gets boring as it keeps you constantly on your toes by a steady influx of customers, rush hour (which is a more fast paced part of your day) as well as several chores and sometimes even robberies (!) where you get to identify your assaulter. There are also several challenge stages for specific food groups which can get REALLY difficult to complete, but help you lead your restaurant toward your 5 star goal.
Gameplay gets more fast paced as you progress and can be pretty stressful, but is also very rewarding when you manage to get that perfect combo streak at the end of the day. If you are into this time sensitive serving "genre", this game will keep you hooked into it for hours at a time.

I mean, it has its flaws, I'm not gonna lie but you can't go past the feels that it brings from the original saga. I love all the Tomb Raider games, and this one is no different. The crazy and nonchalant story and the awesome enemies make the game what it is. Now yes, it has a lot of flaws, which can be explained by the early realease by the company (even before it was actually finished), pressured by the investors. And that sense of non-completion is palpable throughout all the game. The controls are the same as in TB4 (The last revelation) and TB5 (Chronicles) but somehow, although this is a newer game, they feel clunkier and less dynamic. Some enemies are really hard to kill (Boaz) and you don't always know what to do, but that is the signature move of this games, thou. Once you know your way around the creatures it is easy to bring them down (except for Boaz, that prick is a hard cookie), but in the way you may lose a lot of ammo and health. But, the save system actually saves you from that, if you're at least decent playing video games. One thing that did bothered me were the glitches and bugs scattered all over the place, but I can't blame the programmers for not having been allowed to actually finish the game and polish it. However, the graphics are pretty cool, considering the realease year and the rushed completion. They don't look like next gen of course but they have a nice rounded-shaped  form which doesn't make you believe that you're actually playing Minecraft. So, all in all, Tomb Raider 6 is an awesome (yet flawed) game that fans of the saga could enjoy, though it demands a lot of time and patience from the player. And yes, you WILL want to throw your keyboard through the window a couple times, but that's what we are in for, right?

As a long-time fan of the Tomb Raider series, I must confess- this is the only game in the entire franchise I dread playing, for a number of reasons. How is it even possible to make a misstep with such a beloved IP, and in such a grand scale? I'm not quite sure, but our boys at Core Design managed to do it. But is how the game turned out really their fault?
Kiiiiiiiinda.
Back around 2002-2003 Eidos was suffering through some serious financial troubles, and had to reallocate where time and money was being spent. Several projects being published by Eidos were unfortunately canned or put on hold during this time- including Kronos' Fear Effect: Inferno (rip). As Eidos' cash cow, you could imagine why the Tomb Raider franchise was exempt to this. Core Design was trying to beat everything they could out of the potential for the PS2, promising that Lara's next day out would revolutionize how adventure games are made. By Q2 2003, Angel of Darkness would both be somewhat near finished, and would have been delayed twice already- but Core still needed more time. Eidos ended up putting their foot down and hurried it along for release just in time for the live-action film and counterpart "Tomb Raider: The Cradle of Life" , select copies of the PS2 version of Angel of Darkness also came with free ticket vouchers to go see the movie! Great deal, right?
And then you played the game.
So what makes this game so terrible? Well, there's a lot of things. But before we get into all that, let's talk about the positives this game brings-
1. By far, the best part about this game would be both the sound design and soundtrack. Composed by Peter Connelly and Martin Iveson, the music is passionate, and really lets you feel like there's a lot at stake in Lara's predicament.
2. New inventory system. This is a mixture of bad and good- I like that there's a number of recovery items now that affect you in varying strengths, that you can buy and sell items, and so on. BUT the way the system is incorporated is very weird. It's like they just copypasted the pause menu and put numbers on it.
3. Graphical options. Oh my GOD. Click that setup button on the starting menu and you will feel like you're in the future with how many things you can fiddle with. This game came out 12 years ago, and it has a leg up on many AAA games in just how you can alter your game to your liking.
And that's about it.
OOOOOOOOOKAAAAY. Now for my favorite part.
The most heinous offender in this game would be the how the game handles. The controls are floatier than my fat♥♥♥♥♥coated in astroglide across an ice cap. It feels like they just tried to streamline the old grid-based movement system from previous games, which ironically makes jumping across gaps a lot harder. This is also the first game in the series to incorporate mouse control for the camera, and that seems like a well-needed improvement for the game, until you discover that it A) only works on the X-axis, B) moves lara around in whatever direction you're looking. Lara can still do flips and shoot and all that jazz, but it all feels so slow and clunky now. Frankly, most scripted animations in this game feel the same way. It kind of makes getting chased by a police helicopter through the streets of Paris lack a certain urgency through Lara's actions. You can sneak around, too, I guess. You'll only use this function maybe like two or three times in the whole game, and even then, you're only using it because that's when it's required. I find it hilarious that the every previous game has incredibly linear pathing, yet feels so much better to play with.
Angel of Darkness now features a unique dialogue system. This is revolutionary because you have the choice of picking between a whopping TWO options when speaking to the quantity of emotionless mannequins that are known to populate Paris. (I learned a lot about Paris playing this game, did you know there's only one harlot in the entire ghetto?) The greatest part about this dialogue system is how amusing it is that these convos often lead to two very differing results. My personal favorite being A) make a deal and get a bunch of cool things, B) uhhhhhh you get shot.
GOOD IDEA: Introduce RPG elements to an adventure game to increase the replay value, create various pathways/solutions to obstacles that can be utilized via whatever skills/stats you have (See: Deus Ex series)
BAD IDEA: Introduce RPG elements to an adventure game and make only one solution to every obstacle, making it impossible to progress unless you've levelled the one stat you need, making "skill trees" merely a fetch quest (See: this game)
This is also the first game where you can plays as someone who isn't Lara, you get to play as chirugai-wielding badboy and Nine Inch Nails frontman, Kurtis Trent (Reznor). You only play as him in the last third of the game (in Prague), and even then you play as him for maybe like an hour or two. That's about it.
Getting back to my previous point about the development process, a lot of people like to excuse this game because it was rushed by Eidos to fit in with the then-upcoming film release. But, you have to think about how much more "finished" this game could have been. It had started development with the turn of the millenium, and was originally slated for a Q4 2002 release- but was delayed until June 2003, and at that point, they still asked for some more time. Given that the entire story of the game was told, (yet unresolved, as there were originally supposed to be two games after this one to finish the arc it began) and a basic flow/design for the game's progression was established, you have to wonder what one more time extension really could have resolved. Sure, there'd be less bugs, but it wouldn't fix the rest of the game.
Between the bland, boring gameplay, the misplaced RPG elements, the terrible controls, I'm really wondering why I even bought this game on steam in the first place, I played it and hated it back on the PS2, so I can't imagine why I bothered to spend money on this game again. Maybe I just like to torment myself, maybe I just like to drop cash on garbage.
Bottom line: this game blows, don't waste money like I do.

Atmosphere. It’s not the sluggish controls, or the missing textures, or the plot inconsistencies, or Lara’s hilarious death cry that make this half-baked mess worth revisiting. It’s a game world in which everything you see and hear oozes with the atmosphere of a film noir. It’s a game world that rivals Shadow of the Colossus in its loneliness, Max Payne in its bleakness, and Resident Evil in its sense of growing dread. It’s a place we never thought we’d see Lara go, and a place we’ll never see her go again.
From the onset, we’re plunged into the seedy urban backdrop of Paris, and immediately it feels foreign, alien - there is no Eiffel tower in the distance, no idyllic boulevards, nothing to imply any sense of comfort or hospitality. Instead we explore back alleys with barking dogs chained to the walls, rain falling on dumpsters that need emptying, drainpipes running along decrepit buildings that at a glance might resemble an ancient tomb.
In The Angel of Darkness, the exotic has not been replaced with the urban - the exotic has been replaced with the decaying and the abandoned. In this respect, the locales featured in the game are more similar to previous instalments than first assumed, and they retain the same sense of danger and peril, cranked up to eleven.
This is partly because of an engrossing story that sees Lara accused of a crime she cannot recall committing. She’s on her own, stalked by police determined to bring someone, anyone in, to feign progress in their investigation of a series of violent murders. Suddenly Lara’s status as a world famous adventurer counts for nothing - her only friend is dead and she’s by herself in an unfamiliar country. Worse yet, none of this is her choice - she has not chosen to be in this situation, and instead it is one she is forced to fight her way out of. It’s the setup to a rewarding plot well ahead of its time for 2003, marred by a few glaring flaws, but absolutely worth sticking out to its conclusion. There is a real sense of action here, both intelligent and thrilling.
Sometimes, however, the danger conveyed stems from unreliable controls, glitchy physics and trial-and-error platforming/combat. Earlier Tomb Raider games were not easy, but gameplay mechanics were in place that guaranteed consistency - a standing jump would always perform exactly as expected, as would a running jump, and even the simpler but essential action of walking could be depended on to save Lara from falling off a ledge, usually to the sound of cracking bones. In The Angel of Darkness, a more conscious use of these actions is required - walking may see Lara decide to drop down and grab the end of a ledge at a crucial moment, a standing jump with the wrong trajectory or too close to a wall may see her veer off in the wrong direction, and simply drawing a gun can be followed by all manner of movement hiccups. A poorly implemented upgrade system doesn’t help, giving Lara further jumps and a higher level of “grip” at regular intervals, presumably to offer a new element to platforming, but in reality only succeeding in making it harder to tell whether or not she’ll be able to clear that gap.
Like most of the game’s design flaws and technical issues, this can be overcome by more patient gamers by a save system that can be used on-the-fly. From there, it’s a relatively smooth journey through around 30 levels of varying quality, each accompanied by one of the game’s saving graces, a haunting soundtrack that works as the perfect compliment to dark backstreets, unearthed tombs and industrial complexes acting as a front for something far, far more sinister. Cutscene direction enjoys similar success - arguably the game’s best moments are watched, not played - achieving a cinematic quality rivalled in 2003 only by the likes of Metal Gear Solid and Final Fantasy, not in terms of graphical fidelity but by a visual flair that goes beyond merely taking the audience from point A to B. Lara turns off the power, unwittingly unleashing a failed experiment (and setting up a boss fight for later), and we see the brutal havoc it leaves upon escaping its enclosure.
The Angel of Darkness is a beautiful disaster. Very little works as it should - the equilibrium of platforming, puzzles, and action perfected over the previous five instalments has been replaced by a Frankenstein of gameplay mechanics that, in spite of whatever intentions the developers might have had, do nothing in their existing form to enhance the overall experience. The game, then, is not for everyone. Yet there is enough here to entertain over its roughly 12 hour length, and if you can overlook the obvious issues, you may be lucky enough to catch a glimpse of the masterpiece that could have been.

Mud shifting underneath me.
The echoes of screaming soilders and fallen teammates surround me.
Crawling past razor sharp barbedwire as I try to find cover from the enemy's whizzing bullets that distort my hearing.
Finally, I get close enough to the trenches, but hidden enough so that I blend in with my surrounding environment.
Grenade explosions go off by me as I see my squadrons bodies collapsing and being thrown into the air.
The screams get louder and louder, but I know that I must concentrate on my shot.
The only visibility that I have is the glare off of my enemies helmets from the sunlight reflecting off of the rain on their helmets.
I line up my shot....*bfff*
I start picking off my enemies hiding behind their trenches like flies.
I shift my iron sights to the right and I make eye contact with one particuluar enemy.
Time slows down as we both take a deep breath and focus on one another knowing that one of us won't make it out alive.
I fire my shot....and my body goes limp.
Verdun is the WW1 game that we never thought we needed. It's surreal realism of battling in the trenches, equipping gas masks, and taking your time on each shot you take adds to the excitement. Verdun isn't just some war gam. It's a war simulation that tests your patience. You will die...a lot. But that adds to the realism. You can barely get away with a bullet graze, as the kills usually take only one hit. You have to use teamwork and tactics to flank and take advantage of your enemies weak points. There are a variety of gamemodes, but trenchwarfare is the most popular, and for good reason. I would highly suggest putting your money into this game if this sounds like something up your alley. The developers listen to complaints, and fix bugs and glitches, along with updating the game as well. Take advantage of any sales that go on if the normal price is out of your price range.

One of the greatest online multiplayer FPS games of the old and also most of the current generations, there is a single player mode to do a standard match with bots but the true value in this game is freely mod-able community servers, which has kept the game alive and feeling fresh to players for ages, i'd give it 5 stars but the only thing is its lacking in value if you dont have an internet connection all the time.
You can spend hours and days on end looking through the list of servers running all kinds of game modes, Jail Break, Gun Game, Zombie Escape, Zombie Riot, Surf, to name a few and even some servers that dont have anything to do with shooting, like MiniGames servers where its a course you have to maneuver through without falling.
Garrys Mod is an adaptation to CSS mixed with a little HL2 so if you like the other Source Engine games then CSS is for you, CS:GO has community servers as well but with all the hype of the "matchmaking" modes nobody even looks at the Mod servers, so if you like the gameplay change of community servers then CSS is for you, but if you like the standard style multiplayer matches like in Call of Duty then you probably wanna go for CS:Global Offensive.
I used to run an old laptop with a 2.14 Ghz single core AMD Sempron CPU and an AMD Radeon 4200 with 320MB with a 2x2 ft box fan on my table to cool the laptop, so if your systems a little better you should run things fine on all low settings as long as your system doesnt get too hot, and remember that with laptops and gaming heat is always your enemy.

is a unique interactive visual novel, developed by
and first released on Steam in april 2013. The game is based on the novel with the same title by John Buchan, which got quite well-known thanks to its being the inspiration for Ian Flemmings
books. The novel tels the story of Richard Hannay, a bored-to-death gentleman who all of a sudden finds himself in the eye of an espionage storm. Buchans story has its flaws: some plot-turns come across as unbelievable, but the characters are drawn very fine indeed, as is the time period against which the plot evolves.
Buchans novel is followed very closely in the game, which does an excellent job in transferring the overall feel and atmosphere of the period and place during which the action takes place: London, Scotland and the English countryside early summer 1914, just before the outbreak of the First World War. The developers achieved this by using a brilliantly designed and executed visual style, with a lot of hand-drawn images.
Actually, the story is told in several different ways, all with their own level of interaction. The narrative part of the novel is being projected on the screen, with the player having to click through the different lines. But the game manages to introduce variety even in this simple mechanic: the tempo of the clicking varies: sometimes a screen is held onto longer, while at other times clicks has to done much faster. Dialogues are being voice-acted in a very convincing way, some self-contained stories are even being projected as short movies. There is some point-and-clicking too, although this is allways clearly indicated and not designed as a challenge or puzzle. All in all, the variety in interaction between player and game helps a lot to draw one into the story.
The awesome visuals and interesting storytelling are accompanied by a soundscape that mostly stays in the background, punctuating some important actions without drawing any attention to itself. A bit more of these, and a more convincing musical envelopment would have painted the period even better I believe. But this is only a minor quibble. More problematic are the click-and-drag actions one has to perform to unlock doors or achieve other minor tasks. These feel tucked on, and do not integrate well within the overall concept.

My favorite terrible game.
Try to follow me on this one...
The ally AI is atrocious and more often than not they will simply charge into the line of fire and stand there (enemy fire and your own alike), forcing more mission restarts than any game ever should require. They are♥♥♥♥♥♥on a zombie useless and will almost never contribute in any way, you just wish they would back off and take cover so you can take out the targets at your own pace instead of frantically trying to kill them before they blow away your moron partner. Which is ironic because the enemies seem to understand cover and have pinpoint accuracy, and sometimes even shoot through objects to destroy you (especially the helicopters
Missions are a chore and you simply want to close your eyes and be done with them. More often than not they take multiple tries, not due to difficulty, but simply bad design. The escort missions in this game are the worst I've ever seen in a sandbox. You will have to do each one several times so you can figure out where your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI partner is going so you can clear out the 10 shotgun wielding enemies laying in way to insta-kill them(this has been the case in EVERY escort mission, even your CIA mentor buddy [the guy that apparently taught you everything you know] does nothing but stand out in the open while dozens of mobs mow him down...)
They give you so many tools to work with but refuse to allow you to use them. For example you will face helicopters in several missions where there are no turrets/tanks, normally you could just grapple hook onto them and toss the pilot out, but they will always add a second person so this is made impossible. It forces you to shoot out the passenger while him and the gattling gun on the helicopters are gunning you down with pinpoint accuracy. On top of that if you can even hit him you're lucky as most of the time he is on the opposite side and cant be shot at until it makes another pass. This is not fun in any way shape or form and forces you to forego some great weapons because later in the game you more or less need the RPG to not get destroyed.
Ammo is scare when you need it, and abundant when you dont. You will find yourself picking up random weapons constantly just to have a gun.You can always call a drop but its just not viable mid mission and either way you are forced to buy the weapon again simply for some ammo which in the beginning of the game will suck up every dime you make. This could have been fixed by making the ammo reserve larger ( its laughably small even with full upgrades ).
Hit-boxes are just terrible, and for some reason headshots seem to not matter if you are more than arms length away. The games auto aim just puts every shot into their stomach no matter where you aim, hell you can even aim a few feet to the left and still every shot is a gut shot. It would seem enemies have the same auto aim when it comes to shooting you and its beyond frustrating.
Now, with all that is wrong with the game (and trust me there is a LARGE amount of♥♥♥♥♥♥wrong with it) I couldn't recommend this game any more, and it comes down to one simple thing.
The gameplay is amazing!
When you're not on a mission you will be blowing up silos of fuel, or hooking enemies to nearby cars and watching them get dragged away, and just overall causing MASSIVE amounts of damage to the people and buildings of this random south american country.
This game does sandbox right. Remember those tools I told you about that are rendered useless by the games mission structure? Well that problem is gone when you're just messing around in the world. Enemies feel fair and don't come in such large numbers, so you are able to deal with them any way you please. Want to throw someone off a cliff? Go ahead! How about tying a guy to a rocket/airplane and watching him turn into a glint in the sky? Its not only possible but its easy since you aren't constantly running from unending enemy fire.
The graphics and visuals of this game are flat out stunning. Textures/models looks good, and the draw distance of this game is absurd ( as is the map size ). You can literally drive for hours and not hit the edge of the map, its scary how they managed to get a map this size to not only run this good, but to also show you SO much of it at once. Makes me wonder what GTAs issue is.
So to wrap this up, the game itself as a game is bad. The missions/AI/pacing and just about everything else relating to story progression is just terrible (aside from the "Blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up to unlock stuff" system). But as a sandbox "I'm going to just blow off some steam" kind of game, its top notch. I found myself dragging♥♥♥♥♥through every mission wishing it was over, and once it finally concluded I perked right up as this game is at its best when you are let off the leash and allowed to experience the world as you see fit.
Don't expect a good story, memorable characters, or immersive gameplay (nothing sucks you into a world like redoing a mission ten times because your AI partner gets himself killed in seconds...). Go into this game looking to simply mess some♥♥♥♥♥♥up and have a good time and I promise you this will also be your favorite bad game.

I was a bit frustrated at first with this game as it had all of the right elements for a good game in my opinion, cool story, first person, spooky atmosphere but alas, I could not get it to play. Luckily the developer got the game to run despite its quirkiness and off I went! Firstly, this game is only 99 cents, and it is way worth that much money. So much of the time big games will have beautiful graphics and  but absolutely no storyline, just shoot and be shot at. This game, however, has a very interesting story behind it which has kept my interest so far. A quick synopsis~You wake up in a van with no knowledge of what happened nor who the person is who has abducted you. This stranger (or is it a stranger?)  subsequently dumps you in the middle of what at first appears to be the woods. After some walking around you discover that in fact you are in an abandoned town . It has a bit of an open world feel but it is small. Despite this, it is very nicely done and delivers a good creepy atmosphere.  I wont write more about the story but this scenario grabbed me. Yes, the graphics are a little clunky but there are moments of very pretty scenes like the night sky with a full moon that make up for this, and there was a few little oddities like one has to jump up to get on the sidewalk to walk as if there is a small wall around the sidewalk but otherwise the game ran well and is definitely worth it if you like a creepy tale, exploring, puzzles and a mystery to solve. I enjoyed it quite a bit~ 8/10 (with a bit of smoothing this game could be a ten I think)

The Walking Vegetables is a 16-bit rogue-like/action game, where your main objective is to explore, fight, take loots, survive and discover new areas.
It seems that at 1980’s, an evil alien race has invaded Earth, turning all vegetables into crawling, bawling, mauling abominations. You are about to join Department Radical, the grooviest police force on Earth to clean all this mess and return the peace to the streets.
You have to play several chapters divided in areas where an army of vegetables (carrots, potatoes, onions an so on...) are going to try to kill you. There are multiple buildings filled with enemies too, where you can fought through for a loot or for a some keys to unlock chests and some other buildings. There are a shop too to improve you weapons or buy medical kits and at the end of each area you are going to beat a boss.
The guy is easy to control using four arrows to move and mouse to aim and shoot. You can use several weapons (two of which are active and the rest selectable via a mouse wheel), a melee weapon and a a rechargable item that you can unlock. There are awide range of weapons and it's a good point that you can press the mouse button to shoot continuosly instead of destroying it, clicking thousands of times on it.
Tha main character and all the vegetables are well defined but, in general, graphics are very pixelized trying to emulate the games of 80's
Music sounds well at the first ten minutes but then it turns a little bit annoying. Sounds are quite good too and the sound of weapons are nice.
The game is not very difficult but scenarios are wide and there is not checkpoints so, five bars of life sometimes are very few to complete the chapter.
The game has achievements but it has not trading cards. I encourage to developers to add them in next releases.

It's a rather short experience, and while it is interesting, I cannot recommend it due to it's design choices, glitches and technical problems.


. Interesting story, though it tries too hard
. It is not a linear game, you can explore the city all you want, and piece the story together at your own pace
. Focuses more on storytelling and ambience rather than jumpscares.
. Attention to detail can be found throughout the city.
. Voice acting is ok.
. Gameplay is janky (you have to jump to get on stairs, sidewalks, even doorways)
. Lighting is all over the place, some doors flash white.
. Some really weird design decisions: there's a flashlight in one of the city's buildings, but you can't take it, you have to keep your lighter.
. The lighter doesn't light anything.
. I kept hearing footsteps, the whole game, even when I was standing still. (not sure if it's a glitch)
. The menu doesn't work properly, I can only press the "Play" button, "Continue" and "Quit" don't work.
It's a nice effort, and the game designer, Cameron, is a real nice guy. If he and his crew can fix all these little technical problems, it would be an above average game.

This is certainly a game I recommend everyone who likes strategy games try, but keep in mind that less hardcore strategy gamers wont enjoy it nearly as much due to it's in depth nature. The learning curve of the game is steep, to say the least, and many people will find it needlessly complex. People like me, however, love the extra depth to the game, the ability to micromanage and customize armies, politics, research, and relations with other countries. It doesn't take too long to get a hang of how the game works if you hit pause and play around with it a bit, or you could go through tutorials or online guides on how to play the game. Overall a wonderful game, if a bit slow on lesser-end computers.

Cons:

Deceptively simplistic, addictive and well worth the price.

‘The Angel of Darkness’ is, without question, the worst game in the Tomb Raider series. But is it a BAD game?
I decided to find out for myself. I’d seen the reviews on Steam. I’d read articles devoted to explaining WHY this game was as bad as it is. If it turned out to be a bad game, I only had myself to blame. Still. I sat through the opening credits. Something I didn’t notice the first time was that the credits are presented like the opening of a movie, which does a really good job of setting up the atmosphere for the rest of the game.
The next part is – jarring – so much so that I nearly stopped playing then and there.
Let’s take a step back for a moment. In ‘The Last Revelation’, Werner Von Croy was introduced as Lara’s estranged mentor, but by the end of the game, it seemed that whatever hostility existed between them had lifted. This was only further enforced by the events of ‘Chronicles’, the previous game to this one.
So when Lara suddenly HATES Von Croy and seemingly MURDERS him, it literally comes out of nowhere. To the game’s credit, this is actually a decent opening. Just really poorly timed.
So, after this shocking scene, you take control of Lara for the first time. This is where the game’s first issues are made apparent. The controls are WORSE than the Playstation games!
Do the original games have bad controls? ANSWER: I don’t know. They’re so well refined that, once you get used to them, it’s near impossible to tell. Why then, with a control scheme so similar to the originals, can I say, with certainty, that the controls for ‘Angel of Darkness’ are bad? Maybe it’s the fact that you start at a S-L-O-W walk before you run? Perhaps it’s the twitchy turning (don’t worry Officer, I can walk in a straight zig-zag, just give me an hour).
Overall though, the controls aren’t that bad | (To Be Continued in… Advanced Controls – Basic Combat).
The hub level ‘The Parisian Ghetto’ is where the game really begins. There’s a lot to do and a lot to interact with, including people! A first for the Tomb Raider series. The level of detail here is outstanding. While things do tend to move slowly during this part, it’s all carefully designed to support the story and introduce various characters. This is also the first time you have access to Von Croy’s Journal. In addition to acting as a Journal for Lara’s thoughts and objectives, the Journal also contains information and clues related to the story and future puzzle. In particular, these elements add a greater interaction and depth to the story than any previous Tomb Raider game.
Interacting with the characters leads to a variety of quests that need to be accomplished, all of which lead to the best part of the entire game: ‘The Louvre’ and the ancient tomb beneath it.
Everything from the Sewers beneath the Louvre to the end of Von Croy’s apartment is PHENOMENAL! The music, which was already good to begin with, gets even better, and perfectly matches the atmosphere of each level. The puzzles, though sometimes a bit linear, are excellent, polished, and masterfully executed. And the grand puzzle at the end is some of the best that Tomb Raider has to offer! The story was already proving to be very strong, but by the end of Von Croy’s Appartment, I was CONVINCED this was a good game (And then the Internet said, “Oh Yea?!” and everything turned to♥♥♥♥♥♥.
As much as I would praise the first half of ‘Angel of Darkness’, it has its – obvious – rough edges.
Advanced Controls – Basic Combat: We tried. We couldn't make them worse.
Combat is AWFUL! This is the first unforgivable sin of ‘Angel of Darkness’. And nowhere is this MORE apparent or frustrating than with the first boss.
ISSUE 1: It takes FOREVER to draw or holster a weapon. There’s nothing wrong with having somewhat of a delay. But when it feels like I could play three OTHER games in the time it takes… This is made FAR worse by the fact that the ‘holster weapon’ function is sometimes unresponsive. [Welcome to Dial-Up Combat.]
ISSUE 2: When in combat mode, you are ALWAYS facing your opponent. What makes this even WORSE than issue 1 is that if you want to move in any direction other than forward, you hop. The ONLY direction you can run in is TOWARDS THE ENEMY! No, this is NOT an Easter Egg, and Lara is NOT a Bunny!
In previous Tomb Raider games, combat wasn’t perfect. But the level of freedom and responsiveness made it a fun and versatile system. Here, combat is beyond restrictive! The first boss is a clever and creative puzzle boss, but the combat system transforms it into a hellish frustration.
If you manage to get through the unfortunate frustration of the first boss, the game rewards you with some AMAZING action sequences and a PERFECT closing to the first part of the game.
If you’re smart, you’ll stop playing at this point. I’m not saying that the second half doesn’t have interesting ideas, puzzles or story (it DOES or I could hate it more), but the execution is a DISASTER! The second unforgivable sin.
Remember how you had to solve a HUGE non-linear puzzle and overcome a clever (if frustrating) boss to get the first ‘plot item’? A small puzzle room with two skeletons hides the second…
Remember the amazingly detailed hub level with its various social puzzles and numerous quests? One person, one quest (though the quest IS decidedly cool).
Remember that brilliant story that was perfectly paced, cleverly written, with interesting characters? Screw story! Let’s have the main villain kill off his lackeys because they looked at the moon the wrong way.
…WHAT THE HELL HAPPENED?!
To understand WHY the second half is so – underwhelming, it is necessary to look at the development history of this project.
Originally, ‘Angel of Darkness’ was conceived to take place over four different locations, making up four sections of the game, each as detailed and refined as the first. In order to meet deadlines, two sections were cut entirely. Personally, I think THIS more than anything DESTROYED the story. They should have cut the game in half and ended on a cliff-hanger.
In addition to development being under extreme time pressure, the second Tomb Raider movie was about to be released, and ‘Angel of Darkness’ was FORCED to be release in conjunction. This killed ANY chance of the second half receiving ANY sort of refinement.
What makes this worse is that the second half is not devoid of good ideas or puzzles. The fish puzzle is actually quite clever! The fish AI is pathetic, so much so that you can easily bypass the fish without solving the puzzle. Worse still, I suspect this was meant to be a larger puzzle than what is present in the game.
The plants in the ‘Bio-Research Facility’ make that section the most beautiful in the entire game! In addition, the plants are designed to be traps! And were never used as anything but decoration.
I’ve already mentioned how disappointing the puzzle for the second ‘plot item’ is. But the doorway leading to it is AMAZING!
So, is this a bad game? Yes.
Despite that, I LOVED the first half of ‘Angel of Darkness’. I even loved parts of the second half! I wanted this to be a good game, but the second half was just too flawed.
As a fan of the Tomb Raider series, there’s enough positive elements that this game should not be overlooked.
However, for the average gamer, I can not recommend this game.
