Just Cause 2 is a legendary over the shoulder sandbox shooter along the lines of Grand Theft Auto without the charm. The game focuses on destruction, deep controls and doing whatever craziness you'd like to do. You play as Rico Rodriguez and you've been sent in by the government to mess things up like a kitten in tissue paper on an island nation that seems giant by gaming standards. You have the option work for different factions / gangs that have their own agendas. The gangs are a nice touch and you'll see them battle each other on the island while civilians run and hide. Its a nice AI dichotomy.
Since the game is set on a bunch of giant islands, the terrain is gorgeous and diverse. You'll see lush green jungles beneath icy mountains, then go into those icy mountains and down into sandy deserts. After that, you can take a boat for a ride across beautiful blue waters, then hijack a jet and surf on top of it into a golden sunset while dodging missiles. Everywhere in this game is a gorgeous place and there are tons of places to visit and blow up. There doesn't seem to be any interiors, but that is fitting for a game so beautiful with good traversal diversity.
The controls are deep, but they allow you to do a lot more than your average over the shoulder sandbox shooter. You have your standard, run, jump, gunfire, reload, grenade, toggle guns, toggle grenades buttons, but you also have the infamous grapple hook. This hook is what the Bionic Commando reboot was missing. Double pressing it will send you instantly zipping to wherever it latched onto. Traversal is made super easy, climbing up buildings with the hook, but not just that, but you have a parachute that is used to glide around. Simply hit the jump button while in the air to deploy the chute. Pressing and holding the grappling hook will grapple something, but then when you hold it, aim at something else and release the button, you've now tethered two things together, which results in hilarity. Tether a moving car to the ground, to watch the car flip over. Tether a NPC to a rocketing propane tank and watch them blast off. Not just that, but there is plenty of car combat. Normal games would have you just get in a car, not this game, you can get on top of the car to shoot things, or you can slip down in front or behind the car to shoot things using the car for cover as its moving. You can take over moving vehicles, with easy quick time events that show a struggle instead of just kicking a person out from behind the wheel.
Combat is pretty easy, you just aim the cursor and fire. There is no aim button, if your cursor is remotely near anyone or anything, you will see a red highlight around the logical target. So if you the player have terrible aim, Rico Rodriguez will still shoot the target. In terms of holding guns, you can hold one two handed gun and two one handed guns. There are throwable explosives and you can toggle between two types. You can also melee enemies with the grappling hook.
With so much control freedom, you can tackle missions any way that you want. Such as a car chase mission where you need to escort the driver, do you grappling hook vehicle to vehicle, taking out enemies and struggling to knock out the driver? Do you tether the other vehicles to the ground and watch them crash, or do you use your parachute to hover over the action and blow up the other vehicles? The choice is yours. It is an excellent game to do what you want.
Missions themselves give you easy to follow objectives as if they were steps to follow. Open the gate, take out that rocket launcher, take out those snipers, pick up that item, grapple onto that helicopter, and so on. The objectives are marked with red and easily found with how far away they are. If you try to deviate too far from a mission location, the game will warn you and start a 10 second counter. This keeps the intensity on and prevents people like me from exploiting things.
Outside of missions, there are plenty of things to do and they're all marked on your map. Well you need to visit the location marked on your map before you find what it is there to do. Things such as races, time trials, destroy bases and loot villages. Destroying locations and looting villages each has a percentage attached to it. To loot a village, you need to find 100% of things hidden there. Things like vehicle parts, weapon parts, cash boxes and even liberate the village from propaganda buses. Thankfully when you get near something findable, it will show up pointing out where you are, but you need to be very near it. This saves you from detailed searching. It is the same for ammo boxes and health cabinets.
As for the bases, you need to find things and blow up things such as towers, generators, gas tanks, communication towers and surface-to-air missile launchers, each will make up 100%. It is fun for explorers to seek out every nook and cranny, but I can understand if getting 100% would feel like a chore.
When you create chaos or break any sort of law, the local military will be sent after you. At first it'll be simple things hunting you down, but if you keep creating chaos, your 'heat' level will go up and more soldiers will come after you. How do you reduce your heat level? Hide. Yep hide in the jungle and after time your red heat will go to orange heat and start dropping down. This is good for keeping the focus on what you were doing before you created heat. With plenty of jungle in the game, it is pretty easy to ditch any heat you might have.
Sadly the enemies feel pretty dumb. No one takes cover when you're putting bullets into them, even if enemies are next to cover, but I guess people play for the fun of doing what they want, not the challenge. In car chases enemy vehicles will just ram other objects. It leads to some laughable moment. They'll just drive off cliffs when you hit the brakes. I can understand scripted events like running into a gas station, but otherwise it is hilariously bad.
The game is pretty easy even on normal with regenerating health. Not just that, but health pickups from cabinets seem well placed. If you die, you go to the last checkpoint. Sometimes the checkpoints are further back than you think, but that's the only thing that really presents a punishment in the game.
The real downside to the game is that it seems to crash once every few hours back to the desktop. Luckily the game has an autosave feature.
To top all of that off, there is a free Multiplayer MOD that allows every player into one world together for chaos to ensue. Is it worth $15? Sure.... but it has been on sale before at $2.50. Keep that in mind.

Verdun is something that tries puts you in the boots of a real soldier in WW1, and while it can never accomplish it completely, it can show you a fraction of what a soldier felt. The fraction of their fear, their hopelessness and sometimes their comradeship. However, this is only one side of the game. While it's important, people talk about it too much. The other side of Verdun is it is, in fact, a game you can tell because it's fun to play, which no one ever says.
The things that make it historically accurate are the same things that make it the best hardcore game I've ever played. Kills are satisfying and are never handed to you. Any victory is something you have to fight for, any skill you have is skill you've earned. It does take a while to become more than cannon fodder as the learning curve is pretty steep. As someone who has put in the time to come over it, I'd say this game is definitely worth a buy.

The chronological successor to the Victoria series, what Hearts of Iron 3 lacks in graphical prowess it makes up for in Political, Technological, Historical, and Military depth. Even though the game significantly shortens the play period to 12 years, it makes every second of it enjoyable.
With the rise of the Commitern, Facist, and Allied powers, you take on the role of any country present in the WW2 period, and must make the choice of either going to the aid of Great Birtain and France, the invading Eastern Europe by Germnay's side, or crossing the Volga in a counterattack with your Soviet allies.
While it has the makings of great game, HOI 3 falls flat in some places. The shorter times span means that some situations repeat themselves, and the variety in playthrouhgs is diminished. Playing as a nation with a small military and population (i.e. Ireland) means you can't play a very active role in the war, and fighting the better armed and trained Axis or Allied forces would mean certain death.
8/10, a great game with it's share of faults, but still great.

If you like grand strategy wargaming, then this is the best one there is....provided you get at least the first two expansions, and preferably all three. People love to complain that its graphics are bland or unimpressive, but those people are looking for an RTS or shooter with lots of eye candy. This game is all about the grand strategy. Others may complain about the AI not being smart enough, but they overlook the fact that this is the best grand strategy AI ever written for a PC game and no PC based AI is ever going to be a match for a decently operated human mind. Now the specifics:

Cargo Commander is a really underrated gem. The basic gameplay is simple; you activate the magnet on your little spaceship, then run and gun through pods full of aliens trying to collect loot. Each 'sector' is procedurally generated based on its name, so there are a near-infinite amount of 'sectors' to explore. It does a great job of capturing the loneliness that must exist on someone away from their family, isolated in the void. Your son even sends you drawings! The one thing I don't like is the difficulty; because levels are procedurally generated, they don't really come in a learner-curve, and can be kind of mixed up. This wouldn't be so bad except you can't try out a new sector until you collect a 'sector pass' in a level you haven't found one in yet. So if you get some difficult sectors you can be stuck with them for a while...

Bit of a disclaimer: So far I've only played Scythe on Tabletopia so far.
So honestly, it's not the best digital tabletop game (I'm comparing it to Sentinels of the Multiverse and Talisman digital versions). There aren't built-in systems to make sure you do your turns right and it's got the loose-ness of a sandbox game, so you can mess up like accidentally un-stack all the encounter cards.
That said, it does what it sets out to do very well: allow you to get together with friends without having to rendezvous at the same place and play cool board games. Plus, another HUGE advantage is that if one of your friends has the game, you don't have to pay a single cent to play with them.
Tabletopia isn't perfect but it's damn good at doing what it does.

I can't imagine what this would do to someone with epilepsy, but it would definitely be very bad. As it is, I had to turn it off after playing the same level for about five minutes and not being able to make the jump because it was changing between screens so rapidly and the colors were so bright that I couldn't take it. And I'm not epileptic, I've never had this kind of problem with a game before. So yes, I recommend it, in short doses to people who aren't bothered by strobes of light and color. But I can't imagine myself playing this for an hour or two straight, it's really more of a "take five minutes to enjoy the soundtrack" kind of game.

Okay, let's get these facts straight and true:
- HIS/HITS is NOT designed to be a SIMULATION at ALL.
- There are controls for mouse, Gamepad, and Keyboard only. I have personally verified all 3
- This game is by NO MEANS P2W, I can NOT STAND those PoS games that are (WoT/WoWP)
-There is a full screen mode, it is in the settings, so try and actually LOOK AROUND for what you are complaining about
!!!Most of the negative reviews are by those who simply hop in for 5-10 minutes, find no outright eye-candy, and come in with undue bias towards anyhting remotely non-SIM.!!! So far, EVERY complaint listed by the top 15 Negative Reviews are non-existant, or outright clouded by wrong expectations.
Now for the review:
HITS is a game GREAT for those who are looking for a fun, laid-back MMO based on ~1930s-1950s aircraft, whether Prototypes, Paper Planes, or "normal" military aircraft. This game is by no means a looker, but is well optimized for laptop users and those with aging desktops. Hell, I can run it with my backup Integrated GPU on my spare laptop with no lag. (2.5 GhZ OC)
The game is somewhat faction based, with you being a PMC allied with either the Axis Nations or the Allied Nations, with you being able to make a character for both factions if you so choose. You get 3 Nations aircraft, regardless of which "Nation" You choose, in addition to Gunners [Heavy Fighters] and Bombers, [Dive Bombers, and traditional level-flight types] and these trees are quite fleshed out, and, if they continue bringing in aircraft from the Original HITS, there will be many more.
The economy is quite easy to adapt to, and is partly player driven through trading of just about everything (Recommended way of buying things outright) and requires not a single dime of your $$$ to enjoy. All you can buy with real cash is minor details such as nose art, or minor other details for your aircraft which offer anything from 10% increased EXP to 10% Increased Drop Rates for missions. There is no Premium membership [!!!!] and nothing is more than a few $$ to buy.
Cons:
-Some questionable translations, though if you speak Deutsch it is fine
- Minor text issues on item drops, but is easily negated.
- Ok Graphics, but not designed to be a showhorse of such.
Overall, I would rate at 8.5-9.0 out of 10.

Probably one of the best skillful party games out there as opposed to most party games being a luck competition. It features online and local play allowing it fulfil all of the party game requirements. Ultimate Chicken Horse is a party platformer in which each player attempts to reach the end goal on various maps. At the start of each round however each player is given a party piece which is some form of platform, obstacle, or bonus that can make the course harder or easier. So naturally the longer you spend on the level the more stuff that gets added and so the complexity rises, as does the difficulty.
In order to make this gameplay work there is An Excellent score system that offers different points for various things. A few of the examples would be; completing the level, killing another player with your own trap, being the only player to reach the goal, being the first player to reach the goal and a few others. Although you may be thinking now "Well how does anybody win if every player reaches the goal each time?", and to answer that they included a very good system of not giving any completion points if none or all players reach the goal. Especially so if everyone reaches the goal where the only way to score points would be to have collected a coin.
Due to this it encourages players to try and make the course difficult enough in order to try and stop their opponents (or could be friends I guess) from reaching the goal while also allowing themself to reach it. This can result in many hilarious outcomes which I have come across like ferris wheels with spinning saw blades attached or really precise jumping puzzles only to find that the platforms are all ice-covered. There is an abundance of creativity out there for this game in the 10 very different levels it has to offer so far.
That does bring me to talk about a slight downside about the game which is that even though having up to 4 players creating a platforming course at once can be very entertaining the game starts to lack a bit when playing with only 2 people so it is recommend to have at least 3 people (including yourself) to play it with.
Another great thing about the game is the various modes available to it. There is the default Party Mode which is what I have been talking about exclusively above as this is the main part of the game, but there is also a Creative and Free Play modes where you can create custom courses that can be saved and played at any time. As I am not much of a creative player I didn't spend much time on this but for those out there who enjoy creative platforming this is a very could feature and I can see some very difficult and challenging courses being made.
Overall, Ultimate Chicken Horse is already a well established game in the party games genre in my opinion and it still being updated with new features! If you're looking for a good game to play locally or online with friends then this will most definately serve that purpose.

Angel of Darkness was the last of the "Von Croy Trilogy" as well as the last of the Core Design Tomb Raider made games. It was the first "smooth" graphics Tomb Raider game ever made, meaning no polygonic characters or blocky locations. The game had excellent detail on the characters as well as the locations. But great visuals don't lead to a great game, when the controls don't function right. Apparently this game was in production for a few years, and to have it be released at the same time as the second Tomb Raider movie "Cradle of Life" it was rushed into the gaming market without fixing the bugs or glitches. In the past, the only difficulty you deal with in the Tomb Raider games is the environment of the levels and the obstacle of traps and enemies. In this game, you are handicapped with limited controls, glitches, and a hanging meter every time you need to travel across a ravine or ledge by hanging off it with only your hands holding you up while going across. Had these issues been resolved this could of been a playable game. But I am unable to give it mercy when the game is frustrating in control wise and not level wise. I can understand what they were trying to do, they were attempting to experiment with new challenges, gameplay, and situations to differ from the older games. Which that is fine, I am open to new experiences for the Tomb Raider games but if you don't focus on the gameplay of the game no one will care about what those new experiences were. At the time this game was released, only three million copies got sold, and was cited as a market failure. It was such a disaster that it nixed the planned sequals to follow up and Core Design ended up ditching Tomb Raider which ended up in the ownership of Crystal Dynamics. I would love to of seen a follow up to this game, which was going to be titled "Tomb Raider: The Lost Dominion" which would of explained how Lara Croft escaped from the Temple of Horus as well as the fate of Kurtis Trent, who was an interesting character who became the first playable male protagnogist in a Tomb Raider game. But with the reputation this game has, I don't think we will ever see him in another Tomb Raider game again. Thus Angel of Darkness ended the first line of the Tomb Raider franchise and is if not the weakest game in the entire franchise. Lesson to be learn, never rush the prodcution of a game and be sure the controls don't suck.

A lot of reviews of Tomb Raider The Angel of Darkness critziese verious aspects of the game, such as the awakward controls, gameplay bugs and the darker nature of lara. None of these reviews give a background to why it has all of these flaws. This isnt really going to be a review of the game. I would recomend reading other reviews to find out about the acual game. This is just for players to read and to take into mind why the game has all these flaws.
Here's the backstory to why the game was rushed (which I have adatpted from Wikipeda - I won't tell if you don't ;) )
AOD started development in 2000, with the intention to create a new Tomb Raider game to compete with new action games and to also take advantage of the PS2's hardware. The team spilt into two groups, one working on Tomb Raider Chronicles, and another to work on AOD. Tomb Raider Chronicles had pushed the PSX to it's technical limits, so it was another resion to create a game with the PS2.
After Chronicles had been completed the first version of the game was scrapped by lead Programmer Richard Morton as the game had became to overambitious for the PS2. Only the basic story had been developed. Development started again from the begining.
It was inteneted that Angel Of Darkness would have two sequals to them to continue the story.
The Angel of Darkness was unveiled  in March 2002 at E3. Problems with the game were sensed at an early stage.
A release date was announced for November 2002, but the game got delayed into spring 2003 to  benefit from additional marketing support from Lara Croft Tomb Raider: The Cradle of Life, the sequel to the original 2001 movie.
Despite the delays, the company pushed Core Design to release the game in time for the marketing support. In order to meet the deadline, areas of the game containing key narrative elements had to be cut; one of the losses was the explanation of how the character survived the events of The Last Revelation.
Among other concepts that needed to be cut were two further locations, character animations, sound bites, and unique gameplay elements involving Kurtis.
Some completed environmental assets also ended up being cut by mistake. Some of those elements were also deliberately left out by the team, who wished to bring them into future games.
The team at Core Design later said that they felt Eidos forced them to get the game out before it was ready. The game was also reportedly submitted eight times to Sony before its release. The game went gold on 18 June 2003, two days before its original release date. The game was finally released in the summer of 2003, alongside The Cradle of Life.
The game received strong initial sales, mostly driven by an aggressive advertising campaign. However The game received mixed to negative reviews from critics. critizing the controls, graphics and overall gameplay.
The Angel of Darkness caused multiple problems for the Tomb Raider franchise. Paramount Pictures faulted The Cradle of Life‍ '​s relatively inadequate box office performance on the poor critical reception, and backlash the video game received from its fans. The head of Core Design, Jeremy Heath-Smith, resigned after the release of the game,  and plans for a sequel called The Lost Dominion,part of a proposed trilogy created using the game's engine, were scrapped.
Eidos Interactive took the production of Tomb Raider games away from Core Design and assigned them to Crystal Dynamics, who has been making the Tomb Raider games ever since.

Just Cause 2 is a legendary over the shoulder sandbox shooter along the lines of Grand Theft Auto without the charm. The game focuses on destruction, deep controls and doing whatever craziness you'd like to do. You play as Rico Rodriguez and you've been sent in by the government to mess things up like a kitten in tissue paper on an island nation that seems giant by gaming standards. You have the option work for different factions / gangs that have their own agendas. The gangs are a nice touch and you'll see them battle each other on the island while civilians run and hide. Its a nice AI dichotomy.
Since the game is set on a bunch of giant islands, the terrain is gorgeous and diverse. You'll see lush green jungles beneath icy mountains, then go into those icy mountains and down into sandy deserts. After that, you can take a boat for a ride across beautiful blue waters, then hijack a jet and surf on top of it into a golden sunset while dodging missiles. Everywhere in this game is a gorgeous place and there are tons of places to visit and blow up. There doesn't seem to be any interiors, but that is fitting for a game so beautiful with good traversal diversity.
The controls are deep, but they allow you to do a lot more than your average over the shoulder sandbox shooter. You have your standard, run, jump, gunfire, reload, grenade, toggle guns, toggle grenades buttons, but you also have the infamous grapple hook. This hook is what the Bionic Commando reboot was missing. Double pressing it will send you instantly zipping to wherever it latched onto. Traversal is made super easy, climbing up buildings with the hook, but not just that, but you have a parachute that is used to glide around. Simply hit the jump button while in the air to deploy the chute. Pressing and holding the grappling hook will grapple something, but then when you hold it, aim at something else and release the button, you've now tethered two things together, which results in hilarity. Tether a moving car to the ground, to watch the car flip over. Tether a NPC to a rocketing propane tank and watch them blast off. Not just that, but there is plenty of car combat. Normal games would have you just get in a car, not this game, you can get on top of the car to shoot things, or you can slip down in front or behind the car to shoot things using the car for cover as its moving. You can take over moving vehicles, with easy quick time events that show a struggle instead of just kicking a person out from behind the wheel.
Combat is pretty easy, you just aim the cursor and fire. There is no aim button, if your cursor is remotely near anyone or anything, you will see a red highlight around the logical target. So if you the player have terrible aim, Rico Rodriguez will still shoot the target. In terms of holding guns, you can hold one two handed gun and two one handed guns. There are throwable explosives and you can toggle between two types. You can also melee enemies with the grappling hook.
With so much control freedom, you can tackle missions any way that you want. Such as a car chase mission where you need to escort the driver, do you grappling hook vehicle to vehicle, taking out enemies and struggling to knock out the driver? Do you tether the other vehicles to the ground and watch them crash, or do you use your parachute to hover over the action and blow up the other vehicles? The choice is yours. It is an excellent game to do what you want.
Missions themselves give you easy to follow objectives as if they were steps to follow. Open the gate, take out that rocket launcher, take out those snipers, pick up that item, grapple onto that helicopter, and so on. The objectives are marked with red and easily found with how far away they are. If you try to deviate too far from a mission location, the game will warn you and start a 10 second counter. This keeps the intensity on and prevents people like me from exploiting things.
Outside of missions, there are plenty of things to do and they're all marked on your map. Well you need to visit the location marked on your map before you find what it is there to do. Things such as races, time trials, destroy bases and loot villages. Destroying locations and looting villages each has a percentage attached to it. To loot a village, you need to find 100% of things hidden there. Things like vehicle parts, weapon parts, cash boxes and even liberate the village from propaganda buses. Thankfully when you get near something findable, it will show up pointing out where you are, but you need to be very near it. This saves you from detailed searching. It is the same for ammo boxes and health cabinets.
As for the bases, you need to find things and blow up things such as towers, generators, gas tanks, communication towers and surface-to-air missile launchers, each will make up 100%. It is fun for explorers to seek out every nook and cranny, but I can understand if getting 100% would feel like a chore.
When you create chaos or break any sort of law, the local military will be sent after you. At first it'll be simple things hunting you down, but if you keep creating chaos, your 'heat' level will go up and more soldiers will come after you. How do you reduce your heat level? Hide. Yep hide in the jungle and after time your red heat will go to orange heat and start dropping down. This is good for keeping the focus on what you were doing before you created heat. With plenty of jungle in the game, it is pretty easy to ditch any heat you might have.
Sadly the enemies feel pretty dumb. No one takes cover when you're putting bullets into them, even if enemies are next to cover, but I guess people play for the fun of doing what they want, not the challenge. In car chases enemy vehicles will just ram other objects. It leads to some laughable moment. They'll just drive off cliffs when you hit the brakes. I can understand scripted events like running into a gas station, but otherwise it is hilariously bad.
The game is pretty easy even on normal with regenerating health. Not just that, but health pickups from cabinets seem well placed. If you die, you go to the last checkpoint. Sometimes the checkpoints are further back than you think, but that's the only thing that really presents a punishment in the game.
The real downside to the game is that it seems to crash once every few hours back to the desktop. Luckily the game has an autosave feature.
To top all of that off, there is a free Multiplayer MOD that allows every player into one world together for chaos to ensue. Is it worth $15? Sure.... but it has been on sale before at $2.50. Keep that in mind.

There are some game that are just the usual rubbish that just are games and nothing more. But there are the exceptions- games that push the limits of what it means to be a game. And I personally think "The 39 Steps" pushes the boundary the most, because it's hardly a game. Does it have fine points about it? Sure! It's got a great soundtrack, excellent voice actors, great background sounds, and well-done backgrounds. But I feel like how I felt with playing "Over the Void". All of this seems to be covering up how little the game actually has to offer. I played the game in roughly 3 hours because that game made me move at that pace. If I was in full control of the speed of the story, I bet I'd be done in roughly less than an hour. All the gameplay is melted down into clicking. Nothing complicated. Nothing at stake. Which really undermines the purpose of the achievements of the game. Oh, you clicked 15 times in this game! Ding!
I don't mind point-and-click games but usually if you have some control of choice over the game. And choice over a game doesn't have to mean the way the story turns out. Sometimes the choice could be how you handle a situation, what steps you take to get somewhere, what items you use on an object. And 39 Steps takes all choice away and turns the game into a tourist ride of fun places around Scotland... PowerPoint Style. But it's a well-designed PowerPoint, I'll give it that!
The story is decent. I never had read the 39 Steps, but I knew what to expect from older novels and this one's no different... the pacing is about as slow as a turtle trying to swim through maple syrup, and it doesn't help with the gameplay being slow, either. Sure, slow stories can be just as effective and the story in 39 Steps has it's moments, but there are a lot of long drags, and one particularly occurs with so much repetition you forget what's supposed to happen in the story. But the story, the good and bad parts, I feel I should give no credit to the the designers or the game's total score. I feel like it'd be better placed in a book review, since the designers just cherry-picked their favorite quotes of the story and threw the words in while an intense chase scene in occuring, undermining any slight tension the player might have been feeling.
If you want to experience the 39 Steps, or you're a connoiseur of PowerPoints, this is perfect for you. I happen to be a gamer that prefers to actually play a video game, rather than watch it with short intervals of clicking.

TL;DR - I'd recommend picking it up when it goes on sale or if you know you've got friends to play it with, as the campagin is hopelessly short and there's not much endgame content without the Wild Run DLC. Still incredibly enjoyable if you like cars, exploration, or customization.
-Cars. There's a lot of them, a wide variety of real life brands, and there's some pretty extensive visual customization for almost all of them.
-Microtransactions exsist, but almost all of them are shortcuts that you can eventually reach in the base game, or are simply visual components.
-It's always online, but I've never experienced any server difficulties.
- Geography is completely boned up, but many of the cities or landscapes capture the essence of the town they smulate. Someone living in San Francisco won't recognize many streets, but it still feels like the city.
- Game sometimes can seem empty. Civilian foot traffic is low in cities, and occasionally traffic is sparse.
-Devlopers are still actively involved and relasing content, so that's pretty cool.
The storyline is the video game equivalent of a wet piece of toast - bland, uninspiring, and so generic that you completely forget about it. There's some pretty cringey dialogue, some pretty bad voice acting, and your protagonist is an unrelatable walking cliche. Once you hit the cap of level 50, it's a short MMO-style grind to max out your car, and then it seems like you're done with the game.
This is when the Wild Run DLC becomes a lfiesaver. It introduces weekly and monthly challenges against other people, inspiring you to come back again and again. It adds real end game content, and I highly recommend it.

Bethesda Game Studios did a good job recreating the moribund, post-apocalyptic world which is called Fallout, taking it from the old yet legendary isometric perspective and giving it an absolutely different, FPS/TPS view.
Those who begin their adventure as the Lone Wanderer have an immense, dangerous world waiting ahead of them, with plenty of quests to be taken, mysteries to be solved and adversaries to be turned to green puddles of goo. Everything in the game, including weapons, character design and the whole atmosphere itself was made as accurately as possible to correspond with the original Fallout: A Post Nuclear Role Playing Game, although as true as that might sound, a feeling that the original Interplay designers would have their own vision and concept of a sequel (if they would still have rights, resources, personnel and the possibility to
such a sequel) still persists in the mind. Nonetheless, Fallout 3 does an outstanding job in showing a dark, retro-futuristic world the fate of which ended horribly wrong. Our protagonist is a vault dweller, "born" and raised in a deep, metal, underground vault which acted as shelter during The Great War. The plotline of Fallout 3 is at first twisted and unclear, in other words perfect for a game with an open-world setting. Having the freedom to either follow the main questline or to go wherever you desire in search for weaponry, experience and bottle caps (meet and greet the new currency of the post-apocalyptic world) the game gives you plenty of opportunity to go out and explore the Capital Wasteland. During the course of your adventures, you will find vast Metro Tunnel systems, caves, hideouts, abandoned buildings, Vaults (your vault isn't the only one out there) military installations and much much more to raid and pillage, taking the pre-war technology and other goodies for your own use.
The NPC's in the game are all very unique, often having their own attitude and personality. The dialogues, even though they aren't really as dark in humor as the text in the original Fallout 1 and 2, are still worthwhile to listen to, just as much as the atmosphere in Fallout 3 is worthwhile to immerse yourself in, luckily the world is deep enough. There are many unique factions in the game, all of which have their own, almost always conflicting philosophy, thus waging war against one another. Some of these factions found their way to Fallout 3 straight from the classic originals while the others were added by Bethesda. These factions, such as the Brotherhood of Steel or the the Brotherhood Outcasts, only make the overall plotline more deep and interesting, frequently leading the player away from the his main quest course to devote time for other, less significant, but not less thrilling matters.
Fallout 3 is a game which every RPG loving player should acquire. Not only is this the successor to something which is more than just a game, this is a successor which conveys the original atmosphere in a very accurate, although in my opinion, not the most complete way.

Dark Souls 2 is the black sheep of the Souls series, usually placing last or second to last on many people's list of favorite Souls games. Oddly enough though, as a guy who has been playing the Souls games since Demon's Souls on the ps3, Dark Souls 2 has been the only one in the series that I have come back to for consistant replays. This maybe due to the fact that this game has the best PVP in the series hands down, with the most enjoyable NG+ (also, unlike the original Dark Souls, it has a second half that isn't complete♥♥♥♥♥♥and is actually worth the trouble of going through to see the ending).
It's mostly down to personal preference whether you'll like this game or not, though. I personally think it's sprawling but overall linear approach (which is very Demon's Souls-eques, minus the arch-stones) isn't as terrible as everyone makes it out to be. Oddly enough though, Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne are smaller and (at least for me) feel a lot more linear (especially in comparison to Dark Souls 1) yet don't recieve nearly as much flack.
That's not to say there aren't problems in Dark Souls 2. The fact that they brought back the "Nexus"-styled hub-world of Demon's Souls which is the only place you can upgrade in is a step down from Dark Souls 1 (this is also a problem Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3 as well). There is also the problem of despawning enemies, which can make the game both easier and harder at the same time and cause balancing issues. The bosses are mostly "dude's in armor" and follow the same "lern d attac pattrn 2 win" which has become the norm for the series rather than the more original and intresting (although by no means perfect) boss fights in Demon's Souls (then again, the "Looking Glass Knight" was rather original, as he spawns PVP players through his shield).
People also bring up the E3 trailer from 2013, and get pissy because the graphics got downgraded. Yes, that does suck and there isn't much of an excuse, yet it's not like they were straight up flaunting cut content as well as better than in-game graphics like they did with Bloodborne's early trailers (Ebrietas in Cathedral Ward, cut arcane stuff, these graphics
). While most of the DS2's E3 trailer did have better graphics than the final release, at least most of what was show was in the final game. It's not like it was Halo 2's 2003 E3 demo where they advertised a straight up different game.
TL;DR Dark Souls 2 is a flawed game that gets a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥even though it improves on a lot of things that Dark Souls did (it even has a worth-while second half that isn't complete garbage). It also recieves♥♥♥♥♥♥for things that Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3 are still doing yet don't get♥♥♥♥♥♥for (mostly because they aren't Dark Souls 2).
So, if you are new to the Souls series or if you were put off intially by fans bandwagoning on the hate train because "Dirk Sulz 2 sux lol", I recomned picking this version up and giving it a try (or a second chance) as it comes with the base game as well as all the DLC for a decent price.

The Walking Vegetables is an interesting little game. I honestly nearly wrote it off when I first checked it out, but I'm really glad I gave it a shot; it's a fast paced and fun rogue-lite shooter with a rather unique theme.
Something I really loved about the game is how the theme is used to create some very visually distinct enemies. Every enemy type is a different vegetable which allows, at a glance, to know not only what I'm facing but allows me to figure out what to expect. Lemons? They will leave pools of harmful lemon juice. Broccoli, on the other hand, will charge at me; while leeks will try to ambush and so on. With the game's more fast paced combat, having that instant recognition of the different enemy types is a definite plus.
Another thing about the combat I really liked is that it didn't feel as reliant on the rolls of the dice as other games in the genre. When I lost it always felt like it was due to a lack of skill on my part and not having enough power though my guns and pick ups. I always had options to overcome bad luck by simply killing more of the horde for money or hitting optional buildings for more rolls of the loot dice and objects to destroy for chances of drops. I never felt like I was out of options and I was under-powered, just lacking in the skill to make it further.
That's not to say there's aren't things I dislike about the game. One thing I didn't care for was sheer lack of info the game provides. Now, I realize that figuring things out on your own is, for the most part, a staple of the genre. However, hiding gameplay mechanics seems a bit much to me and a lack of tutorial does just this. Perhaps the greatest example of this is in melee and that melee weapons can be used to knock back bullets to kill enemies. The only place the game made mention of this, when I spent time in the game, is in the tool tip of an unlockable skill as its requirement. This seems like a pretty key game play element that is hidden and does make wonder if I am missing other important things.
Speaking of skills. The other thing I didn't like is how slow it is to unlock things in the game. While I don't want all the skills handed to me, but some of them are a rather long grind to unlock, even ones that you would naturally unlock by playing the game. Destroying 3,000 objects, for example, to unlock a single skill. Weapons also seem to unlock rather slowly, requiring a currency, called rad rocks, to unlock new drops via the in game store. While the dev did drop by my video to say that there's ways to get them that I didn't find yet, at least at the start of the game, until you find what the dev was hinting that, it's a bit of a slog to get new guns in the drop pool.
Overall, I really enjoyed my time with The Walking Vegetables. It's a silly concept that has been developed well into a fast paced, unique rogue-lite. To top it all off, the game is getting a lot of post-launch support with new enemies, modes, and of course bug fixes. While the game may not be as deep as others in the genre, it has a lot of style and fun that makes it well worth a look.
Version Played: Post-Launch Patch 1, 10/02/17

Lara gets framed for murder, so her solution to 'clearing her name' is to strut about Europe aggressively threatening people and going on a killing spree in one of Paris' most popular tourist attractions...
...Okay it's fun to rip this game to shreds, but if you're a Tomb Raider fan, particularly of the Core Design era, it's unmissable, being Core's last addition to the series.
First, it should be noted that this game is actually UNFINISHED due to problems between Core and Eidos during development. Because of this there are bugs, incomplete sections and large gaps in the story. However, there is still much to be enjoyed about the story, atmosphere, audio and visuals, and this still remains as one of my favourite games of the series.
Here' a more detailed insight:
I've found the replay value of this game to be immense. Because of all the incomplete content, hidden areas, alternate routes and detailed environments you find something new upon every playthough. It's like exploring a beta product, which it basically is.
The graphics are amazing for their time (2003) and have aged well, however they need to be set up correctly before you start the game which can be confusing at first.
The soundtrack is excellent, with Peter Connelly and the London Symphony Orchestra working their magic. The main theme particularly stands out.
The story is more ambitious and engaging than any previous entry in the series. However there are patches that are completely missing due to cut chapters during the rushed release. This is especially clear at one point when Lara expresses familiarity with a character she has never met during the game.
The controls are different from previous games and can take some getting used to but in my opinion they actually make sense, and you may find yourself struggling to return to the old system after a lengthy play-through. Remapping may be required for keyboards lacking the number-pad. I also suggest you don't use the mouse.
The gameplay is slightly crippled by Core's last-minute decision to switch control methods, making the movement seem a little sluggish and dis-jointed at times. This can be frustrating at first but can be forgotten about over time. However the animations are realistic and smooth.
Dialogue options are available but for the most part are pointless or for comedy value.
The strength upgrade system is quite amusing; how Lara has to beat down doors etc. in order to “Feeel stronger” and be able to jump further. You may dislike this aspect of the game but some may see it as a more fun method of obtaining secrets. The stamina bar makes climbing a more stressful experience, having to make sure the bar doesn’t run out before you’ve reached your destination. Again, whether you like this or not comes down to personal preference.
There is also a very basic stealth system that doesn't seem fully incorporated. There are little to no opportunities to actually use it throughout the entire game. There are also hidden moves that Lara can perform including backflipping off ledges and pushing blocks using the Classic animation, but you'll have to find those out for yourself...
In addition to Lara you also get to play as Kurtis, who was supposed to have supernatural abilities for the player to control, and a spinning blade as a primary weapon. Unfortunately the only evidence of this now is in cutscenes, some of which are placeholders, making his gameplay significantly duller than it should have been.
I recommend this game despite its many flaws. If you can keep an open mind and a sense of humour, give it a chance and you may be surprised/intruiged.

Also pssst....stick through the end credits for a little easter egg.

UCH is a charming competitive platformer designed for both casual party crowds and masterful try-hards. You control one of (currently) 7 hand-drawn animal characters as they frantically try to make their way to the exit. You compete against 3 other players as you each choose a random item, platform, or trap from the Party Box and place it anywhere on the level. Your aim is to strategically hinder your friends while keeping it in line with your own skill to pass. It quickly gets hectic as gravity-defying platforms are scattered all around, as traps, teleporters, and projectiles threaten you with a close shave.
Each animal has the same movement stats and control the same way, with your decision only up to how you like their dance animation, sounds, and outfits. You can crouch under hazards (but not crawl), slide on and jump off of most walls, sprint, and dance. Though you cannot double-jump, your critter can reach far distances if you know your limits and make use of your environment, even if other players give up. Many traps can be used as makeshift platforms; likewise innocent platforms can end up knocking the fuzzy fellows into a trap if placed right (aka somebody hits their head and that causes them to jump differently than they expected).
Points are earned for different qualifications and matches can be close if players of similar skill play together. (There is now a handicap option if leeway needs to be made, however. This reduces points earned by the higher-skilled player by a percentage) You earn points for completing the map, but with bonuses for being the only player to survive, coin collection, trap kills, first to the exit, and so forth. Any of these may be turned off by the host, with many other options such as a placement timer, point/time limit, item disables, etc. The game is highly customizable, especially now with the added freeplay and level creation modes. Even in regular levels, expect crazy contraptions to be built with the moving platforms combined with the glue item.
Despite its toony casual appearance, the movement system is very competent and it is possible to become a very experienced player over time. Characters have friction and stop quicker if they have less momentum. Holding sprint while wall-jumping will cause your animal to jump back slightly farther than wall-jumping without holding sprint, leaving it up to you to decide which to be doing at the time. You can hold up while wall-sliding to slide slower, allowing you to time a critical jump near traps. Tapping jump will do a smaller hop instead of a full leap. You will be able to get in tune with the controls and deaths will start to feel less like the game screwing you over, and more of what precise button presses you have to make to survive.
The game supports gamepads and keyboards equally effectively, allowing many controllers and keys to be detected. Both types can be rebound to your taste, even with one action bound to two separate buttons at once. The kicker is being able to play with local friends while playing online at the same time, with multiple controllers (or one player on keyboard) being used at the same time. The control methods are very refined and the devs are staying on top of game bugs constantly.
Overall, I highly recommend this game as a very good party game and platformer for all skill levels. Whether you intend to be a more casual player wanting to party with your friends, shouting at their obnoxious trap placements, or a "pro player" eager to know the ins and outs of the game, still shouting at the ridiculous speed the level spirals out of control, it's bound to be a fun and hilarious experience for many people.

Bethesda Game Studios did a good job recreating the moribund, post-apocalyptic world which is called Fallout, taking it from the old yet legendary isometric perspective and giving it an absolutely different, FPS/TPS view.
Those who begin their adventure as the Lone Wanderer have an immense, dangerous world waiting ahead of them, with plenty of quests to be taken, mysteries to be solved and adversaries to be turned to green puddles of goo. Everything in the game, including weapons, character design and the whole atmosphere itself was made as accurately as possible to correspond with the original Fallout: A Post Nuclear Role Playing Game, although as true as that might sound, a feeling that the original Interplay designers would have their own vision and concept of a sequel (if they would still have rights, resources, personnel and the possibility to
such a sequel) still persists in the mind. Nonetheless, Fallout 3 does an outstanding job in showing a dark, retro-futuristic world the fate of which ended horribly wrong. Our protagonist is a vault dweller, "born" and raised in a deep, metal, underground vault which acted as shelter during The Great War. The plotline of Fallout 3 is at first twisted and unclear, in other words perfect for a game with an open-world setting. Having the freedom to either follow the main questline or to go wherever you desire in search for weaponry, experience and bottle caps (meet and greet the new currency of the post-apocalyptic world) the game gives you plenty of opportunity to go out and explore the Capital Wasteland. During the course of your adventures, you will find vast Metro Tunnel systems, caves, hideouts, abandoned buildings, Vaults (your vault isn't the only one out there) military installations and much much more to raid and pillage, taking the pre-war technology and other goodies for your own use.
The NPC's in the game are all very unique, often having their own attitude and personality. The dialogues, even though they aren't really as dark in humor as the text in the original Fallout 1 and 2, are still worthwhile to listen to, just as much as the atmosphere in Fallout 3 is worthwhile to immerse yourself in, luckily the world is deep enough. There are many unique factions in the game, all of which have their own, almost always conflicting philosophy, thus waging war against one another. Some of these factions found their way to Fallout 3 straight from the classic originals while the others were added by Bethesda. These factions, such as the Brotherhood of Steel or the the Brotherhood Outcasts, only make the overall plotline more deep and interesting, frequently leading the player away from the his main quest course to devote time for other, less significant, but not less thrilling matters.
Fallout 3 is a game which every RPG loving player should acquire. Not only is this the successor to something which is more than just a game, this is a successor which conveys the original atmosphere in a very accurate, although in my opinion, not the most complete way.

This game's nice. Maybe not GOTY, but most things work well enough.
The structure is simple enough - to beat the campaign (which is something you'll do multiple times), you have to get past several "chapters", each concluding with a boss fight. Areas consists of a large "hub" (which has paths to other areas and constantly spawning enemies), multiple "objective areas" (where you fight a number of enemies to unlock the path to the boss), multiple buildings (which are also filled with enemies and can be fought through for loot) and a shop.
The player can carry multiple ranged weapons (two of which are active and the rest selectable via a wheel-menu), a melee weapon, and a rechargable item (effects from use vary).
Choices of enemies/bosses per area, building layouts, item drops, etc. are randomized, which has it that you encounter familiar hand-crafted elements but in different pattern on each session.
A single session can take between 20 to 60 minutes depending on how many optional paths you decide to take - sticking with a few weapons and taking only required paths generally has you looking to finish one session in 30 minutes or less. Par for "speedrun" unlock is 15 minutes (which I was able to beat with 12m after several attempts).
Performing specific objectives unlocks "skills", which stick between sessions and influence one or other aspect of the game (e.g. increasing health, making some attacks more powerful, or changing equipment the player starts with). You can pick several of these to be used for a session (eventually up to 4 at once). Other things that persists between sessions is "meta-currency" awarded for beating bosses (which is used to unlock new weapons/items).
I'd say that the game is well-rounded in terms of difficulty - enemies come in multiple shapes and forms, but so do weapons, and the fact that you can find and carry multiple of them at once allows to prepare for most situations. Bosses are manageable, switching between several patterns. Achievements mimic in-game skill unlocks and should be managable enough with some practice and strategy (many unlock conditions are much easier met with specific equipment/skill combinations).
Artwork is distinguishable enough and generally stylish. The game makes use of several visual effects by default, which can be disabled in settings menu.
Audio is fine. Using some of the melee weapons (such as "shivs" and throwing stars) too quickly allows to reach the point where sounds of preceding attacks start to cut out before finishing.
Music is remarkably catchy and fitting.
I was able to unlock all skills/achievements in ~12 hours (counting a few offline), though I'm yet to unlock a number of weapons.
Subjects of consideration:
- "tongue of steel" skill (which prevents player from taking damage when walking over pools of fire/acid) is more or less a requirement with a number of bosses, as arenas can be small and dancing between boss, enemies, and hazards can be a trouble.
- Either by design or not, but the fact that melee weapons deflect all projectiles in front of the player and have generally high attack rate has it that you may very well just swing them constantly. Multiple other games in the genre share this mechanic and it is only a little unfortunate when the game's balance is built around this. Too late to change anyway.
- With keyboard controls, when moving straight into an obstacle, the character seems to simply pick clockwise direction. This makes for a bit of inconvenience in first few hours of play, as the usual behaviour in such cases is to have the character move towards the nearest corner (i.e. pick direction that has a shorter walk distance until movement in original direction can be resumed) if at all in such situation.
Overall, it's worthwhile.

Cargo Commander is a unique 2d platformer/shooter. The goal of the game is to find each piece of cargo, you do this by exploring various sectors. There's a near infinite (you type in a name for the sector, which is than used to generate the sector) and then you explore various containers within the sector to find cargo. You'll also find a variety of enemies, weapons and sector passes, the latter of which is used to unlock more sectors. Asides from that, there's some unique features within the gameplay it's self: Your character has a drill which can be used to break through containers, being in space means you'll often times find yourself being affected by gravity and more. It's all about finding the most efficent way to get through containers to find the cargo. Asides from that, there's some other random elements that I found to be cool - Each sector has a highscore, and you can loot the dead bodies of people that have died playing in that sector. Collecting cargo will net you various unlocks, that range from new features, such as journey mode, a mode that has you exploring one sector for a high score to things that improve your character in the main game. You'll get the ability to upgrade your guns, drill, HP etc, you'll get the ability to start with certain unlocks and more. Overall, I had fun with Cargo Commander, my biggest complain would have to be it can get repetetive easy, even with the infinite amount of sectors, there's just not enough variety within the individual containers to make it entertaining for hours on end.

Paradox is a developer whose games most people will either love or hate. Furthermore, most people who like one Paradox game seem to like most or all of them, as they are almost all different takes on the grand strategy genre. I am a fan of other Paradox games I have played, namely Hearts of Iron II and Europa Universalis IV, but I found Hearts of Iron III to be buggy and unmanagably complicated. Complicated with a capital C. For example, you'll be creating order-of-battle hierarchies that take into account things like HQ placements and radio range, micro-managing logistics and supply routes, etc. Like other Paradox games, the tutorial is woefully inadequate, but unlike other Paradox games I've tried, there just wasn't enough fun in the early stages for me to push through the steep learning curve. People say the expansions do a lot to mitigate the problems with the base game, and I don't doubt it, but if the game needs these expansions so badly, they should've been released as patches, not as paid content.
If you enjoy extremely deep and realistic war games and don't mind bugs, this just might end up being one of your favorite games of all time. If you find micromanagement tedious, it probably won't be. I have spent literally hundreds of hours on Paradox games, mostly playing Darkest Hour and Europa Universalis IV with my friends, but this game just kind of left me feeling a bit overwhelmed by choice, and underwhelmed with fun.

These are the words I so beautifully chose to review the game with after having just finished it 100%. Having cooled down a bit and after taking a step back, I realize that a more detailed review is in order. After all, Dark Souls II: SOTFS wasted 166 hours of my life.
Nedless to say, I did not enjoy this game. Why play it to completion then, I hear you ask? Because Dark Souls II was the last game in the critically acclaimed series that I had yet to conquer. Having heard it was the worst game in the series, I had purposefully abstained from playing it until I had finished the other games, so that it would be easier for me to complete, being used to the souls-games and all. But oh boy was I wrong. Because this is
like the other games.
Dark Souls II is a souls game in name only. Sure, it has all the elements of a souls title. It has conveluted lore, item descriptions for every item, dodgerolling, Estus Flasks, punishing deaths and of course;
bosses. But it also adds new mechanics which expand upon the formula established in the original Dark Souls, such as a 5% loss of maximum health every time you die (which can only be negated by using an item that is not easily accessible early on), the ability to respawn bosses by burning bonfire ascetics (and increasing the difficulty of an entire area in the process) as well as a new stat extending the invincibility of your rolling.
Kinda wierd how none of these things were implemented in the later games in the series, huh?
Let's start with the bosses. There are 41 bosses. That is a lot of bosses, which explains why 6 of them are straight up reskins or literally just 2 of the same boss, and also why two of the bosses are a regular rat with the addition of a mohawk and a boss consisting of a couple of regular monsters put into a room. The design is for the most part uninspired, uninteresting and just plain boring. There are exceptions of course, but hardly enough to justify this lazy design.
To complete the game 100%, you have to do a lot of stuff.  (duh). But four achievements in particular require you to obtain every spell in each repective class of magic; Sorcery, Miracle, Pyromancy and Hex. And oh boy is this fun. There are some spells that require you to gain rank 3 in a specific covenant to obtain. In every other souls game, this rank is usually obtained by getting 30 of a specific item. But not in Dark Souls II. 500. You have to get 500 points in a PvP-arena to get a pyromancy. These points are given based on the outcome of the fight; if you win a fight, +1 point, but if you lose, -1 point. This means that you effectively have to win 500 matches against other players. In a game where the only players that remain active are either pros or hackers, this is not fun. Luckily, there is an alternative; Chancellor Wellager. This dude will sell you every spell that is unrealistically hard to obtain (or impossible of you are playing offline), as long as you are playing on NG++. However, Wellager is located at a pretty end-game location. This means, that in order to get every achievement, you have to complete the game almost 3 times. This is manageble, but in no way is it fun. Hitboxes suck, area and enemy design is meh, bosses are not nearly as hard or interesting as in Dark Souls, and the game is so much f****** longer than it needs to be.
Along your journey through Dark Souls II, you will meet a bunch of NPCs. Some of these have unique achievements associated with them. Two of these NPCs in particular,
and
have achievements that require you to summon them at 3 boss fights, have them survive said boss fights, and then talk to them at some specific locations. This would not be too bad, were it not for the AI of these NPCs. They tend to fall of cliffs. A lot. And every time this happens, you have to respawn at a bonfire, resummon them, make your way to the boss and pray that they survive. Sometimes the locations where you summon them are in the middle of an area, so every time they die you have to clear a lot of enemies so that they arrive at the boss with maximum health. Not a huge issue, but it gets real frustrating real quick.
All in all, Dark Souls II is a horrible game
that is artificially enlongated by filler bosses, bland areas and an unnessecarily long "first half". This is why I can
playing it.

"We Need To Go Deeper" tries to emulate the sense of venturing in a submarine together with a group of friends into the unknown and discover new tools, upgrades and biomes.
- UI is very bland and lacking of sound
- Juxtaposition of low and high-def artwork together as menu and loading backgrounds
- Lack of in-game tutorials
- Very little character customization with only 1 available starting tool
- Low interactability with existing items in the game world.
- Adventuring is too basic without any sense of danger, as sleeping(restoring health) does not come with any drawback.
- Co-op is very limited to people either manning the submarine or manning the guns onboard the ship (or in rare cases, repairing). When you land, everyone is basically playing a mini platformer mashing buttons to attack.
- Little differentiation between each player in terms of character and roles in the strategy of the game.
- Game is too repetitive and upgrades are too in your face as the treasures you obtain are either cash (to be exchanged for character cosmetics) or direct upgrade, eg. "Rotation speed increased".
- Art is somewhat unique, and I can understand other people who might like it, though not to my taste.
- The design at the start might be too ambitious and if features are continually added and implemented with perfection of execution, this game might have potential.
This game has very little to offer for me without any semblance of story or goal and existing features require little creativity to be employed.

At first when I saw all the negative reviews, I didn't want to download this game, but then I saw a positive review saying that the game isn't meant to be realistic or like war thunder in any way. So I thought: Well since most of the negative reviews hates on the game's flight models and stuff, and the game isn't supposed to be realistic, and it's actually supposed to be an MMORPG but with planes, I decided to give it a shot.
Here are the pros and cons:
Pros: - Easy to learn
- Don't have to pay to win or to have fun
- Tons of planes
- Tons of missions
- Missions can be played in co-op, or alone
- PvP and PvE modes
- Can run smoothly on any computer
- No lag
- Easy to level up
- Easy to get new upgrades
- Not a grind fest, making money and getting unlocks and rewards is quick and easy.
- Lots of parts and items to upgrade your plane with
- Storage warehouse for un-used items
- Tons of Quests that gives you bonus rewards
- Extremely detailed tutorial quests to teach you how to play the game
- Fun to play
Cons: - The game's graphics look like it's from 1996
- The damage model is just a simple health bar, no individual components that can take damage
- Can't do barrel rolls or loops
- No plane engine sounds
- All guns sounds the same
- You can fly through enemies without taking damage
- Only 3 different death animations for planes, 1: The plane's engines starts burning, and a wing breaks off, and the plane spirals to the ground and explodes. 2: The plane's engines starts burning, and the plane spirals to the ground and explodes. 3: The plane doesn't burn or anything, it just spirals to the ground and explodes.
- No throttle control

Overall I find it fun to play the game, even though the controls and gameplay is really simple and easy, and the graphics are from the 1990's. It just feels fun to play, and there's a lot of content. Even more content than some AAA games. It has almost as much content as War Thunder. Lots of maps, planes, missions, weapons, upgrades, and so on. If this game had tanks like War Thunder, then I would say they have the same amount of content. It's still a great game though.
Long story short: Great game, great fun, tons of content, no grinding for money or levels, you should totally try it out!

I'm so disappointed with this game, there's a lot of good, but there's a lot of bad as well.
The Crew is a game made by Ivory Tower and published by Ubisoft. The Crew is an MMO where you explore the US with your crew which consists of you and your friends.
Story wise the game follows on Alex Taylor. You are a rookie racer and your brother is the founder of a nation wide racing group called the 5-10. You want to join, but before you can prove yourself, your brother is murdered by another 5-10 named Shiv who teamed up with a corrupt FBI agent. A few years pass and an agent by the name of Zoe comes by with a deal, help her put both of them behind bars and you become free. But you need to work up the 5-10 chain before you can get to Shiv, so you need to build a crew from all over the country.
The Crew offers a one time campaign which you can play solo or with friends. A lot of the events are identical in every region. Get to a state, find the next member of your crew, do jobs for them and repeat in an other country to work your way to Shiv. Some of the missions, include time trials, races, chases, take down missions and destroy missions where you have to destroy shipments of stuff.
The graphics and the entire map are incredibly well designed. I've spent 5 hours alone on driving around and seeing the sights and trust me it's incredibly fun and at the time of me writing this review I still haven't explored the entire map, so there's a lot more to explore.
The gameplay itself, is pretty decent. The game offers you different type of cars, like circuit, raid, dirt, street and perf cars which you can use to drive on different types of terrain.  A lot of them handle differently, like the circuit vehicles are incredibly fast, but brake terribly, raid vehicles can drive through all the terrain, so you can use them to drive up on mountain areas.
The game also has online races, but you can forget doing Crew events cause literally no one is playing the crew races, every event is solo only and the matchmaking is some of the worst stuff, I have ever seen. If someone in the lobby has terrible internet, tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ You will be stuck on the message that say's trying to reconnect the player having problems. The game doesn't kick him out and trust me sometimes it gets annoying when in a single race the game pauses the race multiple times trying to reconnect other players.
The game also suffers from really big issues, like AI rubber banding players in the top position. and the AI in the lower positions give up on the races trying to ram each other of the road when they get the chance to do so. The game also suffers from clipping issues where you ram something so hard your car will get stuck in whatever you hit.
The game overall is a really fun game, but a lot of major issues make this game not worth the full price. On a discount I can safely say you can get the game and you will not be disappointed, by the game.
Final Rating:
6/10 - Only buy on a discount

UCH is a charming competitive platformer designed for both casual party crowds and masterful try-hards. You control one of (currently) 7 hand-drawn animal characters as they frantically try to make their way to the exit. You compete against 3 other players as you each choose a random item, platform, or trap from the Party Box and place it anywhere on the level. Your aim is to strategically hinder your friends while keeping it in line with your own skill to pass. It quickly gets hectic as gravity-defying platforms are scattered all around, as traps, teleporters, and projectiles threaten you with a close shave.
Each animal has the same movement stats and control the same way, with your decision only up to how you like their dance animation, sounds, and outfits. You can crouch under hazards (but not crawl), slide on and jump off of most walls, sprint, and dance. Though you cannot double-jump, your critter can reach far distances if you know your limits and make use of your environment, even if other players give up. Many traps can be used as makeshift platforms; likewise innocent platforms can end up knocking the fuzzy fellows into a trap if placed right (aka somebody hits their head and that causes them to jump differently than they expected).
Points are earned for different qualifications and matches can be close if players of similar skill play together. (There is now a handicap option if leeway needs to be made, however. This reduces points earned by the higher-skilled player by a percentage) You earn points for completing the map, but with bonuses for being the only player to survive, coin collection, trap kills, first to the exit, and so forth. Any of these may be turned off by the host, with many other options such as a placement timer, point/time limit, item disables, etc. The game is highly customizable, especially now with the added freeplay and level creation modes. Even in regular levels, expect crazy contraptions to be built with the moving platforms combined with the glue item.
Despite its toony casual appearance, the movement system is very competent and it is possible to become a very experienced player over time. Characters have friction and stop quicker if they have less momentum. Holding sprint while wall-jumping will cause your animal to jump back slightly farther than wall-jumping without holding sprint, leaving it up to you to decide which to be doing at the time. You can hold up while wall-sliding to slide slower, allowing you to time a critical jump near traps. Tapping jump will do a smaller hop instead of a full leap. You will be able to get in tune with the controls and deaths will start to feel less like the game screwing you over, and more of what precise button presses you have to make to survive.
The game supports gamepads and keyboards equally effectively, allowing many controllers and keys to be detected. Both types can be rebound to your taste, even with one action bound to two separate buttons at once. The kicker is being able to play with local friends while playing online at the same time, with multiple controllers (or one player on keyboard) being used at the same time. The control methods are very refined and the devs are staying on top of game bugs constantly.
Overall, I highly recommend this game as a very good party game and platformer for all skill levels. Whether you intend to be a more casual player wanting to party with your friends, shouting at their obnoxious trap placements, or a "pro player" eager to know the ins and outs of the game, still shouting at the ridiculous speed the level spirals out of control, it's bound to be a fun and hilarious experience for many people.

This is a hard platformer where you invert gravity instead of jumping. There's nothing quite like it.
The game has simple mechanics, but the level design makes the most of them. It's is tough but mostly fair, checkpoints are frequent. Finding the correct timing and route through a room is sometimes a bit of a puzzle.
It's short by itself, but VVVVVV has great replay value IMO, and there's optional collectibles, extras unlocked by getting those, and a level editor with >10h of good preinstalled content. Some of these extras are very hard.
The physics are a bit annoying in that precision takes practice, but once you're used to them it's not much of a problem.
The visuals, room names, and great energetic music create a lighthearted atmosphere that makes it fun to keep trying.
Thanks to an accessibility menu VVVVVV isn't just for hardcore gamers without disabilities, and most people can have a good time playing it.

Adapted from the 1915 John Buchan novel, The 39 Steps is a political thriller that takes place in early 1900's Europe where a bored Scot is quickly introduced to one of his neighbors who reveals an assassination attempt on a Greek head of government that will take place in less than a month. After learning of this conspirary the protagonist, Richard Hannay, ends up falling into a journey that he never imagined.
The main thing you need to know about The 39 Steps before you go into it is that it is not a game of puzzles, collectibles or skill, it is a interactive game that tells a story and you are there for the ride. You click through Hannay's thoughts, then sit back and watch/listen to the character's dialogue as they reveal new clues and hints that keep you guessing through 20 segments that are nicely broken up. You can leave off at any of these points or just leave a bookmark if you need to leave in a hurry. Sometimes there are sections where you click around a room to look at objects and various texts, some of which are incredibly detailed and could probably take a good amount of time to read. There are never that many moments where you feel like you are in control of these "investigation" parts though, usually the only things that are interactive in the rooms are the objects that need to be clicked on, and there are is an indicator on the bottom that lets you know how many objects there are left to see in the scene or that you have already looked at.
The fact that you are never controlling Hannay's thoughts or making important character decisions is never a problem in The 39 Steps though. The text is excellently placed and animated during certain scenes making it tense at one moment and beautiful at another. The choices made such as there never really being a full image of a human character while they are speaking to one another makes you think about who these characters are and why the developer decided to depict them that way.
For those that are intersted in a good story in the form of a video game The 39 Steps is incredibly interesting and thrilling throughout. I would highly suggest it to anyone that enjoys visual novels, point and click games or the original book.

Like other paradox developed games, this is a Grand Strategy game on the Clausewitz Engine. It is set in world war II, and the leadup to that war. Build divisions of 2 to 5 Brigades, then organize those Divisions into corps, Armies, Army Groups, and Theaters. Carefully manage your production to keep dissent, supply, production, and upgrades in balance. Spy on your enemies, and keep yourself in power. This game is the micromanager's dream. The game is a real time strategy, but you can pause time to assess, rethink, and react. In fact, in a well set up game 80% lf the time you play will be spent paused, especially in the middle of a war, working out just how you'll move.
Don't want to micromanage? Give the AI control and master the individual elements without having to worry about the others. This game is propped up as a decent game on Gameplay, and Gameplay alone. If you don't like the graphics, wait till HoI 4 comes out, and you might get better graphics. As is, I reccomend this game to any strategy nerd out there, those who liked EU3, and the other paradox game should also find this a fitting final game in the four game quartet.
